# AISC Education Channel - Operations Knowledge Base

Source: the AISC Education YouTube channel (https://www.youtube.com/@aisceducation), 270 videos enumerated 2026-06-24.
Lens: direct operations value for Your Company, a structural steel fabricator and erector in Houston TX (AISC member takeoff, fabrication, erection, in-house PE stamp, Tekla detailing, field bolting, joists, anchor rods, the ACP project).

Method. Every video was triaged by title and duration into Tier 1 (direct ops value: connection design, erection, fabrication, detailing, AISC 360, AISC 341 seismic, bolting, welding, construction management, cost/estimating, anchors), Tier 2 (design and analysis fundamentals, framing and floor systems, fireproofing, sustainability, BIM, bridges with fabrication or erection overlap), or Tier 3 (skipped: student steel bridge competition, K-12 and student outreach, promotional gameshows, model-viewer and VR teaching aids, and the short Steel Reel teasers). Tier 1 and Tier 2 were watched; Tier 3 was skipped. Watch depth: a curated visual-heavy Tier 1 core was watched deep (full transcript plus sampled 1024px slide frames through the /watch pipeline); the remaining Tier 1 and all Tier 2 were watched at transcript depth (full cleaned caption transcript, the reliable spoken record, mined for spec citations and procedures). Per-video entries live beside the consolidated file in research/aisc-edu/<videoid>.md.

Doctrine note. Spec section numbers, table numbers, Design Guide numbers, and any weights in these entries are quoted from what the presenter said or showed. They are a study aid, not a system-of-record. Any number that would enter a bid or a stamped calculation must be re-verified against the current AISC Manual, the controlling Specification, and bridge/aisc_validator.py. This honors verify-do-not-generate.

## Coverage Summary

Total videos enumerated: 270. Tier 1: 125. Tier 2: 107. Tier 3 skipped: 38.
Watched (Tier 1 + Tier 2): 232 (26 deep with frames, 206 transcript). Entries written: 232.

# TIER 1 ENTRIES - Direct Operations Value

## Introduction to FHWA Bridge Welding Reference Manual
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tOtLvoS8yrE | Duration: 1:31:25 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
Ronnie Medlock of High Steel Structures introduces the FHWA Bridge Welding Reference Manual, a roughly 300-page free download that explains and complements the AASHTO/AWS D1.5 Bridge Welding Code for designers, materials engineers, and shop-oversight inspectors [01:36][07:49]. The manual covers weld anatomy, welding processes, WPS and welder qualification, workmanship and hydrogen control, inspection and NDE, fracture control, fabrication and constructability details, and the engineer's role [08:23 through 09:54]. A recurring thread is the comparison between the bridge code D1.5 and the structural welding code D1.1, since D1.5 is excellent for bridges but not always the right code for non-bridge transportation steel [10:55][26:49].

### Spec References
The speaker named these standards aloud: AWS D1.5 Bridge Welding Code (paragraph 1.2.2 for approved base metals, Table 4.1 for material-electrode classifications) [27:50][28:20]; AWS D1.1 Structural Welding Code [26:49]; AWS D1.6 for stainless steel welding [82:51]; ASTM/AASHTO A709 as the bridge steel family (the 2015 D1.5 referenced A709 broadly, the 2020 edition lists grades 36, 50, 50W explicitly) [29:21][29:52]; A7 as a legacy steel without chemistry control [84:54]; A709 grade 50CR weathering stainless [82:20]; the AWS A5 consumable specifications that the D1.5 electrode classifications point to [87:32]; AWS A2.4 welding symbols [71:42]; and AISC Design Guide 21 on welded connections by Duane Miller [73:01]. The presenter did not cite AISC 360 or AISC 341 sections, which is expected for a bridge-code talk.

### Technical Details
Arc welding melts both base and weld metal through a roughly 6,000-degree arc against steel that melts near 2,800 degrees, with a shield protecting the arc from contaminants [13:29][15:03]. The processes covered are shielded metal arc (stick), flux-cored arc (gas-shielded or self-shielded), gas metal arc including metal-cored wire, submerged arc, and electroslag [15:34 through 21:42]. Submerged arc is the workhorse of bridge fabrication because it mechanizes well and uses large 3/32 and 5/32 inch wires versus the 0.052 to 0.05 inch wires of FCAW and GMAW, depositing far more weld metal for big flange and web butt splices [20:41][21:11]. GMAW short-circuiting transfer is prohibited by the bridge code for thick material because its low heat will not fuse the base metal, though it is useful for thin stock [18:39].

### Fabrication Notes
Approved welding procedures are required for all bridge welding, and fabrication cannot begin until procedures are approved, so reviewers must return WPS approvals in time [34:04][35:05]. WPS qualification is documented by a PQR using a wide single-side groove in one-inch plate with all-weld-metal and tension tests, and because qualified weld metal overmatches the base metal the tension specimen always fails in the base metal [35:36 through 37:41]. Prequalified standard joints in the code carry detailed fit-up tolerances; a fabricator can show a root face from zero to minus one-eighth on a quarter-inch detail and gets an added plus or minus 1/16 on the shop floor, but changing any setting or skipping a required backgouge turns the joint non-standard and forces requalification [30:55 through 33:34]. Hydrogen control drives much of the practice: keep consumable coils sealed until use, store stick electrodes in heated rod ovens, and apply thickness-based preheat, with optional post-heat the fabricator may add since D1.5 prescribes preheat but not post-heat [46:19 through 47:19].

### Erection Notes
Field welding is presented as fully viable when D1.5 controls are followed, used effectively for retrofits and for clean aesthetic structures where a bolted splice was not wanted [72:00][72:30]. Self-shielded flux-cored is noted as the option for remote or field situations without shielding gas [17:36]. When field-joining complete built-up girders with full-penetration web and flange welds, use a weld access hole at the corner to avoid a quality problem at the weld intersection [66:54]. The talk is bridge-oriented and does not cover crane, rigging, or member-erection sequencing in the building-steel sense.

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Named discontinuities include incomplete fusion, hot (solidification) cracks, slag inclusions, undercut, overlap, craters, porosity, spatter, arc strikes, base-metal laminations and lamellar tearing, and hydrogen-assisted cold cracks [41:15 through 42:47]. The code prohibits arc strikes and spatter [41:46]. Hydrogen cracking needs the combination of hydrogen, stress, and a susceptible (hard) microstructure, avoided by using prescribed A709 steels and checking older steels with a carbon-equivalency formula in D1.5 [43:48 through 44:48][85:25]. NDE methods are magnetic particle for surface cracks, radiography, ultrasonic, and phased-array UT; the Hoan Bridge intersecting-weld crack from constraint plus a discontinuity is the cautionary failure, but the lesson was misconstrued into a wrong belief that welds should never touch [47:50 through 65:52].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Process choice is a productivity and cost lever: stick is versatile but slow, FCAW and GMAW are mid-range, and submerged arc is the most productive for the long mechanized welds bridges need [23:14 through 23:44]. Phased-array UT is presented as better and cheaper to run than RT because results are immediate, the equipment is portable, it needs no radiation standoff or night shooting, and it inspects T and corner joints that RT cannot, with Florida DOT correlation work supporting its acceptance [52:29 through 57:40]. Constructability choices move cost directly: outside-only fillet welds on a box beat full-penetration welds, single-pass fillets beat multipass, thickness transitions are preferred over width transitions to keep one girder line and one-pass equipment usable, and the manual advises checking local fabricator equipment preferences before detailing [67:24 through 71:29][78:07].

### Your Company Application
This is the AWS D1.5 bridge code, distinct from the AWS D1.1 building-steel code Mario Gutierrez runs to, but several principles map cleanly. Mario's welding program benefits from the same hydrogen discipline (sealed consumable storage, heated rod ovens, thickness-based preheat) and the same prequalified-joint logic: any deviation from a standard joint detail forces requalification, which Tekla detailing and our in-house PE should respect when authoring connection details and weld symbols per AWS A2.4. For Ivan's takeoff, the cost story is that process and joint selection drive labor, and submerged-arc-friendly long welds and single-pass fillets are cheaper than full-penetration multipass welds, which is a useful sanity check on welded-connection labor on any heavy job such as ACP. AISC Design Guide 21 (Miller, welded connections) is the building-steel companion worth holding in our reference set. Doctrine flag: NONE. This is bridge-code education applied as reference only; it does not change our AISC member weights from aisc_validator.py, our D1.1 building-steel welding posture, or our CEO-locked rates.

## Simple Connections Simplified
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dVE_udNdt1o | Duration: 1:30:50 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This NASCC Steel Conference session, presented by Tim Holtermann (PE/SE, Canam Buildings, SJI Engineering Practice Committee chairman) and Jeff Martin (PE, Vulcraft-Verco) and sponsored by the Steel Joist Institute, walks through the "simple" connections that actually consume coordination time on a steel job: how open-web joists and joist girders attach to their supports, and how steel roof and floor deck attaches to the structure and to itself. The thesis is that no single connection is correct in isolation. Joist end anchorage, deck support fasteners, deck side-lap fasteners, and hung loads each have several code-compliant options, and the cheapest compliant combination depends on erector preference, regional product availability, and whether wind uplift or seismic diaphragm demand controls [01:30][50:00]. The recurring theme is to standardize the spec to the simplest detail that satisfies the heaviest member rather than chasing per-member optimization.

### Spec References
The session is SJI-centric and deck-standard-centric, not an AISC 360 talk. Citations stated on slides or spoken: SJI bearing-connection and end-anchorage tables keyed to joist designation (K1-12, LH02-06, LH07-17, DLH10-17, DLH18-25, JG) [04:30][11:00]; SJI 44th edition catalog [47:30]; SJI Code of Standard Practice for bolted bridging requirements [16:20]; OSHA steel-erection bolting rule for tie joists and spans over 40 ft on steel supports (Subpart R intent, "fabricated to allow for field bolting," "fully bolted unless constructability does not allow") [02:00][07:15]; AISC snug-tight definition applied to joist seat bolts, and the note that the slotted seat is NOT an AISC slip-critical connection [03:00][06:30]; AWS, with the explicit point that arc-spot (puddle) welds and arc-seam / arc-top-seam welds are NOT AWS prequalified, so WPS and PQR are required [54:30]; AISI S100 and AISI S310 for evaluating deck and deck connections [88:35]; SDI roof, floor, and non-composite deck standards and the SDI diaphragm design procedure [69:30][88:30]; a new SDI deck-design manual for deck attached to cold-formed framing, addressing shear-tension interaction at fasteners [74:25]. Bolt grades named: A307 and A325. No AISC 360 section number, AISC 341 seismic provision, RCSC clause, or Design Guide number was cited; for those, general principles, no section cited.

### Technical Details
Joist end anchorage scales with joist series. K-series and the smallest LH take a 1/8 in by 2-1/2 in fillet and a 1/2 in A307 bearing bolt; LH02-06 step up to 3/16 in by 2-1/2 in; LH07-17 and DLH10-17 go to 1/4 in by 2-1/2 in with 3/4 in A307; the largest DLH18-25 and joist girders need 1/4 in by 4 in welds, and joist girders over 50 plf self-weight require two 3/4 in A325 bolts [04:30][11:30]. Frame 0004 shows the full SJI table verbatim. Bridging now carries specified weld sizes, starting at a 1/8 in by 1 in fillet good through LH-15, and bolted bridging uses a 3/8 in A307 through K-series and LH-12 [15:30][16:20]. Diagonal bridging must be joined at the X intersection because the design takes the unbraced length from that center point [16:40]. For deck, three support-fastener families exist: welds (strongest, slowest, leave burn marks), power-actuated fasteners (5 to 6 times faster, slightly lower strength), and self-drilling screws (#12 or #14 per SDI), with PAF capacity sensitive to chord thickness so the pin must match the support [50:00][56:00]. Arc-spot puddle welds carry a 1/2 in effective / 3/4 in visible and a 3/8 in effective / 5/8 in visible call-out, an east-versus-west naming difference shown on frame 0015 [52:00]. Side laps use button punches (cheapest, weakest), screws, top-seam / arc-top-seam welds (strongest single connection), or proprietary clinch connections that match weld system capacity at button-punch speed [62:40][66:00].

### Fabrication Notes
The joist manufacturer carries most of the shop scope here. Seat bolts only need snug-tight because web-member geometry blocks a power tool from fully tensioning them, so a tensioned bolt is neither required nor practical [06:30]. Where a bolted seat is detailed but the bolt is omitted in the field, the empty slot must be welded inside the slot first, then supplemented on the seat edges away from the slot to reach required length [07:15][08:00]. Skewed bearings under 15 degrees should be avoided by skewing the joist full-length to the far beam or by adding a manufacturer-supplied header roughly one foot off the skew intersection [08:30][10:00]. Beam-to-joist and beam-to-joist-girder connections (shear tabs, 5x5 connection angles full chord depth, coped seated underslung beams) must be coordinated with the joist manufacturer because the added load and the angle location can conflict with interior web members, and webs are not guaranteed to all sit inside [29:00][31:00]. Field drilling of joist chords or webs to hang trade items is not permitted, especially the bottom tension chord [41:00].

### Erection Notes
Bolted-and-welded joist anchorage is the industry norm on steel bearings over 40 ft because OSHA requires bolts on tie joists and long spans, and slotted-hole bolts alone may not laterally brace the support compression chord [02:00]. Horizontal bridging welds are minimal (often 1/8 in by 1 in) but the angle stock is thin, so a careless erector burns holes through the lap; frame and slide photos show rejectable burn-through [17:30]. Deck installers carry strong fastener preferences that are often unknown until the installer is hired, so the spec should leave a compliant range rather than dictate one method [50:30]. Support-attachment pattern naming (36/7, 36/4) means two welds per support on interlocking deck but one weld serving both sheets on nested deck, a real source of field miscount [70:00]. Deck laps on open-web joists should land over a chord angle, not the center of the joist, and butt joints either land both sheets on one chord angle or provide a defined load path between chord angles [79:00].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Named failures: an omitted seat bolt leaving a weak welded ribbon next to the slot [07:15]; burn-through and sloppy laps on thin bridging angle [17:30]; field-coped outriggers and field-drilled chords, both discouraged [27:30][41:00]; wrong PAF pin for chord thickness, illustrated by a project where four different pins appeared in every bay and joists were color-coded by paint to sort them, a near-impossible inspection [57:00]. Weld washers must not be used unless deck is thinner than 22 gauge, a point on which AWS, AISI, and SDI agree [58:30]. SDI specifically prohibits welding 22 gauge nested deck [54:00]. Button-punch quality has no easy field check beyond pushing on it [63:30]. The closing field-fix anecdote, an engineer called out to certify that dents in delivered deck were acceptable, underlines that deck overload and handling damage drive callbacks [87:55].

### Bid / Cost Implications
This is the estimating spine of the talk. Welds are the most expensive and slowest deck attachment; power-actuated fasteners install 5 to 6 times faster at nearly the same system capacity; the cheapest compliant system is often more, faster fasteners rather than fewer, stronger ones, and lighter-gauge deck with more fasteners can beat heavier deck with fewer [50:00][90:00]. A 36/7/4 hybrid (7 fasteners at sheet ends, 4 at interior supports, 37 fasteners over 6 spans, frame 0019) buys strength near a full 36/7 at the fastener count of a 36/5, a direct material and labor saving [69:30]. The recommendation to standardize all girder bolts to A325 and all girder welds to 4 in when girders are mixed trades simplicity for a small premium and avoids field sorting [05:00][12:30]. Specifying parallel deck attachment only where lateral load actually transfers, instead of at every parallel member crossed, removes cost with no structural benefit [75:50]. Hung-load and chord-thickness decisions made early avoid expensive field rework.

### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, this defines the joist-anchorage line items by series: weld size and bolt grade/diameter scale with K, LH, DLH, and JG, and joist girders over 50 plf jump to 1/4 in by 4 in welds plus two 3/4 in A325, which Ivan should pull from SJI weight tables, not assume; the deck attachment pattern (36/4 versus 36/7 versus 36/7/4 hybrid) materially changes deck-labor cost and is a real bid variable on ACP. For Mario's shop and welding crew, the snug-tight-only rule on seat bolts, the slot-fill weld sequence when a bolt is omitted, and the warning that arc-spot and arc-seam deck welds are not AWS prequalified (so a WPS/PQR is needed) are directly actionable on the floor and in the field. For Paul's safety scope, the OSHA over-40-ft and tie-joist bolting requirement is the governing field rule. Tekla detailing should standardize the girder anchorage to the simplest heaviest-case detail and avoid sub-15-degree skewed seats and field copes. Deck-to-wall anchorage and chord-thickness/pin coordination tie to anchor-rod and field-bolting workflows. Conflict with Your Company doctrine: NONE. The session is conventional structural steel, joists, and deck with no PEMB language, and it reinforces the verify-do-not-generate posture, since every fastener capacity and weld size traces to SJI, SDI, or AISI tables rather than a generated number. Note that supplier and manufacturer names appear in the source (presenters' employers and named proprietary fasteners); per Tier 1 rules those stay off any client-facing Your Company output.

## Erection Engineering of High-Rise Buildings
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gq1bmrn22Q8 | Duration: 1:33:34 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
Timothy Nelson of Degenkolb Engineers covers erection engineering for steel high-rise structures, the temporary-condition analysis the erector and its engineer own before the permanent lateral system is fully in place [04:09]. The thesis is that as buildings go all-steel (no concrete core), use delayed mega-brace lateral systems, and push height and speed, more responsibility shifts from the structural engineer of record to the erector and its engineer for the in-between construction stages [06:42][77:46]. He organizes the talk into five topics: wind and seismic demands during construction, structural complexity and erection tolerances, pushing height limits with delayed lateral systems, erection aids and lifting lugs, and tower-crane support [07:13].

### Spec References
AISC Code of Standard Practice Section 7.10.3, temporary support must secure the bare framing against loads likely during erection including wind, and need not consider unpredictable loads such as hurricane, tornado, earthquake, explosion, collision [08:46]. ASCE 37-14 (design loads on structures during construction), reduced wind-velocity provisions Section 6.2.1 keyed to construction period [12:56][13:28], shielding provisions Section 6.2.2 (first three rows no reduction, 15% on subsequent rows) [17:06][17:37], and seismic Section 6.5 allowing up to 80% reduction on mapped spectral accelerations (0.2 x Ss and 0.2 x S1), R = 2.5, with Fa and Fv taken on unreduced Ss and S1 [25:21][26:25][26:56][27:26]. ASCE 7-10 wind, qz and equation 29.5-1 [12:25][13:59]. AISC Design Guide 10 (low-rise) used as a shielding reference [16:03][18:39]. ASCE "Wind Loads for Petrochemical and Other Industrial Facilities" [16:34][19:42], AS/NZS 1170.2 [16:34][20:12], and the Shapiro and Shapiro "Cranes and Derricks" 2011 textbook [16:34][20:42]. OSHA 1926.754 structural stability (no more than 8 stories or 30 feet between erection floor and uppermost permanent floor, no more than 4 floors of unfinished bolting/welding above the foundation) [39:53][40:25] and OSHA's 300-pound load at 18 inches eccentric for connection adequacy [55:36]. FEMA 355D (2000) gravity-connection stiffness equation [46:08], AISC Steel Construction Manual ASD/LRFD for erection-aid design [57:44], the David Ricker Engineering Journal paper (1991) and the ASME below-the-hook standard for lifting-lug factor of safety [62:23][62:53].

### Technical Details
The trust-tower wind analogy treats an unclad partial frame as exposed surface area on beams, columns, and braces; an unclad frame can pick up more wind than the clad finished building, and the audience poll confirmed wind base shear is "sometimes" higher during construction [09:47][81:18][82:21]. For a 60-story all-steel case study (13 to 15 foot stories, 250 by 80 foot plate), averaging five shielding standards gave about 70% of the ASCE 37 unshielded baseline north-south and 81% east-west, supporting roughly a 25% shielding reduction [15:31][22:47][23:48]. Seismic example for Degenkolb's San Francisco office: Ss 1.5g reduced to 0.30 (80%), Fa 1.0 on unreduced Ss, two-thirds of Sms, then R = 2.5 yields a coefficient near 0.08, low enough that judgment may override it back up to about 0.2 [29:32][30:04]. The R = 2.5 reflects that a partially connected ductile system (BRB, brace frames with collectors and diaphragm) may fracture before developing its full R = 6 to 8 ductility [27:26][27:56].

### Fabrication Notes
Box columns are increasingly common and very heavy, on the order of 50-plus tons over a few stories once gusset plates, stiffeners, and wall thickness are counted [54:03]. A complete-joint-penetration splice on a box column of 3 to 4 foot plan dimension can take days to over a week to weld off [54:35]. Lifting-lug demand requires an attentive unfactored weight takeoff capturing all supplemental plates and any consolidation rods or plates inside a concrete-filled box [61:20][62:23]. Erection-aid gravity load is carried in bearing through the PJP root face or by oversized backing bars placed above and below so they bear on each other, keeping gravity out of the bolted aid [58:46][59:18]. Bare metal-deck diaphragm capacity is governed by support attachments (welded stud, spot weld, powder-actuated fastener, screw) and side-lap connections (seam weld, button punch), with side-lap spacing of 24 versus 12 inches swinging total capacity significantly [48:50][49:21][51:57].

### Erection Notes
On 181 Fremont (800 feet, all steel, three-tier external mega-brace plus perimeter secondary moment frame) the erector measured building lean from differential column elastic shortening and building twist as the mega-braces engaged, and set certain columns intentionally out of plumb to land within the AISC Code of Standard Practice global envelope of 3 inches in and 2 inches out at the top [31:05][32:38][33:41][34:12][35:14]. A staged "dashboard" spreadsheet interpolated column XYZ positions at each level across three erection phases versus theoretical, shared with the GC; SAP2000 staged-construction was an alternative [34:43][35:44]. Mega-braces slid through intermediate floors (braced length only, no lateral transfer except at top and bottom nodes), leaving about 20 stories erected without the primary lateral system [42:30][43:33]. Temporary lateral support sources: secondary moment frames (with corner bottom flanges left unwelded to avoid Vierendeel action), gravity-connection partial fixity, slotted-hole brace connections that allow shortening slip before being tightened slip-critical or welded, and early welded-down deck diaphragms [44:06][45:06][47:10][48:14]. Heavy stick-built transfer trusses were false-worked off the perimeter excavation shoring (cutter-soil-mix wall with steel soldier beams at 4 feet on center) using sloped temporary columns to avoid touch points in the slab [37:19][38:21][38:51].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Crane-supplier tie-in demands are frequently undocumented as to ASD versus LRFD level, often generated from overseas codes, and have not always tracked the ASCE wind transition, so the speaker assumes ASD when unsure [68:03][68:34][69:04]. In one case the manufacturer-supplied tie-shoe holes could not pass even the largest bolts under the supplied demand, resolved with very high-strength bolts rather than reaming [70:38][71:08]. A box tube at a tower-crane tie-in was under-stiffened at the top and made audible noise as it distorted, alarming the site and requiring an OSHA conversation [75:11][75:42]. Wind-tacking deck is called out as inadequate to develop deck strength; an expedited proper weld-down is required [51:26]. Lifting-lug checks 5 and 6 (welds to the box wall and localized box-wall effects) are where problems most often arise, especially with thin walls that cannot develop the lug welds [64:58][65:29].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Heavier gauge deck or tighter connection spacing to gain temporary diaphragm strength carries a cost the erector must weigh, and the deck gauge is often left to the contractor rather than fixed on the structural drawings, so it must be confirmed early [51:57][52:27][50:23]. Knowing whether the decker works for the steel erector or the GC changes the schedule dynamics for how fast deck gets laid and welded after erection [50:54]. The load-spreading crane scheme demanded deck welded down across many floors right at the leading edge, a "huge obstacle" that had to be explained and bought into early [73:09][73:40]. Multi-day to multi-week CJP box-column splices keep elements on engineered erection aids far longer than a couple hours, raising the engineering and temporary-steel cost [54:35][55:05]. Lifting lugs use a factor of safety of about 5 (between ASME below-the-hook categories B and C) on nominal steel capacity given single-point lifts over streets and workers [62:23][63:25].

### Your Company Application
This is squarely erector-and-its-engineer territory and reinforces that Your Company's in-house PE stamp should own temporary-condition checks (wind on bare frame, erection-aid and lifting-lug design) rather than assume the EOR covered them. For Mario's shop, the box-column splice timeline and CJP weld-off duration argue for engineered erection aids on heavy lifts, with backing bars sized to carry gravity in bearing, all under AWS D1.1 procedures already in his lane. For Ivan's takeoff, lifting-lug design needs an exact unfactored assembly weight including supplemental and consolidation plates, which ties directly to the aisc_validator.py member weights and to flagging deck gauge as a confirm-before-pricing input. Paul's safety scope maps to the OSHA 1926.754 limits (8 stories / 4 floors unfinished bolting or welding) and the 300-pound erection-aid load. Tekla detailing should carry slotted-hole brace connections and lug/erection-aid plates as modeled temporary steel. Most of Your Company's work is low- to mid-rise conventional steel where mega-brace and tower-crane content is aspirational, so on the ACP project the directly usable items are anchor-rod and column plumb tolerance against the AISC envelope and the deck weld-down sequence, not high-rise climber cranes. Doctrine flags: NONE. The talk uses conventional structural steel framing throughout with no PEMB language, and it never asserts a member weight that would conflict with the validator.

## Erection Engineering of Low-Rise Buildings
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TJP57O8XudU | Duration: 1:37:14 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is part two of a three-part AISC series on steel erection, presented by Ben Miller of Ruby and Associates. Erection engineering is the design of a temporary system that maintains stability of the structure during each stage of steel erection [05:33]. The key teaching is that the engineer of record (EOR) designs only for the final completed condition, while the erector is responsible for stability of the bare steel frame at every intermediate sequence, and incomplete structures may not be stable without temporary measures [06:43]. There is no governing code that prescribes erection design loads, so the erection engineer works from standards and guides and applies significant engineering judgment [12:39]. A low-rise building is defined per ASCE 7-10 as having a mean roof height of 60 feet or less that does not exceed the least horizontal dimension [04:30].

### Spec References
The following were cited verbatim on slides or by the speaker: IBC 2018 Section 2205.1 (design, fabrication, and erection per AISC 360) [09:00]; AISC 360 Section M4.2, secure the structure for dead load and erection loads with temporary bracing per the Code of Standard Practice [09:21]; AISC Code of Standard Practice Sections 7.10.1, 7.10.2, 7.10.3, and 7.10.4, with 7.10.3 requiring temporary supports sufficient to secure the bare frame against loads likely encountered including wind, and 7.10.4 keeping them in place until the lateral-force-resisting system and connecting diaphragm elements are installed (slide 15, frame at [10:13]); ASCE 7-10 (low-rise definition and velocity pressure); ASCE 37-14 (Design Loads on Structures During Construction) Chapter 6, Section 6.2 Wind and 6.2.1 Design Wind Speed factor table and Section 6.2.2 Frameworks Without Cladding shielding rules (slides 17 and 19, frames at [14:12] and [17:50]); AISC Design Guide 10 "Erection Bracing of Low-Rise Structural Steel Buildings" with Figures 2-1 and 2-2 and the German DIN 1055 stacking-factor equation (slide 23 at [20:22]); ASCE 7-10 Section 29.4 solid signs / Figure 29.4-1, and Section 29.5 Lattice Frameworks with equation 29.4-1 and Figure 29.5-2 (slide 34 at [37:17]); OSHA requirement of four anchor rods per column to resist a 300 lb load at 18 in from the column center [71:13]; AISC Figure 11-2 for the four-bolt single-angle connection [75:42]; and the PCI architectural precast concrete code for panel stability after erection [50:57].

### Technical Details
The construction-period wind reduction factor scales the 50-year basic wind speed: less than six weeks 0.75, six weeks to one year 0.8, one to two years 0.85, two to five years 0.9 (ASCE 37 section 6.2.1 table, slide 17) [14:42]. A worked Michigan example took a 115 mph strength-level speed to 92 mph at the 0.8 factor, yielding 15.7 psf at 60 ft with Kz 0.85, exposure B, directionality 0.85 [16:08]. Shielding of repetitive parallel elements applies 100 percent of wind on the first three rows and a 15 percent reduction on the fourth and later rows (ASCE 37 section 6.2.2) [17:39]. Design Guide 10 adds a stacking factor eta from Figure 2-2 keyed to spacing-to-depth ratio a/d and solidity ratio phi; for wide-flange beams and columns the solidity ratio is 1.0 [22:48]. A worked bay (W21x50, 40 ft span, 10 ft spacing, 20 members) gave eta about 0.36, rounded up to 0.4 for conservatism [25:02]. Two ASCE 7 methods (solid-sign Cf 1.9 and lattice-framework Cf 1.8) gave comparable base shear, roughly 7,000 lb per grid for sequence 101 [38:56].

### Fabrication Notes
The presentation is erection-focused, but several fabrication and detailing items surface. The preferred anchor-rod detail moves the four rods outside the column footprint so a wind-induced 32 kip-ft base moment runs at about 90 percent utilization, versus 146 percent concrete breakout when the rods sit inside the footprint [73:46]. Moment connections detailed with flange CJP welds (slide 64 typical beam-column flange moment connection, top and bottom flange CJP, web bolts to develop the reaction) give zero frame action until the field welds are complete [74:11]. The speaker recommends the EOR show optional bolted moment-connection details on design drawings so the erector has flexibility, since a bolted connection can be partially populated (top four and bottom four bolts) for temporary frame action [74:50]. For HSS bracing, knife-plate gusset connections with shop-installed lug plates carrying a shackle are preferred for cable-brace terminations [44:45].

### Erection Notes
Each erection sequence is analyzed as its own standalone building, with wind applied per sequence and temporary bracing sized to the resulting base shear [29:51]. Temporary bracing is typically steel wire-rope cable with turnbuckles for initial tensioning, terminated at a keeper angle on the back of the column so the choker cannot slide [42:38]. Three X-brace configurations trade quantity against cable force (single-story X braces give lower force but more locations; a brace bypassing a floor halves the locations but forces metal-deck cutting and higher cable force) [40:13]. Bracing must remain until the permanent lateral system and diaphragm connections for that portion are installed [47:00]. Long-span trusses need checks both under hook (pick-point selection so chords are not overstressed) and at set (top chord becomes the compression member); a rule of thumb is slenderness L/r under 80 likely stable, over 100 likely needs secondary bracing, and the example W12x40 top chord at L/r 150 required guy cables to dead-men [66:54]. OSHA requires each member end secured with two bolts or equivalent before release from the crane [53:55].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The most expensive failure shown was a lack of communication on a precast-shear-wall job where the structural steel frame had no lateral system of its own; the precast designer never accounted for incidental steel lean-on load, forcing a hard W14x74 brace system and a 5 kip lean-on limit, a cost not in the original bid [56:00]. A common detailing trap is the four-bolt single-angle connection: per AISC Figure 11-2, strain incompatibility means only the two interior bolts are fully effective, so capacity is overestimated [75:42]. Anchor rods inside the column footprint failing concrete breakout at 146 percent under temporary wind is another named failure [73:02]. Cable braces that slide down a column because the choker only bites on itself, with no physical keeper, were flagged as having no test basis for relied-upon friction [43:42].

### Bid / Cost Implications
The dominant cost message is that nonstructural-only lateral systems (precast shear walls, tilt-up) can multiply temporary-bracing cost, and the precast lean-on coordination gap on Example Project 2 created a change cost outside the bid [56:00]. Bringing the erection engineer in early lets the team substitute bolted for welded moment connections and choose anchor-rod layouts that avoid temporary cable bracing entirely, speeding erection and cutting brace-location count and end-termination labor [74:50]. The shielding and stacking-factor methods directly reduce the temporary wind load and therefore brace sizing, so the analysis method chosen has a real cost lever [25:02]. Staged-construction lock-in forces should be reported to the EOR so the owner, not the erector, decides the acceptable percentage of additional locked-in force [96:21].

### Your Company Application
For Tekla detailing and the in-house PE stamp, this is the basis for our erection-procedure deliverable: per-sequence wind analysis with the ASCE 37 construction-period factor, Design Guide 10 stacking factors, cable-brace sizing, and a documented brace-removal trigger tied to the permanent lateral system. Anchor-rod work (Ivan takeoff plus PE design) should default to rods outside the column footprint where wind base moments govern, since that is the detail that keeps utilization workable; flag any EOR base-plate detail that boxes rods inside the footprint. Mario's shop and welding scope should note that flange-CJP moment connections give no temporary frame action until welded, so sequence planning must not assume fixity before the detailing gang finishes; the four-bolt single-angle trap (AISC Figure 11-2, two interior bolts effective) is a shop-drawing review check. Paul's safety scope maps to the OSHA four-anchor-rod 300 lb rule and the two-bolt-per-end release rule, both hard stops in erection sequencing. For ACP project controls, precast or other nonstructural lateral systems are a bid-risk flag: confirm in writing the lean-on limit and who braces what, because that gap is an out-of-bid cost. No conflict with Your Company doctrine; this reinforces the verify-do-not-generate posture, since the speaker stresses judgment and per-sequence checks over assumed numbers. DOCTRINE FLAG: NONE.

## The Erector's Perspective
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tDl6_Y8_XlI | Duration: 1:34:48 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
Tim Duke (corporate QC and risk director, Williams Erection and Atlanta Steel Erectors, ironworker since 1998) walks the full erector workflow from bid through topping out. The thesis is that an erector reads the same drawing set a fabricator does but prices it against field reality: crane reach, weld access, lift weights, stability under construction, and weather. He shows how the AISC Code of Standard Practice allocates scope between erector, fabricator, owner's designated representative for design (ODRD), and general contractor, and how connection-detail choices and weld type drive both cost and schedule [01:24][11:30][39:56]. The video is light on verbatim AISC 360 section numbers and heavy on Code of Standard Practice Section 7, AESS, AWS weld type, and erection-engineering practice.

### Spec References
AISC Code of Standard Practice, Section 7 Erection, with subsections shown on a slide: 7.1 Method of Erection, 7.2 Job-Site Conditions, 7.3 Foundations Piers and Abutments, 7.4 Lines and Benchmarks, 7.5 Installation of Anchor Rods Foundation Bolts and Other Embedded Items, 7.6 Installation of Bearing Devices, 7.7 Grouting, 7.8 Field Connection Material, 7.9 Loose Material, 7.10 Temporary Support of Structural Steel Frames, 7.11 Safety Protection, 7.12 Structural Steel Frame Tolerances, 7.13 Erection Tolerances, 7.14 Correction of Errors, 7.15 Cuts Alterations and Holes for Other Trades, 7.16 Handling and Storage, 7.17 Field Painting, 7.18 Final Cleaning Up [11:30 slide 19]. AESS Table 10.1 of the Code of Standard Practice, with AESS category C noted as custom [14:42]. AWS D1.1 prequalified joint details cited generically for the CJP volume calc, and "D1.8" named for seismic welding qualification [18:05][40:54]. A spec slide referenced the older "Specification for Structural Steel Buildings, Allowable Stress Design / Plastic Design" because that is what the job specced [05:54]. The S001 general-notes slide cited CSI spec Section 05 12 10 for the seismic-load-resisting system (SLRS) [17:40 slide 26]. No AISC 360 chapter or table number and no RCSC section was stated aloud or shown.

### Technical Details
The S001 General Structural Notes slide lists material specs by shape: wide flanges and WTs ASTM A992 Grade 50; miscellaneous plates and continuity plates A572 Grade 50; angles and channels A36; rectangular and round HSS A500 Grade B; bolts A325 N unless otherwise noted; anchor rods F1554 Fy=36ksi unless otherwise noted; threaded rods A36; steel joists per Steel Joist Institute; welding electrodes E70 with CVN per spec; welded studs A108 headed studs Type H4L or S3L [17:40 slide 26]. Note SS-2 designated members and connections as part of the SLRS, SS-3 required natural beam camber upward, SS-4 allowed splices only where indicated, SS-5 required hot-dipped galvanized finish for weather-exposed members and embeds, and SS-6 capped drain holes at 1 1/8 inch diameter [slide 26]. Systems shown include high-rise cores (W14x1440 core columns), bowstring trusses on bents, 350-foot transfer trusses carrying a nine-story building, brace frames, canopies, slab-edge bent plate, precast embeds, and elevator separator beams [26:54][58:55][66:00].

### Fabrication Notes
The erector asks the fabricator for things that move work into the shop where it is faster and safer: assemble frames and shoring in the shop, button-punch deck side laps, shop-attach angle supports and embed tabs so they are not field-fit, and punch a 13/16 inch diameter hole roughly 1 foot from each beam end for the safety-cable tie-off system [07:19][33:22][34:46 slide 56]. He flags details that fabricate hard: a tube elevator-separator beam cut to exact length to sit against a concrete embed almost always needs field cut or lengthening because cast concrete is rarely true, so request welded shear tabs with a couple of bolts or a seat angle instead [23:30]. One precast/galvanized embed held a 1/64 inch tolerance over the whole element, called out as exceptional fabrication given hot-dip galvanizing warping [48:52]. Bevel depth for the PJP option was set to satisfy the loading, using the 2020 AWS weld nomenclature.

### Erection Notes
Stability under construction is the erector's controlling concern. An engineered stability plan is required when the contract documents specify it AND when the structure cannot resist environmental plus erection loads before completion, so the correct answer to the poll was "both" [78:51]. Plans are stamped by an engineer licensed in the project state, carry general erection notes, temporary erection aids, and step-by-step sequences (X01.1, X03.1, etc.) with circle-slash place-keeping, and must involve the superintendent and general foreman so the field crew is bought in and does not improvise [58:55][72:25][93:00]. Wind limits are explicit: braces designed for 25 mph are expected to fail above it, and trusses cannot be set above a stated 15 mph until columns are guyed to dead men or taken down; cranes carry anemometers reporting gust and sustained wind [59:14][89:24][90:02]. Crane selection covers cost, capacity, boom length, and site prep; a 31000 lattice crawler at ~2500 ton capacity needs 137 trucks and five weeks to assemble [82:01]. Heavy picks are both calculated and weighed on the operator's load cell before swinging, since rigging, paint, bolts, and welds can push a pick over chart at the margins [68:28]. Specialty methods shown: Hillman-roller truss push at an arena (100-ton rollers, two per truss, bolted lifting saddle, no welds), strand-jack sky-hook for 300-ton transfer trusses, a derrick over a parking deck that could not carry a 500-ton truck crane, and a helicopter to remove a tower crane [44:01][55:37][65:46].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The recurring failures are detail-driven, not weld-quality counts. Overhead-position fillet welds at slab-edge closure plates and vent-plate supports are slow and access-limited, so the "not so good" versus "good" detail review pushes for a top-side weld, a plug or slot weld for uplift, or a slotted bolted connection that can be adjusted in and out [20:46 slide 33]. Brace gussets fished in after the beam bend many bolts unless an oversized erection hole is provided [25:44]. CJP welds get 100 percent ultrasonic testing, and a welder who blows out a heavy CJP may get two chances before going home, which is why interpass cleaning on CJP is religious [42:55]. Members found overstressed mid-erection trigger a thorough investigation; the first check is whether the stamped sequence was followed to the letter, with responsibility falling on the plan creator or the erector depending on findings [90:50].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Weld-type selection is the headline cost lever. A CJP column splice on heavy shapes was computed at 690 cubic inches, 193 pounds of weld, 230 pounds of wire at FCAW efficiency, about 35 pounds deposited per 8-hour shift, for a 6.5 man-day splice (roughly a week on a 10-hour shift) per connection [40:02]. Converting to a PJP sized to resist the indicated loads plus a 200 kip-ft erection moment, where research confirmed CJP was not required, cut it to about 1.9 days at ~50 pounds deposited per day, with magnetic-particle plus visual testing replacing UT [42:55][slide 56]. Erection-plan engineering itself runs from a few thousand dollars for one truss to several tens of thousands on large projects [84:16]. Erectors bid off piece counts, beam and column weights, bolt counts and sizes (long 1-1/8 inch bolts slow pin-driving), and weld weight rather than tonnage; AESS, seismic welding qualification, and special electrodes are explicit cost drivers [06:30][14:42][18:05]. Derrick rental at $3,500/month beat a 500-ton truck crane at $4,000/day [55:37].

### Your Company Application
This maps directly onto Your Company's full erector-plus-fabricator scope. For Ivan, the takeoff discipline mirrors ours: piece counts for columns, beams, trusses, studs, bracing, decking, plus a weld-weight calc on heavy splices, all of which should run member-by-member through aisc_validator.py rather than tonnage x psf, and the A992/A572/A500/A36 and F1554 anchor-rod material map belongs in our material screen. For Mario, the CJP-versus-PJP weld-volume math (deposition rate, interpass cleaning, UT on every CJP) is a direct shop-and-field productivity model and ties to his AWS D1.1 lead role, with D1.8 flagged when a job is seismic; preheat for heavy splices used propane rosebuds staged ahead of welders so welder wage goes to welding not heating [88:00]. For Paul, the safety content is concrete: engineered cable systems, the 3/8 inch top-and-mid-rail perimeter cable at 8-foot posts that is for fall protection only while the crew is present and then flagged off, and the 13/16 inch tie-off hole the fabricator must punch. Tekla detailing should bake in erection-ease moves Tim asks for (oversized erection holes in non-permanent gusset connections, slotted bent-plate connections, shop-attached embed tabs, top-of-column lifting holes). The in-house PE stamp is exactly the erection-stability-plan author role he describes, and his wind-limit and weighed-pick rigor is the standard to hold on ACP project controls. Anchor-rod F1554 callouts and tolerance reinforce our anchor-rod design and setting workstream. DOCTRINE FLAGS: NONE. He confirms our verify-don't-generate posture (weigh the pick, do not trust calculated weight alone; price member-by-member) and uses no PEMB language.

## Bracing Connections
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LPUhN4zoZaA | Duration: 1:36:16 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is AISC Live Webinar Session 4 of the "Connection Design for Moment Frames and Braced Frames" series, presented by Dr. Brad Davis (University of Kentucky) on March 11, 2020, covering brace-to-gusset and gusset-to-frame connection design [00:48]. The talk splits into basic bracing connections, a single gusset connected to one member, and heavy corner connections where a gusset ties into the beam-column corner and carries enormous loads [01:53]. The unifying method is to trace every limit state from the brace side across to the supporting member, then for corner gussets pin down the indeterminate internal force distribution with the uniform force method and the lower-bound theorem [38:39]. The recurring tool for sizing the critical plate section is the Whitmore section, a 30-degree load spread off the connection length [08:35].
### Spec References
Speaker and slides cite, verbatim: Manual Figure 9-1 for the Whitmore section [08:39]; spec section J4.4 for plate compression with Lc/r limit of 25 and section E3 for flexural buckling above that [11:43]; Design Guide 29 (vertical bracing connections) for K-factor selection (0.5 to 1.2) and for complete worked examples [12:26]; weld strength equation J2-3 and the Manual shortcut equation 8-1 on page 8-8 using 1.392 kips per sixteenth per inch for LRFD [13:01][14:02]; Manual Table D3.1 for shear lag factor [18:42]; Manual Part 9 prying procedures starting near page 9-10 [22:48]; slip-resistance equations J3-4 and J3-5a with the case-of-SC factor near the end of section J3.7 [26:49][31:54]; pretension Table J3.1 (minimum 28 kips for the example bolt) [27:58]; Table J3.2 for Fnv = 54 ksi and Fnt = 90 ksi [31:11][70:57]; Manual Part 13 and Design Guide 29 Chapter 4 for the uniform force method, the lower-bound theorem, and KISS method, with equation 13-1 setting alpha and beta [38:54][41:49][49:07]; Manual Tables 7-1 and 7-2 for bolt strengths [66:58]; weld minimum size Table J2.3 [63:00]; web local yielding equation J10-2, web local crippling J10-D4, web compression buckling J10-D8 [69:00][74:53][75:33]; column shear G2-1a [73:19]. Design Guide 24 is named for spreading load through an extended plate [73:51]. No AISC 341 seismic provisions are cited; this webinar is non-seismic connection design.
### Technical Details
The Whitmore section spreads the brace load 30 degrees each side over the connection length; where it runs off the plate edge it does not control and the gross plate width times thickness governs [09:39]. Plate compression uses J4.4 yielding when Lc/r is at or below 25, otherwise E3 buckling with Lc = KL, and K is taken from DG29 examples, often 0.5, sometimes 1.2 for a gusset welded only to the beam [11:57][86:51]. For corner gussets the six interface forces (Hc, Vc, Mc, Hb, Vb, Mb) are statically indeterminate; the lower-bound theorem lets any statically admissible and safe force field be used, and the force field giving the highest predicted strength is closest to true [42:46]. The uniform force method eliminates gusset moments by routing all resultants through the work point, with alpha (face of column to connection center at the beam) and beta (top of beam to connection center at the column) constrained by equation 13-1: alpha minus beta tan(theta) = eb tan(theta) minus ec [49:18]. Slip resistance is reduced by the ksc factor (0.697 in the example, about a 30 percent reduction) because the applied tension component pulls the plies apart [29:26].
### Fabrication Notes
For an HSS brace, the common shop process is to slot the brace, fit it over the gusset, set one erection bolt, then field-weld the HSS [04:27]. T-stem or claw-angle connecting elements are shop-welded to the brace and field-bolted to the support [05:03][37:03]. The gusset is usually shop-welded to the beam and field-bolted to the column, via an end plate, a single shear-type plate, or double angles [37:46]. Fillet welds are preferred over CJP for the long gusset-to-beam interface to save cost [56:16]. One non-obvious fabrication rule: the gusset-to-beam fillet weld is increased by 25 percent for non-uniform force distribution even when the design says no moment, citing the Hewitt-Thornton work referenced as the Chris U and Bill Thornton paper [55:28]. Weld effective length often needs engineering judgment, and the speaker knocks a quarter inch off the computed length where the plate runs in at a sharp angle and the weld is not fully built out [16:13].
### Erection Notes
The slotted-HSS-over-gusset detail is explicitly an erection sequence: slot, drop over gusset, one erection bolt, then field weld [04:33]. End-plate and shear-plate gusset-to-column connections are field-bolted while the gusset-to-beam weld is shop work, so the corner assembly is partly shop and partly field [36:51]. The brace itself field-bolts to the gusset [37:12]. The talk does not cover crane, rigging, temporary bracing, or erection-stability sequencing; its erection content is limited to which connections are field versus shop.
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The headline field problem is detailers throwing horizontal short-slotted holes into the gusset-to-column shear plate (and the beam-to-column shear tab) by habit, because they look like ordinary single-plate shear connections, when in fact these carry large axial transfer force; the speaker is on a live job with about 50 such connections needing reinforcement [52:53][53:24]. Root cause is a communication gap: the engineer of record often hands the fabricator only the brace axial load, omitting the beam reaction Rb, the transfer force Ab, and whether the column is HSS (needed for Qf), so the detailer has no idea axial exists in that joint [50:51][90:43]. Single-bolt brace connections are discouraged because block shear and shear-lag (connection length near zero) make them very weak [91:56]. Slotted holes in a beam-to-column joint generally will not work even slip-critical because per-bolt slip force is only about 9 kips [90:11]. Forgetting the beam-to-column connection at the corner is named as a frequent and costly omission [03:50].
### Bid / Cost Implications
The choice of force field directly affects connection economy; the KISS method zeros Hc and Vb for a quick safe answer but typically yields heavier, less economical connections than the uniform force method [44:02][46:39]. The 25 percent weld increase on the gusset-to-beam interface adds weld metal on every heavy gusset and should be carried in any connection-weld takeoff [55:28]. Heavy corner connections can drive large beams (a generous spandrel beam is preferred over a W8 because Vb can hit 200 to 300 kips) and may require column web stiffeners; in the worked example the W14x99 column failed web compression buckling and needed added stiffeners, a real fabrication add [75:55][52:42]. Incomplete EOR force data (only brace axial given) generates RFIs and rework, the kind of scope risk that belongs in a bid clarification rather than absorbed silently.
### Your Company Application
This video is the methodology reference for Your Company's heavy braced-frame bid and detailing work, mapping cleanly onto our in-house PE stamp and Tekla detailing. The slotted-hole warning is a direct QC gate for Tekla detailing and for in-house PE review: any gusset-to-column shear plate or corner shear tab carrying transfer force must not get default horizontal slots, and the PE stamp should confirm the EOR provided beam reaction Rb, transfer force Ab, and column HSS status, not just brace axial. For Ivan's takeoff, heavy corner connections imply added gusset plate, claw angles, end plates, the 25 percent gusset-weld uplift, and likely column stiffeners, so member-takeoff through aisc_validator.py should flag braced bays for connection-material allowance rather than assuming a clean brace axial. For Mario's shop and welding scope, the slotted-HSS-over-gusset erection-bolt-then-field-weld sequence and the shop-weld gusset-to-beam fillets are the standard processes to plan and to weld to AWS D1.1 with 70 ksi electrodes as shown. Field bolting uses A325 and A490 with Table J3.2 strengths and slip-critical checks where the EOR specifies them. This is conventional structural-steel connection design with no PEMB content. Doctrine conflict: NONE.

## Introduction to Seismic Connections
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gqCdO8zB0gA | Duration: 1:33:24 | Upload: 2020-03-04 | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is AISC Live Webinar Session 3 of the "Connection Design for Moment Frames and Braced Frames" series, taught by Dr. Owner Atherton of Virginia Tech, on the design of steel seismic connections. The governing theme is ductility, defined at [02:14] as the ability to deform inelastically without significant loss of strength, with structural steel reaching a material ductility ratio of 100 to 200 [02:46]. Seismic design works because an earthquake acts more like an applied displacement than an applied force [03:29], so as system ductility rises the required strength and material quantity fall while connection detailing, welding, and inspection cost rise [04:19]. The talk drills into two systems, the special moment frame (SMF) and the special concentrically braced frame (SCBF), and the connection rules that flow from capacity design and the post-Northridge testing regime.
### Spec References
ASCE 7 mapped spectral accelerations and Table 12.2-1 (the 85 listed seismic systems, R and omega-naught factors) and section 14.1, which references AISC 341 [09:09, 09:24]. AISC 341 Seismic Provisions: Table A3.1 for Ry [10:17, frame SCBF example], section B1.1 / D1.1 highly ductile compactness limits [frame, transcript], section E3.4a strong-column-weak-beam [transcript], section E3.6f and E3.6f.2 continuity plates [frame 11], section E16B item C beam-to-column behavior [75:16], section F2.5c protected zone (middle quarter of brace) [59:05], and section F2.6c.1 required tensile strength Tu = RyFyAg [frame 14]. AISC 358 prequalified moment connections, listing 10 connection types, with the RBS design procedure citing 358 sections 5.8 and 5.6 [frame 9]. AISC 360 Specification: Chapter D and Table D3.1 shear lag cases (case 5 circular HSS, case 2 general), Chapter E column buckling, section J4 connecting-element yielding and block shear, and section J10 / J10.8 concentrated forces for continuity plates [frames, transcript]. Welds use CJP beam-flange-to-column and demand-critical filler-metal toughness; no specific AWS D1.1 clause number was spoken or shown.
### Technical Details
SMF conformance requires full-scale cyclic testing to 0.04 radians (4 percent story drift) while retaining 80 percent of nominal plastic moment, provable three ways: an AISC 358 prequalified connection, a connection prequalified by others, or project-specific qualification testing [12:26, 73:01]. The 358 menu includes the reduced beam section (RBS), bolted and welded end-plate, bolted flange plate, and welded unreinforced flange-welded web (WUF-W), plus proprietary types. The worked RBS example (W36x150 beams, W14x455 column) computes the probable maximum moment Mpr using Cpr (1.15 for A992), Ry (1.1), and the effective plastic modulus, projects it to the joint center, and verifies strong-column-weak-beam at a ratio of 1.04 [frame 10, transcript]. The SCBF example designs a brace connection for an HSS 6.875x0.500 A500 Gr. B brace (Ag 9.36 in2, Fy 42 ksi, Ry 1.4), giving Tu = 550 kips and a capacity-design compression demand of 444 kips, sized through a 5/8 in A572 Gr. 50 gusset checked for Whitmore yielding, block shear (970 kips), and gusset buckling (599 kips), with a 2t fold line of 1.25 in and a 1 in by 1 in reinforcing bar to restore effective net area [frame 16, 60:00 to 72:18].
### Fabrication Notes
The RBS flange cut is a shop operation that relocates the plastic hinge away from the column weld [transcript ~RBS]. End-plate connections are shop welded with no weld access holes, which the speaker notes gives well-controlled welds [transcript]. The beam web to column flange is a CJP weld detailed per 358 section 5.6 using a 3/8 in shear tab as weld backing [frame 11]. The brace-to-gusset slot is cut 1/8 in wider than the gusset thickness, which reduces the brace net section and usually forces added reinforcement [67:44]. The knife-plate variant lets the brace slot weld around the plate end to make the effective net area equal the gross area, avoiding reinforcement, at the cost of one more piece and more welds [56:48, 91:24]. Continuity plates are required when column flange thickness is below the t-limit (in the example tcf 0.855 in versus tc-lim 1.50 in, so plates required) [frame 11].
### Erection Notes
The video is design and detailing focused and does not walk through field sequencing, crane, or rigging procedures. The one field-relevant geometry point is the 2t (or elliptical) fold line in the gusset, a clearance zone that must stay clean so the gusset can hinge and accommodate brace rotation; the speaker advises against letting bolted beam-gusset angles encroach on that fold line because restraining the hinge is a bad idea [82:00, 56:48]. Bolted brace connections may need slip checked only for oversized holes, where slip demand can be capped by overstrength loads; standard holes do not require slip-critical design here [frame 14].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The Northridge 1994 earthquake produced fractures in hundreds of SMF buildings, typically at the beam bottom-flange to column-flange weld [11:25]. Named contributing causes were the bottom-flange backing bar acting as an effective crack starter, poor weld quality, the composite slab effect, low-toughness weld filler metal, and weak panel zones that kinked the column flanges [12:02]. The post-Northridge fix is mandatory full-scale qualification testing for all SMF and IMF connections [12:26]. Protected zones (middle quarter of the brace, brace ends, and the entire gusset connection per 341 F2.5c) allow no attachments, welds, or defects, to prevent premature fracture in yielding regions [59:05]. Demand-critical welds at column base plates and beam-to-column joints carry additional filler-metal toughness requirements [58:23].
### Bid / Cost Implications
The speaker is explicit that higher-ductility systems trade material for connection cost: in high-seismic zones the material savings outweigh added connection and inspection cost, but in low-seismic zones (East Coast, Midwest, where wind often governs) the connection detailing cost can exceed the material saved, making an R=3 system without seismic detailing more economical [04:24, 78:00]. System choice drives R factor (6, 7, 8 for high ductility) and therefore both tonnage and detailing scope. For estimating, seismic connections add full-scale-tested prequalified detailing, demand-critical weld filler metal, continuity plates, gusset reinforcement bars, and added NDE, all cost that does not appear in a plain gravity-frame takeoff.
### Your Company Application
For Ivan takeoff, a seismic project means tonnage is only part of the story; the bid must carry continuity plates, gusset reinforcement bars, knife plates, and the labor of demand-critical CJP welds, so flag any drawing set noting AISC 341, 358, SMF, SCBF, IMF, or "demand critical" and price the connection labor separately rather than folding it into a flat per-ton rate. For Mario and AWS D1.1 welding, demand-critical welds require higher-toughness filler metal and the protected-zone rule bars any tack, attachment, or arc strike in the brace mid-quarter, brace ends, and gusset, which the shop and erectors must respect. For Tekla detailing, the 2t fold-line clearance, the 1/8 in brace slot oversize, the 3/8 in shear tab used as weld backing, and the SH plastic-hinge offset are modelable detail dimensions taken straight from AISC 358. For the in-house PE stamp, only a stamped engineer selects the system, runs strong-column-weak-beam, panel-zone, and capacity-design checks; the takeoff tool verifies member weights through aisc_validator.py and never generates these seismic capacities. Houston is low-seismic, so most Your Company work, including ACP, will not be SMF/SCBF, but the cost lesson is the standing rule: confirm the seismic system before pricing connections. Doctrine conflict: NONE.

## Moment Connections, Part 2
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vZDIxAfN9Tk | Duration: 1:32:57 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
Dr Brad Davis teaches fully restrained (FR) moment connections for wind and low-seismic (R=3) applications, focused on two bolted types that develop prying action: T-stub bolted moment connections and end-plate (moment-in-plate) connections [01:32][02:02]. The unifying idea is that negative moment is decomposed into a flange force couple, the tension flange force is delivered to the bolts through out-of-plane bending of the T-flange or end plate, and that bending can create fulcrum contact at the plate tips that pries the bolts so bolt force exceeds the static demand [02:32][03:33]. The governing design strategy is to size the plate for thick-plate behavior so the plate does not bend appreciably, no fulcrum forms, and the prying force Q goes to zero [05:38][11:55].
### Spec References
The speaker cited AISC Manual Part 9 prying provisions pages 9-10 to 9-14 (and Q-sub-r equation 9-19a near the bottom of page 9-12, plus a Q equation on 9-13) [05:06][87:59]; spec equation J3-1 for bolt design tensile strength with phi=0.75 [11:23][16:39]; Table J3.2 for nominal tensile stress fnt=90 ksi (A325) [16:39][72:02]; the slip-critical equation J3-4 with Table J3.1 minimum pretension Tb=28 kips for a 3/4 in A325 [33:09][33:41]; spec section J3.2 for bolt strength [49:07]; shear-yield equation J4-3 and shear-rupture equation J4-4 [21:20][22:20]; effective hole-diameter rule per section B4.3b [22:20]; web-local-yielding equation J10-2 [25:29]; weld shortcut equation 8-2 with the 1.5 directional increase [73:02]; minimum fillet from Table J2.4 (3/16 in) [73:32]; Manual figure 12-1 connection-classification curve and the 0.2 fixed-end-moment FR threshold [42:27]; AISC Design Guide 16 (wind and low seismic) and Design Guide 4 (higher seismic, used for the column-side flange-bending yield-line check) [36:48][76:06]; the Kennedy split-T model for end plates [05:38][49:07]; interaction equation 9-1 (moment-axial-shear) raised speculatively in Q&A [91:39].
### Technical Details
Thick-plate behavior is confirmed when flange thickness reaches t-NP, derived by setting Mu = phi*Mp of the flange where Z = p*t^2/4 and Fu (not Fy) is used per the 14th edition calibration [12:26][13:30]. Key prying dimensions are b (stem face to bolt center), b' = b - db/2, a, a', and the tributary flange length p capped by the 1.75-to-1 load spread [08:44][10:21]. End-plate flexural strength uses yield-line analysis: the geometric yield-line parameter Y and yield-line location s are tabulated in Design Guide 16 (s is the same in every configuration) so the designer avoids the calculus minimization [44:30][59:26]. Three bolt behaviors exist: thick (Q=0, B=F), intermediate (B=F+Q), and thin (B=F+Qmax with four plastic hinges) [49:38][50:39]. The flush-plate 1.25 gamma factor (1/0.8) artificially raises usable plate strength so the connection classifies as FR; extended plates use gamma=1.0 [43:28][64:10].
### Fabrication Notes
The end plate is shop-welded transverse to the beam, then field-bolted to the column [35:14]. Weld design caps the beam-flange-to-end-plate weld at the larger of demand or 60 percent of flange strength to avoid an undersized weld in a high-stress region [60:29]. Web welds split into zone 1 (max of horizontal web stress or 60 percent of web strength) and zone 2 (sized for end shear) [61:32]. The worked example resolved to a quarter-inch double-sided fillet at the flange and 3/16 in double-sided fillets full-height on the web [73:32][75:36]. The recommendation is no weld access hole with CJP welds, plate width capped at flange width plus 1 in, and minimum bolt pitch of db plus 1/2 in (small bolts) or db plus 3/4 in (larger) to fit the tightening tool [64:42][65:15].
### Erection Notes
This webinar is design-focused and does not cover crane, rigging, sequencing, or field bracing procedures. The only erection-relevant point is that the end plate arrives shop-welded and is field-bolted to the column, and the design assumes compression-side bolts carry the full vertical shear (confirmed correct in the polling question, with friction at the joint cited as added margin) [77:38][78:44].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Lab failures at Virginia Tech showed thin end plates and fin plates bending into fulcrums so bolts failed in combined tension and bending rather than straight tension, with plate deformation large enough to separate the plates by about six inches [04:05][04:35][51:42]. An MBMA test specimen mistakenly shipped with only two top bolts ruptured those bolts in straight tension with thick plates not bending [50:39]. The polling questions exposed two common misconceptions: that increasing bolt gauge or decreasing flange thickness reduces prying (both increase it), and the correct lever to reduce prying is higher specified Fu, which raises the no-prying threshold [79:47][81:18].
### Bid / Cost Implications
The thick-plate option yields a thicker plate with smaller-diameter bolts and a simpler design path; the thin-plate option gives the thinnest plate with bolts about one size larger and a much more complex calculation [55:47][58:22]. For estimating, the example showed light weld volume (a quarter-inch flange fillet and 3/16 in web fillets), so weld labor on a clean thick-plate moment connection is modest [73:32]. Choosing thick-plate trades a little more plate steel for fewer engineering hours and avoids the prying-force calculation entirely [56:18].
### Your Company Application
For Ivan takeoff, every bolted moment connection should be screened thick-plate vs thin-plate early since that drives plate thickness, bolt diameter, and weld size, and member weights must still route through aisc_validator.py rather than any hand figure quoted in the webinar. For Tekla detailing and the in-house PE stamp, capture Y and s from Design Guide 16 tables per end-plate type and enforce the gamma=1.25 flush / 1.0 extended factor plus the FR classification check at figure 12-1. For Mario shop welding, the flange weld holds at the larger of demand or 60 percent of flange strength and the two-zone web weld rule applies, all to AWS D1.1 with the manual equation 8-2 sizing; the no-access-hole-with-CJP guidance should reach the welders. For field bolting, A325 pretensioned end-plate bolts are not slip-critical and do not require faying-surface prep or the extra slip inspection, but any SC flange-plate connection (class A, mu=0.30, Tb=28 kips, J3-4) does, and Paul Guerrero should note prying-related bolt-bending failures are a real rejection mode on thin plates. No conflict with Your Company doctrine: this is conventional structural-steel moment-connection design, no PEMB language, and no supplier names beyond the generic MBMA test reference. Doctrine flag: NONE.

## Moment Connections, Part 1
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L6R9bqhxrnM | Duration: 1:34:16 | Upload: 2020-02-19 | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
This is AISC Live Webinar session 1 of 4 (Connection Design for Moment Frames and Braced Frames), taught by Dr. Brad Davis from slides originated by Dr. Thomas Murray. It covers fully restrained (FR) moment connections for wind and low-seismic frames, not high-seismic, so AISC 341 seismic detailing is largely out of scope here. The design model throughout is that the beam end moment is resolved into a flange force couple, the flanges carry the moment, and the single web plate carries only direct shear with no eccentricity [09:52][10:47]. Three connection families are taught: directly welded flange, flange-plated welded, and flange-plated bolted, followed by the six column-side limit states and a full worked example [01:58][32:48].

### Spec References
The example and slides cite, verbatim: AISC 360 Specification J10 plus Design Guide 13 as the column-side references [33:00]; flange local bending Spec J10.1, web local yielding J10.2, web local crippling J10.3, web compression buckling J10.5, transverse stiffener design J10.8, web panel-zone shear J10.6(a) [frame slide 46]; tension flange plate yielding Spec Eq. J4-1 with phi 0.9 [frame slide 18]; tension rupture and block shear Spec J4.3 and Eq. J4-5 [18:33][26:34]; compression plate yielding/buckling Spec J4.4 and Chapter E section E3 with Lc/r = 25 cutoff and KL = 0.65L [21:18][frame slide 26]; shear-lag for the flange plate Table D3.1 case 4 [15:09]; local buckling slenderness Table B4.1a case 1 (unstiffened) and case 7 (stiffened) [19:46][65:11]; reduced flexural strength at flange holes Spec F13.1 [29:36]; weld combined-strength directional rule J2.4(b) [17:13]; minimum fillet weld and base-metal check J2 pointing to J4 [66:14][68:21]; doubler-plate shear strength Chapter G section G2.1(b) with kv 5.34 [52:15][73:00]; bolt shear-transfer limit state user notes in J3.6 and 14th-edition Manual J3.10 [86:36]; AWS D1.1 Clause 4.3 for the doubler-plate weld [74:41]; and weld Design Guide DG2 section 4.3.3 plus AISC 341-2016 commentary E3.3 for doubler welding background [76:01]. The two CJP-develops-MP papers cited are by Larry Muir and Bo Dowell, a 2012 Modern Steel Construction article [92:02].

### Technical Details
The example is a two-sided directly welded flange connection: W24x103 beams (A992) at Mu = 882 kip-ft and Vu = 75 kips each side, into a W14x159 column (A992) with axial load 1200 kips above and 1335 kips below and a story shear of 90 kips [53:57]. The beam moment decomposes to a flange force of 450 kips (882 kip-ft / 23.5 in moment arm = beam depth minus flange thickness) at each of the four flange points [57:38]. Column flange local bending gave phi-Rn 398 kips, web local yielding 370 kips, web crippling 556 kips, so half-depth stiffeners are needed at the tension points and full-depth transverse stiffeners are required top and bottom [58:53][60:01]. Net stiffener forces came out 80 kips per pair (450 minus the governing column limit), and the panel-zone shear was Vu = 810 kips (450 + 450 minus 90) against a column web strength of only 259 kips after the high-axial reduction (alpha-Pr 1270 kips exceeds 0.4 Py 934 kips) [70:20][70:43].

### Fabrication Notes
The directly welded flange connection is shop-fabricated by welding the single shear plate to the column and beveling the beam flange ends with weld access holes; the CJP flange welds with backing are then made in the field downhand [04:53][05:25]. PJP welds are explicitly not recommended for directly welded flanges because filling a beveled flange from one side leaves a natural crack/stress riser at the root on the far side [82:43][16:14]. Fillet-weld sizing for flange plates uses the Manual shortcut 1.392 kips per sixteenth per inch (times 1.5 for transverse loading), and the spec J2 minimum fillet is 1/4 in, which governed the stiffener welds in the example [08:00][66:14]. Final example fabrication: two 1/2 x 6 A36 stiffener plates top and bottom with 1/4 in double-sided fillet welds, clipped 1-1/2 in at corners to clear the column fillet, plus two 3/4 in Gr.50 doubler plates one each side of the web [63:01][frame slide 79][frame slide 87].

### Erection Notes
The connection is designed to keep field welding downhand and avoid overhead welds, which is why the bottom flange plate is made wider than the beam flange so its welds run on the accessible top face, and the top plate is made narrower [11:29][84:30]. Overhead welding is defined as the welder getting under the joint and holding the electrode upward, which is undesirable, so connection geometry is chosen to avoid it [84:30]. Field sequence matters: the plate-to-column weld must be completed before the plate-to-beam welds to account for weld shrinkage [12:11]. The backing bar at the directly welded flange relaxes the beam-length erection tolerance at the flange-to-column gap [05:31]. Flange-plated bolted connections set the top flange plate 3/8 in high above tabulated beam depth to absorb beam-depth and out-of-square mill tolerances (Manual Table 1-22) [24:24].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
PJP on a directly welded flange is called out as a defect-prone choice because of the embedded root crack, and a single-sided fillet on a directly welded cantilever flange has the same problem [82:43][83:55]. Flange holes in a bolted flange-plated connection trigger reduced flexural rupture (Spec F13.1) and can prevent developing beam Mp, so when the EOR requires the connection to develop the full beam capacity a holed flange-plated detail will not pass [29:36]. The bolt shear-transfer limit state is commonly misread: the strength is the sum over all bolts of each bolt's effective (minimum-of-five) strength, not the single weakest bolt applied to all (the older conservative poison-bolt method) [86:36]. Panel-zone shear is the classic counterexample where shear, normally non-controlling, governs and gets hammered by the flange force couples [47:00].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Doubler plates and transverse stiffeners are explicitly described as expensive and undesirable, so the speaker steers design toward column sizes that avoid them [50:52]. In the worked example a moderately sized W14x159 column under a fairly ordinary 882 kip-ft moment still required both full-depth stiffeners and two 3/4 in doubler plates, which is real added shop labor and plate that an estimate must carry. The recurring fabrication driver is avoiding overhead field welds, since downhand welding is faster and cheaper, which shapes plate widths and shop-versus-field weld choices [84:30]. Where a small cantilever or stub can be shop welded, fillet welds replace field CJP welds and cut cost [06:32].

### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, the lesson is that a moment-frame bid cannot stop at beam and column tonnage from aisc_validator.py; panel-zone shear and column-side limit states routinely add stiffener plates and doubler plates that are separate priced material and weld length, and the example shows a normal-looking joint needing both. Mario's shop and welding scope maps directly: directly welded CJP flanges with backing, no PJP on flanges, 1/4 in double-sided fillets at stiffeners and doublers, and the AWS D1.1 Clause 4.3 doubler-plate weld are exactly the WPS calls he runs under his D1.1 authority, and the downhand-versus-overhead distinction drives how columns get rolled in the shop. Tekla detailing should carry the plate-to-column-before-plate-to-beam weld sequence, the corner clips to clear column fillets, and the 3/8 in high-set on bolted flange plates for tolerance. The in-house PE stamp owns the J10 limit-state checks and DG13 force-distribution model; anchor rods, joists, and ACP controls are not addressed in this session. No conflict with Your Company doctrine: this is conventional structural steel, no PEMB language, and all weights and rates still route through aisc_validator.py and bid_rates.py. Doctrine flag: NONE.
