## Erection Engineering Basics 101
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jctrXmHRfd8 | Duration: 1:00:34 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
Will Jacobs of Stanley D. Lindsay defines erection engineering as engineering tied to developing an erection sequence, in collaboration with the fabricator and erector, that keeps the structure stable under all applicable temporary loading at each stage of construction, plus effective communication of that to fabricator, erector, and GC [01:00]. The work consists of designing temporary bracing and shoring, reviewing and modifying the permanent system to carry temporary forces, and reviewing connection design forces to create alternate force paths or upgrade connections [01:30]. He stresses that the structural drawing note "the structure is stable only in its completed form" assumes the building appears fully built, while the real problem is getting from point A to point B safely [03:33]. The two recurring themes are collaboration and communication, especially listening to the ironworkers who implement the plan [02:01].
### Spec References
Cited verbatim or near-verbatim by the speaker: IBC 2018 points to AISC 360 for design, fabrication, and erection of structural steel [04:03]; AISC 360 Section M4.2, the structure shall be secured to support dead, erection, and other anticipated construction loads with temporary bracing per the Code of Standard Practice [04:33]; AISC Code of Standard Practice Section 7.10.3, the erector shall determine, furnish, and install all temporary supports [05:04]; ASCE 37 (he serves on the committee, cites the 3714 update, i.e. ASCE 37-14) as the governing standard for loads on structures during construction [06:04]; ASCE 7-10 / 7-16 for permanent wind speeds [09:08]; AISC Design Guide 10 for low-rise steel building erection and shielding [06:35]; AISC Design Guide 1 for the anchor-rod bending lever arm of 0.5 times plate thickness plus washer over two [27:02]; ASME BTH for below-the-hook lifting devices, the ASME B30 crane series, and ASME P30.1 for load-handling and critical-lift planning [06:35]; OSHA minimums of four bolts per column, no double connections, and a 300-pound load at 18 inches from the column face [08:08]. "Wind loads for petrochemical facilities" is cited for the deck shielding reduction 1 minus 0.2 times A-floor-beam over A-sub-s [19:52].
### Technical Details
Construction wind is the controlling load. The bare frame behaves like a row of separate logs, each with its own drag factor of roughly 1.8 to 2.0 for a standard beam, so cutting pressure in half and then doubling it by drag lands back near the permanent pressure [13:48]. ASCE 37 shielding is very conservative: no reduction on the first three rows and only 15 percent on the fourth and later rows [14:19]. Pressure varies with velocity squared, so a 20 to 30 percent velocity change can swing force 70 percent [11:46]. Reduction factors in ASCE 37 let a sub-six-week inland job take 0.75 of permanent speed, with the caveat that erecting during hurricane season in a hurricane-prone area forbids the reduction and demands ability to re-brace within two or three days [09:39]. The continuously monitored daily work period is commonly set near a 30 mph reported (cell-phone-app) wind, converting to roughly a 45 mph three-second-gust design [11:16]. Member axial capacity changes drastically with stage: a 35-ft W18x35 with no deck holds about 20 kips axial, about 52 kips with metal deck, and about 250 kips with a concrete slab because buckling shifts to the strong axis [35:45].
### Fabrication Notes
The cheapest fixes are made in the fab and design phase, not the field. Upsizing an anchor rod is minuscule in material cost since the labor is the same: a 3/4-inch Grade 36 rod carries about 6,800 pounds shear versus nearly 40 kips for a 1-1/4-inch Grade 55 rod, roughly six times stronger [28:32]. Connection type drives temporary capacity, so connections should be laid out anticipating temporary axial loads, ranked end-plate or moment best, then double angles, single plates (strong in tension, weaker in compression), single angles poor, and seated connections having nothing [33:40]. Feeding revised member forces to the connection designer as a simple PDF markup before connections are designed avoids costly redesign or, worse, rework after detailing and fabrication [48:06]. A swap from W18x35 to W16x36, one pound per foot heavier but about 50 percent better in axial, is a cheap fabrication-stage change [36:47].
### Erection Notes
The Code of Standard Practice leaves "determine" to the erector, so not every strip mall needs a sealed plan, but oddball framing, long-span trusses, and stability-sensitive metal buildings warrant an erection engineer [05:04]. Sequencing should start at the braced bay and move outward, which often conflicts with a GC who wants to start at one end, so engaging the GC early on sequencing prevents temporary-bracing problems [42:29]. Daily piece-count capacity, from an informal survey of erectors, runs about 30 to 35 columns and main beam lines and about 40 joists for low-rise, and about 25 columns and main girders, 35 filler beams, and four to five fabricated truss assemblies for mid-rise, with hydro cranes cutting counts 5 to 20 percent and high-profile or miss-fab work reducing counts further [44:33]. The temporary period per ASCE 37 runs from the first column until the building is clad and becomes the permanent diaphragm condition [56:22]. Cable bracing lashed to column bases is inconsistent; a stop angle resists the choke riding up the column, confirmed in pilot tests at Virginia Tech where low cable angles broke the cable while higher angles produced slip [37:17].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Undersized anchor rods are the named recurring failure: a 14x300-something base plate with an HSS14 brace on only four 3/4-inch rods worked in the final loaded condition through friction but fails when setting the column unloaded [28:02]. Cable braces pulling up and sideways bend or rupture anchor rods before grout or encasement, and the lever arm grows badly with shim packs and no grout [26:31]. A jersey-barrier deadman is deceptive: a 3,600-pound barrier pulled at 50 degrees yields only about 600 pounds of usable load because the uplift kills friction, the mechanism that collapsed the Indiana State Fair stage in August 2011 under about a 60 mph wind [30:04]. A 2011 Texas collapse drew an OSHA citation for lack of ASCE 37 planning [16:19]. Misaligned holes patched with field weld are shown as a connection-quality failure [33:10]. Inspection is itself a gray area: ASCE 37 does not speak to inspection requirements, so the firm self-inspects at key stages [54:13].
### Bid / Cost Implications
Erection-engineering scope must be set in the bidding stage, because carrying erection-engineering money when competitors do not can lose the job, so the bid package should flag whether a sealed erection plan is genuinely required [50:40]. Bids on larger jobs should include a construction wind study, described as inexpensive with strong return, since a recent study gave a 43 percent force reduction under six weeks and about 20 percent for longer periods, which flows directly into lighter bracing, connections, and temporary foundations [51:10]. Bids should also carry allowances for added connection-design load cases, extra temporary brace detailing and fabrication, and base-building modifications, the last of which can sometimes reduce cost by making erection more efficient [52:10]. Early design-assist involvement lets the erection engineer influence the permanent design and eliminate or reduce temporary bracing cost [24:59].
### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, this confirms that bracing, deadmen, shoring towers, and a construction wind study are biddable scope to be flagged at bid time, not absorbed silently, and that the construction wind case can govern over the permanent case for an open frame. The anchor-rod guidance maps directly to Your Company's anchor-rod design-and-setting workstream: upsizing to a 1-1/4-inch Grade 55 rod at the design stage is cheap insurance against cable-brace bending, and the in-house PE stamp should run the M4.2 / Code of Standard Practice 7.10.3 staged-stability check and the Design Guide 1 lever-arm check on column bases. Tekla detailing should carry temporary-condition member swaps (for example W18x35 to W16x36) and any embedded cable loops or stop angles before fabrication so Mario's shop is not adding them in the field. Paul's safety program aligns with the OSHA four-bolt and 300-pound-at-18-inch minimums and the ASCE 37 planning duty that OSHA has cited, and field bolting plus joist setting should follow a braced-bay-outward sequence coordinated with the ACP GC, with daily piece-count expectations (roughly 30-35 main members, 40 joists low-rise) feeding ACP project controls. Doctrine conflict: NONE. The conventional structural-steel framing here fits Your Company positioning, and although the speaker mentions metal-building stability, that is methodology only and no PEMB language enters our outward work.

## Fundamentals of Connection Design: Shear Connections, Part 2
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=alj4-kHZt0U | Duration: 1:33:10 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is the final session of a four-part AISC series taught by Dr. Brad Davis, covering the design of four shear (simple) connection types: single angle, single plate (shear tab), unstiffened seated, and stiffened seated [01:38]. The unifying theme is that every simple shear connection must be flexible enough to behave as a pin, which requires demonstrated rotational ductility so the small end moment that develops can be relieved rather than fracturing the connection [02:11]. Each connection is placed at the lower-right of the AISC manual beam-to-column classification curve, treating the member and connection as pinned once ductility is ensured [01:38, 02:11].

### Spec References
Sections cited by the speaker: Table J3.4 (bolt edge distance limits) [17:08, 22:12, 32:00], Table J3.2 (nominal bolt shear stress Fnv, including the embedded 0.9 end-loaded factor) [32:30, 42:53], Section J10.2 (bearing length not less than K design) [58:30, 88:52], Section J4 / Equation J4-3 (shear yielding of the angle) [62:06], Section F11 (rectangular-plate flexural buckling, used for plate buckling) [39:44, 40:16], Table J2.4 (minimum fillet weld size) [54:50], and Commentary Figure C-J4.2 for the UBS block-shear case [50:36]. Design aids named: manual Table 10-9, 10-11, 10-12, 10-8, 7-6, 7-7, 8-4, 8-10, 9-4, 15-3, and Equation 9-2 (Tmin) and Equation 9-15 (Cb) [09:26, 11:29, 24:18, 43:23, 70:25]. Bolt and weld grades cited: F3125 Grade A325N bolts and 70 ksi (E70) welds [29:26]. Manual Part 10 design procedures are noted as not code-required [89:53].

### Technical Details
Single angle connections use two distinct eccentricities, e-sub-A for angle design and e-sub-B for bolt design, equal only for a single bolt column [04:48]; the outstanding leg adds angle flexural yielding (phi Fy times t L-squared over 6) and flexural rupture through the holes (phi Fu times Z-net, phi 0.75) [07:23, 07:55]. Conventional single plate (shear tab) limits are: one bolt column, 2 to 12 bolts, A not over 3.5 in, weld at least 5/8 of plate thickness both sides, and plate or web no thicker than Table 10-9 max [16:38, 17:38]. Ductility is achieved by "plowing," keeping the plate thin enough that bolts bear-deform it [18:08]. Extended single plate connections drop those limits and add plate buckling (Section F11 with Cb floor of 1.84) and shear-flexure interaction (a von-Mises-type squared inequality, phi 1.0 shear and phi 0.9 bending) [37:40, 39:44]. The worked extended example was a half-inch by 9 by 15 in A36 plate, six 7/8 in A325N bolts in two columns, W14x43 beam to a W14x90 column, V-u 30 kips, governed near 0.932 on interaction [42:21, 53:42]. Seated connections rely on web local yielding and web local crippling to set required bearing length L-sub-B, with setback taken as 3/4 in (1/2 in nominal plus 1/4 in beam-length tolerance) [58:00, 66:18].

### Fabrication Notes
The single angle is shop-welded or shop-bolted to the supporting member so the beam simply lands and bolts to the leg parallel to the web during erection [06:21]. Shear-tab plates are shop-welded to the support with double-sided fillet welds, sized at 5/8 of plate thickness so the weld develops the plate and no explicit weld strength calc is required [13:00, 28:26]. Holes on the support side of a single angle must be standard, not slotted, so the angle cannot rotate the beam end out of bearing; beam-side holes may be standard or short slots [05:51]. For stiffened seats the stiffener-to-seat weld must match the size of the stiffener-to-column weld so the horizontal weld works with the vertical [68:54]. A 5/16 in fillet was noted as completable in one pass [54:19].

### Erection Notes
Single angle connections eliminate the double-angle double-sided shared-bolt erection problem, since there is only one angle [03:17]. Seated connections (both unstiffened and stiffened) are favored for erection safety: the beam is set on the seat and bolted down, with no double-sided bolt access issue, then a stability top angle (minimum 1/4 in) is installed to keep the beam from rolling [55:22, 64:09, 73:00]. Seated connections are specifically convenient at a column web [56:26, 64:40]. Single angle connections are not recommended for laterally unbraced beams such as in industrial framing [03:47].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The speaker flagged outdated handout slides: a deleted Table 17-1 reference for the single-angle eccentric coefficient [10:28] and a weld-eccentricity dimension that earlier slides located to the wrong point [62:37]. A conceptual error addressed in Q&A is assuming no moment on the bolts because plowing puts the rotation at the bolt line; test data over 20 to 30 years show real bolt eccentricity, so eccentric bolt shear is still checked even though it changes the result very little [83:14, 84:16]. No NDE or weld-defect rejection criteria were discussed; the failure modes covered are design limit states (flexural rupture, block shear, plate buckling, shear-flexure interaction, web punching shear), not field inspection rejections.

### Bid / Cost Implications
Connection-type selection is a cost lever: shear tabs are the simple, few-part default, but only carry low to moderate reaction, so a handful of higher-reaction beams must escalate to double angles or tees, which costs more parts and labor [13:30, 14:36]. Single angle connections trade fewer parts against possibly larger angles, bolts, or welds because bolts act in single shear [03:17]. Seated connections add a part (the top angle) but speed erection [55:52]. The manual design aids (Tables 10-8, 10-9, 9-4, 15-3, and the eccentric C tables) exist to cut engineering time, which is real estimating value when these connections repeat across a job [09:26, 67:51].

### Your Company Application
This is detailing-and-shop content. The single-angle support-side standard-hole rule and the shop-weld-the-angle-first practice are Tekla detailing constraints and shop-prep notes for Mario's crew [05:51, 06:21]. The 5/8-of-plate-thickness weld-develops-the-plate rule and the one-pass 5/16 in fillet observation tie directly to Mario's AWS D1.1 weld sizing on shear tabs and seats [28:26, 54:19]. The "plowing" ductility requirement and the plate-thickness caps are checks our in-house PE stamp owns on every simple connection, and the bolt grades here (A325N / F3125, E70 weld) match standard field bolting; confirm pretension versus snug-tight per the project spec since this webinar covers strength not RCSC installation. For Ivan's takeoff, the lesson is that shear-tab-defaulted framing with a few high-reaction beams forces heavier connection types, a quantity and labor delta worth flagging on ACP if the connection schedule shows mixed types. Conflict with Your Company doctrine: NONE. All section numbers above are quoted only as the speaker stated them; none were invented, consistent with verify-don't-generate.

## Fundamentals of Connection Design: Shear Connections, Part 1
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9OnNk3wHfQ8 | Duration: 1:35:45 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
Dr. Brad Davis teaches the design of simple (shear) beam-end connections, the most common connection type in a steel building. The governing idea is that a shear connection is designed as a pin even though a real moment-rotation curve shows some end moment [02:56]. This works because the connection is detailed for rotational ductility: the pin is placed at the most flexible side, which is back at the face of the support [03:18]. Ductility is achieved by keeping plate and angle material thin (5/8 in cap), using wide bolt gauges or widely spaced vertical welds, and never welding across the top of an angle or end plate [05:43]. The session walks the load-path / limit-state tracking method through two connection families: shear end plates and double angles (welded-bolted, bolted-bolted, bolted-welded).
### Spec References
J4.3 and Eq. J4-3 for block shear and shear yielding [15:29][36:36]; Eq. J4-4 for shear rupture / web base-metal at weld [37:48] (slide cites Spec Table J2.5 routing to J4-4) [37:48]; Table J2.4 minimum weld size [39:03]; commentary figure C-J4.2 for the U sub BS = 1.0 vs 0.5 cases [16:21]; Section F11 as supplemented by manual pages 9-9 and 9-10 for double-coped web lateral-torsional buckling [22:39]; Chapter F pattern and the 1.6 M sub Y cap on coped-web flexure [21:11][67:31]; Section J2.2b User Note for weld returns (slide 76) [64:35]; Table 8-8 and Table 8-3 (C and C1 electrode coefficients) for the eccentric C-shape weld group via instantaneous center of rotation [55:43][59:51]; manual Table 1-1 for the T and detailing properties [08:13]; manual Table 9-2 (S net) and the companion volume 2 Table 9-A (Z net) for coped sections [27:17][27:48]; manual pages 9-6 through 9-9 for single-coped flexure equations [20:00].
### Technical Details
Single-coped flexural strength follows a chapter-F slenderness pattern with lambda = h0/tw, lambda P = 0.475 sqrt(k1 E / Fy), and a modified plate-buckling coefficient k1 = max(fk, 1.61) where k depends on c/h0 and the adjustment factor f depends on c/d (slide 28) [21:19][29:30]. The worked W14x30 A992 example with a 3 in deep, 8 in wide cope gives h0 = 10.8 in, S net 8.37, Z net 15.1, lambda 40 landing between lambda P 23.4 and 2 lambda P, so inelastic buckling controls at Mn 517 kip-in, phi Mn 465 kip-in [27:00][31:14]. The eccentric C-shape weld group resolves through Table 8-8 with k = kl/l = 2.25/8.5 = 0.265, x interpolated to 0.0465, A 0.307, yielding a weld design strength of 100 kips [55:43][59:43]. The bolted-welded knife connection uses the elastic vector method: uniform vertical weld force plus a linearly varying horizontal force over the bottom 5/16 of the weld length, summed as vectors at theta zero [69:53][71:05].
### Fabrication Notes
The beam is not cut to exact length; design assumes a plus or minus 1/4 in length tolerance, and holes are dimensioned from one end so the far-end edge distance absorbs the error [08:39]. The standard fix is a 1/2 in setback to absorb the plus tolerance and subtracting 1/4 in from the design end distance to cover the minus tolerance, applied in block-shear and tensile-rupture areas [09:46][55:25]. Shear end plates are the exception: they require the beam cut to near-exact length with no plus tolerance, which is why they are uncommon in the US [33:11]. End plates need no holes in the beam, only welds [33:11]. Horizontal slots in welded-bolted double angles let one angle size fit varying web thicknesses across many connections [50:13]. Connection depth should be at least T/2 (manual recommendation, not spec) for erection stability [07:45]. Effective weld length subtracts one weld size per end that stops at the air, L minus 2w [11:20].
### Erection Notes
Stability during erection drives the T/2 minimum connection depth recommendation [07:45]. The shared-bolt problem at a double-sided column-web connection is an erection safety issue: it is resolved with an extra bolt row on one beam, a temporary or permanent erection seat, never the old "suicide connection" where an ironworker holds a beam with a spud wrench after releasing the crane [47:12][48:28]. Bolted-welded (knife) connections require the bottom flange coped so the web can be lowered, or knifed, down between angles already shop-welded to the column; cope the bottom not the top so a hung-up beam puts slack in the sling rather than increasing crane-line tension [63:31][64:58].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The presenter flags a printing error in the first printing of the 15th edition manual where a 1.84 limit read "less than or equal to" but should be "greater than or equal to," corrected in the second and third printings [25:34]. Welding across the top of an angle or end plate destroys the ductility assumption and makes it not a shear connection [65:38]. Forgetting to deduct the beam-length tolerance understates block-shear and tensile-rupture demand. Using Z net alone on a coped web can yield at service loads, which is why the 1.6 M sub Y cap exists [67:55]. No weld-profile acceptance/rejection imagery or NDE failure photos appear; this is a design-method session, not a QC inspection session.
### Bid / Cost Implications
Connection-type selection has direct cost weight. End plates save drilling holes in the beam but demand tight length tolerance [33:11]. Bolted-welded knife connections are chosen when a column flange is too thick to economically drill, so welding to the face beats drilling [64:01]. Double angles are the strong fallback used on the few high-load connections where a lighter connection type fails everywhere else [47:44]. Thick column flanges, shared-bolt resolution, and erection seats all add labor and detailing that a takeoff should anticipate. The video is a design course and states no dollar figures or schedule durations.
### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, the beam-length tolerance and 1/2 in setback rule mean coped-beam quantities and edge distances should be carried with the 1/4 in deduction baked into any block-shear check, and connection-type choice (end plate vs double angle vs knife) should be a flagged estimating input, not assumed. For Tekla detailing and the in-house PE stamp, the single- and double-coped flexural checks, the Table 8-8 eccentric weld-group method, and the F11 / pages 9-9 to 9-10 lateral-torsional buckling path are the exact limit states our connection calc package must cite, and aisc_validator.py supplies the W14x30 / 2L3x3x5/16 section properties that feed S net and Z net lookups. For Mario's shop and welding, the 5/8 in thickness cap, the no-weld-across-the-top rule, effective weld length L minus 2w, and weld returns per J2.2b User Note are AWS-adjacent shop practices worth posting at the weld stations. For Paul's safety program, the shared-bolt erection hazard and the bottom-cope knife-connection drop sequence are concrete field-bolting safety talking points that align with our no-suicide-connection posture. No conflict with Your Company doctrine: DOCTRINE_FLAGS NONE.

## Fundamentals of Connection Design: Fundamental Concepts, Part 2
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h6bMo3AweJA | Duration: 1:28:33 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
Brad Davis (University of Kentucky, AISC Committee on Manuals and Textbooks) teaches the second of four sessions, covering eccentrically loaded bolted and welded connections, directly loaded tension connections worked as a full light-bracing-connection example, and compression connections (beam bearing plates and column base plates) [01:34]. The unifying method is the load-path walkthrough: trace force from the member through each component to the support and check every applicable limit state, where the weakest limit state controls the design strength [12:23][13:26][31:34]. He repeatedly contrasts the older elastic/vector method (conservative to very conservative) against the instantaneous center of rotation (ICR) ultimate-strength method, which is more rational and is what the AISC Manual design tables actually use [02:34][76:29].

### Spec References
Verbatim citations made by the speaker: Manual Table 7-7 and Table 7-1 (eccentric bolt groups and single-bolt shear strength) [04:05][06:09]; Table 8-8 and Table 8-3 with the C1 = 1.0 weld-material coefficient (eccentric weld groups) [07:40][09:17]; Section D2 and Section J4.1 (tensile yielding and rupture) [13:26][13:58]; Table D3.1 shear lag factor U, cases 1, 2, and 4 [14:59][44:23]; Section B4.3b for the effective hole diameter and the stagger s-squared-over-4g term [20:36][21:06]; Section J4.3, equation J4-5 (block shear) [21:37][22:40]; Section J3.6 user note and 14th-edition Manual Section J3.10 user note (bolt bearing/tear-out/shear-rupture effective strength) [37:42]; Manual page 9-4 for the Whitmore section [28:25]; Section J4.4 (plate compression buckling, Lc/r limit of 25, otherwise Chapter E) [25:17][26:20]; Design Guide 29 for K effective-length values and Whitmore examples [27:22][78:08]; Section J10.2 (web local yielding) [49:34]; Section J10.3 equations J10-5a and J10-5b (web local crippling) [51:40][60:58]; Section J8 with equation J8-2 (concrete bearing/crushing) [53:12][83:50]. That is 14 distinct cited spec/Manual locations.

### Technical Details
Eccentric groups use coefficient C from the table times the single-bolt or per-16th weld strength; an eight-bolt 3/4 inch A325 bracket at 8 inch eccentricity gave C = 2.93 and 52.4 kips [05:05][06:39]. Shear lag U = 1 - xbar/L, with xbar from Table 1-7 for angles; a long-leg-back-to-back double angle gave U = 0.85, a 15 percent rupture reduction [34:38][71:08]. Net area subtracts an effective hole diameter of bolt diameter plus 1/8 inch (1/16 to standard hole, another 1/16 effective), so a 3/4 inch bolt uses 7/8 inch [33:36]. Block shear takes the minimum of shear rupture (0.6 Fu Anv) or shear yield (0.6 Fy Agv) plus tensile rupture (Ubs Fu Ant), Ubs = 1 for directly loaded connections [22:40][23:44]. The Whitmore section spreads load at 30 degrees from the connection ends to set the critical-section width [28:55]. Web local yielding uses critical length Lb + 2.5k (end) or 5k (interior) with K-design, not K-detailing, and phi = 1.0 [50:39][51:40].

### Fabrication Notes
The session is design theory and does not walk shop processes, but several inputs are direct fabrication and detailing parameters. Hole sizing is explicit: a standard hole for a 3/4 inch bolt is 13/16 inch nominal, and the effective diameter for net-area math is 7/8 inch [40:15][33:36]. Bolt stagger geometry (the s-squared-over-4g term) is a detailing decision that adds net-section strength and must be modeled when present [21:06]. The K-design versus K-detailing distinction matters because the smaller K-design decimal governs bearing-plate cantilever length and web checks, and using the larger detailing value would be unconservative [51:40][59:27]. Weld size enters as D, the number of 16ths (a 5/16 weld is D = 5), and the per-inch shortcut value of 1.392 kips per 16th per inch applies at theta = 0 [11:21][47:30].

### Erection Notes
No dedicated erection, sequencing, bracing, or rigging content appears; this webinar is connection design at the desk, not field procedure. The closest field-relevant items are the support-side limit states the speaker repeatedly flags but does not compute because the support is unknown, for example column-flange local yielding behind a gusset, which is the kind of check the erection and detailing team must close out once the support member is fixed [12:55][48:02].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The speaker names physical failure modes seen in lab specimens rather than inspection rejections: block-shear tear-out of a plate or angle along two longitudinal shear lines plus one transverse tension line [22:07][22:40], and a Whitmore-section tensile rupture at the end of a stiffener in a hanger-type test where the far plate carries almost no stress [28:55]. The worked bolt-by-bolt shear-transfer example predicts the realistic mixed failure: bolt A tears out the angle end, bolt B fails in bolt shear rupture, bolt C tears out the plate end [43:19]. A live-call correction warns to cross out the erroneous 0.85 in the second concrete-bearing term on the handout, a genuine errata catch [71:46]. The polling questions flag two common misconceptions: that Part 7 and 8 tables use the elastic method (they use ICR) and the scope of the Whitmore section [76:29][78:08].

### Bid / Cost Implications
No pricing, schedule, or estimating content is presented. The indirect cost lever is that the ICR method baked into the Manual tables recovers capacity the conservative elastic method would leave on the table, so designing eccentric bolt and weld groups off the tables yields fewer bolts or shorter welds for the same demand, which trims fabrication material and labor [76:29].

### Your Company Application
This session is the connection-design backbone for Tekla detailing and the in-house PE stamp: every limit state walked here (tensile yielding/rupture, shear lag, block shear, the J3.6 bolt-bearing/tear-out/shear-rupture effective strength, Whitmore, plate buckling, web local yielding/crippling, concrete bearing, plate bending) is what the stamping PE must show on a bracing or base-plate calc package. The 7/8 inch effective hole diameter, K-design selection, and U = 1 - xbar/L shear-lag math are concrete checks the detailer should encode so Ivan's takeoff member sizes survive connection design rather than getting upsized late. Mario's shop crew benefits from the hole-size and weld-size (D = number of 16ths) discipline; field bolting on grade-A325 double-shear joints ties to the per-bolt shear values pulled from Table 7-1. Base-plate concrete bearing (A1, A2 spread at 2:1, phi = 0.65) is the direct anchor-rod-and-baseplate workstream and a good ACP project-controls checklist item. Doctrine flags: NONE. Content is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language, no supplier names, and AISC weights still route through aisc_validator.py per Hard Rule 5.

## Fundamentals of Connection Design: Fundamental Concepts, Part 1
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=myhliC9s658 | Duration: 1:30:41 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is session one of a four-part AISC webinar by Dr. Brad Davis covering the fundamentals of bolted and welded connection design under the 2016 AISC Specification, LRFD method. It establishes the design inequality (required strength must not exceed available strength), resistance factors, steel material properties, the four connection families, beam-to-column classification, the load-path approach to identifying limit states, and the per-bolt and per-weld strength checks. The unifying method taught is to visualize force traveling from one member through the connection into the support and to check each limit state it crosses [18:16].

### Spec References
The speaker cited these verbatim: AISC 360-16 Specification for Structural Steel Buildings (Chapters B, D, J); AISC Steel Construction Manual 15th edition; RCSC Specification for Structural Joints Using High-Strength Bolts 2014 edition (Manual Part 16); AWS D1.1 (named as important but not detailed) [03:03-03:35]. Section-level: J3.6 (bolt tension and shear strength) [32:36, 47:33], Table J3.2 (nominal tensile and shear stresses Fnt/Fnv) [33:43], J3.8 (slip strength) [33:43-36:18 area, 47:33 slip], Table J3.1 (minimum bolt pretension) [38:50], Table J3.3 (hole dimensions) [30:02], J3.3 (minimum spacing) [53:12], Table J3.4 (minimum edge distance) and Table J3.5 (slot/oversize increments) [53:43-54:13], J3.10 (bearing and tear-out) [45:29], B4.3b (effective hole diameter for hole-related limit states) [43:58], J2.4 (weld rupture) [55:14], equation form J2-5 directional factor [56:46], J2.4(b) (weld-group ductility) [57:50], Table J2.4 (minimum fillet weld size) [63:31], J2.2b (maximum fillet weld size along edges) [64:33], Table J2.5 pointing to J4 and J4.2 (base-metal strength in shear) [66:37-67:08], Manual Table 7-14 (bolt thread length) [22:50], Manual Table 2-5 (material properties) [49:37]. Design Guides named: Design Guide 16 (PR moment connections) [17:46], Design Guide 17 (figure 5.2 end-loaded connection) [36:18].

### Technical Details
Resistance factors: 0.90 for ductile limit states such as tension yielding, 0.75 for non-ductile such as tension rupture, bolt shear, bearing, tear-out, and weld rupture [06:49-07:52]. Material defaults taught: plates A36 (Fy 36, Fu 58); angles now A529 Grade 50 (Fy 50, Fu 65); beams and columns A992 [07:52-08:54]. Bolt groups: A307 machine bolts (60 ksi); Group A high-strength F3125 grades A325/F1852 and A354 grade BC (120-125 ksi); Group B F3125 A490/F2280 and A354 grade BD; and a super-high-strength group F3043/F3111 not yet readily available [21:48-22:50]. Four hole types are standard, oversized, short-slotted, long-slotted, with standard as the default [30:02-31:34]. Three diameters are used: effective hole diameter (nominal + 1/16) for hole-related checks, nominal hole diameter for tear-out, and bolt diameter for bearing [43:58-45:29]. The directional weld factor (1.0 + 0.5 sin^1.5 theta) raises fillet strength up to 50 percent at theta 90 but reduces ductility [56:16-57:50]. A handy unit: a 70-ksi fillet weld at theta 0 carries 1.392 kip per sixteenth-inch leg per inch of length [61:30-62:00].

### Fabrication Notes
Slotted holes are a shop consolidation tool: horizontal slots in web angles absorb web-thickness variation across beam sizes and vertical slots in flange angles absorb beam-depth variation, so the fabricator can cut one angle pattern that fits many beams [31:34-32:36]. In AISC teaching sculptures, painted bolts are shop-installed and unpainted bolts are field-installed [11:03]. Larger bolts (over 7/8 inch) get a 1/8-inch standard-hole clearance rather than 1/16 because of bolt-and-hole tolerance problems installing big bolts [30:34]. Slip-critical faying surfaces require Class A (clean mill scale, mu 0.30) or Class B (prepared surface, mu 0.50) [25:57, 38:20]. The 5/16-inch fillet is the practical economy threshold: it lays in one pass, while 3/8 needs three passes (roughly 3x cost) and 1/2 needs about six passes (6x cost), so lengthening a weld to stay at 5/16 is preferred over thickening it [69:42-71:14].

### Erection Notes
Bearing-type connections only need snug-tight, defined per RCSC as a few impacts of an impact wrench or the full effort of an ironworker on a spud wrench, enough to bring plies into firm contact [24:56-25:27]. Slip-critical and pretensioned connections require one of four RCSC pretension methods: turn-of-nut (snug then rotate through angle theta from RCSC Table 8.2, a function of bolt length; one-third turn when length is at or under 4D), calibrated wrench (wrench calibrated on site with a Skidmore-type device, shuts off at target), direct tension indicators (DTI nubs flatten and a feeler gauge confirms the gap closes), and twist-off bolts (spline shears off at proper pretension) [26:29-30:02]. Slip-critical joints add field inspection and surface prep that bearing joints do not [25:57, 40:22].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The named failure modes are bolt shear rupture, bearing (steel piling up at the hole edge under contact pressure), and tear-out (shear planes at 0.6 Fu tearing a plate segment free), shown from lab specimens [44:29-46:00]. Tension-side failures are tension yielding, tension rupture with shear lag, and block shear [18:46-20:16]. A common detailing error in welds is undercutting the upper plate: welding too high along a plate edge removes the corner and leaves an apparent throat larger than the real effective throat, which is why max fillet size along edges thicker than 1/4 inch is held to plate thickness minus 1/16 [64:33-66:07]. A common analysis error, caught in the poll, is using the nominal hole diameter plus 1/16 for tear-out clear distance; tear-out uses the nominal hole diameter only, while the extra 1/16 applies to tension rupture, block shear, and bolt shear rupture [72:16-74:30]. RCSC discourages torque charts because the torque-to-tension relationship depends heavily on thread friction [79:08-80:11]. Slip-critical connections are warned against as a careless default because of their surface-prep and inspection cost [40:52-41:25].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Slip-critical connections are explicitly called expensive relative to bearing type because of faying-surface preparation (especially Class B), tightening procedures, and inspection, and the speaker's bottom line is to specify them only where genuinely needed rather than blanket them on drawings [40:22-41:25]. Weld cost scales with passes, not just leg size: doubling a fillet from 5/16 to 5/8 doubles strength but costs about 6x, and stepping 5/16 to 3/8 buys little strength for about 3x cost, so 5/16 is the economic sweet spot [69:42-71:14]. Twist-off and DTI hardware carry their own per-bolt cost and care requirements that a snug-tight bearing joint avoids [29:31-30:02].

### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, this validates pricing connection labor by limit-state count and bolt/weld type, and the material defaults map straight to aisc_validator.py inputs: A992 beams/columns, A36 plate, and the move to A529 Grade 50 angles (Fu 65) that Ivan should confirm is reflected in the shape data. Mario's shop crew benefits from the slot-consolidation lesson (one angle pattern across many beams) and the hard 5/16-pass economy rule, plus the undercut and minimum/maximum fillet-size limits as weld QC checks under AWS D1.1. Paul's field bolting program should standardize on snug-tight for bearing joints and reserve the four RCSC pretension methods for pretensioned or slip-critical joints, with DTI or twist-off being the simplest to inspect. For Tekla detailing, the painted-versus-unpainted shop/field convention and the three governing diameters (effective hole, nominal hole, bolt) should be wired into connection macros and hole charts. The in-house PE stamp work uses the J3 and J2 sections cited here as the citable basis for connection calcs, and the A529 angle adoption is a verify-against-Manual-Table-2-5 item before it touches a stamped drawing. For ACP project controls, flag slip-critical callouts early because they drive surface-prep and inspection cost. Doctrine conflict: NONE. This is conventional structural steel content with no PEMB language, and the A529 Grade 50 angle switch is a confirm-then-adopt note, not an override of locked rates.

## Truss Design and Construction
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KHYmUafNFMg | Duration: 1:26:59 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This webinar by Thomas Meyer of Magnusson Klemencic Associates teaches the full design workflow for what he calls a "straight over tackle" steel truss, a generally 2D long-span truss carrying floors or roofs, with decking at the top chord, a free open bottom chord plane, and a truss stability system [01:03][01:35]. The flow is design criteria, geometry, member shape selection, analysis, member design, connections, and stability, closing with a worked 90-foot span example [02:07]. The recurring theme is that long-span trusses behave differently from beam-and-girder floors: self-weight and connection-material weight are significant, serviceability and vibration often govern, and depth has an optimization sweet spot rather than a "deeper is always better" rule [02:38][11:30][72:22].
### Spec References
The speaker cites AISC Design Guide 11 (floor vibrations, with a note that a second edition has superseded the first edition shown) as the acceptance criteria source for walking and rhythmic vibration [08:18][31:15]; AISC 360 for member design checks of combined axial and bending forces [34:23][66:36]; the AISC Code of Standard Practice for camber tolerance of L/800 measured to the nearest support [07:17]; AISC Design Guide 29 for truss-end connection design analogous to vertical bracing connections [50:01]; and ISO 10137 for uncoordinated group-walking vibration criteria [29:44]. Acceleration limits cited: 1.5 percent g for airports, shopping malls, and indoor pedestrian bridges, 5 percent g for outdoor pedestrian bridges, and 2 percent g for diners adjacent to a dance floor [08:49][09:20][09:52].
### Technical Details
Span-to-depth ratios for the flat part of the weight-optimization curve are roughly 12 to 15 for roof trusses, 8 to 10 for strength-controlled floor trusses, and 6 to 8 for vibration-controlled floor trusses [14:04][14:35]. Web layouts covered are Pratt (longest diagonals in tension), Howe (longer members in compression, faster load path to support), and Warren (diagonals carry both tension and compression); the firm most often uses Warren for lighter truss weight in daily practice [16:09][76:41]. Chord force is estimated as WL squared over 8 divided by effective depth [11:30]; in the example a hand statics check gave 667 kip end shear, 16,750 kip-ft midspan moment, and an estimated 2,130 kip chord force under 1.2D plus 1.6L, against a computed 2,109 kip chord and 1,100 kip end diagonal [61:54][62:24][64:30]. Connection material runs about 15 percent of member centerline-to-centerline self-weight for a well-proportioned truss [53:05].
### Fabrication Notes
Member shapes: web members commonly double angles, HSS, or wide flanges; chords commonly wide flanges, HSS, or WT, with connection ease and architectural exposure driving the choice [22:01][23:34]. Chord-size changes at splices create filler-plate conditions; a filler thicker than 1/4 inch triggers a reduced bolt value, welding the filler to develop force, or extra bolts per AISC requirements [25:04][39:34][40:04]. Double-angle bolting rules: a leg under 6 inches allows one row, 6 inches allows two staggered rows, 8 inches allows two inline rows; stitch plates are required for compression members [44:12][44:42]. Slotting and wrapping an HSS over a thick gusset removes net section and can require an exterior patch plate, ideally welded in the shop [45:18][45:51]. The recommended posture is consistency: one bolt diameter, one N or X choice, one slip-critical or bearing choice across all connections [37:32].
### Erection Notes
Shipping governs splice location; full prefabricated trusses are rarely feasible (a 90-foot floor truss shipped whole only because the fab shop was down the road), so the engineer must talk to the contractor about truck limits and material sourcing to locate splices [19:51][20:56][21:28]. A photo shows ironworkers driving bolts into misaligned holes with sledgehammers, so field welding must be available as a fit-up fallback [38:33][39:03]. The preferred truss connection welds in the shop and bolts in the field [46:23]. Top-chord bracing assumptions must be carried through: if each floor beam braces the chord at 10-foot spacing, each of those beams must be designed for the bracing axial load [34:53][35:25]. Stability requires diaphragm trusses at the top-chord plane, bottom-chord tie beams with diagonals, attention to bracing stiffness not just strength, cantilever tips, and chord axial-load reversals [54:11][55:44][56:14].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The speaker frames most failures as design and detailing traps rather than weld or bolt rejections. Scheduling gussets by table without drawing the geometry produces connections that "work technically" but are clearly wrong, so each scheduled gusset should be drawn to verify geometry [43:11][43:42]. Eccentricity between gusset, knife plate, and HSS at an end connection becomes "RFI number one" if the centering assumption is not stated on the drawings [46:53]. Other named pitfalls: deep incoming beams clashing with a shallow W14 chord, doubler plates from net-section loss (avoid by upsizing the member), unsupported deck over a web-horizontal W14 needing shim support, and negative roof drainage or ponding from uncontrolled deflection [24:04][47:53][48:54][07:17]. No specific bolting or NDE rejection categories are named in this design-focused talk.
### Bid / Cost Implications
Truss weight is the cost driver and is non-linear with depth: past the optimization low point, longer web members add weight faster than chord savings reduce it, so over-deepening costs money [11:30][72:22]. Deeper trusses also add cladding, floor-to-floor height, and longer vertical-transport and duct runs, making the true optimum a whole-building cost conversation with contractor and architect [13:04]. Critically for estimating, drawings often go out to bid with members shown but no connection information on a delegated-connection job, so the bidder must add roughly 15 percent of centerline member weight for connection material, more when loads are high or proportions are poor [52:35][53:05][53:36]. The worked example showed flipping one tension diagonal to compression cut a chord moment from 2,200 to 1,500 kip-ft and trimmed truss weight from 58.1 to 55 tons, a real material saving from a layout change [68:47][69:47][70:18].
### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff through aisc_validator.py, the load-bearing rule is the ~15 percent connection-material add-on over centerline member weight on any delegated-connection truss bid; the validator gives clean shape weights but the estimate must carry the connection uplift, and that fraction climbs with high loads or large gussets [53:05]. Mario's shop and welding scope maps to the shop-weld, field-bolt connection the speaker favors, plus the double-angle row/stagger rules, stitch plates, and filler-plate handling at chord-size changes [44:12][46:23]. Paul's safety lens applies to the sledgehammer fit-up photo: misaligned holes driving manual force in the air is an erection hazard worth a fit-up tolerance check before the truss leaves the shop [38:33]. Tekla detailing should draw every gusset rather than schedule blind, and state the eccentricity centering assumption to kill RFI number one [43:42][46:53]. The in-house PE stamp owns the span-to-depth, vibration (Design Guide 11), camber L/800, and stability-stiffness calls. For joists, note this is custom built-up trusses, not catalog open-web joists, so it does not change Your Company joist pricing. Field bolting consistency (one diameter, N or X, slip-critical or bearing) is a shop-and-field discipline item. ACP controls: splice-location-by-shipping is a project-controls coordination point with the erector. DOCTRINE FLAGS: NONE; this is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language.

## Are You Properly Specifying Materials?
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EBE1c_R9gQ4 | Duration: 1:01:33 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
Larry Kruth (AISC VP of Engineering and Research, former VP at Douglas Steel Fabricating) teaches how to specify the correct, current ASTM material designation for each structural shape and fastener, and the preferred (usually most economical) grade [01:04][01:34]. The controlling lesson is to avoid over-specifying, which he frames as a square peg chipped to fit a round hole where every chip costs money, and under-specifying, a round peg in a square hole that leaves the design short of its required properties [06:17][07:19][07:49]. The webinar is built on Jonathan Tavares' April 2018 Modern Steel Construction article, part of a series AISC updates on a 3-year cycle because material designations change [01:34][03:10].
### Spec References
Cited verbatim: Specification Section A3 (material descriptions and ASTM designations) [08:53]; AISC Code of Standard Practice Section 6.1 (shop standard material) [09:23]; Steel Construction Manual 15th edition Tables 2-4 (shapes), 2-5 (plates and bars), 2-6 (fasteners), 14-2 (anchor rod washers) [11:28][12:29][33:34][41:18]; ASTM A6 (shape dimensions and tolerances) [05:46][21:22]; ASTM A992, A572, A529, A588, A913, A500 Grade C, A847, A1085, A1065, A53 Grade B [13:31][33:42]; ASTM F3125 with grades A325, A490, F1852, F2280 [33:34], plus F3111, F3043, F3148 (TNA), A563 nuts, F436 washers, A959 DTI [35:04][38:11]; RCSC specification Section 2.4 and Table 6.1, www.boltcouncil.org [38:11]; ASTM F1554 grades 36/55/105 with supplement S1 [39:46]; ACI 117 (anchor rod placement tolerance) [41:18]; AWS A5.36, A5.20, A5.29 filler metal [42:19]; AWS D1.1 clause 7.2.6 type B for shear studs [43:55]; ASTM A786 floor plate, A759 crane rail, A709 bridge steel [43:21][44:25]; AISC Design Guide 21 on welding by Duane Miller [42:50].
### Technical Details
W shapes are ASTM A992 (always 50 ksi, no grade suffix); A588 gives atmospheric corrosion resistance at 50 ksi yield and 70 ksi tensile but costs more; A913 serves very large shapes in grades 50, 65, and 70 [13:31][14:03][14:34]. HP shapes moved from A36 to A572 Grade 50 in 2016 [10:25][22:54]. Rectangular HSS is A500 Grade C at 50 ksi (replacing the old Grade B at 46 ksi); round HSS at A500 Grade C is 46 ksi; A1085 lets you use the true wall thickness instead of A500's 0.93 design factor, caps yield at 70 ksi, and adds a 25 ft-lb CVN at 40 degrees F [23:25][25:05][26:06]. Steel pipe is A53 Grade B at 35 ksi and is not the same as round HSS [28:41][29:11]. Plates and bars are A36 (to 8 in, dropping to 32 ksi above) or A572 Grade 50 (to 4 in) [31:27][32:31].
### Fabrication Notes
WT and ST tees are not rolled at mills; they are W and S shapes split down the middle in the fabricator's shop, so they inherit the parent shape's material spec [22:23]. A913 grades 50 and 65 do not require weld preheat, a real shop saving since preheating a very heavy section in cold weather (around 30 to 32 degrees F) can take up to 24 hours to reach welding temperature; grade 70 still needs preheat [16:37][17:07]. Over-specifying drives shop cost: a C12x20.7 will work as a stair stringer but the MC12x14.3 (with its 2-1/8 in flange that lets a handrail post weld flat without crimping) buys less material for the same job [19:46][20:18]. A53 pipe carries an added hydrostatic test cost that a structural round HSS avoids [30:53].
### Erection Notes
Anchor rod field issues dominate the erection content. Hole diameters in Manual Table 14-2 are oversized and coordinated with ACI 117 placement tolerances, and washers are sized to cover the hole and thick enough to develop the required strength; washers may be square or round [41:18][41:49]. Kruth stresses specifying F1554 Grade 55 with supplement S1 (weldable) so the field crew can weld a threaded extension or tie to the base plate when a rod is set too low or out of projection [40:48][57:56]. Grade 105 is high strength but never weldable, so a low-set Grade 105 rod cannot be field-corrected by welding [40:48][58:59].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The recurring error is specifying outdated designations: A500 Grade B instead of Grade C, A36 HP shapes, or A992 Grade 50 (the grade suffix is wrong) [13:31][23:25]. Over-specifying (Charpy V-notch on all material, 70 ksi where 50 works, atmospheric corrosion steel where not needed) passes inspection but wastes money [06:48]. Confusing steel pipe (A53 Grade B, 35 ksi) with round HSS (A500 Grade C, 46 ksi) misstates strength [29:11]. Specifying F1554 Grade 55 without S1, or assuming Grade 105 can be welded, sets up a field failure when a rod needs correction [57:56][58:59].
### Bid / Cost Implications
Correct specification is a direct cost lever: A992 is cheaper than A913, A588 carries a premium over A992, A1085 carries a premium over A500, and the F3125 super-high-strength bolts (F3111, F3043) are unavailable in the US [16:06][26:06][31:59][35:04]. Kruth closes that proper specification eliminates RFIs and the substitution questions ("can I use this instead?") that consume estimator and PM time [48:05]. The 16th edition Manual rebases all connection-material tables from 36 ksi to 50 ksi, so connection takeoffs priced off the 15th edition assume the wrong default grade [45:29][46:00].
### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, lock the current designations into aisc_validator.py lookups: W as A992, HP and connection material default to A572 Grade 50 (16th edition basis), rectangular HSS as A500 Grade C, and never carry A992 Grade 50 as a string. On anchor rods, our design-set-and-tolerance workstream should standardize F1554 Grade 55 S1 weldable and flag any Grade 105 callout as field-uncorrectable, with washer holes per Manual Table 14-2 and ACI 117. Mario's welding lead can claim the A913 grade 50/65 no-preheat saving on heavy sections and should treat shear studs under AWS D1.1 clause 7.2.6 type B, with filler at 70 ksi (A5.20/A5.29/A5.36); Paul's safety scope is not touched here. The over-specify warning supports flagging client general notes that demand Charpy or 70 ksi where 50 ksi works, a candidate RFI on ACP. Doctrine conflict: NONE. ArcelorMittal, Nucor Yamato, Gerdau, and Steel Dynamics are named by the AISC speaker as A913 rolling sources [15:35] and are recorded here as evidence only, not for client output.

## What Your Fabricator Wishes You Knew About HSS
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MU7Hpo8sSb0 | Duration: 56:13 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
Kim Olson of Force Consulting, technical consultant to the Steel Tube Institute, presents fabricator feedback gathered from five AISC-certified shops and SimCorp on why HSS gets a reputation for being expensive. The thesis is that HSS material is often economical (HSS columns run roughly pound-for-pound equal to wide flange, and the lack of a weak axis gives more efficient column use), but the savings get thrown out the window through poorly considered connection details and standard details copied from set to set [03:00, 04:54]. The recurring lesson is design the member with its connection and tube wall tolerances in mind, because the local wall strength of a flexible HSS at the joint can control the connection capacity, unlike a wide flange support [48:00, frame_0021].

### Spec References
The speaker cites these by name. ASTM A500 (current structural tube spec, permissible-variation tolerance tables) and its 0.93 design wall factor tied to AISC B4.1 [49:41]. ASTM A1085 (newer spec replacing A500, tighter wall tolerance, single yield Fy 50 to 70 ksi, removes the 0.93 factor, CVN 25 ft-lbs at 40 F) [49:22, frame_0022]. ASTM A847 appears on the tolerance-table slide alongside A500/A1085 [frame_0019]. ASTM A53 (coated round pipe, advised against in favor of A500) [39:39]. AISC 360 Chapter K (HSS connection checks behind the STI HSS Connex tool) and AISC 360 reduced bearing values for pin-type bolted connections [48:37, 32:00]. AWS D1.1 limited effective throat for flare-bevel groove welds, and the 6G welder certification for tube-to-tube CJP without backing [18:33, 28:12]. AISC Code of Standard Practice Section 10 governs Architecturally Exposed Structural Steel, with Section 10.2.8 stating HSS seam welds are acceptable as produced [37:00, 38:43]. Slide footer cites the HSS Design Guide: Section Properties and Design Information, and Packer and Henderson Figure 3.28 for overlap detailing [frame_0019, frame_0011]. Bolts shown on details are A325-N [frame_0004, frame_0006].

### Technical Details
Four wide-flange-beam-to-HSS-column shear connections were ranked least to most expensive: shear tab (cheapest), WT, double angle, then through plate (about four times the cost of a single plate) [06:46, 08:48]. Four moment connections of similar capacity were compared: PJP weld to the face (most economical, needs 5/8 inch wall), CJP weld, through plate, and cutout/wrap plate; the through and cutout options allow a thinner wall near 3/8 inch [12:55, frame_0006]. For trusses the matched connection that architects prefer is harder and costlier than a stepped connection where branch members land on the tube flat, defined as the width minus four times the wall thickness [17:01]. Round HSS in trusses can roughly triple connection cost versus rectangular [24:10]. Larger and thicker tubes carry bigger corner bend radii, and radius varies producer to producer, which matters when welding two tubes end to end [29:42].

### Fabrication Notes
A500 outside-flat tolerance is 0.020 in up to 2.5 in, scaling to 0.01 times the large flat dimension above 5.5 in; the slide gives an H/B ratio table for square and rectangular tube [42:54, frame_0019]. Worked example: an HSS 12x4 can vary about 0.18 in across the 4 in face and 0.12 in across the 12 in face, so two tubes can stack a quarter inch of slop at an end-plate joint [43:25]. Round tube out-of-round tolerance is 0.75 percent of OD over 2 in; straightness is 1/8 in per 5 ft [45:12, 45:51]. A tube-to-tube fillet weld is about two hours of fit-up; the same joint as a CJP is one to one-and-a-half days plus inspection [29:01]. Push fillet welds up to about 1/2 in before stepping to PJP, then CJP only if required [27:46]. Laser/profile cutters and robotic welders (common in Japan for round HSS columns and moment frames) are lowering tube fabrication cost [25:53, 26:41]. Specify removal of the inside flash weld and the seam-weld orientation explicitly, since neither is a default [38:43].

### Erection Notes
Erection content is light. HSS gives tighter dimensional control and resists twisting during handling and erection, which is why it suits AESS [38:03]. Double-angle shear connections may need the beam double-coped for erectability [07:58]. Temporary bolted erection aids are normal for field-welded AESS and can be removed; the Japanese robotic system welds stub beam/stub column assemblies in the shop, flies them out, and field-connects an infill beam between columns [26:41, 41:03]. A questioner noted HSS connections lend themselves to shop welding then field bolting because of limited access to the tube interior; the presenter agreed much shown work can move to field welds [52:01].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Through-plate connections passed from set to set as a default detail are the headline error, including a case where an all-around weld symbol forced welding the through plate inside the tube, so the shop chopped off the column top and rewelded it, and a crucifix two-direction through plate that required cutting the column in half [09:46, 10:42, 11:00]. Sizing welds to develop full member yield strength rather than the actual applied load is a common overdesign that drives cost [22:00]. Specifying tube-to-tube CJP welds where fabricators report the inspection often is not done or is done improperly [28:39]. Putting all welds ground smooth on AESS drawings is called out as a needless cost; the Code of Standard Practice only asks for a reasonably smooth and uniform weld [41:11]. Overlapped truss joints detailed per the unacceptable case in Packer Figure 3.28 (missing the hidden weld plate at the through member) lose strength [frame_0011].

### Bid / Cost Implications
A single through plate adds a full extra hour of shop time per connection; on a frame with forty or fifty of them that compounds fast, and the speaker notes bumping a 3/16 in wall to 1/4 in to avoid a through plate is often cheaper overall [10:00, 09:27]. CJP and through-plate moment joints are the two priciest options once material, fit-up, and inspection are included; the tube-to-tube CJP swing from two hours to over a day per joint is the clearest schedule hit [16:01, 29:01]. Round HSS roughly triples truss connection cost, though cost per pound for round versus rectangle is the same for equal A500 sections, so an efficient round can still win on total price [24:10, 53:51]. AESS under Code Section 10 carries a real premium and should be specified only where the element is genuinely close to view [37:00].

### Your Company Application
Ivan's takeoff and estimating should flag through-plate, tube-to-tube CJP, and AESS scope as cost drivers and price the shop-hour deltas this video quantifies (one extra hour per through plate, two hours versus a day-plus for fillet versus CJP tube-to-tube); aisc_validator.py covers the member shape, but connection labor is the swing. Mario's shop and welding lead role maps directly: prefer fillet then PJP over CJP, watch weld symbols so an all-around mark does not force an interior weld, and account for producer-to-producer corner radius when welding tubes end to end; the 6G certification note (AWS D1.1) is a welder-qualification check for any field CJP. Tekla detailing should default to shear tab and stepped truss joints, reserving through plates for genuine drag/axial-transfer cases, and should fix HSS seam orientation per Code 10.2.8 on AESS. The in-house PE stamp should size welds to the applied load not full member yield, and use the A1085 thicker-wall, single-50-ksi-yield path to dodge the 0.93 factor when capacity is tight. Field bolting through tubes needs longer-than-stock or hollow bolts and the AISC 360 reduced pin-type bearing values. No conflict with Your Company doctrine: this is methodology, conventional structural steel, no PEMB language, no supplier names harvested, and all spec numbers are speaker- or slide-stated. DOCTRINE_FLAGS: NONE.

## AISC Research:  Seismic Evaluation and Retrofit of Concentrically Braced Frames
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JJR5GX3SU4M | Duration: 1:24:35 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
Charles Roeder and Dawn Lehman present roughly 15 years of NSF and AISC funded research on the seismic behavior, evaluation, and retrofit of concentrically braced frames, contrasting modern special concentrically braced frames (SCBF) against the non-ductile braced frames (termed NCBF) built before 1988 [00:00, 07:45]. The controlling principle is capacity-based design: connections, beams, and columns are designed for the expected capacity the brace will actually deliver in an earthquake, not the force the brace was designed for [06:14, 09:17]. The desired failure is a ductile brace fracture after large cyclic deformation, and the design goal is to develop multiple "links" of yielding (a chain analogy) so secondary yield mechanisms add deformation capacity before the brace fractures [13:23, 16:30].

### Spec References
Speakers cited AISC 341 seismic provisions for SCBF and OCBF, the R=3 provision, ASCE 41 (existing steel evaluation, the current standard being replaced), the proposed AISC 342 standard (named repeatedly, with chapters C for component evaluation, D/E for modeling) [42:42, 49:24], ASCE 7-16 spectra and the 1979 UBC for comparison [52:35], the Whitmore section method and the recommended 3-4-5 (37 degree) gusset spread angle versus the traditional 30 degree [18:31, 19:01], the 2t linear gusset clearance model versus the elliptical (8t) clearance model [17:30, 20:02], and "demand-critical welds" [10:47, 27:10]. Block shear was noted as a relaxed criterion not yet approved by AISC [19:31, 79:05]. No AISC 360 chapter, table number, or Design Guide number was stated.

### Technical Details
A brace in compression buckles, forms a mid-length plastic hinge, and loses compressive capacity over cycles as it is repeatedly straightened, so braces are matched in tension-compression pairs [03:38, 05:10]. Three deficiency categories drive retrofit: cross-sectionally slender braces (high b/t, the most severe, common in pre-1988 frames) [50:58, 53:34], undersized non-demand-critical welds (brace-to-gusset and the interface welds between gusset, beam, and column) with demand-capacity ratios greater than 1 [37:31, 56:18], and weak Chevron beams and columns [63:36]. The balanced design procedure designs the brace-to-gusset weld for the brace tensile capacity and the gusset-to-frame weld for the gusset plate capacity, uses the elliptical clearance for a thinner more compact gusset, and deliberately permits gusset yielding, bolt-hole elongation, and beam yielding as secondary mechanisms [17:00, 66:13, 78:33]. The proposed AISC 342 models the gusset as a rotational spring with a rigid end zone over the full column-side gusset length and about 3/4 of the beam-side length [47:52, 48:22].

### Fabrication Notes
The headline retrofit is filling a slender hollow HSS brace with concrete (pea gravel mix so aggregate is not too large), with the concrete deliberately stopped short of the gusset connection so it does not stiffen the end and make the brace stronger rather than more ductile [25:35, 77:33]. A form is set inside the brace to hold the gap from the gusset, then concrete is poured through a hole at the far end [77:33, 78:03]. Weld overlays add metal to undersized welds to bring them to demand-critical size and behaved well in testing [27:10, 37:31]. For thin beam webs at the connection, a cover plate is recommended so the web reaches about 75 to 80 percent of the gusset plate thickness [72:23, 74:58]. The example brace named for retrofit economy was an HSS 8x8x3/8 [70:17].

### Erection Notes
This is a research and retrofit webinar, not an erection-sequencing talk, so field crane, rigging, and sequencing procedures were not covered. The closest erection-relevant guidance is the gusset clearance detail that physically allows the brace to buckle out of plane during the earthquake, and the note that the lateral system is often not continuous vertically and column splices are a concern in older buildings [18:00, 68:46]. No specific bracing or shoring sequence for new erection was given.

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Pre-1988 frames almost universally used overly slender braces, Chevron configurations sized only for design loads (one fifth to one tenth of current requirements), and welds that were undersized and not tough (not demand-critical) [10:17, 30:16]. Double shear plates joining web and gusset separately work against each other and perform worse than a single continuous shear plate [27:40, 30:48]. Failure of the vertical shear plate connecting gusset and beam to column is a severe problem because beam and column then separate [27:40]. Applying the 2t linear clearance to a rectangular plate produces huge oversized gusset plates and poor performance [80:36, 81:06]. Over-conservatism is itself an error: an oversized gusset or beam reduces inelastic deformation capacity, so members should be sized to what they need, not bigger [21:33, 22:34].

### Bid / Cost Implications
The research repeatedly frames retrofit choices as cost decisions. Filling a brace with concrete is called the more economical option versus replacing the brace, and was the correct answer to the assessment question on the HSS 8x8x3/8 [50:58, 70:17]. A weak beam (DCR up to about 2.5) does not change collapse probability, so replacing all the beams in a building is unnecessary cost, a stated money saver [64:40, 65:43, 67:13]. Properly retrofitting brace, weld, and gusset yields the same collapse probability as a code SCBF, with a 2475-year collapse probability between 5 and 20 percent [67:44, 68:14]. Single continuous shear plates and existing welds can often be kept and overlaid rather than removed and replaced [78:33].

### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, this reinforces that brace and gusset weld sizing keys off expected brace capacity, not design force, so any SCBF/braced-frame bid should price gusset welds and demand-critical weld material against the brace tensile capacity rather than the analysis load. For Mario's shop and welding crew, the demand-critical weld concept, weld overlays, and the brace-to-gusset versus gusset-to-frame weld distinction map directly to AWS D1.1 procedure and any seismic supplemental requirements, and the concrete-fill-with-gap detail is a specific fabrication step (set internal form, pea gravel mix, stop short of the gusset) worth a shop note. For Tekla detailing and the in-house PE stamp, the elliptical clearance and 3-4-5 (37 degree) Whitmore angle produce more compact gusset plates than the legacy 2t/30 degree rules and should be the modeled default on seismic braced-frame work. The b/t slenderness and bolt-hole-elongation points connect to aisc_validator member checks and field bolting. Doctrine flag: NONE. This is a seismic high-region (Seattle/West Coast) research talk; Houston is low seismic, so treat the methodology as reference for any seismic-region or retrofit bid rather than standard Gulf Coast practice, and keep the no-PEMB conventional-steel positioning intact since all of this is conventional structural braced-frame work.

## Concrete Filled HSS
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1fzqBwZKLJQ | Duration: 1:02:43 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
Jason McCormick (University of Michigan) teaches the design of concrete filled hollow structural sections (CFTs) governed by AISC 360 Chapter I, treating the member as a composite of a steel HSS shell and an internal concrete core that develop composite action [01:02]. The webinar covers section classification, four analysis methods, and the design requirements for axial tension, axial compression, shear, flexure, and combined compression-plus-flexure, then closes with research on lightweight foam fill as a seismic alternative to concrete [01:32]. The central theme is that filling an HSS shifts the local-buckling classification favorably (more sections become compact) and lets the concrete carry compression, giving smaller, cheaper steel sections with added stiffness, ductility, and fire resistance [05:04].

### Spec References
The cited references are AISC 360 Chapter I (the governing CFT chapter, named repeatedly), Chapter G for HSS shear (the 0.6 Fy Aw yield/buckling approach) [37:23], Chapter H interaction equations for combined axial-plus-flexure [39:59], Chapter C second-order analysis and Appendix 7 amplified first-order / direct analysis method [40:30], AISC Design Guide 6 for the interaction approach (noted as based on concrete-encased, not filled, and an earlier spec) [39:59], and ACI 318 for the reinforced-concrete shear contribution [38:26]. Material standards named: ASTM A500 Grade B and C, and ASTM A1085 Grade A [07:08]. Manual and document tables cited verbatim: Table 5-4 (HSS tension capacity) [21:28], Table 6-4 (rectangular/square compression-flexure interaction) and Table 6-5 (round) [33:47][34:18], and the AISC Design Examples Volume 15 worked CFT designs [30:43]. Steel Tube Institute design manuals and a forthcoming HSS concrete-fill design guide (Zhao, Packer, Wang, McCormick) were noted as resources, not requirements [56:48].

### Technical Details
Strength material caps: HSS yield used in strength calcs is limited to 75 ksi, rebar to 80 ksi [07:08][07:40]. Normal-weight concrete is 3 to 10 ksi, lightweight 3 to 6 ksi, the 10 ksi ceiling reflecting limited research and a behavior change above it [09:12]. Sections classify as compact, non-compact, or slender by the lowest element slenderness; the compact/non-compact limit for rectangular CFT is 2.26 sqrt(E/Fy) versus 1.40 sqrt(E/Fy) for bare HSS, and round goes from 0.11 to 0.15 E/Fy [12:14][12:45]. Four analysis methods: plastic stress distribution (compact, used for the Manual composite tables), strain compatibility (non-compact/slender, max concrete compressive strain 0.003) [40:55], elastic stress distribution, and effective stress-strain [16:54]. Concrete compressive stress is taken at 0.85 f'c for rectangular and 0.95 f'c for round (hoop confinement) at the plastic level, dropping to 0.70 f'c for non-compact and slender sections where the wall cannot confine the dilating concrete [17:54][22:31][26:04]. Phi for the composite member is 0.75 axial and 0.90 flexure, versus 0.90 for a bare HSS, which can make a bare HSS calc out higher than the filled one [28:37][30:12]. A1085 permits the full nominal wall thickness; A500 must use 0.93 times nominal because of the +/-10 percent tolerance [08:42].

### Fabrication Notes
The HSS shell acts as its own form, eliminating formwork [05:04]. Mills now produce dual-grade B/C HSS, so specifying Grade C captures the higher yield you are likely already getting [08:11]. When filling from the top, do not let concrete free-fall more than three to five feet to avoid segregation and to avoid damaging a thin HSS wall on impact; pumping from the bottom is the alternative but a cap plate then needs vent holes [50:40][51:10]. If internal rebar is used, the mix design and bar spacing must allow full placement, and self-consolidating concrete is recommended to fill voids around reinforcement [51:40][52:11]. Detail the top of the column for a shrinkage void; shrinkage can leave the concrete short of any cap plate so a load assumed to bear on concrete may actually land on the tube [06:07][52:11].

### Erection Notes
The webinar is design-focused and gives little field-erection sequencing. The erection-adjacent content is load introduction: the external force can be applied to the HSS only, the concrete only, or both, and the transfer must be detailed accordingly with attention to shrinkage [47:38][48:08]. Load transfer uses one mechanism only (no superposition): direct bearing via a bearing plate, shear connection via steel headed studs or steel channel anchors, or direct bond [49:39]. The load introduction length is the connection length (for example a shear-tab length) plus 2B or 2D, extendable only in the direction of the applied load [50:10][50:40]. A load may not be applied directly to a slender HSS wall because premature local buckling would prevent transfer into the concrete [49:08].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Named pitfalls: letting concrete fall more than three to five feet causing segregation or wall damage [51:10]; ignoring shrinkage so an assumed concrete bearing actually loads the tube [06:07][48:08]; rebar interfering with through-plate or other connections in a reinforced CFT [06:37][52:11]; and forgetting net-section fracture and block shear at tension connection regions, which Chapter I does not cover [20:57]. On the calculation side: superimposing shear strengths of the steel and the reinforced concrete is not allowed (take the larger of HSS-alone, concrete-alone, or HSS-plus-rebar) [37:23][39:28]; superimposing load-transfer mechanisms is not allowed [49:39]; and in the piecewise interaction the D-point can drop below the nominal curve and become unconservative, so the simplified C-to-B straight line is the safe fix [44:36][45:06]. The simplified rectangular concrete-area method (ignoring rounded corners) always reads slightly high, so re-run with corners when capacity is close [25:34].

### Bid / Cost Implications
The economic case for CFT is reduced steel: filling moves most HSS into the compact category, so smaller, thinner shells reach full capacity, cutting steel cost [05:35]. Eliminated formwork and reduced external fire protection are direct cost savings [05:04][05:35]. The counterweight is that the composite phi of 0.75 (axial) can erase the concrete benefit on lightly governed members, so a section may not be worth filling if the bare HSS already works [30:12][30:43]. Estimating must price the concrete-fill operation, mix design, and trade coordination as added scope, and reserve the more rigorous calc effort (corner-accurate areas, piecewise interaction) for members near their limit [06:37][25:34][45:38].

### Your Company Application
For Ivan, CFT is a takeoff item with two material streams to count: the A500 Grade C or A1085 HSS tonnage through aisc_validator.py plus a concrete fill volume and any internal rebar, with the 0.93 wall-thickness factor applied to A500 sizes per [08:42]; flag that filled members carry added concrete-pour and coordination scope so the bid is not steel-only. For the in-house PE stamp, the design path is AISC 360 Chapter I with the 0.85/0.95/0.70 f'c stress levels and the 0.75 axial / 0.90 flexure phi factors, and the Chapter H or Table 6-4/6-5 piecewise interaction; verify the bare-HSS-can-govern case at [30:12] before claiming a fill benefit. For Mario's shop, the controlling fabrication rules are the three-to-five-foot free-fall limit, cap-plate vent holes when bottom-pumping, and SCC where rebar crowds the section [50:40][51:40]; load-transfer detailing (bearing plate, headed studs, or channel anchors over the 2B/2D introduction length) ties directly to our connection and anchor work [49:39]. For Paul, the relevant safety item is controlled concrete placement and crane/pump positioning during fill, not addressed in detail here. Tekla detailing must carry the fill, vent holes, and the studs/anchors and bearing plates in the connection model. Doctrine flags: NONE. This is conventional structural steel content (CFT columns and beams) with no PEMB language, and it does not touch BID_RATES or any locked rate.
