## The Manufacturing of Structural Steel Shapes
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=COxc2Qja5m8 | Duration: 1:36:46 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
This is Session 2 of the AISC Night School series "Steel Construction from the Mill to Topping Out," presented by two plant metallurgists from a Blytheville, Arkansas structural mill [00:00]. It covers how hot-rolled wide-flange shapes are actually made: scrap melting in the electric arc furnace, ladle metallurgy, continuous casting of beam blanks, reheating, and rolling, with the controlling theme that producing structural steel to ASTM grade is a controlled and predictable process where the producer "knows what the test results are going to be when the scrap is purchased" [86:49]. The mechanical and chemical properties (yield, tensile, Charpy toughness, weldability) are set by chemistry plus thermomechanical control rolling, not by fabrication. For a fabricator the value is understanding what a mill test report (MTR) certifies and why the numbers come out the way they do.

### Spec References
Cited verbatim by speakers or shown on slides: ASTM A992 (typical wide-flange grade), ASTM A572 Grade 50, ASTM A588 / A588B (weathering), ASTM A36, ASTM A913 (quench-and-self-tempered, grades 50/65/70), ASTM A500 (HSS grade B/C, raised in Q&A), ASTM A690 (a marine/corrosion grade, named at [08:52]), and ASTM A6 governing tensile coupon/test geometry [01:17]. Charpy V-notch is governed by the ASTM A673 family (CVN supplementary toughness; specimen and machining requirements discussed [01:23] though the A673 number was not spoken). AWS D1.1 and D1M are named only as committees the presenter sits on [01:34]. No AISC 360 section, no AISC 341 seismic section, no RCSC clause, and no AISC Design Guide number was cited; this is a materials-production talk, not a connection-design talk. Slide 18 carries the full chemistry/mechanical table reproduced below.

### Technical Details
Slide 18 (frame captured) gives the controlling spec limits per grade. A992: carbon 0.23% max, manganese 0.50-1.60%, max carbon equivalent 0.45 (0.47 for >2 in. flange thickness), yield 50-65 ksi, tensile 65 ksi min, yield/tensile ratio 0.85 max, elongation 18% in 8 in. A572-50: carbon 0.23 max, yield 50 ksi min, tensile 65 ksi min, elongation 18%. A588B: yield 50 ksi min, tensile 70 ksi min, corrosion index 6.0 min, elongation 18%. A36: carbon 0.26 max, yield 36 ksi min, tensile 58-80 ksi, elongation 20% [09:31 to 14:34]. Strength is pulled from microalloy additions (vanadium, columbium/niobium at roughly 0.15/0.10/0.05% max) rather than carbon so the steel keeps good Charpy toughness and weldability [10:21]. The A992 max carbon equivalent and 0.85 yield/tensile cap exist for seismic ductility, ensuring enough energy absorbed before fracture [14:17]. A913 reaches grade-65/70 properties through in-line quench-and-self-temper rather than added alloy, so a grade-65 A913 keeps the weldability of A992 grade 50 [14:46 to 16:30]. Toughness is improved by lowering finishing/control-rolling temperature (1680 F cited as a low common figure) and driving sulfur down, at the cost of mill risk and broken rolls [01:25, 93:00].

### Fabrication Notes
This video is about mill production, not shop fabrication, so it offers no cutting, fit-up, drilling, or shop QC procedure. The fabrication-adjacent content is reading the MTR the mill ships with the steel: the heat number, chemistry, carbon equivalent, yield, tensile, elongation, and any supplementary Charpy results are the certification the fabricator relies on for grade and weldability [09:31]. Weldability is governed by carbon equivalent (A913 sets 0.38/0.43/0.45 by grade as a spec limit), and a lower carbon equivalent eases shop welding [15:44]. Tensile coupons are cut full-thickness to ASTM A6 geometry with a 2 in. gauge coupon, weld heat-affected zones removed before testing [01:17].

### Erection Notes
No erection, field-sequencing, bracing, crane, or rigging content. The series title references "topping out" but this session ends at the rolling mill and the test lab. One frame shows a mill-floor column on an anchored base under a press, but it is test-equipment foundation, not a structural erection detail.

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Framed as material defects rather than shop or field rejections. Excess residual elements (copper, nickel, chromium, tin, antimony) make steel brittle and must be minimized through scrap-recipe control [12:17, 12:57]. Excess sulfur and phosphorus degrade properties and Charpy performance, so A992 holds them tighter (0.035 P max, 0.045 S max on slide 18) [10:52]. A992 and A588 can never be dual-certified because A992 caps chromium at 0.35% while A588 needs a chromium minimum for weathering, an incompatibility that would show as an out-of-range MTR [91:47]. Heat treating then welding will change the heat-treated strength, a caution raised in Q&A [89:04].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Yield (in the metallurgical sense of usable tonnage out per ton melted) is repeatedly tied to cost: oxidizing iron in the furnace is yield loss, fewer beam blanks per crop is yield loss, and better yield is improved cost [31:23, 11:31, 71:49]. Achieving tight low-temperature Charpy values (CVN at -20 F or -50 F for Arctic work) is expensive because it forces very low sulfur and low rolling temperatures that strain rolls, so toughness supplements carry real cost and producers may decline the toughest charts [92:15]. The practical bid takeaway is that specifying CVN supplements or premium grades (A913, A588 weathering) above plain A992/A572-50 raises material cost and can affect availability.

### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff and aisc_validator.py, this confirms A992 as the default wide-flange grade and A572-50 as the standard for plates and angles, with A588 only where weathering is specified, which is exactly the grade logic the validator should default to; it does not change any AISC weight, since weight is geometry not metallurgy. For Mario's AWS D1.1 welding, the carbon-equivalent and weldability framing is the link: a low-carbon-equivalent A992 or A913 welds without trouble, and the MTR is where to confirm chemistry before setting preheat. For the in-house PE stamp and any seismic job, the A992 0.85 yield/tensile cap and capped carbon equivalent are the ductility basis to cite. When a spec calls Charpy supplements or A588 weathering, flag the cost and lead-time premium to estimating rather than pricing it as plain A992. No conflict with Your Company doctrine: this is conventional structural steel material science, no PEMB language, no supplier names harvested (the presenting mill is named in the video but not carried here as a sourcing reference). DOCTRINE FLAGS: NONE.

## Let's Talk Seismic -- In Language We Can All Understand
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zoHqvcN7osA | Duration: 1:00:00 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
This is a public-communication and risk-literacy talk by structural PE Brent Maxfield, not a steel detailing or connection-design session. The thesis is that earthquake magnitude alone tells you almost nothing about damage; what matters is the shaking intensity at a given site, which Maxfield calls "the shake in the quake" [03:41][12:40]. He argues engineers should stop saying "MCE earthquake" and instead say "MCE shaking intensity / response acceleration / ground motion" so owners and the public understand what code design actually buys [32:58]. The driving message for any builder or owner is that code-conforming buildings are life-safety designs that can be heavily damaged or made disposable after a major event, not earthquake-proof [31:22][50:35].

### Spec References
No AISC 360, AISC 341, AWS D1.1, RCSC, or Code of Standard Practice sections are cited; this webinar contains no steel-specific provisions. The standards and tools named are the 2000 IBC (origin of the MCE concept) [31:56], the risk-targeted MCER defined as a 1-in-5,000-per-year collapse risk with shaking having a 2 percent probability of exceedance in 50 years and a target of no more than 10 percent probability of collapse at MCER for a typical Risk Category II building [35:09][36:12], the USGS Modified Mercalli intensity scale 1 to 10 and ShakeMap product [12:40][13:13], the 84th-percentile (one standard deviation above median) collapse-prevention basis [29:49], FEMA P-58 with SP3 software for performance-based loss and recovery estimation [49:00], and the USRC building rating system (certified / silver / gold / platinum) tied to two-thirds MCER design-level shaking [48:30]. FEMA "functional recovery" is named as the coming code direction [55:13].

### Technical Details
Maxfield separates magnitude (affects rupture area and shaking duration) from site shaking intensity (acceleration, sometimes velocity, depending on structure period) [06:27][19:23]. He uses a percentile/natural-variation model (4th, 50th, 84th, 98th percentile shaking) to show that one fault rupture cannot be pinned to a single shaking level; distance to fault, fault type (strike-slip versus normal), hanging-wall versus footwall position, soil profile softness, and depth to rock shift the predicted range [26:37][56:47]. Two-thirds MCER is the "design" level event; MCER is roughly a 50 percent larger ground motion than the design level, which is why an essential building tuned to be operational at two-thirds MCER may not be operational at full MCER [42:22][43:53].

### Fabrication Notes
No fabrication content. The talk addresses no shop processes, fit-up, member sizing, tolerances, or QC, so there is nothing here for Mario's shop floor to action.

### Erection Notes
No erection content. There is no field procedure, sequencing, bracing, rigging, or site-coordination material in this session.

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
No connection rejections or inspection failures are discussed because the talk is non-technical. The "errors" Maxfield names are communication failures: engineers letting owners believe code buildings are earthquake-proof, conflating magnitude with shaking, and not disclosing that cladding-failure checks are not required at MCER in the current code [40:47][45:57]. He flags that aftershocks can collapse buildings that survived the main event and that MCER-level buildings are often demolished afterward for economic reasons [40:47][41:18].

### Bid / Cost Implications
The cost framing is owner-facing risk versus cost: code sets the MCER level as a balance, designing to a higher percentile (toward 98th / "bulletproof") is uneconomical, and resilience or functional-recovery design above code adds cost, sometimes on the order of about half a percent of building cost per the FEMA P-58 / SP3 discussion, in exchange for less damage and faster recovery [29:19][34:06][49:33]. None of this changes steel takeoff quantities, AISC weights, or unit rates; it is a basis-of-design and owner-expectation conversation, not a pricing input.

### Your Company Application
Value here is conversational and qualifying, not technical. For Ivan's estimating and any ACP-style project-controls intake, capture the seismic design basis (Risk Category, design shaking level, whether resilience or functional-recovery goals exceed code) as a scope question to the GC or EOR, since those drive the lateral system and connection demand that the detailing and tonnage follow, but take all such criteria from the stamped structural drawings and the in-house PE, never from a video. This talk gives Owner and Joseph plain-language framing to set realistic seismic expectations with owners without overpromising. It offers nothing actionable for Mario's welding, Paul's NCCER safety program, Tekla detailing, anchor-rod design or tolerance, joists, or field bolting. Doctrine flags: NONE.

## Design of Column Reinforcement
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xltavaJQaGg | Duration: 1:04:52 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
Bo Dowswell (ARC International, AISC Committee on Specifications) teaches how to design reinforcement for axially loaded wide-flange columns using welded reinforcing plates, where the failure mode is flexural buckling [02:25][03:25]. The talk covers four linked problems: partial-length reinforcement that must be set back from framing members, the effect of preload (the load present on the column when the plates are welded on), a notional-load analysis that replaces the effective-length method, and how to size the reinforcement welds [09:01][09:32]. The central practical idea is that if the reinforcement is "stabilizing" you can ignore preload and just add preload plus postload as a total load into the spec [18:57].

### Spec References
The spoken references are: AISC 360 Chapter E flexural buckling provisions and specifically Section E3 for wide-flange columns [10:02][10:32]; Section C2.3 for the reduced stiffness EI star equal to 0.8 times tau-sub-b times E times I [41:41]; the tau-sub-b equation from the spec [42:11]; Section H1.1 combined biaxial bending and compression interaction equations [46:46]; and the AISC Code of Standard Practice column out-of-straightness tolerance of L over 1000 [40:08]. He cites the AISC Engineering Journal column-stepped-column effective-length tables published in 1969 [15:06], and a prior 2013 AISC webinar "Design of Reinforcement for Steel Members" (parts 1 and 2) for the allowable-stress preload method and local buckling [25:11][25:41]. He references Blodgett's welding book for weld-shrinkage distortion control [38:38].

### Technical Details
Reinforcement types in rough preference order are: two flange plates (his favorite, easy to design and install, leave roughly 1 inch land at the flange tip for field fit) [03:55][04:25]; flange plates plus a web plate when more weak-axis stiffness is needed [04:25]; a single-sided plate when only one flange is accessible [05:25]; a box (closed) section for torsion and large weak-axis gain [05:56]; and continuous four-sided reinforcement only when load is too high to set back [06:59]. The stabilizing-reinforcement test is that the reinforced radius of gyration R-sub-R must be at least 0.85 times the original R-sub-O [19:28][60:40]. The concept rests on tangent-modulus behavior: a preloaded section yields and loses stiffness, so the elastic reinforcing plates carried far from the neutral axis (flange tips) resist buckling [22:06][23:09]. Partial-length reinforcement is modeled as a stepped column using the moment-of-inertia ratio I-sub-R over I-sub-O and the length ratio L-sub-R over L, with K factors K-sub-S1 (set back one end) and K-sub-S2 (set back both ends); a worked example reads K-sub-S2 of 1.139 at ratio 2.5 and L-sub-R/L of 0.5 [15:39][17:19][17:49]. The notional-load method applies a uniform lateral load W-sub-N equal to P-sub-R divided by (125 times L) when out-of-straightness is within tolerance, or 8 times P-sub-R times delta-sub-D over L squared when it exceeds tolerance, then uses K equals 1, the EI star reduced stiffness, the B1 moment multiplier, and the H1.1 interaction with P-sub-C replaced by the squash load P-sub-NS [40:39][42:41][47:17].

### Fabrication Notes
The dominant shop concern is weld-shrinkage distortion that can push the column out of straight beyond the Code of Standard Practice L over 1000 limit [38:08][39:08]. Two-sided reinforcement lets welders stagger and alternate passes side to side to balance shrinkage, an art the shop knows better than the engineer; single-sided plates give far less control over distortion [38:38][39:08]. Detailers should hold a land of roughly 1 inch (the AISC manual notes about a half inch for certain weld sizes) between flange tip and plate so the field can shift the plate during fit-up [03:55][04:25]. Web-plate and box reinforcement are slowed by beams, struts, and vertical-bracing gusset plates framing into the web, which often force the plate to be cut short [04:55][05:56].

### Erection Notes
Reinforcement is typically a retrofit on an erected, loaded column, so plates are welded in place rather than dismantling the frame [12:03][12:33]. Reinforcement must be set back from work points where beams, struts, or gusset plates frame in, commonly about a foot and sometimes pulled back three or four feet for economy when column strength allows [12:33][13:03]. The plate must extend past the theoretical cutoff point by the anchor length D-sub-RT to develop the load in the plate [51:20][53:21]. He avoids welding across the bottom end to stay away from overhead welds [55:54].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The named failure risks are column out-of-straightness exceeding L over 1000 from weld-shrinkage distortion, which voids the plain spec equations and requires the extra notional-load moment [38:08][39:38]; welded flange-tip tension residual stresses (welding overrides the original compression residual stress at the tip and can actually raise capacity by about 6 percent in the tests) [30:50][31:24]; and, for bolted reinforcement, using non-slip-critical bolts, which lets oversized holes (a sixteenth each) slip and create a large initial rotation before the bolts engage [62:46][63:16]. A common design oversight is missing that the controlling cross section can be at the end of the reinforcement, not only at column mid-height [36:36].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Setting reinforcement back further than strictly required saves plate, weld, and engineering labor while reducing distortion, so the setback decision is a direct cost lever [12:33][13:03]. Treating stabilizing reinforcement as a simple total-load case avoids running two finite-element models (one before and one after reinforcement) and skips the per-section allowable-stress hand calculations, which he states saves substantial engineering time and yields higher usable loads [33:28][33:58]. Choosing the simple two-plate flange detail over web or box reinforcement reduces welder time lost to web obstructions [04:55].

### Your Company Application
This is a connection and member-reinforcement design topic for the in-house PE stamp and Tekla detailing, not a routine new-build takeoff item, so it surfaces mainly on retrofit or load-increase scopes. For Mario's shop and welding lead it is directly relevant: stagger and alternate the plate welds to hold the L over 1000 straightness tolerance, leave the roughly 1 inch land for field fit, and avoid overhead welds at column bases per [38:38][55:54]; route any weld procedure through AWS D1.1 as our standard. For Ivan's estimating, a column-reinforcement scope is priced on plate weight plus weld length and the setback decision, and aisc_validator.py supplies the wide-flange section properties (I, r, area) the stepped-column ratios depend on. Paul should note the overhead and in-place welding hazards on retrofit work. If reinforcement is ever bolted rather than welded, the PE must specify slip-critical bolts per RCSC pretension, which ties to our field-bolting standard. No conflict with Your Company doctrine: conventional structural steel, no PEMB language, no supplier names. DOCTRINE FLAGS: NONE.

## Steel Bridge Fabrication
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FglCqdCewkY | Duration: 1:28:00 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is an AISC live webinar (session L1, October 12 2017) on how steel plate girder and tub girder bridges are fabricated, presented by Dr. Karl Frank, retired chief engineer at Hirschfeld Industries [00:02]. The central message is that a steel bridge is a modular, custom-built product fitted in the shop so the field work is reduced to bolting splices with a wrench [02:05]. Girders are deep, thin-webbed, unsymmetrical composite plate sections custom-developed from a clean sheet rather than picked from a rolled-beam table, to produce a strong, ductile structure [03:39]. The talk walks the full shop sequence: order plate, splice and trim, cut camber, weld web-to-flange, fit stiffeners, splice, inspect, blast, paint, ship.

### Spec References
The speaker cites the AASHTO bridge design specification for girder proportioning limits (web slenderness near 120, flange b/t at 9.2 for Grade 50, flange thicker than web) [04:41][06:14][08:18]. Welding and inspection are governed by AWS D1.5, the bridge welding code, explicitly named, with preheat and interpass temperatures from D1.5 Section 1.5 and maximum amperage by process from Table 5.1 [25:24][28:30][74:41]. Narrow gap electroslag welding was adopted into D1.5 in 2010 after a federal moratorium was lifted in March 2000 [37:51]. Phased-array UT is noted as now recognized in D1.5 [65:48]. Heat input is measured in kilojoules per inch with each pass within 10 percent of the overall average [27:59].

### Technical Details
Plate girders are three plates (two flanges plus web) with stiffeners; tub (box) girders use the same web-to-flange welding but assemble two webs into a box with cross frames [02:37][54:22]. Span-to-depth ratio of 25 to 30 sets the starting depth; webs held under a 137 slenderness avoid longitudinal stiffeners; top flange runs about two-thirds the area of the bottom flange [05:11][16:03][07:16]. The compression-flange-to-tension-flange stiffness ratio limit matters because pushing toward a tee section voids the lateral torsional buckling equations [10:24]. Fusion welding melts a consumable electrode and base metal; rapid cooling in the heat affected zone can form hard martensite, which preheat is used to prevent by slowing the cooling rate [16:33][24:21]. Residual (locked-in) tensile stresses are unavoidable, are not calculated, and are accounted for in the specifications through the inelastic compression-flange curve [55:24][57:29].

### Fabrication Notes
Fabricators do not stock plate; they order on award, with Grade 50 at 4 to 8 weeks and 70W out to 10-plus weeks, plate length capped near 80 feet by rail cars [13:27][14:28]. Submerged arc is the most common process; flange butt welds bevel the plate, weld multiple passes one side with run-off tabs, then flip, air-arc gouge the root to sound metal, grind, and weld the back [33:44][36:17]. Welder qualification runs through a weld procedure specification backed by a PQR from tested plates (all-weld-metal tension, Charpy V-notch, side bends, macro etch, plus RT, and UT for narrow gap electroslag), good typically one to five years [26:28][30:04][31:06]. Flange thickness transitions should be made at field splices and the plates nested so several flanges are cut from one slabbed assembly, turning eight separate welds into two [45:35][47:08]. Quarter-inch stiffeners are disliked because the dual-arc stiffener welder burns through them [53:50].

### Erection Notes
Field assembly is mostly bolting splice plates with cranes and shoring towers; the shop guarantees fit so erection goes fast [02:05]. Heat curving for sweep is done after the flange is attached to the web but before stiffeners go on [82:11]. At most two curved girders are laid down together because stacking curved pieces climbs into the air [66:20]. Shipping drives design: girders up to about 12 feet tall ship upright on single permits; over 120 feet long needs special superload permits and added days; very deep girders may ship web-horizontal, and a stiffening truss can be added for lateral torsional buckling capacity in transit [73:39][74:11]. Rail is standard, with barge as a last resort, as on the Tappan Zee girders [73:05].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The case study where an estimator assumed a 3/8 inch flange dimension was a misprint and bid 3/4 inch, then was forced to build the 3/8 inch flanges that failed the b/t and flange-thicker-than-web limits, ending in a bolted cover-plate retrofit, is the headline lesson: pay attention to a detailer RFI [10:55][12:26]. Visual inspection rejects non-uniform fillet welds; magnetic particle finds surface and near-surface cracks on fillets; radiography (gamma or x-ray, cobalt-60 above three inch plate) and ultrasonics find internal volumetric flaws, lack of fusion, and lack of penetration [57:29][59:04][61:10]. A flaw above the allowable threshold is gouged out, rewelded, and reinspected [81:06]. Adding bolts that are not needed (one splice shown had 312 bolts and 936 holes, another 634 bolts) drives field cost [67:22][68:24].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Material is bought only after award, so lead time (4 to 8 weeks Grade 50, longer for 70W) sits on the schedule front end and cannot be compressed [14:28]. Changing flange width within a field section rather than at a splice raises cost about 35 percent because the weld can no longer be slabbed [48:44]. HPS 70 thick plate behaves like gold: a 12 by 80 foot plate may be bought just to rip one 21 foot piece of 2.5 inch plate, so vary plate width across girders, not thickness, and extend plates to a common point for slabbing [51:17][52:18]. Virtual assembly (laser-tracker hole measurement plus computer-fit splice plates) eliminates hand drilling and multiple physical lay-downs, measuring to under a thousandth of an inch, which is the major speed and cost win [68:24][75:12].

### Your Company Application
For Ivan, the 3/8 inch flange case is a direct warning against assuming a stated dimension is a misprint at takeoff: a wrong member input scales the whole bid, so flag and RFI rather than auto-correct, which matches our verify-don't-generate and source-it-don't-assume rules. For Mario, the welding content (submerged arc, FCAW, preheat by thickness, run-off tabs, root gouging, fillet sizing by plate thickness) is AWS D1.5 bridge code, not the D1.1 building code Mario certifies under, so any bridge work would need separate D1.5 procedure and welder qualification; on building jobs the preheat, heat-input, and martensite logic still transfer. For Paul, radiography is a real radiation hazard requiring standoff distance and is typically run at night outdoors, a site-safety control to capture if RT ever enters our scope. For Tekla detailing, the laser-tracker virtual-assembly model parallels our coordinate-model and fit-up approach and supports pushing fit responsibility into the shop. The bolt-count economy point reinforces minimizing field bolting on our splices. Doctrine flag: this is bridge fabrication under AASHTO and AWS D1.5, outside Your Company's conventional building structural steel and D1.1 scope, so treat the spec citations as reference, not as building-bid authority; AISC member weights still come only from aisc_validator.py. No PEMB conflict. Otherwise NONE.

## Steel Material Properties
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=loRrbAjhZBw | Duration: 1:23:31 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is NSBA Night School Session 3, "Steel Materials," presented by Dr. Carl Frank, chief engineer at Hirschfeld Industries [00:00]. The talk explains where structural steel strength comes from and ties it back to fabrication and welding. Strength is a function of chemistry and heat treatment: steel is hot rolled in the austenite (gamma) phase, then cooled through a transformation to a ferrite-pearlite microstructure, and strength can be raised by alloying, by quench-and-temper, or by inline thermo-mechanical controlled processing (TMCP) [11:50][12:52][13:24]. The recurring theme is martensite control: cooling too fast forms hard, brittle martensite, and the same risk appears in the weld heat-affected zone, which is why chemistry is controlled for weldability and why preheat slows the cooling rate [14:24][20:36][24:45]. The scope is bridge steel, where toughness, fracture-critical sampling, and bolt rotational-capacity requirements go beyond ordinary building practice [01:31][28:24].
### Spec References
Cited verbatim by the speaker: ASTM A709 as the consolidated bridge-steel specification with seven grades (36, 50, 50W, HPS 50W, HPS 70W, HPS 100W) [26:49][27:19]; legacy specs A7, A36, A514 (T1, 100 ksi), A572 Grade 50, A588/A242 weathering, and rolled-section spec A992 [25:49][27:54][58:00 ref]; the new bolt spec ASTM F3125 that consolidates A325, A490, and twist-off grades, ordered as "F3125 Grade A325" [55:22][80:00]; ASTM A1010 (stainless-type corrosion-resistant bridge steel) [52:13][72:32]; HSS specs ASTM A500 (noted not for dynamically loaded structures) and the newer ASTM A1085 with Charpy V-notch, carbon-equivalent, corner-radius, and tighter wall-thickness control [53:49][73:07]; anchor-rod spec ASTM A1554 (now F1554 in practice) grades 36, 55, 105 [65:15]; and ASTM A354 Grade BD high-strength rod, flagged as stress-corrosion sensitive [66:20]. Temperature zones 1, 2, 3 set Charpy test temperatures [50:10].
### Technical Details
Steel transforms from face-centered-cubic austenite to body-centered-cubic ferrite plus carbide (cementite), forming the lamellar pearlite microstructure; structural steel sits near 0.2 percent carbon [09:16][11:19]. Fracture toughness is the controlling property for bridge tension members: a Charpy V-notch (CVN) specimen, 10 mm square with a center notch, measures fracture energy versus temperature, and toughness in ksi-root-inch is estimated as the square root of CVN times 12.5 [39:13][40:16]. A temperature shift converts impact-rate Charpy results to bridge loading rate (about 75 percent of the shift), so the Charpy is tested above the lowest anticipated service temperature [37:40][39:44]. A worked example: 50 ksi steel, lowest service temperature 0 F, gives roughly a 105 F shift, so the steel is tested near room temperature (70 F) and must average about 25 ft-lb across three specimens to tolerate a 1-inch through-crack [40:47][41:17]. Bolt installation tension is 70 percent of tensile strength; a 7/8-inch A325 has a 39 kip minimum pretension [58:36].
### Fabrication Notes
A709 carries fabrication-side requirements beyond building steel: Charpy V-notch testing for tension members (not compression), extra material requirements and weld-repair limits for fracture-critical members, and heavier sampling [28:24][35:36]. Sampling frequency steps up by product: heat-based Charpy sampling for Grade 50 and 36; plate-based testing for heat-treated grades (HPS 70W, HPS 100W) because each plate has unique heat-treatment character; and P-frequency testing at both plate ends for all fracture-critical grades unless normalized [51:11][52:13]. Quench-and-temper is done by reheating into the austenite range, water-quenching to martensite, then tempering at 800 to 1200 F, with higher tempering temperature giving softer, tougher product [15:28][16:30]. HPS 70W is the workhorse, available to 4 inches, generally quenched-and-tempered by one producer over 1 inch, with TMCP grades reaching longer plate lengths (heat-treat furnaces limit plate length to roughly 50 feet) [31:28][33:32].
### Erection Notes
The strongest field-procedure point is snugging: the purpose is to draw the plies into firm contact so that tightening adjacent bolts does not loosen already-tightened ones, and this crosstalk control is the single most important step regardless of the final tightening method [62:42][63:13]. For turn-of-nut, match-mark the nut and bolt after snugging so final tightening can be verified visually; for direct-tension indicators the snugging is done the same way [63:13][63:44]. Checking installed bolt tension with a torque wrench is called unreliable and unnecessary [63:44]. The San Francisco Bay Bridge case shows the erection-sequence trap: A354 BD rods were stored in the pier cap during construction, sat in trapped rainwater for a couple of years, then were tensioned by hydraulic jacking and fractured by stress-corrosion cracking [66:52][67:54][79:26].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The Point Pleasant (Silver) bridge collapse of 1967 is the anchor case: heat-treated 1060 high-carbon steel eye-bars with low toughness, where a brittle fracture grew from a corrosion crack only about an eighth of an inch deep after 40 years, too small to find in service inspection, and the two-eye-bar member had no redundancy [42:52][46:04][48:08]. This drove the Charpy V-notch toughness requirement and the fracture-critical concept [48:38][49:10]. Galvanized-bolt failures are named: over-tapped nuts without lubrication cause thread galling and stripping, so the rotational-capacity test in F3125 Appendix 2 verifies the nut-bolt assembly together [58:03][60:40]. Using torque to control tension is shown failing: a poorly lubricated bolt reads high torque with little tension [61:41]. A325 above 1 inch historically dropped in strength, now corrected to 120 ksi for all diameters [56:26].
### Bid / Cost Implications
Material selection drives cost directly here. Weathering steel costs about 10 percent more than non-weathering but offsets that by eliminating painting and field maintenance, netting roughly the cost of painted steel [29:56]. A1010 corrosion-resistant steel costs substantially more and is limited to 2 inches, so it is reserved for hostile coastal or near-water spans, not general use [52:13][72:32]. HPS 70W enables hybrid girders, pairing a lower-strength web with a higher-strength flange where strength is needed for flexure, which is a material-optimization and weight play at the pier and in long-span tension flanges [31:58][32:29]. Plate-length limits from heat-treat furnaces (about 50 feet for Q&T versus longer TMCP) can force splices on long members and should be checked before committing a section [33:32]. Galvanized fasteners carry over-tapping and rotational-capacity testing overhead [57:01].
### Your Company Application
Your Company is a building fabricator, not a bridge shop, so the A709 bridge spec, fracture-critical sampling, and zone-based Charpy testing are reference context, not our default building scope (positioning stays conventional structural steel). The transferable items map cleanly to our workstreams. For Mario and the AWS D1.1 welding line, the preheat-controls-martensite logic and the heat-affected-zone caution apply directly to thick or higher-carbon material and to the cold-weather preheat point [24:45][76:17]. For field bolting, the snugging-first and match-mark discipline, plus the rule that torque-wrench tension checks are unreliable, should be standard crew practice; note the bolt spec is now F3125 (order as F3125 Grade A325), which Ivan should reflect in takeoff and spec callouts and the in-house PE stamp should reflect on details [55:22][80:00]. For anchor rods, the spec the talk points to is A1554 (F1554 in current practice) grades 36/55/105, all galvanizable, and the hard warning is to never use high-strength A354 BD rods galvanized under sustained tension near water, which ties to our anchor-rod design, setting, and tolerance work [65:15][70:29]. For HSS, A500 is not rated for dynamic loading and A1085 gives tighter wall tolerance (no 10 percent thickness discount), relevant when ACP or any job has cyclic or crane loads. DOCTRINE FLAGS: NONE. No conflict with Your Company doctrine; AISC shape weights still come from aisc_validator.py and rates stay CEO-locked.

## Quality Control and Quality Assurance
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=C2PFj9YZ_mw | Duration: 1:29:44 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is the final session of the AISC night-school series "from the mill to topping out," presented by Larry Owner (former VP at Douglas Steel Fabricating, now AISC). The talk demystifies AISC 360 Chapter N, which became the single recognized source for special inspection of structural steel under the IBC. The central distinction is that Quality Control (QC) is provided by the fabricator and erector controlling their own work, while Quality Assurance (QA) is provided by others (third party, EOR, or AHJ) to assure the quality was met [29:55, 30:33]. Every inspection task in Chapter N is tagged either Observe (random or intermittent check) or Perform (must be done on each joint, each weld, each bolt) [51:09]. The recurring theme: if an inspection is not documented, it was not performed [32:08].
### Spec References
AISC 360 Chapter N is the controlling document, with cited sections N1 general provisions, N2 fabricator/erector QC program, N5.1 QC tasks, N5.3 coordinated inspection, and N6 approved fabricators/erectors [30:01, 31:31, 34:19, 37:00, 38:36]. Cited tables include Table N5.4-1 (inspection tasks prior to welding) and on-slide Table N5.4-3 (inspection tasks after welding, frame 5). Section M2.5 appears on the special-inspection list (frame 3). AWS D1.1 clauses are cited verbatim: 6.3 (WPS available), 6.2 (consumable certs and material ID), 6.4 (qualified welder), 5.17 (no welding over cracks), 6.5.2 scope of examination (Observe, "at suitable intervals"), and 6.5.3 extent of examination "size and contour of a weld shall be measured with suitable gauges" (Perform) [12:53, 27:42, 28:22, 86:52]. AWS D1.3, D1.4, and AWS A5 filler-metal documents appear on inspection lists [07:57, frame 3]. RCSC (Specification for Structural Joints Using High-Strength Bolts) sections 2.1, 9.1 (manufacturer certs / fastener marking), 7.1 (tension calibrator) and Figure C2.1 are cited [13:52, 21:03]. ASTM F3125 / F1852 (TC bolts) and ASTM F1554 (anchor rods) are named [17:59, frame 3]. IBC references: 2009 Chapter 17, sections 1702 and 202 (continuous/periodic definitions), 2018 sections 1704.2.5.1 and 1705.2.1 [25:17, 26:39, 40:09, 41:02]. Code of Standard Practice Section 6.1 is cited for material identification [32:53].
### Technical Details
QC inspects against the approved shop and erection drawings plus reference standards; QA uses those same documents AND the design drawings/specifications as an extra check that information transferred correctly from design into the shop/erection set [34:37, 35:37]. Coordinated inspection (N5.3) lets a single party perform a task that QC and QA share, but only if the EOR and the AHJ approve the QC procedures as meeting QA criteria [36:18]. Perform tasks require an actual measurement on each item; Observe tasks are random or intermittent. Every weld must be visually inspected for crack prohibition, weld/base-metal fusion, crater cross section, weld profiles, weld size, undercut, and porosity (Table N5.4-3, frame 5). Fillet welds and most CJP welds can be inspected visually with a fillet gauge for size and a tape for length; not every weld needs NDT [16:38, 48:58].
### Fabrication Notes
A fabricator's quality management system must spell out written procedures for engineering/detailing, contract review, document control, drawing preparation, RFI tracking, drawing issuing and change control, purchasing/material control, prequalifying sublet detailers and sublet fabricators, material identification, and each shop operation (cutting, welding, drilling, bolting, surface prep, painting) [52:35 through 57:43]. Pre-installation verification (PIV) per RCSC 7.1 requires testing three bolts per lot (not per keg) in a Skidmore-Wilhelm tension calibrator; the RCSC commentary permits direct tension indicators (DTIs), which are also produced in lots, to serve as the tension calibrator, avoiding a Skidmore on every jobsite [18:35, 21:46]. TC bolts marked "A325 TC" are F3125 / F1852; bolts are stored in dust-tight containers because lubrication is critical, and the keg lot number ties the bolt back to its PIV test [17:59, 20:29]. Douglas Steel added a voluntary welder identification system (welder number/symbol stamped at each shop weld) and a matching bolter identification system, neither required by Chapter N, so a defective weld or loose bolt can be traced to the person for retraining [43:04, 46:50].
### Erection Notes
The erector's QC program mirrors the fabricator's but for field work: field bolting procedures, field welding procedures, and a nonconformance reporting procedure [58:42]. Owner recommends, though Chapter N does not require, a site-specific safety plan and a site-specific erection plan that establish where the crane sits and how material reaches the right location [58:56]. Field inspection does not require crawling over every bolt: if proper bolting training and PIV were done, TC bolts and fillet/CJP welds can be inspected largely visually for size and length [48:37]. A simple field inspection report keyed to column grid lines (for example grid A1-A3, levels 2-3) records pieces installed, bolts installed per procedure, field welds at all detailed locations, who did it, the date, and any incomplete items [49:14].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Several real Douglas Steel nonconformances are shown. A clip angle detailed 4-1/2 inches to the first hole instead of 3 inches (detailing error) was field-fixed with field-welded clips [60:55]. Missing shop clip angles on piece 57B1 were sent to the field and installed (frame 17) [61:36]. Erectors cut a frame apart thinking it would not fit and could not reassemble it, forcing a rebuild [61:56]. The most serious failure: an HSS 20x8x1/2 (piece 123B1) detailed with a temporary two-bolt connection for erection per OSHA, intended to be field-welded top and bottom, but the field-weld section bubble was never cut on the erection diagram; the weld symbol was missed, the bolt bent and failed under load after concrete pour (CAR #008, frames 18 and 21) [62:37, 64:32]. The corrective action added a detailing-standard note requiring a section bubble at every field-welded joint. A separate case: sublet clip angles (mark 6A209, which was the subfabricator's code for 2-9/16 gauge, unknown to the shop) arrived with no holes in the CNC file; a night-shift CNC operator wrongly halved the 5-1/2 inch gauge to 2-3/4 and added holes himself, producing the wrong gauge on a large quantity that reached the field where holes would not line up (frame 19) [68:47, 73:55].
### Bid / Cost Implications
Owner argues nonconformances should be measured not by raw count but as cost as a percent of yearly sales: most quality programs call a program excellent under 5 percent, and Douglas Steel ran around 0.2 percent even in its highest-count year (141 NCRs in 2012) [77:58]. Counterintuitively, a rising NCR count can mean a healthier reporting culture, not a worse program, because people are comfortable reporting [78:36]. Being an AISC-certified (approved) fabricator lets the AHJ waive third-party QA inspection (NDT itself is never waived, only the requirement that a third party perform it), which removes duplicate inspection cost, but the fabricator must still issue a certificate of compliance [37:39, 82:00]. The closing point ties quality to bid value: "the bitterness of poor quality remains long after the sweetness of low price is forgotten" [79:54].
### Your Company Application
This video is a direct template for a Your Company Chapter N quality manual and maps cleanly onto the team. Tekla detailing should carry the standing rule from CAR #008: every field-welded joint gets a section-bubble cut on the erection drawing so the detailer and checker both see the weld is required, and the checker must verify against the design drawings, not just match the model. Mario Gutierrez owns the Perform-task reality that every weld is measured for size and contour with gauges per AWS D1.1 6.5.3, plus a welder ID stamp tied to each shop weld so a bad profile traces to a welder for retraining, which fits his AWS D1.1 welding-lead role. Paul Guerrero owns the site-specific safety plan and the field bolter-ID and PIV records. Ivan's takeoff and the in-house PE stamp connect to the QA cross-check: design-drawing information must transfer correctly into the detailed set, and aisc_validator.py already enforces verify-don't-generate on member data. Field bolting maps to PIV three-bolts-per-lot with the DTI-as-calibrator shortcut; anchor rods map to ASTM F1554 on the inspection list. For ACP controls, adopt the NCR-as-percent-of-sales metric and route every NCR through engineering to find the broken procedure. Doctrine conflict: NONE. The verify-don't-generate posture, confidence tagging, and document-control discipline all align with this material.

## Field Fixes and Solutions
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yI69Nu6pwQI | Duration: 1:35:09 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
AISC Night School Session 7, presented by Dr. James Fisher (December 3, 2018), is a working catalog of how a fabricator, erector, and engineer of record diagnose and repair steel that does not fit or perform in the field. Fisher's organizing rule is that labor, not material, drives the cost of a fix, so the cheapest fix is the one prevented by good detailing and the second cheapest is the one solved by adding steel [03:56], [04:19]. He frames every problem as get accurate information first, act immediately to limit delay charges, determine whether a fix is even required, then coordinate the paperwork sign-off before engineering the repair [03:19], [04:55]. The bulk of the session is anchor rods, which he spends a half hour on because the problems recur far too frequently [02:43], [29:00], followed by columns and beams, camber, shear studs, fit-up, reinforcing, and member-selection guidelines.

### Spec References
ASTM F1554 governs anchor rods, with color-coded product marking A36 blue, grade 55 yellow, grade 105 red, grade 55 available to 4 in diameter and grade 105 to 3 in, plus optional supplement S1 for weldable grade 55 [24:16], [24:46], [25:02]. AISC Manual Table 14-2 (15th edition) gives anchor-rod hole, washer, and washer-thickness sizes [25:18]. AISC Design Guide 1 addresses base-plate and anchor-rod design including pier development [26:52]. OSHA 1926.755 sets the four-anchor-rod minimum and the 300 lb at 18 in eccentric iron-worker load [27:42]. AISC Code of Standard Practice section 6.4.4 gives camber tolerances and the column plumb tolerance is H/500 [41:02], [31:41]. AISC Specification Appendix 6 gives stability bracing forces for out-of-plumb columns [31:08]. AISC Manual Table 1-22 lists ASTM A6 mill tolerances on beam depth, up to 1/4 in over theoretical [50:04]. AISC Spec Table J3.3 caps reaming at oversize-hole diameters, with the standard 1/32 in per ply and note 3.3 allowance [65:15]. AISC Spec sections J1.8 and J1.9 permit bolt-weld and weld-rivet load sharing, J1.9 requiring weld strength at least 25% of required [62:57], [64:11]. AWS section 7.6 covers shear-stud qualification [44:24].

### Technical Details
Anchor rods that are too short can be repaired by welding a threaded extension, a coupling nut, cutting and epoxy anchors, or welding the base plate to the rod, with the hard limit that you cannot weld to high-strength 105 ksi rods [09:33], [09:54]. Fisher repeatedly steers to larger-diameter A36 (F1554 grade 36) rods over high-strength rods precisely because A36 is weldable and ductile enough to cold-bend or heat-straighten when bent [10:14], [16:59]. A nut is acceptable when the rod top is at least flush with the top of the nut; below that you must check thread shear strength [91:20]. Weld shrinkage shortens a CJP weld by roughly 1/8 in, which accumulates into out-of-plumb columns on long column lines [32:27]. ASTM A6 mill tolerance lets a beam over-run theoretical depth by up to 1/4 in, the root cause of continuity-plate and wing-plate misfits [50:04].

### Fabrication Notes
Camber is measured in the unstressed position in the shop and cannot be verified once the member is on the job site, so any camber dispute is settled at the fabricator [41:22]. Members to camber are filler beams, composite floor beams, girders, and trusses; do not camber spandrels, cantilevered or moment-connected or braced beams, torsion-loaded members, beams under 20 to 25 ft, beams with webs 1/4 in or thinner, or any camber under 3/4 in, and use a heavier beam instead [34:11], [35:43], [36:36]. Continuity plates should be detailed thicker than the beam flange, Fisher's example being upper stiffener 1/4 in greater and lower 3/8 in greater, to absorb A6 tolerance [47:46]. End plates are detailed short about 1/8 in each end for A6 and fabrication tolerance [33:48]. Embed plates use 1/2 in minimum for deck bearing and 3/4 in for beam bearing as heat sinks, and should always be oversized in plan because they are routinely mislocated [53:06], [52:50].

### Erection Notes
The four-rod OSHA minimum gives erectors a false sense of security; partly erected steel under wind must be evaluated separately, since anchor rods sized only for the 300 lb at 18 in load will not hold a frame [27:58]. Fisher cites a 40 ft HSS-column building in Utah that collapsed in a 30 to 35 mph wind because a joist girder was left sitting unattached on a column top, and notes that an oversized anchor-rod substitution shifted the failure from rod breakage to footing tip-over [07:43]. Out-of-plumb columns beyond H/500 are braced using Appendix 6 forces, or the column is freed by cutting and re-setting anchor rods with epoxy [31:01]. Anchor-rod templates must be wood or steel firmly fastened to the formwork, often just 2x4s spanning to the foundation edge, so concrete placement does not drift the pattern; problems arise when the concrete contractor rather than the erector sets the rods [22:24], [88:05]. Leveling nuts suit light one- to two-story loads with a thick washer to prevent punching; heavier loads use shim stacks or setting plates, and shims can be left in place [89:01], [23:26].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Recurring failures named are anchor rods too short, too long, bent over (a bulldozer over snow-covered plates), rotated 90 degrees, or set in the wrong position, including a 1,300-rod project that had to be redone after a detailer dimensioned the setting plate wrong [20:46]. Base plates punching through leveling nuts is fixed by jacking and grouting [23:26]. Shear studs that snap during the bend-over inspection (bent at least 30 degrees, often by sledgehammer) signal a miscalibrated stud gun, qualified per AWS 7.6 [43:43]. Fit-up failures include weak-axis moment connections, continuity plates the same thickness as the beam flange, bolted holes that do not align on heavy bracing connections, and beams that do not fit between wing plates because two fabricators built columns and beams without coordinating beam over-run [45:58], [49:12]. Crane-runway fatigue cracking concentrates at tieback locations [78:41].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Fisher's central estimating message is that on a fix, labor is the expense and material is cheap, so the engineer should sharpen the pencil to see if a fix is even needed before money is spent and an argument over who pays begins [03:56], [04:01]. He recommends designing beams for about 10% extra concrete thickness because over-screeding is predictable, since extra steel is cheaper than chasing an overstressed member or a field reinforcement [42:26], [42:50]. He flags expensive specification habits: CJP welds are easy to call out but costly, doubler plates should be designed out by picking a thicker-web column, and minimum edge distances detailed too tight leave no room to ream, so add 1/8 in to edge distances as insurance [72:42], [73:11], [66:54]. He also notes engineering fees on a fix are legitimate and should be discussed openly with the team [04:55].

### Your Company Application
This session is a direct checklist for Your Company's anchor-rod workstream and Mario's shop. The F1554 grade-36-over-high-strength rule and the no-weld-to-105-ksi rule should be standing constraints in our anchor-rod detailing and any field-repair WPS Mario writes, and the Table 14-2 hole and washer sizes plus Design Guide 1 pier development belong in our Tekla anchor-rod templates. The A6 depth tolerance (Table 1-22) and the practice of detailing end plates and continuity plates oversized feed straight into Tekla detailing and into Ivan's takeoff, since a thicker continuity plate is a few pounds of steel against a costly field weld. The 10% extra-concrete design margin and the camber-measured-in-shop rule support our verify-don't-generate posture on composite-deck and joist jobs, and the H/500 plumb tolerance with Appendix 6 bracing is a clean reference for our in-house PE stamp on erection-stability questions. For Paul's safety file, the OSHA 1926.755 four-rod minimum plus Fisher's warning that it does not guarantee wind stability reinforces requiring an engineered stability check, not just four rods, before crews climb. The firmly-fastened template guidance is the practical answer to anchor-rod setting tolerance, and the joist end-diagonal story is a field-coordination caution for ACP joist work. Doctrine conflict: NONE. Note the video predates the 16th edition AISC Manual our aisc_validator.py wraps; the cited table numbers (14-2, 1-22, J3.3) are 15th-edition and should be re-confirmed against current tables before quoting on a live bid.

## Erection Engineering: Stability During Construction
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ECCIeyWO8JY | Duration: 1:12:32 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This 2018 AISC Night School session (Session 6), presented by Benjamin Miller PE/SE of Rubin Associates, covers erection engineering: keeping a steel frame stable in its incomplete, sequenced condition during construction [00:02][01:32]. The EOR is responsible for stability of the final completed structure only, which exists once the final diaphragms, steel, and connections are buttoned up [06:13]. At every intermediate sequence the lateral system is incomplete, so the erector must add temporary measures, and the erection engineer designs them [06:45][03:36]. The thrust of the talk: an open, uncladded steel frame can draw far higher wind force than the finished building because of larger drag coefficients and longer unbraced lengths, so temporary bracing is engineered to the same probability of exceedance as the final design, not to a casual everyday wind [49:38][52:12].

### Spec References
Cited verbatim by the speaker: AISC Code of Standard Practice (AISC 303) Section 7.10.1 parts A and B (EOR identifies the lateral force resisting system and any required erection sequence) [08:15][22:43]; Section 7.10.2 (EOR identifies non-structural elements of the lateral system) [17:04]; Section 7.10.3 (loads the erector need not consider) [25:51]; Section 3.1.2 part B (EOR shows shears, moments, axial and transfer forces for members and connections) [12:29]. Also cited: ASCE 37 (Design Loads on Structures During Construction), specifically Chapter 6 wind, Section 6.2.1 wind-speed reduction factors, and Section 6.2.2 shielding [07:15][39:11][41:49][42:51]; ASCE 7 with Figure 29.5-2 force coefficients [43:23][46:01]; IBC; the Steel Construction Manual (14th edition design example referenced) [33:34][68:03]; SJI Technical Digest 9 (handling and erection of steel joists and joist girders) [07:15]; AISC Design Guide 10 (low-rise buildings) [07:15]; and PCI Architectural Precast Concrete, 3rd edition [57:48].

### Technical Details
Wind during construction starts from ASCE 7 pressures, then ASCE 37 Section 6.2.1 allows a wind-speed reduction tied to construction duration; a sub-six-week erection earns a 0.75 factor on wind speed, which, squared into pressure, yields about 56% of design pressure [39:42][42:21]. ASCE 37 Section 6.2.2 permits a 15% shielding reduction on the fourth and subsequent elements (85%), while the first three rows take 100% [42:51]. That relief is offset by force coefficients of 1.6 to 2.0 for flat-sided open framework from ASCE 7 Figure 29.5-2, governed by solidity ratio; roughly 1.95 for a single wide-flange [43:23][46:33]. In the 14th-edition example the construction east-west base shear hit 429 kips against a final design base shear of 170 kips [47:34][48:05]. Truss element stability was analyzed under hook versus at-set: chords web-vertical gave a top-chord unity of 5.9 at set (needing bracing before crane release), but turning the chords horizontal dropped the same members to 0.85 [60:20][61:54][62:26].

### Fabrication Notes
Detailing choices drive how much temporary bracing the field needs. A flange-plate moment connection using a WT instead of a double angle makes all four bolts strain-compatible and effective for moment, where the angle leaves the middle two bolts largely ineffective per the AISC Manual; the WT version let them skip temporary cable bracing on those moment lines [70:05][70:36]. A welded HSS-to-gusset joint with a single 3/4-inch erection bolt loaded by the HSS sidewalls (HSS 8x8 example) was limited to about 750 lb in bending, essentially zero stability until field welds are placed [70:36][71:37]. A bolted knife plate with four corner bolts is preferred because the erector can develop capacity at set and drop some cable bracing [72:07]. Base-plate detailing matters: moving anchor rods outside the column shape rather than inside reduced a wind-column base anchorage from 146% to a workable utilization without changing anchor size or embedment, only enlarging the base plate [68:03][69:04].

### Erection Notes
The erection engineer needs a blocking (sequence) plan from the erector, modeled tier by tier (column-splice to column-splice), then loads each stage per ASCE 37 including staged material, wind, and any snow/ice [35:38][36:09][37:39]. Temporary cable bracing is sized to the engineered event, not to a 20 to 25 mph site wind, which is why erectors see "so much bracing" [52:12]. Cable detail: wrap the column about 18 inches up with a turnbuckle to keep the cable taut, and weld an angle across the back of the column so the wrapped cable cannot ride up under 70 mph loading [54:14][54:45][55:16]. Erectors dislike wire rope over 1/2 inch; this job used two lines of 5/8-inch wire rope rather than going to 3/4 inch [52:42][53:43]. Temporary bracing must stay until the permanent lateral system and its diaphragms are in place per the Code of Standard Practice, even after all steel is erected [38:09][56:18]. Where a steel frame ties into perimeter precast erected first, cable bracing was too flexible for the precaster's load limits, so hard braces (W14x74 noted) replaced cables [56:48][58:49].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
This is a design webinar, so it names design and documentation failures rather than weld or bolt rejections. The recurring failure is incomplete EOR documentation: not fully describing the lateral load path and diaphragm-to-frame load transfer, not stating whether column anchorages are pinned or fixed, and not identifying non-structural lateral elements or how long temporary bracing must remain, which forces early RFIs [09:51][11:26][22:13][39:11]. An ambiguous shoring note (10 kips per joist versus 5 and 5) needed a phone call to resolve [24:18][25:19]. A specification that referenced both Code of Standard Practice and ASCE 37 created a direct contradiction on hurricane loading; the erector is flagged to red-flag this and resolve it by RFI, exclusion, or bid clarification [27:23][31:31][33:03].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Bringing erection engineering in earlier can save schedule and reduce temporary measures, for example starting erection at a braced frame line to engage the permanent lateral system sooner [05:10][15:30]. Conflicting spec language carries real cost: the hurricane-contingency plan was dropped because implementation cost was excessive, a decision reached jointly with owner and GC [32:31]. Bracing magnitude is a cost driver because construction base shear here was 2.5 times the final design shear, so material staging, cable runs, and the deck contractor cutting deck around bracing all add field cost [48:05][56:18]. Detailing that lets the erector release a pick under self weight or drop a brace line (WT moment connections, bolted knife plates, horizontal truss chords) directly reduces erection labor and rented bracing [62:26][70:36][72:07].

### Your Company Application
For Tekla detailing and our in-house PE stamp, the connection choices that cut field bracing map straight onto our work: prefer WT over double-angle flange-plate moment connections where the middle bolts would otherwise be ineffective, prefer bolted knife plates over single-erection-bolt welded HSS-to-gusset joints, and place anchor rods outside the column shape so wind-column base plates are not overstressed at tier one. That last point ties directly to our anchor-rod design, setting, and tolerance workstream: a slightly larger base plate with anchors outside the flanges took a base anchorage from 146% to acceptable. Ivan should capture, at takeoff, whether the set states the lateral system, the diaphragm load path, and anchorage fixity, and raise an RFI when absent rather than assuming, consistent with our ask-before-guessing and SF-sourcing discipline. Paul Guerrero's safety scope intersects the OSHA column-anchorage climbing loads and the requirement that engineered temporary bracing stay until the permanent diaphragm is in. For ACP project controls, sequence-locked dead-load moments (the 55 kip-ft example) and super-elevation of cantilever ends argue for tracking erection sequence as a controlled deliverable, not a field improvisation. DOCTRINE FLAGS: NONE. The content is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language, no supplier names, and no conflict with our rates, AISC-validator, or verify-don't-generate rules.

## It Doesn't Get Built Without the Erector
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Wou7aR18MR4 | Duration: 1:32:11 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is the erector's view of the steel project, presented by Phil Torchio (retired president of Williams Enterprises) in AISC Night School Session 5. It walks the full erector lifecycle: how erectors get work from fabricators, how an erection estimate is built piece by piece off the drawings, how the AISC Code of Standard Practice (COSP) allocates responsibility, how crane and hoisting capacity drives the whole plan, and how the field actually sets and welds the steel. The recurring theme is that the erector sells labor and hoisting, prices in pieces and crane picks (not tons), and that detail geometry and weld type are the real cost drivers, not headline tonnage [08:24][09:50].
### Spec References
AISC Code of Standard Practice, Section 7 Erection, cited section by section on a slide: 7.1 Method of Erection, 7.2 Job-Site Conditions, 7.3 Foundations Piers and Abutments, 7.4 Lines and Benchmarks, 7.5 Installation of Anchor Rods Foundation Bolts and Other Embedded Items, 7.6 Installation of Bearing Devices, 7.7 Grouting, 7.8 Field Connection Material, 7.9 Loose Material, 7.10 Temporary Support of Structural Steel Frames (ODRD), 7.11 Safety Protection, 7.12 Structural Steel Frame Tolerances, 7.13 Erection Tolerances, 7.14 Correction of Errors, 7.15 Cuts Alterations and Holes for Other Trades, 7.16 Handling and Storage, 7.17 Field Painting, 7.18 Final Cleaning Up [14:57][15:55]. AWS D1.1 named, with AWS D1.8 cited as the supplemental seismic welding standard requiring qualified WPS and a separate welder qualification for moment connections [21:05][21:48]. AWS A2.4 cited for the 2020 change to the PJP weld symbol convention from S(E)/D(S) to D(S) where D is the depth of groove and S is the size of weld [50:54][51:24]. The AESS (Architecturally Exposed Structural Steel) category matrix from COSP is discussed by category, AESS 1 through 4 plus Category C custom [18:37].
### Technical Details
The reference building is a 26-story rectangular braced-frame office tower in downtown Charlotte (300 Tryon), chosen as a clean erector case. The lateral system is a stiff braced core: vertical X and tubular K bracing in the core, so once the core is plumb the building is plumb and few stability cables are needed [28:36][29:36]. Bottom-shaft built-up columns are W14x1400 at Fy=65 ksi, a 30-foot starter shaft weighing about 42,000 pounds, with diagonals marked W14x145 carrying P=790k to 850k T or C from the design drawings [28:36, frame slide 39/45]. The frame moment column splice detail calls a CJP single-bevel groove for flanges and web, prepped with a 30-degree bevel and 3/8 inch root, the most efficient field joint prequalified in D1.1 [48:12]. COSP plumbness and erection tolerances are illustrated by the standard nomograph, with the caveat that intentionally non-plumb columns (Football Hall of Fame example) require the contract to define work points explicitly [17:54]. The AESS matrix scales finish quality by sight distance, AESS 2 beyond 20 feet, AESS 3 within 20 feet, AESS 4 touchable by the public; Category C is a pure custom architect direction that does not inherit the other AESS elements and requires a visual sample [18:37].
### Fabrication Notes
The erector relies on the fabricator to detail for field constructibility: lifting holes in columns to pin the column hitch, drilled holes in beams for catenary fall-protection lines and safety cable, cable posts for interior openings, and bolted rather than welded field connections where the erector needs to plumb before final weld (parapet kicker diagonals, K-brace tubular connections wanted as 2-bolt so a diagonal stays put) [10:50][27:37][29:48]. Shop assembly of small trusses and roof frames is agreed at the pre-detailing meeting under the contract clause that assemblies be shop-done where practical; large trusses cannot ship assembled [90:06]. For framing into concrete the erector wants the fabricator to supply a welded angle seat or welded shear tab with slotted holes because embeds and concrete are never exactly placed, and elevator-separator beams cut slightly short [25:46][51:58]. Bent plate is shipped loose (welded-on plate stops beams nesting on the truck and the bent-plate edge must stay straight for curtain wall) [80:54]. The galvanized 1/64-inch-tolerance wind-turbine embed shows fabrication QC far tighter than AISC standard, with the fabricator engineer computing both dead-load deflection and concrete float of the embed during placement [58:38].
### Erection Notes
Hoisting governs the plan. On 300 Tryon the GC furnished tower cranes (Peiner SK 415, L4 boom); at the 133-foot lift radius crane capacity is 22,025 lb, limited not by radius but by an 11,000-lb two-part hoist, and an imposed 85 percent safety factor drops allowable to 18,720 lb, which would cap a W14x1400 pick at only 13 feet [30:55][frame slide 45]. The fix: bring in a 275-ton hydro to set the first-tier full columns, then cut upper columns in half and reeve four parts of line on the tower crane, gaining three floors of work while splices are welded to hold schedule [32:50]. Steel is specified delivered to the hook; the erector unloads, checks webs vertical, shakes out on dunnage in a graveled lay-down area, then Christmas-trees up to five beams on a bull tail with a multiple-lift procedure [82:11][85:55]. Sequence plan is set jointly by erector and fabricator, sized by lay-down area and site access (Charlotte allowing trucks only 6 to 7 am), and is generally not stamped unless erecting over occupied space (the McLeod hospital over-build had the whole erection plan stamped) [84:48][86:37]. Marshaling steel to a remote yard is avoided as pure added cost [84:55].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The detail-review slides flag the bad-vs-good edge-of-slab condition (A3 vs A4 on S300): the rejectable detail buries an intermittent 3/16 fillet 2-inch-on-12 weld under the bent plate where the welder cannot reach without angel-wing or rolling scaffold, so a plug or slot weld through the bent plate or a bolted bent-plate support angle with slots is preferred [24:06][frame slide 33]. Deformed bar extending over the top flange is called a tripping hazard and a reason to keep the bent plate off the beam [25:46]. Loose stud plates that sink in the pour should be tack-welded to hold elevation for precast [26:10]. CJP column splices receive ultrasonic testing, and the speaker notes the allowable for a PJP is intentionally lower than a CJP because the code anticipates a welder takes extra care on a joint he knows will be UT'd [52:02]. Flange misalignment at the splice is corrected with a 150-ton porta-power between the flanges to seat a tight backing bar before welding [49:58]. Silica dust is the current exposure concern, mitigated with HEPA drills on concrete connections [37:17].
### Bid / Cost Implications
The estimate is built in pieces and crane picks, not tons; GCs and fabricators convert erection price to dollars-per-ton only as a negotiating metric [09:50]. The headline cost lesson is the CJP-to-PJP conversion on the W14x1400 splices. A full-capacity CJP flange weld holds about 498 cubic inches of weld plus 108 root and 83 in runoff tabs, roughly 193 lb of weld needing about 230 lb of flux-core wire; at 35 lb deposited per shift that is 6.5 man-days per splice. Converting to PJP sized to the actual design tension plus a 200 kip-ft erection load drops it to about 95 lb of flux core at 50 lb deposited per day, 1.9 man-days, saving about 1,800 dollars in direct cost per joint plus large schedule savings [48:52][52:02]. Pricing builds true direct cost first, then a markup (you can mess with markup, never direct cost), then base sales price plus alternates [37:42][frame slide 62]. Contract risk is real: flow-down clauses, pay-when-paid as a condition precedent, requirement-to-proceed-without-change-orders, and liquidated damages the erector tries to cap near 1 percent of contract price [42:01][44:01][frame slide 66]. Weather show-up pay, 440 three-phase power, builders-risk deductibles, and CCIP/OCIP terms are all priced in [37:42][frame slide 17].
### Your Company Application
This video is a direct playbook for Your Company as a combined fabricator-erector. For Ivan's takeoff, mirror the estimate slide: count columns/beams/girders/joists, stud count, vertical X-or-K and horizontal bracing, deck SF, deck edge angle and bent plate, then compute moment-connection and column-splice weld weight as explicit cost drivers, run through aisc_validator.py for member weights rather than trusting LLM math, and price in crane picks not tons. The CJP-to-PJP conversion is a concrete value-engineering lever Mario and the PE stamp can apply: when a splice CJP is sized for full member capacity but the actual demand plus an erection allowance is lower, an in-house PE can stamp a PJP that cuts weld volume and man-days dramatically, with the AWS A2.4 2020 D(S) symbol convention noted for detailing. Mario's AWS D1.1 work gains the D1.8 supplemental note: seismic moment connections need qualified WPS and a separate welder qualification, so screen ACP and any seismic job for that requirement. Tekla detailing should bake in erector-friendly features (column lifting holes, beam holes for catenary and safety cable, bolted-before-welded kicker and brace diagonals, welded angle seats with slotted holes at concrete embeds, loose bent plate). Paul's safety scope maps to the fall-protection content (catenary lines, clamp-on or welded stanchions, HEPA silica drilling). Anchor-rod and embed tolerance work ties to COSP 7.5 and the wind-turbine 1/64-inch embed extreme. For ACP project controls, the Tower Steel Erection sequence table (sequence number, location, description: receive/crib/shake out, stand and plumb columns, box columns with at least 2 bolts per connection, weld splices, install plumb cables per stability plan, final bolt-up/deck/perimeter cable) is a ready template. Doctrine flag: NONE. Note only that the video uses tons-per-dollar as a GC metric while Your Company prices erection in pieces; both are compatible, and nothing here conflicts with the locked BID_RATES or the verify-don't-generate rule.
