## Connection Design as the Fabricator's Representative
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zEUATyZFOEo | Duration: 1:31:59 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is AISC Night School 18 Session 4, presented by Chad Fox PE SE of Ruby and Associates, on the role of the delegated connection designer who works as the fabricator's representative [01:14]. The thesis is that when the engineer of record (EOR) selects delegated design under the AISC Code of Standard Practice, the fabricator's connection engineer must design every connection as its own free-body diagram with a clear understanding of load and load path, while continuously steering geometry toward shop and field efficiency [37:54]. The whole bid-to-build workflow is framed around counting connection types, writing RFIs to remove costly conditions, and choosing repetitive sizes because the cost of a steel building is more about labor time than material weight [57:35].
### Spec References
Code of Standard Practice (COSP) Section 16.3 of the manual [01:42]; COSP referenced in Specification Section A4 [04:53]; COSP Section 3.1.1 three connection-design options [05:35]; COSP Section 3.1.2 EOR-provided info [08:46]; main-member reinforcement options 3A and 3B with price/schedule adjusted per Sections 9.4 and 9.5 (slide pg 17); COSP Section 4.2.3 fabricator change requests [16:28]; COSP Section 4.4 review by ODRD/ODRC (slide pg 23); COSP Section 4.6 RFI process (slide pg 25); COSP Section 7.10 lateral-force-resisting-system description [30:46]. AISC 360 (Specification): Chapter J overall, J2 welding, J3 bolting, J4 connecting-element checks [38:46]; J2-5 fillet-weld directional-strength increase up to 50 percent [62:37]; Table J2.1 groove-weld effective throat [62:37, slide pg 73]; J3.2 minimum bolt spacing 2-2/3 d, 3d recommended [66:34, slide pg 77]; Table J3.4 minimum edge distance [67:32]; J5.2 bearing-bolt fill reduction over 1/4 inch [76:46]; J3.8 slip-critical fill reduction [76:56]; J10.7 and Manual Part 2 top-flange stability [48:42]; Chapter K and Manual Parts 9 and 10 for HSS [38:55, 79:11]; F11 gusset out-of-plane bending and H1 combined axial plus bending [71:35, slide pg 83]. Manual tables/figures cited: Table 1-1 K-det vs K-design [68:34]; Tables 2-4 and 2-5 material selection [56:50]; Table 4-14 critical compression stress [71:56]; Tables 7-14, 7-15, 7-16 bolt clearances [66:51]; Table 7-15 entering/tightening clearance ASTM F3125 A325/A490 (slide pg 77); Tables 8-12 weld passes [62:08]; Table 8.2 PJP/CJP prequalified welds [63:22, 64:58]; Tables 10-14a/b/c skewed shear tabs [46:50]; Figures 8-11, 8-13, 8-14 weld/shelf access [65:53]; Fig 10-32 top-of-steel seated options (slide pg 55); Fig 7-6 prying neutral axis and Fig 9-4 prying variables (slide pg 86). RCSC specification for structural joints using high-strength bolts, in Manual Section 16.2 [78:11]. AWS D1.1 Structural Welding Code Steel [78:35, slide pg 92]. AISC Design Guides cited by number: 4 extended end plates, 13 column stiffening, 16, 17 high-strength bolt primer, 21 welded connections primer, 23 constructability, 24 HSS connections, 29 vertical bracing connections [70:01, 79:39, slide pg 92]. Blodgett Design of Welded Structures cited as outside reference [78:48].
### Technical Details
COSP gives the EOR three options: design all connections, let an experienced detailer select prequalified Manual-table connections, or delegate design (Option 3), with 3A and 3B newly clarified in the 2016 COSP for member reinforcement at connections [05:35, 09:31]. Main-member reinforcement is not connection material, so under 3A the EOR designs it, and under 3B the EOR shows project-specific concepts plus estimated quantities so all bidders price the same scope; if neither is shown, reinforcement is excluded from the bid and later designed by the connection-design PE in final configuration [08:59, 09:52]. Connection-type families covered include simple shear (single and double angle, shear tab, extended shear tab), bracing (gusset, uniform force method), and moment connections (bolted flange plates, extended end plates, false-flange transfers). The uniform force method in Manual Part 13 and Design Guide 29 breaks brace force into gusset-to-beam and gusset-to-column components, and Special Case 2 lets the designer shift the vertical brace component through the gusset-to-column connection to relieve an overloaded beam-web-to-column joint [72:47].
### Fabrication Notes
Move fit-up and assembly to the shop because shop labor is more efficient, tools are available, access heights are lower, and weather is controlled, which usually means shop welding or bolting and field bolting [57:05]. Select readily available material from Tables 2-4 and 2-5: A992 for W and WT shapes, A36 default for channels and angles, and either A36 or A572 Gr 50 for plate since plate cost differs little [56:50]. Fillet welds are preferred, single-pass at 5/16 inch or smaller, and efficient to about 3/4 inch [36:43, 61:43]; PJP welds rank next and a groove weld with a 1/8 inch land plus thicker base material is often cheaper than a CJP of the same size because no backer bar is needed [63:50, slide pg 73]; CJP welds are least preferred because of material prep, backer bars, stringent inspection, and certified welders [64:58]. Watch K-detail dimension for clearances versus K-design for calculations, use standard flange gauge from Table 1-1, and respect fillet radius when squeezing material via Figure 10-3 (riding the fillet) [68:34, 67:11]. Flange plates are oversized in depth to absorb mill rolling variation, then filled with shims, and made wider or narrower than the beam flange to allow corrective fillet welds if bolt holes misalign [76:06, 77:06].
### Erection Notes
The designer must keep the ironworker safe; OSHA erectability requirements sit in Manual Part 2 and govern minimum bolt-up when erecting members [51:43]. Opposing beams framing into column webs or girders over columns require a staggered connection or an erection seat so the first beam stays supported while the second is brought in and bolted, shown in Fig 10-2 [53:25, slide pg 60]. Freestanding columns need four anchor rods and must resist a 300 lb force at 18 inches from the outer column face in any direction, a load case the base-plate designer (usually the EOR) must include [52:45]. A real lesson learned: gussets for fillet-welded HSS braces detailed too tight could not be rotated into position, forcing a week of redesign, so the fix is a maximum-setback dimension at the brace end so the detailer can place it for field fit [70:26]. Slip-critical bolts with oversized or slotted holes ease erection because they tolerate fit-up error, whereas bearing bolts erect faster only when holes line up [85:34].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Envelope-loading confusion is the most common issue: a building with 50 load combinations yields max and min member loads from different combinations, so nodes show apparent through-forces and often lack equilibrium, triggering RFIs to confirm true forces [37:51, 39:15]. Eccentric work lines are a red flag, illustrated by an 8 inch offset producing M = 347 ft-k with no moment listed on the design drawings, which may be a modeling error needing member up-sizing (slide pg 47). Long copes where a shallow beam (W8, 3/16 web) frames into a deep girder (W36) over a 12 inch cope length risk flexural buckling and block shear, fixed by up-sizing to W12 or reinforcing the web per Manual Part 9 [42:09]. Other recurring problems are details copied from prior projects that may not tell the whole story [22:02], stocky beams with no room for shear material, four-inch-flange moment beams with no bolting room, and too many members at one node, which Design Guide 23 and 3D BIM help avoid [50:12].
### Bid / Cost Implications
The slide cost-breakdown pie for erected structural steel is roughly material 28 percent, fabrication 46 percent, erection 26 percent, so less weight is not less cost and up-sizing for repetition is generally favorable [29:13, slide pg 35]. Connection material alone can be 5 to 30 percent of total tonnage, which estimators must not ignore [50:38]. The connection designer's fee is built by counting each connection type, estimating design time per type, and summing; cost drivers that push the fee up are lack of information, lack of clarity, obvious errors, and main-member reinforcement, while repetition of sizes and forces lowers design, detailing, and fabrication cost [27:04, 27:22, 27:55]. The bid-phase count example slide shows W33x152 girders and HSS8x8 braces with axial loads tagged per location (for example A = +/- 80k), demonstrating that loads belong at each node for an efficient bid [35:00, slide pg 35]. Transfer forces released by RFI after bid, or RFI-driven member up-sizing, can constitute a change to contract documents and a legitimate change order [88:23].
### Your Company Application
This video is a direct playbook for Your Company's in-house PE stamp and Tekla detailing flow. Ivan's takeoff should mirror the bid-phase count method: enumerate connection types, flag where the EOR gave half-uniform-dead-load instead of actual shears, and treat connection material as 5 to 30 percent of tonnage rather than a flat allowance, which complements aisc_validator.py member weights since the validator does not carry connection steel. The eccentric-work-line and node-equilibrium checks are concrete count-gap and RFI triggers we should encode before pricing, and the cost pie (fab dominates, material is a minority) reinforces our doctrine that SF-times-psf is ROM only and that repetition lowers true cost. For Mario, the fillet-single-pass-at-5/16, PJP-with-1/8-land-over-CJP, and weld-access guidance map onto AWS D1.1 WPS selection and shop welder qualification; for field bolting, lock the two-bolt-size rule with a 1/4 inch diameter gap (the slide shows 3/4 inch A325 Group A and 1 inch A490 Group B, both ASTM F3125) to prevent wrong-bolt installation. For Paul Guerrero's safety scope, the OSHA four-anchor-rod and 300 lb-at-18-inch column-stability requirement and the erection-seat / staggered-connection rule for opposing beams are erection-sequencing and anchor-rod-tolerance items to carry on ACP and similar jobs. Doctrine conflict: NONE. The conventional-structural-steel framing here matches our positioning, and nothing instructs us to surface supplier names, material costs, or PEMB language.

## Steel Fabrication : A Virtual, Detailed Tour of the Steel Fabrication Process
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6CFDIBILmZ8 | Duration: 1:32:19 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is AISC Night School 18 Session 3, presented by Chris Crosby PE CWI, operations manager at Cianbro Fabrication and Coating (the auto-caption mishears the firm as "Jam bro"), a medium-sized bridge and building fabricator in Georgetown, Massachusetts [00:36][01:22]. Crosby walks the full fabrication chain in five stages: detailing, project management, production, shipping, and quality control [03:53]. His recurring framing is that nothing starts until he has "drawings and steel" [05:01]: detailing produces the drawings, project management procures the steel, and only then can the shop start making sparks [05:39]. The tour follows material flow through a real plant, receiving, cutting, hole-making, layout, fitting, welding or bolting, cambering, cleaning, coating, and shipping [45:43].

### Spec References
The talk is dense with cited references, all stated on slides or aloud. Preferred material grades are in the Steel Construction Manual Tables 2-4 and 2-5 (shapes, plate, bar), with fasteners in Table 2-6 [13:57][15:36][slide 22]. Column splices are in Manual Table 14-3 [22:02][slide 31]. The Code of Standard Practice (COSP) Section 4 covers approval documents: 4.1 owner responsibility, 4.2 fabricator responsibility, 4.3 use of digital files, 4.4 approval, 4.5 documents not furnished by the fabricator, 4.6 the RFI process, 4.7 erection documents [26:21]. COSP Section 3.1.1 gives the OSDR three connection-design options [29:54]. COSP 6.1 covers material identification, 6.2 thermal cutting, 6.4 fabrication tolerances, and 6.4.4 camber tolerances [47:31][53:39][63:54][71:02][slide 102]. AISC 360 (the steel spec) Section M2 covers thermal cutting and M2.5 hole-making, with Section N referenced for the spec chapter and Section A3 / 2.1 for material identification [47:31][56:25]. RCSC Section 3.3 gives hole sizes, Section 4 defines snug-tight, pretensioned, and slip-critical joints, and Section 7 covers pre-installation verification [56:37][61:54]. AWS D1.1 is the structural welding code, with QC tolerances at 5.21 (joint dimensions), 5.22 (welded member dimensions), and 5.23 (weld profiles) [60:40][71:33][slide 102]. SSPC surface-prep classes (SP5 white metal, SP10 near-white) are cited for cleaning [64:48]. Preferred grades named: WF A992, HSS A500 Gr C, channels A36/Gr 50, angle A36 and Gr 50, S and I shapes A36, plate A36 and A572 Gr 50, anchor rods F1554 Gr 36 or Gr 55 [14:01][16:38][slide 22].

### Technical Details
Connection types discussed are double-angle clip angles (bolted-bolted, welded-bolted) and shear tabs, chosen by shop equipment and skill rather than by load alone [17:44][88:26]. Column splices shown are a full-penetration flange splice with a bolted web [23:42]. Systems covered include multi-story moment frames, trusses, plate girders (built-up, with SAW and flange butt splices), a football stadium, and a pedestrian bridge [38:50][20:35]. The model-based detailing workflow generates the Advanced Bill of Material (ABM) for mill ordering and also spits out filled bolt quantities and erector point-to-point lists [10:11][85:48]. Cambering is by mechanical hydraulic ram or by heat (vees applied to web and flange, with temperature-indicating crayons to avoid overheating), to offset dead-load deflection; tolerances per COSP 6.4.4 [63:08][82:43].

### Fabrication Notes
Material identification and traceability run from receiving to the point of assembly per AISC 360 2.1 and COSP 6.1 [47:31]. On receipt, a visual inspection per A6 catches kinks, bends, and flange tilt; non-conforming pieces are set aside for QC disposition [47:55]. Each piece is marked with heat number, PO number, job number, and size, then staged by yard location; a pull ticket plus a nested cut list releases it to the floor, and mill test reports are filed behind the PO for traceability back to heat [48:27][51:34]. Cutting uses horizontal bandsaws for wide flange, channel, and large angle; CNC plasma and oxyfuel burn tables for plate (oxyfuel for thick plate); and an angle master (punch-and-cut) for angle, flat bar, and small channel [52:48][53:49]. Holes are drilled or punched per AISC 360 M2.5 and RCSC 3.3 [56:25]. Layout uses a flange-gauge template and soapstone, with automated scribing of part marks and weld symbols on more-automated lines [58:25]. The whole shop runs under an AISC-certification quality management system with documented, implemented procedures for every step, control of nonconformance, and corrective action [67:54].

### Erection Notes
Erection drawings are the "jigsaw puzzle" instructions tying piece marks to locations; the erector's needs (column splice type, perimeter cable holes, perimeter-railing bolt holes, and shop-versus-field assembly decisions) must be settled at kickoff so the detailer draws once [21:01][24:22]. Whether pieces ship as large shop assemblies or stick-build in the field drives crane sizing and field crew size [25:23]. Sequencing (which corner to start) is set at the project kickoff with the GC and erector in the room; Crosby recounts a large Indiana job that started in the wrong corner and caused major problems [33:34][88:13]. Shipping limits constrain assembly size: standard flatbed 8'-6" wide, 5'-0" bed height, 48 or 53 ft; legal load up to 8'-9" wide, 13'-6" high, 55 ft; permit/signage to 14 ft wide and 85 ft; super-loads beyond that need escorts, with very long pieces (130-135 ft) on special trailers or barge [65:48][slide 98].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The named field and process errors are scope-of-supply gaps (missed lintels, stair and rail items, davits) that surface as field calls [07:43]; starting detailing or erection in the wrong corner [33:34]; and web buckling when cambering, especially on superlight members, if the ram presses only at midspan instead of hitting three to five points along the beam [82:55][83:47]. Visual receiving inspection per A6 rejects kinked, bent, or flange-tilted mill material for QC disposition [47:55]. Crosby notes that bolts shipped to the field too early "grow legs and walk off," so bolt lists are pulled from the model only after shop drawings go out for approval [86:16].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Mill ordering drives schedule and cost: large-tonnage jobs go to the mill against published rolling schedules (which show roll dates but not whether tonnage is already sold, so you still phone the mill), in bundle quantities and minimum truckloads of roughly 42,000 to 48,000 lb; small jobs buy from a warehouse/service center [10:11][36:00][40:05]. Preferred grades matter because they are readily available at the mills; off-preferred grades cost time and money [13:30]. Standard stock choices (96-by-240 plate, 20 ft flat bar and angle, 21 ft HSS, mill-bundle clip angles) reduce drops and handling [37:30][38:14]. Connection-type choice is an economics decision: a highly automated drill-line shop bolts faster, a high-skill welding shop welds faster, so the standard detail is set to the plant, not the other way around [17:44][88:26]. CVN (impact) and other ASTM A6/A992 supplemental tests, when the OSDR requires them, add mill cost and must be ordered up front [35:23].

### Your Company Application
Maps directly to Your Company workstreams. Ivan's takeoff is the ABM and mill-order step: the talk validates building a measured member list from the model before pricing, and the Table 2-4/2-5/2-6 and F1554 Gr 36/55 grades line up with bridge/aisc_validator.py and the A992/A500/A572 inputs Ivan should hold to. Mario's shop and welding work covers fitting, AWS D1.1 welder qualification and WPS submittal, and the bolted-versus-welded standard-connection call that should reflect Your Company's own equipment and crew skill, with RCSC Section 4 joint types and Section 7 pre-installation verification (3 bolts per lot per diameter/length, turn-of-nut) governing field bolting. Paul's safety scope is reinforced by the filtered-air welding hoods, perimeter cable holes, and pre-bolted perimeter-railing holes that let the erector guard the edge immediately. Tekla detailing is the model-to-ABM-to-bolt-list pipeline, including auto-scribed part marks and weld symbols. The in-house PE stamp question is answered cleanly at [80:01]: design documents and any option-3 fabricator-engineered connections need a PE stamp; shop drawings themselves should not be stamped (they are an interpretation), and when an EOR asks for a seal the right move is an RFI requesting a review letter instead, which Joseph and the PE should adopt as standing policy. Anchor rods tie to F1554 grades; joists and deck appear under buyout submittals (certs of conformance, coatings, joist and deck shop drawings). For ACP controls, the COSP Section 4 submittal sequence, RFI logs, and connection-design option (3.1.1) belong in the project register. Doctrine flags: NONE. The presenter names mills (Nucor-Yamato, Steel Dynamics, ArcelorMittal) generically as the speaker's own examples, so they are reported as cited, not added as Your Company supplier references; do not carry them onto any client document.

## The Manufacturing of Structural Steel Shapes
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bhy5zrqTxo8 | Duration: 24:58 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is AISC Night School session two, presented by two plant metallurgists from a mill in Blytheville, Arkansas, covering how structural shapes are made from scrap to finished beam, not how they are fabricated or erected [00:02]. The core teaching is mill metallurgy: chemistry control, the grade specifications a fabricator reads on a Mill Test Report (MTR), and the production sequence of scrap yard, electric arc furnace (EAF) melting, ladle metallurgical furnace (LMF) refining, casting to beam blanks or blooms, reheating, and rolling to finish length [02:09]. The recurring theme is that strength is bought through controlled micro-alloy additions rather than carbon, to preserve weldability and Charpy V-notch toughness [10:15].
### Spec References
ASTM grades named: A992 (typical wide-flange grade), A572 grade 50, A588 grade B (weathering), A36, A913 (quenched and self-tempered, grades 50/65/70), and A690 (marine piling) [09:14][14:53][08:44]. The carbon equivalency (CE) formula is stated to be carried in A992 and used as the weldability indicator [05:43]. Welding-standard committees named: AWS D1.1 and AWS D1M (one speaker is a committee member and CWI), plus ASTM A102 committee work [01:09]. No AISC 360 chapter, AISC 341 seismic section, RCSC clause, or Design Guide number was cited in this metallurgy session.
### Technical Details
Structural carbon runs roughly 5 to 10 points (0.05 to 0.10 percent) with iron at about 97 to 98 percent; low carbon protects toughness, ductility, and weldability [03:09]. Manganese is the main strengthener after carbon at about one-sixth the strengthening effect, near 1 percent in A992, A572, and A588, and it ties up sulfur to improve rolled surface [04:42]. Micro-alloys vanadium and columbium (niobium) strengthen by grain refinement through nitride and carbide precipitation during rolling, at very small additions (15, 10, 5 max) [07:44]. A588 must hold copper, nickel, and chromium (chromium 40 to 70) inside ranges and meet a corrosion index of 6.0 or higher to qualify as a weathering grade [13:22]. A913 reaches grade-65 properties at grade-50 weldability through in-line quench and self-temper, and its CE is spec-set at 0.38, 0.43, and 0.45, with a mandated Charpy V-notch [14:53].
### Fabrication Notes
This session does not cover shop fabrication, fit-up, or QC. The only fabrication-adjacent content is upstream weldability: CE indicates heat-affected-zone hardenability and potential cracking, which the mill controls by chemistry while the fabricator controls cooling rate, preheat, and filler metal [05:43]. A992 carries a yield-to-tensile ratio for seismic ductility, and elongation across grades runs about 18 to 20 percent [13:52].
### Erection Notes
No erection, field procedure, sequencing, bracing, or rigging content appears in this video. It ends inside the EAF charging step.
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
No inspection failures or rejection categories are discussed. The closest content is the impurity controls the mill enforces: phosphorus held to 0.035 max on A992 and 0.040 elsewhere, sulfur to 0.05 max, and aluminum minimized because excess makes steel very brittle [10:46][12:51]. These are chemistry limits, not field rejections.
### Bid / Cost Implications
Scrap chemistry drives steel cost: lower-residual scrap (number one heavy melt) is the premium feed and the cleaner, lower-residual the charge, the cheaper the resulting steel; residual copper, chrome, nickel, and molybdenum bump yield and tensile by 3 to 4 KSI as a side effect [19:53][07:14]. For estimating, the practical takeaway is that grade choice (A992 versus A913 versus A588 weathering) carries a real material-cost and availability difference that should be sourced, not assumed.
### Your Company Application
For Ivan, this confirms reading the MTR grade and CE before takeoff and treating A992, A572-50, A588, and A913 as distinct line items with distinct cost and lead time; A913 is the grade to watch where weldability at higher strength matters. For Mario and AWS D1.1 welding, the CE and HAZ-cracking discussion reinforces matching preheat and filler to the delivered grade, since the mill controls chemistry but the shop controls cooling and preheat [05:43]. A588 weathering steel and A913 are conventional structural steel grades, fully consistent with Your Company positioning and with no PEMB language. This video has no anchor-rod, joist, field-bolting, Tekla, PE-stamp, or ACP-controls content. Doctrine conflict: NONE.

## Night School 6, Session 3: Bracing Connection Details and Prying Action
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=96MiMz1MYZ8 | Duration: 1:27:53 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
William A. Thornton (cives, TR Higgins 1995) teaches the three common bracing-connection details at a column and the AISC 14th edition manual prying-action method that governs two of them. The three details are double clip angles, shear tabs or shear plates, and end plates [02:08]. Prying action is the additional bolt tension Q that develops when a relatively flexible fitting (column flange, WT, clip angle, end plate) bends, so the real bolt force P+Q exceeds the applied demand T [10:25][12:01]. Clip-angle and end-plate connections require a prying check; the conventional single-column shear tab does not, which is its main advantage [05:13][14:33].
### Spec References
Speaker-cited references: the prying requirement appears in the 2010 AISC Specification (14th edition manual) and in every spec since the 7th edition (about 1970), worded as required tensile strength shall include any tension from prying produced by deformation of connected parts [09:22][09:54]. Detailed method is Part 9 of the 14th edition manual [10:25][22:51]. Appendix 3 paragraph 3.2 (fatigue) requires elastic stress including prying, and the manual prying method is NOT elastic [33:16][68:00]. Bearing shear-tension interaction is Specification Section J3.7 [44:36]; slip-critical interaction is Sections J3.8 and J3.9 [57:03][62:48]; bolt strengths from Table J3.2 (also Manual Tables 7-1, 7-2) and pretension from Table J3.1 [42:31][65:28]; slip-critical shear from Manual Table 7-3 [58:08]. He also names AASHTO 10.32.3.3.2 for elastic fatigue prying Q [33:48]. The F-sub-y to F-sub-u change traces to Swanson, Engineering Journal 2002.
### Technical Details
The simplified model is the Struik and de Back two-hinge model (Delft, 1969), with the bolt force placed at the inner edge of the bolt and moments M1 at the stem line and M2 at the bolt line [14:33][15:35]. Geometry: a is toe-to-bolt-center, b is bolt-center-to-fitting-face, with a-prime and b-prime adjusted by half a bolt diameter, rho equals b-prime over a-prime, and delta equals 1 minus hole-width over tributary length p [16:06][49:13]. T-sub-C is the fitting thickness that fully develops the bolt design strength B; any thickness beyond T-sub-C wastes material [23:54][50:49]. Since the 13th edition, F-sub-u (not F-sub-y) is used in the flange-bending limit because strain hardening lifts capacity, while phi stays 0.9 [22:19][23:23]. Alpha-prime locates the design in admissible space: greater than 1 means the fitting controls (use alpha=1), less than 0 means the bolts control (use alpha=0), between 0 and 1 means both control [34:19][35:22]. Two reciprocal algorithms, analysis and design, return the same connection [38:55][55:28].
### Fabrication Notes
Clip angles are praised for ease of fabrication because the beam is cut slightly short with a setback of about half an inch, and angle placement absorbs over-run or under-run [03:09][03:40]. Rolled angles have a maximum thickness around an inch; common stocked thicknesses are quarter, five sixteenths, three eighths, half, five eighths, three quarters, seven eighths, and one inch, so you cannot always hit an exact required thickness [04:11][52:53]. End plates are hard to fabricate: the beam must be cut to exact length and the plate tends to curl from weld heat, which can compromise the out-to-out dimension; fillers correct under-run or over-run [07:47][08:19]. Shear tabs eliminate drilling thick column flanges, a major fabrication saving on heavy columns with three to four inch flanges [05:13][76:25].
### Erection Notes
Shear tabs erect the easiest: the beam with gusset attached is slipped in sideways, set on a drift pin at each end with a bolt or two, the erection crew moves on, and the bolt-up crew finishes [05:13][78:30]. Double clips and end plates need the piece slid down between or onto column flanges, which is slower. End plates minimize pieces but leave little erection tolerance [68:00]. Thornton cited a power-plant job where switching from double clips to shear tabs let the customer report the job came in about two million dollars under estimate, and an erector offered a deductive of fifty dollars per beam to convert clips to shear tabs [76:25][78:30].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The recurring design error is ignoring prying and assuming the bolt sees only the applied tension when the real force is T+Q, which can be much higher on a thin or flexible fitting [12:32]. Failing to check the column flange itself: even an adequate clip or end plate can be governed by a thinner column flange, so prying must be evaluated on both sides of the connection [08:51][13:32]. A real field consequence named was buildings ending up wider at the top floor than the bottom because end-plate weld curl and column over-roll were not managed [74:50]. He warns against welding double angles at their toes to a column, calling it ineffective with no published method, and advises designing as if column stiffeners are absent rather than relying on partial stiffening [82:36][70:14].
### Bid / Cost Implications
Detail choice is the cost lever. The shear tab is the most economical of the three: easiest to fabricate (no flange drilling), no prying analysis, and easiest to erect [77:27]. Avoiding drilling of thick column flanges is the largest fabrication saving on heavy jobs, with the two-million-dollar power-plant example and the fifty-dollar-per-beam erection deductive as concrete figures [76:25][78:30]. Over-thick fittings beyond T-sub-C add no capacity and only waste material and money [50:49]. The worked example showed a connection that looked like it had four to five times margin on raw bolt tension (29.6 vs 6.5 kips) drop to a real available strength of 10.4 kips per bolt once prying was applied, so screening on raw bolt values overstates capacity [43:35][51:51].
### Your Company Application
For Ivan takeoff and estimating, the detail-selection logic is the cost driver: default to conventional single-column shear tabs at columns to cut flange drilling, prying analysis, and erection time, and flag clip-angle or end-plate details as higher fabrication and erection cost. For Tekla detailing and the in-house PE stamp, the Part 9 prying method (T-sub-C, alpha-prime, rho, delta, F-sub-u not F-sub-y, J3.7 bearing and J3.8/J3.9 slip-critical interaction) is the governing check on every brace-to-column connection carrying axial plus shear, and the column flange must be checked on both sides. For Mario shop work, the half-inch setback on clips absorbs beam length tolerance, while end plates need exact-length cuts and weld-curl control to avoid out-to-out drift. For Paul safety and field bolting, the shear-tab drift-pin-then-bolt-up sequence is the cleaner erection method. Anchor-rod and base-plate prying and seismic anchor design were explicitly deferred by the speaker to a later session, so do not treat this video as guidance on anchor-rod prying [84:09][85:10]. Doctrine flags: NONE; this is conventional structural steel content with no PEMB language and no supplier numbers to surface.

## Night School 6, Session 5: Vertical Bracing Connections - Corner Connection Part 2
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BgOAwTEitLU | Duration: 1:32:00 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
William A. Thornton works a complete high-seismic corner bracing connection for a Special Concentrically Braced Frame (SCBF), an HSS brace into a single hinge plate (knife plate) that releases in-plane brace buckling rather than the usual out-of-plane two-T hinge zone [02:04][02:34][09:09]. The connection uses an extended shear plate to the column web and is solved by the Uniform Force Method Special Case 4, which models the column-web connection as if it were a column flange by taking the section out to the centroid of the bolt group [29:30][61:13]. The whole design chases four sub-connections (brace-to-gusset, gusset-to-column, gusset-to-beam, beam-to-column) and shows that nearly every limit state is loaded close to 1.0, unlike the non-seismic case in the prior session [07:46][60:08].

### Spec References
AISC 341-10 seismic provisions Section F2.6a (brace tensile demand Ry Fy Ag) [08:16][08:47]; F2.6a-2 (compressive demand, lesser of Ry Fy Ag and 1.14 Fcr Ag) [11:24]; F2.5b3 (slot-reinforcement attached for expected strength) [27:00]; F2.6a ductility three options, simple-connection 0.025 rad [35:13]. AISC 360 specification equation E3-4 (elastic/critical buckling) [10:22]; Section J4.4a (slenderness under 25, buckling not a limit state) [16:01]; block-shear equation J4-5 [17:34][38:04]; Table D3.1 case 6 for shear-lag X-bar [22:48]; Table J3.2 bolt shear [37:45]; local web yielding formula J10-3 [66:25]. AISC Manual 14th edition Table 7-7 (C-prime, instantaneous center, here 172) [38:17] and Table 10-2 buckling stress with phi (41.2 ksi) [20:09]; Manual Part 9 and Part 10 (extended shear-plate ductility, ~0.03 rad rotation) [35:43][74:00]. ASTM A325-N bolts and ASTM A500 HSS, all Grade 50 plate [07:15][07:46]. RCSC is named as a committee Thornton serves on but no pretensioning clause is cited [01:02].

### Technical Details
The brace is an HSS 5x5x3/8 (Fy 46, Ry 1.4) at 45 degrees, tensile demand 398 kips, compressive demand 312 kips at KL/r 63.1 [08:47][10:52]. The hinge plate is 1 in by 10 in Grade 50, sized for tension yield, checked for rupture (457 kips) across the 5/8 in slot, and confirmed against side-sway buckling at KL/r 12.5 using a hinge width of 3t per Taiwan and University of Washington research rather than the usual 2t [12:24][14:59][33:00]. The gusset settles at 1/2 in, sized by block shear and the Whitmore section (30-degree spread, length 21.8 in), which Thornton stresses is the main tool for checking gusset buckling along the line of action at K=0.5 [17:34][18:34][19:39]. The slotted HSS net area falls below gross, so it gets a pair of 3/8 in by 2-7/8 in reinforcing plates sized to stay inside the 3-5/16 in workable flat for fillet welding on the flat face [22:15][24:50].

### Fabrication Notes
The hinge plate is slotted to receive the gusset, not the reverse, because gusset stresses are less well known than the hinge plate [13:59]. Slot width is gusset thickness plus 1/8 in for assembly; the HSS net section subtracts the 1-1/8 in slot per wall [14:29][22:48]. Reinforcing-plate length is 6 in weld plus 6 in weld plus an erection clearance dimension X that the detailer cannot fully fix because it depends on how the erector inserts the brace [27:59][82:01]. In practice the reinforcing weld is run continuous, though technically you need 6 in of weld before the slot starts and 6 in after load transfers into the hinge plate [83:35][84:05]. Final fillet welds: gusset-to-beam 1/2 in for the first 6-3/4 in (one-sided because the beam flange is blocked and shipped flush), 1/4 in for the remaining 15 in, and a missing weld symbol on the reinforcing plates should read 1/4 in by 6 in [64:52][67:26][68:00].

### Erection Notes
Brace cut length is the work-point-to-work-point length (17 ft) minus twice the pull-back at each end (3 ft 7 in per end), giving an unbraced length of 118 in [09:18][09:49]. The erection clearance X in the slot exists only so the brace can be jockeyed into place after the beam and gusset above are set; Thornton has seen 1 in, 2 in, and up to 6 in used depending on the erector's sequence [82:33][83:03]. The beam ships flush at the cope, which limits the gusset-to-beam weld to one side over part of its length [65:22].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Historically, gussets that ran the brace connection far out on unsupported plate buckled along the line of action; roofs came down and crews had to jack the structure and add reinforcing plates, which is exactly the failure the Whitmore buckling check now prevents [21:11][21:42]. A biaxial block-shear interaction check on the shear plate first came out at 1.14, over by 14 percent, forcing a move from a 1/2 in to a 5/8 in and ultimately 3/4 in plate [46:42][58:01]. Thornton flags that slotting the HSS directly to the gusset with no hinge line is a design error unless you then design for the full flexural strength of the brace, 1.1 Ry Fy Z [73:41][74:13]. A reviewer question confirms the slot reinforcement is mandatory because the provisions require effective net area to exceed gross, even though one researcher reported never seeing a slot failure in testing [80:28][81:28].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Thornton notes the connection is compact for shipping (about 4 ft from beam bottom flange to plate tip) even with 18 in of plate sticking out, so it is well within shipping limits [70:02][70:32]. He repeatedly points out where you could sharpen the pencil: the shear plate could drop from 3/4 in to 5/8 in if you do not assume worst-case biaxial loading, and the 18 in of 1/4 in fillet could shorten to 10 to 12 in with larger welds, though the 10-bolt count fixes the minimum plate length either way [58:01][70:32][70:50]. He distinguishes the conservative one-off hand calc (cover every worst case) from a vetted computer program that could refine each load case, accepting deliberate overkill to guarantee coverage on a manual design [53:25][53:56].

### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, this is the seismic premium made concrete: an HSS brace connection in an SCBF carries a 1 in hinge plate, two slot-reinforcement plates, a heavy 3/4 in extended shear plate, and a 33 in deep bolt group with 10 to 11 bolts, far more steel and labor than the non-seismic double-clip connection. For Tekla detailing, the slot must be longer than the reinforcing plate by an erection X dimension, the hinge plate is slotted (never the gusset), and reinforcing-plate width must respect the HSS workable flat so Mario's crew fillet-welds on the flat, not the radius [24:50][82:01]. For Mario's shop, welds are A325-N bolting plus 1/4 in and 1/2 in fillets with minimum fillet governed by the thinner of gusset or HSS wall; the beam ships flush at the cope, so plan one-sided access there [64:52][71:34]. For the in-house PE stamp, the controlling references to capture in a calc package are AISC 341-10 F2.6a demand equations, Manual Part 10 ductility (plate yields before bolt/weld fracture, 0.03 rad), and the Whitmore buckling check; note that Uniform Force Method Special Case 4 is not in the AISC Manual and rests on the lower-bound theorem, so a reviewer may question it [29:30][77:24]. Doctrine flags: NONE. This is conventional structural steel, no PEMB language, and AISC weights and member properties still route through aisc_validator.py rather than these spoken numbers.

## Night School 6, Session 4: Vertical Bracing Connections - Corner Connection Part 1
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p3lIEY5YNh8 | Duration: 1:33:14 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
William Thornton works one full wind/low-seismic corner bracing connection start to finish, an SD example out of the AISC 14th edition Manual using the uniform force method (UFM) [02:07][03:44]. The key teaching point is that a single brace-to-corner connection is really four connections, each with its own limit-state stack: brace-to-gusset, gusset-to-column, gusset-to-beam, and beam-to-column [02:40]. The design sequence starts at the brace-to-gusset interface because that sets the gusset geometry, then walks the forces through each interface [05:16][77:31]. Many limit states repeat across the four interfaces, so once a check is shown it is skipped on later interfaces [03:11].

### Spec References
Cited verbatim by the speaker: AISC 14th edition Manual and Specification (ASD example) [03:44]; Spec Section J3.6 implied via block shear Section J4.3 (block shear equation) [11:29][50:33]; Table 7-1 bolt single-shear values [05:46]; Table 7-15 not cited; Table B3.1 (now D3.1) shear-lag U cases, case 2 [07:52][08:22]; Table J3.2 bolt tensile/shear strengths, Group A bolts [38:34][78:34]; Table 4-22 critical-stress table for KL/r [27:06][27:36]; Manual Part 1 (X-bar tables) [08:53]; Manual Part 8 weld tables, Table 8-8 (eccentric C-shaped weld coefficient) and Table 8-3 (electrode C1) [55:46][57:50][58:22]; Manual Part 13 (couple distribution discussion) [35:54]; Manual equation 9-3 (T-min weld/base-metal) and equation 9-33 (prying Q) [46:52][59:28]. References to AISC Engineering Journal papers (Gross 1990 K=0.5 gusset effective length; Dowswell 2006 gusset buckling; Hewitt/Thornton 2004 weld ductility 1.25 factor) and a Modern Steel Construction Whitmore article (July 2011) [27:36][28:06][63:43][82:11].

### Technical Details
Brace is a WT6x22.5 (A992 Gr 50), brace force plus or minus 75 kip, brace slope 43.6 degrees, UFM angle from vertical 46.4 degrees, gusset is a 3/8 inch plate A36 [03:44][04:14][13:00]. Eight A325 bolts, 3/4 inch diameter, threads excluded, standard 13/16 holes, 3 inch spacing, single-shear ASD value 11.9 kip each so 8 x 11.9 = 95.2 kip > 75 [05:16][05:46][06:16]. Whitmore section length 15.9 inches spread at 30 degrees each side, buckling K = 0.5, KL/r = 41, Fcr/Omega = 19.7 ksi giving 83 kip > 75 [25:31][26:31][27:06][29:06]. UFM geometry: beta-bar 8.5 inches (centered on the 16-7/8 inch gusset edge), ideal alpha 11.5 inches, but the 20 inch weld forces alpha-bar = 10.5 inches; the ideal value must be used in r = 24.2 or the forces will not close [31:43][33:20][33:50]. Resulting interface forces: Vb 25.4, Hb shear 35.6, Mb 25.4 kip-in, Vc 26.3, Hc 18.8 kip [34:20][34:51][35:23].

### Fabrication Notes
The gusset is a 3/8 inch A36 plate; double angles are 4x4x3/8 Gr 36 with horizontal short slots in the outstanding leg and 1-1/4 inch edge distance [04:14]. Minimum fillet weld for 3/8 inch plate or 3/8 inch angle is 1/4 inch, and every weld in the example is checked against that minimum and against the gusset base-metal shear-rupture T-min (gusset-to-beam T-min works out to 0.101 inch < 3/8) [58:22][65:45][59:28]. The 20 inch horizontal gusset-to-beam weld length is prescribed up front [03:44]. Holes are standard 3/4 inch (13/16 nominal) unless noted; net-section and shear-lag effects from the WT stem being unconnected drive the U = 0.874 reduction [04:14][08:22][08:53].

### Erection Notes
This is shop-detailed connection design, so explicit field/crane/rigging procedure is light. The practical erection-driven guidance: use the same beam depth on both sides of the column to avoid eccentricities on transfer forces, and use decent-size beams and columns because a brace node-connected in the analysis model may carry 400 kip the beam never "sees," making a tiny beam impossible to connect without doubler plates and stiffeners [76:31][77:01][77:31]. The 1/2 inch setback at the brace and the gusset-to-framing fit-up dimensions are fixed by the UFM geometry [33:20].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Block shear of the WT and of the gusset is the most-emphasized failure mode, with separate tear-out paths for shear and for the axial component [10:58][51:03][52:06]. Bolt capacity is wrong if only single shear is checked: five limit states apply per bolt (bolt shear, bearing on main material, bearing on connection material, tear-out on main, tear-out on connection), take the least of the five for each bolt and sum [18:41][22:25][49:13]. A recurring engineer error is picking a brace member without regard to how it connects, ignoring net-section and shear-lag loss [07:20][77:31]. Using alpha-bar instead of ideal alpha in the UFM r-term makes the forces fail to balance [33:50]. Block shear of the beam is NOT checked for the vertical component because the beam is not coped and there is no recognized failure mode for ripping out the top flange [73:58].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Thornton answers a direct cost question: total engineering hours for one connection like this, from receiving loads to issuing a design sheet, runs about an hour, sometimes 20 minutes if connection pictures can be reused from prior jobs [78:35][80:09][81:11]. The calculations themselves run fast with in-house software, but data input is about 10 minutes and drawing/checking dominate the rest; AutoCAD pictures are not auto-generated from the calc [80:09]. Anyone doing these professionally needs a spreadsheet or hard-coded program; doing more than a couple by hand is uneconomic [79:07][81:11]. Economy levers when a connection will not work: change the force distribution (special-case Delta-Vb), enlarge a too-compact gusset, or upsize the beam/column [75:30][76:01].

### Your Company Application
This is the canonical worked example for Your Company's in-house PE stamp on conventional braced-frame corners: the four-interface sequence, UFM geometry, and the full block-shear/Whitmore/prying/weld stack are exactly what our connection design sheets must show, and the 1-hour-per-connection figure is a usable basis for Ivan to price engineering hours folded into fab and erection rates [78:35][80:09]. For takeoff through aisc_validator.py, every member here (WT6x22.5, 4x4x3/8 angles, the gusset plate) must pull its weight and section properties from the validator, never from LLM math, and the WT net-section/shear-lag warning reinforces our "verify, do not generate" rule on member selection [07:20][09:57]. Mario's shop crew gets the 1/4 inch minimum fillet for 3/8 inch material and the threads-excluded A325 bolting basis as concrete WPS/fit-up inputs [58:22][05:46]. The five-limit-state-per-bolt rule and block-shear-for-both-directions are good Tekla detailing QC checks. No conflict with Your Company doctrine: this is conventional structural steel, no PEMB language, A325 bearing-type bolts in standard holes with no slip-critical claim. Doctrine flags: NONE.

## The Splice is Right
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aVtV6LWfoMg | Duration: 1:29:44 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is a five-speaker Pecha Kucha session covering column, truss, and member splices across the full lifecycle: design (Carol Drucker), fabrication (Sylvie Boulanger), erection (Larry Owner of Douglas Steel), welded connections (Duane Miller of Lincoln Electric), and architecturally exposed structural steel splices (Tara Mayer Bulic). The governing theme is that a splice is for shipping, handling, and constructability, and is "right" when it is simplified, the complex welding stays in the shop, and the field splice is direct, accessible, and discreet [06:43][17:11][41:32]. A splice is distinct from a connection: it rejoins one continuous member that was cut for transport, so it should disappear from view [51:57][89:06].
### Spec References
Speakers cited the following: AISC Manual Part 14 for standard gravity column splices [07:15]; Manual splice "type 8" carrying both PJP and CJP welded options, with Manual PJP sizes matching the spec minimum PJP sizes by material thickness [08:16]; ASCE 7-05 (ASD) and ASCE 7-10 (LRFD) for wind, plus ASCE 37 for construction-period loads with its wind-velocity reduction factor [07:46]; the AISC Seismic Provisions requiring gravity columns to carry shear equal to the least plastic moment strength at the splice over column height, with intermediate/special concentric braced frame and BRB columns at twice that, and the 2016 seismic provisions newly allowing PJP welds in IMF/SMF splices "with restrictions" where CJP had been required [10:22][11:24]; the AISC specification compression-splice stability force of 50% of compression acting in tension, or shear/moment from 2% of compression for members other than columns [12:59]; AISC Design Guide 1 base plates [10:22], Design Guide 4 extended end plates [13:32], and Design Guide 10 erection bracing listing bending failure of the base plate, buckling of anchor rods, and anchor-rod pullout [39:28]; the 14th edition Manual fill-plate rule capping the bolt reduction at 15% [15:05]; OSHA 1926 Subpart R, specifically 1926.756 (300 lb eccentric load 18 in from the column face) and 1926.760 plus the perimeter-column 48 in extension and 42 to 45 in cable-hole provisions [30:38][31:10]; RCSC for the limited slip-critical range and the bearing X/N bolt thickness check [81:07]; AWS D1.1 preheat thresholds [77:18].
### Technical Details
Gravity column splices need minimal calculation and the contractor can pick any Manual Part 14 type [07:15]. With tension or lateral load the splice must be designed; first check whether tension exists at all, and with an envelope solution pair minimum axial with maximum moment so compression is not overstated [09:19]. Built-up and box-column welds are analyzed as a line weld (force per unit length over available stress to size the throat), with a plastic stress-block method available to cut bolts or weld size [09:50]. Truss splices distribute force by area (shear lag U = 1 when each element is connected) or assign all tension to the flanges with the web taking shear [14:35]. Sharing axial load between bolts and welds in one splice is a "no-no" due to strain-compatibility [16:08].
### Fabrication Notes
The repeated fabrication principle is to push complex welding into the shop where it is controlled and leave a simple direct splice for the field [17:11][19:17]. Order material only after the splice location is fixed; a shop CJP splice was used to extend a member to allow a bolted field splice [15:37]. In the shop a PJP is preferred over CJP to cut weld volume, but field splices trend CJP for fit-up [15:37]. Weld access holes on CJP truss splices must be remembered so the web is not lost, and they can be large enough to see daylight through [16:40]. Trial fit-up of complex splices in the shop or yard is a core "splice is right" tip: a two-story transfer truss was laid on its side filling the whole shop, splice plates used as drilling templates for shim and diagonal, and the bottom chord was never released until the top fit and was re-bolted before shipping [23:24][24:24]. Heavy three to three-and-a-half inch column splice plates take one welder a week each, involving web plates, preheat, heating/warming, and final bolting [27:27].
### Erection Notes
Larry Owner framed erection around OSHA Subpart R and constructability. Column splices are located five feet above finished floor so splice plates do not interfere with the perimeter safety cable, since OSHA's 48 in is a minimum not a maximum, and 60 in is a convenient working height [33:46][41:01]. Columns should not run more than two stories due to weak-axis bending under the eccentric erection load plus wind [34:48][41:01]. Erection aids or two channels on either side of the web stabilize a welded splice before the weld is made, then are removed [36:52][37:54]. Where an upper shaft is smaller, move the gauge line and keep a flat (not tapered) splice plate [36:20]. The column-to-concrete base is itself a splice: oversized washers dropped over the anchor rods keep shim stacks from being kicked over and preserve base elevation [40:29]. Field welding skill loss is managerial and experiential, not technological; preheat is the welder's friend in cold weather [62:18][77:18].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Named failures: anchor-rod pullout, buckled anchor rods, broken-off anchor rods, kicked-over shim stacks, and base-plate bending failure during erection [39:28][40:29]. Putting the column splice at mid-height or too low forces a worker into a man-lift and can violate Subpart R when splice plates sit where the perimeter cable belongs [32:12]. CJP welds specified where a PJP or bolted detail would do are an over-design that draws fabricator pushback; engineers of record are urged to give forces rather than dictate CJP [16:08][84:29]. The X-bolt field risk is the wrong-length bolt from the bolt bag leaving the nut not flush, requiring careful inspection and a bold cloud on the erection diagram [81:07]. Bad welds: incomplete grinding that looks worse than as-welded, and over-polishing that removes weld strength and takes paint unevenly [49:22].
### Bid / Cost Implications
The headline number: a bolted splice of a W14x730 tension chord needed about 6,900 extra pounds of steel and 128 high-strength bolts, while a welded version used roughly 70 pounds of weld metal, and contractor pricing showed a 79% cost reduction for the welded connection [42:34][43:37]. Butt-plate column splices are the most cost-effective when architecture allows [11:57]. Bearing bolts in oversized holes can cut truss-splice bolt count by 50% versus slip-critical [13:32], and an X-bolt is a 25% strength gain essentially for free when the ply thickness already creates the condition [83:12]. Engineering-record CJP defaults and "pay the EOR for the forces" practice add avoidable cost [85:29]. AESS adds attention and cost: distance-to-view (a 20 ft threshold) decides where to fuss, since beyond 20 ft splices need far less remediation [50:56][51:26].
### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, the W14x730 example is the case to encode: a welded shop splice can replace thousands of pounds of bolted-splice steel and over a hundred bolts, so the splice-method assumption materially swings tonnage and bolt count fed through aisc_validator.py. Mario's shop and welding lead role maps directly to the weld-in-shop, bolt-in-field doctrine, the PJP-over-CJP shop preference, weld-access-hole discipline, and the AWS D1.1 preheat rule (preheat to 70 F below 32 F, stop at 0 F for welder comfort) [77:18]. Paul's safety scope is the OSHA Subpart R content verbatim: the five-feet-above-floor splice rule, 48 in perimeter-column extension, perimeter-cable holes, and the 300 lb eccentric load [30:38][41:01]. Tekla detailing should fix splice locations before material order, keep two-story column lifts, draw splices in detail to check bolt installation tolerance and conflicts, and flag X-bolt connections boldly on erection drawings [14:35][82:10]. For anchor rods, adopt the oversized-washer practice and the Design Guide 10 erection-bracing failure modes for ACP base-plate setting and tolerance. NONE of this conflicts with Your Company doctrine; the Tier 1 verify-don't-generate rule is reinforced, since all weights and splice forces still route through aisc_validator.py and the in-house PE stamp, not LLM math.

## 8_Seismic Design in Steel_Concepts and Examples_Part 8
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LR7rwuL1vbg | Duration: 1:27:15 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
This final session of Rafael Sabelli's eight-part AISC seismic series covers the design of buckling restrained braced frames (BRBF) end to end, applying capacity design. The braces are the fuse: size them first against 100% of the story shear, then run a plastic mechanism analysis (PMA) to find the maximum tension and compression forces those braces can impose on beams, columns, and connections, then design those protected elements for the amplified force [05:15][70:28]. The maximum brace forces include a strain hardening factor omega and a compression overstrength factor beta drawn from manufacturer testing, so the system is a design partnership between the engineer of record and the BRB manufacturer [16:27][70:58].

### Spec References
The speaker cited: redundancy factor rho of 1.3 and the B2 second-order factor [08:19]; ASCE 7 stability index theta greater than 0.1 (B2 above 1.1) for required displacement amplification [37:52]; AISC 341 torsional bracing requirement at the chevron connection point and the AISC 341 rule that bolted joints in a seismic load resisting system be pretensioned with a Class A faying surface and no slots in the direction of loading [56:14][82:46]; main Manual Table 4-1 (column compression), Table 4-22 (F-critical), Table 7-1 (bolt shear), Table 8-4 (eccentrically loaded weld coefficient C) [28:42][34:17][43:27][48:01]; Design Guide 1 for base plate flexure [62:20]; the Dowswell 2006 / Engineering Journal paper on effective length factors for gusset plate buckling, the NIST NEHRP Seismic Design Tech Brief No. 11 on BRBF, and the 2017 SEAOC proceedings "Design of Chevron Gusset Plates" by Sabelli and Lee Harbor [49:03][73:33][74:05].

### Technical Details
BRB area is set so phi*Fy*A equals the brace force, using the lower bound of the allowed Fy range 38 to 46 ksi and an expected RyFy of about 42 ksi, with round-up increments of 1/4 in to 5 sq in, 1/2 in to 10 sq in, then 1 in [11:21][15:26]. Selected areas ran 2.0 sq in at the roof to 5.5 sq in at the base [14:25]. PMA design stresses were about 68 ksi in compression and 59 ksi in tension using beta 1.15, omega 1.4, RyFy 42 ksi, producing a governing overstrength ratio near 2.2 at the second floor versus the code default of 2.5 [18:30][20:00]. In a chevron, the beam carries a net vertical load proportional to (beta minus one) of the vertical brace component because compression capacity exceeds tension [22:33]. Final design used a W10x77 compression column (753 kips per Table 4-1), a W18x55 beam, and a 32 in by 18 in tall "mega gusset" with stabilizing top and bottom flange plates [28:42][46:28].

### Fabrication Notes
The engineer specifies the BRB to the manufacturer either by area (for example 5 sq in) or by design strength (for example phi*Psc of 200 kips), and must state clearly whether phi is included [11:21][12:24]. Gusset thickness is often dictated by the BRB core plate thickness, so the fabricator cannot freely pick a plate gauge [40:55]. A rule of thumb from fabricators is a chevron gusset length of beam-length over six (48 in here against a 40 in to 42 in minimum); a far longer required gusset signals going to a heavier beam [31:16][55:12]. Where the beam web is thinner than the gusset, a web doubler is added to match thickness and raise block-shear/tear-out strength [51:39]. Drag-element shapes were quarter sections of HSS rather than double angles specifically so they would not interfere with the gusset-to-base-plate fillet weld [66:24].

### Erection Notes
Bolts are kept 4 in off the bottom of the gusset plate for erection access [42:56]. For the beam-to-gusset double-shear connection the engineer asks for tack welds for erection so the gusset plate does not fall off and the bolts can all be driven straight through once the beam is set, instead of staggering bolts [50:36][51:08]. Anchor rods at the base plate are shown deep-bolted, and the base plate column connection is CJP welded to allow inelastic rotation to come out of the column [58:18][65:53].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The session frames pitfalls more than rejections. Making braces stronger than needed forces stronger and costlier connections, beams, and columns, so over-rounding is penalized downstream [15:56]. Relying on gravity-column shear to carry part of the frame force is not code-compliant, which is why gravity columns are commonly pinned [81:14]. A Q&A point noted the Whitmore section tension check (30 degree fan from the bolt group) must still be run on the gusset [81:45]. Designing anchor rods for combined shear and bending would push rods from 1-3/4 in to 3 in, so a separate shear load path is preferred [63:21].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Ductile detailing yields more economical buildings because the required strength is reduced and large inelastic drifts are accommodated through ductility rather than brute strength [71:59]. Brace areas were "pretty tightly designed" with at most about 10% round-up, which keeps connection and member sizes down [15:26]. BRBs are proprietary manufactured items, so brace pricing, the stiffness factor (about 1.4 here), and the beta/omega factors come from the manufacturer brochure or direct consultation, and that information must be in the bid model and the connection design [35:17][41:25]. Gusset design is increasingly shared with the brace manufacturer, which shifts connection-engineering scope and must be coordinated on load path and design responsibility [63:51][70:58].

### Bolting / Welding Summary
Two manufacturer-specified bolted brace cases appeared: a 338 kip / 294 kip brace using four 1-in A490X bolts in double shear with a 3/4-in grade 50 gusset (bolt shear 396 kips per Table 7-1, bearing 339 kips, block shear 349 kips) [42:56][43:27]; and a beam-to-gusset case using five A325X bolts in double shear with tack welds for erection [50:36]. Per AISC 341 these bearing-type joints are built as pretensioned with a Class A faying surface, and there is no advantage to designing them slip-critical [82:46]. Welds: gusset-to-beam/column fillets sized off Table 8-4 (two 5/16 in and two 3/8 in fillets in the two gussets), base-plate flange CJP welds specified as demand critical with demand-critical web welds, and S1 supplement specified for anchor-rod weldability on the grade 55 rods [48:01][61:19][65:53].

### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff this confirms BRBs are proprietary line items, not aisc_validator.py rolled shapes: capture brace area or design strength, the Fy 38-46 ksi band, the manufacturer beta/omega/stiffness factors, and price them off the manufacturer brochure, while the columns, beams, and gussets remain conventional AISC shapes that run through aisc_validator.py (W10x77, W18x55 here). Tekla detailing should carry the "mega gusset" with stabilizing flange plates, the L-over-six chevron gusset rule of thumb, the 4-in bolt-standoff and web-doubler-to-match-gusset notes, and the HSS drag elements clear of the base-plate weld; Mario's crew gets the tack-weld-then-bolt sequence and AWS demand-critical weld filler on base-plate flanges. The in-house PE stamp owns the capacity-design load path and must coordinate scope and load path in writing if a BRB manufacturer assists the gusset design, and anchor-rod work (grade 55, 1-3/4 in, deep-bolted, S1 weldable, separate shear load path) maps to Your Company's anchor-rod design/setting workstream. Doctrine conflict: NONE. The system is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language.

## 7_Seismic Design in Steel_Concepts and Examples_Part 7
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XVY9ldxereY | Duration: 1:28:44 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
This is the third live session of Rafael Sabelli's eight-part AISC seismic-design series, covering the full design of a steel special moment frame (SMF) on a four-story example building [00:02][01:04]. The governing idea is that an SMF is controlled by drift, not strength, so members are sized to the drift limit first and strength checks (which run well below a demand-capacity ratio of one) come last [03:39][04:10][75:23]. The worked example uses a prequalified reduced beam section (RBS) connection and carries the design from member selection through the panel zone, the beam and column strength, the base plate, and the anchor rods [02:37][57:01].

### Spec References
Cited verbatim by the speaker: AISC 358 (prequalified connections), specifically Section 5.3 for RBS member restrictions [10:50]; AISC 341 seismic provisions, with highly ductile member requirements in Section E3, demand-critical welds, protected zones, and the 2010-vs-2016 minimum column flange thickness rule [05:12][20:32][45:11][93:00]; AISC 360 for strong-column-weak-beam, web local yielding, web crippling, flange local bending, panel zone shear, the B2 second-order factor, and the C-sub-M / B1 rule [23:38][37:29][67:00]; AISC Design Guide 1 base-plate-with-large-moment method [58:02][62:07]; ACI bearing equation with the square root of A2-over-A1 spread for grout [61:06]; AISC manual Table 14-2 (anchor-rod washers) and Supplement S1 (weldable anchor material) [68:15]; ASCE 7 for drift limits, the stability factor theta, and Section 12.8.7 P-delta load factors [31:52][34:26][83:44]; NIST/NEHRP Seismic Tech Brief No. 2 on steel SMF and Farzad Naeim's Seismic Design Handbook as references [18:28][75:54].

### Technical Details
The RBS beam is limited to a rolled or built-up I-shape, 36 in deep max, 300 lb/ft max, flange thickness 1.75 in max, span-to-depth ratio at least seven, with seismically compact flanges checked at the center two-thirds of the reduced section [10:50][11:22]. Flange reduction (dimension C) runs 10 to 25 percent per side, dropping flexural strength roughly 15 to 30 percent; the example took a 27 percent cut of the plastic section modulus [12:22][38:32]. Strong-column-weak-beam is screened with a plastic-section-modulus ratio kept above 1.5, and the example pair (W14x132 column, W24x62 beam) finally cleared it at 1.44 against a Z-ratio of 2.1 [23:38][43:39]. Drift design landed at a period near 1.5 seconds and a base shear about 60 percent of the strength-design shear, with the bottom-story B2 at 1.06 and theta at 0.07, both inside limits so K equals one [29:44][33:24][34:26].

### Fabrication Notes
The shop cuts the RBS radius into both flanges per the A, B, C dimensions from AISC 358, and compactness is verified at the reduced center two-thirds width, not the full flange [13:22][14:53]. The column required continuity plates (driven by the minimum-flange-thickness check, 1.17 in needed vs 1.03 in available) and a roughly half-inch doubler plate from the 937-kip panel zone demand [45:41][46:43][47:14]. A key optimization message is that going to a heavier column (W14x176) and a lighter beam eliminated both the continuity plates and the doubler, removing significant shop labor at the cost of a little added steel [49:49][50:53]. Connection completion (not detailed in the example) includes removing weld tabs and backing bars at the demand-critical CJP welds [73:52].

### Erection Notes
RBS keeps inelastic strain in a protected zone away from the column face, with lateral bracing required just outside the hinge region; the example needed bottom-flange braces about every 5 ft (50 times an r-sub-y of about 1.4) while the top flange was braced continuously by the composite deck [11:52][51:54][52:25]. At the column base the design uses double-nutted anchor rods top and bottom, four per side on a 32 in by 32 in plate, with debonding of the rods from the concrete so the rods can elongate and the connection can rotate for ductility [59:33][68:15][73:22]. Shear at the base is best taken out by bearing of the base plate edge or by friction (a 0.4 coefficient on the flexural compression gave 102 kips), not through the anchor rods, which makes for poor bending elements [66:10][67:13].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The session frames "failures" as design rejections rather than weld defects: selecting a beam too deep or too heavy for RBS prequalification, or one that is not seismically compact, only to have it rejected at the prequalification check [05:12]. Web local yielding came out "just barely no good," driving the continuity-plate requirement, and the panel zone failed without a doubler [45:11][46:43]. Treating the moment-frame column base as a true pin is called unrealistic because the connection cannot actually accommodate the large inelastic rotation; assuming a fully rigid base can be unconservative for member selection because real foundation flexibility adds to first-story drift [85:18][86:19]. The speaker also warns that the AISC 358 blanket 10-percent drift increase for RBS is overly conservative (real effect is 2 to 5 percent if modeled directly) [20:00].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Continuity plates and doubler plates are the cost levers: tighter lateral brace spacing (every 5 ft vs every 7.5 ft) adds a few braces, but spending on a heavier column to delete continuity plates and doublers usually nets a cheaper, more economical frame [48:15][50:53][75:54]. Connection-type choice carries direct cost trade-offs: WUF-W is cheap and easy for small buildings, RBS adds flange-cutting, and bolted flange-plate or bolted end-plate connections appeal to erectors who want to avoid field welding and the inspection/NDE that comes with it [07:14][08:14][08:44]. Anchor-rod sizing has cost weight too: tension-only design allowed 1.5 in grade 55 rods, while forcing shear and bending through the rods would have pushed all eight to 2 in or even 2.25 in diameter [65:10][66:10].

### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff this confirms that SMF member counts cannot be inferred from drift sizing alone; continuity plates, doublers, and RBS flange cuts are real shop quantities that ride on the column-beam pairing, so a measured member takeoff through aisc_validator.py plus the connection schedule is required, not a per-ton assumption. For Mario the demand-critical CJP welds at the beam flanges, web, and column base per AISC 341 set the WPS and weld-toughness and tab/backing-removal scope, and AWS D1.1 procedure and welder qualification should be staged before those joints. Anchor-rod work maps directly to our anchor-rod design/setting/tolerance stream: grade 55 weldable rods (Supplement S1), debonded and double-nutted on a heavy 2.75 in base plate, with shear taken by bearing or friction rather than the rods; the in-house PE stamp owns the strong-column-weak-beam, panel-zone, and base-plate-large-moment (Design Guide 1) checks, and Tekla detailing must carry the protected zones, RBS geometry, continuity plates, doublers, and the shear load path the example left undesigned. No conflict with Your Company doctrine; this is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language, and it reinforces our verify-don't-generate posture on AISC weights and connection counts. DOCTRINE FLAGS: NONE.

## 6_Seismic Design in Steel_Concepts and Examples_Part 6
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=J9sCpBLMZ4c | Duration: 1:27:05 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
This is session 6 of Rafael Sabelli's eight-part AISC night-school series on seismic design in steel, covering building lateral analysis and diaphragm design for a building that uses special moment frames (SMF) and buckling restrained braced frames (BRBF) [01:02]. The first half walks through lateral analysis methods in ASCE 7, load cases, accidental torsion, structural modeling, stability and second-order (P-delta) effects, and developing strength-level design forces [02:36]. The second half develops diaphragm forces, shear, collectors and collector connections, chord forces, capacity-design forces, and analysis around a diaphragm opening [03:37]. The recurring theme is that moment frames are usually drift-controlled while braced frames are strength-controlled, and that everything in the lateral system carries an amplified design force from the P-delta effect [37:37].

### Spec References
ASCE 7 cited throughout: equivalent lateral force procedure and modal response spectrum analysis, vertical-distribution exponent K table, diaphragm classification Section 12.3.1.2 (rigid where concrete-filled deck span-to-depth is under 3) [08:16], the related 12.3.1.1 and 12.3.1.3 [79:17], the stability check in Section 12.8.7 with the theta coefficient [32:57], and the diaphragm-force equation with omega-sub-O collector amplification starting at seismic design category C [76:39]. The base-shear scaling changed from 85 percent (ASCE 7-10) to 100 percent (ASCE 7-16) [05:10]. AISC 360 cited for the direct analysis method, effective (equivalent) length method, and first-order analysis method with their B2 limits of 1.5, the 0.8 and tau-sub-B stiffness reductions, Appendix 8 (B1 and B2 magnification), and the Chapter H beam-column interaction [25:46]. A325N bolts and AISC Manual tables 7-1A, 10-10A, and 3-19 are named for the collector connection [67:29]. Constrained-axis flexural-torsional buckling tables come from an Engineering Journal paper, 2013 quarter 4 [62:18]. Reference documents named: AISC Seismic Design Manual, an NCSEA guide to diaphragms/chords/collectors, NIST Tech Brief No. 5 on composite steel deck and concrete-filled diaphragms, and Farzad Naeim's Seismic Design Handbook [74:36].

### Technical Details
The example building uses SMF in one direction with reduced beam section (RBS) connections and BRBF in the other, on rigid concrete-filled-deck diaphragms [16:31]. Base shears were 271 kips for the SMF and 331 kips for the BRBF; vertical distribution used K of 1.21 for the SMF (period near 1 second) and 1.125 for the BRBF [13:57]. Accidental torsion at 5 percent of building dimension drove each frame line to 55 percent of base shear, a 10 percent increase [13:26]. BRBF modeling multiplied work-point-to-work-point brace stiffness by a stiffening factor KF of 1.4 (range 1.2 to 1.8, from manufacturer literature, varying with connection type, brace area, and length) [22:12]. Calculated B2 factors were all below 1.1, allowing K of 1 and the effective length method [41:44]. Diaphragm collector design used omega-sub-O of 3 for the SMF; a roof diaphragm force of 142 kips gave 71 kip reactions, and capacity-design brace forces were 118 kips tension and 135 kips compression with a 179 kip horizontal component [57:42]. The collector beam was a W18x50 checked for constrained-axis flexural-torsional buckling (386 kips capacity at 13 ft), with composite flexural strength of 516 kips from Table 3-19 requiring 33 studs [62:49].

### Fabrication Notes
The session is design-focused, but a few items touch fabrication. The collector W18x50 uses 3/4 inch shear studs at 24 inch spacing for seismic shear transfer, with 33 studs needed to develop the composite flexural capacity from Table 3-19 [59:45]. The collector connection is a single shear plate, A36, 3/8 inch thick, with two 1/4 inch fillet welds proportioned to exceed the plate strength so weld checking is satisfied once the plate works [66:59]. The speaker warns that changing column size at the floor in the analysis model, when the actual splice is roughly 4 ft above the floor, can introduce error in any tonnage calculation pulled from that model [17:33]. No preheat, WPS, welder qualification, or NDE detail is given.

### Erection Notes
No field erection sequencing, crane, rigging, bracing, or site-coordination content appears in this session. It is an analysis-and-design webinar; the actual SMF and BRBF member and connection design is deferred to sessions 7 and 8 [85:56]. No erection notes available for extraction beyond the design intent that the BRBF acts as a pinned truss and the SMF carries the lateral load in its direction.

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The speaker flags engineering errors rather than shop or field rejections. The most emphasized is K-factor miscalculation: he recommends avoiding hand-calculated K factors because engineers commonly get them wrong with leaning columns, and instead using the first-order then direct analysis method [30:56]. A second-order analysis that omits gravity load is not actually second-order, since the destabilizing P-delta effect needs the gravity load present [31:57]. Mixing load-combination factors (1.2 on one term and 1.0 on another) between the seismic mass and the P-delta gravity load is called out as inconsistent [38:39]. He notes B2 must never exceed 1.5 for a seismic design because ASCE 7 stability would not allow it [26:17]. Tonnage error from column-size modeling shortcuts is the one item that maps to a takeoff/estimating risk [17:33].

### Bid / Cost Implications
The equivalent lateral force procedure is slightly conservative and can drive members one or even two sizes larger than modal response spectrum analysis, a direct tonnage and cost difference [04:38]. BRBFs are increasingly chosen over special concentrically braced frames (SCBF), now used even in one- and two-story buildings, which shifts which system is most economical on a given job [85:26]. Sizing moment frames for drift first rather than strength is presented as the efficient design path, avoiding wasted effort on members that drift later forces to grow [82:22]. The model-derived tonnage caution at [17:33] is the clearest estimating-accuracy flag: tonnages pulled from an analysis model can be off if column sizes are placed at floor lines rather than true splice points.

### Your Company Application
The tonnage-from-model warning at [17:33] is the load-bearing item for Ivan: any tonnage harvested from an analysis model is approximate because the model places column-size changes at floor lines, not at true splice elevations roughly 4 ft up, so a bid-grade takeoff still needs a measured member count through aisc_validator.py rather than a model tonnage dump. The collector connection is a clean Tekla and Mario reference: a single A36 3/8 inch shear plate, four 7/8 inch A325N bolts at 3 inch pitch, two 1/4 inch fillet welds sized to develop the plate, plus 3/4 inch studs at 24 inches for seismic shear transfer. None of this conflicts with Your Company doctrine; the content is seismic high-category (California-type) special-system design well outside our typical Houston conventional-steel low-seismic scope, so it is a methodology reference, not a stamp-ready procedure for an in-house PE. DOCTRINE FLAGS: NONE. The webinar names a brace manufacturer's brochure only generically, so no supplier-name rule is touched.
