## 5_Seismic Design in Steel_Concepts and Examples_Part 5
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ui_ytffLODo | Duration: 1:31:15 | Tier: 1 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
Rafael Sabelli (Walter P Moore) opens the live portion of the AISC night-school series with the planning phase of seismic design for a four-story steel office building, special moment frames (SMF) in the long direction and buckling-restrained braced frames (BRBF) in the short direction [01:35][05:11]. The session covers system selection by seismic design category, effective seismic weight, period and base-shear determination, a wind-versus-seismic comparison to pick governing members once, the full set of horizontal and vertical irregularity checks, and construction of the seismic load combinations [04:09][62:17]. The unifying idea is capacity design: protect connections by forcing yielding into a controlled location (reduced beam section in the SMF, the brace core in the BRBF) and size everything else for the force that location can deliver [30:51][72:06].
### Spec References
Cited verbatim by the speaker: IBC 2015 with ASCE 7-2010 loading, AISC 360 (steel), ACI 318 (concrete), AWS D1.1 (structural welding), with AISC 341 required for seismic and AISC 358 for the prequalified connection [08:18]. Also AWS D1.8 seismic welding supplement [08:50]; AISC 360 Chapter N (QC/QA, NDT) [26:15]; AISC 341 Chapter J (seismic QA, demand-critical welds) [27:48]; AWS D1.1 Section 6 and AWS D1.8 Section 7 quality requirements [28:18]; AISC 341 Section A3.3 for the 2 in plate CVN requirement (20 ft-lb at 70F) [20:33][80:47]; AISC 358 Section 5.7 (named in the poll) [76:41]; ASCE 7 Tables 12.2-1, 12.3-3, drift tables in Chapter 11, and the SDC tables [17:30][38:00][62:48]; AISC Design Guide 1 for anchor-rod field fixes [21:34]; ASTM grade-supplement S1 for weldable Grade 55 anchor rods [21:04].
### Technical Details
Materials: beams and columns A992 Fy 50 ksi with Ry; sections over 1.5 in flange thickness need specified CVN toughness, thinner flanges are exempt [19:03]. A913 Grade 65 (Grade 70 in 2016) permitted for SMF and BRBF columns [20:03]. Connection plates A36; base plates Grade 50, and plates over 2 in require CVN 20 ft-lb at 70F per AISC 341 [20:33]. BRB core is A36 with an added expected-yield window of 38 to 46 ksi so connections can be designed at about 42 ksi expected strength [23:37][24:37]. Weld filler is 70 ksi, CVN 20 ft-lb at 0F generally and 40 ft-lb at 70F for demand-critical welds where inelastic strain is expected, valid because lowest anticipated service temperature stays above 50F in conditioned space [22:36]. The RBS moves the plastic hinge off the column face and reduces beam stiffness, which is accounted for in the 2 percent drift check [30:51][32:21].
### Fabrication Notes
QC and QA come from AISC 360 Chapter N, with tables for welded and bolted joints listing tasks before, during, and after, plus NDT frequency rates [26:15][26:46]. AISC 341 Chapter J adds the more stringent seismic requirements over Chapter N, including demand-critical weld provisions, and AISC 358 adds requirements for the prequalified RBS [27:48][58:00]. Jurisdictions may approve a fabricator or erector to run QC in the shop without a parallel third-party QA inspector where the authority having jurisdiction allows it [26:46]. CVN testing is required only for plates over 2 in and sections with flanges over 1.5 in because thinner material reliably shows adequate toughness, so testing thin material wastes effort [19:33][80:47].
### Erection Notes
This planning session does not walk through field sequencing, crane, or rigging. The erection-relevant content is anchor-rod handling: Sabelli recommends specifying weldable Grade 55 anchor rods (supplement S1) so a too-short or mislocated rod can be field-fixed by welding an extension, with the standard fix shown and treated in AISC Design Guide 1 [21:04][21:34][22:05]. Grade 36 rods are always weldable and Grade 105 are never weldable [21:04]. Column splices sit above the second floor in this layout [06:43].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
BRB core material that comes in below 36 ksi is rejected for not meeting A36, and material between 36 and 38 or above 46 ksi is set aside because it falls outside the tightened expected-yield window [23:37][24:07]. A too-short or mislocated anchor rod is the named field problem, solved by the welded extension when weldable rods were specified [21:34]. The poll confirmed the common misconception that only one standard governs seismic QA: AISC 360 Ch N, 341 Ch J, 358 5.7, D1.1 Sec 6, and D1.8 Sec 7 all apply (answer F, all of the above) [76:41]. A second poll corrected the belief that aligning center of mass with center of rigidity removes torsional irregularity; accidental torsion still applies [78:14].
### Bid / Cost Implications
The governing-load logic is the cost message: size members for the controlling effect (seismic governs this building for both strength and overturning) and verify the other effect rather than designing twice, which cuts engineering effort [40:38][44:13][48:25]. BRBs are a tested proprietary system; 100 to 1000 kip braces are readily available, above 1000 kip they become special and availability plus test coverage must be verified, and manufacturers often assist with connection design [33:23][25:13]. Demand-critical welds, CVN toughness testing on thick plate, pretensioned bolts with prepared faying surfaces, and the added 341/358 QA all add fabrication scope and inspection cost that a seismic bid must carry.
### Your Company Application
For Ivan takeoff, a seismic SDC-D job changes the bill: A992 beams and columns plus A913 Grade 65/70 columns, Grade 50 base plates, CVN-tested thick plate, A325 pretensioned bolts (threads excluded, Class A faying or better) on the seismic system, A490 bolts at BRB gussets, and weldable Grade 55 anchor rods all need explicit line items and cannot be priced as plain material [19:03][20:33][43:00]. Mario's shop and welding scope expands: demand-critical welds need 70 ksi filler at 40 ft-lb/70F CVN, WPS per D1.8, and the heavier QA of 341 Chapter J beyond 360 Chapter N, so welder qualification and inspection hours rise. Paul should note demand-critical welds and CVN-toughness handling as added inspection hold points. Tekla detailing must carry the RBS cut geometry, protected zones, and the BRB gusset connection that matches the manufacturer's tested configuration. The in-house PE stamp work that drives base-plate and anchor-rod design must use the amplified (overstrength) seismic load on base plates and anchor rods, though not on the foundation [89:36][90:06], which ties directly to Your Company anchor-rod design, setting, and tolerance practice and to the Design Guide 1 weldable-rod fix. No conflict with Your Company doctrine: this is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language. Doctrine flag: NONE. Note for doctrine, any tonnage or weight figures used downstream must still come from bridge/aisc_validator.py, not from this webinar.

## 1_Seismic Design in Steel_Concepts and Examples_Part 1
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oFSH4qj637w | Duration: 1:29:50 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is session one of an eight-session AISC Night School course taught by Rafael Sabelli of Walter P Moore, covering the principles of effective seismic design in steel [00:00]. The central idea is that steel structures resist earthquakes not by remaining elastic but by accepting controlled inelastic damage, which lets the engineer design for reduced forces using a response-modification factor R [33:57][41:38]. The chain that produces a ductile system runs from ductile material to ductile section to ductile member to a properly proportioned system, where strong connections force yielding into predictable fuse elements [62:46][127:00]. Proportioning, not raw strength, is the controlling discipline: seismic design is described as keeping inelastic demand at locations that can yield and away from locations that would fracture [56:35][114:00].
### Spec References
The speaker names AISC 341 (the Seismic Provisions) as the building code document that defines expected material strength [57:06]. He cites the expected yield relation FYE equals RY times FY, and gives A992 with specified minimum FY of 50 ksi, an RY of 1.1, an expected yield of 55 ksi, and a defined upper bound of 65 ksi [57:38][58:09]. He references the AISC Seismic Design Manual (2010 edition matching the 2010 provisions, with a 2016-provisions edition forthcoming) and the AISC Facts for Steel Buildings volume on earthquakes by Ron Hamburger [02:32][03:33]. R-factors stated for systems: SMF, BRBF, EBF and steel plate shear walls at R of 8; SCBF at R of 6; IMF at R of 4.5; OMF at R of 3.5; OCBF at R of 3.25 [64:19][66:55]. No AISC 360 chapter, AWS D1.1 clause, or RCSC section is cited by number in this session.
### Technical Details
The session is conceptual: response spectra built from single-degree-of-freedom oscillators, the constant-acceleration, constant-velocity, and constant-displacement regions of a spectrum, and the relation that increasing stiffness shortens period [24:08][71:05]. Yielding effectively lengthens period and adds hysteretic damping, both of which lower acceleration demand and are bundled into the R factor [69:00][71:00]. Material behavior is tied to restraint: a smooth coupon yields and necks, but triaxial restraint (notches, thick beam-flange-to-column-flange welds) suppresses yielding and pushes the steel toward brittle rupture per the von Mises yield surface [45:47][48:54]. Section ductility requires seismically compact members with tighter b/t and h/tw limits than ordinary compact sections so full yield develops before local buckling [52:29][53:00].
### Fabrication Notes
The fabrication-relevant content centers on the highly restrained beam-flange-to-column-flange weld, which the speaker repeatedly flags as a location where ductile A992 steel cannot deliver ductility because of triaxial restraint and thick column flanges [48:54][49:25]. The design answer is to move yielding off that joint using cover plates, haunches, or a reduced beam section (RBS) where the flanges are cut back so the reduced beam, not the connection, is the weaker fuse [55:33][56:04][56:35]. Access-hole geometry must be configured to avoid local rupture, and holes or other cross-section reductions are to be avoided in yielding regions [51:58][105:00]. Expected material overstrength of 10 percent up to as much as 60 percent must be carried into capacity-design proportioning, with strain hardening of roughly 10 percent for ordinary braces and around 40 percent for BRBF and EBF elements [57:06][59:10][59:40].
### Erection Notes
This conceptual session does not cover field erection sequencing, crane or rigging, or site coordination in any specific way. The closest erection-adjacent point is the requirement for lateral bracing of moment-frame beams at frequent intervals so the beam can develop flexural yield rather than lateral-torsional buckling, which has implications for where bracing connections land in the field [53:31][54:32].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The dominant failure named is the pre-Northridge beam-to-column moment connection, which did not deliver the anticipated ductile behavior at the joint and drove the post-1994 testing requirements [86:39][87:11]. The session also names brittle fracture at the restrained beam-flange-to-column weld, premature local buckling of non-compact or slender sections, flange rupture, and gusset/brace connection fracture at slotted brace-to-gusset connections that historically failed in tests and in earthquakes [49:25][55:02][55:33]. A specific proportioning error is called out: after Northridge, owners made every beam the same W36 to economize on connection testing, which overloaded the lower stories and concentrated all damage in the first couple of floors [86:39][89:14]. Column plastic hinging top and bottom of a first-floor column is shown as a soft-story mechanism to avoid [65:53].
### Bid / Cost Implications
The economic argument is explicit: designing every structure to stay elastic (R of 1) is reasonable only for facilities like nuclear plants and is uneconomical for normal buildings, so codes accept inelastic damage to save construction dollars [28:46][41:38]. Higher R systems carry lower design force but require more detailing and tighter section limits, so the cost trade is detailing effort and section selection against member size [64:19]. The owner conversation flagged is that code-minimum seismic design protects life but does not guarantee continued operation or low repair cost, so hospitals, manufacturers, and asset-sensitive owners may pay for performance above code [40:35][41:05]. The Northridge example shows that economizing on connection qualification testing by standardizing one beam size produced a worse, more damage-prone structure, a false economy [88:12][89:14].
### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, the practical hook is that seismic systems pull members toward seismically compact shapes and add reinforcement (cover plates, haunches, RBS cuts) at moment connections, so a seismic job is not priced like a gravity job; the member takeoff through aisc_validator.py should expect heavier, stockier sections and extra connection material, and the FYE equals RY times FY relation (A992: 50 ksi specified, 55 ksi expected, 65 ksi upper bound) is the validated material basis, not LLM math [57:38][58:09]. For Mario's shop and welding lead, the central message is that the beam-flange-to-column-flange CJP is a restraint-critical location where weld quality and access-hole geometry decide whether the connection fractures, which maps directly to AWS D1.1 welder-qualification and joint-prep discipline even though no clause number is stated here. Tekla detailing should model the RBS cuts, cover plates, and haunches exactly as designed since proportioning, not strength, is what makes the fuse work, and the in-house PE stamp on a seismic frame must carry the AISC 341 capacity-design logic. Houston sits in low seismic demand, so most Your Company work is OMF/OCBF territory (R of 3.5 and 3.25) with light detailing, but any seismic-category job or out-of-region bid must flag the heavier requirements. Doctrine flags: NONE; this content reinforces the verify-don't-generate and aisc_validator-only weight rules.

## 4_Seismic Design in Steel_Concepts and Examples_Part 4
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=awRerj-stq0 | Duration: 1:26:29 | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This session four of the AISC Night School, presented by Rafael Sabelli of Walter P Moore, teaches the seismic design of buildings as a system of interlocking codes rather than a single document [00:32][02:04]. The central concept is the risk-targeted maximum considered earthquake (MCE sub R), a ground motion defined so that a code-conforming building has no more than a 10% chance of collapse if that shaking occurs, calibrated on paper to no more than a 1% chance of earthquake-induced collapse in a 50-year period [09:52][11:23][12:24]. The design force chain takes the MCE spectrum, multiplies by 2/3, divides by R over I sub E, and the result is the very reduced level structures are actually proportioned to, with real performance coming from ductility and overstrength embedded in the R factor [13:55][24:40].
### Spec References
The speaker cites the following by name. ASCE 7-10 and ASCE 7-16 (loads, analysis requirements, system limits) [03:36][03:05]; ASCE 7 section 12.8.2.1 for the approximate period formula [27:46]; International Building Code and the 2016 California Building Code as the adopting state code [02:35][03:05]; ASCE 7 Chapter 14 as the chapter that adopts material standards [04:39]. AISC 360 (specification for structural steel buildings, member and connection strengths, stability analysis) [06:15][07:15]; AISC 341 (seismic provisions, proportioning, detailing, material restrictions) [07:15][07:46]; AISC 358 (prequalified connection standard for SMF and IMF) [08:17]; ACI 318 [04:39][06:45]. AWS D1.1 (structural welding code, adopted by reference) and AWS D1.8 (seismic welding supplement, toughness and other weld requirements for the seismic load resisting system only) [06:45][08:47]. SEAOC Seismic Design Manual Volume 1 and Finley Charney's ASCE 7 seismic loads guide are named as further resources [77:19].
### Technical Details
The code hierarchy is layered: ASCE 7 gives loads and analysis, AISC 360 gives element strengths, and AISC 341 gives proportioning and detailing, a division the speaker confirms in a poll [78:23][79:25]. R factors run to 8 for the most ductile steel systems; special concentrically braced frames carry R of 6 with much of that from overstrength, and cantilever column systems carry low R because of low overstrength [26:14][26:44]. Risk category (one through four) drives the importance factor I sub E (1.0, 1.25, 1.5) and the drift limit (2% H for risk categories one and two, lower for three and four) [16:57][19:33][20:04]. The structural period is taken from the approximate formula T sub A = C sub T times height to the X, capped at CU times T sub A for the strength check, with CU near 1.4 in high-seismic regions [27:46][29:49][30:19]. The omega sub O overstrength factor (ranging two to three) amplifies forces for collectors and elements supporting discontinuous frames and walls [33:22][33:52]. Stability is checked through the stability coefficient theta capped at 0.25, and redundancy gives rho of 1.0 for well-distributed systems or 1.3 for few or poorly distributed elements [35:24][37:28][37:58]. Diaphragm forces are applied one level at a time, not simultaneously, plus separate transfer forces in dual systems [53:19][54:20].
### Fabrication Notes
This session is loads and analysis, so direct shop fabrication content is light, but two items carry to the shop. Collector members are typically wide flange with discrete bottom-flange bracing and are checked for constrained-axis flexural torsional buckling where a composite or perpendicular steel deck restrains the top flange, which changes the controlling unbraced length the detailer and shop must honor [55:20][56:22][58:22]. Stair connections in the seismic system are detailed with slotted holes so the stringer can move in its stiff direction during story drift, and the shop must fabricate those slots so they do not bind and still carry gravity load [68:08][68:40]. The seismic weld toughness rules that the shop and welder follow come from AWS D1.8 as adopted by AISC 341 [08:47].
### Erection Notes
Direct erection sequencing and rigging are not covered in this loads-focused session. The relevant field-side point is that diaphragms brace the gravity columns at every story so the columns can use the story height as their unbraced length; that load path must exist in the completed structure, meaning deck and its connection to the framing are part of the lateral system, not just gravity [51:46][52:16]. Seismic separation joints at property lines and thermal breaks must preserve a designed gap so adjacent structures do not pound, which the field has to lay out and protect [69:41][70:43].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The session frames conceptual design errors rather than inspection rejections. Named pitfalls: reading a too-flexible period from an analysis model and using it unbounded, which understates required base shear, so the code caps the period at CU times T sub A [29:19][29:49]; designing lower-level members only to the ELF force distribution, which underloads them and leads to failure there, the reason the supplemental diaphragm force exists [53:19]; placing a non-ductile moment connection in a ductile special moment frame, which the speaker says he would not do [64:01]; hard-connecting stiff stairs so they act as unintended non-ductile braces and then fail [67:37][68:08]; and taking maximum modal drift at one floor minus another in a modal response spectrum analysis, which is invalid because signs are lost and drift must be tracked mode by mode [46:39][47:09].
### Bid / Cost Implications
Several choices in this session move cost. Modal response spectrum analysis tends to produce far less overturning than the equivalent lateral force procedure, which can yield real economy on overturning-resisting elements [46:39][47:09]. Heavy cladding tends to be seismic-governed and light cladding wind-governed, so the controlling load case and therefore the steel weight shifts by cladding type regardless of what the bare base shear suggests [74:48][75:18]. Seismic systems carry top-heavy overturning and omega-amplified collector and column forces, so even when wind and seismic base shears look similar the seismic overturning demand can drive heavier members [75:48]. Higher risk category means lower drift limits and higher importance factor, which stiffens and therefore adds tonnage to the lateral system [19:33].
### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, this session is a reminder that seismic governs member size through overturning and omega-amplified collector and column forces, not just base shear, so a takeoff that scales tonnage off SF without the controlling load case can miss heavy lateral members; flag the seismic design category and risk category as inputs that change the steel weight, consistent with our verify-don't-generate posture. For Tekla detailing, the constrained-axis flexural torsional buckling treatment of collectors and the slotted-hole stair connections are detail-level requirements the model must carry, and AISC 358 prequalified connections (for SMF and IMF) plus AISC 341 protected-zone and AWS D1.8 weld toughness rules drive how Mario's shop and welders prepare those joints. The in-house PE stamp work touches risk category, importance factor, R selection, and the period cap directly. Most Your Company work is in lower-seismic Houston, so much of this high-seismic detailing may not bind on a given bid, but the system-of-codes framing (ASCE 7 loads, AISC 360 strengths, AISC 341 detailing, AWS D1.8 welds) is the correct reference structure for any seismic-governed job and for ACP project controls if that site carries seismic demand. Doctrine flags: NONE. No supplier names, no PEMB language, and no fabricated section numbers or weights were introduced; only sections the speaker stated aloud are cited.

## 3_Seismic Design in Steel_Concepts and Examples_Part 3
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pK-eQAwk05w | Duration: 1:31:42 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
This is session three of AISC Night School "Seismic Design in Steel," written and presented by Rafael Sabelli of Walter P Moore, covering the seismic design of braced frames [00:03]. The controlling idea is capacity design: the brace is the ductile fuse, and every other element (connections, columns, beams, gussets, base plates) is proportioned to resist the maximum force the brace can deliver so the fuse acts as a fuse [10:50][20:36][44:42]. Three ductile systems are taught. The special concentrically braced frame (SCBF) gets its inelastic drift from brace tension yielding (expected strength RyFyAg) and controlled compression buckling [07:17][13:21]. The buckling-restrained braced frame (BRBF) uses a steel core that yields in both tension and compression because a sleeve plus grout and a bond interrupter prevents the core from buckling, giving nearly symmetric behavior [36:32][39:06]. The ordinary concentrically braced frame (OCBF) instead limits inelastic demand through higher strength and a low R factor of 3.25, and is used mainly for low industrial and metal-type buildings [03:09][62:09].

### Spec References
The speaker cites AISC 341 (Seismic Provisions), including the 2016 edition for multi-tiered braced frames [66:16][127:00] and the requirement that the three connection-fixity options are all allowed by AISC 341 [62:40]. He references AISC 360 Chapter E compression provisions, specifically the 0.877 factor that he removes to get the 1.14 maximum compression force (RyFy cap) [24:13][50:50]. AISC Design Guide 29 (brace connection design) is named repeatedly for gusset K factors and gusset design, drawing on Bo Dowswell's work published in the AISC Engineering Journal [55:57][56:58][80:36]. The R factor of 6 for SCBF is discussed [09:18]. The AISC Seismic Design Manual is cited for the three brace-buckling accommodation methods (linear fold line, knife-plate, elliptical hinge) and beam-to-column connection examples [30:24][60:35]. Material specs cited: A500 (Grade B historically, now Grade C preferred) and the newer A1085 with tighter controls and Ry of 1.25 versus A500 [74:24]. Two NIST technical briefs (SCBF and BRBF) are listed as resources [80:36]. ASCE 7 is cited for design base shear and drift requirements [44:42].

### Technical Details
Braces are sized for their compression capacity because earthquake load reverses, which creates overstrength since tension capacity (RyFy) can be two to three times compression capacity; that overstrength is part of the R factor [09:18][10:19]. SCBF braces have high compactness limits (thicker HSS walls spread strain and resist local kinking) and slenderness limits [17:30][24:45]. Buckling plane is controlled through end fixity (pinned in one plane, fixed in the orthogonal) and brace shape (round HSS has equal radius of gyration both axes; a wide flange has a clear weak axis), so designers tune K and r per axis to force buckling in the chosen plane [25:15][27:18]. Two plastic mechanism analyses are required for SCBF: condition one uses maximum tension (RyFy) and maximum compression (1.14 times design, capped at RyFy) for columns, gussets, and base plates; condition two uses post-buckling compression at 0.3 times maximum (0.342 when multiplied out) to capture unbalanced beam forces and drag-through forces [50:20][51:21][105:00]. BRBF needs only one mechanism analysis since tension and compression are similar; maximum tension is omega times RyFyAg (strain hardening 30 to 50 percent) and maximum compression is beta times omega times RyFyAg (compression overstrength 10 to 25 percent), both from testing [46:47][96:00]. Prohibited and penalized configurations: K-bracing into a column mid-height is prohibited for SCBF, BRBF, and OCBF; single diagonals are allowed only with the overstrength factor of 2; tension-only bracing is allowed only for OCBF [64:42][70:00][65:12].

### Fabrication Notes
A1085 HSS is preferred for seismic projects because of tighter dimensional controls and a higher Ry of 1.25; the speaker advises verifying that the chosen HSS shape is actually available through AISC service center listings or the fabricator [74:56]. For brace-to-gusset slots, the slot for gusset width should be one eighth inch wider than the plate (not one sixteenth) so the erector can maneuver the brace while keeping fillet welds small enough to bridge the gap [73:23]. Slot length should be about 2 inches longer than the final position to give erection maneuverability, and the design should anticipate the brace ending anywhere within a 2 inch zone with sufficient lap and reinforcement length [73:53]. Gusset fold-line detailing: minimum width of the linear fold line is twice the gusset thickness, with a recommended extra inch for tolerance; the knife-plate method uses about three times the knife-plate thickness [31:26][65:00]. Special welds with toughness requirements are required at column splices and at the ordinary-moment-frame beam-to-column connections used to accommodate rotation [67:47].

### Erection Notes
Erection tolerance drives the slot detailing: the deliberate one eighth inch slot oversize and the 2 inch extra slot length both exist to let the erector get the brace into place [73:23][73:53]. Brace buckling produces large out-of-plane movement (rule of thumb: about 10 percent of brace length), so the field layout and architectural coordination must keep the brace clear of sensitive elements such as glass curtain walls; configuring in-plane buckling can avoid hitting a facade [69:19][70:19]. Critically, the gusset fold line that allows the brace to buckle must not be restrained by concrete composite deck or a ground-floor slab cast against it, which would defeat the hinge [70:51]. Protected zones cover essentially the entire brace and connection; do not connect metal studs, handrails, or other attachments in areas of anticipated inelastic strain since that creates a fracture initiation point [71:51][72:21].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Named connection limit states to check: brace net section fracture, block shear fracture in the brace and in the gussets, weld fracture at interfaces, and gusset buckling [55:27]. A specific bad practice called out is using very thick gusset plates with very thin beam webs, which the University of Washington guidance warns against [55:57]. Designing a connection weaker than the brace is a primary failure: the connection fractures before the brace yields, causing sudden loss of frame strength and stiffness [11:20]. Restraining the gusset fold line with a slab, or attaching architecture to the protected zone, are detailing errors that prevent the intended ductile buckling and can create falling hazards [70:51][71:21]. Column fracture under the rotational demand of a gusseted fixed beam-to-column connection was observed in the UC Berkeley test program [59:02]. Designing the middle column of a brace bay for near-zero seismic axial (because elastic analysis shows it at the neutral axis) is a mistake; plastic mechanism analysis gives the real unbalanced design force [49:19].

### Bid / Cost Implications
The unbalanced vertical force in inverted-V and V (chevron) configurations forces a substantial beam, so chevron framing drives heavy beams into the SCBF system and adds tonnage [63:42][64:12]. BRBF braces are proprietary specialty items (the speaker names Nippon Steel, Star Seismic acquired by CoreBrace as generic vendor examples) and in practice must be bought from a manufacturer that has done the required testing, which means specifying a brace not from a specialty manufacturer is difficult and the brace design is largely the vendor's domain [40:42][86:22]. Multi-tiered braced frames are noted as generally not economical when done as SCBF, with BRBF the better choice for that geometry [66:46]. Capacity design inflates connection, column, base plate, and beam sizing well above the elastic demand, so these frames carry connection-heavy detailing and material premiums that must be priced.

### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, treat any seismic braced-frame job as connection-heavy and capacity-governed: beams in chevron bays and columns and base plates sized to brace overstrength will be heavier than an elastic read of the plans suggests, and BRBF braces are vendor-priced proprietary assemblies that belong as a specialty line, not a plain member weight from aisc_validator.py. For Mario's shop crew, the gusset fold-line width (twice gusset thickness plus tolerance), the one eighth inch slot oversize, and the column-splice and demand-critical-type welds with toughness requirements are the fit-up and welding items to control, all under AWS D1.1 plus AISC 341 toughness callouts. For field bolting and erection, the 2 inch slot length and one eighth inch width are intentional erection tolerances; Paul's crews must protect the brace and connection protected zones (no tack-on attachments) and must keep the gusset fold line free of slab encasement. Tekla detailing should carry the protected-zone marks, the fold-line dimensions, and brace out-of-plane buckling clearance (about 10 percent of length) so field clashes with architecture are caught in the model. The in-house PE stamp work must include the two SCBF plastic mechanism analyses (condition one at RyFy and 1.14 maximum compression; condition two at 0.3 post-buckling) and Design Guide 29 gusset checks. Note A1085 HSS with Ry 1.25 as the preferred seismic brace stock when sourcing. Doctrine conflict: NONE. This is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language, and the vendor names appear only as the speaker's generic BRBF manufacturer examples, not as Your Company supplier references.

## 2_Seismic Design in Steel_Concepts and Examples_Part 2
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nR_4iv_Mboo | Duration: 1:28:32 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
Rafael Sabelli (Walter P Moore) teaches Session 2 of the AISC Night School seismic course, covering special and intermediate steel moment frames. The controlling idea is capacity design: the beam flexural plastic hinge is the intended fuse, so the frame is proportioned for flexural yielding to form in the beams at each end while columns, panel zones, and connections stay essentially elastic [10:54], [16:41]. This prevents soft-story mechanisms and avoids yielding the high-axial-load columns. The session walks the portal-frame sub-assemblage from inflection point to inflection point as the basic unit of the frame, derives beam shear from the probable plastic moment, then derives column moment, column shear, and panel zone shear from that beam capacity [29:06], [30:09].

### Spec References
Speaker-cited: AISC 341 (Seismic Provisions), with explicit mention of the 2010 vs 2016 editions for the probable-moment strain-hardening factor and the strong-column-weak-beam ratio in "Chapter E" (M*pc/M*pb) [37:36], [86:33], [88:05]. AISC 358 the Prequalified Connection Standard, which sets the 1.15 strain-hardening factor adopted in 2016 (the 2010 provisions used 1.1) [38:10], [77:00]. AISC 360 for panel zone shear strength and concentrated-force limit states [61:33]. AWS D1.1 for welding (cited generically as the welding code violated in pre-Northridge practice) [51:33] and AWS D1.8 (Seismic Supplement) for weld dams not allowed, the large clip dimensions on continuity plates, and demand-critical weld toughness [53:39], [60:59]. The probable beam moment is Mpr = 1.1 (2010) or 1.15 (2016) x Ry x Fy x Z, with Ry x Fy = 55 ksi for A992 [37:36]. The 2016 PJP column-splice rule requires at least 85 percent effective throat [57:48].

### Technical Details
Connections discussed: reduced beam section (RBS, four bites out of the flanges to make a weak zone away from the column face) [13:31], [67:48]; welded unreinforced flange welded web (WUF-W) [55:43]; bolted flange plate and bolted end plate [68:19]; proprietary SidePlate, Kaiser bolted bracket, ConXtech ConXL two-way connection on a concrete-filled box column, Simpson Strong Frame, and the TT connection (2016 additions) [69:20], [69:53], [70:27]. Key geometry symbols: Mpr probable moment at hinge, Sh offset (about half beam depth from column face), Lh hinge-to-hinge length, Mcl moment at column centerline [34:25], [37:04]. Strong-column-weak-beam ratio greater than 1.0 addresses story mechanisms; a ratio well above 2.0 is needed to actually prevent column flexural yielding [78:07]. Panel zone shear equals the full change of column shear across the beam depth, reduced by the story column shear [43:46]. M*pc accounts for axial demand: ZcFy minus the axial term using the overstrength load combination [87:33].

### Fabrication Notes
The beam-flange-to-column-flange CJP groove weld is the critical fabrication detail. Modern practice CJP-welds the beam web to the column flange rather than bolting it, so the web participates and unloads the flanges [54:40], [64:37]. Backing bars (3/8 inch steel) are tacked, and tacks are incorporated into the final weld; weld tabs create run-off so starts and stops fall outside the joint [65:11]. At the bottom flange, current detailing removes the backing, back-gouges, reweld with a reinforcing fillet, and grinds smooth to remove the unfused notch that acted like a built-in crack starter [52:37], [55:43], [65:44]. Weld access holes are enlarged to relieve restraint and spread strain. Higher-toughness weld filler is mandatory at demand-critical welds. Continuity plates need large clips per AWS D1.8 to keep welding on the flat web [60:59]. Ultrasonic testing inspects the finished CJP for inclusions and discontinuities [66:15].

### Erection Notes
Stability bracing is required at the column and near (not within) the plastic hinge location, plus bracing at a defined spacing along the beam [71:00]. An adequate composite deck can replace the brace adjacent to the plastic hinge per the seismic provisions [71:34]. Protected zones, roughly one beam depth in from the column face, prohibit field attachments such as shot pins, low-toughness tack welds, deck puddle welds, and similar in the hinge region [72:06]. Column splices and column bases are also demand-critical weld locations and need that toughness and detailing in the field [72:39]. The speaker did not discuss crane, rigging, or lift sequencing.

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The Northridge lessons are the core failure catalog: bottom-flange CJP weld fracture and fracture into adjacent base metal [48:57]. Causes named: high strain at the column face with no demand relief, bolted (slipping) webs that forced the flanges to carry web moment and shear, weld access holes that failed to relieve restraint, column flange bending without continuity plates, low-toughness weld filler, beam material that ran grade 50 instead of the assumed grade 36 (so strong-column-weak-beam math worked only on paper), unfused steel backing acting as a 3/8 inch built-in crack, weld dams not allowed by AWS D1.8, too few weld passes, and poor welding and inspection that let welders do things AWS D1.1 prohibited [49:27], [51:02], [53:09]. Bottom-flange welds are most defect-prone because the welder reaches through the web access hole and must start and stop there [53:39].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Seismic moment frames carry real fabrication labor and material cost beyond gravity framing. Cost drivers a takeoff must price: demand-critical high-toughness weld filler, backing removal plus back-gouge plus reweld plus grind at every bottom flange, enlarged weld access holes, CJP web welds, continuity plates and doubler plates where local limit states come up short, and full UT inspection of every moment connection [60:29], [66:15]. The session shows a redesign trade where a heavier column with a lighter beam keeps the same sub-assembly stiffness but can eliminate continuity and doubler plates [63:06], a tonnage-versus-shop-labor trade worth flagging on a bid. Prequalified RBS or WUF-W connections per AISC 358 avoid the cost and schedule hit of project-specific qualification testing.

### Your Company Application
For Ivan, a moment-frame seismic job is not priced like gravity steel: the takeoff must add demand-critical weld filler, backing-removal labor, continuity and doubler plates, and UT on every moment connection, and should surface the heavier-column-lighter-beam trade as an estimating option. For Mario as AWS welding lead, this maps directly to D1.1 plus D1.8 demand-critical procedures: enlarged access holes, web CJP, remove-backgouge-reweld-grind at the bottom flange, no weld dams, correct pass count, high-toughness filler. For Paul, the protected zone (about one beam depth from the column face) bans field attachments and tack welds and is a real field-control item. Tekla detailing must model RBS cuts, continuity and doubler plates, access-hole geometry, and protected-zone callouts. For the in-house PE stamp, the strong-column-weak-beam check, panel zone shear per AISC 360, and Mpr derivation per AISC 341/358 are the governing calcs. Anchor rods tie to the column-base discussion: rods are sized for worst-case uplift (no live load, 0.9 dead, vertical earthquake up), while column compression adds base-plate overstrength [79:43]. No conflict with Your Company doctrine: this is conventional structural steel, no PEMB language, and all member weights still route through aisc_validator.py rather than any number spoken here. Doctrine flags: NONE.

## Design of Underhung Hoist and Crane Girders
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WL4juwP5XrU | Duration: 1:32:40 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
The webinar (Lucas Toggle, AISC, 2017-05-18) covers design of underhung bridge crane runway girders, where the hoist and trolley travel on a bridge girder whose end trucks ride on the bottom flange of the runway members suspended from the roof framing [01:32][02:35]. The controlling theme is that underhung (bottom-flange-loaded) runway design differs from top-running crane design: there is no single governing code, so the engineer assembles criteria from several documents, and strength and deflection are usually not the governing checks. Torsion, fatigue, local flange bending, and local web tension under the wheel typically control [71:43][73:14]. Practical underhung capacity is 10 to 15 tons because of local flange bending effects, with typical jobs running 1 to 7.5 tons [06:47].

### Spec References
Cited by the speaker: AISC 360 Specification for allowable strength and fatigue (free download) [13:27]; AISC 360 Appendix 3 fatigue provisions and Table A-3.1 stress categories with threshold stress range F-th and allowable stress range F-SR [41:26][44:29][45:00]; AISC 360 Chapter H for combined loading and biaxial bending, equation H1-1b [38:47][60:42][88:20]; Section F2.2 for F-critical and equation F4-2 for the cap-channel section [59:37][63:24]; AISC Design Guide 7 (industrial buildings, includes a top-running crane example) [14:03]; AISC Design Guide 9 (torsional analysis, references the AISC torsion design manual) [14:34][38:47][39:17]; AISC Steel Construction Manual Table 1-19 (combined wide-flange-plus-channel properties) [62:21]; ASCE 7 (impact factors, 20% side thrust, 10% longitudinal tractive) [13:27][22:44][77:24]; ASME NUM1 (reduced impact factors) [13:27][79:27]; AIST Technical Report 13 (load combinations, end-stop forces) [14:34][25:18][91:23]; CMAA 74 (service classes, Table 2.6-1; installation tolerances Table 1.4.1-1) [14:34][18:40][26:22]; IBC 2015 and ANSI standards for enclosed/patented track [70:07][79:27]. A 2005 Modern Steel Construction article is cited for the cantilever K-sub-C method [35:06].

### Technical Details
Design loads are maximum wheel load (bridge weight distributed to end trucks plus rated hoist-and-trolley load near one end truck), vertical impact 0 to 25% of wheel load, lateral side thrust 20% of rated capacity plus hoist and trolley weight (bridge weight excluded), longitudinal tractive 10% of maximum wheel load, plus end-stop force [21:14][22:14][24:15]. Side thrust and tractive forces act horizontally at the top of the bottom flange, perpendicular and parallel to the runway respectively, and are distributed to each wheel [49:39][77:54]. Bottom-flange loading increases lateral-torsional-buckling resistance, allowing up to a 40% C-sub-B increase per Structural Stability Research Council guidance (the example used a 1.4 multiplier) [32:30][33:34][60:09]. Deflection limits are L/450 vertical (wheel load without impact) and L/400 lateral [27:06]. Fatigue need not be checked below 20,000 cycles or where stress is fully compressive [42:57][43:27]; the worked example used ASTM A992, a W16x57 wide flange versus a W16x36 plus C12x20.7 cap channel [58:36][62:21].

### Fabrication Notes
The major shop cost driver is the runway splice: it needs a complete-joint-penetration weld at the bottom flange, ground smooth for a continuous running surface, with the backer rod removed and the CJP tested [51:49][52:50]. Leaving the backer rod in place drops the fatigue stress category (lower F-th and C-f constant), so removal is a fatigue requirement, not optional cleanup [46:04]. Cap channels add shop labor to weld two shapes together plus the channel weight, and do not resist lateral force or aid local flange bending, so a wide flange alone is often the lighter, cheaper choice unless the cap-channel section is roughly 20 lb/ft lighter [29:25][65:59][66:30]. Avoid notches, holes, cover plates, and transverse welds on the tension flange; clamped attachments are preferred over welded or bolted ones to limit stress risers [46:35][47:07].

### Erection Notes
Runway beams must be installed straight, parallel, and at constant elevation to the CMAA 74 tolerances, which are tighter than the AISC Code of Standard Practice and must be flagged to the contractor early and shown on the construction documents [26:22][55:25]. Sample CMAA tolerances: span 3/16 to 3/8 in, lateral runway straightness 3/8 in total with 1/4 in per 20 ft rate of change, and a tight differential-elevation tolerance between the two parallel runways [27:24][28:25]. Splices go near (but not at) vertical supports for safe access, away from the maximum negative moment [52:20]. Details should provide vertical, lateral, and longitudinal adjustability (shims, through-bolts with adjustable nuts, clamping) for rail alignment and to absorb dead-load deflection of the superstructure [55:25][55:56]. An initial runway survey verifies installed tolerances, and periodic maintenance must continue through service life [72:14].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The named recurring error is treating underhung design like top-running design and assuming strength or deflection governs, when torsion, fatigue, and local effects usually control [71:43][73:14]. Clients sometimes specify CMAA Service Class E or F for an underhung crane, which is wrong because E and F apply only to top-running cranes [43:59]. Unintended continuity introduced through connection plates between simple-span ends is a detailing trap [30:25]. Excessive deflection in the supporting structure is cited as a cause of a substantial number of crane problems and failures, so building members supporting the runway must meet the crane deflection criteria, not the looser L/250 to L/300 building limits [80:28][81:30]. A runway surface gap over the crane manufacturer's limit (often 1/16 in) causes wheel binding [83:06].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Splices are explicitly called expensive (CJP weld, grind, backer-rod removal, NDE), so continuous-span runways are favored to minimize them, and a checklist is recommended for repeat designs [30:56][51:49][74:15]. The example shows the cap channel forcing the wide flange up from a W16x57-class member toward a heavier W16x50-plus-channel build because of local flange bending, illustrating that adding material can raise both weight and cost rather than lower it [64:58][65:28]. Pre-engineered clamps are reported to save up to 17% versus fabricated clamps and carry manufacturer QC and dimensional/impact testing, where fabricated clamps have no standardized testing and depend entirely on shop workmanship [69:06][68:06]. Engaging the crane manufacturer and joist supplier early reduces rework risk, since SJI has no fatigue design standard for joists [55:56][56:30].

### Your Company Application
For Ivan, crane-runway scope is a member takeoff problem with a heavy connection premium: each runway splice carries a CJP-weld-plus-NDE cost that Tonnage-by-weight alone misses, and a cap-channel alternative must be priced against the lighter plain wide flange (the 20 lb/ft rule of thumb) rather than assumed beneficial, all member weights pulled through aisc_validator.py. For Mario, the controlling shop items are the bottom-flange CJP runway splice ground smooth with backer rod removed (an AWS D1.1 CJP under fatigue category rules) and the discipline of no welds, notches, or holes on the tension flange. For Paul and field crews, CMAA 74 installation tolerances are tighter than the AISC Code of Standard Practice and require an initial runway survey, which is a coordination and inspection scope to capture, not a casual set. For Tekla detailing, the plan/elevation Tekla model shown in the webinar matches our workflow; details must carry vertical, lateral, and longitudinal adjustability and avoid accidental continuity at splice plates. For our in-house PE stamp, this is exactly the kind of single-component design that gets overlooked: the stamp must cover torsion (Design Guide 9), fatigue (Appendix 3 Table A-3.1), and local web/flange effects, not just strength and deflection. Joist interaction matters because SJI has no joist fatigue standard, so any ACP-style job with crane runways on joists needs the joist manufacturer engaged early with our fatigue criteria, tracked in ACP project controls. Doctrine flag: the webinar repeatedly references pre-engineered metal buildings as a host structure for these cranes; that is the speaker's context only and must NOT migrate into any Your Company outward language, which stays conventional structural steel with no PEMB terminology (Tier 1 brand rule). Otherwise NONE.

## Stiffeners and Doublers - Oh My!
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wzVCON-baSw | Duration: 1:27:18 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
Carol Drucker (Drucker Zajdel Structural Engineers) teaches why doubler and stiffener controversies arise on projects and how to prevent them through correct design, detailing, and clear assignment of design responsibility [01:00]. A doubler is a web reinforcing plate; the main case is the column panel zone at beam-to-column flange moment connections, where the offset top and bottom flange forces drive an increased horizontal shear (shear flow, VQ/It) across the zone between flanges [02:01][04:34]. A stiffener (continuity plate) reinforces the column at the same connection for the local flange limit states. The controlling design move stressed throughout is to verify the actual panel-zone shear against the column strength rather than assume full beam moment capacity, because that assumption can require doublers on nearly every column [34:58][35:29].
### Spec References
Cited verbatim by the speaker: AISC Design Guide 13 (Charlie Carter, doubler/stiffener design, written 1999 against the 1993 spec) [06:42][21:25][40:08]; AISC Design Guide 29 (Bill Thornton and Larry Muir, Chevron effect) [15:38]; AISC 360 Section J10.6 (panel-zone shear, elastic and plastic range equations, axial-load dependent) [36:32]; Chapter G and equation G2-1 (doubler sizing, shear) [38:36][76:21]; Section G2.1 (minimum doubler thickness for shear buckling) [76:21]; J10.7 (unframed beam ends restrained against rotation) [46:23]; J10.1 flange bending, J10.2 web local yielding, J10.3 web crippling (with new Qf factor in 2016) [54:11][55:14]; equation J2-5 (50% weld strength increase for load perpendicular to weld axis) [71:39]; Table 4-1, Tables 9-x equation 9-50, Table 14-4 [65:58][66:31][70:05]; Manual Part 10 encroachment table [09:19]; Manual Part 15 bracket procedure for partial-depth stiffeners [50:34]. AWS D1.8 2016 (seismic supplement to AWS D1.1) provides the pre-qualified doubler weld configuration as a bevel PJP not requiring UT [11:24][27:13]. Code of Standard Practice Section 3.1.1 (2005/2010 and 2016) on showing column web doubler plates [26:43][29:23]. ASCE 7 load combinations referenced for the worked example [63:54].
### Technical Details
Doubler weld configurations: flush doubler groove-welded into the column radius, or a thickened doubler prepped to clear the radius and fillet-welded to the flange; the effective thickness of a thickened doubler is the thickness at the toe of the fillet, not the full plate [06:42][07:45]. Thin doublers are 1/4 to 3/8 inch, thick over 3/8; thin can be square cut with limited radius override, thick must be prepped (30 degrees common) [08:48][09:50]. AWS D1.8 prequalifies a 30-degree prep with no radius override; override is allowed if three macro-etch tests show fusion and no cracking [11:54][12:25]. Panel-zone strength reduces sharply when axial load approaches the squash load (alpha PR over Py above 0.4 triggers reduction) [31:57][74:47]. Stiffener minimums: width one-third beam flange minus half column web; thickness the greater of width/16 or half the element delivering the force; partial-depth stiffeners acceptable except web crippling now needs 3/4 depth in the 2016 spec [47:58][49:32]. Stiffener eccentricity limited to 2 inches with effectiveness interpolated from 100% to 65% per DG13 [58:48].
### Fabrication Notes
The fabricator-friendliest detail is the thickened doubler with a single-pass 5/16 fillet to the column flange; the offset doubler with a spacer plate is the least fabricator-friendly [05:38][16:38]. Ask the fabricator early for the maximum doubler thickness before splitting into two plates, typically 1/2 to 5/8 inch [06:42]. Increasing doubler thickness to provide land for a single-pass fillet can beat increasing the fillet leg size [07:45]. Stiffeners are clipped at the web to clear K detailing and at the flange to clear k1; welding in the k area is allowed for wind/low seismic if the clip is 1.5 inches past the radius and the weld stops short by one weld size, because rotary-straightened W-shapes have low toughness there [51:05][51:35]. Fitting both stiffener ends to bear is time-consuming (fit, file, repeat), so usually only one end is finished to bear with a 5/16 fillet on the other [62:19].
### Erection Notes
This webinar covers connection design, fabrication economy, and design-responsibility allocation; it does not address field erection, sequencing, bracing, crane/rigging, or site coordination. No erection-specific guidance was given.
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The recurring failure is UT rejection of doublers groove-welded into the column radius: as the doubler overrides the radius a gap forms behind it, producing questionable UT results; the speaker cited a project where the shop inspector insisted on UT, several welds failed, and the team requalified them as PJP by accounting for root Z-loss [10:52][14:04][14:36]. Welding in the k area has caused cracking of W-section members in fabrication [51:35]. A design error named is missing the panel-zone shear entirely because 3D line-element analysis (the speaker showed RISA output) reports constant column shear with no panel-zone spike [30:56]. Over-conservatism by specifying full beam moment capacity instead of actual moments is flagged as a job-killer [31:57]. Outdated references (the old red book plug-weld rule based on the 1978 spec) cause unnecessary requirements [40:38].
### Bid / Cost Implications
The office cost study (14x90 column, two W24x55 beams, 350 kip-ft, half-inch stiffeners and doublers sent to multiple fabricators) found: thickened doubler prepped to clear the radius saved 25% over the groove-into-radius baseline; upsizing the column ~20 lb/ft to W14x109 saved 15%; the cheapest option in every case was upsizing the column to drop the stiffeners and using a thickened doubler with a single 5/16 fillet [22:29][24:03][25:07]. Eliminating both stiffeners and doublers was 8% more costly because heavier 14-columns above W14x132 jump over $200/ton [25:38][20:53]. The seismic manual notes upsizing a column 50 to 100 lb/ft for a clean shaft is often cheaper than doublers [19:50]. On a price-per-ton (unit weight) job, the upsize-and-add-tonnage option pays the fabricator more while cutting shop labor, so it is the fabricator-preferred choice [25:07]. Pricing across fabricators varied widely, so confirm with the actual shop [24:34].
### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff and bid screening on moment-frame jobs, the controlling estimating decision is whether doublers/stiffeners are excluded or delegated: per Code of Standard Practice 3.1.1 the 2016 edition now requires conceptual details and quantities (or an allowance) on the drawings at bid time, but engineers still write contrary exclusions in specs or typical details, so Ivan must read those exclusions before pricing or risk an unfunded RFI fight over who pays for doublers [26:43][28:19][29:23]. This is a real bid-risk line item to flag, and the cost study gives Ivan defensible ratios (thickened doubler -25%, modest column upsize -15%) to advise the EOR or carry an allowance. For Mario's shop and welding lead role, the actionable details are the AWS D1.8 prequalified 30-degree PJP doubler weld (avoids UT), the single-pass 5/16 fillet preference, the k-area weld restriction on rotary-straightened W-shapes, and the macro-etch test path for radius override [11:54][51:35]. For our in-house PE stamp on delegated connection design, use J10.6 with the actual moment breakdown (dead/live/lateral) and column axial load rather than full beam capacity, since the worked example showed the difference between ~100% and ~26% of columns needing doublers [34:58][35:29]. AISC weights stay sourced from bridge/aisc_validator.py; this content informs connection scope and cost, not member weights. No conflict with Your Company doctrine; this is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language.

## Steel Specifications Unraveled
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WfmWj-KqWKE | Duration: 59:07 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is a one-hour AIA/PDH webinar by John Baier, principal at SMBH Inc. (Columbus, OH), on how a structural engineer edits and structures the steel project specification so it agrees with the general notes and the drawings [00:30][03:32]. The thesis is the three-part CSI MasterFormat section structure (Part 1 General, Part 2 Products, Part 3 Execution) applied to Division 5 metals, the goal being a short, coordinated, internally consistent spec where any single piece of information lives in only one place to avoid conflicting data [13:39][09:36]. It is a specification-writing and coordination talk, not a connection-design or welding-procedure talk.

### Spec References
Cited by name: CSI MasterFormat with 50 divisions, Division 5 metals (with Division 3 concrete, 6 wood, 9 painting referenced for coordination) [08:04][08:36]; section number 05 12 00 ("oh five one two zero zero") for structural steel [60s, 28:50]; AISC 341 referenced on seismic jobs [19:17]; the AISC Code of Standard Practice, specifically Chapter 10 for AESS categories now matching IBC 2016's reference [47:49][48:21][49:10]; SDI specification for steel deck and SJI specification for joists [19:47][36:02]; IBC Table 1604.3 for deflection criteria [37:06]. Material/product references: ASTM A1085 50 ksi HSS [33:57], A325 bolts [21:18], A490 for tension-control bolts [34:28], A307 bolts for shear and joist-to-column [34:59]. AISC fabricator certification and the IAS accreditation alternative [26:44]. SP2/SP3 surface-prep cleaning levels and galvanizing G60/G90 coatings [31:25][41:40].

### Technical Details
The talk covers material grade selection in Part 2 including the A1085 50 ksi HSS chicken-and-egg between engineers and producers [33:57], bolt-grade retention (keep A325/A490/A307 as the job actually uses, delete the rest), and the three tension-control installation options the spec can leave open to the fabricator: turn-of-nut, tension-control spline bolts, and direct tension indicators [34:28][35:29]. ASD versus LRFD must be stated so reported reactions and loads are unambiguous [20:17][36:32]. Joist topics include SJI camber (no camber, per-SJI camber, or engineer-specified, with a span/camber table) and the masonry-wall-adjacent deflection concern, plus bridging now left to the manufacturer rather than drawn row-by-row [38:36][40:07]. Deck topics include profile, depth, gauge, single/double/triple span, and the unshored-span trap where omitting yield strength (40 ksi versus a manufacturer's higher value) changes allowable unshored span from 8'-9" to 9'-9" on the same 2-inch form deck at a 5.5-inch slab, 20 gauge [43:44][44:48].

### Fabrication Notes
Quality assurance hinges on requiring an AISC-certified fabricator (or IAS-accredited alternative); if certification is not required, the engineer must add Part 2 source quality control because certification is what removes the need for an inspector to enter the shop and inspect welds [26:44][27:47]. For non-certified small or rural shops, the fallback is qualifying language such as ten years of successful experience on comparable projects [27:15]. Galvanizing requires specifying no quench for steel that will later be painted, since the water bath leaves impurities that defeat primer adhesion [31:55][32:25]. Relief holes in galvanized closed shapes must have a named party responsible for plugging, because trapped water that freezes can split the member, a quarter-million-dollar exposure on a big job if left as a change order [32:55][33:26]. Acoustic deck batts on cellular deck must be factory-installed [45:18].

### Erection Notes
Part 3 Execution governs the field: erection requirements, whether certified erectors are required, and field quality control [22:21]. Most owners now hire the testing agency rather than the contractor, driven by the special-inspections regime, and the spec must state this so the contractor does not carry it in the bid while still requiring the contractor to coordinate timely inspector access [22:52][23:23]. Field protection and repair of shop-primed steel is addressed, and tension-control connections with turn-of-nut require getting the inspector on site at the right moment to inspect [23:53][24:24]. A movement noted over the prior decade is leaving steel unprimed (plain) during erection where it is concealed in the final product [30:55].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The recurring failure mode is conflicting information held in two places (spec versus general notes versus drawings), which the talk addresses with a "strictest provision shall govern" clause naming all three documents [09:36][56:25]. Concrete pitfalls named: speccing deck without a yield strength and getting an unexpectedly short unshored span [44:48]; failing to assign relief-hole plugging [33:26]; quenching galvanized steel that must later be primed [32:25]; speccing double-span deck on a single-span canopy condition [42:44]; and unintentionally adding cost by requiring primed or painted roof deck that the project does not need [07:34]. The talk is about spec-drafting errors, not weld/bolt rejection statistics.

### Bid / Cost Implications
Cost discipline is a theme: on large warehouse jobs with acres of deck and joists, specifying unneeded primer or paint on roof deck adds real per-square-foot cost the developer scrutinizes [07:03][07:34]. G90 galvanizing versus standard G60 is usually a custom order that adds schedule time [41:40]. A spec that omits certification or testing requirements distorts a public bid because some bidders carry those costs and others do not, so a complete spec keeps the bidding field level [52:12]. Leaving the three tension-control methods open lets the fabricator pick the cheapest installation [35:29], and letting the joist manufacturer set bridging lets them compete on analysis and erection time [40:07].

### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff and bid screening, this confirms why the spec and general notes must be read together before pricing: deck primer/paint, G90 versus G60, unshored-span limits, and certification/testing requirements all move cost and belong in the count assumptions, not guessed. It reinforces our verify-don't-generate posture, never harvest deck gauge or yield from one place when the controlling number may sit in the drawings. For Mario's shop and welding QC, the AISC-certification point is direct: our certification is what keeps a third-party inspector out of the shop for routine weld inspection, so the cert is a cost and risk lever, and the no-quench-before-paint and relief-hole-plugging rules are shop-floor catches worth a standing checklist. For anchor rods and in-house PE stamp, the delegated-design submittal note (say explicitly when calculations must be signed and sealed) maps to our connection and embed design [18:16]. For joists, the SJI camber and manufacturer-set bridging guidance applies directly. Paul's safety scope is untouched: the speaker states specifications deliberately stay out of means, methods, and safety, leaving those to OSHA and other requirements [57:50]. Doctrine flags: NONE. The conventional structural-steel framing (structural steel, joists, deck, miscellaneous/secondary) matches our positioning with no PEMB language present.

## New Developments in Connection Design
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wUvOCLDJHQ8 | Duration: 1:28:35 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This webinar, presented by Bo Dowswell (PhD, PE, principal at ARC International, an AISC connection-design researcher), covers the revised design procedure for coped beams that moved from the 14th to the 15th edition AISC Steel Construction Manual [02:21][11:40]. The core change is the shift from an elastic allowable-stress-design approach to a strength-based procedure that lets the engineer take credit for the inelastic or potentially plastic strength of the cope, and removes the old limits on cope geometry [11:40][80:33]. A cope is the notch cut in a beam flange and web so the beam can frame to a supporting member, single cope when only the top flange is cut, double cope when top and bottom flanges are cut for equal-nominal-depth framing [03:25][04:26]. The talk treats shear, flexural, axial, and combined-load strength for both single and double copes, with single-cope flexure modeled as local buckling (a short WT cantilever) and double-cope flexure modeled as lateral-torsional buckling [42:20][80:33].

### Spec References
Cited verbatim by the speaker: AISC 360 Section J4.2 for shear yielding of connection elements [16:46]; Chapter F three-part local-buckling curve for WT members and the lambda_p / lambda_r slenderness transition [20:25][21:29]; Section J4.1 for tension yielding of the cope, designed as a tension member [43:53][75:53]; Section E7 for local buckling and effective area A_e of slender compression members [44:54]; Section D7 used to derive the simplified axial-strength equation [46:57]; Section F11 (added between the green book and the 2016 spec) for rectangular cantilever-beam flexural buckling, used for double copes [55:36][56:38]; Section J4.4 for flexural (column-type) buckling of double copes, with KL/r <= 25 allowing tension yield without reduction and KL/r > 25 sending you to Chapter E [76:23][77:27]. The buckling adjustment factor f carries over unchanged from the 14th edition Manual [28:50]. Source material is the Cheng, Yura and Johnson report from University of Texas (Ferguson Lab) and an AISC Engineering Journal paper "Plastic Strength of Rectangular Connection Elements" [08:31][26:10][83:31]. A known errata: the Manual C_B range should read greater-than-or-equal-to 1.84, not less-than-or-equal-to [64:36].

### Technical Details
Shear strength uses the 0.6 von Mises factor times F_y times gross shear area A_gv = H_o times t_w, where H_o is the remaining depth at the cope [16:46][17:19]. Single-cope flexure is a local-buckling problem on a short WT-like cantilever of length e (eccentricity from supporting-member face to cope face), with critical stress from classical plate buckling (Timoshenko / SSRC) using a plate coefficient that is theoretically 0.61 but corrected by the empirical adjustment factor f and a K_1 cope-length term [18:53][27:17][31:24]. Tom Murray's simplification set lambda_p = lambda_r / 2 from the experimental data so lambda_r need not be computed [23:33][24:36]. Axial strength uses an effective area A_e per E7 with its own K_a coefficient (1.28 for long copes where C/H_o >= 1.64, higher for shorter copes) [44:54][47:28][48:05]. Double-cope flexure goes to F11 after computing L_b and C_b from Manual equations developed by Dowswell and Robert White via finite-element models, where L_b is simply the average of top and bottom cope lengths (an estimate originally suggested by Professor Yura) [56:38][66:08][68:42]. Buckle shapes confirm the bottom cope barely affects strength [59:47].

### Fabrication Notes
The cope itself is the controlling shop-cut feature; longer and deeper copes than the standard cope are common in practice, driven by skewed framing (a 45-degree skew increased one cope length about 40 percent) and equal-nominal-depth double-cope conditions [04:57][05:28][06:29]. Dowswell flags that fabrication and handling can introduce the geometric imperfections the design curve cannot credit: welding distortion, getting bumped in shipping, or roughly a sixteenth of an inch of out-of-flatness from cutting the cope itself [73:52][74:22]. Because the test specimens used to set the curve did not have measured imperfections (out-of-flatness, initial twist, residual stresses), the Manual curve is held conservative rather than raised [73:21][73:52]. A galvanized double-cope example is shown, so coping interacts with galvanizing [04:26].

### Erection Notes
The presentation is connection-strength focused and does not cover crane, rigging, or sequencing. The one erection-adjacent caution is lateral-torsional buckling of the overall beam: with the long copes now permitted, the end connections will not restrain the beam the way the pinned-end assumption implies, so an unbraced (or not-yet-braced) coped beam has greatly reduced LTB strength and the engineer of record must check it separately from the connection [08:00][80:33][81:04]. This matters during erection before decking or bracing is in place.

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The talk is design-method rather than inspection-failure oriented, so no specific weld rejection or bolt-inspection failures are named. The governing failure modes discussed are cope buckling: local buckling of the single-cope web in compression, lateral-torsional buckling of the double cope, and shear yielding along the cope plane, with most real copes failing inelastically or elastically rather than reaching the plastic moment because H_o is too deep [05:28][07:30][52:01]. The combined-load checks show long copes fail by axial-flexure interaction and short copes by axial-shear interaction [49:13][50:19].

### Bid / Cost Implications
No dollar figures or schedule estimates appear. The practical takeaway with cost effect is that the 15th-edition strength procedure recovers inelastic capacity and removes the old cope-geometry limits (single cope previously limited to half member depth and twice member depth in length; double cope to 20 percent depth), which can qualify deeper or longer copes that the elastic method would have rejected, reducing the need for reinforcement on skewed and equal-depth framing [13:42][14:12][80:33]. The judgment-heavy axial and combined-load checks mean coped-beam connections on heavy or skewed members carry engineering effort that should be priced into connection-design scope [10:02][49:13].

### Your Company Application
For Tekla detailing and the in-house PE stamp, this is the governing method when a shop-cut cope is deep, long, or skewed: single copes check as local buckling per the Chapter F WT curve, double copes as lateral-torsional buckling per F11 with L_b as the average of top and bottom cope lengths, and both pull the section properties at the cope rather than the full section. For Ivan's takeoff, skewed and equal-nominal-depth connections drive longer copes and added connection-design effort, which should be flagged for estimating rather than assumed standard. For Mario's shop crew, the note that cutting the cope can leave roughly a sixteenth of an inch of out-of-flatness, and that welding distortion erodes the as-designed capacity, supports tight cope-cut QC and fit-up control. Tonnage and AISC weights stay sourced from aisc_validator.py; this video informs connection design and detailing judgment, not member weights. No conflict with Your Company doctrine: conventional structural steel, no PEMB language, no supplier names, and it reinforces verify-do-not-generate since the speaker repeatedly stresses engineering judgment over blind equation use [10:34][70:46].
