## Part 2: Seismic Design for Non-West Coast Engineers
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MmRG7YH-LvM | Duration: 1:03:07 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
Mike Engelhardt (UT Austin) introduces earthquake engineering for engineers outside high-seismic regions, with the second half focused on steel [00:31]. The governing idea is that we do not beat earthquakes with strength, we survive them with ductility, trading elastic strength for controlled yielding [00:31, 09:17]. ASCE 7 sets the lateral strength and stiffness demand, and AISC 341 (Seismic Provisions for Structural Steel Buildings) supplements AISC 360 to tell us how to build ductility in through ductile detailing [08:47, 31:50]. The unifying method is capacity design: pick fuse elements to yield, detail them for ductility, then make everything else stronger than the fuse so the fuse yields first [33:24, 55:01].
### Spec References
Speaker cited, by name: ASCE 7-10 (moving to ASCE 7-16), AISC 341 (2010 edition shown, Seismic Provisions for Structural Steel Buildings) [10:18, 31:20], AISC 360 (main spec) [31:50], ACI 318 for concrete [09:48], AISC 358 (Prequalified Connections for Special and Intermediate Steel Moment Frames for Seismic Applications) [61:07], and AWS D1.8 (the seismic supplement to D1.1) [61:38]. Reference documents named: FEMA P-749, FEMA P-750 (NEHRP Recommended Seismic Provisions, the source document for ASCE 7), FEMA P-751 (design examples), NEHRP Seismic Design Technical Briefs No. 2 steel SMF, No. 4 nonlinear analysis, No. 5 composite steel deck diaphragms, No. 8 steel concentrically braced frames [57:35, 58:36]. No AISC 360 chapter/section or J-table numbers were spoken in this part; those are not invented here.
### Technical Details
Seismic Design Category (SDC) A through F controls everything and depends on geographic location, soil/site class (A hard rock through E soft clay, F site-specific, default D), and the building risk category 1 through 4 (most buildings are category 2) [10:49, 11:50, 16:28]. Spectral accelerations S_S (short period, about 0.2 sec) and S_1 (1 sec) come from ASCE 7 maps or the free USGS lat/long tool, are modified for soil, then multiplied by 2/3 for the design spectrum [12:20, 14:23, 17:59]. Base shear V = C_s times building weight, where the elastic demand is divided by the response modification factor R [25:40, 26:42]. R values stated: special moment frame R=8, intermediate moment frame R=4.5, special concentrically braced frame R=6, undetailed systems R=3 (allowed only in SDC B and C) [28:17, 29:47]. Systems covered: special/intermediate/ordinary moment frames (beam flexural yielding is the fuse), special/ordinary concentrically braced frames (brace yields in tension, buckles in compression), eccentrically braced frames (shear-yielding link 2 to 3 ft long is the fuse), buckling restrained braced frames (steel core yields tension and compression, casing prevents buckling), and special plate shear walls (thin web plate buckles then yields in tension field) [36:01, 39:36, 44:42, 49:19, 53:27].
### Fabrication Notes
Fuse-element detailing rules are deliberately simple: no high-strength steel (Grade 50 or less, because higher strengths tend to be brittle), low width-thickness (b/t) ratios to delay local buckling, and good lateral bracing because beams want to twist [34:26]. EBF links require many fitted stiffeners welded in to handle shear buckling, which Engelhardt calls one of the more costly detailing features [46:45, 47:16]. BRBs are proprietary and bought from certified manufacturers (Star Seismic, CoreBrace, Nippon Steel named) because the required qualification testing is not affordable to replicate; the brace is a debonded steel core sliding inside a grout-filled HSS casing [49:49, 51:22]. AISC 341 carries a quality control / quality assurance section that grew directly out of Northridge welding-quality failures [55:32]. Welding done correctly is about 90 percent of the battle of keeping a steel building standing [61:38].
### Erection Notes
The talk is design-oriented and does not walk field sequencing, crane, or rigging. The erection-relevant content is that lateral frames are placed only in selected locations, not everywhere, because they are expensive, while the rest is gravity framing [36:01]. Braces must point in both directions so that as half buckle the other half carry tension [43:11]. Connections must be detailed to let a brace rotate when it buckles (in-plane or out-of-plane) rather than tear the connection apart, which is a fit-up and gusset-geometry concern that carries into the field [44:12].
### Bolting / Welding
This part cites welding standards, not bolting. Welded beam-to-column moment connections were the central Northridge failure, where connections fractured instead of the beam yielding as intended [05:40, 06:13]. For high-level seismic detailing the controlling welding documents are AISC 358 prequalified moment connections plus AWS D1.8, the seismic supplement to AWS D1.1 [61:07, 61:38]. No bolt grades (A325/A490), no RCSC pretension or turn-of-nut method, and no electrode or preheat values were stated, so none are recorded here.
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Named real failures: 1985 Mexico City, a 21-story welded steel building collapsed onto a 14-story steel building [04:38]. 1994 Northridge, no collapse but widespread brittle fracture of welded beam-to-column connections, plus fractured HSS brace and brace connections and a cracked heavy base plate, all non-ductile behavior the design philosophy did not intend [05:40, 06:13, 06:44]. 1995 Kobe, welded beam-to-column fractures, brittle fracture of heavy welded box columns, brace-connection failures, and residual drift [07:14, 07:45]. The recurring lesson is a fracture or buckling limit state reaching capacity before the chosen fuse yields, traced largely to welding quality [32:22, 55:32].
### Bid / Cost Implications
SDC drives everything downstream: SDC A (Austin) requires essentially no seismic design, B and C calculate forces but usually skip ductile detailing, and D, E, F demand full California-level detailing even far from California [22:08, 23:09]. Dividing the elastic force by R gives very low design lateral forces (16 percent of building weight in Santa Clarita, 6.5 percent in Memphis for an R=8 SMF), so members and foundations are economical, but the offset is real money spent putting ductility in, since ductility is not free [29:47, 30:50]. EBF link stiffeners and BRB proprietary braces are concrete cost adders, and special detailing pulls in AISC 358, AWS D1.8, and a QA/QC program that adds inspection scope [46:45, 51:22, 55:32]. Site-class geotechnical work can justify a class above the default D and save money [16:58].
### Your Company Application
For Houston (Harris County), Texas is low-seismic, generally SDC A or B, so most Your Company work uses undetailed systems designed like wind (R=3) with no AISC 341 ductile detailing, and Ivan's takeoff should confirm the SDC from the structural general notes before assuming seismic scope is absent. The doctrine value is the capacity-design and fuse logic, which maps cleanly onto our verify-don't-generate posture: if a set does invoke AISC 341 (an out-of-region GC, a higher risk category, or a Memphis/out-of-state job), the bid must flag demand-critical welding, AISC 358 prequalified moment connections, AWS D1.8, EBF link stiffeners, or BRB proprietary braces as cost and schedule adders, and Mario's welding plus the in-house PE stamp must address D1.8 and the QA/QC program rather than default D1.1. Anchor-rod and base-plate work ties to the cracked-base-plate Northridge failure, reinforcing that column bases must develop the fuse capacity in any detailed system. No conflict with Your Company doctrine; this is methodology, not PEMB language, and the conventional structural steel positioning holds. DOCTRINE FLAG: NONE.

## Lean on Bracing for Steel I Shaped Girders
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ABoxRE5o9bs | Duration: 1:26:08 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This NSBA webinar by Jamie Ferris of TxDOT teaches lean-on bracing, a method of preventing lateral torsional buckling in steel I-girder bridges by letting several girders lean on one or two cross frames at each brace location through top and bottom struts, rather than placing a full cross frame in every bay [06:43][07:14]. The controlling failure mode is lateral torsional buckling, a lateral translation accompanied by twisting of the cross section, and the critical stage is deck placement when the bare steel must carry the entire construction load [02:35][03:05]. Cross frames and diaphragms act as torsional bracing because they control twist of the cross section, and a designed lean-on layout cuts the number of those braces while still meeting stability requirements [03:35][07:45]. The method derives from TxDOT research project 1772 at the University of Texas at Austin and applies to straight bridges with or without skew [10:23][07:14].
### Spec References
This is a bridge webinar, so citations are AASHTO LRFD, not AISC building spec, with three exceptions noted. Cited: AASHTO 6.8.2 tension check [49:40], AASHTO 6.9.4 compression check [49:40], AASHTO 6.13.2 bolt check for struts and AASHTO 6.13 generally [49:40][67:33], AASHTO 3.4.2 for the 1.5 construction load factor [59:17], and the AASHTO 20-degree skew threshold above which bracing must be normal to the girder lines rather than parallel to the skew [13:25]. AISC is referenced for the cross-sectional distortion expression in AISC Appendix 6 developed by Dr. Joe Yura in the 1980s [34:44], and the lateral imperfection of unbraced length over 500 times girder height is noted as consistent with the torsional bracing provisions of AISC [47:33][48:07]. Background strength work cites Yura report 1239 "Bracing of Steel Beams and Bridges," 1992 [46:24].
### Technical Details
Total torsional system stiffness combines cross frame stiffness, cross-sectional (web distortion) stiffness, and in-plane girder stiffness as springs in series, so the total is always smaller than the smallest component, and required stiffness is twice the ideal stiffness divided by a 0.75 resistance factor for an LRFD-compliant value [30:42][32:12]. Web distortion is the dominant reduction term: the portion of web outside the brace depth can distort, an effective web width of N plus 1.5H is used with the web spreading at a 0.75-to-1 slope, and for slender built-up webs (h over tw greater than 58) the web is split above and below the brace and recombined in series [35:14][36:25][36:55]. A worked example with a 48-inch web showed the 24-inch lower region contributing 185,400 kip-in/rad versus 1,459,400 for the 12-inch upper region, proving distortion is non-linear with depth [40:07]. Brace strength uses an initial imperfection of Lb/500 times girder height, with brace moment equal to brace force times brace height equal to required stiffness times the imperfection [47:33][48:37]. The design example was a three-span continuous straight I-girder bridge, zero skew, 46 ft wide, five girders at 10 ft spacing, 92-inch web at 0.6875 inch, 24-inch flange at 1.5 inch [50:29][57:46][58:16].
### Fabrication Notes
Cross frames are called out as one of the more expensive parts of a steel structure, so cutting their count directly reduces shop fabrication cost [17:30][08:15]. The tension-only cross frame configuration uses four angles with one diagonal in compression and one in tension; the slender angles do not perform well in compression so designers neglect the compression member and design only for tension, and the same angle size is typically used for all struts and cross frame members to simplify procurement (areas A_d and A_c treated as equal A_b) [43:11][44:12]. Connection plates carry holes for fit-up bolts at each corner of the cross frame [85:10]. Fewer and right-sized braces also reduce fatigue-prone details, since oversized standard cross frames attract larger live load forces that drive fatigue cracking near brace locations, especially on skewed supports [08:47][09:18].
### Erection Notes
Lean-on bracing reduced fit-up problems and let contractors erect girders faster than typical plate girders, saving schedule [08:15][17:00]. The framing plan must be built around the actual girder erection sequence, ideally after talking to contractors about lifting order, and TxDOT lays full cross frame lines at bearing and at field splice locations to prevent twist while the bridge is partially installed [52:00][55:12]. When erection side is known the cross frame layout follows a natural S-shape; when either side may start it becomes a mirror image with more cross frames [55:42][81:34]. On the 19th Street underpass, heavy struts were tied together and lifted with the girder, then untied and attached to the adjacent girder by ironworkers once set, and girders were left at the second splice point for about 18 months for traffic control with no stability issue [21:04][22:34][17:00]. Conventional bracing would have needed 80 cross frames there versus 28 with lean-on [19:02]; the design example dropped 148 conventional cross frames to 80 [68:33].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The recurring field problem is brace fit-up difficulty, worst near skewed supports, which lean-on bracing mitigates by replacing hard-to-fit cross frames with struts [14:55][70:36]. Fatigue cracking found during routine maintenance inspections around cross frames and diaphragms is the named in-service failure, caused by large stress concentrations from cross frame forces under truck traffic and aggravated by skew and by oversized standard braces [08:47][09:18]. No weld rejections or bolt inspection failures are named; TxDOT field-welds cross frames after a fit-up erection bolt and reports good results because it has good field welders and steel inspectors [04:06][04:37].
### Bid / Cost Implications
The core economic argument is fewer cross frames, which lowers fabrication cost and erection cost, reduces fit-up labor and construction timeline, and simplifies future inspection and maintenance [08:15][73:09]. TxDOT explicitly endorses the method for the right straight-girder projects in its design manual chapter 3 section 14 because of fabrication and erection savings [72:07]. For heavily skewed bridges, a partial application that removes cross frames only in problematic areas (the Lake Conroe SH 105 example) captures savings without redesigning the whole bridge [69:04][70:36]. The savings scale per structure, so for a multi-line bridge the stiffness, strength, tension, compression, and bolt checks are run for each line of braces across the width [68:33].
### Your Company Application
This is bridge work (AASHTO), so it does not directly govern a Your Company building bid, but the cost lever transfers cleanly: on any I-girder or wide-bay frame, Ivan's takeoff should treat cross frames and bracing as a cost driver and flag where engineered lean-on or strut substitution could cut piece count, fabrication, and field labor, while routing all member weights through aisc_validator.py rather than trusting the lecture math. The Lb/500 imperfection and the deck-placement-is-the-critical-stage point reinforce Paul Guerrero's erection-stability planning: bare steel must be braced for the construction case before any deck or concrete load, and partially erected girders need full brace lines at splices and bearings. Mario's crew should note the TxDOT practice of an erection fit-up bolt at each cross frame corner followed by field welding after girders are set, which matches conventional field-bolt-then-weld sequencing and the fit-up-bolt detail belongs in Tekla connection plates. The tie-and-lift handling of heavy struts is a rigging note for field bolting and crane planning. Conflict with Your Company doctrine: NONE; this is methodology, conventional structural steel, no PEMB language, no supplier names, and no rate or AISC-weight claims were imported.

## Part 1: Seismic Design for Non-West Coast Engineers
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=R87hxvDoxX8 | Duration: 59:41 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
This is the first of a two-hour AISC webinar by Micah Engelhardt (University of Texas at Austin) aimed at engineers with no earthquake-engineering background, and it stays at the fundamentals level on purpose [00:30]. The central teaching is that earthquake load is an inertia force, mass times acceleration, so F equals MA, and lighter buildings draw less force [30:56][31:28]. The second core idea is the design philosophy embodied in the building codes: we do not design ordinary buildings to stay elastic in a strong earthquake because that is uneconomic, so the goal is to prevent collapse and save lives while accepting substantial damage [51:11][52:11]. The mechanism that makes this possible is ductility, inelastic deformation capacity, and the closing point is that in a strong earthquake the maximum load a building sees is set by the building's own lateral strength, not by the strength of the quake [54:15][58:22]. All steel-specific content (AISC 341, welded connections, ductile detailing) is explicitly deferred to Part 2 [02:33][03:03].

### Spec References
Spoken references are to loads-and-philosophy documents rather than to fabrication standards. The speaker cites ASCE 7-10 for approximate-period rules of thumb (number of stories divided by ten for a moment frame under 12 stories, and a height-based formula T sub a equals a coefficient times height raised to a power, coefficients from a table) [44:57][45:27][45:59]. He names AISC 341, the Seismic Provisions for Structural Steel Buildings, but only as a preview of Part 2 [03:03]. For further reading he cites FEMA P-749 (introduction to the NEHRP recommended seismic provisions) and FEMA P-750 (the precursor to ASCE 7), both noted as free [52:11][53:45]. He uses the term risk-targeted maximum considered earthquake as the code design event [53:13]. No AISC 360 chapter, AWS D1.1 clause, RCSC provision, table number, or Design Guide number is cited; this is a loads and philosophy lecture, not a connection-design one.

### Technical Details
The lecture builds the response-spectrum concept from a single-degree-of-freedom elastic model with mass, a damping ratio (typical two to five percent of critical), and elastic stiffness K, combined into a natural period T [37:44][38:44]. Using the 1994 Northridge Newhall firehouse record (peak ground acceleration 59 percent g), a 0.25-second building amplified to about 2.2 g, a 0.5-second building to about 1.25 g, and a 1.0-second building to about 0.7 g, illustrating resonance [40:49][41:52]. Period correlates strongly with height: roughly 0.25 s for a 2.5-story building, 0.5 s for five stories, 1.0 s for ten stories, with low-rise buildings hit hardest because they resonate with typical ground motion [41:20][47:01]. Soft soil shifts the spectral peak to longer periods and can bring tall buildings into resonance, as in 1985 Mexico City [48:33][34:36]. A worked example takes spectral acceleration of 1.5 g times building weight to show an elastic structure would see an inertia force of 150 percent of its weight, an order of magnitude above the 10 to 20 percent code design force, the gap being covered by ductility [49:38][50:40].

### Fabrication Notes
No fabrication, tolerance, fit-up, or shop QC content appears in this hour. Shop-level steel detailing is held for Part 2 [02:33][58:53].

### Erection Notes
No erection, field-procedure, sequencing, bracing, or rigging content appears in this hour.

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
No connection-level inspection failures or rejections are detailed here, since the content is conceptual. The one concrete steel-performance note is that steel buildings in Northridge suffered fractures at welded connections, which the speaker flags only as a preview of a Part 2 discussion [29:23]. Building-collapse modes named as life-safety failures are unreinforced masonry, non-ductile reinforced concrete, and soft-story tuck-under parking levels [55:15][27:22].

### Bid / Cost Implications
The economic argument running through the talk is that designing to stay elastic in a strong earthquake is not affordable, so codes trade strength for ductility because ductility is generally less costly than strength [57:51]. The cost is accepted damage: choosing ductility is described as making a deal that the building will be damaged in a strong event [57:51]. Lighter structures attract less seismic force, which ties mass reduction to demand reduction [31:59]. None of this is steel-pricing or estimating detail; there are no rates, tonnage rules, or per-SF figures in this hour.

### Your Company Application
For Houston, this hour is context rather than a procedure: the takeaway is that seismic is not only a West Coast concern and the Gulf-coast / central-US designer should not assume zero seismic detailing, though Houston itself is low-hazard. The actionable steel content for Your Company (AISC 341 ductile detailing, demand-critical welds, protected zones, the Northridge welded-connection fractures) is in Part 2, so Ivan's takeoff, Mario's AWS D1.1 welding scope, and Tekla seismic-connection detailing draw nothing concrete from this session yet. Practical near-term use is limited to estimating intuition: lighter framing and correct period assumptions matter when a job carries any seismic design category, and a low seismic category should be confirmed from the project's ASCE 7 design data, not assumed. No conflict with Your Company doctrine. The conventional-structural-steel positioning is unaffected; no PEMB language and no supplier names arise. DOCTRINE_FLAGS: NONE.

## Designing of Strengthening for Existing Steel Members
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c2f5et7z-PA | Duration: 1:36:03 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
Joe Schuster of Simpson Gumpertz and Heger, co-author of the second edition of AISC Design Guide 15 (Rehabilitation and Retrofit), teaches how to evaluate and strengthen existing steel beams, columns, and connections when loads change [04:10][04:40]. Triggers for strengthening include added stories, change of occupancy (for example office at 50 psf live load converted to assembly at 100 psf), heavier finishes or dead loads, reframing for stairs and elevators, and repair of fire, impact, or corrosion section loss [05:41][06:11][07:43]. The method is verify by analysis: pull current loads, determine the historic member's actual material and cross-sectional properties, check available strength to the current AISC specification, and design reinforcing only where the demand exceeds the existing capacity [12:49][30:25].
### Spec References
AISC Specification Appendix 5 (evaluation of existing structures), with Section 5.3 evaluation by analysis and Section 5.4 evaluation by load test; sections 5.2.2 through 5.2.6 for required material tests including 5.2.6 for bolt and rivet strength [11:47][12:49][16:28][25:48]. Strength provisions from chapters B through K of the current specification, specifically chapter E (E3-4 elastic buckling, E6 and E6.2 built-up column welds), chapter F (F4.2 singly symmetric LTB, F13.3 cover plates), chapter I (concrete encasement), and chapter J (J2.2 weld minimums, J3.2 nominal shear, J1.9 reinforcing existing connections with welds, J1.10 sharing load between rivets and slip-critical bolts) [40:14][53:12][43:17][67:24][71:28][82:14]. The load test uses factored gravity 1.2D plus 1.6L held one hour with recovery to within 10 percent [14:23]. Design Guide 15 supplies historic shape tables and material specs; Design Guide 11 supplies historic rivet tensile values [29:00][79:09]. External codes cited: IEBC (repairs, additions, alterations, the 5 percent stress and substantial-damage thresholds), ASCE 7, ASTM A370, ASTM F606, and historic steel grades A7, A9, A36, A307, A502 grade 1, A325, A490 [08:43][13:21][17:58][25:48][81:13].
### Technical Details
Substantial structural damage means a lateral element reduced more than 33 percent or a gravity member supporting 30 percent of the building reduced more than 20 percent; additions or alterations that raise member stress over 5 percent must meet the current IBC [09:44][10:47]. Historic A7 and A9 (1901) carried 55 ksi tensile and yield at half the tensile; A36 became common after 1963 and grade 50 after the 1970s [19:32][20:12]. Weldability is judged by carbon equivalent: under 0.45 is weldable with standard procedures, 0.45 to 0.6 needs preheat to slow cooling, over 0.6 favors a bolted detail [21:43][22:43]. Beam reinforcing shifts the plastic neutral axis by welding a plate, WT, or angles to the bottom flange; the worked example raised a W12x16.5 from a plastic section modulus of 20.6 to 26.6 cubic inches with a 5 inch by quarter inch plate over only the 7.5 ft of overstress plus development [33:30][41:45]. Loaded columns lose strength near welds because steel above roughly 650 degrees weakens; designers treat the 1 to 1.5 inch zone around the weld as inactive and check the remaining section against the load present at welding [64:23][64:53]. Column preload may be ignored if the reinforced least radius of gyration stays at or above 85 percent of the original [65:54].
### Fabrication Notes
Limit heat input to loaded members: prefer fillet welds over groove welds, use the smallest adequate weld size, use intermittent welds, avoid overhead welding and welding across stress lines [24:48][25:18]. Verify weldability before fabricating reinforcement, by inspecting existing welded connections, by a carbon-equivalent chemical test, or by a tab-plate test (quarter inch by 2 by 2 plate with a 5/16 inch fillet, struck with a mallet, sound if the fracture runs through the weld not the interface) [23:14][23:45]. Make reinforcing plates wider than the existing flange so they weld topside; in the example the 5 inch plate beat the 4 inch flange [40:45]. Termination welds develop yield times area (45 kips on the beam plate, 108 kips on the column plate), and a weld across the plate end lets the side welds equal plate width rather than 2W [44:20][45:23]. Asymmetric single-side column plates risk welding distortion and P-delta and must be quantified [62:51].
### Erection Notes
This is rehab field work inside occupied buildings, not new erection. Shore before cutting rivets or replacing connections so the joint does not deform; if four of five rivets carry the in-place load, rivets may be swapped one at a time without shoring [81:43][81:13]. Shear-stud retrofit cores discretely through the slab, protects the top flange, controls coring water against the space below, then fills with non-shrink grout [57:47][58:49]. When the underside is inaccessible the team cut the slab topside and rewelded deck as demolition progressed [60:50]. New infill beams, props, and jacking-out of preload must follow loading sequence because added members only carry loads applied after install [54:12][51:37].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Over-conservatism is the named failure: bumping member or weld sizes adds heat and distortion to a loaded member and can cause cracking or P-delta [24:48][62:51]. High carbon causes low ductility and cracking, high phosphorus causes brittleness and weld cracking, high sulfur causes porous welds [21:43][22:13]. A tab-plate fracture at the weld-to-base-metal interface signals unweldable steel [23:45]. Coring can damage the top flange or hit slab reinforcing [57:47]. An unstiffened seat deforms too much before engaging load, so a stiffened welded seat with bolted seat-to-beam connection is required for ductility [84:14][85:47]. Combining new welds with existing bolts in one new joint is normally barred for stiffness incompatibility; the J1.9 and J1.10 allowances are the exception for existing riveted joints [82:44][83:14].
### Bid / Cost Implications
The strength-based current-code approach lets a much smaller plate replace a large tube that an old allowable-stress check would require, cutting steel and weld [39:42][41:45]. Reinforcing only the overstressed length matters: the column example reinforced the middle half and lost about 1 percent capacity while roughly halving plate and weld; intermittent staggered welds further cut deposit [76:33][77:05][46:53]. Load testing is rarely chosen because field survey plus analysis is cheaper than instrumenting and loading a structure [13:52]. Reliable project records remove the cost of coupon pull-testing to ASTM A370 [17:58]. Sharpening dead loads, live-load reduction, clear spans, and LRFD over ASD can each save reinforcing [34:00][34:30].
### Your Company Application
Ivan can use the Appendix 5 flow for any retrofit takeoff: a strengthening bid is a measured member takeoff of the existing shape (depth, flange width, average flange thickness through Design Guide 15) feeding aisc_validator.py, never SF times psf, and it carries the 5 percent stress trigger that decides whether a member even gets priced. Mario's crew owns the heat-control welding discipline (fillet over groove, smallest size, intermittent, no overhead, tab-plate verification before production) under AWS D1.1, and any weld to pre-1963 steel needs a carbon-equivalent or preheat call before the WPS is set. Paul should treat rivet swap and slab coring as shored, sequence-controlled operations with overhead and water-damage exposure. Tekla detailing must model partial-length plates, development welds, and the plate-end weld exactly, and the in-house PE stamp ties the strengthening calc to current-spec section numbers. Bolting work maps to A325 or A490 swaps under RCSC and the J1.10 slip-critical sharing rule; in-house anchor-rod and joist scope is not touched by this webinar. No conflict with Your Company doctrine: this is conventional structural-steel rehab with no PEMB language and no supplier names. Doctrine flag NONE.

## Steel  Framed Stairway Design Pt 2
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aAkFcgVtQoM | Duration: 1:30:44 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is part 2 of an AISC webinar by Adam Friedman (author of the then-forthcoming AISC Design Guide 34, Steel-Framed Stairway Design), focused on seismic design of steel stairs as nonstructural components, the new ASCE 7-16 serviceability provisions for accommodating inter-story drift, and the delegated-design relationship between the structural engineer of record (SER) and the fabricator's specialty structural engineer (SSE) [01:03][02:34]. The central message is that an egress stair must either be detailed to move freely during a seismic event (sliding or ductile connection) or be locked up and designed as part of the building's seismic force resisting system; the worst outcome is a stair that inadvertently acts as an unintended brace and draws force it was never designed for [22:41][50:00].
### Spec References
Cited verbatim by the speaker: IBC Chapter 16; ASCE 7-2016 Chapter 2 (load combinations), Chapters 11, 12, 13; ASCE 7 Section 1.4.2 (general structural integrity for SDC A); ASCE 7 Chapter 13 nonstructural components; equation 13.3-1 (horizontal seismic design force Fp); Section 13.1.3 (component importance factor Ip); Table 13.5-1 (ap, Rp, overstrength); Table 13.6-1 (mechanical/electrical components); equations 13.3-3 (Fp min) and the 1.6 SDS Ip Wp max; Section 13.3.1.2 (vertical seismic force, 0.2 SDS Wp); Sections 12.4.2.1 and 12.4.2.2 (vertical seismic in combinations); new Section 13.5.10 (egress stairs and ramps serviceability); Section 13.3.2.1 (seismic relative displacement Dp/DpI); equations 13.3-6 and 13.3-8; Table 12.12-1 (allowable story drift); ACI 318-2014 Section 17.2.3.1 (anchorage overstrength, SDC C and higher); AISC Specification Section G1 (shear), Manual Table 3-12 (flexural values), AISC Code of Standard Practice, NAAMM (NAMM) stair manual, AISC Design Guide 11 second edition (vibration), AISI cold-formed spec, ACI 117 (concrete tolerances), ASTM C90 (CMU tolerances), ASTM A384 (galvanizing warpage safeguard), ASTM A500 Grade C (HSS).
### Technical Details
The horizontal force simplifies for an egress stair to FP stairs = 0.24 SDS Wp times [1 + 2(Z/H)], using Ip 1.5, ap 1.0, Rp 2.5, with Z/H conservatively 1.0 [11:19][26:30]. ASCE 7-16 Table 13.5-1 splits the old single line into egress-stair members (ap 1.0, Rp 2.5, overstrength dropped from 2.5 to 2.0) and a new fasteners/attachments line (ap 2.5, Rp 2.5), which raises bolt/weld/dowel forces about 250 percent versus 7-10 [06:14][08:16]. Seismic displacement DpI from Section 13.3.2.1 can be 1 to 2.5 inches per roughly 8 feet of height difference and can exceed 4 inches on tall towers, which then conflicts with the IBC 4-inch-sphere guard opening limit [27:50][28:23]. Section 13.5.10 gives three accommodation options: (A) sliding connection with oversized/slotted holes plus keeper plates or end stops, accommodate DpI or 0.5 in min; (B) bearing detail without a stop, accommodate 1.5 DpI or 1 in min; (C) metal supports with rotation capacity, 1.5 DpI or 1 in min with no brittle failure modes permitted [19:01][20:33]. Locking the stair at both ends forces it into the building model designed for the structure overstrength, minimum 2.5 [22:10]. The deformation-to-force check (PL/AE rearranged) showed a 1-inch imposed movement on a C12x20.7 stringer over a 12-foot span generating about 1,224 kips, illustrating why rigid both-end details are unworkable [39:07].
### Fabrication Notes
The worked stringer example used a rectangular HSS 12x2x1/4 ASTM A500 Grade C with checkered-plate treads and risers, sized through Specification Section G1 and Manual Table 3-12 [56:42][57:13]. Landing diaphragms are framed like conventional floors, the speaker's preferred method being deck plus concrete over metal deck; some fabricators use stiffened plate or thicker checker/diamond plate, but quantifying built-up-beam tread/riser capacity is hard because the web-height-to-thickness ratio fails AISC and AISI local-buckling criteria, pushing designers to finite element or rational methods [44:14][46:17]. Galvanizing was covered: prefer matched fasteners and metals, watch piece-size and assembly-size limits at the galvanizer's kettle, and guard against warpage per ASTM A384 [74:18][75:22]. Tolerances are cleanest when all parties adopt the AISC Specification, Manual, and Code of Standard Practice; concrete tolerances per ACI 117 and masonry per ASTM C90 are looser, so a quarter-inch minimum to half-inch preferred gap absorbs the variation [71:44][73:17].
### Erection Notes
A practical drift detail sets a threaded rod with a jam nut and washer plate cast into the slab depth so the erector can drop the stair, cut loose, add the top washer and finger-tight upset nut, and keep moving without waiting on the concrete pour, an explicit schedule efficiency [32:29][32:59]. When concrete is not yet placed and the stair is used during construction, temporary blocking must be provided until the slab is poured [33:00]. The speaker stressed field access for bolting where a stringer sits a half inch off a concrete or masonry core wall, the possible need for flange block-outs at shear tabs, and confirming whether masonry is in place before the stair is set, with temporary supports as needed [75:53][76:24]. Maximize repetition in framing and connections, build erection aids that let a crew drop each stair assembly in and keep moving, and field-verify dimensions against actual construction rather than the plan gap [76:24][73:47]. Avoid field welding on galvanized work; shop-weld and field-bolt where possible [74:49].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The headline failure mode is the stair becoming an inadvertent load path: in a moment-frame building a rigidly tied stair acts as a brace, becomes the stiffer seismic force resisting system, and fails at the stair connections or in the members because nobody designed it for that [23:42][24:12]. Brittle limit states (bolt shear, weld rupture, weld fracture) cannot govern when relying on option C rotation capacity [20:33][37:01]. Construction errors flagged include concrete or debris dumped into the movement gap or oversized hole, which destroys the seismic displacement allowance and becomes a maintenance concern [38:03]. Specification mismatches were called out as a frequent source of rejection and RFIs, especially stock or purchased specs with an arbitrary quarter-inch deflection limit never reviewed for the project, and conflicts between the project spec and the design drawings [66:35][67:06].
### Bid / Cost Implications
If the drawings show no stair bracing, that bracing is not in the fabricator's price, so a fabricator or delegated designer should raise it before bid or clarify by RFI rather than absorb it later [48:54][49:24]. The Code of Standard Practice rule that design drawings govern over the spec means that if a delegated-design spec is paired with detailed stair drawings, a bidder will assume the SER already completed the design; conceptual or suggested details must be labeled as such in the bid documents [65:32][66:03]. Large seismic displacements are explicitly described as very costly and difficult to accommodate, so the delegated designer should request accurate per-floor drift values from the SER rather than defaulting to the conservative equation 13.3-8 upper bound [28:23][55:00]. Scope and seal expectations, including any request that the SSE seal fabricator-created shop drawings, must be settled at the bidding stage, not at submittal, since many fabricators have no in-house PE and a third-party engineer sealing drawings created by others raises jurisdiction and liability problems [69:38][71:44]. Stock quarter-inch deflection limits drive avoidable cost across design, fabrication, detailing, and erection [67:06].
### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, treat stair bracing, drift connections, and expansion-joint covers as scope that is invisible on incomplete drawings; price them or file an SF/scope RFI rather than assume omission, consistent with our verify-don't-generate and drawing-completeness gates. For the in-house PE stamp, the seal discussion maps directly: confirm scope and what our stamp covers at bid time, never agree to seal shop drawings we did not create, and provide sealed calculations with our own sketches as the submittal. For anchor rods, the ASCE 7-16 change drives anchor and embed forces up roughly 250 percent (ap 2.5) with an overstrength of 2.0 to 2.5 per ACI 318 17.2.3.1, so any seismic-region stair-to-concrete base connection needs that higher demand designed and the field-set drift detail (oversized hole, finger-tight upset nut, kept-clear gap) flagged to Paul and Mario. For Mario's shop crew, the AISC weight and member values (HSS 12x2x1/4 A500 Grade C) must come through aisc_validator.py, not LLM math, and galvanizing per ASTM A384 plus matched fasteners belong on the traveler. For Tekla detailing, model the movement gap, keeper plates, and slotted/oversized holes explicitly so erection sequencing (drop-and-go drift detail before slab pour) is captured. For ACP controls, the delegated-design partnership posture (SER provides per-level plans, drift values, and code criteria; conflicts resolved by RFI early) is the register and communication discipline to enforce. No conflict with Your Company doctrine: NONE. The content is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language, and supplier names are not introduced.

## Steel  Framed Stairway Design Pt 1
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wXnsH3L6JSo | Duration: 1:30:47 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is part one of a two-part AISC webinar by Adam Friedman of CSD, previewing the then-forthcoming AISC Design Guide 34, Steel-Framed Stairway Design [01:05][32:18]. The thesis is that stairs and handrails are formally outside the Code of Standard Practice scope, defined there as "other steel" items, yet the speaker strongly recommends adopting the full AISC suite as the reference standard so the detailer, fabricator, and erector all share one set of expectations [04:52][06:01]. Part one covers stairway components and classes, code-driven layout (IBC vs OSHA), gravity loading, design methodology (sloping-beam vs horizontal-plane, simple-span vs frame analysis), and common member and connection types. Seismic, serviceability for drift, and delegated design are deferred to part two [02:54][87:50].
### Spec References
Cited verbatim on slides or by the speaker: AISC Code of Standard Practice 2016, Steel Construction Manual 15th edition, AISC Specification for Structural Steel Buildings 2016 [04:52]. AISC Specification Appendix 6, Section 6.3 for stringer bracing by tread/riser stiffness and strength [78:30 mis-stated as "appendix 6.3"]. AISC Manual Table 3-18a (deflection L/100) and Table 3-18b (stress 24 ksi LRFD / 16 ksi ASD) for checker plate [52:57][53:45]; AISC Manual Tables 17-12 and 17-13 for material weights/densities [37:21]; Manual Table 1-13 (HSS) and Table 1-5 (channels) for section properties [frame 0020]; Manual Table 3-8 for channel shear/moment allowables [71:58]. Manual Part 7 bolts, Part 8 welds, Part 9 connecting elements, Part 10 shear-plus-axial, Parts 11 and 12 moment connections, Part 13 bracing [frame 0017][62:33]. Design Guide 24 Hollow Structural Section Connections and Design Guide 29 vertical bracing connections [frame 0017][63:46]. IBC Chapter 10 means of egress, IBC Chapter 16 structural design, IBC Section 1011.5.4 (3/8 in riser tolerance) [20:35], IBC Section 1014.8 handrail projection [21:21], IBC 2015 Table 1604.3 deflection limits [frame 0012][41:58]. ASCE 7-16 including commentary Chapter C3 dead-load material table [37:21]. OSHA 1910 Subpart D as revised January 2017: 1910.25 stairways, 1910.28 duty to have fall protection, 1910.29 fall-protection systems, 1910.25(c)(4) 22 in width, 1910.36(g)(2) 28 in exit-route width, Table D-2 under 1910.28(b)(11) handrail locations [26:09][27:55]. AWS D1.1 referenced for an out-of-tolerance fit-up weld [65:54]. Also AISI North American cold-formed steel spec and ASTM A786, A53 Gr B, A500 Gr B/C, A36, A1085, TMS 402 [53:54][60:02].
### Technical Details
Five stair classes (industrial, service, commercial, architectural) and geometric types (straight, parallel/switchback, angled, scissor, circular, curved, alternating-tread/ship ladder) are defined per the NAAMM stair and railing manuals, which the design guide updates structurally [06:43][07:45]. IBC risers run 4 in min to 7 in max with a 3/8 in tolerance between adjacent risers; the speaker recommends designing to 6-5/8 in so field misfit at the top or bottom riser stays code-legal [19:31][20:35]. IBC tread 11 in min, guard top 42 in, handrail 34 to 38 in, 1-1/2 in finger clearance, 4 in sphere infill rule [frame 0006][24:06]. OSHA post-2017 allows steeper geometry (9-1/2 in tread, 9-1/2 in riser), 42 in guard, 30 to 38 in handrail with 2-1/4 in finger clearance, 19 in sphere [25:21][27:00]. Gravity live loads from the IBC 2015 / ASCE 7-16 slide: stair tread 300 lb concentrated on 4 in^2 or 100 psf uniform (non-concurrent); landing 100 psf; guard top rail and handrail 200 lb point or 50 lb/ft any direction; infill 50 lb over 1 sq ft [frame 0011][37:57]. OSHA uses five-times-normal live load or a 1,000 lb concentrated load, 60 psf recommended floor minimum [39:46][41:30]. Design methodology: sloping-beam and horizontal-plane methods give near-identical reactions (1.83 vs 1.82 kip in the example) so either is acceptable; adjust stringer self-weight by the slope ratio when using horizontal-plane [44:05][45:25]. Simple-span (pin plus roller) is preferred and most conservative for deflection; a pinned-pinned frame analysis is statically indeterminate and produces large axial reactions from arching/catenary action that must be carried by connections and supports [45:45][47:01].
### Fabrication Notes
Build in tolerance: design risers below the 7 in absolute max so fabrication and erection variation does not push a riser out of code [19:53]. Lay out guard pickets center-to-center on a 4 in module so the clear opening lands near 3-3/4 in rather than a hard-to-hold 3.99 in [24:48]. The speaker favors a carrier angle under pan treads over direct welding to the stringer because it gives fit-up tolerance in the shop [51:58]. Stringer-member fit-up is a real shop constraint: a nominal "1-1/2 in pipe" is 1.90 in OD per A53 Gr B, and if an architect actually wants a 1.50 in OD member that is custom tubing and a separate, costlier buyout, so send an early RFI [60:51][61:43]. The MC12x14.3 was specifically rolled with a wide enough 2-1/8 in flange to seat a 1.90 in OD pipe post in a channel stringer; mismatched post and channel flange widths force a poor weld [66:01]. Checker plate is typically ASTM A786 with a wide yield-stress range, so call out the grade and verify availability with the fabricator before relying on Table 3-18b [53:54]. Grating and many treads are buyout items with manufacturer load tables; verify ADA and IBC opening size in grating treads on egress stairs [54:43].
### Erection Notes
The speaker's heavy-industrial background shows: switchback stair flights were preassembled on the ground and craned into a 350 ft modular tower as ready-to-use construction access, set in three-story-tall sections by one of the largest cranes in North America [09:11][09:30]. Leaving the slab-edge angle or pour stops loose for field installation buys plus or minus one inch of erection adjustment all around the opening [35:27][frame 0010]. Post-supported and hanger-supported landings with four support points are preferred because they erect as independent, freestanding units; integrated landings spanning between stringers complicate erection and lateral analysis [56:54][58:25]. Separate stair flights that keep top-of-steel low let each flight serve as construction access as soon as it is set [58:53]. Provide a partial tread or 5 to 6 in of clear space at stringer-to-floor connections so a welder has field access or a post-installed anchor can be installed without the stair in the way [32:31][33:35].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Field-modified industrial stairs where a mechanical or plumbing line was run straight through the stair, cutting the stringer, are called a life-safety failure inspectors should watch for [10:17]. Specifying the seven-inch absolute max riser then "borrowing" tolerance from it is a violation that cannot be cured elsewhere [19:53]. Architect-versus-fabricator pipe-size confusion (1-1/2 in nominal vs 1.5 in OD) surfaces as a shop-drawing-review dispute when it should have been an early RFI [61:43]. Frame 0018 shows the named failure: a pipe post that did not fit the channel stringer flange, producing an oversized, irregular field weld that does not meet AWS D1.1 [65:54]. Arbitrary spec deflection limits like a copied "1/4 in max" with no stated basis (live or total, finish or vibration driven) drive oversized members and bid variance; the speaker tells engineers to challenge them [49:36][50:03].
### Bid / Cost Implications
Adopting the AISC suite up front removes scope gray area among detailer, fabricator, and erector, which reduces RFI churn and field rework cost [05:57]. An unexplained tight deflection limit (the copied 1/4 in spec) materially changes member size and stiffness and "could have a big difference in terms of cost based on what fabricator or contractor bid the job," so it is a bid-risk flag to clarify before pricing [50:21]. The pipe-OD confusion is the clearest cost trap: a custom 1.50 in OD tube is more expensive than A53 1.90 in pipe and should be caught at bid or early design, not at shop-drawing review [61:17]. Reusing the building's standard connection type on the stair maximizes repetition for design, detailing, fabrication, and erection and avoids field errors, which is a direct labor-cost lever [62:00]. Frame analysis instead of simple span generates large axial connection forces, increasing connection and supporting-member cost, so the method choice has a price [47:31].
### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, this confirms that stairs sit outside the Code of Standard Practice "structural steel" definition, so stair tonnage, channel stringers, pipe/HSS guards, pan or grating treads, and landing steel should be a clearly separated bid line, and the AISC member weights still come through aisc_validator.py (MC12x14.3, C12x20.7, A500 HSS, A53 pipe are all standard shapes). The 1-1/2 in nominal pipe equals 1.90 in OD point is a concrete RFI trigger Ivan should encode when an architect calls a railing size. For Mario's shop and welding, the carrier-angle fit-up preference, the MC12x14.3 wide-flange-channel for pipe-post seating, and the frame-0018 AWS D1.1 fit-up failure are direct guidance: control post-to-stringer fit so the fillet meets D1.1 rather than masking a gap with weld metal. For Paul's safety file, the OSHA Subpart D 2017 changes (42 in guards now on industrial stairs and platforms, handrails newly required) and the cut-stringer life-safety photos support stair and platform fall-protection checks. Tekla detailing should carry the 6-5/8 in riser target, center-to-center picket layout, loose slab-edge angle for plus or minus one inch field play, and the building's standard shear connection reused on stairs. The 200 lb / 50 lb-per-ft guard loads and IBC Table 1604.3 deflection limits (Span/360 live, Span/600 for tile finishes, Height/60 cantilever guard post) are in-house PE stamp inputs. Anchor relevance is the post-installed anchor and deformed-bar-anchor load-path guidance at guard-post-to-slab connections plus leaving field access for setting them. Doctrine conflict: NONE. Nothing here touches BID_RATES, names a supplier, or conflicts with conventional-structural-steel positioning; treat all numbers as the speaker's design-guide recommendations, not Your Company rates.

## Effective Bracing of Flexural Members and Systems in Steel Buildings and Bridges
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oy2JqXNZzqM | Duration: 1:04:30 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
This is the 2018 TR Higgins lecture by Todd Helwig (UT Austin) on stability bracing of I-shaped flexural members, focused on torsional bracing through cross frames and diaphragms [00:00, 02:03]. The governing idea is that effective bracing of a beam against lateral-torsional buckling requires both adequate strength and adequate stiffness, and that you can brace a beam either by stopping lateral movement of the compression flange (lateral bracing) or by stopping twist of the cross section (torsional bracing) [03:03, 03:33]. A beam or girder is considered fully braced at a location if you stop twist of the section [04:35]. The talk then drives toward two findings that matter in practice: connection eccentricity in cross frames can soften real stiffness 50 to 80 percent below the simple truss model [17:57], and a "system buckling mode" can control in narrow girder units regardless of how tightly you space the cross frames [33:23, 35:24].

### Spec References
The speaker repeatedly cites AISC Appendix 6 for torsional bracing stiffness and strength, naming the stiffness equation as Equation 6-6 and the cross-sectional distortion equation as residing in Appendix 6 [04:35, 26:38, 27:08, 30:46]. The distortion equation is attributed to Joe Yura's work in the late 1980s [26:38]. On the bridge side he cites AASHTO interim specifications: the system buckling mode equation went into the 2015 interims with capacity limited to 50 percent of the critical load, then was modified in the 2017 specifications up to about 70 percent with a Cb-type system factor (1.1 partially erected, 2 for continuous), and the cross frame reduction factor R sits in AASHTO Chapter 4 commentary as a 0.65 factor [37:28, 38:30, 39:00, 58:55]. No AISC 341 seismic section, AWS D1.1 clause, RCSC provision, or numbered Design Guide is cited. The distinct citations captured are AISC Appendix 6, AISC Equation 6-6, AASHTO 2015 interim, AASHTO 2017 spec, and AASHTO Chapter 4 commentary.

### Technical Details
Total torsional brace stiffness behaves as springs in series: 1 over beta-T equals 1 over the brace stiffness plus 1 over the cross-sectional distortion stiffness plus 1 over the in-plane girder stiffness, so beta-T is always smaller than the smallest component [30:46, 31:21]. Cross-sectional distortion is controlled with a transverse web stiffener, and the Appendix 6 equation models the participating web width as the brace width plus 1.5 times the web depth H, propagating at a 0.75-to-1 slope each side [27:08, 27:38]. For a single-diagonal cross frame the tension diagonal braces the compression diagonal when connected at midpoint, so the compression diagonal can be designed on half its length for buckling, true both in-plane and out-of-plane [15:22, 56:19]. The in-plane stiffness factor scales with girder spacing squared and a girder-count factor that climbs fast (12 for two girders, 32 for three, up to 77 for five), which is why the effect only bites on narrow two- or three-girder units [29:46, 30:16].

### Fabrication Notes
Cross frames are among the most expensive components on a bridge on a per-pound basis because they are almost entirely fabrication: cutting, welding, and flipping the frames to make welds, with heavy handling [10:15]. The split-pipe stiffener detail (a round pipe split in half and welded to the web and both flanges) is called out as a fabrication win because it gives a perpendicular weld regardless of skew angle, avoiding the awkward bent-plate connection plates that follow a skew, and it creates a closed shape that delivers warping fixity [44:34, 45:04, 45:34]. Cross frames are fabricated square to fit between the girders, which the speaker uses to argue the worst-case critical-shape imperfection is unlikely because it would require diagonals of different lengths [40:00, 40:30]. The test girders for the tub-girder study were fabricated at a named fabricator (Hirschfeld) [49:08].

### Erection Notes
Erection sequence shapes the imperfection: simulating cross frame installation one frame at a time, pulling the girders straight, installing the frame, then releasing, converts a critical-shape imperfection into a milder pier sweep, which lowers brace forces [40:30, 41:01]. Two real construction failures anchor the erection lesson. A Houston bridge widening on twin I-girders (170 ft span, 17 ft cross frame spacing, 8 ft girder spacing) began twisting during deck casting and reached about 10 inches of bottom-flange kick at half the pour before it was caught and stripped back [31:21, 32:22]. The Marcy pedestrian bridge in upstate New York collapsed in 2002 during deck placement with no top lateral truss, killing a worker, behaving like a twin I-girder system [33:23, 33:54]. The takeaway is to provide a top lateral truss on narrow units and to tie all girders with at least one full cross frame line per bay across the width when using lean-on bracing, both for the system mode and to keep deflection uniform during casting [34:24, 63:08, 63:38].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The headline error is modeling cross frames as pure truss (line) elements in commercial software, which ignores bending from eccentric single-angle connections and overestimates stiffness 50 to 80 percent [17:57, 19:30]. Concentric details (double-angle or Z-frame) agree well; eccentric single-angle X and K frames do not [18:58, 23:03]. A vivid real consequence: TxDOT chased a phantom fatigue problem on a heavily skewed bridge because the overstiff model told them to enlarge cross frames, which attracted more force and worsened the apparent problem, ending in a roughly 500,000 dollar added girder line for a non-problem [24:35, 25:05, 25:36]. The other systemic failure is unbraced-length and bracing-spacing thinking on narrow units: closer cross frame spacing does not fix the system buckling mode because the two girders buckle together in a half sine wave largely insensitive to spacing [35:24, 36:26].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Cross frames are flagged explicitly as one of the most expensive per-pound items on a bridge, driven by fabrication labor (cutting, welding, flipping, handling), so cross frame count and detail choice carry real cost weight [10:15, 10:45]. Lean-on bracing reduces the number of cross frames materially in the cited projects: 15 intermediate frames cut to 7, and 80 frames cut to 28 on a 60-degree skew, with better fatigue behavior and easier fit-up near supports [43:03, 44:04, 44:34]. The modeling error has direct dollar exposure (the 500,000 dollar TxDOT fix) and the split-pipe and lean-on details lower both fabrication and inspection cost because fewer weld details need to be looked at [25:05, 43:34, 44:04]. Offsetting bracing lines four to five feet off the support reduces congestion and force [42:32].

### Your Company Application
This is a bridge-heavy webinar, but the transferable items for Your Company are torsional bracing of flexural members during erection and the cost of fabricated bracing. For Mario's shop and welding line, the split-pipe stiffener perpendicular-weld lesson and the warning that frame-flipping welds drive cost are directly useful when detailing stiffeners and cross-bracing. For Tekla detailing and the in-house PE stamp, the key caution is that line-element truss models of eccentric single-angle braces overestimate stiffness 50 to 80 percent (AASHTO uses a 0.65 reduction in Chapter 4 commentary); any framing-stability or beam-bracing check on narrow walkway or canopy frames should account for cross-sectional distortion (Appendix 6 transverse stiffener) and the in-plane stiffness effect, which the speaker explicitly says applies to building walkways of two or three girders such as a hotel link bridge [55:15]. For Paul's safety scope and erection, the Marcy and Houston cases reinforce that narrow girder pairs need a top lateral truss and at least one full cross frame line per bay before deck casting, and that erection sequence (pull straight, install, release) controls imperfection. For Ivan's takeoff, treat fabricated cross frames and bracing as labor-heavy per-pound items, not bulk steel weight. This material does not touch anchor rods, joists, field bolting grades, or ACP controls, and AISC weights still come only from bridge/aisc_validator.py. Doctrine conflict: NONE.

## What Engineers Need to Know about Steel Erection
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hrRyM4V89oU | Duration: 1:03:16 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
Curtis Mayes, P.E., director of pre-construction and engineering at LPR Construction and a member of the Research Council on Structural Connections since 2006, argues that the engineer of record can remove most field erection risk before the construction team is even on the job, mostly by specifying intent rather than relying on assumptions. The thesis is that erectability is a design decision: connection choice, anchor-rod sizing, tolerance management, weld access, and a clearly drawn lateral load path all get locked in on the contract documents, and a constructible building costs less and is safer to put up [02:42][14:30]. The talk is structured around specifications, safety, connections, lateral force resisting systems, and sharing the BIM model with the fabricator and erector [03:00].
### Spec References
AISC Code of Standard Practice cited repeatedly: 7.10.1 temporary support of structural steel frames including the lateral force resisting system and special conditions [04:00], 7.1.2 that accumulated mill and fabrication tolerances shall not cause erection tolerances to be exceeded [05:18], and 7.10.3 that the erector is not to consider loads from unexpected events such as hurricanes, tornadoes, earthquakes, explosions, and collisions [15:05]. OSHA Subpart R column-stability provisions shown verbatim on the slide: 1926.755(a)(1) minimum of four anchor rods per column, 1926.755(a)(2) anchor-rod assembly and column-to-base-plate weld designed for a 300 lb eccentric gravity load 18 inches off the column face in each direction, 1926.755(a)(3) level floors or pre-grouted leveling plates, leveling nuts, or shim packs, 1926.755(a)(4) competent-person evaluation for guying or bracing, and 1926.756(d) column splices designed for the same 300 lb at 18 inch load [16:57][27:31]. AISC Manual 13th Edition Table 14-2 is cited on a slide for oversized holes in base plates [frame 10]. ASCE 37 is named for construction-period and hurricane loads [15:31]. A Steel Erectors Association of America (SEAA) and National Institute of Steel Detailers (NISD) detailing guide is shown. No AWS D1.1 clause numbers, no AISC 341 seismic sections, and no RCSC section numbers were stated.
### Technical Details
Tolerance accumulation is the recurring failure mode. On an HSS 16x8x3/8 rolled to an arc, the cold rolling changed the section to roughly 15.5 inches tall by 8.375 inches wide, so 3/8 inch of width growth across about 20 bays accumulates into a major top-of-steel mismatch unless intermediate dimensional QC checks are specified [06:00][08:04]. Two behavior case studies: an athletic facility where the EOR specified a column detailed 1 inch out of plumb and a truss fabricated 1 inch short so that removing the shores pulled the column plumb under dead load [09:11], and a seven-bay crane-rail mill building whose arched roof spread the perimeter columns up to about 1.5 inches under dead load, throwing crane-rail alignment off [11:04][12:58]. Slots manage this: short slots placed sparingly, on one beam end roughly every five bays for beam-to-column-flange lines and roughly every ten bays for web connections, keep the building in line without forcing the erector to space every member [34:41][frame 14]. For long-span trusses, orient the top-chord web horizontal so the section is stable to lift; a 145 ft, 160,000 lb truss with a W14x370 top chord is unliftable web-vertical and erectable web-horizontal at the same weight [36:32].
### Fabrication Notes
Preferred shop connections favor single-sided erectability: shear-tab and extended shear-plate connections are easy to land, while shared-bolt through connections and beams into both column webs slow the erector even when they are cheaper to fabricate [21:41][22:54]. The favored column splice is four shop-welded inner plates on square-cut upper and lower shafts with bearing transfer and slip-critical bolts, aligned to the inside flange so W12 and W14 sizes match, avoiding any field bevel cutting [28:46]. Keep bolt diameters at least 1/4 inch apart and avoid two bolt grades at one diameter, because a 1 inch and a 7/8 inch bolt look nearly identical and a 1 inch bolt can drop into a 7/8 inch oversized hole, creating QC and traceability errors [37:57][frame 15]. Shop welding is normally gas metal arc or submerged arc with bare-wire electrode, which suits the enclosed shop with no wind to blow shielding gas away [59:54]. Specify oversized holes in all plies (not just one) on complex frames so pins land on theoretical geometry with full adjustability [31:28][frame 13].
### Erection Notes
Preferred free-standing column support uses a single center shim pack with the anchor rods left to rock and plumb the column, anchor rods extended outside the base-plate footprint, and an extra inch or two of base-plate edge distance reserved for field slotting if a rod is off [24:19][25:31]. With a shear key, use leveling nuts and leveling plates rather than shim packs on the pocket edge, which can spall and create a hazard [26:18]. Provide two temporary through bolts at brace connections instead of OSHA's one-bolt minimum so the erector can pin the first hole and bolt the second safely [20:04]. Extend one claw angle about 3 inches so braces rotate into a gusset without a sandwich-clearance fight [30:00]. On steel deck, avoid single-span deck (ironworkers call it a widowmaker) and prefer screws or button punch over welded side-laps where diaphragm demand allows [57:53]. Field welding is normally flux-cored arc with a gooseneck stinger; stick welding is now only incidental in the field [59:26]. LPR modeled cranes, rigging, modules, shoring, and bracing inside the fabricator's shared Tekla model to plan erection [49:28].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The headline field failure was the seven-bay crane-rail building: the arched roof spread the columns under dead load, so crane girders sitting on the column seats had to be physically repositioned, described as a mess; the speaker's stated root cause is the arched roof geometry, which a straight tee-to-tee roof would have avoided [60:53][62:39]. Other named errors are tolerance accumulation that surfaces three-quarters of the way through a job and forces rework [14:20], anchor rods designed only for the OSHA 300 lb at 18 inch load, which the slides show as 0.6 ft-kip versus 9.72 ft-kip at 15 psf wind, eight to sixteen times too small for real wind [18:50][frame 8], slots placed everywhere driving up cost and reducing quality, mismatched 1 inch and 7/8 inch bolts landing in the wrong holes, and overhead welds specified by default when the underside weld is often not structurally required [40:04][41:25].
### Bid / Cost Implications
The fillet-weld cost table (priority 5 slide) prices a 100 kip load at $55.00 per labor hour and sets 5/16 inch fillet as the 0 percent cost baseline at one pass; going to 3/8 inch jumps to two passes and 67 percent more cost for only an incremental capacity gain, and a 1 inch fillet runs 11 passes at 244 percent over the 5/16 baseline [43:31][55:55][frame 22]. The practical bid rule is 5/16 inch is the optimum and typical maximum field fillet, because production is governed by passes, not throat. Short slots are nearly free because they stay bearing-type and avoid slip-critical surface prep and pretension cost; the only penalty is a slightly reduced bearing capacity per bolt [53:55]. Hurricane load planning is an extraordinary measure that roughly doubles to 2.5x normal construction wind pressure, so the EOR should keep it as builder's risk per COSP 7.10.3 or call for separate pricing [15:56]. Truss top-chord orientation and connection choice change erection hours at identical material weight, so they are estimating inputs, not just analysis details [36:32].
### Your Company Application
Ivan's takeoff should treat erectability as a cost driver: flag rolled or cambered HSS, arched roofs, crane-rail bays, and long-span trusses for tolerance-accumulation contingency, and price field fillet welds at 5/16 inch as the sweet spot since the pass-count curve here mirrors our own weld-hour assumptions through Mario's shop. Mario's crew should default to flux-cored arc in the field and gas-metal or submerged arc in the shop, prefer 5/16 inch fillets, and hold the 4 inch weld-access and 45 degree visibility rules when judging detail constructibility. Paul should carry the two-bolt brace rule, the single-span deck widowmaker hazard, and the shear-key shim-spalling hazard into JHAs. For Tekla detailing and the in-house PE stamp, this validates extending one claw angle for rotation, the four-plate bearing column splice, single-sided shear tabs, and short slots placed every five bays (flange) or ten bays (web), plus designing anchor rods for 15 psf wind on the free-standing column face with rods outside the base-plate footprint and 1 inch minimum diameter, well above the OSHA 300 lb floor; oversized base-plate holes cite AISC Manual Table 14-2. On ACP controls, model erection aids (cranes, shoring, bracing) in the shared Tekla model and document the lateral load path on the drawings so the field sequence is unambiguous. Doctrine conflict: NONE. This is conventional structural steel, no PEMB language, and it reinforces our verify-do-not-generate posture (AISC weights and rates stay in aisc_validator.py and bid_rates.py; the $55/hr and pass counts here are the speaker's illustrative figures, not Your Company rates).

## Design Tips for Constructible Steel-Framed Buildings in High-Seismic Regions
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=opFTacNZh_s | Duration: 1:32:31 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
John Hooper (MKA, Seattle) and Scott Eden cover how to design constructible steel lateral systems in high-seismic regions, defined as Seismic Design Category D and higher, the trigger for AISC 341 [02:03]. The central teaching is the fuse-and-capacity-protect model: pick the seismic system, size the fuse exactly to demand and never oversize it, then capacity-protect everything around it (columns, foundations, connections) [20:52][21:23]. Low seismic lets you use R=3 and AISC 360 with almost any configuration; high seismic forces defined, ductile systems with height limits and detailing rules [01:31][09:40]. Eden's half is a parametric study showing that deeper moment-frame columns (versus the traditional W14) cut frame weight 12 to 34 percent because drift, not strength, governs special moment frames [74:54][75:24].

### Spec References
AISC 360 (R=3 low-seismic baseline) [01:31]; AISC 341 seismic provisions, triggered at SDC D, cited for the ASFY full-tensile-capacity SCBF brace-connection rule and for orthogonal bracing penalties at moment-frame connections [02:03][86:44][90:35]; AISC 358 prequalified moment connections, including Chapter 9 (Kaiser bolted bracket, authored by Eden) and the WUF-W (welded unreinforced flange, welded web) used in the study [27:53][68:16][68:46]; ASCE 7 Chapter 12 design base shear, the systems table with 84 line items (20 usable for steel in high seismic), R=8 for SMF, the 160-ft height rule, and the period amplification allowance [09:40][10:41][22:53][60:42]; ASCE 7-10 for rho and omega-zero application to FX and FPX diaphragm forces [42:18]; AISC Seismic Design Manual including Table 8-1 for collector unbraced lengths and the new steel moment-frame base examples Eden contributed [46:23][47:54][58:38]; NIST seismic technical briefs (Sabelli on steel-deck/composite diaphragms, Eden on steel moment frames), free downloads [38:43][58:38].

### Technical Details
Systems covered: special and ordinary concentrically braced frames (OCBF limited to 35 ft, pushing designers to SCBF), buckling-restrained braced frames, eccentrically braced frames, special/intermediate/ordinary and special-truss moment frames, and steel plate shear walls [02:33][10:11][06:07]. Drift governs SMF, with a 2 percent limit for Risk Category II and 1 percent for Risk Category IV (health care), which makes tall moment frames costly [23:55][62:43]. The deep-column study held the strong-column-weak-beam ratio just above 1.0 (baseline pairing 1.06) and the normalized drift near 1.0 for an apples-to-apples comparison, throwing out moment ratios above 1.5 and drift ratios outside 0.9 to 3.0 [70:51][72:24]. Column flexural drift contribution dropped 43 percent (16.6 to 8.9) moving from W14 to deep sections [73:54]. The caveat: deep RBS columns can show local column instability / lateral-torsional buckling at the unbraced bottom flange; specimens were W14x283 and W18x211 columns with W30x132 beams, and continuity plates corrected the instability [80:31][82:35][83:37].

### Fabrication Notes
Gusset plates are the strongest constructability tip (Sabelli's work): avoid one-size-fits-all scheduling that takes the worst alpha and beta across cases and builds a plate that was never actually designed, avoid the forced 30-degree Whitmore fan that drives oversized plates needing edge stiffeners, and instead specify the gusset width directly on the drawings, allowing a 2-to-6-inch work-point offset for efficiency [32:05][34:37][35:39]. A web doubler is worth about 50 lb/ft of column weight per a Herrick fabricator, so upsizing the column to delete a doubler is often cheaper [28:30]. Fabricators want a clean column (no doubler plates, no continuity plates); the deep-column study notes you almost always still need a doubler when the beam-column ratio is held at 1.0 [76:26][76:56]. Match AISC 358 prequalified details exactly, do not redraw code details, and state explicitly any deviation so it can be priced [52:28][52:58].

### Erection Notes
Crane pick capacity runs roughly 25,000 to 30,000 lb, so member size and splice frequency must be planned for large-volume spaces with 30-to-50-ft unbraced columns and 60-to-70-ft braces [12:43]. Splice columns no more than every two levels, three if possible, never floor by floor because that slows erection [29:00]. The two-story X is the preferred braced-frame configuration because it has only three connections per bay versus five for a single-story X [30:33][31:35]. Hooper stresses prefab and pre-erection meetings, getting the engineer in the field to catch problems early, and confirming the WPS up front so everyone is aligned [54:28]. Brace angle should stay 40 to 50 degrees, and brace-frame aspect (height to length) should stay at or below 5, with 10 the practical ceiling [29:32][63:13].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Over-designating demand-critical welds: engineers mark everything demand-critical to avoid thinking, which fabricators called lazy because it spends money and slows schedule where the spec does not require it [54:59][55:29]. The SCBF chevron economy problem raised from the floor: engineers of record size braces for buckling strength but design the gusset connection for the full tensile capacity (ASFY required by AISC 341), forcing an oversized beam and an uneconomical connection; both presenters said they switch to BRBF to make that go away [85:43][86:44][87:14]. Oversized fuses break the capacity-protection economy [20:52]. Redundant general notes and specs that disagree, and referencing only the latest code edition instead of a specific dated standard, cause field confusion [51:27][51:57]. Omissions and tolerance issues hurt more in high seismic because fixes are harder (a bad BRB may need full replacement) [53:28].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Concrete dollar figures stated: special moment frame about $30/SF versus brace frame about $18/SF, dropping to $16/SF with disciplined repetitive grid spacing [13:44][15:16]. A transfer beam, transfer truss, or sloping column costs $20,000 to $40,000 each [17:18]. Deep caissons run about $1 million each; foundations are roughly 20 to 25 percent of cost [25:57]. A chevron SCBF beam balloons to a W36, while a BRBF chevron beam stays around W24 [30:03][38:13]. Deep-column moment frames save 12 to 34 percent frame weight plus indirect savings on column-splice weld passes and inspection [83:37]. Fabricators need accurate tonnage early and must know what is included: connections, and specifically anchor-rod connections to the foundation [49:55][50:26].

### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, the anchor-rod note is direct: state explicitly whether tonnage includes connection steel and anchor-rod-to-foundation steel so the bid is apples-to-apples, and confirm against aisc_validator.py weights rather than LLM math [50:26]. The clean-column / web-doubler trade (a doubler equals roughly 50 lb/ft of column) and the gusset-scheduling waste are direct guidance for Tekla detailing and connection design, and the SCBF chevron ASFY problem says to flag any chevron SCBF as a likely cost outlier versus BRBF in early screening [28:30][32:05][86:44]. For Mario's shop, deeper columns mean thinner flanges and fewer weld passes at splices, and over-designating demand-critical welds should be avoided per the AWS-tied WPS discipline [54:59][80:00]. For Paul's safety, the 25,000-to-30,000-lb crane pick ceiling drives splice planning [12:43]. The in-house PE stamp work ties to the capacity-protection method and the specific-dated-standard referencing rule [51:57]. Doctrine flag: NONE. The webinar is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language, and all figures here are quoted from the speakers, not generated. Note that any rate transfer to a Your Company bid must still use the CEO-locked BID_RATES in bid_rates.py; the $/SF and per-item figures above are the presenters' regional numbers, not Your Company pricing.
