## Drawing and Specification Requirements for Seismic Design
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gr3G7fNniVI | Duration: 1:31:45 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
This 2016 AISC webinar by Larry Muir (AISC director of technical assistance) and Tom Sable (principal at Englekirk) covers what information the engineer of record must show on contract documents for a seismic project, defined as one that must meet AISC 341 the seismic provisions, versus a non-seismic project that only meets AISC 360 [01:02-01:32]. The driving message is that a fabricator bids what it sees in the contract documents, so missing or unclear seismic requirements lead to bids that come in at a fraction of the real cost and to change orders later [03:33-04:33]. Muir frames AISC 341 as a supplement to AISC 360, which applies to all projects seismic or not [11:37-12:07].

### Spec References
AISC 341 seismic provisions, including Section A4 (information to be shown on drawings), Chapter J (seismic inspection requirements), Chapter K (qualification testing of moment connections, stated as "I believe it's chapter K") [38:07], and the commentary chapter on demand-critical welds (stated as "Chapter D, I believe") [85:50]. AISC 360, with Chapter N for quality assurance and inspection [19:47, 47:19]. AISC 358 prequalified connections for special and intermediate moment frames. AWS D1.1 structural welding code and AWS D1.8 its seismic supplement (item 13 on assembly order/welding sequence [18:14, 55:08]; demand-critical weld definition; weld-access-hole welder qualification test [73:36]; tapered transition detail [76:38]). RCSC specification for structural joints using high-strength bolts, with the speaker noting there is no seismic supplement to the bolting spec [13:09]. IBC Section 1603 (seismic design parameters on drawings), 1704 / 1704.3 (special inspections), 1704.5 (structural observation) [43:12-48:20].

### Technical Details
Demand-critical welds are required only where AISC 341 lists them: groove welds at column splices and bases in higher-ductility systems (IMF, SMF, special truss moment frames, special cantilever columns, SCBF, EBF, BRBF, steel plate shear walls) and groove welds at beam-to-column connections in those systems, with the exception that beam-to-column groove welds are demand critical even in an ordinary moment frame [25:26-27:27]. The Code of Standard Practice gives three connection-design options: engineer completes all connection design, an experienced detailer selects from the AISC manual tables, or design is delegated to a licensed PE working for the fabricator [13:39-15:11]. Protected zones, lowest anticipated service temperature (the 50 degree F limit), and RBS dimensions A, B, C, and R are required drawing items [54:07, 72:34-73:05]. Backing-bar treatment depends on location: to the inside of a section (top flange of a moment beam, or a column base plate where backing is inside) the backing may stay with a contouring or reinforcing fillet; to the outside (bottom flange) the backing must be removed, back-gouged, and a smooth transition provided; butt-splice CJP welds at column splices generally need no backing removal [28:57-32:31, 89:27-90:58].

### Fabrication Notes
Muir recommends the engineer leave welding process, sequence, and technique to the fabricator's shop floor unless there is a very specific reason, since the shop owns the risk of weld cracking [18:45-19:47]. AISC 358 prequalification limits constrain fabrication: there are no prequalified connections to the weak axis (web) of a column, only built-up cruciform, box, or plated wide-flange columns provide four flanges; HSS options are limited to one concrete-filled HSS column option and one HSS beam option, with no prequalified HSS-column-to-HSS-beam joint [37:06-38:38]. RBS connections require rolled wide-flange or built-up I-shapes with limits on depth, weight, flange thickness, span-to-depth and width-to-thickness ratios, and lateral bracing [39:39-40:39]. A992 is not mandatory; A36 plate and grade 50 are explicitly allowed in AISC 358, and requiring all steel to be A992 can make a project unbuildable [23:53-24:56].

### Erection Notes
Anchor rods drive erection accuracy: grade 36 or 55 usually work for gravity, but seismic often needs grade 105, which cannot be welded, so a misplaced grade 105 anchor rod is very difficult to correct in the field [60:17-60:48]. SCBF gusset plates that buckle out of plane need a free-to-bend fold/bend line, and where the gusset is embedded in concrete or a metal-deck diaphragm a compressible material (about 1.5 inches, the detail says Styrofoam) must surround it so the bend line can form [80:15-82:18]. Structural observation focuses on first-time conditions, the first SMF connection for example, to confirm the contractor and inspector have read the design intent correctly [49:21-51:28].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Muir groups recurring problems as imagined requirements: belief that all steel must be A992 or grade 50, belief that all welds in the seismic force resisting system must be demand critical, and belief that all backing must be removed, none of which AISC 341 requires [23:23-25:26]. Sable adds that engineers sometimes throw up their hands and mark every weld demand critical, which wastes the owner's money [53:35-54:07]. The most frequent and costly error ("public enemy number one") is designing an IMF or SMF without first confirming a prequalified AISC 358 connection exists for the chosen members, which can force an expensive owner-funded testing program under AISC 341 [34:34-37:06]. Inspectors and detailers also confuse weld backing with weld run-off tabs; removing a tab does not require removing the backing [90:58]. Connection configurations are sometimes desired but not defined, violating the Code of Standard Practice when design is delegated.

### Bid / Cost Implications
The webinar's central cost point is that an informal study put a special moment frame (R near 8) at roughly 2.5 times the cost of an R-equal-3 system, because ductile detailing adds cost even though base shear drops [08:36-10:06]. Incomplete bid documents leave the fabricator a choice: bid what it sees and fight change orders later, or bid what it thinks the engineer wants and price itself out, which penalizes the most knowledgeable bidder [10:06-11:37]. Per the Code of Standard Practice, anything required but not in the contract documents is a scope change that justifies a price and schedule adjustment [07:35-08:36]. A discovered need for a physical connection-testing program is a cost a fabricator would not have carried in a bid [39:09].

### Your Company Application
For Ivan and the takeoff through aisc_validator.py, the bid-screen should flag any AISC 341 seismic project and check that the contract documents state the seismic force resisting system, R factor, demand-critical weld locations, and a confirmed AISC 358 prequalified connection before pricing; an SMF or IMF without a confirmed prequalified connection is a LOW-confidence, change-order-prone bid that needs an RFI, consistent with our verify-don't-generate and ask-before-guessing doctrine. Mario's AWS D1.1 crew must hold the AWS D1.8 demand-critical filler-metal and the weld-access-hole welder qualification, and the shop should resist engineers who over-specify welding sequence, since that decision belongs on the shop floor. Tekla detailing must carry protected zones, RBS A/B/C/R dimensions, backing-removal versus contouring fillet by flange location, and gusset bend lines with compressible material. For anchor rods, the grade 105 non-weldable warning maps directly to our anchor-rod design/setting/tolerance workstream: misplacement is costly to correct, so setting tolerance and template QC matter more on seismic bases. Paul's safety and field-bolting work intersects with RCSC pretension on SFRS sheets. No conflict with Your Company doctrine; conventional structural steel positioning holds and no PEMB language appears. NONE.

## Working with Large Trusses
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=B2zTYoGWhvo | Duration: 1:14:50 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This webinar (PDH code 5669) by Colin Hughes of a Southeast/Texas fabricator and Sylvie Boulanger of Super Metal (Montreal) is a fabricator-and-erector view of large trusses, not a connection-design lecture [00:34]. The governing theme is that the optimal number of splices in a truss is zero, fabricated in one shop piece when shipping and crane capacity allow, and that every downstream decision (splice type, camber method, member shape, erection sequence) is driven by transport limits, shop and field crane capacity, and site access [04:42][05:12]. The recurring engineering message is that fabricators should engineer camber themselves and look early for opportunities to size members to their advantage, because "if the engineer is off it is oops, if we are off it is ouch" when pieces will not fit [38:31].

### Spec References
No AISC 360 section numbers, table numbers, AWS D1.1 clauses, RCSC sections, or Design Guide numbers were spoken aloud. General principles, no section cited. The only named references are bolt grade A490 and bolt grade A449 (1 and 1/8 inch) [09:46][35:55], a "75% bearing contact, no more than 2/100 inch separation" machined-fit acceptance criterion stated as a project requirement [42:38], steel at 65 ksi [11:48][44:43], the turn-of-nut bolt method [74:10], and a reference to "Carol Drucker load-path recommendations" for keeping plate bending and eccentricity low [40:34].

### Technical Details
Truss types covered: a 70 foot HSS 3D architectural truss in Charlotte [03:40], a fabricated-in-one-piece pedestrian bridge at the NASCAR Hall of Fame [07:14], a multi-splice bolted truss over the RSA judicial building in Montgomery supporting eight floors [09:46], an 8th Avenue Place transfer truss (74 ft by 36 ft, 136 short tons, carrying two 45-story columns, 8,500 kips compression and 3,500 kips tension, members to W14x730) [34:19][35:55], a cantilever conveyor truss in Labrador launched like a bridge [43:40], stacked full-story student-residence trusses in Manitoba with one room per diagonal [51:22], and ASS welded 3D trusses at Calgary airport (largest 45 tons, shortest 14) [62:10]. Chord member choices: WT (web doubles as connection material for lapped HSS or angle webs), wide flange for larger loads, HSS for less horizontal bracing, with the "bird beak" mitered HSS node rotated 90 degrees and welded all around [16:54][20:26][20:57]. A W6x26 coped at both flanges could not be made to work and needed cope reinforcement plus web doublers; a heavier W16 with a thicker web would have avoided that [19:26].

### Fabrication Notes
Camber is built two ways: rolled chord members (smooth, no extra shop grinding, but often from a specialty plant with long lead time) or straight segmented members cut and angled to hit specific deflection callouts (uses mill stock but adds shop labor) [13:49][14:49]. Cambered chords are detailed twice, once in the full building model with infill, columns and posts, and once as the truss alone in its own model [15:51]. Heavy bolted splices were match-drilled in the shop so plates fit in the field [10:47]. On 8th Avenue Place, preassembly used fill-in-the-blank checks (staff not allowed to pre-check the box) and total stations for accuracy, and heavy bearing plates were machined to the 75% contact, 2/100 inch flatness criterion [39:33][42:38]. Calgary used jigs and a rotator so welding always sat in a good position for both quality and appearance, with a two-tier AESS standard: distant steel gets a good weld with no grinding, close-up steel gets grinding [63:42][64:43].

### Erection Notes
Large trusses are often erected twice, once in the fabricator's own yard for fit-up verification (RSA truss assembled in the backyard, a 3D pedestrian bridge laser-measured against detailing drawings) and once on site [22:27][23:27]. Field-welded splices need shoring towers and alignment aids that are later removed and scrapped (Duke Energy building) [12:49]. The Manitoba stacked truss came up crooked because it was rigged at two pickup points when four were required, corrected once the rig was fixed [58:00]. Calgary erection assembled pairs on the ground, set them on an adjustable "Swiss knife" temporary tower, installed four struts between them, then removed the tower [67:21]. Temperature mattered: some Manitoba trusses would not fit until crews retried in the cooler early morning [60:38].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The Labrador cantilever truss is the cautionary tale: at launch none of the base plates fit, so every hole was field-oversized; then the GC delayed grouting and the cantilever load crushed the unsupported column shims "like butter," tilting the truss onto the existing building [46:17][47:18]. The fix was a same-day-engineered jacking and shimming rig (supporting beam, lifting beam, hydraulic jacks, repeated jack-and-shim) that recovered position while keeping the original anchor rods, after which the contractor grouted immediately [49:51][50:51]. Other named misses: the W6x26 double-cope that could not be designed, the Manitoba two-point pick, and Manitoba trusses quietly retried at dawn because of thermal fit. Slip-critical oversized holes were called out as a strength penalty that forces more bolts (a 200-bolt splice would balloon to 300 to 400) [10:47][11:17].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Field-welded CJP splices were quoted at roughly 40 man-hours of welding per location (about 20 hours per flange) on the RSA chords (W14x730 and W14x65, 65 ksi), versus faster, cheaper bolted snug-tight connections [11:48][12:19]. The over-200 A490 bolts at 1 inch and over a foot long were special-order long-lead and expensive [09:46]. Spending more up front on a slightly larger WT, W16, or full-square HSS section repeatedly avoided larger downstream fabrication cost for cope reinforcement, web doublers, and gusseting [17:24][19:26][68:23]. Specifying the launch-and-engineer scope on the Labrador job thinned the bidder field. Field-oversizing every hole "made a real difference in how we managed the project" budget [47:18].

### Your Company Application
This maps cleanly to Your Company workstreams. For Ivan's takeoff: model splice count, lead-time bolts, shoring towers, and double-erection (yard plus field) as explicit line items, and flag the WT/W16/full-square upsize trades early, since the heavier section is often the cheaper bid. For Mario: the 40 man-hours-per-CJP-splice figure and the strong "bolt over weld in the field" preference are direct shop and field planning inputs, as is the two-tier AESS finish rule (no grinding on distant steel, grind only close-up). For Tekla: detail cambered chords twice, the building model and a truss-only model, and use total stations or laser checks at yard preassembly. For our in-house PE stamp: engineer camber in-house rather than trusting the design number, and protect load path per the Drucker-style minimal-eccentricity approach. For anchor rods: the Labrador failure is the lesson to never let a GC defer grouting under a cantilever and to preserve anchor rods during any base-plate rework. The 75% machined-bearing, 2/100 inch flatness criterion is a usable fit-up acceptance metric for heavy bearing splices on ACP-type controls. DOCTRINE FLAG: NONE. The content is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language and no conflict with Your Company doctrine; the only caution is that no AISC section numbers were cited aloud, so any spec basis must be added from our own references, not invented from this video.

## Design of Reinforcement for Steel Members - Part 2
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=clNpsHmgaUQ | Duration: 1:33:14 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
This webinar by Bo Dowswell PE PhD covers how to reinforce existing steel beams and columns that are already carrying load, with the central problem being the preload, defined at [02:34] as the portion of total load present on the member at the time reinforcement is added. Because you usually cannot strip a member to zero load before welding plates or angles onto it, the reinforced section only resists the post-reinforcement load, so superposition must combine pre-reinforcement deflection on the bare section with post-reinforcement deflection on the built-up section [05:07]. The session strings together several short interrelated topics (deflection, torsional constant J, stitch welds, welding to loaded members, built-up column shear flow, plate buckling between welds) and closes with a 25-minute composite beam reinforcement example [61:26].

### Spec References
Cited verbatim by the speaker: Section D4 (tension members) and J3.5 for stitch weld spacing on faying surfaces [17:28]; the maximum stitch-weld spacing P equals 24 times the thickness of the thinner part joined with a 12-inch cap [18:31]; Chapter J intermittent (stitch) weld minimum length of 4 times weld size and 1.5 inches minimum [16:21]; Table B4.1A case 7 with lambda_r equals 1.4 times sqrt(E/Fy) for column local buckling [45:26]; Section E6.2 for stitch-weld spacing in built-up columns, non-staggered P_max equals 0.75 times t times sqrt(E/Fy) capped at 12 inches, staggered allows 1.12 and 18 inches [48:28]; Appendix 8 Section 8.2 amplified first-order analysis with B1 [42:14]; Manual Table 3-23 for moment and shear as a function of X [41:12]; the Code of Standard Practice out-of-plumb tolerance delta_o equal to L/1000 [38:06]; Chapter F has no provision for plate buckling between welds on beams, so a Chang and Johnston era reference is substituted [51:11]; composite beam example I.1 from the AISC design examples and Commentary Section I3.2 for effective moment of inertia [62:26][79:39].

### Technical Details
The torsional constant J differs between individual behavior (sum the J of each plate and the wide flange) and integral behavior with a continuous weld, where the larger moment arm produces a much greater J, sometimes 3 times higher [09:14][13:17]. Stitch-welded members fall between these limits, and shape-builder software computes integral J which is unconservative for lateral-torsional buckling when welds are intermittent [12:47]. For welding to loaded members, elevated base-metal temperature drops modulus, yield, and ultimate strength; an ineffective zone W_y of 1 inch for stick welding and 2 inches for self-shielded flux core is knocked out of the section, measured from the far face, and section modulus rather than plastic modulus is used to avoid a residual kink [28:20][29:23]. Built-up column shear flow VQ/I and anchor force MQ/I cannot be found directly because columns have no known transverse shear, so a notional uniform load W_n equal to P_r/(125L) is applied to mimic the L/1000 out-of-straightness moment, then amplified by B1 for second-order effect [38:37][42:14].

### Fabrication Notes
Stitch welds lower cost through less deposited weld and produce much less shrinkage distortion, which matters because weld-induced out-of-straightness sharply cuts column strength [14:50][15:21]. Minimum stitch length is 4 times weld size and at least 1.5 inches so the arc has room to establish a sound weld [16:21]. To limit heat into a loaded member the speaker recommends small-diameter electrodes, low current, stringer beads instead of weave beads, controlled interpass temperature (300 F for thin material, commonly 600 F max on a WPS), letting passes cool, and monitoring with temperature crayons [20:06][21:40][22:43]. Shelf dimension matters for fit-up: leave about 0.5 inch of horizontal shelf for a 3/16 fillet so the welder can reach the joint, more if the part may run out of tolerance [67:35].

### Erection Notes
The presentation is field-reinforcement focused, so erection content is woven into the welding discussion rather than crane or sequencing guidance. The speaker stresses getting the erector's WPS in advance and reviewing it to confirm the heat-input process will not overheat a loaded beam or column [20:06]. Overhead welds are roughly 25 percent as productive as horizontal welds, so reinforcement is detailed to allow horizontal welding where possible [67:04]. Long reinforcement is a handling problem in the field: a 45-foot 2.5 by 2.5 angle is very flexible and hard to handle, which drove the decision to use partial-length reinforcement [76:32][84:24].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The named failure mode is corrosion entering the gap between back-to-back double angles with no stitch plates, where trapped moisture (the speaker suspects coal dust held it) corroded the steel and the expanding corrosion product cracked the connecting weld [18:00]. The spacing rules in J3.5 and D4 exist specifically to keep the faying-surface gap small enough to prevent that corrosion. A second pitfall is trusting shape-builder software for J on stitch-welded members, since it returns integral J that is unconservative for the actual intermittent condition [12:47]. A third is using plastic section modulus near a hot weld, which can leave a permanent kink as the weld cools [29:23].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Stitch welds reduce welding cost and outweigh the small added cost of laying out and measuring the intermittent pattern [14:50]. Partial-length reinforcement is more economical than full-length and is preferred, with the theoretical cutoff point selected by iteration to minimize weld and material length [33:55][76:32]. Overhead welding at about 25 percent productivity is a real labor multiplier to price against horizontal welding [67:04]. The composite example shows the iteration cost directly: a strength-only cutoff at 15.5 feet (rounded conservatively to 14) failed the deflection check and had to grow to a 39-foot reinforcement length, which the speaker would avoid in practice due to handling difficulty [78:07][84:24].

### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, reinforcement and retrofit scopes should price partial-length plates or angles, account for stitch versus continuous weld length, and add the overhead-welding labor factor when access forces it; the 0.5-inch shelf-dimension rule affects plate sizing. For Mario as welding lead, the heat-input controls (stringer beads, interpass-temperature limits, the WPS review against AWS D1.1 parameters) and the J3.5 stitch-weld geometry (4 times weld size, 1.5 inch minimum, 24t and 12-inch spacing cap) are directly shop-actionable, and the corrosion-cracked double-angle case is a clear QC teaching example. For Tekla detailing, stitch-weld spacing per E6.2 and the buckling-between-welds limits govern how intermittent welds are placed on built-up members. The in-house PE stamp work maps tightly to this content for any reinforce-existing-member design, including the notional-load method for column shear flow. This is verify-don't-generate territory: every spacing limit, J value, and section property must run through bridge/aisc_validator.py and the cited spec sections rather than LLM math. No conflict with Your Company doctrine; this is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language.

## Design of Reinforcement for Steel Members - Part 1
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LclgSYUL6Oo | Duration: 1:31:38 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This webinar by Bo Dowswell, P.E., Ph.D. of ARK International covers the strength and stability design of structurally reinforced existing steel members, specifically columns under flexural buckling and beams under lateral torsional buckling [01:03]. Reinforcement enlarges the cross section to carry added load (building extension) or to restore strength lost to damage, corrosion, or fatigue [02:03], [02:33]. The two governing themes are the controlling effect of geometric imperfections (rolling tolerance, P-delta, and weld distortion) on a reinforced member's strength [10:40], and whether reinforcement is "stabilizing" (radius of gyration of the reinforced section at least 85% of the original), which lets the designer neglect preload [32:36], [67:08].

### Spec References
The speaker cited AISC 360 (2010) Section E3 flexural buckling with the inelastic and elastic critical-stress equations, the elastic case being 87.7% of the Euler stress [10:08], [10:40]; Chapter H for combined axial-plus-moment beam-column design of singly symmetric reinforcement [08:05], [15:30]; Chapter C and Appendix 8 (B1 amplification factor) for second-order P-delta effects [11:11], [15:30]; Section F2 for doubly symmetric I-shapes, with Section F4 required for singly symmetric I-shapes (including web local buckling and the rule that J is taken as zero when the flange moment-of-inertia ratio is at or below 0.23) [58:16], [62:22], equation F4-2 referenced for the preload modification [78:23]; and the AISC Code of Standard Practice straightness tolerance of L over 1000 [09:07], [14:29]. He also referenced the Blodgett weld-distortion equation and an AISC Engineering Journal step-column paper (over 40 years old) plus the 1989 green-book ASD manual for non-stabilizing reinforcement [16:31], [27:23], [36:09]. No AISC Design Guide number, AISC 341 seismic section, AWS D1.1 clause, or RCSC bolting provision was cited; this presentation is member design, not connection or bolting design.

### Technical Details
The column design procedure runs seven steps: pick reinforcement type, estimate size, compute reinforced-section properties, assess geometric imperfections on flexural buckling, assess preload effect, assess partial-length reinforcement effect, then check strength per E3 [03:34], [07:05]. Doubly symmetric reinforcement is preferred because singly symmetric reinforcement shifts the centroid toward the added plate, creating an eccentric moment, and bows the member away from the weld [07:35], [08:05]. Total out-of-straightness delta-sub-D after welding sums rolling tolerance, P-delta, and weld distortion; if it exceeds the L/1000 tolerance delta-sub-O, the member is checked as a beam-column with a first-order moment of P-sub-R times (delta-D minus delta-O), amplified by B1 [11:44], [15:00]. Partial-length reinforcement (plates pulled back from member ends) is modeled as a step column using tabulated effective-length factors K-sub-S1 and K-sub-S2 (both greater than one, applied to reinforced-section properties), entered with the reinforced-to-original moment-of-inertia ratio and the length ratio [26:52], [29:27]. The worked example (W14x90, 18 ft, Fy 50 ksi, 300 kip preload, 1100 kip total factored LRFD load, 3/4 by 12 plates pulled back 4 ft each end) yielded K = 1.04, design strength 1500 kips against 1100 applied, and the bare W14x90 yield check of 1190 kips confirmed the end "ear" plates were unnecessary [39:53], [45:11]. For beams the controlling check is lateral torsional buckling per F4, with a step-beam C-prime-sub-B reduction factor beta-sub-LTB for partial-length reinforcement based on the setback-to-length ratio D-sub-R over L [70:40], [71:41].

### Fabrication Notes
Weld distortion scales with the square of the fillet leg size per Blodgett, so a 3/16 fillet may hold a member within L/1000 while doubling the leg roughly quadruples distortion to about a half inch, outside tolerance [18:04], [18:34]. Stitch welding reduces distortion, speeds the job, and lowers cost, with a reduction factor R-sub-S equal to stitch length over center-to-center spacing [19:11], [20:12]. Welding only one side of a partial-length plate kicks the column sideways, so symmetric welds and sequences that minimize distortion are specified by drawing note [22:16], [52:27]. Welding heat is a fabrication hazard on loaded members: a transverse weld can render an entire bottom flange ineffective, while a longitudinal weld removes much less, handled by an effective-width method that deletes the heat-affected strip from the section [55:31], [82:33]. A bottom-flange plate is the speaker's preferred reinforcement because it clamps in place for easy fit-up and welds downhand, whereas a WT welded overhead runs about four times the cost of a downhand weld [52:27], [54:31].

### Erection Notes
The webinar centers on shop and design work, with limited field content. The key field point is that field welders cannot remove all preload before reinforcing an in-service member: industrial and power-plant columns may carry 60 to 100 kips of preload during welding, which is the entire reason the preload and stabilizing-reinforcement checks exist [06:35], [38:11], [48:18]. Doubly symmetric reinforcement gives field welders a chance to balance shrinkage from both flanges and keep the post-welded member within the L/1000 straightness tolerance [08:36], [22:16]. No crane, rigging, sequencing, or shoring procedures were discussed.

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The dominant defect is excess weld distortion pushing the post-welded member outside the Code of Standard Practice L/1000 straightness limit, driven by oversized fillets, one-sided welding, or singly symmetric layouts [18:34], [22:16]. The speaker flagged that upward camber from a bottom-flange weld can crack an attached floor slab if not anticipated [51:26], and that welding heat on a loaded member can reduce flange strength enough to fail a beam or column [55:31], [82:33]. He warned of an unconservative calculation trap: when computing the M-sub-BR ratio for the step-beam factor, the actual J must be used rather than J equal to zero, or beta-LTB comes out too large [73:43]. No third-party inspection, NDE, or rejection categories were named.

### Bid / Cost Implications
Cost drivers named explicitly: weld position (overhead WT reinforcement runs about four times the cost of a downhand bottom-flange plate) [54:31]; weld volume, since stitch welds cut welding time, cost, and distortion versus continuous welds [19:11]; and matching reinforcement plates left and right to reuse one plate and one weld detail rather than fabricating odd tab or wing plates [23:47], [25:51]. The worked example shows good engineering deletes unneeded steel: the end ear plates were dropped after the bare-column yield check passed, removing distortion, cost, and schedule [45:43]. The trade-off between unloading a column (a months-long plant shutdown that may cost more than building a new unit) and designing for preload is itself a major schedule and cost decision [06:35].

### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, reinforcement and retrofit scopes must be priced from a measured plate-and-weld member takeoff through aisc_validator.py, not from SF-times-psf, since plate sizes come from iterative section-property calcs and the validator holds the W14x90 and WT properties Dowswell pulls "straight out of the manual." For Mario as welding lead, the actionable rules are downhand bottom-flange plates over overhead WTs, stitch welding to cut distortion and labor, balanced weld sequences to hold L/1000, and awareness that weld heat on a loaded member reduces flange strength. Paul's safety scope intersects where members are reinforced under live preload (welding on a column carrying 60 to 100 kips), which warrants a load-path and shoring review before any field weld on an in-service frame. Tekla detailing should carry the standing note "welding shall use techniques and sequences that minimize distortion" plus the post-welded L/1000 acceptance criterion. The in-house PE stamp work maps directly: E3, Chapter H, Appendix 8, F2, and F4 are the governing sections for any reinforcement design we stamp. This content does not touch anchor rods, joists, field bolting, RCSC pretension, or AISC 341 seismic, and it is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language. Doctrine flag: NONE.

## Vertical Bracing Connections - Analysis and Design
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Qr2mYsXSR4s | Duration: 1:04:05 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is an AISC overview of Design Guide 29, Vertical Bracing Connections, presented by Larry Muir and Bill Thornton, both members of the AISC Committee on Manuals and the Committee on Specifications task committee on connections [01:33]. The governing principle is the lower bound theorem of limit analysis: a connection is safe if the designer picks any force distribution that satisfies equilibrium (Statics), does not exceed any limit state, and has enough ductility to redistribute load without fracture [18:58][19:29]. This works because force is attracted to stiffness, a yielding member sheds load to stiffer elements, and steel is inherently ductile so redistribution occurs [20:00][20:30]. The practical tool for choosing that distribution is the Uniform Force Method (UFM), a geometric method that produces only shear and normal forces on each gusset interface with no moments, so the resultants intersect at a single workpoint [25:41][26:11].

### Spec References
The talk cites AISC Design Guide 29 (the subject, about 400 pages) and notes the examples are keyed to the 2010 AISC Specification, later revised to the 14th Edition [07:44][33:58]. UFM equations and the Alpha-Beta geometric relationship are referenced to Part 13 of the AISC Manual [04:38][09:48]. The seismic discussion cites AISC 341 (called "341-10") special concentrically braced frame provisions, the comparison R=3 system, and the AISC 341 end-rotation requirement of about 0.025 radians [09:16][55:41][57:45]. Extended single-plate ductility is per Part 10 of the AISC Manual (about 0.03 radian capacity) [57:15]. A directional weld strength increase of 1.0 + 0.5(sin theta)^1.5 is cited [61:50]. Historical sources named: Ralph Richard (UFM research), Bo Dowswell (gusset stability), Abolitz and Warner 1964 AISC Engineering Journal (yield line), and a forthcoming Pat Fortney and Thornton Engineering Journal paper on the Chevron effect [25:41][12:54][37:01][43:43].

### Technical Details
UFM special cases: Case 1 is a non-concentric workpoint that induces moment into beam and column but can give a more economical gusset [27:13]; Case 2 dumps part of the beam-to-column reaction up through the gusset when the beam-to-column shear is too high to detail economically [28:15]; Case 3 connects only to the beam or only to the column for very shallow or steep brace bevels, accepting a moment [29:49]; the new Case 4 connects to a column web (or flange) by taking the eccentricity e-sub-c out to the first column of bolts, using a deeper section to resist eccentricity rather than assuming e-sub-c equals zero [30:20][31:23]. Appendix A generalizes UFM by removing geometric constraints and folds the beam reaction directly into the force determination [09:48][48:25]. Appendix C covers gusset stability with both centerline Whitmore buckling and edge buckling, noting AISC 341 commentary now says edge buckling is typically not a concern, so many gussets are "compact" where yielding governs over buckling [12:21][17:58]. Appendix D handles transfer (drag) forces across a column.

### Fabrication Notes
The design guide favors brace-to-gusset details where the connecting element provides out-of-plane stiffness: angle legs, WT stems, HSS walls, or flange plates, and avoids lapping plate on plate ("pushing on a chain") [16:27][16:58]. Detailing dependency is explicit: a milled top-cord bearing plate cannot be detailed until the beam is known, because rolled-section mill work is not perfect and the bearing edge must be milled to match the inside profile of the column or beam flange [52:33][53:04]. The talk gives a direct shop choice between a 3/8 inch fillet weld with a fitted, milled bearing edge versus a 5/8 inch weld (roughly double the welding cost) that carries all load and needs no milling, and says only the fabricating shop can decide [52:33][53:04]. A 5/8 t weld is used so the plate yields before the weld fractures (extended shear-tab theory) [38:35].

### Erection Notes
Field connection methods shown include double-angle and single-angle braces field bolted to the gusset, cruciform four-angle bolted attachments to a wide-flange web, HSS bird-mouth slotted and field welded onto the gusset, and shop-welded slotted flange plates that provide a field-bolted connection out to the member flanges [14:24][15:27]. Extended tab (single-plate) connections push the bolts out beyond the column flanges so the erector can "slap everything up against the side of the tab plate and field bolt it," which is faster in the field [32:24]. Drilling through thick jumbo-column flanges and webs lets the drill drift, which makes getting the bolt into the hole a field headache, so replacing drilled double-angle clips with a modest welded connection saves erection time [31:53][32:24].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The headline error is unauthorized field or shop welds that break the engineer's assumed force distribution: adding a weld between a beam flange and the connection sucks extra load into the adjacent bolts, can overload or rupture those bolts, destroys the assumed uniform bolt distribution, and may then require a stiffener [54:10][54:40][55:11]. The configuration must replicate what the engineer assumed; a connection assumed simple must stay close to simple [55:11]. Detailing trial-and-error pitfalls named: a 3 inch bolt spacing can produce a block shear failure on a thin web even when the bolts check out, fixed by adding bolts or opening to 4-1/2 inch spacing [50:59]. Over-stiffening gusset edges for edge buckling is called out as a common but usually unnecessary practice [12:21].

### Bid / Cost Implications
The seismic example pairs an SCBF design with an R=3 design of the same frame so a fabricator bidding a job can see exactly how AISC 341 changes connection cost relative to a non-seismic design [09:16][09:48]. The biggest stated number is two coal-fired power plants where the connection design saved an estimated 2 million dollars versus historical cost, mostly from using extended and conventional single-plate tabs instead of double-angle clips on jumbo columns [31:23][31:53]. The recurring cost driver is the "ugly design load," an inflated UDL-based beam reaction (the example would imply roughly 3,000 psf, a load no real floor carries) that forces uneconomical Special Case 2 or beam-reaction-distribution work purely to satisfy the contract reactions on the drawings [29:18][47:22][48:56].

### Your Company Application
For Ivan, the Special Case 2 and Appendix A beam-reaction work is the estimating flag: when drawings give UDL-based "ugly design loads" rather than actual reactions, connection design balloons and the bid must price that detailing, so reactions on the contract drawings drive connection cost the way SF drives tonnage. For Tekla detailing and the in-house PE stamp, the lower bound theorem plus UFM (Part 13, special cases 1 to 4) is the design basis, with milled bearing plates that cannot be detailed until the beam size is fixed. For Mario, the welding lesson is firm: do not add a flange weld the engineer did not assume, since it overloads adjacent bolts; honor the assumed force distribution and use the directional strength increase and the 1.25 ductility (rid) factor on transversely loaded welds where the design specifies it [59:47][60:17]. For field bolting, extended single-plate tabs beat drilled double-angle clips on thick jumbo columns, both for fab time and to avoid drill drift that fouls field bolt entry. Anchor-rod and column-base relevance: Design Guide 29 adds brace-to-column-base cases (flange and web, with a yield-line web check) that the older Manual did not cover, useful for our base-plate and anchor work. Doctrine conflict: NONE. This is conventional structural steel methodology with no PEMB language, AISC weights still come from aisc_validator.py, and rates stay CEO-locked.

## Seismic Load Paths for Steel Buildings
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vFvN6JwYADc | Duration: 1:28:54 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
Raphael Sabelli of Walter P Moore teaches the complete seismic load path for steel buildings, the path that connects every mass in the structure down to the foundation. The central idea is the fuse concept, also called capacity design [09:43] [11:15]: yielding elements (beams in a moment frame, braces in a braced frame) act as fuses that are deliberately weaker and more ductile than the protected elements (columns, collectors, connections), so inelastic deformation happens where it is wanted. Because design forces are reduced far below the maximum considered earthquake (MCE), the speaker explains the ASCE 7 reduction chain: take the MCE spectrum, multiply by 2/3 to reach the design-basis level, then divide by the R factor [04:35] [05:05], so an R=8 structure designs for roughly one twelfth of MCE forces [06:37]. The talk then walks the load path through foundations, diaphragms, chords, collectors, and ends on deformation compatibility for non-load-path elements like stairs.
### Spec References
The speaker repeatedly cites ASCE 7 for the load-reduction process, the omega-sub-zero (overstrength) factor, ASD load combinations for foundation stability, LRFD load combinations, and the C-sub-d deflection-amplification factor [04:18] [25:10] [74:06]. He names the AISC Seismic Design Manual (five-volume, which he chaired) as the source for the collector axial-strength tables [62:50] and as a general reference [77:13]. He cites AISC 360 Chapter E for compression / flexural-torsional buckling of collector beam-columns [61:16]. He references ASCE 7-22 as the first edition addressing a member spanning across a seismic joint [72:36], and a NIST / NEHRP technical brief on diaphragms in steel-frame systems as a free download [32:25] [76:42]. Seismic systems are named generically: special moment frame (SMF), special concentrically braced frame (SCBF), and eccentrically braced frame (EBF) [02:01]. No AWS D1.1 clause, RCSC pretension clause, or specific table number was stated aloud, so those are not cited here.
### Technical Details
Three diaphragm types are covered: bare steel deck welded or screwed or shot-pinned to framing, concrete-filled or composite deck, and horizontal steel truss diaphragms for industrial roofs [29:49] [31:53]. Diaphragm rigidity drives the analysis method: a flexible diaphragm (about an order of magnitude more flexible than the frames) is a determinate system solved like a beam, while rigid and semi-rigid diaphragms are indeterminate and need a 3D building model [42:16] [44:18]. The speaker stresses that a flexible diaphragm is not a simple span; multi-span and cantilever conditions get envelope chord forces, and seismic loads reverse so diagrams must be enveloped both ways [46:21]. Collectors are beam-columns with combined gravity flexure and seismic axial load; their compressive strength may be governed by constrained-axis flexural-torsional buckling when a composite deck restrains the top flange, which most software ignores in favor of conservative minor-axis buckling [60:46] [62:20]. The talk also covers the backstay effect in tall and podium buildings, where a shear reversal drives a force into the backstay diaphragm larger than the building base shear [38:43] [39:44], and P-delta thrust accumulating through gravity columns into the diaphragm [34:58].
### Fabrication Notes
This is a design webinar, so shop fabrication detail is light. The fabrication-relevant content is connection type selection for collectors and gravity beams: single-plate (shear tab) and double-angle connections from the manual carry large rotation capacity, single-plate connections tested at UC Berkeley exceeded 10 percent rotation [67:27], and typical connections are detailed for 3 percent rotation capacity within the design range before seismic drift is added [67:57]. For higher collector forces the speaker describes a welded top-flange detail (introduces eccentricity) or welding both flanges to make a moment connection, plus the extended single-plate method with a double column of bolts for added strength [65:26]. Collector reinforcement embedded in a composite deck must be sized for a width that keeps unconfined concrete stress below 0.5 f-prime-c [58:13]. No WPS, electrode, preheat, or weld-procedure tolerance was stated.
### Erection Notes
Erection-specific procedures, crane, rigging, and sequencing are not addressed in this design-focused webinar. The closest content is the stair-isolation detail meant to keep stairs off the seismic load path: tie one end hard (often a fully welded connection at the top) and tie the other end flexibly with a slotted-hole angle connection at the bottom so the stair moves with the upper diaphragm [69:34] [70:04], with the bolt deliberately made weak enough to shear before tearing up gravity support if drift exceeds the slot [71:06]. The speaker also stresses maintaining adequate building separation to prevent pounding, especially where mismatched story heights let one building strike another mid-column rather than at a deck [71:36] [72:06].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The speaker names several recurring design mistakes rather than shop inspection rejections. Assuming a flexible diaphragm is always a simple span is called a mistake many people make [46:21]. Placing a member with zero axial capacity where a multi-span moment diagram is assumed to cross zero is warned against, because the true zero location is uncertain [46:52]. Failing to tie a bare-joist-and-deck diaphragm together so it can pull apart is flagged [48:55]. Counting on foundation rocking or uplift to limit forces is discouraged because deep foundations carry large unaccounted overstrength [29:18], and the ASD-versus-LRFD mismatch can make a footing appear stable under one combination and not the other [25:10]. Letting stairs act as unintended brittle braces, and underestimating seismic drift past the detailed slot length, are both called out [69:02] [71:06].
### Bid / Cost Implications
In the closing Q&A the speaker addresses system selection cost directly [86:34] [87:34]. A fully elastic structure would be very strong and very expensive, which is why the R-factor reduction is used [05:35]. Choosing a special (high-R, ductile) system versus an ordinary (low-R) system is a real cost trade: special systems carry added inspection cost and possibly added erection time, while ordinary systems carry the cost of heavier foundations and the rest of the structure designed for higher accelerations [87:34] [88:05]. The speaker advises weighing not just steel tonnage but inspection, erection, and foundation costs together. Backstay overturning moments are described as very expensive to design for, so reducing them benefits structural economy [38:10].
### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, the system-selection cost discussion maps to the bid: special seismic systems add inspection and erection cost while ordinary systems add foundation and tonnage cost, so a seismic job needs the system type confirmed before pricing, and member counts still come from schedules and framing-plan marks through aisc_validator.py, never from a per-square-foot guess. Mario's shop and welding crew touch the collector and connection details: shear tabs and double angles for ductile gravity connections, and welded top-flange or both-flange welds where collector forces are high, with any such weld driven by the project WPS rather than this webinar. Paul's safety scope ties to the stair-isolation detail and the post-earthquake egress logic, since stairs must stay usable for evacuation and first responders. Tekla detailing should model the slotted stair connections, collector chord lines, and seismic-joint bracket bearing length so the field gets the movement allowance right. The in-house PE stamp work should pull from the AISC Seismic Design Manual collector tables and ASCE 7 reduction chain cited here; anchor-rod design and field bolting follow the connection demands but no RCSC pretension clause was stated to cite. Doctrine flags: NONE. This is conventional structural steel content with no PEMB language and no conflict with Your Company rules.

## Where Did That Force Come From? Combining Diaphragm Braced Frame Force
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Lr_k78ess2k | Duration: 1:26:55 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
Raphael Sabelli of Walter P Moore presents a design methodology for reconciling three inconsistent force sets that meet where a diaphragm collector enters a braced frame: base shear forces (wind or seismic, in red), diaphragm acceleration forces Fpx (yellow), and capacity-design mechanism forces from yielding fuse members (blue) [01:33][04:07][05:10]. He is explicit that this is engineering judgment bridging a gap between ASCE 7 and the AISC seismic provisions, not a code requirement [02:04]. The method builds two or three artificial load cases, solving each connection by statics: case one uses the vertical distribution or mechanism forces and tends to govern vertical forces, case two swaps in the Fpx collector force with a statical adjustment and tends to govern horizontal forces, and a third case captures the post-buckled condition for special concentrically braced frames [22:09][67:02].
### Spec References
ASCE 7 (cited as "ASCE 7" / "A7") for the equivalent lateral force vertical distribution and the diaphragm Fpx forces; AISC 341 seismic provisions for the capacity-design connection forces and the special concentrically braced frame analysis at Section F2.3 (two analyses: maximum tension plus maximum compression, then maximum tension with compression degraded to 30 percent) [04:38][65:59][69:42]. The Omega-sub-o overstrength factor is applied to collector connections starting in seismic design category C [08:14][23:11]. Systems named by their code designations: R=3, ordinary concentrically braced frame at R=3.25, and the higher-R special concentrically braced frame (SCBF), eccentrically braced frame (EBF), and buckling restrained braced frame (BRBF) [08:14][39:05]. Material and strain-hardening factors cited: Ry for material overstrength and a 1.1 factor for BRBF connections, and 1.25 strain hardening on the EBF link yield strength [42:42][43:13].
### Technical Details
Forces are resolved at the gusset-to-beam and gusset-to-column joints using the uniform force method (or a variant), then statics gives the beam axial force, the beam shear, and the connection forces [13:19][14:53]. For modal response spectrum analysis the speaker introduces a purple set: signs are lost to the square-root-of-sum-of-squares, forces are not statically balanced, the engineer assigns directions, and section cuts must track each quantity mode by mode because differences between modal combination maxima are mathematically meaningless [26:49][29:53]. For SCBF the post-buckled case three drives a large axial drag force through the beam along a zigzag load path once compression braces lose roughly 70 percent of capacity [49:55][80:15]. In the worked four-story example, the SCBF connection horizontal force jumped to 266 kips under the post-buckled case three against only 10 kips in the elastic analysis [60:16].
### Fabrication Notes
This is a structural design webinar on how connection design forces are derived, so it does not cover shop fit-up, cutting, or QC processes directly. The fabrication-relevant takeaway is that the connection designer should be given the full set of corresponding force cases (case one, case two, and case three where it applies), because handing over only the lumped maximum of each component produces a statically inconsistent set that forces another conservative adjustment downstream [35:29][62:22].
### Erection Notes
The webinar does not address erection sequencing, bracing, rigging, or crane work. Its physical content is the in-service load path: after compression braces buckle and degrade, force must zigzag through beams to a tension brace or to an out-of-plane braced frame 30 to 40 feet away via diaphragm shear, which is a permanent-condition behavior rather than an erection procedure [80:15].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
No weld or bolt inspection failures are named. The design errors flagged are conceptual: assuming the brace forces are zero when diaphragm forces are applied, which would lead to a connection that can fail [07:42]; applying all Fpx forces simultaneously, which grossly overestimates shear and overturning demand [20:04]; over-conservatively increasing the brace-below force instead of reducing the brace-above force, which the speaker calls inconsistent with the code [25:49]; and using differences between modal combination maxima, which is meaningless [29:53].
### Bid / Cost Implications
The choice of collector load-path assumption (for example 33/33/33 across three bays versus 100 percent into the center bay, or a shortened collector that discounts part of the building width) directly changes how heavily the connections are designed and therefore the connection material and shop labor [21:07][74:29]. The post-buckled SCBF case can drive a connection from 10 kips to 266 kips of horizontal force, so a frame priced without it would be badly under-detailed [60:16]. Communicating three corresponding force cases rather than one lumped envelope avoids piling conservatism on conservatism, which trims heavier-than-needed connection steel [35:29].
### Your Company Application
This is a connection-force-derivation methodology, so its relevance is mostly to Tekla detailing and any in-house PE stamp work where Your Company derives or checks seismic connection forces for braced-frame jobs: the detailer and stamping engineer should expect three corresponding force cases from the EOR and should reject a single lumped-maximum force set as statically inconsistent [35:29][62:22]. For Ivan takeoff, the load-path and Fpx assumptions materially change collector and gusset connection weights, so a braced-frame estimate cannot assume light connections without confirming the seismic design category and whether SCBF post-buckled forces apply [21:07][60:16]. There is no joist, anchor-rod, field-bolting, or AWS welding content to map to Mario or Paul here. No conflict with Your Company doctrine: the content is conventional structural steel and the speaker is careful to label his method as judgment, which aligns with the verify-do-not-generate posture. Doctrine flag: NONE.

## Welding - Special Applications
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Oq85-3nZsZQ | Duration: 1:43:01 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
Dr. Duane K. Miller of Lincoln Electric, chair of the AWS D1 structural welding code committee, walks through the ten miscellaneous welding topics that became Chapter 12 of AISC Design Guide 21 (welding) [02:38][03:08]. These are the frequently asked field questions that did not fit elsewhere: extending anchor rods, welding anchor rods to base plates, welding on coated steels, welding heavy/jumbo sections, welding under high restraint, welding HSS, welding AESS, welding on existing structures, plus butt welding and heat shrinking (the last two were skipped for time) [03:08][102:23]. The through-line is weldability driven by steel chemistry and the fracture-mechanics control of toughness, residual stress, and crack size [49:59].

### Spec References
AISC Design Guide 21 (welding), specifically its Chapter 12 miscellaneous topics, Chapter 7 (welding procedures), Chapter 15 (weld safety), and page 62-63 historic-steel and anchor-grade discussions [02:38][09:20][94:06]. AISC Design Guide 15 by Roger Brockenbrough for historic steel properties [94:37]. AWS D1.1 structural welding code Section 5.15 (surface cleanliness), Table 4.5 limitation of variables, and the fillet weld break test [29:27][40:48][42:50]. AWS A3.0 (welding terms, weldability definition) [05:41]. AWS D19.0 (galvanized welding, now obsolete, last updated 1972) [38:46]. ANSI/AWS Z49.1 (safety in welding and cutting) plus AWS fact sheets 1, 21, 25 [31:01][32:31]. ASTM F1554 anchor-rod grades 36/55/105 with optional Supplement S1, and ASTM A325, A354, A307, A36 [09:51][13:34]. ASTM A6 Supplement S30 (jumbo CVN at centerline, t/4 depth) with 20 ft-lb at 70 F requirement [54:03]. The 2005 AISC 13th edition specification shop-painting clause and Section M4 [28:23][28:54].

### Technical Details
Weldability is governed by carbon content compounded by alloy, and is inversely related to hardenability; low-carbon low-alloy steels weld best, and sulfur and phosphorus drive hot cracking [06:46][08:17]. F1554 is the preferred anchor-rod spec, but grade 36 carries a manganese footnote, grade 55 has no carbon or alloy limits unless ordered to Supplement S1, and grade 105 (105 ksi yield) is essentially uncontrolled chemistry and a near-guaranteed weldability challenge [10:24][19:45]. Suppliers often substitute grade 55 for an ordered grade 36, so weldability must be verified case by case via a lab chemistry check and the carbon-equivalency equations on the mill test report [11:27][15:07]. Heavy/jumbo shapes (former group 4 and 5, example W14x730 with 5 in flange, 3 in web, 22 in depth) have a segregated higher-carbon, lower-toughness core that becomes problematic only in tension joints, which is why CVN is now sampled at the centerline t/4 location [44:55][53:33]. Fracture is controlled by three variables: toughness, residual or applied stress, and crack size, and triaxial tensile stress at a weld access hole removes the shear needed for ductility per the Mohr-circle argument from Gensamer (1941) [49:59][57:40][66:24].

### Fabrication Notes
For anchor-rod extensions, first check mechanical options (coupler nuts, undercutting and milling the base plate); if welding, use a weldable-steel doughnut washer with the ID matched to the rod OD as a shelf and runoff tab, grind the extension to a chisel point, weld one side, back-gouge the root, weld the second, then grind flush, and never use a plug weld (no tension capacity) [04:40][20:17][22:18]. On heavy sections, AISC mid-1980s rules require preheating to 150 F before thermal cutting the access hole, grinding to bright metal, then MT or PT inspection to start crack-free; the preferred practice drills the access-hole radius on the drill line to avoid the hard-to-grind radius notch [72:33][73:04]. Access holes are enlarged (height 1.5 t-sub-w, min 1 in, max 2 in; length on the W14x730 reaches about 15 in) specifically to keep flange-weld and web-weld residual stresses from interacting [69:27][70:29]. Reduce weld volume with a double-V groove, sequence so the final high-residual passes land away from the core, and use higher-toughness filler (20 ft-lb at minus 40 F for weld metal) [70:29][55:38].

### Erection Notes
The recurring field trigger is anchor rods set too deep (no thread engagement, rod below the base-plate plane) or too shallow, which tempts crews to field weld; the speaker's first answer is a mechanical fix and telling the rod-setting contractor not to set too deep [03:39][16:40][24:21]. The EDS/Plano suspended-truss case study shows the erection strategy for jumbo work: make the complicated nodes in the shop and leave simple butt splices for the field where the welder has better access away from the column, and leave the large access holes open after they have done their residual-stress job [75:40][77:42]. When welding on existing structures under load, place the work lead as close to the weld as possible so welding current does not stray through conduit, HVAC ducting, or gas lines [99:15][99:46].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The Orlando Civic Center jumbo bottom-chord tension truss fractured in the base metal (not the weld) at the weld access hole during night erection in the late 1970s, traced to small access holes terminating in residual tension plus pre-existing PT-detectable notches and gouges [42:50][67:24][72:03]. Named failures include plug welds in tension on anchors (no capacity), tack welds on the inboard side of a rod-end nut (can crack the rod), incomplete fusion through a heavy galvanized coating so strength rides only on the zinc, severe porosity from zinc sublimation, and zinc-induced centerline cracking [22:18][23:50][36:41]. Inspecting welds after heavy paint or dipping can mask discontinuities, so visual inspection must occur before painting [34:36][35:08]. Lamellar tearing still occurs with large through-thickness CJP welds, most often at plate edges and fabricated-box corner joints [74:05].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Welding choices carry direct cost. Continuous AESS welds cost more than intermittent welds and add distortion, so caulk between welds can be cheaper where strength does not require a full weld [90:29]. AESS demands mockups painted in the final finish and viewed from the actual installed distance (a 30 ft-high truss judged from 30 ft), and the AISC AESS document supplies estimated premium costs by category for use with architects [88:55][93:35]. Critical coated-steel applications require WPS qualification by test rather than relying on prequalified procedures and mocking up the thickest coating condition, which adds qualification time and cost [39:46][40:17]. HSS connection detailing can force a member-size change, and overlapped HSS joints need multiple cuts (more fit-up risk) versus a single-cut gapped connection [80:47][84:20].

### Your Company Application
Anchor-rod work maps directly to Your Company's anchor-rod design/setting/tolerance workstream: standardize on F1554 grade 36, and when a set-too-deep risk exists, order to Supplement S1 up front so welded extensions are defensible, with Mario verifying weldability by chemistry and carbon equivalency on the MTR before any field weld, never a plug weld. Ivan's takeoff should flag jumbo shapes (heavy W-shapes in tension) for the Supplement S30 CVN requirement, enlarged access holes, 150 F preheat, and PT/MT, since these add shop hours that a plain tonnage rate misses. Tekla detailing should adopt the shop-complicated-node, field-simple-splice sequencing for any heavy truss and the drilled access-hole-radius detail. Paul's safety program should pull Z49.1 and AWS fact sheets 1, 21, 25 for galvanized fume and metal-fume-fever toolbox talks. The in-house PE stamp should drive the AESS category, mockup, and weld-extent decisions before bid so the architect's expectation is priced, not absorbed. Doctrine flags: NONE. This is conventional structural steel content with no PEMB language and no supplier names introduced.

## SteelDay 2012: 50 Tips for Designing Constructable Steel Buildings
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3hkoFY05N6s | Duration: 1:31:19 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
Clifford Schwinger, PE of The Harman Group teaches constructability as the art of structural engineering: the goal is the lowest total cost of a steel frame, not the lowest tonnage. His four principles are that simplicity equals economy, that least weight does not always equal least cost, that fewer pieces means greater economy, and that it is all about the connections [07:46]. He estimates roughly half the cost of a steel frame building is tied in some way to connections, because once the mill steel reaches the shop nearly everything that follows (detailing, drilling, coping, shipping, field connecting) is connection work [10:57]. The single most important tip is to show the reactions, moments, and axial forces on the contract drawings so connections are not over-designed for two to four times the real demand [09:21]. His tips target R=3 gravity and routine lateral systems, not high-seismic systems [05:41].

### Spec References
Cited verbatim by the speaker: AISC 360-10 (3610) [20:45]; AISC 341-10 (34110) seismic provisions, with Section D2.2 stating bearing-bolt shear values are permitted even when R is greater than three if holes are standard or short-slotted with the load perpendicular to the slot, provided bolts are pretensioned and faying surfaces prepared as for slip-critical [25:26]; AISC 303-10 (30310) Code of Standard Practice for delegating connection design and for required drawing information [31:36]; Table 3-6 ("table 36") uniform load capacities in the Steel Construction Manual [14:36]; Specification equation J10-1 ("j101") for checking whether stiffeners can be eliminated at hanger/concentrated-load points [74:56]; ASCE 7-05 and ASCE 7-10 ("c705 and asce 710") R-factor tables, with ordinary steel concentrically braced frame R=3.25 and ordinary steel moment frame R=3.5 [67:13]; AISC 360-05 ("3605") cited only as the prior edition that had used "slip critical" language now deleted [23:55]. He also references the AISC Steel Construction Manual, the Manual design examples, the Engineering Journal, and the AISC Steel Solutions Center as resources [33:09].

### Technical Details
Bolt grades named are A325 and A490, with a worked example that a fabricator standardizing on 7/8 in A325 will jump to a larger diameter such as 1-1/8 in A490 rather than swap grade at the same diameter when forces exceed economical A325 capacity [45:32]. Slip-critical connections are genuinely required only with oversized holes, or with slotted holes loaded parallel to the slot; all other cases usually accept pretensioned bearing bolts [21:50]. All slip-critical bolts are pretensioned but not all pretensioned bolts are slip-critical, and the two terms must not be used interchangeably [24:56]. Tension members in braced frames and trusses should be held to about 75% of yield capacity, because net-section loss at bolt holes governs and A992 (Fu/Fy = 65/50 = 1.3) is less forgiving than A36 (58/36 = 1.61) [43:00][82:08]. Strong-axis column moment of inertia is about 2.5 times the weak axis for W-shapes, so orient moment-frame columns for strong-axis bending [69:15].

### Fabrication Notes
Short-slotted holes with snug-tightened bolts are permitted for most shear connections and are needed to accommodate fabrication tolerance, temperature change at erection, and end rotation from camber; requiring standard holes at both ends of a cambered beam can make it impossible to bolt into place [30:32]. One-sided connections (single angle and single-plate shear tabs) are safe and economical, are the practical solution for skewed beams, and should not be prohibited [27:26]. Camber rules: do not camber moment-frame, braced-frame, short, or light beams, do not over-camber, do not specify camber under 3/4 in, and do not require camber be verified after erection because some camber dissipates [76:58]. Plate-girder web-to-flange welds are usually small fillet welds sized for shear flow, not CJP, and only the engineer of record knows the shear flow, so the EOR must provide shear and moment diagrams rather than delegate the weld sizing [59:26]. Favor fillet over groove welds and avoid arbitrary all-around or CJP moment welds [62:04].

### Erection Notes
Frame girders to column flanges and beams to column webs, since girders carry heavier reactions and seat more easily against a flange without sharing bolts [70:17]. Configure framing so no more than one beam frames into any one side of a column and so skewed connections are minimized; orient columns square to braced frames, preferably to the flanges, and never skew a braced-frame column [37:54]. Verify that members can physically be installed: the speaker recounts a field call where a correctly designed but tight HSS-brace gusset could not be rotated into position [64:11]. Keep brace and truss diagonals between 35 and 55 degrees so the connection stays compact [63:39]. Fewer beams means fewer connections and fewer crane picks, so maximize slab span (for example 3 in deck versus 1-1/2 in deck) to drop member count [64:42].

### Bolting and Welding Requirements
Bolting per AISC 360-10: use bearing bolts in standard or short-slotted holes for the majority of shear connections; reserve slip-critical for oversized holes or slots parallel to the load [21:50]. Even under AISC 341-10 Section D2.2 with R greater than three, design for bearing-bolt shear values but pretension the bolts and prepare faying surfaces as for slip-critical [25:26]. Pretensioned (not necessarily slip-critical) bolts or welds are required for the listed connections including column splices in tall buildings, beam-to-column connections in tall buildings, supports for large cranes, and supports for machinery or impact/reversal live loads [51:00]. Welding: strive for downhand or vertical welds, size plate-girder fillet welds for shear flow, and avoid unnecessary CJP welds [62:04]. No AWS D1.1 clause, electrode, preheat, or NDE procedure was cited; this is a design-constructability webinar, not a welding-procedure session.

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The headline error is the drawing note "connections shall be designed to support the full shear strength of the member," which is wasteful and hard to achieve once a beam is coped and holes are punched, especially in grade 50 steel [13:31]. A second common note, designing connections for 150% of the Table 3-6 uniform load capacity, is usually overly conservative but can be dangerously under-strength near a concentrated load: his W24x76 example shows a 113-kip connection demanded where the real reaction near the load is 234 kips [14:36]. Other recurring bad notes: requiring all connections be slip-critical, prohibiting one-sided connections, mandating all 3/4 in bolts and all standard holes, and arbitrarily requiring loads "in any direction" when they do not occur in all directions [18:44][27:26][29:31]. Failing to coordinate with the mechanical engineer produces unanticipated beam web penetrations discovered only at fabrication [55:21].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Roughly half of a steel frame's cost is connection-related, so over-specified connection notes add real cost without adding safety [10:57]. Fabricators price on tonnage and complexity together, not tonnage alone; stiffeners at every moment connection and "gingerbread" little pieces drive up the dollars-per-ton, with a change-order anecdote of small pieces billed near $8,000 per ton against a $2,000 per ton base [51:11][72:20]. Delegating connection design to the fabricator under the Code of Standard Practice is the more cost-effective path because each shop applies its preferred bolt diameter and detail [44:31]. But the EOR must still show reactions and any required stiffeners and web doubler plates on the bid drawings, because a fabricator cannot price accurately without knowing where stiffeners are required [57:55].

### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff and bidding through aisc_validator.py, the half-the-cost-is-connections rule means a pure tonnage-times-rate number understates complex skewed or heavy-connection jobs; flag connection complexity and gingerbread as a cost driver, consistent with our verify-don't-generate posture on the SF-driven estimate. The required-drawing-information rule (reactions, stiffener and doubler locations per Code of Standard Practice) is a drawing-completeness gate item: if a set lacks reactions or stiffener callouts, raise an RFI before pricing rather than assume full-strength connections. For our in-house PE stamp, the 75%-of-yield ceiling on braced-frame and truss tension members and the bearing-versus-slip-critical distinction are direct design rules; specify pretensioned bearing bolts in standard or short-slotted holes by default and reserve slip-critical for true cases. For Mario's shop, prefer fillet welds sized for shear flow over CJP, prefer single-angle and shear-tab one-sided connections, and use short slots to absorb camber and tolerance. For anchor rods, adopt square base plates with standardized square anchor-rod patterns keyed to column family (one pattern per W12, one per W14) rather than per-column edge distances, which reduces field setting confusion on ACP and every job [73:23]. For Paul's safety scope, the field-installability check (the HSS gusset that would not rotate in) supports a pre-lift constructability review. Doctrine conflict: NONE. The webinar is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language, and nothing here overrides BID_RATES or AISC validator weights.
