## Fastener Fundamentals
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rt6D-p5BgO8 | Duration: 1:34:01 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
This is a fastener-engineering deep dive on structural bolting from a bolt-manufacturer's perspective: how high-strength bolts are made, what threads and coatings actually do to performance, how torque, tension, and angle relate, and what goes wrong on real jobsites. The unifying idea is the torque-tension-angle curve [35:00, 64:00]: torque and tension are linear only in the elastic range, and over 50 variables (surface roughness, temperature, install rate, helix angle, stiffness, humidity) move that relationship [61:00]. Because structural bolts are intentionally tensioned well into yield, a practice the speaker calls a "no-no in every other engineered fastener application," our industry designs many of a good fastener's best traits (long threads, matched sets, controlled K factor) out of the product to meet code, which is why field problems concentrate in large-diameter, high-strength, coated bolts [73:00, 90:55].

### Spec References
RCSC Specification, with the snug-tight definition quoted verbatim from both the 2000-2004 revision ("the tightness that is attained with a few impacts of an impact wrench or the full effort of an ironworker using an ordinary spud wrench to bring the plies into firm contact") and the 2009 revision ("the condition that exists when all of the plies in a connection have been pulled into firm contact ... and all of the bolts ... tightened sufficiently to prevent the removal of the nuts without the use of a wrench") [92:00]. RCSC's four approved pretensioning methods: turn-of-nut, calibrated wrench, DTI (direct tension indicator) washers, and twist-off (tension-control) bolts [70:00-72:00]. RCSC rule that a fastener altered from its tested condition (e.g. rust) must be re-qualified [82:17], the 1-in-20 ply slope limit before a bevel washer is required [90:33], and the RCSC determination that a shear plane in the thread transition zone may be treated as full body [84:30]. ASTM bolt specs by number from the slides: A325 / A325M and F1852 (Group A), A490 / A490M and F2280 (Group B), and A354 Grade BD, with A354 quoted directly that pretensioned use above 50% of tensile strength should carefully consider the head, tensile, nut, washer, test, and inspection requirements of A490 [75:00]. Coating specs cited on the Group-A/B matrix: B695 zinc mechanically deposited (Group A only), F2329 zinc hot dip (Group A except twist-off), F1136 zinc/aluminum (Group A or B except twist-off), F2833 zinc-rich base with aluminum organic/inorganic (Group A or B except twist-off), and F1941 electrodeposited (Group A hex only) [77:00]. AISC manual and AISC minimum design tension are referenced; Dacromet and Geomet named as the proprietary processes the F1136 spec was written around. The AWS D1.1 welding code is not discussed in this video.

### Technical Details
Group A bolts run 120 ksi tensile, Group B run 150 ksi [72:00]. Group A is medium-carbon, oil-quenched (moderate quench) with low quench-crack risk and better ductility; Group B is the higher-risk family, and the speaker has seen more quench cracks there, especially as A490 began getting coated [89:00]. Thread terms shown: root, flank, crest, pitch, major and minor diameter, 60-degree thread angle, with the internal/external thread geometry (H/8, 3H/8, 5H/8, H/4, P/2, P/4) [43:00, 46:00]. K-factor reference values: K=0.20 for as-received bolts and nuts with no supplemental lube (highly variable), K=0.10 to 0.17 with wax or other lubricant, and K=0.28 for HDG-coated bolts with no lubricant [61:00]. Turn-of-nut works because it pushes the bolt up onto the plastic plateau where tension varies little even as degrees change a lot; without lubrication a 180-degree install spec plus the allowed +60-degree tolerance can get close to the fracture point [69:00-70:00]. Snug tension is highly variable, ranging from roughly 10 to 300 degrees of rotation; even a spud wrench at ~60 degrees can develop 20,000 to 25,000 lb on a 7/8-in bolt [68:00].

### Fabrication Notes
Bolts are made by cold forming or hot forming; the hot-form progression is steel bars, hot-form nut blank, descale (sometimes), quench-and-temper heat treat, tapping, plating/coating if required, lubrication if required, inspection, packaging [24:00, 31:00]. Large-diameter and long parts are the hard cases: harder to heat-treat uniformly, prone to die fins and body swell that affect hole size, and hard to keep straight through many thick plies [37:00]. Most stress sits on the first few nut threads nearest the grip, and many quality problems trace to poor heat treatment or thread quality and fit [37:00]. For coatings the nut threads must be oversized for clearance, which raises the nut minor diameter, lowers proof-load capacity, and can shift the failure mode from bolt tensile to thread stripping; bolt-tensile and nut-proof-load tests are run on fixtures and do not correlate to assembled-fastener behavior [80:00]. The speaker's own QC caught a quench crack in a coated A490 on receipt inspection and scrapped the entire lot [78:00]. He stresses matched assemblies, controlled K factor, and not over-tensioning coated fasteners.

### Erection Notes
All four tensioning methods depend on first reaching a true snug-tight condition, which is the weak link because snug is so variable in the field [92:00]. Twist-off bolts give single-side install and shear the spline when the calibrated torque is reached; DTI washers measure preload by compression and come as gap-measuring or silicone "squirter" types, placed under the head or nut [71:00]. The strongest field recommendation is to move away from impacting (impact-wrench) tools toward non-impacting, non-reacting electric or pneumatic tools: they are quieter, preserve coating integrity, and prevent driving coating off corners and threads, which can wreck an otherwise good install [66:00, 67:00]. A practical failure shown was a bolt that slipped into bearing and bound in the steel so badly the crew could not turn it to develop tension, fixed by attention to hole size; another was installing from the head side, which twists off bolt heads from body friction in the hole [79:00, 80:00]. Match-marking, witnessing, and sign-off can still pass a bolt that has already partially stripped its first thread and a half on slick coated fasteners [81:00].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Named defects and rejections: quench cracks (described as potentially horrible, running through the thread root, and rising with coated A490) versus seams and bursts (usually cosmetic forging defects with ASTM permissible limits) that often cause unjustified project shutdowns [76:00-78:00, 123]. Also: improperly mated components and missing engagement reported as thread stripping (counterfeit or defective material that is really just too little engagement), head bursts, fatigue, torsional and tension failures, lack of installer training, and head twist-off from head-side install [74:00-80:00]. Mixing inch-series washers onto metric fasteners cracked the washers because the under-head radius forced them apart [79:44]. Over-tension is now common on slick coated fasteners and has produced limited stress-corrosion / delayed-fracture cases in coated A490 from micro stress cracks in the thread roots [81:00]. Improper storage (rust-through covers, water-filled buckets) and improper handling (bolts dumped on the ground, lots mixed) appear as field failures [85:00]. On rust, RCSC requires re-qualification of any altered fastener; the speaker won't put a number on acceptable rust [82:00].

### Bid / Cost Implications
The opening thesis is explicitly commercial: "the difference between panic and understanding is slight, but can mean thousands of dollars," and informed bolt decisions cut downstream problems and project compromise [15:00]. Quench cracks force scrapping and segregating whole lots, and burst/seam panic shuts down projects for cosmetic defects, both of which are avoidable schedule and cost hits with the right receipt-inspection knowledge [76:00, 78:00]. The Group-A versus Group-B trade is a sourcing decision: Group A buys availability, ductility, easier coatings, and "less risk" while Group B buys strength, and the 80/20 rule is that 80% of problems land in the 20% of bolts that are large-diameter, high-strength, and coated, so the speaker and the engineer should both get nervous about a 4140 2-in high-hardness coated bolt [72:00, 90:55]. Specifying A354BD to reach sizes above A490's 1.5-in cap means calling out heavy-hex dimensions and invoking A490 test requirements (mag particle, carb/decarb, max tensile) with the supplier, which is a procurement and QC scope item [75:00, 88:00].

### Your Company Application
Field bolting and Mario's crew: the move from impact wrenches to non-impacting, non-reacting tools and a real understanding of snug-tight and turn-of-nut directly informs our erection bolting procedure and the +60-degree tolerance risk on coated bolts; pair this with the RCSC four-method framework when Paul writes the field-bolting and installer-training portions of the safety and QC plan. Anchor rods and in-house PE stamp: the A325/A490/A354BD grade logic, the 1-in-20 bevel-washer rule, and the A354 "invoke A490 testing" guidance map onto anchor-rod and large-diameter connection callouts our PE produces and onto setting tolerance and hole-size coordination. Ivan's takeoff: bolt grade, coating spec, and matched-assembly requirements are real cost drivers, so bolt and coating selection (Group A default, Group B only when strength demands it) should be a flagged line in estimating rather than a silent assumption, consistent with verify-don't-generate. Receipt inspection at the shop should screen for quench cracks on coated Group-B lots and not panic-reject cosmetic bursts/seams, a concrete QC routine for Mario and our incoming-material check. This is general fastener and bolting practice, not joist or ACP-controls specific, and it carries no AWS D1.1 welding content. Doctrine conflict: NONE.

## Weld Inspection: What Matters and What Doesn't
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jhxRagJo644 | Duration: 1:34:48 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
This is a Duane K. Miller (Lincoln Electric, Manager of Engineering Services) lecture for AISC on separating weld discontinuities that actually impair structural performance from cosmetic features that do not, so that inspection effort and repair money go where they matter. The thesis runs through the W. Edwards Deming "Out of the Crisis" frame at [07:54] (the system belongs to management, not the welder) and the James Cameron "rightist" quote at [03:57]: weld it correctly for the loading and service condition, then stop. The talk works from AWS A3.0 discontinuity definitions through the five NDT methods, the AISC 360 and AISC 341 inspection-task tables, and into fitness-for-service and fatigue, arguing that acceptance criteria are workmanship limits set by what a qualified welder can produce, not a hard boundary of suitability for service.

### Spec References
Captured verbatim from slides: AISC 360-10 Specification Section N5.4 with Tables N5.4-1 (Inspection Tasks Prior to Welding) and N5.4-3 (Inspection Tasks After Welding) at [23:42] and [1:30:50]; AISC 360-10 Section 5b "CJP Groove Weld NDT" requiring UT by QA on all CJP groove welds in tension butt, T- and corner joints in material 5/16 in. (8 mm) or greater for Risk Category III or IV of ASCE/SEI 7 Table 1-1, and on 10% of those welds for Risk Category II, at [11:51]; AISC 341-10 Seismic Provisions Chapter J Section J5 "Inspection Tasks," subsection 2a "k-Area NDT" requiring MT (magnetic particle) crack testing of the web k-area after welding of doubler plates, continuity plates or stiffeners, at [1:22:56]; AWS A3.0 Standard Welding Terms and Definitions (incomplete fusion definition) at [15:48]; AWS D1.1:2010 Structural Welding Code Steel, Commentary C-6.8 "Engineer's Approval for Alternate Acceptance Criteria" and Clause 5 Fabrication, at [1:03:11]; the SAC Steel Project Report SAC/BD-00/06 (Shaw) round-robin UT study, AWS D1.1 acceptance criteria, at [55:17]. Table N5.4-3 footnote cites visual inspection of the web k-area within 3 in. (75 mm) of the weld.

### Technical Details
The five NDT methods (the "Big Five" at [1:26:53]) are visual (VT), dye penetrant (PT), magnetic particle (MT), radiographic (RT), and ultrasonic (UT). PT greatly enhances visual inspection, is low cost, works on non-magnetic material, and is very effective on surface-breaking cracks but cannot see subsurface flaws (slide at [31:36]). RT principles are shown via the film-density model at [35:33]: discontinuities read darker, thicker sections lighter, with edge-effect transitions. UT acceptance under AWS D1.1 uses an indication rating or "dB" value, and the SAC round-robin found broad scatter in that rating and that on average 16% of rejectable indications were false calls at locations with no implanted discontinuity [55:17]. Fatigue and fracture mechanics close the talk: a single-edge crack has a stress-intensity K-I about 1.58 times that of a through-thickness crack of equal length [1:11:05], and a worked fatigue example predicts 281,765 cycles for a crack to grow from 0.25 in. to 2.25 in. [1:07:08].

### Fabrication Notes
Table N5.4-1 (prior to welding) is the shop's first gate at [23:42]: WPSs must be available (P for both QC and QA), and fit-up of groove welds must be checked for joint preparation, dimensions (alignment, root opening, root face, bevel), cleanliness of the steel surfaces, tack weld quality and location, and backing type and fit. Table N5.4-3 (after welding) at [1:30:50] makes QC and QA both Perform welds cleaned, size/length/location, visual acceptance (crack prohibition, weld/base-metal fusion, crater cross section, weld profiles, weld size, undercut, porosity), arc strikes, k-area, backing and weld tab removal where required, and documentation of acceptance or rejection. The fitness-for-service argument at [1:03:11] is the core fab message: Clause 5 criteria reflect what a qualified welder can produce, not a structural failure boundary, so not every flagged discontinuity needs a repair. Jumbo sections warrant extra inspection for low toughness, thermal cutting, richer composition steel, high restraint, high residual stress, and reduced redundancy [1:18:59].

### Erection Notes
The repair-cost curve at [1:07:08] is the erection lesson: complication of repairs rises sharply from fab to erection to completion, so a discontinuity caught and dispositioned in the shop is far cheaper than one chased in the field after the member is set and loaded. The k-area MT requirement under AISC 341 J5 applies where continuity plates, doubler plates, and stiffeners are welded into the column k-area, which is field-relevant on seismic moment-frame connections [1:22:56]. The talk does not cover crane, rigging, bracing, or sequencing in detail; its erection content is about where repairs happen and why earlier is cheaper.

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Named discontinuities and failures: incomplete fusion (IF), defined per AWS A3.0 as fusion that did not occur between weld metal and the fusion faces or adjoining beads, illustrated at [15:48] and again as a fillet-weld root condition at [43:27]; misalignment (high-low) at [19:45], shown as a profile defect with associated radiographic indication; and the full visual reject list from Table N5.4-3 (cracks, lack of fusion, bad crater cross section, out-of-tolerance profiles and size, undercut, porosity). The most important inspection failure named is the false call: the SAC UT round-robin found 16% of rejectable indications were at locations with no real discontinuity [55:17], which means UT scatter itself drives unnecessary repairs. The Tub Girder case at [1:15:02] makes the point that an unrepaired weld can be left in service when the loading is cyclic shear at low stress range with adequate throat and defined toughness.

### Bid / Cost Implications
NDT scope scales with Risk Category and is a direct cost line: 100% UT on tension CJP welds for Risk Category III or IV versus 10% for Risk Category II is a measurable difference in QA hours and schedule per the Section 5b slide at [11:51], so the bid must price NDT to the building's risk category, not a flat assumption. The repair-complication curve at [1:07:08] argues for shop QC investment over field rework, since the cost of a given repair multiplies through erection and completion. False-call rejections (16% in the SAC study) are pure waste, so an estimate that buys disciplined VT and right-sized NDT avoids paying for repairs that fix nothing. Jumbo sections and seismic k-area MT add inspection scope that must be carried where those conditions exist.

### Your Company Application
For Mario (AWS D1.1 welding lead), this maps directly to the shop fit-up gate: enforce the Table N5.4-1 pre-weld checks (WPS available, root opening, root face, bevel, cleanliness, tack quality, backing fit) and the Table N5.4-3 post-weld visual acceptance list as the in-house QC checklist, and use the Commentary C-6.8 principle to disposition cosmetic discontinuities rather than over-repair. For Paul (safety/QA coordination) and the in-house PE stamp, the NDT-by-risk-category rule means the bid and the QA plan must read the building's ASCE/SEI 7 Risk Category and set CJP UT percentage accordingly, and seismic moment-frame jobs trigger k-area MT under AISC 341 J5 that the PE should call out on the connection details. For Ivan (takeoff/estimating), NDT scope is a risk-category-driven cost line, not a flat add, and false-call repair waste is a real number to factor when comparing UT-heavy specs. Tekla detailing should carry backing, weld-tab, and k-area inspection notes so the requirements survive into the shop. On ACP controls, the repair-complication curve supports a shop-QC-first posture with documented acceptance or rejection per weld. Doctrine conflict: NONE.

## Practical Steel Metallurgy
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=InwUp3TmZzs | Duration: 1:31:53 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
This AISC webinar, presented by Doug Reese Evans of Steel Dynamics, teaches the working metallurgy a structural steel user needs without going deep into theory. It is organized around four practical questions: what is the difference between iron and steel, why are there multiple grades of steel, how can a mill control chemistry, and if I retest a product will I match the mill test report. The controlling idea is that steel properties come from chemistry plus microstructure together, not chemistry alone [56:25], and that grain size from rolling reduction can drive strength more than alloy content does [62:35]. The takeaway for a fabricator is that grade names are context labels on the same underlying material, mill test report values are nominal not exact, and retesting on the wrong coupon gives misleadingly different numbers.

### Spec References
This is a material-and-grade talk, not a connection-design talk, so the citations are ASTM and AASHTO material specs rather than AISC 360 chapters, AISC 341 seismic sections, AWS D1.1 clauses, or RCSC. Cited verbatim by the speaker: ASTM A572 grades 42, 50, 60, 65 [29:12]; ASTM A588 grades A, B, C, K [29:12]; ASTM A36 [29:12, 36:30]; ASTM A992, published 1998 [29:12, 34:52]; ASTM A709 with T1/T2/T3 and F1/F2/F3 suffixes [33:22, 33:52]; AASHTO M270 (metric, 345 MPa equals 50 ksi) [31:49, 32:19]; ASTM A6 for permitted chemical variation across a heat and the tensile-variability annex [75:57, 76:29]; ASTM A370 for coupon location and the full-thickness plate-strap specimen versus the 0.505 round [78:35, 79:05]; ASTM A913 quench-self-temper [79:37]. Charpy energy minimums were stated: 15 ft-lb non-fracture-critical and 25 ft-lb fracture-critical, with service-temperature zones such as 0 F (T1) and minus 30 to minus 60 F (F3) [33:22, 34:22]. No AISC 360 or AWS section was cited; treat any connection-spec need as general principles, no section cited.

### Technical Details
Steel is iron alloyed with up to 2 weight percent carbon; above 2 percent it is cast iron, which forms graphite flakes that act as stress risers and is unsuitable structurally [06:37, 22:34]. Cast steel is not cast iron and can be engineered to normal carbon-steel chemistries [24:35]. Iron is allotropic, transforming from face-centered-cubic austenite to body-centered-cubic ferrite on cooling; austenite holds 2 percent carbon, ferrite only 0.02 percent, and the rejected carbon forms cementite, giving the ferrite-pearlite microstructure [14:23, 15:24, 17:27]. Slow cooling gives pearlite, fast cooling gives bainite or brittle martensite [19:29]. Finer grain size raises strength because dislocations pile up at grain boundaries, and grain size is set mainly by rolling reduction: a light shape gets more reduction and finer grain than a heavy one [60:32, 62:35]. The practical illustration: a W14x398 carries more chemistry yet lower yield than a W16x36 because the heavy flange sees less reduction and coarser grain [63:06].

### Fabrication Notes
The fabrication-relevant content is metallurgical rather than shop-process. Carbon equivalent is the key number for weldability: it folds alloying elements into an equivalent carbon figure to predict heat-affected-zone behavior, and higher carbon content trades weldability and ductility for strength [85:47, 86:18]. Killed steel matters for clean welds and sound sections; aluminum or silicon additions tie up dissolved oxygen so no carbon-monoxide voids form, and continuous-cast structural product is fully killed [71:49, 73:22]. Laminar tearing is driven by inclusion level and type, shows up mainly at weld joints, and is reduced by cleaner steel practice; rolled steel is anisotropic for laminar tearing even though it is isotropic at yield [82:40, 83:43]. No fit-up tolerances, shop QC steps, or AWS weld procedures were given in this talk.

### Erection Notes
No erection content. The webinar covers material production and grade identification only, with no field procedures, sequencing, bracing, rigging, or site coordination discussed.

### Bolting / Welding
No bolting content (no A325/A490 grades, no pretension or turn-of-nut, no RCSC method cited). On welding the talk stays at the metallurgy level: weldability is governed by carbon equivalent and microstructure, cementite-rich high-carbon zones are brittle and unweldable while low-carbon ferrite is weldable [17:27], and laminar tearing concentrates at weld joints and improves with lower-inclusion steel [82:40]. No electrodes, preheat values, joint types, or NDE methods were specified, and no AWS D1.1 clause was cited.

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The most actionable failure mode for a fabricator is retest mismatch. A third-party lab that lacks capacity for the full-thickness ASTM A370 plate coupon often substitutes a 0.505 round, which samples a local lamination rather than the through-thickness average and can report exaggerated, location-dependent yield, especially in thick shapes or A913 quench-self-temper material [78:35, 79:05, 79:37, 80:07]. The core area of a heavy W shape (ASTM 1.5 in, AISC 2 in or greater) has the coarsest grain and the worst sulfur and phosphorus segregation, so it reads lowest in strength and elongation [77:33, 78:03]. Historic errors named: brittle cast-iron railroad bridges that fractured under load [24:35], and the standing specification warning against acid Bessemer steel because that process could not remove sulfur or phosphorus [48:48].

### Bid / Cost Implications
The multi-certification point is the estimating lever: a single mill-rolled shape can simultaneously satisfy A36, A572-50, A709-50, and A992, so the same physical steel carries four grade names and the grade is a context choice, not a different product [37:01, 39:33]. A992 cannot always be supplied in light single angles because the section is too light to hit the alloy and carbon levels the grade requires [40:04]. Specifying a fracture-critical or low-temperature Charpy suffix (A709 F-grades, 25 ft-lb) adds testing and cost over the plain base grade [33:52]. The historical cost contrast (Bessemer steel far cheaper than puddled iron) underlines that grade and process selection have always been cost decisions [47:47].

### Your Company Application
For Ivan in takeoff, this confirms that A992 wide flange, A572-50, A36, and A709-50 can be the same shape under different grade names, so substitution review should treat them as context labels and check the specified grade against availability (the A992-light-angle limit is a real procurement gotcha to flag). For Mario as AWS D1.1 welding lead, the carbon-equivalent and killed-steel points reinforce why mill test reports and CE values belong in weld-procedure planning, and why laminar tearing is a joint-design and material-cleanliness issue, not a welder-skill issue. For the in-house PE stamp, the ASTM A6 annex and A370 coupon discussion give defensible language when a client retest disputes a mill test report: nominal values match, exact values do not, and a 0.505 round on a thick shape is the wrong coupon. For Tekla detailing and thick-flange members, note the core-area variability when through-thickness properties matter. No conflict with Your Company doctrine: the conventional-structural-steel positioning holds, no PEMB language appears, and all grade and spec numbers here are quoted from the speaker, not generated. DOCTRINE FLAGS: NONE.

## Analysis and Design of Chevron Brace Connections with Flat Bar Gussets: Part 2
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fiypKXKVLU8 | Duration: 1:34:46 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
Patrick J. Fortney (Cives Engineering, vice chair of the AISC seismic design manual committee) extends Part 1 to seismic chevron brace connections, the V and inverted-V configurations in a Special Concentrically Braced Frame (SCBF) [04:10][05:12]. The governing idea is capacity design: the connection and the frame are not designed for elastic analysis forces but for the expected strength the brace can deliver, so the brace itself becomes the energy-dissipating fuse that buckles and yields in a code-level event [07:13][89:54]. The work flows through expected tension yield (RyFyAg), expected buckling strength, expected post-buckling strength (30 percent of buckling), a hinge/fold line that accommodates out-of-plane brace buckling, protected zones, and a mechanistic two-load-case analysis of the beam [12:19][16:56][20:06].

### Spec References
The presenter cites AISC 341-10 (Seismic Provisions) repeatedly: Section 8.3.2 on using expected material strength for limit states within the member that set the required strength [08:43]; Table A3.1 for Ry and Rt factors [10:16]; Section F2.6c for brace connection tension and compression requirements [12:19]; Section F2.5b for sizing the welds attaching the reinforcing plate [41:58]; Section F2.4a for beams assuming braces carry no gravity load [17:59]; Section F2.4b for beams intersected by braces away from the column [22:08]. From AISC 360 he cites Table D3.1 Case X for shear-lag X-bar [78:23], Section G2 (and G2-1 the h/tw limit) for beam shear [76:43][77:13], Section J4.2 for connecting-element shear [76:43], Section J10 for web panel-zone (stated as not applicable here) [76:10], Chapter H (H1) for beam axial-flexure interaction [81:23]. He also cites ASCE 7 Chapter 12.4 seismic load combinations with overstrength (Omega-naught) [19:04], Design Guide 29 Appendix B for the 2M/L couple figure [51:27], and the AISC Seismic Design Manual elliptical yield-line example 5.3.11 (corner gusset, Reaveley/Roeder University of Washington work) [86:36][87:10].

### Technical Details
For the worked example the braces are HSS4x4x3/8 and HSS5x5x3/8 in A500 Gr. B (Ry 1.4, Rt 1.3), gussets and plate A572 Gr. 50 (Ry 1.1, Rt 1.2) [10:47][27:21]. Expected tension is RyFyAg = 398 kips; expected buckling uses Ry inside Fe, giving 1.1 times buckling = 176 kips for connection design, and post-buckling = 0.3 times 176 = 52.8 kips [28:24][32:09][33:11]. Buckling length is end-of-brace to end-of-brace, not work point (here 197 in after subtracting an assumed 36 in pull-off), with KL/r = 105 against the 4.71 limit of 118 [13:22][29:59]. The hinge/fold line is drawn perpendicular to the brace line of action, offset 2t (two times gusset thickness), crossing the free edges; he treats 2t as a minimum clearance and provides extra for fabrication and erection tolerance [14:22][56:12]. Connection limit-state checks shown: weld brace-to-gusset (401 vs 398), shear rupture of brace walls using design wall thickness 0.349 in with Rt (853 kips), gusset buckling via Whitmore width with K=0.65 and Fcr from Table 4-22 without Ry, gusset tension yield (402), net-section rupture with computed X-bar 1.64 and U=0.909, and the gusset-to-beam weld using 2M/L converted to an equivalent normal force [34:46][72:00][51:27].

### Fabrication Notes
The brace is slotted over the gusset; the slot width is gusset thickness plus 1/8 in (e.g. 3/4 in gusset gives a 7/8 in slot) so an over-rolled or undercut slot still slides on, centering the brace with about a 1/16 in gap each side [42:31][87:00]. The reinforcing plate must restore the slotted net section: its effective net area must be at least the brace gross area and its Fy at least the brace Fy (Gr. 50 plate over Fy 46 brace satisfies this) [15:23][41:27]. Plate-to-brace welds are sized on the plate expected strength (Ry 1.1, here 55.6 vs 46.4 kips) and run on each side of the reduced section with enough length overlap [15:53][41:58]. The X dimension (slot beyond the gusset edge) drives the reinforcing-plate length on shop drawings, and the detailer must verify the HSS workable flat so the plate sits flush and there is room to weld both sides [16:24][42:31].

### Erection Notes
The X slot dimension must be large enough that the erector can drop the brace into place [16:24]. The 2t hinge clearance carries a deliberate tolerance margin so field fit-up does not pinch below 2t and obstruct the intended brace buckling [56:12][57:50]. Protected zones (gusset, center quarter of the brace, and a zone of length B equal to the out-of-plane brace depth adjacent to each connection) must be shown not only on structural drawings but explicitly on shop drawings and erection drawings, with no welded attachments, studs, or direction aids placed in them [16:56][59:23][60:26].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Fortney names several traps. Pulling Fcr from Table 4-22 for the brace buckling check is wrong because the table values omit the Ry factor needed for expected strength [32:09]. Double-counting the phi factor by reapplying it to Table 4-22 values that already embed it [36:49]. Forgetting that connection-design compression carries a 1.1 amplifier while the frame mechanistic analysis does not, so the beam analysis divides the connection compression by 1.1 [20:37][61:28]. Using Section J4.2 instead of G2 for the connection-region (panel) shear can miss the G2-1 h/tw slenderness limit and overstate strength [77:13]. He also flags omitting beam axial-flexure interaction when the brace horizontal components are carried through the beam to the column rather than dumped into the diaphragm (Chapter H1 needed) [78:50][81:23]. Welded attachments inside a protected zone create heat-affected zones and stress hotspots that degrade ductility [73:26].

### Bid / Cost Implications
The mechanistic analysis can force a large beam upsize: the example W24x84 was inadequate in bending (needed 1700 kip-ft, only 840 available) and jumped to a W24x176 (Zx 511 vs 462 required), which Ivan must capture as real tonnage when a chevron SCBF appears in a takeoff [66:11][68:48]. Fortney notes a deeper replacement beam shifts connection geometry and pull-off, so a re-iteration may be needed, adding engineering time [69:51]. On gusset economy he states from running dozens of cases and a paper with Bill Thornton that elliptical yield lines are not more cost-effective than a compact linear fold line with a 10-degree Whitmore spread or a hinge-plate gusset; a flat-bar gusset can work seismically but usually needs shaping to get economical plate thickness and weld length [50:22][24:13][88:15]. He also notes that combining the two gussets into one can be more or less demanding on the beam case by case, with no general rule [82:27][85:03].

### Your Company Application
For Ivan, any chevron or inverted-V braced bay flagged as seismic SCBF is a tonnage risk: price the beam at the mechanistic-analysis size (the W24x176 in this example), not the gravity size, and pull every member weight through aisc_validator.py rather than trusting elastic output. Tekla detailing must build the 2t hinge clearance with a tolerance pad, slot the HSS at gusset-thickness-plus-1/8, set the reinforcing-plate length from the X dimension, and place protected-zone callouts on both shop and erection drawings. Mario's shop and field welders need WPS coverage for the reinforcing-plate welds sized on plate expected strength and an explicit no-weld rule inside protected zones (gusset, brace center quarter, B-deep adjacent zone). Paul should note that after a code-level event these braces are intended to be replaced. The in-house PE must resolve the beam axial-flexure question by RFI to the EOR (load to diaphragm versus through the beam-column connection) before stamping, since it changes the beam check. This is conventional structural steel seismic content, no PEMB language, and there is NO conflict with Your Company doctrine.

## Analysis and Design of Chevron Brace Connections with Flat Bar Gussets: Part 1
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7NqcCokyZWQ | Duration: 1:32:45 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
Patrick J. Fortney (CSD Engineering / SCI Steel) teaches the analysis and design of Chevron (mid-span) brace connections using single gussets, with Part 1 limited to low-seismic and wind applications where AISC 341 strength and detailing do not govern [04:05][56:58]. The controlling idea is that a flat bar gusset places the centroid of the gusset-to-beam interface directly under the point where the brace line of action crosses the flange, so the interface carries only normal and shear forces with no moment, while a shaped single gusset shifts that centroid off the work line and introduces a moment that must be handled [11:18][14:26][34:04]. The method walks a full set of limit-state checks on the brace, the gusset, the welds, and the beam, then builds beam shear and moment diagrams from the interface forces treated as externally applied loads [37:45][55:27].

### Spec References
Cited verbatim by the speaker: AISC 341 (V and inverted-V seismic provisions, two-story X continuity) [56:58][88:44]; net-section tensile rupture Chapter D, Eq. D2-2 with shear-lag U and Table D3.1 / Table B3.1 for xbar [40:25][86:21]; shear rupture Eq. J4-4 (0.6 Fu net shear area) [44:01]; gross tensile yield D2-1 [44:31]; gusset compression buckling Section E3, Eq. E3-1 through E3-4 with the 4.71 root(E/Fy) limit, plus Manual Table 4-22 for available critical stress [45:01][46:08]; gusset interface gross shear J4-3 and shear rupture J4-4 [48:09]; web local yielding Section J10, Eq. J10-2 (with J10-3 near member ends) [50:51]; web local crippling Eq. J10-4 and J10-5a/b [51:52]; web compression buckling in J10 [54:25]; beam flexure Chapter F, Eq. F2-1; beam shear Chapter G, Eq. G2-1 with the 2.24 root(E/Fy) web slenderness limit [55:27]; weld strength Manual Part 8 (1.392 D L LRFD, 0.928 D L ASD, directional 1.0 + 0.5 sin^1.5 theta) [43:30][49:14]; Manual Tables 3-6, 4-22; and AISC Design Guide 29 (vertical bracing), Appendix B Fig. B-1 for the 4M/x equivalent normal force and Appendix C for the Dowswell whitmore reference [36:39][47:39].

### Technical Details
The flat bar moment-free condition gives V1 L1 = H1 eB so the interface sees only the brace horizontal and vertical components, where eB is half the beam depth [33:32]. For shaped gussets the off-centroid distance Delta produces Ma = H1 eB - V1 L1 - Delta1 and Mb = V2 L2 - Delta2 - H2 eB, converted to an equivalent normal force N = 4M/x for weld sizing [34:34][36:09]. Sign convention: tension brace components positive, compression negative [23:45][24:15]. Buckling uses K = 0.70 for a gusset that is not at a member end, r = tg/root(12), and K = 1.0 with the Dowswell 2006 (EJ) approach for whitmore checks [31:57][47:39]. The worked example used HSS A500B braces, A992 Gr.50 wide-flange beam, and Gr.50 (A572-250) plate, with brace 1 at 118 kips tension on a 9.78:12 bevel (Theta 39.5 deg, components 91.1 and 75.1 kips) and brace 2 at 163 kips compression (components -126 and -104) [56:58][59:32][60:03].

### Fabrication Notes
Material guidance: flat bars are commonly A572 Gr.50, also A36 and A529 Gr.50, generally up to 12 in wide and 2 in thick, with width increments of 1/4 in under 3 in, 1/2 in from 3 to 6 in, 1 in from 6 to 12 in, and thickness increments of 1/8 in up to 1 in and 1/4 in above [12:21][13:23]. The key fabrication distinction is that a flat bar has sheared longitudinal edges while plate (shaped) material can be flame cut on all four sides [14:58]. The brace is slotted over the gusset; the slot is sized at gusset thickness plus 1/8 in, and the speaker uses nominal (not 0.93 design) HSS wall thickness when computing net area to allow for hand flame-cutting, grinding of notches, and undercut [40:55][65:50][78:29]. Choose bar width as brace width plus 1 in so a single-pass weld can fill, and target single-pass fillet welds rather than multi-pass to ease shop and field work [27:50][30:54].

### Erection Notes
The slot tolerance is an erection concern: too tight and the erector cannot slide the brace over the gusset, too loose and more weld is needed to bridge the gap [40:55]. In the field the slot can end up bearing on one face of the gusset with the full gap on the other side, or the erector may take time to center it; this is unpredictable, so the detail gives the welder the design weld and relies on the qualified welder to upsize for actual gaps [77:29]. The two-in clear distance from the brace leading corner to the flange is set partly for workmanship, inspection access, and erection fit-up [28:50]. No crane, rigging, or sequencing detail beyond fit-up is covered.

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The speaker flags upsizing the brace-to-gusset weld for the slot gap as a frequent miss; the design weld must be increased in the field to account for the gap, which is the welder's responsibility once given the design value [76:58][77:29]. He notes that omitting the panel-zone shear check on a tension-compression brace pair is an error and agreed it should be checked for single-gusset Chevron connections [80:32]. Two-story X frames are not directly addressed by the AISC 341 V and inverted-V provisions and must be treated carefully; in SCBF the beam must be continuous and the braces discontinuous through the joint [88:44][89:16]. Fouling of adjacent flat bars (x1r + x2r must be >= 0) is a geometry failure to guard against when coding the layout [20:38][29:21].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Economy drives the flat bar versus shaped gusset choice: flat bars use less plate and shorter weld and avoid the interface moment, so they are cheaper at small brace forces, but at high force the short interface forces a larger or multi-pass weld that can erase the saving [09:46][14:26]. The speaker repeatedly favors lengthening the connection to keep a single-pass weld over keeping it short and asking for multi-pass, an explicit labor-cost trade [30:54]. Shaped gussets cost more detailing time up front but cut back-end analysis effort and reduce beam eccentricity, which he judges worth it [18:37][19:07]. Net-area conservatism (nominal wall, slot +1/8) is a deliberate safety margin, not a code requirement, and a reviewer should not mark up the compliant design-thickness alternative [78:59].

### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff this maps to brace-frame jobs where chevron/mid-span connections appear; gusset plate, slot prep, and field weld length all carry quantity and labor weight, and the flat-bar-versus-shaped decision is a real cost lever to surface on a bid. For Mario as AWS D1.1 welding lead, the single-pass-fillet preference, the slot-gap weld upsizing, and the four-weld HSS-to-gusset detail are direct shop and field welding rules; qualified welders are expected to grow the weld for actual field gaps. Tekla detailing should encode the bar-width = brace + 1 in rule, the 2 in clear-to-flange dimension, the fouling check, and the slot = tg + 1/8 in. In-house PE stamp work should run the full D, E3, J4, J10, F, and G limit-state set and confirm panel-zone shear and beam adequacy, since the EOR remains responsible for the beam carrying chevron-induced shear and moment. AISC member weights must still come from bridge/aisc_validator.py, never from spoken example values. Doctrine flag: NONE. This is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language, and the content aligns with the verify-do-not-generate posture.

## Erection Engineering: The Science Behind the Art
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8lhyuhPtkZY | Duration: 1:25:51 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This webinar by Will Jacobs and Clint Rex of Stanley D. Lindsey and Associates covers erection engineering, the supplemental engineering that keeps a steel structure stable in each intermediate stage of construction before it reaches its completed, contract-document form [02:36][03:39]. The premise is the standard structural-drawing note: the structure is stable only in its completed form, and temporary supports for all intermediate stages are the contractor's responsibility, which legally falls to the steel erector [03:08][04:09]. The talk argues that as building geometries get more complex and slender, with more long-span trusses and transfer elements, erector experience needs engineering help to confirm how many braces are needed and whether a member can be picked safely [04:41][57:38].
### Spec References
Cited verbatim: IBC 2012 directs steel design, fabrication, and erection to AISC 360 [07:14]. AISC 360 (14th Edition) Specification Section M4.2 on temporary support and the Code of Standard Practice Section 7.10.3 are the two erection-engineering sections, with the COSP placing duty on the erector [07:45][08:45]. Specification Chapter F flexural design, the scope language on members restrained against twisting at load points and supports [23:36]. Specification Appendix 6 nodal torsional bracing of beams and nodal bracing of columns for brace strength and stiffness [28:16][45:50]. Appendix 8 second-order amplifiers B1 (member stability) and B2, with the EI-star reduced-stiffness term [42:44][43:14]. Specification Section D5 on pin connections (noted as tight-fitting permanent pins, distinct from erection lifting lugs) [10:45]. OSHA: four anchor rods required per erected column, plus column-splice minimum loads and field-only stud application [09:15]. Other standards named: ASCE 37 construction loads, ASME BTH-1 below-the-hook lifting devices, AISC Design Guide 10 erection bracing of low-rise buildings, the Wire Rope Users Manual, SJI Technical Digest No. 9 on handling and erecting steel joists, and an L/1000 sweep tied to ASTM rolling tolerance [11:48][15:23][09:45][64:16][41:12].
### Technical Details
Construction wind is the controlling load surprise: ASCE 37 gives a 25 percent velocity reduction for a construction period under six weeks (0.75 factor), but since pressure scales with velocity squared the force factor is about 0.50, then lattice drag factors up to 2.0 push temporary pressures back above the permanent case [16:53][17:55][18:26]. Running the AISC 14th Edition example building as a structure under construction took base shear from about 170 kips to about 600 kips, roughly three times the permanent wind [19:29]. ASCE 37 sets a 25 psf pre-composite construction live load for concrete placement by hose and its own load combinations with reduced factors such as 0.5 on construction live load [16:23][58:38]. Truss stability uses a smeared wL-squared/8 over depth to get chord force, then treats the compression chord as a standalone column swept L/1000, checked with B1 amplification; KL/r values of 272 and even 590 appear in real trusses and are tolerable because final bracing follows [33:56][41:42][55:34]. Whether truss web members are modeled pinned or fixed to the chords dramatically shifts buckling load (about 1.25 self-weight pinned versus 5.5 fixed), so the engineer scans web end moments (about 2.2 kip-ft at LF 1.4) to justify the assumption [50:22][52:28].
### Fabrication Notes
The speakers stress that temporary steel is hard to fabricate ahead of time so it lays out exactly as planned, which makes field-applied web stiffeners on cribbing beams cumbersome [24:36][25:07]. Instead of shop stiffeners they use the British-standard fake-length method, adding two times beam depth to the unbraced length to capture end distortion in lateral-torsional buckling [25:39][26:41]. The fabricator supplies the real truss weight including connections; comparing it to the bare analytical weight gives a connection factor, typically 1.1 to 1.25, below 1.0 for a fully welded tube truss and up to about 1.5 for a heavy bolted truss [33:56][40:09][41:12]. Field weld holes and bolt holes do not always land where needed, which is why industrial clamps with defined capacities are preferred for restraining temporary beams against roll-over [27:12][28:16].
### Erection Notes
Erectors care most about whether a freestanding truss can be released from the crane and for how long before bracing, which drives the wind question [31:24][32:24]. Long trusses arrive in two or three pieces with field splices that were sized for the final building, not the erection condition, so temporary loads on those splices must be checked; field CJP welds often get a temporary bolted connection so the crew can move on while welders finish [32:24][32:54]. On-hook stability for very slender 226-foot barrel trusses required an eigenvalue buckling analysis to seed a direct-analysis initial shape, weak springs at nodes to prevent numerical instability, and iterating support points until reaching about a 1.4 safety factor, ending in two cranes and four pick points [61:11][66:48][71:26]. The cautionary field story: a truss shipped on its side was picked at midspan, lifted 6 then 12 feet while the ends stayed grounded, and finished with a 7-foot kink matching the predicted buckled shape; the fix was heat straightening and a revised pre-compressed-arch rotation method [72:56][74:58][75:28].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
A box pedestrian truss (Pratt/Vierendeel-style, 14x38 chord turned strong-axis-vertical so weak axis resisted buckling, KL/ry 590) buckled with a kink at midspan as an experienced erector released it from temporary bolted supports; slings still attached caught it, no injuries, and it had to be heat straightened with bolts replaced [54:02][56:37]. The named failure modes are chord buckling from underestimated slenderness, ignored strong-axis and weak-axis moments in Vierendeel chords, and the unanalyzed on-its-side lift kink [55:34][56:05][74:28]. The recurring lesson is that stability problems are not visible to the naked eye on slender structures even to seasoned erectors [57:07].
### Bid / Cost Implications
The speakers note erection engineering pays better and carries liability that ends at job close, unlike some architect work [58:08]. Cost-relevant rules of thumb: assume a truss weighs about 25 percent more than analytical bare weight, and if a member looks too slender to pick it probably is [84:19][84:49]. Reducing assumed wind velocity (for example using 30 mph, where the 25 plf top-chord wind drops to about 4 plf, since crews do not erect above 30 mph) can avoid costly temporary bracing if the erector and owner agree on an alternate scheme on standby [47:52][48:22][19:59]. Deliverable scope drives engineering cost, from a hand sketch to a one-sheeter to a full staged 3D BIM package (one job ran about 70 sheets) [76:31][78:35].
### Your Company Application
This maps directly to Your Company's in-house PE stamp owning erection engineering rather than washing hands with the means-and-methods note: temporary stability, pick analysis, and temporary splice loads are stamped engineering work Mario's crew should not improvise on slender trusses or long-span members. Ivan's takeoff should carry the 1.1 to 1.25 connection factor (up to 1.5 heavy-bolted) when converting analytical truss weight to real picked weight, and flag any long-span or transfer element as needing an erection-engineering review line in the bid. Tekla detailing supports the staged 3D erection-sequence deliverable and the field splice plan; the temporary-bolted-then-field-weld splice pattern fits Mario's AWS D1.1 work and Paul's safety planning around release-from-crane and crane/rigging pick points. Anchor-rod note: OSHA's four-bolt-per-column rule [09:15] aligns with our anchor-rod design and setting scope, and SJI Digest 9 [64:16] applies wherever we set long-span joists. NONE of this conflicts with Your Company doctrine; it is conventional structural steel, no PEMB language, and reinforces verify-do-not-generate since every chord force, B1 amplifier, and connection factor here is a checked calculation, not an assumed number.

## Column Base Connection
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=anmtg3SiGZA | Duration: 1:28:13 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
Dr Amit Kanvinde (UC Davis) presents a multi-year AISC-funded experimental and finite-element study on exposed steel column base connections, testing whether AISC Steel Design Guide 1 (base plate and anchor rod design) is accurate against real test data [00:38, 03:05]. The work runs in two phases: phase one is shear transfer at the base (braced-frame condition, high axial and shear, low moment) [05:47], phase two is axial-plus-flexure (moment-frame base, axial and moment, low shear) [21:34]. The headline finding is that these connections are far more ductile than design assumes, reaching 8 to 10 percent column drift with no brittle failure, and that Design Guide 1 is accurate for friction and anchor-rod bearing but unconservative for shear lugs and overly conservative for compression-side plate yielding [20:57, 56:00].
### Spec References
The speaker cites these by name: AISC Steel Design Guide 1, the base plate and anchor rod design guide, throughout [03:05]; AISC 2010 Seismic Provisions, which already carried some of these findings and were downloadable from the AISC website at the time [09:42], with a questioner naming seismic provisions section 8.3.3 on connection ductility [25:56]; the AISC steel specification, which absorbed the shear-transfer findings [09:51]; ACI 349 (the nuclear standard) as the source of the concrete size-effect penalty method [18:39]; and ACI 318 Appendix D for anchorage to concrete, which the speaker says penalizes headed anchors versus rebar [11:51]. A slide shows the Design Guide 1 shear-key cone equation Vn45 = (4 sqrt f'c) A45 [16:34 frame], and the proposed size-effect equation min of phi-CCD (1/sqrt c)(40/9 sqrt f'c) A35 and phi45 (4 sqrt f'c) A45 [19:20 frame]. Anchor rods are ASTM F1554, called "1554" verbally [25:25], Grade 36 and high-strength 105 ksi. The shear-bracket reference equation on slide 84 cites Mattock and Gaafar 1981, Marcakis and Mitchell 1980, and Harries et al 1997.
### Technical Details
The exposed connection tested is a W8x48 column (about two-thirds scale of a W14) on a base plate over grout over a concrete footing, with anchor rods embedded in the foundation and leveling nuts under the plate for plumbing before grouting [23:00, frame slide 33]. Phase-two test matrix had seven specimens varying plate thickness (1, 1.5, and 2 inch), nominal rod yield (36 and 105 ksi), rod count (four corner rods, one test with eight), and gravity load (0 to 152 kips); rods were 3/4 inch diameter, headed with two nuts sandwiching a washer at the bottom, set deep so concrete pullout did not control, grout 8 ksi [Test Matrix frame slide 37, 48:59, 53:21]. The load-displacement loops are pinched with an intermediate plateau caused by the plate lifting off the yielded anchor rod, with residual moment from the axial pre-stress effect [38:39]. Strain gauges on two sides of each rod read equal, proving the rods carried near-pure axial tension with negligible bending and negligible prying [52:09, 17:58]. The eight-rod test showed the two interior rods do almost nothing; the connection behaves like a four-corner-rod plate [43:55].
### Fabrication Notes
The column-to-base-plate weld in the test specimens was a partial-joint-penetration weld on the outside of the flange with a reinforcing fillet weld on the inside of the column flange, all toughness-rated, sized so the total weld throat develops the column flange rather than the weld fracturing first [14:49]. The closing demonstration shows a base-plate weld fracture where a PJP weld at a column flange corner cracks and the whole flange tears, the failure mode this detailing is meant to prevent [13:42, 14:08]. Phase-one friction specimens deliberately included mill scale on the base plate and shim stacks under the plate to match real erection, conditions earlier test programs had omitted [10:14]. Plate thickness is the fabrication lever that shifts the failure mode between base-plate bending and anchor-rod yielding [49:55].
### Erection Notes
The connection model follows standard exposed-base erection: anchor rods cast in the foundation, leveling nuts set and adjusted to plumb the column, then grout placed under the base plate for uniform bearing [23:29]. Shim stacks under the plate are a real erection practice the friction tests reproduced [10:14]. The footings were stepped in the lab only to hook the strong floor and to keep the bearing confinement realistic, not a field condition [22:00, 27:07]. Anchor-hole size was standard slightly-oversized per Design Guide 1, with washer plates to prevent dishing of the washers, generally not welded in the flexure tests [36:53].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The central design-side error flagged is using the 45-degree cone method for shear-lug or shear-key bearing: it overpredicts blowout capacity by roughly a factor of two (test-to-predicted about 0.5) for foundations larger than about 6 inches edge distance, because concrete fracture, not full stress-block development, controls; the size-effect penalty fixes this to a test-to-predicted of about 1.1 with COV 0.2 [16:20, 19:20, frame slides 24 and 29]. A second design error is treating these bases as fixed on a strength check alone, which does not guarantee stiffness; the base alone contributed more than half a percent of drift at design-level load, so they are between pinned and fixed (pinned is the conservative assumption for column sizing) [33:00, 37:39]. The physical failure shown is a brittle PJP base-plate weld fracture tearing the column flange [13:42]. Biaxial loading dropped major-axis strength 30 to 40 percent, an effect no design guide covers [07:48].
### Bid / Cost Implications
This is a research lecture with no pricing, schedule, or estimating content; cost is not addressed beyond two notes. The speaker observes that Design Guide 1 is so conservative for compression-side plate yielding (off by up to 100 percent) that a designer who drops that limit state and checks tension-side and anchor-rod mechanisms instead can justify thinner, lighter base plates [56:00, 06:00]. He also notes a tension-side hunch or chair detail would avoid plate tension yielding but adds expense, a design tradeoff rather than a default [25:01].
### Your Company Application
The hard takeaway for our anchor-rod work is that the Design Guide 1 shear-lug 45-degree cone method is unconservative; if Ivan or our in-house PE ever sizes a shear lug or shear key for high base shear, the design must apply the concrete size effect, not the bare cone equation, or it can be off by a factor of two. For Tekla detailing and Mario's shop, the validated base-plate weld is a PJP on the flange outside plus a reinforcing fillet inside, toughness-rated, sized to develop the column flange, which matches conventional structural-steel practice and should be the default note over an undersized weld. For anchor-rod design and setting, the study confirms ASTM F1554 rods with leveling nuts, standard slightly-oversized holes, and adequate embedment so concrete pullout does not govern, and confirms Design Guide 1 is fine for friction (mu = 0.45) and anchor-rod bearing. Tell estimators and erectors that exposed bases are flexible, not truly fixed, which matters for drift and for any ACP frame analysis assuming fixed bases. NONE of this conflicts with Your Company doctrine; AISC member weights still come from aisc_validator.py and rates from bid_rates.py, this video changes no validated number.

## Effective Communication Connections
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WTCrvYGRZws | Duration: 1:29:29 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
Dr. Patrick Fortney teaches how the engineer of record (SEOR) and the fabricator-employed connection designer must communicate when connection design is delegated to the fabricator [00:02, 02:06]. The thesis is that misleading, omitted, or contradictory design-document information drives delays, errors, RFIs, change orders, and unanticipated cost, while clear and coordinated communication of scope, governing standards, and design loads lets the estimator capture cost accurately at bid stage [03:38, 04:40, 07:14]. The 2010 AISC Code of Standard Practice was the first edition to explicitly recognize fabricator connection design, and its three options anchor the whole discussion [02:36].
### Spec References
The speaker cites the AISC Code of Standard Practice (AISC 303) 2010, Section 3.1 for the three connection-design options [08:45, 09:16]. He references AISC 360 (with the 2005 and 2010 versions called out by methodology, ASD vs LRFD) [24:12, 25:16], AISC 341 (2010) for the seismic force resisting system [25:16, 53:36], and AISC 358 (2010) for prequalified moment connections [25:47]. Bolting is tied to RCSC (2004 and 2009 versions named) [25:16, 26:20] and welding to AWS D1.1 (2004 and 2008, plus D1.8 2010) [25:16, 26:20, 41:44]. He cites AISC 14th Edition equations J10-9, J10-10, J10-11, J10-12 for web panel-zone evaluation [50:29, 50:59] and Table 3-6 (13th Edition) for UDL beam reactions [44:51]. The AISC Design Examples v14.0 preface is quoted as saying its approach is not the only approach [71:39].
### Technical Details
Code of Standard Practice Section 3.1 gives three options the SEOR must designate for EACH connection: option one, complete design shown on the structural drawings (SEOR responsible); option two, connections selected or completed by an experienced detailer, never designed by them, SEOR still responsible; option three, connections designed by a licensed PE working for the fabricator [09:47, 10:18, 11:19]. The term EM (engineer mandated) means a detail that is 100% designed where the fabricator only details, fabricates, and furnishes [32:57]. Design-load communication is central: simple shear reactions, moments, axial forces, and brace transfer forces must all be provided per the Code [37:03, 42:47]. Panel-zone evaluation requires four possible equations and the designer must know whether the SEOR considered panel-zone deformation on frame stability and the assumed K value, which only the SEOR knows [50:29, 50:59].
### Fabrication Notes
Continuity plates and web doubler plates significantly increase connection cost and can cause integrity problems; a 14x90 column needing a 1-1/2 inch continuity plate showed visible distortion from the welding process [54:36, 55:08]. Fortney promotes "clean columns" as a shared goal and points to AISC free clean-column software and software warnings (RAM Steel flags doubler or continuity requirements at column selection) to eliminate stiffeners during beam-column final selection [55:08, 55:38, 56:10]. Weld symbols must carry a size or a load: a fillet symbol with no size forces an RFI unless a general note assigns AISC minimum welds, and since 2008 AWS D1.1 a groove-weld symbol with no tail note no longer means CJP, so a CJP tail note is required or the designer may only develop the base metal [38:37, 41:44, 42:16].
### Erection Notes
The video is about design-document communication, not field erection, so erection sequencing, bracing, crane, and rigging are not covered. Fortney does note that connection simplification proposed by the fabricator or connection designer can reduce cost and sometimes simplify erection [70:05]. No erection tolerances or field procedures are cited.
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Named failures are document-level: contradictory standards (Note 4 directing LRFD while Note 8 invoked the 9th Edition ASD manual) [23:09]; a seismic R=3.0 labeled ordinary concentric braced frame with details actually showing special concentrically braced frame 2t clearance, traced to details accidentally carried from another project [27:21, 28:22]; R=3 general notes paired with reduced-beam-section and bolted-flange-plate moment details that were really for progressive-collapse, with no note explaining it [29:23]. Incomplete details (a brace-to-gusset fully designed but beam-to-column and gusset-to-column left to the fabricator) and missing weld sizes force RFIs [31:27, 38:37]. UDL over-specification is the recurring error: a girder required to carry 147 kips when the infill beams delivering load were only good for 70 kips, back-calculating to roughly 700 to 947 psf on a commercial floor [44:51, 45:23, 47:26].
### Bid / Cost Implications
Whether the fabricator PE must sign and seal calculations, and separately whether shop drawings must be signed and sealed, must be stated explicitly because each raises the company risk profile and must be priced at bid stage [03:38, 14:23, 17:26]. Requiring calculations for every connection (versus sample calculations plus option-two detailer selection) sharply increases document preparation, submittal volume, and review time, impacting shop and project schedules, so the fabricator must know that up front [18:58, 20:33, 21:05]. UDL and full-plastic-moment specifications are conservative and drive steel cost up unnecessarily; a w24x55 designed for 53 kip-ft when the actual was 300 kip-ft, and a w24x62 designed at 574 kip-ft when actual was 540 kip-ft, change whether continuity or doubler plates are needed [47:26, 53:36, 54:06]. Unaddressed bid-stage RFIs and missing transfer forces become change orders after award [04:40, 56:42].
### Your Company Application
This is the playbook for Ivan's takeoff and for the in-house PE stamp. At intake, Ivan should classify every job against Code of Standard Practice 3.1 (option one, two, or three) and flag explicitly whether the spec requires the fabricator PE to sign and seal calculations and, separately, shop drawings, since both raise cost and risk that the estimate must carry [14:23, 17:26]. The UDL and full-plastic-moment lesson maps directly to our verify-don't-generate doctrine: when a set posts UDL or Mp instead of actual reactions, treat it as a conservative LOW-confidence load that inflates connection size, continuity, and doubler-plate cost, and raise an RFI for actual reactions rather than pricing the conservative number silently. Tekla detailing and our PE should target clean columns to cut welding cost and distortion, and Mario's welding scope should confirm every fillet has a size and every CJP has its AWS D1.1 2008 tail note. For ACP project controls, log option-three sign-and-seal scope, transfer forces, and any standard-coordination conflicts in the RFI register before award. No conflict with Your Company doctrine; the conventional structural-steel framing (braced frames, moment connections, no PEMB language) aligns with our positioning. Doctrine flag: NONE.

## Alternate Methods of Connection Design
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bdoiz4a39SQ | Duration: 1:28:34 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
This 2015 AISC webinar, by Larry Muir (AISC Steel Solutions Center) and Dr Patrick McManus (Martin and Martin), teaches connection-design methods that go beyond what is tabulated in the AISC Manual while still satisfying the AISC Specification [01:02]. Muir draws the line between the Specification (adopted into law by reference in the building codes, written as requirements) and the Manual (guidance only, not a contract requirement, so calling out "design shall conform to the AISC Manual" is improper) [02:36]. Part one covers shear-connection considerations beyond strength, mainly rotational ductility and torsional restraint [03:37]. Part two covers built-up PJP welds, bolt-group analysis by alternate methods, and prying action [37:26].

### Spec References
Specification Section B3.6a defines a simple shear connection and requires sufficient rotation capacity for the analysis-required rotation [05:38]. Section J1.2 permits inelastic but self-limiting deformation to accommodate simple-beam end rotation [06:09]. Section J2.2b limits weld returns to allow weak-axis flexure [07:11]. Chapter F (Section F1) carries the assumption that beam supports are restrained against rotation about the longitudinal axis [24:40]. Seismic Provisions Section F2.6b requires connections to accommodate 0.025 radians of rotation [11:20]. Chapter N requires UT on CJP welds with frequency by risk category [40:35]. Table J2.5 gives weld available stresses [45:20]. Specification Section J3.6 states prying action must be considered when computing bolt tension but does not dictate the method [72:38]. Manual Part 7 (instantaneous center of rotation and elastic bolt-group methods, C-prime, Delta-max of 0.34 in), Part 9 (weld and bolt minimum-size ductility checks), Part 10 (single-plate, shear-tab, and extended-tab design tables), and Part 2 (bearing-support stability) are cited throughout. Referenced studies: McGill University tests on welded shear tabs [21:38], Jim Swanson University of Cincinnati 2002 prying-action summary, and Bill Thornton's prying work that underlies the Manual method [73:10].

### Technical Details
The de-facto test target for simple shear connections is 0.03 radians, but Muir shows a serviceable beam almost never reaches it: 0.003 rad occurs near span = 36x depth, and a beam is usually unserviceable before then [14:57]. Rotation is accommodated by weak-axis flexing of angles, end plates, and WT elements, by bolt plowing (localized bearing), by hole elongation, and by support flexibility; the conventional shear tab gets a max plate-thickness limit and a weld sized at 5/8 of plate thickness so the bolts plow or the plate yields before the weld fractures [10:18]. For built-up PJP welds, a reinforcing fillet lengthens the effective throat: equal fillet and PJP gives roughly a 40 percent (square root of 2) gain, and maximizing the PJP in thick steel with a smaller reinforcing fillet drives the throat to the hypotenuse [43:43]. PJP welds get only a small directionality increase (phi 0.75 to 0.80, about 6 percent) versus 50 percent for fillets [47:53]. Prying action resolves into three limit states (flange hinging, combined mode, bolt tension) selected by the alpha term; the Manual uses Fu not Fy because weak-axis bending and strain hardening reliably reach above-yield strengths [74:42].

### Fabrication Notes
CJP welds are expensive: they need backer bars or back-gouging and rewelding, often weld access holes, and Chapter N ultrasonic testing keyed to risk category [40:03]. Built-up PJP welds avoid UT (Chapter N requires it on neither PJP nor fillet welds), usually avoid weld access holes and backing, and can be the cheaper detail despite needing more weld metal for the same capacity [41:06]. McManus's office tabulates, by plate thickness, double-sided fillet or single-sided built-up-PJP-plus-fillet combinations that match the grade-50 plate strength so the fabricator can choose the economical option in place of a CJP [50:55]. He notes the reinforcing fillet on the back side keeps the backer-bar pseudo-crack internal, which matters for fatigue or high-seismic where the backing would otherwise have to be removed [49:54]. The single-plate 5/8-thickness rule applies to both A36 and A572 grade 50 [52:58].

### Erection Notes
Beams that run continuous over columns can violate the Chapter F torsional-restraint assumption and the pinned-column assumption at once, so stabilizer plates are detailed at the support [31:20]. Beams on bearing plates need stability by building into concrete or masonry with anchorage, by a top-flange diaphragm connection, by a top stability angle, or by an end plate or transverse stiffeners, plus a tie-down to the bearing plate [30:50]. A diaphragm or deck stabilizes the top flange, but during erection that deck is not yet in place, so the erection sequence must keep the beam stable until the floor system is on [30:20]. A common field fix when bolt holes will not make up is to weld the shear tab to the beam web; stopping the horizontal welds short of the holes preserves a free plate length to hinge and accommodate rotation, a behavior the McGill tests support [20:36].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Long or double copes leave a thin web plate with little torsional restraint, and pairing a long double cope with a torsionally stiff double-angle connection is a worse detail than an extended tab because the weak cope section governs anyway [34:55]. Field changes that depart from the Part 10 table limits leave a connection that may fail the Part 9 ductility checks, forcing a search for other rotation sources [12:51]. CJP welds are abused as a default crutch to develop the base metal, carrying needless cost and the heavier Chapter N inspection burden [40:03]. One-sided welding of a built-up PJP without the back-side reinforcing fillet eccentrically loads the weld [49:23]. A failed-UT CJP being patched with a fillet and recalled a PJP is questionable because the inclusion's location makes the PJP effective throat uncertain [87:27].

### Bid / Cost Implications
CJP welds cost more in labor (backing, back-gouging, access holes) and add mandatory UT under Chapter N, so substituting a built-up PJP plus reinforcing fillet, or double-sided fillets, can cut weld cost while matching plate strength [50:55]. The trade is more deposited weld metal against a higher factor of safety with no UT, which is often net cheaper [41:39]. Alternate bolt-group methods (the separation method for drag and collector connections, and the interaction method) let an estimator tabulate a reliable shear-plus-axial capacity rather than re-running the iterative instantaneous-center method per condition, which is faster for repetitive industrial connections [57:37]. The separation method runs about 9 to 17 percent conservative versus the IC method, so it trades a small capacity penalty for predictable, codeable numbers [61:42].

### Your Company Application
For Tekla detailing and the in-house PE stamp, the built-up-PJP-versus-CJP table is a direct cost lever: matching plate strength with a PJP-plus-reinforcing-fillet avoids Chapter N UT and back-gouging on members that do not need a developed CJP, which Mario's shop and the welding WPS work should reflect. Mario's crew should keep the conventional shear-tab discipline (5/8-thickness weld, plate thickness limit, welds stopped short of the holes on any field-weld fix) so connections retain the rotation capacity the design assumes. Field bolting ties to the rotation theme: short-slotted holes and bolt plowing absorb most simple-beam end rotation on shallow beams, so a make-up problem in the field has known engineered remedies rather than improvisation. For Ivan's takeoff through aisc_validator.py this video changes no member weights or AISC shape data; it is connection methodology, and the validated tonnage stays the system of record. Erection and Paul's safety planning should note the over-column stabilizer-plate and bearing-plate stability requirements and the fact that deck-dependent top-flange bracing is absent during erection, so temporary stability is sequenced. Doctrine flags: NONE. All content is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language, no supplier names, and no fabricated section numbers.
