## High Strength Bolting: The Basics
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PmXMTt_JPb8 | Duration: 1:34:51 | Upload: 2016-09-22 | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
Geoffrey Kulak (author of AISC Design Guide 17 and the Guide to Design Criteria for Bolted and Riveted Joints) teaches the behavior and fundamentals of high-strength bolted joints, not connection design recipes. The structural engineer owns four jobs: selecting the bolt type and grade, designing the fastener, the installation, and the inspection [06:00]. Load transfers through a bolted joint in one of two ways, by shear in the bolt plus bearing on the connected material, or by friction (slip-critical), and the design philosophy throughout is to size against the ultimate (failure) load level because steel bolts have no clean elastic benchmark [34:00]. The lecture closes with a worked gusset-plate brace connection that walks slip load, bolt shear, plate bearing, block shear, and gusset buckling end to end.

### Spec References
Cited verbatim on slides or aloud: AISC Standard 2010 (the 360-10 specification, "AISC 2010") as the governing spec [21:00]; the tabulated bolt shear and tension values are in Table J3.2 [43:30]; RCSC (Research Council on Structural Connections) specification, named as the installation/inspection authority paired with the ASTM product spec [05:00, 67:00]; ASTM bolt grades A307, A325, A490, plus tension-control F1852 and twist-off F2280 [slide 12]; ASTM A563 nuts and ASTM F436 washers [slide 12]; AISC Design Guide 17 (High-Strength Bolts: A Primer for Engineers) and the Guide to Design Criteria for Bolted and Riveted Joints, both named as references [93:00]; Bickford's book cited for mechanical-engineering bolting [93:30]. Group A is A325/F1852 and Group B is A490/F2280 [slide 12].

### Technical Details
Minimum tensile strengths: A307 about 60 ksi, A325 120 ksi, A490 150 ksi with a 170 ksi ceiling because steel ductility falls off at that level [03:00-04:00]. Bolt shear strength is about 62 percent of bolt ultimate tensile strength, from the von Mises relationship 1/sqrt(3) = 0.577 confirmed by tests [33:00, slide 31]. The design nominal shear value takes 90 percent of that 62 percent, giving 0.563 Fu, which after threads-in-shear-plane and length effects lands at the tabulated Table J3.2 numbers (68 ksi for an A325 Group A bolt with no threads in the shear plane) [43:00]. Threads in the shear plane drop the value to about 80 percent of threads-excluded [44:00]. A bolt in tension uses the tensile stress area, about 0.75 of the gross pi*d^2/4 area, so P-ult = 0.75 Fu Ab [58:00]. Required pretension is 70 percent of bolt ultimate tensile strength [56:30]. Critically, ultimate bolt shear strength does not depend on pretension, because shear yielding in the bolt dissipates the installed pretension essentially to zero [40:00-42:00]. Slip resistance Rn = mu * Du * hf * Tb * ns per bolt, with mu = 0.30 Class A (clean mill scale, hot-dip galvanized, roughened) and 0.50 Class B (blast-cleaned), Du = 1.13 ratio of installed to specified-minimum tension, ns slip planes [slides 47, 109]. Plate bearing Rn = 1.5 Fu Lc t <= 3.0 d t Fu, reduced to 80 percent when deformation at the hole is a design consideration [slide 63, 61:00-62:00]. Block shear is tension fracture across the net tension area plus shear yield (about 0.6 Fy on the gross shear area) [65:00].

### Fabrication Notes
This is a fundamentals lecture, not a shop-process talk, so fit-up and QC are framed from the inspector's side. All material within the grip of the bolt must be steel; a non-steel layer (the lecturer cites the Kemper Arena failure, a resin-impregnated fiber pad within the grip) is barred and contributed to a collapse [16:00]. Faying surfaces are not painted in slip-critical zones to develop slip resistance [46:30]. Surface condition sets the slip coefficient, so the shop and coatings choice (clean mill scale versus blast-cleaned versus galvanized) directly fixes Class A versus Class B [slide 47]. Short, fat bolts (a 7/8 in A325 or A490 only 2 in long, especially galvanized) can twist off before installation completes because they lack enough thread length to absorb the turn; a rotation test is the check [76:00].

### Erection Notes
Installation starts snug-tight, the full effort of a worker on a 15 in spud wrench or the first impact of an impact wrench, bringing plies into firm contact working from the stiff center toward the edges [25:00, 69:00]. Pretensioning is by calibrated wrench, turn-of-nut, tension-control (twist-off) bolts, or load-indicator (direct-tension-indicator) washers [slide 24]. Turn-of-nut applies 1/3, 1/2, or 2/3 turn past snug depending on bolt length, half turn being typical, which intentionally yields the bolt so the least and most elongated bolts in a joint carry nearly identical tension (50 versus 49-51 kips example) [69:00-71:00]. Calibrated wrench must be calibrated on at least three bolts of that exact grip and re-calibrated when bolt length changes, and you must use washers [68:00]. A handbook torque-tension value is forbidden by RCSC because it is roughly 40 percent off [67:00]. Twist-off of the tip alone does not prove pretension, the calibration is what proves it [79:00]. Snug-tight contact need not be full across the whole joint, since slip resistance is independent of contact area (the inclined-plane physics) [48:00].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Dividing total joint load equally by the number of bolts is wrong in long joints; an extreme 13-bolt-in-line case shows the end bolts take far more shear than interior bolts, which is why a length reduction applies past 38 in of joint [38:00-39:00, slide 40]. Ignoring prying action on bolts in tension undersizes them, prying can add 20 percent or more over P/n (the Kemper Arena lesson) [14:00-15:00, slide 16]. Fatigue cracks in slip-critical members start at edge nicks and scratches, not at the hole, so a nicked or poorly finished plate edge is a real reject in repetitive-load joints [50:00-51:00]. You cannot over-tighten a bolt; if it is over-tightened it simply breaks, so reports of broken bolts point to too-short bolts or insufficient ductility, not over-torque [76:00]. Inspecting for pretension that was never required wastes money, match the inspection to the joint class [72:00].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Do not default to the most conservative joint. Specifying slip-critical or pretensioned bolts where snug-tight bearing would serve costs more to install and more to inspect; field-measured slip is about half a hole clearance (one dime thickness), tolerable for most buildings [29:00-30:00]. Bolt grade and faying-surface choice carry installed cost: tension-control twist-off bolts install from one side, quietly, and need no separate inspector watching every bolt, but the bolts themselves cost more [79:00-80:00]. Turn-of-nut delivers measured pretension averaging 80 percent of ultimate for A325 (about 38 percent over the specified minimum), so the conservatism is already built into the rule and need not be paid for twice [78:00]. The estimating takeaway is to specify the lowest joint class the loading allows.

### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff and estimating, the joint-class decision is a direct cost lever: most Your Company building frames are bearing-type snug-tight or pretensioned, and only fatigue, load reversal, or geometry sensitivity should trigger slip-critical pricing, so the estimate should not blanket-default to slip-critical inspection labor. For Mario's shop and field crews, the installation hierarchy (snug-tight from stiff to edge, then turn-of-nut half turn or calibrated wrench on at least three bolts per grip with washers, re-calibrate on length change) is a clean field checklist, and the broken-short-bolt diagnosis is worth posting. For Paul's safety and QC, the inspection-by-class map (snug-tight bearing, pretensioned, slip-critical) plus the no-non-steel-in-grip rule and the edge-nick fatigue check are concrete acceptance gates. For Tekla detailing, calling out bolt group (A versus B), thread condition (N versus X), faying-surface class, and hole type drives the Table J3.2 values our connections rely on. This reinforces our verify-do-not-generate doctrine: bolt shear, tension, slip, and bearing capacities come from Table J3.2 and RCSC, never from LLM arithmetic, the same way AISC member weights come only from aisc_validator.py. No conflict with Your Company doctrine; this is conventional structural-steel bolting with no PEMB language. Doctrine flag: NONE.

## AISC Live Webinar - Are You Properly Specifying Materials?
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HiRG3tYU7xA | Duration: 1:02:32 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
Charlie Carter (AISC VP and Chief Structural Engineer) walks through how to specify the correct ASTM material standard and grade for every common structural steel product, so that what is drawn matches what is economically available in the marketplace [00:02]. The thesis is that calling out the right ASTM standard pulls in everything that makes the material what you expect: ordering requirements, mechanical properties (yield, tensile, elongation), chemistry, process, testing, cross-section tolerances, defect repair, and reporting [08:47]. The quick-reference source is the table in AISC Code of Standard Practice Section 6.1.1, which lists the preferred (most common) ASTM standard for each product, plus the more extensive material tables in Part 2 of the AISC Manual and the Modern Steel Construction article of the same name [10:19].

### Spec References
Code of Standard Practice Section 6.1.1 material-identification table [10:19]; AISC Manual Part 2 material tables and Table 14-2 anchor-rod hole sizes [12:21][45:55]; ASTM A6 (cross-section definitions for open shapes) [25:43]. Shapes: A992 (W), A913 grades 50/60/65/70 (high-strength), A588 and A847 (weathering), A572 Gr 50 (HP, plate), A529 Gr 50, A36, A500 Gr C (HSS), A1085 and A1065 (large/improved HSS), A53 Gr B (pipe); A513 flagged as unsuitable [37:06]. Fasteners: A325, A490, F1852, F2280 now unified under F3125 as grades [39:08]; F3111 and F3043 (200 ksi); A563 nuts; F436 washers; F959 DTIs; F1554 anchor rods grades 36/55/105 [43:50] with Section 4.1 substitution. RCSC Section 2.4, Section 2.6.2, and Sections 7/8/9 (preinstallation verification, installation, inspection) at boltcouncil.org [42:18][86]. Welds: FEXX 70 ksi, AISC Design Guide 21, AWS A5.36, A5.1, A5.5, A5.20, A5.29, AWS D1.1-15 [47:29]. Concrete coordination: ACI 117 anchor placement tolerances [46:26].

### Technical Details
W shapes are almost all A992 (Fy 50 ksi); A913 is the high-strength alternative with size minimums for the quench-and-self-temper process (W14x90 and up, W12x65 and up, W10x49 and up), and grades 50 and 65 need no preheat while grade 70 still does [16:59][19:31][20:32]. S, M, C/MC, and L shapes sit in the 36-or-50 ksi overlap where the asterisk grade can be A572 Gr 50, A529 Gr 50, or A992 [21:33][38:08]. Rectangular and square HSS are A500 Gr C at 50 ksi yield, but round HSS at the same grade is only 46 ksi, and round HSS is not interchangeable with A53 Gr B pipe at 35 ksi [27:47][33:32]. A1085 holds Fy 50 ksi for both round and rectangular, has a tighter 5 percent wall tolerance that removes the 0.93 design-thickness reduction, plus a max tensile and specified toughness [31:27][56:13].

### Fabrication Notes
The Section 6.1.1 table exists to simplify shop and field material identification: preferred standard grades need no special marking, only off-grade material gets marked, so a fabricator should preserve that marking discipline [10:49]. The MC12x14.3 stringer channel has a 2-1/8 inch flange specifically to land a railing post and make the weld without crimping the pipe or building up weld over an overhang [23:38]. When the wall thickness governs design, A500 product is reduced to 0.93 of nominal, while A1085 and A1065 are used at full thickness [31:57][56:13]. A1085 toughness lets it be used in dynamically loaded welded structures, which plain A500 prohibits [32:31].

### Erection Notes
The headline erection-relevant item is anchor-rod fit at column bases [46:26]. Mike West coordinated ACI 117 anchor placement tolerances, the Code of Standard Practice anchor-rod tolerances, and the 15th edition AISC Manual hole sizes so that rods set by the concrete contractor to ACI 117 receive a base plate fabricated to Code of Standard Practice tolerances using Manual hole sizes, aimed at ending base-fit problems [46:26]. No crane, rigging, or sequencing content beyond base-plate fit is covered.

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The single most common mis-specification named is calling out "A325 anchor bolts," because anchor rods are not bolts; the supplier then quietly furnishes A449 rod cut to length and the buyer believes they got A325 [61:18]. Specifying A513 tube (common in handrails) is a defect because A513 carries no minimum strength level, so yard stock was never ordered to a strength [37:06]. Over-specifying bolts with N, X, or SC suffixes in the purchase order is unnecessary since those are design/installation conditions, not the fastener ordered [57:44]. Stale weld references like AWS A5.1/A5.5 are often wrong because they name stick welding, not the shop processes actually used [48:31]. Welding high-strength heat-treated bolts is cautioned against [59:18].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Specifying the preferred, most-available grade avoids time chasing scarce or pricier alternatives, so correct specification is also the fast and economical path [50:33]. Carter declines to state prices and repeatedly directs the estimator to producer cost sheets and AISC member service centers for live pricing, noting the upcharge for higher-strength steel often does not keep pace with the strength gain, meaning you pay comparatively less per unit of strength [53:07][60:18]. Alternate grades (lighter table shading) should be priced and confirmed with a fabricator or supplier for cost and availability before being assumed [13:52]. A500 Gr B versus Gr C carries no exhaustion lag because mills dual-label and service centers stock the dual product, so the higher strength is free to take [51:35].

### Your Company Application
Ivan's takeoff should default to the current preferred grades through aisc_validator.py: W as A992, HP as A572 Gr 50 (not A36), rectangular/square HSS as A500 Gr C at 50 ksi, round HSS at 46 ksi, pipe as A53 Gr B at 35 ksi, plate as A36 or A572 Gr 50, and never treat round HSS and pipe as interchangeable [27:47][33:32]. For the in-house PE stamp and anchor-rod work, default anchor rods to F1554 Gr 55, never "A325 anchor bolts," and adopt the ACI 117 / Code of Standard Practice / Manual hole-size coordination so anchors set by others on ACP land the base plate clean [43:50][46:26]. Mario's welding should standardize on FEXX 70 ksi filler with WPS references to AWS A5.36 and D1.1-15 (drop stale A5.1/A5.5 callouts), watch the grade 70 A913 preheat requirement, and avoid welding high-strength bolts. Field bolting should specify F3125 grade A325/A490 without N/X/SC purchase suffixes, with RCSC pretension/DTI methods (F436 washers, F959 DTIs) per RCSC Sections 7/8/9. Tekla detailing should carry A513 as a banned handrail tube. Doctrine flags: NONE. This reinforces verify-don't-generate (grades pulled from aisc_validator.py, not assumed) and conventional structural steel positioning with no PEMB language.

## Metallizing - From A to Zinc
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WTs3tSGrEco | Duration: 57:47 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
This NSBA webinar by Brian Raph and Tony Mudis of Can-Am Bridges teaches thermal spray metallizing (arc spray of zinc or aluminum wire) as a corrosion protection system for steel bridges, presented as an alternative to paint and hot-dip galvanizing [00:03][04:09]. Metallizing is a cold line-of-sight spray where two electrically opposed wires arc, melt, and are atomized by compressed air onto a blasted steel surface, where overlapping molten "splats" cool into an armor-like sacrificial coating [05:11][12:49]. Zinc protects galvanically by sacrificing itself to the steel substrate, giving an essentially indefinite service life with minor maintenance [04:41][05:11][27:41].

### Spec References
The presenters cited the following verbatim: SSPC-SP10 near-white blast as the minimum surface prep [06:42][31:17]; ASTM B833 for 99.9% zinc wire [21:35]; the FHWA Tech Brief on slip and creep of thermal spray coatings, authored by Dr. Justin Ocel, October 2014, finding unsealed metallized surfaces meet Class B [40:04][44:09][51:54]; ISO 2063, SSPC-CS 23.00 / AWS C2.23M, and NACE No. 12 as related metallizing standards [44:09]. RCSC Class B slip-critical with a minimum 0.5 slip coefficient was described but not cited by RCSC section number [39:32]. Applicator qualification was attributed to NACE or SSPC certification, no clause number [47:16]. The forthcoming AASHTO/NSBA Steel Collaboration TG8 guide specification for metallizing was referenced with a draft targeted for January [40:35][49:51].

### Technical Details
Adhesion is a mechanical bond into a sharp angular anchor-tooth profile, ideally about 3.5 mils deep with 2.5 mils the minimum, achieved using steel grit rather than round shot [07:42][09:13]. This differs from galvanizing, which is a metallurgical alloy layer that becomes part of the steel [08:12]. Three consumable "flavors" exist for bridges: 99.9% pure zinc, 85/15 zinc-aluminum alloy (denser, not thicker, using about 20% more wire per square foot, roughly $1 to $2/SF more), and 99.9% aluminum (rarely used in bridges, preferred for high-temperature industrial work) [18:01][23:05][24:36]. Zinc gives greater galvanic protection and is easier to spray; 8515 adds chloride resistance for coastal/marine settings; zinc should not be used in service above 140 degrees F [19:34][22:35]. Sealers of low viscosity may be applied to preserve coating weight, though many states leave the coating unsealed and still expect about 30 years before consumption [25:39][27:11].

### Fabrication Notes
Blasting to SSP10 with steel grit is the single most important quality factor, and hand blasting is the dominant method for getting the angular profile; it is a slow, labor-intensive step [06:42][13:50]. Temperature does not affect the ability to metallize, but temperature and humidity control the allowable window between blasting and coating; Can-Am uses an 8-hour blast-to-coat window in its shops to limit flash rust [10:15][11:17]. Because it is a cold process keeping steel under 250 to 300 degrees F, there is no curing or cooling time, no risk of weld damage, and no camber or curvature distortion, so coated girders move through the shop quickly and can be inspected by hand immediately [03:39][14:57]. Overspray zinc is collected and recycled; one plant reported metallizing about a million SF/year yielding 50 to 60 tons of recycled zinc [29:43].

### Erection Notes
Metallizing has no size or shape limitation, so very large box girder units (25 to 30 tons) that cannot fit a galvanizing kettle were metallized, sealed, and erected with no field touch-up [03:08][34:48]. Several projects were coated fully off-site and floated or dropped into place where setting up site blast operations was not feasible, with any shipping damage repaired before reaching the inaccessible site [35:20][35:51]. The coating is rugged enough that shipping or field damage is unlikely [32:47].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
No formal rejection list was given, but failure modes named were: a peened or dimpled profile from round shot instead of the required sharp angular profile, which prevents proper mechanical bond [09:13]; flash rust from exceeding the blast-to-coat window in humid conditions [11:17]; and inaccessible stiffener snipes and acute plate angles that the spray gun cannot reach, which are instead repaired with an organic zinc product like a paint touch-up [45:41][46:11]. Inexperienced applicators struggle to develop the required anchorage profile and uniform application [47:16].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Third-party metallizing runs roughly $12 to $14/SF because the applicator must mobilize cabinets and crews into the shop, while an in-house fabricator that has climbed the learning curve is competitive with a three-coat paint system [52:26][52:57]. The 8515 alloy costs about $1 to $2/SF more than pure zinc and consumes about 20% more wire for the same coverage [23:05]. Small members such as cross frames are not economical to metallize and are better hot-dip galvanized as a complement to metallizing the large girders [54:29]. Metallizing wire is exempt from Buy America (BABA) because it is neither iron nor steel [18:32]. The schedule advantage is throughput: no cure or cool time means immediate handling and inspection [14:21].

### Your Company Application
This is bridge-industry corrosion protection, outside Your Company's conventional building structural steel scope, so most content is reference rather than direct workstream. The transferable item is slip-critical bolting: any coating in a faying surface must qualify for RCSC slip resistance, and the FHWA finding that unsealed metallized surfaces meet Class B (0.5 minimum slip coefficient) is the kind of coating-vs-connection check Mario and the PE stamp should confirm whenever a galvanized or coated faying surface appears on a field-bolted slip-critical joint [39:32][40:04]. For Ivan's takeoff, the standards menu here (SSPC-SP10, ASTM B833) and the rule that small secondary members are cheaper to galvanize than spray-coat is a useful coating-scope heuristic. Doctrine flag: the speakers are from Can-Am Bridges, a named manufacturer; per Hard Rule 4 do not carry that supplier name into any Your Company client output. NONE otherwise.

## Weld Details: The  Good, The Bad and The Ugly
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mRJp75pN0Ho | Duration: 1:34:04 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
Dwayne Miller (chair of the AWS D1.1 structural welding committee, AISC TR Higgins lecturer) teaches twelve principles of correct and proper welded connection design, then walks good, bad, and "ugly" case studies against them [01:52][03:35]. The thesis is that "correct or proper" equals strong enough to transfer all applied load but no stronger than necessary, because over-strength welds are the more common and costly error [04:23][04:40]. The recurring failure mode is the complete-joint-penetration (CJP) weld specified by default to avoid calculating a fillet size, when a minimum fillet would carry the load with a fraction of the deposited metal [05:17][72:23]. The twelve principles are: strong enough, clear and direct load path ("the force goes to the stiff part" / provide a path into the member that lies parallel) [08:15][08:34], welds in low-stress regions [18:44], no stress risers [21:50], not constrained [27:32], do not load the weld in bending [27:50], protect weld toes and roots ("watch your toes, remember your roots") [39:12], a clearly defined throat (avoid the "nothing weld") [42:11], recognize/respect material properties (through-thickness ductility, lamellar tearing) [42:33], easy economical and safe to fabricate and erect [53:02], recognize commercial realities (mill tolerances, weld distortion) [53:16], and aesthetically pleasing [57:14].
### Spec References
AISC 360 Chapter J for weld design and the cartoons/formulas for stresses around tubular connection perimeters [85:33][92:32]; AISC 360 Section J5 for the 50 percent fillet-weld strength increase when loaded transverse to weld orientation [89:51]; a minimum prequalified fillet size in AISC Chapter J, speaker hedged "I think it might be table 2.1" (stated as uncertain, not verbatim) [85:33]. AWS D1.1 for prequalified joint details, the 1/16 inch root-gap limit before correction, and the rule to increase fillet leg by the amount of gap [88:08][89:02]; D1.1 prohibition on discontinuous/butted backing (with tubular exceptions added in 2010) [25:30][27:15]; D1.1 angular distortion limits [55:02]; a specific prequalified detail shown on a slide labeled "TC-U4a-GF" with 30 degree included angle and 3/8 inch root opening [frame: El Paso joint slide]. PJP groove weld throat capacity cited as 30 percent of electrode classification tensile strength times length [93:05]. ASTM A6 (ASM) mill tolerances: flange tilt t plus t-prime less than or equal to 5/16 inch for shapes over 12 inches deep, and HSS out-of-roundness of 0.75 percent of OD over 2 inches [54:43][55:38]. AISC Engineering Journal 1973 article "Commentary on Highly Restrained Welded Connections" (El Paso) [78:41]. Fatigue categories E and E-prime for cover-plate terminations and category F-equivalent stress on the weld [21:15][87:01]. Source study: SAC/BD-97/01 Barsom and Korvink, through-thickness 20 percent reduction-of-area lamellar-tearing measure [frame: SAC slide].
### Technical Details
Load-path geometry controls weld stress: a longitudinally aligned lug loads its weld uniformly, while rotating it 90 degrees produces a peak stress at midlength, fixed by stiffeners or by sizing only the welds in the parallel plane [09:06][10:08]. On round and square HSS the parallel quadrants are at the 3:00 and 9:00 positions, so a bottom lug strains the weld toe and ends unless a bracket reaches those positions or an internal diaphragm is added near the tube end [12:27][15:13][16:48]. Welding residual stress is driven by thermal expansion being roughly ten times yield elongation (a 10 inch, 50 ksi bar elongates 0.17 percent at yield versus 1.8 percent from room temperature to melting) [35:43][36:26]; when three orthogonal shrinkage strains meet at a point (Sigma 1 = Sigma 2 = Sigma 3) the steel cannot exhibit ductility and brittle fracture is likely, mitigated by weld sequencing and weld-access-hole snipes [37:18][38:36]. Through-thickness ductility is the weak axis: conservative through-thickness ultimate is about 80 percent and yield about 90 percent of longitudinal, with reduction-of-area sharply lower, so through-thickness tension loading risks lamellar tearing [51:29][51:44]. Transverse fillets carry more load because the failure throat rotates toward perpendicular, giving about a 38 percent increase before the codified 50 percent [91:16][91:36].
### Fabrication Notes
The "nothing weld" is the central QC concept: a weld that looks like the specified profile but is nothing like it, caused by lack of fusion through the section or by an excessive root gap that shrinks the effective throat [42:47][43:49]. Fit-up must be measured before welds are deposited; D1.1 allows 1/16 inch of root gap without correction, and beyond that the fillet leg is enlarged by the gap amount [89:02][89:18]. Make welds long and small rather than short and large for economy, because doubling length doubles strength while doubling leg quadruples deposited metal, never going below the minimum prequalified size [85:00][85:18]. Welding distortion is real: the Owens Steel box-column-around-a-wide-flange case used physical mockups to prove standard mill tolerance plus weld distortion would leave members out of square, and the fix was a true fabricated box [65:55][66:51]; a heavily reinforced doubler-and-stiffener gusset assembly distorted so badly it needed a porta-power jack to straighten, avoidable by selecting a heavier member [67:45][68:38]. Detail cover plates narrower than the beam flange to avoid flipping the assembly [53:16][53:49].
### Erection Notes
This is a design and fabrication webinar with limited dedicated erection content, but field welding versus field bolting on large trusses is addressed: fabricators prefer shop-welded splices while erectors prefer bolted field splices, and when loads are too large to pass through bolts, field welded connections must be used [62:43][63:18]. One cited project hid an "ugly" multi-bolted continuous bottom-chord connection inside a sleeve and field-finished it to speed construction and meet aesthetics, coordinated around one tower crane and one mobile crane alongside deck and curtain-wall trades [frame: Steel Conference article][63:34]. Several ugly examples were field-welded details (a 5 inch rod to a 3.5 inch plate) where shop conditions would have produced cleaner work [69:34][69:52].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Named failures: the default CJP specified "just in case," "when loads are unknown," or "when no one wants to calculate the weld size" [05:34][07:28]; the discontinuous/butted backing bar creating a transverse stress riser, prohibited by D1.1 and AISC for cyclic loading [25:30][26:23]; the nothing weld from poor fit-up or non-fusion [43:35]; weld toe versus root crack initiation under cyclic load depending on fillet size [41:00]; lamellar tearing through the thickness, the documented El Paso Performing Arts Center (1972) compression-ring failure where a 1 inch plate received CJP welds loaded through-thickness into 2.5 to 3 inch box members, repaired by directly welding thick-to-thick [74:53][76:23][77:33]; the lesson that using a prequalified joint detail does not by itself make a joint suitable, leading D1.1 to add the note that the engineer shall determine suitability of all joint details [80:19][80:36]. Ugly workmanship: melt-through shipped and installed, unremoved weld tabs, and "dingleberries" left unground [83:37][70:07].
### Bid / Cost Implications
The CJP-versus-fillet economics are quantified on a real ugly example [frame: load slide / 71:11]: 24.5 kips of tension on a 5 inch rod is only 1.25 ksi on the rod and 0.23 ksi distributed over the CJP welds, while a minimum 5/16 inch fillet carries it at 1.84 ksi with a capacity of 278 kips, 11 times the demand. The CJP consumed 26 pounds of weld metal versus 0.23 pounds for the minimum fillet, a 96 percent reduction in deposited metal for an equally adequate, better-looking weld [72:23][72:38][72:54]. The standing estimating rule is long-and-small fillets at the minimum prequalified leg [85:00]. Distortion-driven rework (jacking out distortion, scrapping out-of-square members) and field versus shop weld choices carry direct cost and schedule weight [63:02][68:38].
### Your Company Application
For Mario (AWS D1.1 welding lead): adopt "long and small, never below minimum prequalified leg," measure root fit-up before depositing (1/16 inch gap limit, add gap to leg beyond that), keep backing continuous, and protect roots on single-sided PJP joints, all D1.1 anchored [85:00][89:02][41:37]. For Ivan (takeoff/estimating): a CJP call-out is a cost flag, not a strength necessity. Where geometry permits, a minimum fillet runs roughly 96 percent less weld metal, so flag default-CJP details on incoming drawings and price the fillet alternate; this aligns with verify-do-not-generate since the demand check is a short hand calc against AISC Chapter J [05:34][72:54]. For Tekla detailing: model load-path-correct lugs and stiffeners ("force goes to the stiff part"), add internal diaphragms or external brackets on HSS connections, and use weld-access-hole snipes to break up constraint [10:08][16:48][38:36]. For in-house PE stamp: through-thickness lamellar-tearing risk (El Paso, SAC 20 percent reduction-of-area) governs any thick-plate joint loaded through the thickness, and a prequalified detail still requires engineer-of-record suitability judgment per D1.1 [77:33][80:36]. Anchor-rod and base-plate weld sizing, joist seat welds, and field bolting all benefit from the same minimum-fillet discipline. Doctrine flags: NONE. Nothing here conflicts with Your Company doctrine; it reinforces the verify-do-not-generate and source-the-input posture, and the AISC weight database in aisc_validator.py remains the only weight authority. Note the speaker named manufacturers generically in a slide credit (fabricators who supplied examples); these are not Your Company suppliers and were not added to internal supplier lists.

## Understanding the Code of Standard Practice
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2uGymrKGkcU | Duration: 1:30:12 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
This is a 2014 NASCC Steel Conference panel, co-presented with CASE (Council of American Structural Engineers), walking through the AISC Code of Standard Practice (AISC 303) and the changes introduced in the 2010 edition [00:00][22:33]. The Code sets the trade customs and the division of responsibility among the owner's designated representative for design, the fabricator, and the erector, and it defines what must appear in the contract documents so each party can bid and build without guessing. The slide deck title throughout is "2010 Code Changes" and "Code Discussion Topics," organized by the Code's own section numbering. No audio transcript was available for this entry, so every citation below comes from the on-screen slide text.

### Spec References
All references are to the AISC Code of Standard Practice (2010 edition) as shown on the slides: Section 1.9 Commentary on unspecified tolerances [07:31]; Section 3.1 Structural Design Drawings and Specifications and its Commentary, listing required design-document content (a) through (g) and Section 3.1.1 through 3.1.6 [11:16][15:02][18:48]; Section 3.1.2 connection-design options (1) complete design shown, (2) selected/completed by an experienced steel detailer, (3) designed by a licensed PE working for the fabricator [22:33][30:04]; Section 3.1.2 continuation on service-load vs factored-load and LRFD vs ASD, and the PE-of-record written review of substantiating connection information [33:50][37:35]; Section 4.4 and its Commentary on the 14-day approval allotment [45:06]; Section 6.4 Fabrication Tolerances, specifically 6.4.4 camber [52:37][1:00:08]; and Section 7.10 Temporary Support of Structural Steel Frames, specifically 7.10.1 and its Commentary [1:03:54][1:07:39]. The deck also references the AISC Steel Construction Manual as the default source of connection tables when the design drawings provide none [30:04].

### Technical Details
Section 3.1 requires the design documents to state the size, section, material grade and location of all members, all geometry and working points necessary for layout, floor elevations, column centers and offsets, camber requirements, and the joining requirements between elements of built-up members [15:02]. Section 3.1.2 forces the owner's designated representative for design to pick one of three connection paths per connection, which determines who carries the connection-design liability [22:33]. A slide reproduces Figure 1-1 illustrating the column panel zone with column web stiffeners, the kind of detail the design must define rather than leave to the detailer [26:18]. When the detailer completes connections under option (2), the Code says the detailer shall utilize tables or schematic information in the design drawings, and absent that, tables in the AISC Steel Construction Manual or other reference information approved by the owner's representative [30:04].

### Fabrication Notes
Section 6.4.4 sets the camber tolerance and is the most concrete fabrication number in the deck [52:37]. A cambered beam received by the fabricator already holding 75 percent of the specified camber needs no further cambering. Otherwise, for beams 50 ft or less the camber variation is minus zero / plus one-half inch, and for beams longer than 50 ft the allowance is minus zero / plus one-half inch plus an additional one-eighth inch for each 10 ft (or fraction) over 50 ft. The second paragraph of 6.4.4 requires camber to be measured in the fabricator's shop in the unstressed condition for inspection purposes [1:00:08]. A cold-cambering detail slide shows a 45 ft beam with a 24 ft cambered middle zone and the corresponding moment diagram, illustrating that camber is induced over the central span, not end to end [56:23].

### Erection Notes
Section 7.10.1 makes the owner's designated representative for design responsible for identifying in the contract documents both the lateral-load-resisting system and the connecting diaphragm elements that give the completed structure its lateral strength and stability, and any special erection conditions required by the design concept, such as shores, jacks, or loads that must be adjusted as erection progresses to set or maintain camber, hold position within tolerance, or prestress [1:03:54]. The 7.10.1 Commentary explains that 7.10.1(b) covers special requirements inherent in the design concept that the erector could not otherwise know, for example sequentially erected structures where a member must reach a specific elevation in a later step; these must be disclosed so the erector can properly bid, plan, and perform the erection [1:07:39].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The recurring failure mode the panel targets is incomplete or ambiguous contract documents: a tolerance the design concept needs but never specifies (the Section 1.9 Commentary point that the necessary tolerance should be written into the contract documents) [07:31], connections left undesignated so liability is unclear, and special erection or shoring requirements never disclosed to the erector [1:07:39]. No weld-profile accept/reject photos, NDE rejection criteria, or bolting inspection failures appear in this deck; this video is a document-and-responsibility code talk, not a QC defect catalog.

### Bid / Cost Implications
Section 4.4 Commentary states the 14-day allotment for return of shop and erection drawings represents the fabricator's portal-to-portal time, and that in the absence of contrary information in the contract documents, 14 days may be assumed for bidding, contracting, and scheduling [45:06]. When substantiating connection information is part of the submittals, a longer, modified allotment should be written into the contract documents. The panel's "Bubba Says" interludes drive the bidding point home: a schedule no one has actually agreed to is not a schedule, and changing one requirement ripples into what else it affects [03:46][48:52]. The three connection options in 3.1.2 also shift cost and risk, since fabricator-PE-designed connections (option 3) move engineering effort and liability onto the fabricator's price [22:33].

### Your Company Application
This Code is the backbone of the verify-don't-generate posture. Ivan's takeoff should run a drawing-completeness gate against the Section 3.1 (a) through (g) list: if member size/grade/location, working points, floor elevations, column offsets, camber, or built-up joining are missing, the set is review-only and gets an RFI, not a price, which aligns with our SF-and-completeness gate. The 3.1.2 connection question decides whether our in-house PE stamp carries the connection design (option 3) and whether that engineering cost lands in our fab and erection rates per Your Company doctrine; the 3.1.2 continuation also tells us to confirm LRFD vs ASD and service vs factored loads before detailing. Tekla detailing under option (2) must pull connection geometry from the design tables or the AISC Manual, never invent it. For Mario's shop, 6.4.4 is the camber acceptance rule (minus zero / plus one-half inch baseline, measured unstressed in the shop), and 7.10 tells Paul Guerrero's erection planning to demand that shoring, jacking, and lateral-stability-during-erection requirements be in the contract documents before crews mobilize. On ACP project controls, the 14-day drawing-return assumption and the submittal/RFI-system expectations from Section 4 should seed the schedule and the project communication plan. No conflict with Your Company doctrine; the Code reinforces our gate-first, cite-the-source approach. Doctrine flag: NONE.

## Constructability of Structural Steel Buildings: Part 4
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AumoKgJajHA | Duration: 56:46 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
This webinar, presented by Jay Ruby and Jeff Gasr of Ruby and Associates, teaches AISC Design Guide 23 (Constructability for Structural Steel Buildings), focused on Chapter 6, constructability of erecting steel [06:12]. The thesis is that erectors hold field knowledge that should be brought to the design team as early as possible, ideally before bid, to cut cost and schedule through the constructability influence curve, where early decisions cost the least and late changes cost the most [03:38]. A repeated theme is that the least-weight structure is not the least-cost structure [51:05], and that shop and erection labor (not material, which has settled at 25 to 30 percent of total cost) now drive steel delivery cost [04:39].

### Spec References
The speakers cite AISC Design Guide 23 throughout and walk its section numbers aloud: 6.1 complete coordinated construction documents [11:57], 6.2 site constraints [15:32], 6.3 season of construction [17:37], 6.4 sequence of construction [20:11], 6.5 construction schedule [22:15], 6.8 temperature adjustments [35:39], 6.9 special tolerances [37:39], and 6.11 general erection tolerances [51:05]. They cite the AISC Code of Standard Practice repeatedly, naming Section 7.1 (owner's designated representative for construction setting sequence) [20:11], Section 7.10.1 (SE shall define erection-sequence requirements: shores, jacking, elevations) [25:51], and Section 7.10.3 (erector responsibilities, structural stability maintained at all times) [41:48]. They reference ASTM A6 mill tolerances (sweep, camber, flange roll) [37:39], AWS for welded-assembly tolerances distinct from AISC [52:39], and AISE Technical Report 13 for mill buildings with overhead cranes [53:09].

### Technical Details
Connection and member types discussed: anchor rods and base plates, with a base-plate critique that four-bolt patterns can leave corners unshimmed (a two-tier column on leveling nuts and a plate washer is shown) [23:47]. Lateral systems covered concrete cores versus brace-frame substitutions, where Ruby replaced a 2-foot-thick concrete core in a 10-story Detroit building with a brace frame to avoid cure time [15:01]. The stadium case used 90-foot cantilever plate girders (26 of them), a tension tie cable, and an uplift strut redetailed from a welded knife plate to a 3-inch-diameter pin at the bottom and a 3-inch slot at the top for single-pick erection [29:58]. Trusses, double-angle and tee top cords, joists, perlins, and roof deck diaphragms are all treated as stability-critical members [88:00 region near 43:18].

### Fabrication Notes
Steel is fabricated workpoint to workpoint with no temperature input, cut at roughly 60 to 70 degrees in the shop [35:39]. Design Guide 23 Section 6.8 gives the field rule: a 100-foot truss changes length about one eighth of an inch for every 15-degree shift from its fabrication temperature, so a 65-degree shop piece set in a 120-degree desert afternoon must have connection allowance for that growth [36:39]. Fabricators should account for ASTM A6 mill shape tolerances (sweep, camber, flange roll) since special tolerances tighter than A6 are hard to hit [37:39]. Primer weather resistance and whether a top coat is applied are flagged as fab-and-field coordination items affected by season [19:40].

### Erection Notes
Erection guidance centers on single-pass erection, keeping the crane moving west to east or north to south with no comeback work [21:43], and just-in-time delivery so steel goes up fast and consumes less laydown [21:13]. Site constraints per the Code of Standard Practice require access for delivery, laydown space, and room for boom and tail swing; soil bearing for the crane is checked (the example is a Manitowoc 16000 with 220 feet of boom and 180 feet of luffer) [16:36]. Special erection procedures (shores, shore adjustment, jacking, elevation control) belong to the SE per Code Section 7.10.1, and the erection engineer should share building models to catch load reversals from temporary conditions [25:51]. Sun cambering is noted: as the sun heats one side of a column or cantilever, the structure bows away from the sun, which the erector must distinguish from a real elevation error [37:09].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The clearest failure shown is the industrial-facility roof where three bays were erected about 3 feet out of plumb because the 120-ton truss had an L-over-b slenderness of 180 against a target of 80, in a building with no sway frames, a cantilevered bottom-cord diaphragm system, a million square feet under roof, 3/4 mile long by 240 feet wide [45:21]. The fix required an auxiliary crane to set three joists per truss, temporary sway frames every three bays, cable horizontal bracing at the top cord, and cable bracing to supplement permanent vertical bracing that could not take temporary erection loads [47:25]. Other named errors: unshimmed base-plate corners on tall columns [23:47], stripping bolts out of an erected beam below the safety-connection minimum [24:20], and over-tightening a two-point bridle so the top cord goes into tension and bottom cord into compression, reversing the design [44:18].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Design-bid-build offers no reward for quality erectors: bidding against 16 erectors and 12 fabricators, the low bidder wins and hopes there is enough fat left to make money [08:17]. Material cost has flattened at 25 to 30 percent while shop and erection labor climb, so labor is where margin is won or lost [04:39]. Cost drivers to price include temporary shoring towers, welding enclosures (and how many times a welder must be re-enclosed for field welds) [19:09], crane sharing with the concrete contractor on a shared tower crane [22:46], and soil improvement timing that can be pulled forward to save crane mat and schedule cost [16:36]. The hospital case showed schedule compressed from 52 weeks to 35 weeks on an identical design purely by getting erectors, concrete, and crane users at the table early [54:42].

### Your Company Application
This maps directly to Your Company workstreams. Ivan's takeoff and bid review should add a constructability screen on every set: flag base-plate bolt patterns and column shim needs for anchor-rod setting and tolerance, flag any concrete-core lateral system as a brace-frame substitution opportunity that grows our erection scope, and compute truss and girder L-over-b against the 80 threshold to budget temporary sway frames and bracing before they surprise the field. Paul Guerrero should tie the stability-at-all-times duty (Code 7.10.3) and OSHA safe-working-environment language into erection planning, and Mario's crew should carry the Design Guide 23 6.8 temperature rule (one eighth inch per 100 feet per 15 degrees) plus the sun-camber caution into Houston summer sets and field-weld enclosure planning. Tekla detailing can pre-place lift lugs, pin-and-slot strut details, and temporary bracing rather than field-modifying members later, and our in-house PE stamp lets us author the special erection procedures the Code assigns to the SE. ACP project controls should push for the early-at-the-table posture this video proves out. No conflict with Your Company doctrine: the content is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language, and it reinforces our verify-don't-generate and SF-and-takeoff discipline.

## Constructability of Structural Steel Buildings: Part 1
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0BIruFjIYNk | Duration: 1:10:46 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is the primer session in a four-part AISC series on constructability presented by Dave Ruby and Jay Ruby of Ruby and Associates. The thesis is that constructability is a design philosophy, not a one-time event or a value-engineering check at 30/60/90 percent [35:33] [50:42]. The recurring theme is breaking the "silos of influence" where designer, fabricator, and erector each optimize on first-dollar (lowest first cost) in isolation, which does not yield the lowest-cost or most-buildable structure [05:16] [29:27]. The fix is to infuse construction knowledge and a construction professional onto the design team from the feasibility stage forward, not at 30 or 60 or 90 percent [32:01] [32:31].
### Spec References
No AISC 360, AISC 341, AWS D1.1, or RCSC section numbers are cited in this session; it is a philosophy and delivery primer. The speaker references the AISC constructability Design Guide being sold on the AISC website as the companion document but does not give a Design Guide number [01:09]. He cites the Construction Industry Institute (CII), affiliated with the University of Texas at Austin, and its 1989 definition of constructability as "the optimum use of construction knowledge and experience in planning, design, procurement, and field operations to achieve overall project objectives" [20:40] [32:01], plus a 2010 expansion adding building operations and maintenance [36:38]. General principles otherwise, no spec section cited.
### Technical Details
The most concrete technical content is a bay-size framing study comparing 30, 40, and 60 foot bays for the same building envelope [41:22] [43:29]. At 30 foot bays: 11 trusses, 786 joists, 144 bottom-chord braces with 228 connections, 145 struts with 290 connections, 11 columns, 40 diagonals, 111 joints in the bracing. At 40 foot bays: 8 trusses, 72 braces, 74 struts with 148 connections, 8 columns, 30 diagonals. At 60 foot bays: 6 trusses, 450 joists, 102 braces, 36 struts. The point is that tonnage is nearly identical across all three ("throw a blanket over the difference in tonnage") but piece count and connection count, which drive fabricator man-hours, change dramatically [42:58] [43:59]. The cladding hides the difference so the owner cannot tell the bays apart [42:58].
### Fabrication Notes
The session frames fabrication cost as a man-hour problem, not a dollars-per-ton problem [43:59]. Fabricators buy raw steel by the ton, then add man-hours for painting, shipping, handling, cleaning, drilling, welding, and bolting; piece count and detail complexity are the real cost drivers before a fabricator gives a number [37:09] [44:00]. The drivers for a fabricator are stated as numbers of pieces and complexity of details [37:41]. No tolerances, fit-up procedures, or shop QC steps are specified in this primer.
### Erection Notes
Erection is treated through site-coordination and access rather than field procedure. The speaker stresses evaluating site review, truck lay-down, lifting space, and crane positioning, none of which sit on the designer's decision matrix but all of which affect buildability [55:14] [55:47]. He gives the example of congested sites where erection can only run off the street from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. [55:47]. No bracing, sequencing, or rigging specifics are given.
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
No inspection failures, weld rejections, or bolting rejections are named; this primer does not cover NDE or QA/QC. The "errors" discussed are process errors: making the structural system decision weeks before the mechanical engineer is involved [28:55] [57:20], treating BIM as a substitute for full design drawings rather than a tool [24:51] [25:21], and waiting for a 30/60/90 constructability review, which only critiques what was done and never what was not done [35:33] [36:04].
### Bid / Cost Implications
This is the strongest section for estimating. A single connection-type decision on a 52-kip single-shear reaction with six bolts ranges from about $21 (snug-tight, threads excluded from shear plane) to $28 (threads in shear plane), to $31.50 and $38 for pretensioned bearing bolts, to $68 for slip-critical, and that cost is bolts and installation only [39:14] [40:17] [40:52]. A connection redesign on one project cut bolt count from 44,000 to 21,000, a direct man-hour and schedule reduction [41:22]. Reported value-engineering returns: a $20,000 investment yielding $100,000 to $400,000, and a $200,000 investment yielding $1 to $4 million, from a study of 100 to 150 projects [38:44]. Case studies cite roughly $500,000 saved and 17 weeks cut on a 150,000 SF hospital (about $3.75/SF) [46:08] [47:10], $800,000 and 16 weeks on a 105,000 SF Georgia project [47:40], and $4.5 million and 3 months on a 1.2M SF Detroit hospital by switching a concrete core to steel [52:43] [53:43]. The closing argument is that the controlling metric is dollars per square foot, not dollars per ton: one four-option study ran $1,000 to $2,100 per ton but $88.80 to $113.75 per SF [65:48] [66:20].
### Your Company Application
The bay-study and the dollars-per-SF-over-dollars-per-ton message map directly onto Ivan's takeoff and our existing doctrine that SF is the controlling input, not tonnage. This webinar is external confirmation that two framing schemes can carry nearly equal tonnage yet differ sharply in piece count, connection count, and therefore man-hours and price, which is exactly why our member-takeoff-through-aisc_validator approach beats SF x psf and why bid_rates carries separate fab and erection man-hour-loaded rates rather than a single ton number. The bolt-decision cost ladder is a useful Mario and Ivan reference for scoping connection type early (snug-tight vs pretensioned vs slip-critical drives both cost and field-bolting labor). The site-access constraint feeds Paul's erection-safety and ACP project-controls planning. Doctrine flag: NONE. The session uses no PEMB language; its "design build" and "IPD" references are delivery-method discussion, and nothing here conflicts with conventional-structural-steel positioning or the verify-don't-generate rule.

## Constructability of Structural Steel Buildings: Part 2
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iB0NLSM6H68 | Duration: 1:28:28 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
This webinar, presented by Dave Ruby of Ruby and Associates with project engineer Chad Fox, teaches constructability as a continuous design process rather than a one-time review event, built around AISC Design Guide 23 [00:00]. The thesis is that construction knowledge and experience must be infused into design from concept through field operations, not just at the bid stage, and that doing so improves schedule, cost, RFIs, claims, and profitability [05:04][08:09]. The single most repeated operating lesson for a fabricator-erector is that steel cost is driven by piece count, repetition, shapes, connections, and field labor, not by tonnage, so the controlling economy metric is dollars per square foot, not dollars per ton [55:44][62:53][64:23].

### Spec References
The speakers cite AISC Design Guide 23 (Constructability of Structural Steel Buildings) as the governing source throughout [00:00][43:23]. They repeatedly invoke the AISC Code of Standard Practice, which defines what is delivered and installed if the designer specifies nothing different, and which requires the lateral load resisting system to be defined on the documents [20:23][53:42][54:44]. They reference the AISC Specification and Code for steel buildings and its tolerances, including the camber tolerance of minus zero plus one half inch [27:36][27:36][28:09]. Bolt grades named are A325 and A490 [38:16][42:23]. No specific AISC 360 section numbers, AISC 341 seismic sections, AWS D1.1 clauses, or RCSC clause numbers were stated aloud; spec references here are general principles plus the named documents and tolerances only.

### Technical Details
Connection economy was demonstrated with a six-bolt single shear connection carrying 52 kips using 1 and 1/8 inch A325 bolts, where snug-tight threads-excluded is three bolts at $21, threads-included is four bolts at $28, pretensioned rises to $31.50 and $38, and slip-critical jumps to $68 [38:16][39:18][40:50]. The lateral system comparison (chevron double-angle bolted, tension-X double-angle bolted, bolted end-plate moment frame with column stiffeners, and field-welded moment frame) showed braced frames at roughly $1,900 per ton versus moment frames at roughly $2,100 per ton, which masks an $8.83 versus $13.30 per square foot spread [58:19][62:53][64:23]. The L/B stability rule was given: divide member length in inches by flange width, under 80 is stable as set, 80 to 100 needs a lateral stability analysis, over 100 will likely collapse after release and needs erection bracing [49:31][50:32]. Camber is only a means to compensate for concrete dead-load deflection and never establishes elevation; critical elevations must be defined explicitly with their own tolerance [27:36][29:09].

### Fabrication Notes
The standing rule is to maximize shop work and minimize field work, avoid built-up shapes, avoid framing deeper members into shallower ones, and avoid web connections into shallow wide-flange columns; columns smaller than 14 inch are generally not good to frame into and 6 inch columns only suit pass-over conditions [31:10][37:15][37:45]. Designers should use AISC table connections (single shear plates, single and double angles, seated and stiffened seated, standard shear clips) and minimize bolt diameters and grades to hold field inventory down [41:53][42:23]. Detailing cost tracks piece count and repetition far more than tonnage, and the shop worker, like anyone, gets faster and makes fewer errors with repetition [56:14][57:16]. Joints must be drawn to large scale (3/4 inch or 1 inch to a foot, not 1/8 inch) before fabrication to confirm gusset plates do not overlap and that net section governs tension diagonals, since analysis programs size on gross area and miss net-section reductions [44:25][45:26][46:26].

### Erection Notes
Site review is a design input: access, laydown, pre-assembly area, stock area, truck and crane room, and crane type (crawler, tower, luffer) all affect both cost and the feasible structural system [15:18][15:49]. Long-span trusses shipped in pieces must be assembled on the floor, which loads the floor and changes dead-load distribution, because a structure is erected one piece at a time and dead load follows the as-built geometry, not the completed model [16:20][24:31]. Shoring strategy matters: a 150 to 200 foot truss can sometimes be cantilevered to use two towers instead of three, or split into sections to use one tower, which on a tall building is large schedule and cost savings [21:55][22:25][23:28]. Member maximum column length should be maximized to avoid needless splices, but local union rules and the 30-foot safety-net trigger constrain how many stories of column can be set at once [32:41][33:11]. Field fit suffers at stiff truss nodes; reconfiguring brace framing into the weak axis of a chord makes adjustment easier when bolt holes do not line up [67:30][69:34].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The marquee bolting failure was a contractor whose entire project was rejected because he ordered pretensioned bolts and never tightened them; the inspector required the bolts to be tightened [39:49][40:19]. The Millennium Park Frank Gehry project, built within AISC tolerances, ended with steel joints up to 12 inches off the 3D model from deflection, temperature, and construction tolerances, which left the skin 12 inches from its attachment and triggered a major dispute, because AISC building tolerances apply to vertical columns and horizontal floors and locate only work points and floor lines, not the centers of curved structures [34:11][35:43][36:14]. A New York chevron joint with 14x730 columns and 14x550 diagonals was never drawn to scale; the diagonals were undersized because the program checked gross area not net section, producing a first-week claim to upsize to 730s [44:25][46:26]. A New York shear-wall transfer joint with a 14x90 column buried in a 24 inch shear wall carrying about 2,178 kips had no real load path and required a full redesign of the wall reinforcing; the repeated designer response was that it worked in the model [51:37][52:40][53:10].

### Bid / Cost Implications
The central bid lesson is that price per ton is a poor economy metric because it is only a back-calculation (price divided by tons) and hides the real cost drivers; dollars per square foot is the controlling figure [62:53][64:23][64:53]. In the lateral-system study the material cost varied by only $40,000 to $50,000 while shop and field labor swung by about $120,000, so material is a small part of the total and labor and schedule dominate [64:53][65:26]. The Lansing Community College redesign moved beams from 3-foot to 10-foot spacing, cut 700 members and 1,400 connections, removed steel tonnage, and added a fourth floor for $200,000 less than the original, still on schedule [72:37][74:40][75:40]. The Georgia crane building moved trusses from 25-foot to 50-foot spacing, removed about 835 tons, saved close to a million dollars and 16 weeks while making the structure stiffer by adding bottom-chord bracing (72 members to 172) [76:44][78:46][84:25].

### Your Company Application
For Ivan takeoff and estimating, the strongest takeaway is to drive every bid off dollars per square foot and piece count, not dollars per ton, since the L/B over-100 instability cost, slip-critical bolt premiums, and built-up sections are invisible in tonnage but real in price; the $21-to-$68 single-connection spread is exactly the kind of detail aisc_validator.py member data plus a connection-method flag should surface. For Mario shop and field bolting, the pretensioned-bolt rejection story is a direct field-QC checklist item, and the A325 versus A490 inventory discipline (one bolt type per joint, minimize grades in the raising gang's bag) maps to shop kitting and field bolt control. For Tekla detailing and the in-house PE stamp, the rule to draw joints to 3/4 inch or 1 inch scale before fabrication and to check net section on tension diagonals is a detailing gate worth encoding, as is defining critical elevations explicitly rather than relying on camber (minus zero plus one half tolerance). For Paul safety, the spud-wrench connector story and the 30-foot net trigger tie member-length decisions to fall protection. For joists, anchor rods, and ACP controls, the embed-oversize guidance (make the embed two inches larger to fix 50 to 75 percent of mislocations) and the steel-to-concrete-core tolerance mismatch are practical setting-tolerance notes. Doctrine flag: NONE. The dollars-per-square-foot emphasis reinforces existing Your Company doctrine that SF is the controlling input, and no PEMB language appears.

## Constructability of Structural Steel Buildings: Part 3
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wwswlb69lpY | Duration: 1:10:02 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This Ruby and Associates webinar (Jay Ruby and John Matusca) teaches constructability for fabricators, walking through Chapter 5 of AISC Design Guide 23, which addresses fabrication issues [06:43]. The central thesis is that early fabricator and detailer collaboration from project inception, not value engineering after bid and not field means-and-methods, is where a fabricator influences total project cost and schedule [07:13][15:34]. They cite the 1993 Construction Industry Institute definition: constructability is the optimum use of construction knowledge and experience in planning, design, procurement, and field operations to achieve overall project objectives [07:13]. The recurring point is that price per ton is the wrong lens; the real driver is man-hours, piece count, how many times a piece is handled, and number of shipments [03:04][05:07].
### Spec References
The talk is process-oriented and cites few exact sections. Captured references: AISC Design Guide 23, Chapter 5, with named subsections 5.1 complete and coordinated documents [09:18], 5.2 material procurement and shop drawing fabrication [20:39], 5.3 standards [52:00], 5.4 connections [28:53], 5.5 surface preparation [36:12], 5.6 galvanizing and coatings [36:44], and 5.7 shipping and delivery / piece sizes [38:16]. Standards named generically: AISC, AWS, ACI [24:45]; AISC Seismic Provisions for Structural Steel Buildings and the seismic response modification factor R [26:49]; the International Building Code Chapter 17 special inspection requirements [32:30]; AIST Technical Report 13 for mill buildings (tolerances more stringent than AISC) [58:00]; and Factory Mutual guidelines [28:23]. SSPC surface prep was cited as "SSP5 white blast cleaning," a misstatement of SSPC-SP 5 white metal blast [36:44]; treat the speaker's wording as approximate.
### Technical Details
On seismic, the geotechnical engineer sets the seismic site class, then the engineer has latitude in choosing R; a higher R lowers tonnage but drives expensive connections, while a lower R raises tonnage but reduces connection cost, a trade-off where fabricator input is valuable [26:49][27:20]. Member grouping was illustrated with a 20 ft bay of 200 beams where the analysis program optimized to four different sizes (W10x15, W12x14, W12x16, W14x22 as spoken); grouping cuts shop and field tracking overhead even at a small tonnage penalty [17:37]. A truss job with 120 pieces had 56 different truss types; cutting that count saves real money [18:38]. Camber was flagged: software cambers many beams an inch each, when a deeper, stiffer member can avoid camber altogether [19:08].
### Fabrication Notes
Bolted joint considerations include snug-tight versus fully tensioned versus slip-critical, and whether to use AISC standard connections [31:59][32:30]. Welded joint considerations include joint type, how many times a piece must be turned in the shop, welding process selection, and the weld-all-around symbol that is common on drawings but seldom necessary [35:40]. Surface prep and coatings were called frequent overspecification: interior steel not exposed to moisture may need little prep and no paint [36:44][37:14]. Case-study fabrication wins: dropping floor beams a couple inches so deck bears on top rather than coping, which on a roughly 450-beam job saved about 900 copes [46:00]; shop-welding short cantilevers instead of field-welding [45:29]; and a crane-girder design iterated from 60 tons down to 45 tons via a fishbelly so a shop with a 40-ton lift could handle it with an engineered lift [53:16].
### Erection Notes
Erector input is treated as part of the same early team. A laced crane column at about 13.5 ft column-line spacing grew to 14.5 ft over the flanges; the fabricator and erector jointly weighed shipping it as field sticks versus tightening the column gauge and sending an escorted oversize load [38:16]. On the charter steel melt shop, the fabricator laid wide-flange truss top and bottom chords on their sides with same-depth wide-flange web members so a gusset welds on flat with no spacers or shims, which also removed lateral bracing during erection of those trusses [52:14]. The melt shop, roughly 100,000 SF in three structures with the melt bay 110 ft tall housing two 200-ton overhead cranes, went from start of design in January 2005 to substantially erected in November 2005 [50:40][51:10].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The named failure mode is incomplete and uncoordinated bid documents: missing dimensions, missing members, and connection information reduced to general notes, which produce inaccurate bids, RFI floods, extras, schedule delays, lost profit, and an over-budget unhappy owner [10:52][11:24]. A concrete example: a partial fifth-floor plan of a 30-story building showed only a single sketch for a connection carrying significant horizontal force into a concrete shear wall; the real solution was an embedded shear plate detailed in Tekla that bidders did not price [29:56][31:28]. Inspection-cost traps were named: slip-critical connections require continuous special inspection while snug-tight require only periodic, and certain weld types require continuous versus periodic inspection, a large cost the owner bears [32:30][35:40]. Tolerance mismatch was flagged: bidding to AISC tolerances when AIST TR-13 or Factory Mutual applies causes disputes [58:00].
### Bid / Cost Implications
The whole talk reframes bidding around man-hours, piece handling, and shipments rather than dollars-per-ton [03:04][05:07]. An accurate model handed to the fabricator early lets him push a button for material list, piece count, and tonnage, freeing time to plan the work rather than rebuild the takeoff [22:42][44:58]. The headline number: a 144,000 SF four-story hospital under the constructability method versus a similar traditional design-bid-build hospital saved 17 weeks of total project duration (design 10 weeks, zero bid/estimate time, four weeks of award time gained, ABM prep under a day), with a stated steel cost saving that excludes the cost of money over those weeks [48:35][49:08][50:10]. Tightening method, surface prep level, R-value choice, and member grouping each move both fabrication cost and downstream inspection cost.
### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, the lesson is to refuse to price incomplete connection information and to run a drawing-completeness gate before pricing, which matches our existing doctrine; the 30-story shear-wall embed is exactly the count-gap our aisc_validator.py member takeoff and the SF/completeness gates are meant to catch, so flag general-note connections as a low-confidence RFI rather than carrying a minimum-connection assumption. Mario's shop benefits from the grouping, cope-elimination, and shop-weld-versus-field-weld trade-offs, and the snug-tight versus slip-critical and weld-type choices map to his AWS D1.1 welding lead role and to inspection cost we should surface in the GP report. Paul's safety scope ties to the erection items: oversize/escorted loads, engineered shop lifts of heavy girders, and removing lateral bracing during truss erection. Tekla detailing is directly endorsed (the embed plate was a Tekla model), reinforcing our viewport-on-every-bid practice and the value of handing an accurate model early. The R-value, seismic-connection, and anchor-adjacent content supports our in-house PE stamp and anchor-rod tolerance work, and the ACP project controls fit the early-collaboration and total-cost framing here. DOCTRINE FLAGS: NONE. The talk uses no PEMB language and contains no supplier names; note only that the speaker's "SSP5 white blast" is properly SSPC-SP 5, and the W-shape sizes spoken in the grouping example are illustrative, not validated weights.

## Got Stiffness? Designing Better Base Plates
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x_P1EezPXGI | Duration: 54:48 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
Barry Arnold (P.E., S.E., SECB, ARW Engineers, Salt Lake City) argues that lateral-force-resisting and moment base plates fail because engineers oversimplify them with P over n, the applied load divided by the number of anchor rods [07:57]. He says base plates are one of the most important elements in a steel structure, that if the base plate fails during a seismic event it is "game over" regardless of how well the beams, columns, and braces are designed [00:79], and that the real behavior must be captured by modeling the whole assembly (plate, anchor rods, grout, gusset) for relative stiffness, not by a single force divided across bolts [42:38]. The controlling idea is that base-plate and anchor-rod stress distributions are driven by the stiffness of all interconnected elements, so small geometry changes (gusset length, anchor-rod position) produce large force swings [35:44].

### Spec References
Speaker and slides cite: AISC Design Guide 1 and Design Guide 7 as the standing base-plate and anchor-rod references [47:22]; the ACI anchor-design provisions shown on the Allowable Anchor Rod Loads slide as ACI Appendix D, with D.5.2 "Steel Strength of Anchor in Tension" (phi-Ase-futa) and D.5.3 "Pullout Strength" (Np, phi-Np) [frame, ~39:00]; ASTM A563 for the nut bearing surface and ASTM F1554 anchor-rod grades 36, 55, and 105 [frame; 44:00]; and the University of Minnesota base-plate synthesis (free, web) as supplemental reading [47:35]. The speaker references "the steel manual" for nut width but cites no AISC 360 section, AISC 341 seismic section, AWS D1.1 clause, or RCSC clause by number, so weld and bolt detailing in this talk is general principle, no AISC/AWS/RCSC section cited.

### Technical Details
Concrete and grout are modeled as a compression-only spring P=kx; for 3,000 psi concrete on a 1-inch cube ACI implies about 0.003 in displacement under 3,000 lb, giving k of roughly 1,000,000 lb/in, not the 3,000 to 15,000 value most engineers assume [10:14][frame]. A higher spring constant lowers base-plate bending stress but raises anchor-rod force by about 16 to 18 percent through prying [11:35]. Anchor rods are modeled fixed at the base plate and pinned at the embedded end (length set by embedment, grout depth, rod diameter) to capture secondary shears and moments [13:01]. Prying force is governed by material strength (Fy, Fu), plate thickness, leg length, anchor-rod hole location, gauge between rods, applied load, and the spring constant [16:30][frame]. Moving anchor-rod gauge from 4 in to 8 in raised plate stress about 80 percent and anchor-rod force from about 4 percent over P/n to about 30 percent over [18:13]. Concentrating all rods on one side of the column drove a weld peak to 60 kips/in and overstressed the closest rods about 100 percent above the instantaneous-center-of-rotation value [30:56][32:41]. In the worked example, P/n gave 133.33 kips (1200k/9) but the stiffness-based FEM required 218.6 kips, a 63 percent increase; 2-in F1554 grade 55 became grade 105 [frame].

### Fabrication Notes
The anchor-rod capacity table flags a fabrication-relevant limit state that is routinely missed: bearing on the head of the nut or bolt, taken on the partial flat surface of an A563 nut, often controls over steel tension strength even for grade 36 rods [38:18][40:01]. For a 7/8-in rod the partial-nut bearing pullout (phi-Np) is only about 18.4 kips while a grade 105 rod develops 43.3 kips, so the nut bearing, not the rod, sets capacity [frame; 38:32]. Lengthening the anchor rod does not change the bearing area and does not fix this; the fixes are a plate washer, higher-strength concrete (3,000 to 7,000 psi), or a larger rod diameter [40:42][45:00]. The speaker requires continuous special inspection of grout installation because partial or voided grout (truncated cones with a hollow center) destroys the compression bearing the base-plate model assumes [15:35].

### Erection Notes
Grout placement quality is the field item the speaker stresses most: an interview with the grout installer revealed grout shoved in by hand with no packing around the rods and the job left half-grouted, which would leave roughly 50 percent voids under the plate [14:51]. He shows a field photo where a gusseted brace base plate was erected without approved or stamped calculations under contractor schedule pressure, with the supporting calculation later found to be dated 1964, and the connection had to be cut out and re-detailed in place [51:53][52:55]. He also shows a brace base plate with no stiffener on one side and no compression element to push against, which changes the rod and weld stresses [49:53][51:23].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
A study of 426 buildings after major earthquakes found 26 percent of moment-frame base plates and 29 percent of braced-frame base plates with substantial damage [05:52][06:01]. Observed failures were unexpected early anchor-rod failures, excessive anchor-rod elongation, large plate yielding leading to brittle fracture (the speaker calls the base plate a prime breeding ground for brittle fracture), crushing of grout and concrete, and weld failures between the gusset plate and the base plate [06:20]. Named design errors: using P over n, ignoring prying action, ignoring elastic properties and overall assembly stiffness, guessing a low concrete spring constant, arbitrary anchor-rod placement, assuming a thick plate cures everything (it takes over 2 in to negate prying in his simple model), and applying the uniform force method without checking that the base plate and column face are actually rigid [07:57][20:04][21:28]. The single most overlooked check he names is bearing on the nut/bolt head [40:57].

### Bid / Cost Implications
The talk is a design-method study, not a costing talk, so there are no rates or estimating figures, but several findings carry direct cost weight. Designing rods to true stiffness-based demand can mean a 63 percent higher rod force, pushing material from F1554 grade 55 to grade 105 and adding plate washers, thicker plates, or higher-strength concrete [frame; 44:00]. Trimming gusset length to save a little steel can raise anchor-rod force nearly 50 percent and weld peaks substantially, so a small fabrication economy can force a larger, costlier connection [29:18][30:56]. Continuous special inspection of grout adds a real field cost line that the design assumptions depend on [15:35].

### Your Company Application
This maps to anchor-rod design, setting tolerance, and grout for ACP and any lateral or moment column base, and it reinforces several Your Company postures. For Ivan's takeoff, anchor-rod sizing must not be read off P/n alone; the A563/F1554 grade and the nut-bearing limit state can change rod grade and add plate washers, so capture rod grade, washer, and grout f-prime-c as priced items and flag a stiffness check for lateral bases. For Tekla detailing and the in-house PE stamp, this is the verify-don't-generate case: the example where a fabricator built from 1964 calculations and unapproved shop drawings is exactly the failure our governance gates exist to prevent, so base-plate and anchor-rod connection calcs get a stamped, current basis before release. For Mario's shop, the gusset-to-base-plate weld is the cited failure location and deserves QC attention even though the speaker gives no AWS clause number; pair it with a real WPS rather than treating it as incidental. For Paul's field side and erection, grout installation around anchor rods should be a held inspection point, since voided grout invalidates the bearing the design relies on, and anchor-rod gauge and position set in the field must match the detail because small shifts swing forces 30 to 100 percent. No conflict with Your Company doctrine; the talk is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language, and it strengthens our anchor-rod, grout-inspection, and verify-before-fabricate rules.
