## Partially Restrained and Flexible Moment Connections
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SdoZaCu7YLo | Duration: 1:09:25 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
Dr. Louis Geschwindner (AISC VP of Engineering and Research, TR Higgins 2000) walks through the behavior, analysis, and a simplified design method for partially restrained (PR), semi-rigid, and flexible moment connections [00:30][01:32]. The unifying idea is the beam-line plus connection-curve intersection: a beam end develops a moment-rotation relationship from slope-deflection, the connection has its own moment-rotation curve, and equilibrium is where the two cross [19:37][20:09]. Because real connections behave nonlinearly up to a limit state (he shows a tested double-angle-plus-top-and-seat connection that ended in bolt failure), the design must verify the connection actually behaves the way the analysis assumed [18:35][41:24]. The closing "flexible moment connection" method is a modernized version of the old type-2-with-wind approach: design beams as simple, design connections for the lateral-load moment, then add explicit drift and stability checks [42:55][87:00].
### Spec References
AISC types of construction: type 1 rigid, type 2 simple, type 3 semi-rigid, introduced 1946 and carried through the 1989 ASD specification [03:08][03:40]. The 1986 through 1999 LRFD specification redefined these as type FR (fully restrained) and type PR (partially restrained) [05:11]. Section B3.6a defines simple connections and Section B3.6b defines moment connections (FR and PR) in the combined 2005 specification [06:44][07:16]. He cites the 13th edition AISC manual [06:13], the 2005 specification commentary on connection classification (and flags a likely typographical error there: it lists 20 and 2 where the referenced source paper used 0.5) [31:35][32:06]. The 90-percent and 20-percent fixed-end-moment classification thresholds are attributed to Omer Blodgett, "Design of Welded Structures," 1966 [29:01][29:32][31:35]. Source papers: Geschwindner, simplified PR beams, AISC Engineering Journal 1991 second quarter [13:25]; Geschwindner and Disque, "Flexible Moment Connections for Unbraced Frames Subject to Lateral Forces, a Return to Simplicity," EJ 2005 [43:26]; the three-parameter power model and connection databases by Goverdhan (1980s) and Kishi and Chen (1980s) [36:14][36:44]; Kim and Chen connection-stiffness measures in EJ [53:17]; Driscoll 1976 on stiffness ratios [55:22]; stability guidance from Joe Yura on leaning columns and a 10-story limit from a study by Mike Ackroyd [59:26][63:30].
### Technical Details
The beam-line equation comes from slope-deflection: Ma = 4EI/L times theta-a plus 2EI/L times theta-b, with the fixed-end moment wL-squared over 12 [15:29][15:59]. No matter what linear connection is used, a uniformly loaded beam can never be designed for less than wL-squared over 16, which matches the plastic collapse mechanism (wL-squared/16 at each end and at center) [23:48][24:50]. Classification uses the secant stiffness Ks: Ks times L over EI equals 18 for a fixed connection, 0.5 for a simple connection, and 2 at the 50-percent fixed-end-moment middle case [30:32][31:04][31:35]. Connections behave nonlinearly, unload along their initial stiffness, and after enough cycles reach "shakedown," after which they respond linearly within the maximum prior load [40:22][41:24]. Driscoll's three connection types: type A double web angle (0.2 to 0.76 of a rigid girder), type B top-and-seat angle (0.96 to 1.72), type C top-and-seat-plus-web (1.5 to 1.7); the flexible-moment-connection model treats one girder at twice its length as roughly 0.5, conservative for all but the most flexible connections [56:22][57:23][58:25].
### Fabrication Notes
This is an analysis-and-design webinar, so it carries no shop fabrication procedures, fit-up, or QC instructions. The relevant fabrication-adjacent point is the connection family itself: flush end plates, top-and-seat flange angles, double web angles, and flange plates are the typical PR connections, and a stated advantage is that moment capacity can sometimes be achieved with no welded component at all, which simplifies fabrication relative to fully restrained connections [09:49][10:20].
### Erection Notes
No erection sequencing, bracing, crane, rigging, or field-coordination content is presented. The speaker notes only the general claim that PR connections may be simpler to fabricate and erect than fully restrained connections, without procedure [10:20].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The central failure mode shown is bolt failure in the connection at the top of its moment-rotation curve, the practical danger being that the three-parameter power-model equations imply the connection carries moment indefinitely when a real bolt or limit state ends it; designers must check that the connection does not run past its actual limit state [18:35][41:24][45:32]. He explicitly states he did not verify whether other limit states would govern the example connections, so they "may not actually work" [64:33]. He also flags a likely typographical error in the 2005 specification commentary classification numbers [32:06], and the historical misinterpretation that type-2-with-wind connections need not resist gravity moments, which the 2005 specification corrects by requiring the connection behave consistent with the analysis assumptions [50:11][51:13].
### Bid / Cost Implications
PR and flexible moment connections are presented as potentially more economical, with lower total steel weight and simpler fab and erection, but Geschwindner is candid that decades of AISC-sponsored fabricator cost studies comparing PR to FR frames reached no firm conclusion either way, so any cost advantage must be proven case by case [09:49][13:25][30:30]. The barriers to wider use are lack of authoritative literature, no clear guidance on whether they are economical, and no commercially available software [12:53]. For an estimator the takeaway is that a PR or flexible-moment-connection scheme is not automatically cheaper and requires its own engineering study before it can be priced as a savings.
### Your Company Application
This is theory and design methodology, not a takeoff or shop input, so its direct hit on Ivan's member takeoff through aisc_validator.py is light: the validated tonnage path is unaffected and AISC weights still come from the validator. The value is to the in-house PE stamp: if a project engineer ever proposes PR or flexible moment connections to cut tonnage, this webinar is the design-method reference, and the firm must require an explicit drift check, a stability/leaning-column check, and a connection limit-state check before stamping, since the speaker himself flagged bolt failure and unverified limit states. For Mario's shop the practical note is that PR connections (double web angles, top-and-seat angles, flange plates, end plates) can often be all-bolted with no welded moment component, which fits field bolting and reduces shop welding. For Tekla detailing, the connection classification and the requirement that the as-detailed connection match the analysis assumption should be confirmed with the EOR before modeling. Doctrine conflict: NONE. The content stays inside conventional structural steel with no PEMB language, and it reinforces our verify-do-not-generate posture since the speaker repeatedly insists the connection be checked against its real limit state rather than trusted to a model equation.

## Staggered Truss System: Lessons Learned
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sZx5Zt5iSRw | Duration: 58:39 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
The webinar teaches the staggered truss structural system through two completed mid-rise projects: a 14-steel-floor hotel tower over four post-tensioned concrete parking levels in downtown Chicago (Staybridge Suites, 186 ft, 190x60 footprint, 10 ft floor-to-floor) and two rural college dormitories in southern Ohio (each about 45,000 SF, 200 beds, up to seven stories, 10 ft floor-to-floor) [02:02][05:38][07:10]. A story-deep truss sits on every other floor along a column line, and the trusses stagger floor-to-floor on adjacent column lines in the traditional checkerboard arrangement so the floor plank spans from the top chord of one truss to the bottom chord of the next [07:10][12:18]. The system is purpose-built for repetitive modular-dwelling layouts (dormitories, hotels, apartments) with a central running corridor, because the Vierendeel panel of the truss is placed at that corridor [11:48]. The headline benefit is a low floor-to-floor height with everything prefabricated for fast erection.
### Spec References
The presenters cite AISC Design Guide 14 (staggered truss framing) as the primary reference, downloadable free for AISC members [01:32], and AISC Design Guide 19 (fire resistance) for a section devoted to staggered truss protection with UL assemblies, a guide their office co-authored [20:55]. No AISC 360 chapter, AISC 341 seismic section, AWS D1.1 clause, RCSC, or Table number was spoken aloud. The seismic discussion stays general: the speaker notes Design Guide 14 addresses some seismic detailing and that plastic hinge locations are typically detailed in the Vierendeel panel, but cites no AISC 341 section because both projects were wind-controlled [18:22]. Treat every other engineering point here as general principles, no section cited.
### Technical Details
The common truss is a Pratt configuration so the longer diagonals carry tension and the verticals carry compression, with diagonals economically set at 45 to 60 degrees and a Vierendeel panel centered at the corridor [11:48][12:18]. Design Guide 14 suggests double channels for tension diagonals and tubes (HSS) for compression verticals [33:39]. Engineers are told to keep diagonal-member stress ratios at or below about 0.80 to 0.85 so shear-lag and effective-area reductions still permit a workable connection [12:48]. Trusses resist lateral load in the short direction, often giving lateral resistance "for free" once sized for gravity, with rigid moment frames in the long direction; Staybridge instead hid brace frames behind elevator shafts to avoid expensive moment connections [04:06][15:20]. Diaphragm design is treated as central because of the vertical irregularity: lateral force enters the top chord, passes through the web to the bottom chord, then must transfer through the diaphragm to adjacent trusses one bay over since no vertical element sits below that bottom chord. The team drew shear and moment diagrams for every story in both directions and designed chord forces from the diaphragm moment divided by diaphragm depth [25:00][27:32].
### Fabrication Notes
Truss chord flanges must be wide enough for plank bearing on both sides plus the grouted joint over the chord; with a roughly 2 in plank bearing each side and a 4 in grouted joint, chords needed at least 8 in flange width, with 10 to 12 in more ideal [16:50]. Bottom-chord gusset plates run large because the planks must seat on either side (an 8 to 10 in plank plus about 2 in clearance), and pre-composite loads can drive gusset design through whitmore buckling over that length [17:21]. Fabricators debate weight optimization versus truss repetition: designing one worst-case truss and repeating it lets the shop keep a jig and consistent workable gauges, while Staybridge optimized each truss for weight so upper-floor trusses are lighter [29:35][30:05]. Section availability should be confirmed early with a small rural fabricator. Headed (Nelson) studs on the chords are easier to apply in the shop, but the team flagged the shop-applied stud tripping hazard during erection as a coordination item [47:22]. Large completed truss assemblies consume storage space when a delivery-to-erection gap occurs, as happened at Staybridge [39:45].
### Erection Notes
The dormitory specification required a signed and sealed erection plan from the fabricator/erector, and the design engineer ended up assisting that sequence [40:15]. On the stepped hilly site, erection started at the small top-of-hill end to build a stable mass, then worked down [40:45]. The governing erection problem is bracing the truss top chord, which wants to go into compression before the diaphragm exists: the crew used temporary X cable bracing to plumb the frame and carry short-direction load before moment frames and diaphragm were in place, then braced the top chord with cables, set precast to the first Vierendeel vertical, added pipe braces from the top chord down into the precast, removed the cable bracing, and ran the remaining precast, repeating truss by truss [42:18][43:19][44:21]. Pipe braces were anchored with drilled anchors into the precast and a temporary welded tab on the chord, later removed and patched under the topping slab [46:21]. It is advantageous for one erector to set both trusses and plank, and the precast used for erection stability must be detailed in step with the steel [31:07][41:17]. In an urban site with near-zero laydown, two trusses arrive per truck and the crane lifts each truss directly off the truck into place [05:07].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The named field error is treating erection-stability embed plates as a later batch job: at Staybridge the contractor erected nearly a full floor of precast plank with not a single embed plate welded, planning to weld three floors at once, which defeats the embed plates' erection-stability purpose until the engineer required welding as the crew progressed [33:08]. A coordination failure was late MEP input: the electrical engineer (a design-build sub added partway and not on the design team) needed conduit in the plane of the steel, forcing 5 in circular web penetrations through truss chords; circular holes and a forces check avoided expensive angle-and-plate reinforcing [23:29][24:00]. Other recurring issues are gusset plates protruding past the Vierendeel vertical into the finished corridor wall [38:12], combined truss-plus-precast camber eating a 2 in topping down to about a quarter inch [47:52], and an expected crack in the topping along the truss chord line even with fiber and joint reinforcing, since deflection and camber are lost where two precast pieces butt together [48:55]. Plank blockouts at exterior columns and exterior-truss gussets (a 4 ft blockout at one exterior truss) left voids needing a cantilevered-plank or bent-plate detail to support cladding [52:28].
### Bid / Cost Implications
The headline commercial driver is speed: everything is prefabricated, the truck delivers and the crane sets directly, and the speaker cites a referenced Arizona project that erected roughly 12 floors of trusses and plank in about 19 days, with a normal pace of a floor every week or two when well coordinated [54:01][57:08]. An untopped plank system (used at Staybridge and described as AISC-endorsed) removes the concrete subcontractor and wet trades above the foundation, since everything becomes prefabricated trusses, precast plank, and site-mixed grout, saving time and money, but it makes the grouted joints critical for diaphragm shear and demands a willing supplier [51:28][52:28]. The system steel weight came in lower than a traditional composite steel frame; the speaker recalled an order of about 12 to 13 psf from a fabricator study but explicitly would not state it with certainty, and could not recall his own project's number [56:37]. Early involvement of GC, fabricator, and plank supplier is repeatedly tied to cost, and is harder to secure on a hard-bid project [49:57][50:28].
### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, the staggered-truss psf figures here (about 12 to 13 psf, speaker-uncertain) are anecdotal and must never seed a tonnage number; the doctrine member takeoff through aisc_validator.py still governs, and the speaker himself modeling verify-don't-generate by refusing to state the psf without certainty supports that posture. The dorm geometry (24 ft 8 in bays, 48 ft 2 in to 54 ft 2 in truss spans, 45,000 SF per building, 200 beds) is a clean Tekla-detailing test case for repetitive bay grids, and the system maps to ACP project controls through its core lesson that erection sequencing, embed-plate weld-as-you-go discipline, and plank-supplier coordination drive schedule. For Mario's shop crew, watch chord flange width (at least 8 in for plank bearing plus a 4 in grouted joint), oversized bottom-chord gusset plates, and the shop-versus-field timing of headed studs; for Mario's welding lead role, the embed-plate-must-be-welded-as-erected rule is the named field failure to enforce. For Paul's safety scope, the top-chord buckling risk before the diaphragm exists, the temporary X cable and pipe bracing, and drilled anchors into precast are the live erection hazards. The in-house PE stamp directly covers the signed and sealed erection plan the spec required. No AISC 360, 341, AWS D1.1, or RCSC section was cited, so any future Your Company use of this material must add its own validated spec basis rather than borrow numbers from the talk. Doctrine flag: NONE; the content is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language and no supplier names introduced.

## Connection Design: Dealing with Load Path, Transfer Forces and Apparent Lack of Joint Equilibrium
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-_1h4muNI7k | Duration: 1:16:26 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
Bill Merrill, a 43-year connection-design specialist, argues that modern 3D analysis software produces members and reactions in perfect node equilibrium, but the data handed to the fabricator and detailer for connection design is routinely incomplete, specifically the transfer forces that pass from one side of a joint through the connection [09:12][73:54]. The central distinction is between the actual axial load in a member and the transfer force across a connection: they are equal only when the bay containing the load has no vertical bracing (and no horizontal brace contributing an out-of-plane component) [32:51][68:21]. Because envelope forces from 250 load cases are signed and governed by different cases, joints commonly appear out of equilibrium, and the practical job is to design adequate connections anyway by tracing the intended load path, computing transfer forces, and adding selective redundancy [12:51][75:28].

### Spec References
The speaker repeatedly cites the AISC Code of Standard Practice: Section 3.1.2 for the SER's obligation to show pertinent axial and transfer loads [21:37][45:33], and Section 3.1.1 for the engineer-of-record check of panel zone shear / web doubler identification [45:33]. He references the AISC 13th edition Manual for the panel zone shear figure and method [41:49], and contrasts two brace-connection methods named verbatim: the older "direct force method" versus the AISC-endorsed "uniform force method" [46:35][47:35]. He names CJP flange welds as the common moment-connection-to-column detail [42:52]. He cites the common "50% UDL" shear convention for non-composite simple shear connections [69:47][74:25]. No AISC 341 seismic section, AWS D1.1 clause number, RCSC section, or Design Guide number is cited.

### Technical Details
The talk covers a knee brace (kicker) where the beam carries an unshown axial load that must be designed for [16:25]; a stadium raker carrying an 800 kip axial load that overstressed a collateral beam [24:08]; concurrent gravity and wind transfer forces in braced frames, including beams with zero axial load that still carry a transfer load from a brace's horizontal component [29:17]; out-of-plane vertical force in a purlin with no axial load but a major transfer load from the X-component of the brace plus the X-component of the roof horizontal bracing [39:47]; panel zone shear requiring signed moments MU1 and MU2 plus the story shear [41:49]; tension-only and tension-compression bracing load-flow permutations that must be modeled brace-by-brace [46:03][49:11]; a transfer-force algorithm developed over a two-day meeting for a 6,000-node, 4,000-member, 250-load-case airplane hangar [56:00]; and a 439 ft truss continuous over a center tower where knee braces (14x90) and columns (10x49) picked up 164 to 292 kip gravity loads through stiffness, resolved with a redundant node, a chord run continuous to a splice, and a transfer girder checked for the full gravity load [62:06][70:18].

### Fabrication Notes
The fabricator's connection PE (the "CPE") may compute transfer forces for simple topology but should require the SER to provide them for complex topology and loading [40:49][41:19]. The algorithm rule is that every member connects to its supporting gusset for its listed force, then the higher-order transfer terms are summed per joint layer and the smaller of two opposing transverse sums is taken, not the larger [58:31][61:35]. The 439 ft truss detail ran the chord continuously through a fitted node plate to a splice away from the panel point so the large axial transfer was relocated to the splice rather than concentrated at the node [70:50]. Detailing software (SDS2 is named) can silently insert a wrong assumed transfer force when a component is missing, so fit-up forces must be verified against the correct transfer load, not the member's full axial load [31:20][48:08].

### Erection Notes
Erection content is light. The speaker notes false work was needed to hold a cantilever during construction of a diagrid building [03:36], and that the stadium raker error required field retrofit of connections originally designed only for shear [18:00]. A general theme is that without connections the mill would ship straight to site and the erector would send it back, framing the connection as the load-path element the erector relies on [11:20]. No crane, rigging, or sequencing procedure is given.

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Named failures: a W24 beam-to-column connection designed for shear only while the kicker carried 160-plus kips, requiring field retrofit [18:00]; a stadium beam overstressed by an 800 kip raker, a third of the beam cut away and replaced with a larger W24 alternate to avoid heavy web doubler plates [25:08]; a power-industry "yardstick building" where deleting a column and adding wind ties let the ties carry gravity load against design intent, an unsafe redistribution caught only by an in-house review team [50:15][53:55]; detailers modeling the full member axial load (for example 25 kips) as the transfer force when the true transfer was only 5 kips, producing connections heavier than needed [31:20]; and panel zone shear "checked" by canceling equal opposing beam capacities so no doubler appears needed, which is not a valid check without the story shear [44:29].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Missing transfer-force data is a bid-stage risk: the speaker recommends the fabricator bring in a connection engineer at bid time for a preliminary view of heavy connections (the 800 kip raker) to avoid moving to the litigation stage later to recover the money [27:11]. Over-modeling transfer forces (using the full member axial load instead of the true transfer force) makes connections more expensive to fabricate than required [31:20][59:01]. Conversely the hanger-job algorithm was not overly conservative and drew no fabricator complaint, with the speaker noting few want to save a handful of bolts in a large truss connection [61:35]. Two days of up-front transfer-force work on the hanger job is presented as cheaper than rework and disputes [74:57].

### Your Company Application
This maps directly to the in-house PE stamp and Tekla detailing workflow: Your Company's connection PE should flag beams and rakers with missing or unshown axial loads, request transfer forces from the SER per Code of Standard Practice 3.1.2, and never let Tekla or a connection-design routine silently substitute a member's full axial load for the true transfer force. For Ivan's takeoff and estimating, heavy lateral-system connections (knee braces, rakers, truss panel points) should trigger a connection-engineering review at bid time so an 800 kip surprise does not land after award; this aligns with our verify-don't-generate doctrine and the SF-is-controlling principle that a wrong input scales the whole bid. For Mario's shop, the CJP flange-weld moment connections and the relocate-the-splice-away-from-the-node detailing approach are practical fit-up guidance. The 50% UDL shear convention referenced here is consistent with conventional structural steel practice and our no-PEMB positioning. No conflict with Your Company doctrine. doctrine_flags: NONE.

## Connections: The Last Bastion of Rational Design
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ANit-hbBD2o | Duration: 56:56 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
Bill Thornton (CSE Corporation, longtime AISC, ASCE, AWS, and RCSC committee member and chairman of the AISC Committee on Manuals) argues that connection design is the one part of structural engineering still resistant to automation, because almost no software designs real connections beyond the simplest shear tabs, clips, and single angles in the AISC manual [01:31][08:09]. The unifying theory is the lower-bound theorem of limit analysis: any admissible internal force field that satisfies equilibrium and all limit states, with sufficient ductility for redistribution, gives a load less than or equal to the true collapse capacity [25:40][26:10]. The practical corollary he repeats is that the admissible force field that maximizes connection capacity is closest to the real collapse solution, so among several valid methods the one giving the highest capacity is closest to the truth and usually also the most economical [28:10][32:51]. Ductility is the non-negotiable caveat: steel works because it deforms and redistributes rather than fracturing like glass or concrete [27:40][28:10].
### Spec References
The talk is conceptual and cites few exact numbers. Named explicitly: AISC 341-05 seismic provisions [43:06]; the AISC 13th Edition Manual and its CD examples for a boiler-house bracing connection [38:31]; the uniform force method as adopted by the AISC manual committee [22:34]; the Whitmore section with the standard 30 degree spread [43:37]; and the seismic 2t net-section reinforcement requirement for braces [42:35][43:06]. He references a forthcoming AISC Design Guide he and Larry Muir are writing on gusset distortional forces [49:46][52:55] and an AISC Engineering Journal paper on gussets buckling under brace tension [48:46]. No specific J-section, table number, or weld clause was stated, so most details below are general principles, no section cited.
### Technical Details
Three connection families are distinguished: simple shear connections and moment connections, which have an essentially unique load path, and bracing connections, which are highly indeterminate with multiple valid load paths [08:09][19:29]. For static, non-seismic moment connections the flanges carry the moment and the web carries the shear; seismic and AASHTO bridge cases share moment into the web [17:57]. For bracing, he compares the KISS (keep it simple stupid) method from American Bridge and Bethlehem Steel, the parallel force method (Dave Ricker, around 1980-85), and the uniform force method (from Ralph Richard, around 1985-87) [34:23][37:59]. The KISS method puts the brace vertical component on the gusset-to-column and the horizontal on the gusset-to-beam, but it is not admissible unless the resulting couples M-sub-c and M-sub-b are carried in the members [35:24]. The parallel force method works on column flanges but poorly on column webs because it drives load perpendicular to the web; the uniform force method deliberately avoids load normal to a column web [36:57][31:47]. A worked comparison showed the UFM force field giving about 320 kips capacity for a detail where applying the parallel force field to the same hardware gave only about 30 kips [33:22].
### Fabrication Notes
The full-penetration fuse-free connection where every weld develops member strength is presented as the engineer-of-record's dream and the fabricator and shop's nightmare: every weld is CJP and must be ultrasonically tested, which is expensive and slow [51:21][52:23]. Seismic 2t net-section reinforcement forces oversized "barn door" gusset plates with reinforcement at both brace ends, leaving only a short stretchable length (a 9 inch example) [42:35][43:37]. Thornton's economical alternative rotates the brace to buckle in plane: plates welded across the toes of the brace flanges slip between plates extending off the gusset and bolt together, avoiding the large 2t gusset [44:38][45:39].
### Erection Notes
Bracing connections drive roughly 40 to 50 percent of the cost of erected structural steel, much of it in fabrication, erection, and interference with utilities [16:56][38:31]. The all-CJP fuse-free detail sends the erector "through the ceiling" because the joints cannot reasonably be field-tested by ultrasound in that configuration [52:23]. Seismic drift is flagged as an emerging field problem: target seismic drift can approach 2.5 percent (about 1 in 40) versus the 0.2 percent (1 in 500) of older design, which makes the gusset and column try to occupy the same space and generates distortional (frame-action, secondary, kinematic) forces that must be resolved by a fuse, a pin, or member strength [47:44][50:16][50:49].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Filling shear connections with bolts or designing for full UDL or half UDL is shown to be both uneconomical and not necessarily safe: a 3 foot W10x22 designed for half UDL carried a phantom reaction near 62 kips, roughly 8 to 25 times any realistic load, illustrated as an Abrams tank on the beam [11:46][13:21]. A field photo showed a supported beam connection with nearly twice the capacity of the supporting beam connection, both nominally half UDL, which is illogical and unsafe and required a field-added stiffened seat to pick up the summed load [14:54][15:25]. Seismic details that satisfy the letter of the provisions but not the intent are repeatedly criticized: columns too small to develop the braces, and 2t reinforcement leaving a connection likely to be detrimental to real seismic performance [41:34][43:06]. A WT brace with oversized gussets was photographed in the shop as a joke [55:27].
### Bid / Cost Implications
Connections are the only real differentiator between fabricators since everyone buys the same steel, so connection method is where money is won or lost [16:56]. A 40 story building with about 32 bracing connections per floor showed roughly a quarter million dollar fabrication difference between KISS and UFM, more once erection and utility interference are counted [38:31]. A Georgia power-plant SCR/scrubber job came in 2 million dollars below the engineer's KISS-based estimate by using the uniform force method and Larry Muir's variations [39:33]. Seismic detailing alone was cited as adding about 40 percent (and in one case 77 percent) to steel cost, triggering owner meetings to justify the increase, so his advice is to avoid seismic detailing where the design permits [40:34]. Specifying actual reactions and separating gravity from lateral moments lets the connection designer avoid needless doubler plates [18:27][18:59].
### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff and estimating, the headline is that connection method, not member tonnage alone, can swing fabrication cost by hundreds of thousands on a bracing-heavy job, so a bid on indeterminate bracing should flag whether the engineer specified KISS, parallel, or uniform force method and whether actual reactions and split gravity/lateral moments were given; the UDL-versus-actual-reaction issue is a direct estimating lever and pairs with our verify-don't-generate posture. For our in-house PE stamp, the lower-bound and admissible-force-field framework is the rational basis for any connection calc we author, and the uniform force method is the preferred admissible field for column-web bracing. For Mario's shop, the warning on all-CJP fuse-free details is concrete: CJP welds mean mandatory UT, so prefer bolted in-plane-buckling brace details where the design allows. For Tekla detailing, the 2t reinforcement and barn-door gusset sizing should be modeled early so erectors are not surprised. For Paul's safety oversight, the ferry-terminal collapse and the under-capacity supporting-beam example reinforce that connection detailing errors are the failure mode that kills people, not member sizing. No conflict with Your Company doctrine; this material is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language and aligns with our AISC-validated, verify-don't-generate approach.

## The AISC Seismic Provisions: Past, Present, and Future
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mIbyuEnUEek | Duration: 1:33:47 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is Jim Malley's 2010 TR Higgins lecture on the AISC Seismic Provisions (AISC 341), tracing seismic steel design from the 1920s through the 2005 and 2010 editions [11:38][12:09]. The controlling idea is the three-part philosophy of AISC 341: identify a target yield mechanism, designate deformation-controlled ductile fuses where earthquake energy is dissipated, then use capacity design so the rest of the system stays essentially elastic against the forces those fuses can develop [26:42][27:12][28:15]. A key consequence for fabricators is that seismic design works from expected material strength, not minimum specified strength, because the fuse capacity has to be the real capacity, not the floor value [37:35][38:05].
### Spec References
Cited verbatim by the speaker: AISC 341 (seismic provisions, 2005 and 2010 editions) [24:38][26:10]; AISC 360 (main specification) [30:19][90:23]; AISC 358 pre-qualified connections for special and intermediate moment frames [54:00][54:32]; AWS D1.8 seismic welding supplement, newly referenced in 2010 versus the 2005 Appendix W [31:22][41:39]; ASCE 7-05 and ASCE 7-10, including ASCE 7-10 Chapter 16 for nonlinear response history analysis [26:10][53:00]; ACI 318 including Appendix D for anchorage at composite systems and column bases [30:50][49:55]; ACI Chapter 22 for diaphragm coordination [46:48]; FEMA 353 (basis for the Appendix Q quality program), FEMA 695 / ATC 63 (system validation), ATC 3 and ATC 58, and the AISC Seismic Design Manual [73:57][89:52][74:28]. System acronyms named: SMF, IMF, OMF, STMF, SCBF, OCBF, EBF, BRBF, and SPSW.
### Technical Details
Width-thickness limits in ductile elements are stricter than AISC 360, with 2010 introducing the moderately ductile and highly ductile element terms tied to lambda-ps and the plastic limit [44:46][45:46][91:00]. Demand-critical welds require two toughness levels, roughly 20 ft-lb at zero degrees for all seismic welds and 40 ft-lb at 70 degrees for demand-critical welds, both from the FEMA/SAC research [42:11][42:43]. SMF connections must be tested to 0.04 radians of drift, achieved by project test, appendix pre-qualification, or AISC 358; IMF drops to 0.02 radians [53:30][59:07]. SCBF analysis in 2010 adds a two-level check using a 30 percent residual brace compression capacity to capture the unbalanced post-buckling force [63:45][64:46]. EBF links must be designed with strain hardening, about 1.25 for braces and 1.1 for columns, with all three links above a base column taken as yielding simultaneously [68:18][68:48].
### Fabrication Notes
Heavy shapes and plates carry Charpy V-notch toughness requirements on the base material, slightly more restrictive than the older large-truss thickness triggers [38:35][39:05]. Protected zones at plastic hinges are no-fly zones: no curtain-wall attachments, no shot pins for metal deck, only small spot welds for OSHA deck hold-down, and the engineer must mark them on drawings so the shop and field do not disturb them [42:43][43:45][44:16]. AWS D1.8 now governs backing bars, welding procedure specifications, and continuity-plate detailing that the 2005 Appendix W carried [41:39][41:39]. Column splices favor complete-joint-penetration welds because real ground motions move the plastic hinge through the story and can drive near-full column moment at the splice [56:34][57:05].
### Erection Notes
Bolted joints in seismic frames use fully pretensioned high-strength bolts with Class A slip-critical faying-surface preparation but are designed for bearing, so small earthquakes do not slip while major events use the bearing strength [39:36][40:07]. Standard holes are the default; oversized holes are allowed at braces to ease erection fit-up [40:38]. Lateral braces for moment-frame beams must sit roughly one flange width clear of the plastic hinge and never inside the protected zone, and the brace force at a hinge is about 6 percent of the flange capacity, a large number to deliver back into the diaphragm [57:36][58:07][58:37]. Column bases must be designed to the same force as the member above, putting anchorage squarely into ACI 318 Appendix D territory [49:23][49:55].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The speaker shows a Lehigh test photo where a stud connector placed over the middle of the plastic hinge caused a fracture straight through the beam top flange, a direct protected-zone violation [43:15]. He notes the recurring field problem of a plumber or other trade attaching to a protected zone unaware, which then must be repaired with the contractor [44:16]. A second slide shows a lateral brace mistakenly placed in the middle of a plastic hinge because the design engineer did not communicate the zone [58:37]. Appendix Q sets the QA/QC inspection tiers (observe, perform, document), with ultrasonic and magnetic-particle NDE required at CJP welds and other special locations [74:28][74:59][75:30].
### Bid / Cost Implications
Using the seismic provisions in low categories (A, B, C) buys a higher R factor and smaller members, but the speaker is explicit that smaller members do not necessarily mean a cheaper structure once the seismic detailing is added [34:31][35:01]. EBF strain-hardening capacity design can make lower columns humongous and inefficient on tall buildings, which is why nonlinear response history analysis is used to right-size them [79:36][80:07]. The 2010 cycle deliberately relaxed some 2005 rules, dropping the belt-and-suspenders ductile-limit-state requirement on connections to ease bolted-connection design [40:38][41:09]. The mix-and-match concept (special, intermediate, and ordinary connections in one frame based on demonstrated demand) is flagged as a future economic gain [88:51][89:22].
### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, a seismic job (SDC D, E, or F) means demand-critical welds, tested moment connections, and protected zones that all add cost beyond a plain AISC 360 frame, so the estimate must price the detailing tier, not just the tonnage; expected-strength material is a design input, never a member-weight change, so aisc_validator.py stays the weight source. For Mario, demand-critical welds carry the two-level Charpy toughness, AWS D1.8 governs backing bars and WPS, and CJP column splices are the norm, all of which belong in the AWS D1.1/D1.8 welding posture. Paul should treat protected zones as a coordination hazard: signage and trade control so no one shot-pins or attaches into a hinge, plus NDE access for UT and MT. Tekla detailing must carry the protected-zone marks and oversized brace holes; the in-house PE stamp owns the capacity-design forces and the column-base-to-anchor-rod path through ACI 318 Appendix D, which ties directly to anchor-rod design and setting tolerance. ACP is not in a high seismic category in Houston, so most of this is reference rather than active scope, but the bolting rule (fully pretensioned, slip-critical prep, bearing design) and the protected-zone discipline are good practice to carry. Doctrine flags: NONE. Nothing here conflicts with Your Company doctrine; this is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language.

## Performance and Behavior of Gusset Plate Connections
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VSod7wBtGtU | Duration: 1:26:59 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
Two paired papers from an AISC seismic session (session E3) on the inelastic behavior of brace-frame gusset plate connections. Charles Roeder (University of Washington, with Dawn Lehman) presents test-based design recommendations for corner and midspan gussets in special concentrically braced frames [01:02], and Larry Muir (with Bill Thornton) presents the companion work on vertical bracing connections under high seismic drift [57:45]. The unifying finding is counterintuitive: a gusset that is stronger and stiffer than needed performs worse, because the brace must yield and buckle while the connection accommodates large end rotation [30:36]. The design goal is to keep the gusset stiff and strong enough to carry the brace force and no more, so inelastic action stays in the brace and yielding is allowed across the gusset [44:58].

### Spec References
The speakers name design methods and limit states more than coded section numbers. Cited by name: the uniform force method for sizing welds and bolts to the beam and column [13:14]; the Whitmore width established by 30 degree projection on each side [10:43]; the Thornton method (30 degree projection) and modified Thornton method (45 degree) for gusset buckling [19:55]; the standard 2tp clearance rule for brace end rotation [11:44]; AISC seismic provisions and the IBC drift limits [44:58, 59:47]; the expected brace force RyAgFy for tension and RyAgFcr for compression with a 10 percent reserve [08:10]; demand-critical welds for the connection [27:02]; Ry = 1.4 for HSS tubes [09:41]; and an ASCE journal paper (June, prior year) carrying the weld-sizing equation [53:10]. Muir references an in-progress AISC vertical bracing connections Design Guide [58:46] and a Berkeley test written up by Lopez in Engineering Journal [61:54]. No AISC 360 or 341 chapter numbers are spoken; treat the rest as general principles, section not cited aloud.

### Technical Details
Roeder distinguishes corner gussets (supported on two edges, stable but force a large thick plate under the 2tp rule) from midspan gussets (one edge, less stable, rotate more easily) [16:21]. His recommendations: an elliptical clearance of 8tp for corner gussets that cuts plate size by 30 to 40 percent and lets the plate get thinner [29:02]; a 6tp horizontal clearance band for midspan gussets [18:24]; size connection welds to the plastic capacity of the gusset, not the brace force, because gusset bending adds demand beyond the brace tension [28:32]; use effective length coefficient K = 0.65 for corner gussets and K = 1.2 for midspan, with the buckling length taken as the mean of three Whitmore-related dimensions [51:37]. Recommended beta factors replace resistance factors since design forces run near 100 percent above factored loads: 0.9 for net-section yielding and Whitmore tensile yielding, 0.85 for block shear, weld beta near the usual factor [49:35]. Across 27 SCBF tests at UW plus multistory frames in Taiwan, well-designed specimens reached 16 to 20 inches out-of-plane brace buckling before fracture and roughly 2 to 3 percent story drift [25:29, 40:54]. Edge buckling proved an unreliable predictor and is effectively dismissed [20:55]. Muir's papers address distortional (pinching) forces when the beam-to-column angle closes at 2.5 percent drift, with a plate buckling check (three sides simply supported, one free) and fuse, pin, or moved-work-point details to drive distortional force toward zero [60:50, 73:38].

### Fabrication Notes
Welds joining the brace tube to the gusset and the gusset to the beam and column should be CJP of matching metal or fillet welds sized just larger than the steel thickness, set to the gusset plastic capacity [28:32]. HSS braces are slit to slide over the gusset, creating a net-section concern at the slot tip [09:11]. The elliptical clearance both reduces plate size and reduces yielding damage to the beam and column [29:33]. Tapered gussets perform well and improve constructability, though they can need a slightly thicker plate and show more yielding in the welds [46:00]. Muir notes that pinned or hinged fuse details are not easy to fabricate, and that end plates or angles forming a limited hinge are more palatable to a fabricator but cannot transfer large axial force [66:57]. A reduced-section fuse, like an RBS cut, can carry the axial force and still limit distortional force [69:29].

### Erection Notes
Specimens are tested with out-of-plane restraint to simulate the lateral support a slab gives in the real frame [24:59]. For midspan gussets, lateral support is often attached only to the beam web rather than the bottom flange, so stability leans on web stiffness [18:24]. Muir's moved-work-point detail uses long slots, an increased setback from beam end to column face, snug-tight bolts, and a single standard hole as a pivot so 2.5 percent drift occurs without the gusset binding on the column [70:31]. A concern raised was bracing the column through that single bolt; the answer was that added standard holes above and below give three bolts, the column bracing force is only about 1 percent of column load, and inch-and-an-eighth A490 bolts carry ample capacity [71:33]. Bolts are kept snug-tight to allow movement, though pretensioned bolts on clean mill scale would still slot before the gusset buckled [72:34].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The first UW test, built to conventional practice with the 2tp clearance, fractured its welds early because they were sized to brace tension while ignoring gusset bending [27:32]. Making the gusset thicker, the beam heavier, or the connection stiffer consistently reduced ductility by forcing the brace into reverse curvature and shortening the plastic hinge [30:36]. A buckling-restrained brace specimen rotated and effectively buckled because beam-flange fracture let the conservatively designed gusset lose stability [15:19]. Demand-critical welds showed stable crack growth several inches long, initiating around 1.5 to 2 percent drift, treated as expected rather than a defect if cracks stay limited [27:02, 85:26]. Net-section fracture occurred in only 2 of 27 tests, tied to near-fault tension pulls or overly stiff connections [36:14]. A bolted knife-plate-and-tee splice gave poor ductility because bolted connections stack limit states in series [34:08]. Muir's main failure mode is gusset buckling while the brace is in tension, from the closing beam-column angle, which then fractures welds (the Lopez test) [61:54].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Roeder's elliptical-clearance recommendation reduces gusset plate size by 30 to 40 percent and allows a thinner plate, which directly cuts plate weight and welding on every braced bay [29:02]. His pushback on overly conservative net-section reinforcement matters to cost: a strict calculation demanded about 4 square inches of added steel, yet specimens with an inch to an inch and a half, or none at all, did not fracture [35:43]. The beta-factor approach (0.9 net section, 0.85 block shear) yields smaller, more economical reinforcement [50:06]. On test economics, Roeder cites roughly 8 to 9 thousand dollars per single connection test and four to five times that per multistory frame, with about two tons of steel per specimen [55:43, 23:58]. Muir's CJP-everything detail with stiffeners is described as very simple to design but very expensive [65:56], while the fuse and moved-work-point details trade fabrication effort for distortional-force control.

### Your Company Application
For Tekla detailing, the elliptical 8tp corner clearance and 6tp midspan band, plus K = 0.65 corner and K = 1.2 midspan and the mean-of-three Whitmore length, are concrete connection-geometry rules to encode in any seismic brace-frame connection model. For Mario and the shop, the CJP-or-oversized-fillet rule sized to gusset plastic capacity (not brace force) and the demand-critical weld callout are the AWS-side controls; expected stable weld cracking under cyclic test is research context, not a shop acceptance criterion. For the in-house PE stamp, this is the source argument that overdesigning a gusset hurts seismic ductility, useful when an EOR or reviewer pushes for a thicker plate. For Ivan's takeoff, the smaller elliptical gussets and reduced net-section reinforcement lower plate tonnage on braced-frame jobs, but this is verify-don't-generate territory: tonnage still comes from the validated member takeoff through aisc_validator.py, never from these percentages. For field bolting on Muir-style details, note snug-tight slotted-hole intent and A490 use, which the erection crew must not casually pretension. Houston is low-seismic, so most Your Company braced frames fall under Muir's non-seismic note that the 2tp clearance is unnecessary when inelastic drift is not expected [56:43]; flag any genuinely seismic job (out-of-state, high-R) for these rules. No conflict with Your Company doctrine: this is conventional structural steel connection design, no PEMB language, and no supplier names beyond the speaker's generic acknowledgments. Doctrine flag: NONE.

## High Strength Bolting - Why isn't it Simple, the Way it Used to Be?
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kxitGn8zLJ0 | Duration: 1:01:20 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
Dr Peter Birkemoe (University of Toronto) traces high strength structural bolting from the riveting era to the present and explains why bolt design grew complicated as research drove bolt counts down. The central technical lesson is prying action in bolts loaded in tension: how flange flexibility amplifies the bolt force by a prying ratio Q/P, and why pretension, joint fit, and shimming control whether a tension joint survives fatigue [13:55][18:36]. The recurring theme is that fewer, stronger bolts create new failure mechanisms (prying, block shear) that simpler riveted joints never exposed [14:25].
### Spec References
The talk is historical and conceptual, so few clause numbers are spoken. Named documents: the RCSC (Research Council on Structural Connections, formed 1947, first specification 1951, then the Specification for Structural Joints Using ASTM A325 and A490, last edition cited as 2004 with another pending) [08:48][09:19][60:18]; the 1912 American Bridge Company specification from the Carnegie Steel pocket companion [04:07]; and the Guide to Design Criteria for Bolted and Riveted Joints (the "bolt guide" / RCSC Council guide) [28:58][30:30]. The speaker references "the new AISC" requiring a Whitmore-section check on brace ends but cites no section number [51:12]. Fastener grades named: A325 and A490 [09:19].
### Technical Details
Pretension is set near 70 percent of the bolt minimum tensile strength, and a key principle is that pretension does not change ultimate bolt strength; a rigid flange means the bolt does not "see" load until applied tension exceeds pretension [18:36][22:14]. With a real flexible flange the bolt tension rises from first load and at ultimate the relation is applied load plus prying force equals ultimate tension [23:50]. Several prying formulas exist (Douty, DeWolf, Struik/Delft, Kulak/Fisher, Nair, Birkemoe, Kennedy and others), all derived from similar mechanics; the speaker prefers the Delft equation for being intuitive and semi-empirical [29:29][30:00]. Block shear, the square-over-4G rule, shear-tearing models, and Whitmore section (a shear-lag effective-area reduction, distinct from block tear-out) are discussed [39:53][51:44].
### Fabrication Notes
The shift away from "all surfaces shall be painted" to assembling clean or rusty mill-scale steel is central; dry mill-scale or wheel-abraded faying surfaces affect slip behavior [55:04][47:46]. Shimming at the bolt line is required where flanges do not contact, and galvanized shims add zinc thickness inside the grip, which can cause loss of tension, so shim choice matters [37:49][38:19]. The speaker notes that turned bolts (within six thousandths fit, reamed hole) were the old secondary-rivet equivalent [48:16]. A325/A490 pretension target values appear in the RCSC manual by diameter [58:42].
### Erection Notes
Field practice and detailing are decisive for tension joints. Two case studies: a crane girder where a dished bottom flange left gaps at the bolt line, so pretension was lost and bolts fell out under crane load because the flange compressed [33:37][34:39]; and a galvanized HSS bridge expansion strut where bolts torqued in the morning could be loosened by hand in the afternoon, because afternoon sun expanded the member (added compressive P) and erased the induced tension [35:11][36:45]. The cure in both was careful shimming or a better detail. Snug-tight bolts may permit slight slip and are installed mainly to draw plies together and keep nuts on [54:32].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Loss of pretension from soft material in the grip (insulation, excess galvanizing) is flagged as a fatigue-killer; the Hartford arena roof collapse is cited where tension hangers had an insulating layer in the joint leading to low or no tension and poor threaded-fastener fatigue behavior [50:07][50:40]. The "banging bolt" phenomenon: snug-tight joints with fewer bolts than a slip-critical design, on dry mill-scale or wheel-abraded surfaces, slip under service load and emit a loud bang [54:32][55:04]. A field-malpractice warning: torque "cheater" conversion tables (torque to tension) are unreliable and should not be used; follow the RCSC installation and verification methods instead [58:42][60:18].
### Bid / Cost Implications
The historical arc is a cost story: research that recognized true bolt strength cut the number of bolts required for shear and bearing, shrinking connections and reducing fabrication and inspection cost [11:21][13:25]. There is "always pressure to keep connection costs down and reduce inspection requirements" [13:25]. The flip side is that slip-critical designs carry extra bolts that function as a safety and cost factor versus bearing-only designs, and that snug-tight versus pretensioned choice has cost consequences in the shop now that tension-control bolt guns pretension nearly everything anyway [57:08][52:48].
### Your Company Application
This webinar is the doctrinal backbone for Your Company field bolting and QC. For Mario Gutierrez (shop and field crew) it confirms that installation method (turn-of-nut, DTI, twist-off TC, calibrated torque) must follow the RCSC specification exactly and that torque cheater tables are banned; snug-tight versus slip-critical must be specified per joint, and faying-surface condition drives whether banging bolts appear [54:32][60:18]. For Paul Guerrero (safety) the crane-girder and Hartford cases show that loss of pretension is a structural-safety event, so shim-at-the-bolt-line and no-soft-material-in-grip belong in the field checklist. For Tekla detailing, gaps and dished flanges must be designed out and shim packs called on the model. For anchor-rod and field-bolting tolerance work the prying-action lesson means hangers and tension members need rigid-flange or center-shim details to control fatigue. For Ivan takeoff, bolt count is a real cost lever (slip-critical adds bolts) and bolting method affects shop hours. Doctrine flags: NONE. Nothing here conflicts with Your Company positioning; it reinforces verify-don't-generate by deferring all install and inspection rules to RCSC rather than judgment.

## Underlying Concepts to the Seismic Provisions
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=y0uufRnkYhQ | Duration: 1:29:29 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
Dr. Xiaoming Wong presents the two ideas that the entire AISC seismic system rests on: ductility design and capacity design. Because high-seismic ground motion can reach roughly 1g and a building designed to stay elastic at that level would be uneconomical, codes deliberately trade strength for ductility, reducing the elastic force by a ductility reduction factor (R-mu, equal to mu under the New Mark equal-displacement rule, [20:14]). The method is to strategically place "structural fuses," also called deformation-controlled elements per ASCE 41, at chosen locations that are allowed to yield and dissipate energy, while every other member is a force-controlled element kept elastic by capacity design [22:19], [25:21]. Wong's repeated thesis is that the hard, judgment-heavy part of the provisions is capacity design, not ductility detailing, and that a designer must first identify whether each member is a fuse or a force-controlled element before reading any system chapter [29:27], [60:30].

### Spec References
The speaker cites these by name: AISC 341 Seismic Provisions (referred to as the 2005 and forthcoming 2010 editions); AISC 358 prequalified connection document plus its Supplement No. 1 [07:49], [20:00]; FEMA 350 and the SAC program [06:48], [07:18]; AWS D1.8 seismic supplement [08:19]; ASCE 7 (basic vs special seismic load combinations, R, Cd, and Omega-zero tabulated) [10:22], [66:40]; ASCE 41 (deformation-controlled vs force-controlled elements) [22:49], [25:52]; AISC 341 Section 13.2a for brace KL/r limits [49:14]; AISC 341 Section 13.4a (also stated as 13.48-4A) for V and inverted-V brace beam design [80:04]; and the 2T gusset clearance noted as a commentary requirement [49:44]. Older load codes named: UBC editions 1985, 1988, 1994, 1997, the K factor, R-sub-W, and IBC [03:40].

### Technical Details
For special moment frames the target is a plastic hinge in the beam, with the reduced beam section (RBS) the only connection currently prequalified for high-seismic, weakening the beam rather than strengthening it because drift, not strength, governs [37:08], [37:39]. Concentrically braced frames make the diagonal braces the fuse, expected to buckle out of plane (preferred over in-plane) and yield in tension, requiring seismically compact sections with limited b/t, and HSS members tear early at cold-formed corners if b/t is too large [23:20], [48:44]. Eccentrically braced frames make a short beam link the fuse yielding in shear; the EBF is the only system with an explicit deformation check, comparing link rotation demand (gamma) against capacity, where a short shear link gives about 0.08 radian and a long flexural link only about 0.02 radian [54:19], [57:26]. The three code factors are explained physically: R combines the ductility reduction factor and system overstrength Omega-zero (from redundancy and reserve strength), and Cd amplifies elastic drift to estimate inelastic deformation [66:40], [69:47].

### Fabrication Notes
The RBS hinge region and other fuse locations are designated protected zones in every system, where nothing should be attached or welded; Wong specifically warns against shot pins or powder-actuated fasteners fired into the protected zone, because the resulting field repairs may do more harm than the original problem [44:37], [45:08]. Fuse sections must meet seismic compactness tables for flanges and webs to delay local buckling, so material and section selection at the shop matters for ductility, not just strength [42:00]. A key discipline is not to oversize the fuse: an oversized brace or link develops more force, which then drives up the demand on the surrounding braces, beams, and columns under capacity design [83:40].

### Erection Notes
Field detailing must make the intended buckling mode actually happen rather than betting on chance; for braces the gusset must be flexible enough to allow out-of-plane hinging, enforced by the 2T clearance from the corner so the plate can bend [46:40], [50:14]. The commentary notes that the 2T clearance is defeated once a concrete slab is cast against the gusset, so a soft compressible material should be placed next to the gusset to preserve its ability to flex [52:18]. Link lateral bracing is required to stabilize EBF links, with specified strength and stiffness, and lateral-torsional bracing of moment-frame beams limits the maximum unbraced length to ensure the hinge forms [42:31], [59:58].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The central failure shown is a "Pittsburgh style" or pre-Northridge welded moment connection where the intended beam plastic hinge never formed and the welded joint fractured instead, which Wong calls embarrassing because those welds were supposed to be capacity-protected [40:23], [82:00]. Other named problems: thin doubler plates buckling in shear in the panel zone during testing, HSS braces tearing at cold-formed corners when b/t is too high, and shot pins violating protected zones [44:05], [48:44]. He also flags a code-application error he has heard from engineers and building officials: using the amplified (special) seismic load to design the structural fuse itself, which is conceptually wrong because the fuse is designed at the level-two force, not level three [73:23].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Wong states plainly that ductility is not cheap and you have to pay for it through redundancy and detailing in exchange for the force reduction R provides [69:15], [69:47]. Capacity design means braces, beams, columns, and connections must be sized for the expected (not nominal) yield strength of the fuse using a material overstrength factor plus cyclic hovering, so those surrounding members carry real cost premiums driven by fuse capacity, and oversizing the fuse multiplies that cost across the frame [76:27], [83:40]. This is a concept webinar with no dollar figures, schedules, or estimating numbers; the cost message is qualitative.

### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, a seismic-system job means surrounding members (collectors, columns, EBF beams, V-brace beams) are governed by expected-strength capacity demand from the fuse, not by the level-two seismic load, so those members run heavier than an elastic-only read suggests and the takeoff must size them through aisc_validator.py against the capacity case, not the reduced case. For Mario and AWS welding, the demand-critical and capacity-protected welds at moment connections and brace gussets must hold while the fuse yields, and the protected zone is a no-attachment rule the shop and field crews must honor, which ties directly to D1.8 seismic supplement requirements over plain D1.1. Tekla detailing must build in the 2T gusset clearance and link/beam lateral bracing, and Paul's safety brief should flag that shot pins and powder-actuated fasteners are prohibited in protected zones. No conflict with Your Company doctrine: this is conventional structural steel content with no PEMB language, no supplier names, and no rate or AISC-weight claims to verify. Doctrine flag: NONE.

## Specifying Camber: Rules of Thumb for Designers
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zJk5FWaNHH4 | Duration: 55:21 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
Camber is a curvature fabricated into a beam or truss to compensate for deflection induced by loads, taken about the strong axis (bending about the flanges), while bending about the weak axis (about the web) is called sweep [03:38]. Presenter Erica Winterstetter (AISC Great Plains Regional Engineer) frames camber as "more of an art than a science," not a checkbox in analysis software, and a topic learned by trial and error in the field rather than in school [02:36]. The drivers are reduced framing weight and reduced floor-to-floor depth, where going from a W21 to a W18 saves 3 inches per floor that compounds across a multistory facade and MEP stack [04:08]. The controlling rule of thumb: camber is only worth it if it saves at least 5 pounds per foot of beam weight [08:14].
### Spec References
The speaker cites ASTM A6 for mill rolling tolerances of hot-rolled shapes, shown graphically in the 13th edition Steel Construction Manual Tables 1-22 through 1-29 [09:47]. AISC Specification Chapter A references A6, and the Code of Standard Practice Sections 5 and 6 reference ASTM A6 [09:47]. Induced-camber tolerances are in the Manual page 2-28 and Code of Standard Practice Section 6.4.4 [13:00]. The mill-camber tolerance for camber and sweep is 1/8 inch per 10 feet [10:19]. The 80%-dead-load camber guidance traces to two papers at the 1996 NASCC conference [22:56]. The R=3 seismic provision is named to illustrate that nominal pin connections carry minimal fixity [25:29].
### Technical Details
Mill (natural) camber comes from uneven cooling at the mill where flanges cool slower than the web and the beam arcs into a crown; at the A6 limit of 1/8 inch per 10 feet a 30-foot beam gets at most 3/8 inch, usually less, so mill camber is generally not a design factor [09:16]. Induced camber carries a negative-zero, positive-1/2-inch tolerance: a called 1.5 inches cannot finish below 1.5 inches and may run to 2.0 inches [13:30]. Transportation losses can run up to 25% of induced camber, partly offset by that positive 1/2-inch [14:00]. Camber is chosen for one of roughly 150 load combinations, so the floor is flat for only that single case [21:55]. Conservative practice cambers out 80% of permanent dead load (real connections give about 20% fixity versus a theoretical pin-pin); an aggressive stance adds superimposed dead and up to 10% live load, but that SDL-plus-live portion should not exceed 1/2 inch of the total [22:56].
### Fabrication Notes
Camber is induced in the fabrication shop, not the mill, by cold cambering or hot cambering [12:27]. Cold cambering uses a jig with two pressing rams at the third points, deflecting the beam 2 to 3 times the target so it passes the yield point into permanent plastic deflection while the elastic portion springs back as the rams retract; long beams (40 to 60 feet) are pressed at multiple points serpentine-style through the machine [15:02]. The pure tension/compression in the flanges means no residual stress is induced in the flanges, though the web is less clear [17:38]. Hot cambering applies heat at 1100 to 1200 degrees in isosceles wedge patterns (about a 30-degree apex) along web and flange, worked upside down so gravity assists, and costs about 10 times cold cambering (roughly 3 man-hours cold versus 30 hot) [19:46]. Camber is performed after the beam is cut to length and punched or drilled, so square-end members may need re-trimming [25:59]. Camber is verified in the shop in the horizontal position, never in the field [14:00].
### Erection Notes
Per the Code of Standard Practice, beams detailed without specified camber are fabricated so any incidental rolling or shop crown points upward after erection, so a beam never ships already sagging [10:53]. If a beam arrives with 75% of its specified camber from the mill, no further cambering is required, realistically only on a long beam with a low specified camber (a 50-foot beam at 3/4 inch where 9/16 inch falls inside the 5/8-inch mill tolerance) [11:24]. During erection, double-angle connections have enough play to warp into place on a cambered beam; shear-plate, tee, and single-angle connections may need short-slotted holes for fit-up, which do not bump the joint to pretensioned or slip-critical as long as load is perpendicular to the slot [26:33]. Camber differences between adjacent beams, and between cambered beams and joists or non-cambered supports, complicate deck placement and should be transitioned by trimming an adjacent camber [33:54].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Common mistakes include over-specifying camber (the speaker says always round down, specify in 1/4-inch increments only, never eighths or sixteenths, and never call camber below 3/4 inch because transportation losses make it ineffective and shops cannot reliably induce that little) [31:48]. Correcting an over-cambered beam by running it backward through the machine is the wrong fix per AISC because it induces strain weakening and fatigue-type back-and-forth action; the correct correction is mild heat in the 200-to-500-degree range for a few minutes [18:46]. Cambering moment connections (cover-plated, directly welded, or end-plate) is a frequent error because the differential pinches one weld root gap closed and opens the other or forces tapered shim plates [27:38]. Ponding from a flat-set slab elevation can leave shear studs poking through the slab or pull beams into deflection [30:46].
### Bid / Cost Implications
A fabricator bid is roughly 30% raw material and 70% labor and value added, so the economy is in simple, repetitive members and connections rather than minimizing weight [04:38]. At the example pricing (steel near $1,100 per ton, about 56 cents per pound), a $75 cold-camber charge equals about 134 pounds, hence the 5-pound-per-foot break-even; cold-camber quotes ranged $35 to $200 per infill beam depending on width, depth, length, geography, fabricator, and camber amount [07:43]. Hot cambering is about 10 times cold and is reserved for members exceeding cold-camber machine capacity, often plate girders in bridge work [21:20]. A worked example showed a cambered W21x44 jumping to W21x83 and a cambered W18x35 jumping to W18x65 when camber is removed, illustrating the weight-versus-labor trade [38:44].
### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, encode the 5-pound-per-foot break-even and the do-not-camber filters (spans under 24 feet, depths under 14 inches or over 44 inches, webs 1/4 inch or thinner, tapered or point-loaded members) so estimate-grade sizing through aisc_validator.py flags where camber pays versus where it just adds labor; quote ranges of $35 to $200 cold and roughly 10x for hot. For Mario's shop, the cold jig (third-point rams, push 2 to 3x target) and the negative-zero / positive-1/2-inch verification in the horizontal position are the QC standard; correct over-camber with 200-to-500-degree heat, never reverse-press. For Mario as AWS D1.1 welding lead, do not cold-camber beams that will get welded cover plates and avoid cambering directly welded moment connections where root gaps distort. Tekla detailing should set camber after cut/punch and re-trim square ends, use short-slotted holes on shear-plate fit-up, and transition adjacent beam-and-joist cambers for clean deck placement. For joists and field bolting at ACP, match beam and joist camber on column lines and adjust joist seat depth on a cambered girder. The in-house PE stamp should specify 1/4-inch increments, round down, hold the SDL-plus-live portion to 1/2 inch, and account for up to 25% transport loss. Doctrine conflict: NONE.

## SSPC Surface Preparation - Shop Painting of Structural Steel
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oKpWGYZFaR4 | Duration: 1:14:00 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is a three-part AISC conference session on protecting fabricated structural steel: SSPC surface preparation standards (Bill Shope, SSPC), corrosion and fire-protection coatings (Andrew Smith, International Paints), and architecturally exposed structural steel or AESS (Todd Elwood, AISC). The unifying message is that coating performance is bought at the surface-preparation stage, not the paint can. As the coatings speaker put it, "you only get one chance to paint steel properly and that's when it's new" at fabrication [47:12], because mill scale, salts, and contaminants must be removed and a sharp angular profile created before any coating is applied [47:43].
### Spec References
SSPC surface-prep standards named verbatim: SP 1 solvent cleaning, SP 2 hand-tool cleaning, SP 3 power-tool cleaning, SP 5 white-metal blast, SP 6 commercial blast, SP 7 brush-off (sweep) blast, SP 10 near-white blast, SP 11 power tool to bare metal, SP 15 commercial-grade power tool [03:07][12:20][50:14]. Visual guides VIS 1 (dry abrasive), VIS 2 (degrees of rust), VIS 3 (power tool), VIS 4 (water blasting), VIS 5 (slurry) [08:46]. Abrasive standards AB 1, AB 2, AB 3 [12:51]. Certification programs SSPC QP 3 (shop painting) and AISC SPE (Sophisticated Paint Endorsement), being harmonized under ANSI public-comment procedures [15:56]. Coatings standards ISO 12944 for system selection, ISO 4628 breakdown grade RI3, and ASTM B117 salt-spray test [31:18][32:50]. AESS: AISC Code of Standard Practice sections 2.1 (what is structural steel), 2.2 (exclusions: cold-formed, cables, castings), 10.2 (AESS tolerances), 10.3 (fabricator special care), 10.4 (erector special care) [54:51][57:55][58:27].
### Technical Details
Cleanliness levels are defined by foreign matter remaining per nine-square-inch area: SP 5 white metal removes all foreign matter (cleanest), SP 10 near-white allows light staining and is the level typically required to strip all mill scale from new steel, SP 6 commercial allows 33 percent staining, SP 7 brush-off just roughens intact coatings [06:42][07:14][07:45]. The written consensus standard in the SSPC red book always holds legal precedence over the reference photographs [13:21]. Profile matters: angular grit produces a sharp peak profile and far greater surface area for adhesion than round shot, and profile is measured with a profile gauge [47:43][48:13]. Corrosion needs water, oxygen, and an electrolyte; loss can reach roughly 200 microns per year in aggressive atmospheres, faster with pitting [27:15][28:17]. Zinc-rich primers (zinc silicates and epoxy zincs) are the workhorse because zinc sacrifices itself, demonstrated on a scribed B117 panel where the scribe filled with zinc corrosion products and showed no rust [29:48][31:18]. Steel loses about half its strength near 550 C (400 C used offshore as a safety threshold); intumescent coatings swell and char to delay reaching the critical core temperature, rated in minutes (a 60-minute example shown) [37:30][42:35].
### Fabrication Notes
SP 1 solvent cleaning is mandatory before any abrasive or brush blasting so contaminants are not driven into the steel [03:39]. Shop blasting commonly uses centrifugal wheel (automated) machines roughly three times faster than hand-nozzle blasting, up to ten times on repetitive identical pieces, and these suit straight regular members but not unusual shapes [15:24][48:13]. Airless spray is the fastest, most economical coating-application method; brushing and rolling are reserved for small repairs [35:59][37:30]. Recycled shot and grit must be cleaned in a recycler and topped with new abrasive so adhesion is not lost to oil or lead pickup [14:53]. For AESS the Code of Standard Practice 10.2 roughly halves general tolerances; welds get no automatic special treatment, so welds ground smooth, contouring and blending of welds (notably on HSS), continuous versus stitched fillet welds, minimized weld show-through, tighter coping, and removal or grinding of piece marks and mill marks must each be specified separately [57:55][61:01][62:31].
### Erection Notes
Field connections are bolted or welded on site and always require some on-site touch-up painting, with SP 2 and SP 3 the methods typically specified for field work [49:00]. Field surface prep by scraper, wire brush, or needle gun is slow, unpleasant, often poorly done, and risks polishing the surface, which harms coating adhesion [49:44][50:14]. The Bristle Blaster (a wire brush with kinked bristles that impact rather than brush) was cited as new technology able to produce field steel clean enough for zinc silicates [50:44]. For AESS, Code section 10.3 requires the fabricator to take special care in handling and shipping, and 10.4 requires the erector to minimize visible erection damage; erection field aids should be removed if the architect or engineer requires it [58:27][63:03]. A closing audience exchange treated shimming for proper member fit-up as an erection tolerance issue rather than a specific AISC requirement [70:53][71:55].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The recurring field dispute is contractors specified to SP 6 commercial blast but effectively held to SP 10 near-white, since SP 10 demands more labor and abrasive [05:40][11:19]. Agreed comparator panels rust over time and give a false target unless sealed with a clear lacquer barrier [10:19]. Applying coatings over existing corrosion or polishing the surface during field prep both compromise adhesion [28:47][50:14]. The named AESS failure mode is the disconnect where engineers specify only to the Code of Standard Practice yet expect seamless ground-smooth welds and tight fit-up that the bare code does not guarantee [59:00]. A concrete example: a castellated beam (cut and rewelded) supplied for a 60 to 70 ft high gymnasium roof drew a dispute over ungrounded welds that no occupant could ever see, money that should not have been spent [66:38].
### Bid / Cost Implications
Coatings deliver their protection at only about 0.1 to 0.3 of total project cost, an easily justified spend against an unprotected frame [25:43]. SP 10 costs materially more than SP 6 in labor and abrasive, so the prep class written into a spec directly drives the blast line item [05:40]. ISO 12944 ties system thickness to environment and required life, with example systems ranging from 160 microns (C2) up to 335 microns (C5I, fifteen-year durability), each thickness a different material cost [35:26][36:29]. Heavier steel has a smaller surface-to-volume ratio and needs less intumescent thickness, so section factor drives fire-protection cost [42:35][44:37]. The AISC AESS brochure includes a cost matrix showing AESS can add roughly 100 to 200 percent for the highest category-one steel (within 20 ft and touchable), with a user-defined column so only the wanted items (for example welds ground smooth) are priced rather than the whole category [64:04][66:07][68:11].
### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff and estimating, surface prep is a real cost lever: the spec class (SP 6 versus SP 10) and the ISO 12944 environment category and DFT should be read off the coatings spec and priced as distinct line items, and any "blast and prime" assumption flagged LOW until the prep standard is confirmed. AESS scope is a margin trap; the AISC cost matrix categories (1 within touch, 2 within 20 ft, 3 above 20 ft) give Ivan a defensible basis to price welds-ground-smooth, mill-mark removal, and tighter coping only where the occupant sees them, and to RFI the GC when a set says AESS but omits which items per Code 10.2. For Mario's shop crew, the order is solvent clean first, then blast to the specified SP class with an angular profile, then coat, with airless spray for production and brush only for repairs; field touch-up at bolted and welded connections is SP 2 or SP 3 and must avoid polishing. For Paul, the session underscores blasting and coating PPE and respiratory hazards (silica or silicosis from silica sand abrasive, lead pickup when stripping old paint) [14:23]. Tekla detailing should carry AESS designations and weld-finish callouts per member so the shop sees them. This complements our anchor-rod and field-bolting work without conflict. Doctrine flag: NONE. One watch item: the brand rule bars PEMB language, and AESS positioning (engineered, architecturally exposed conventional steel) is fully consistent with our conventional structural steel stance, so no conflict.
