## Composite Steel Joists - Standards and Code of Standard Practice
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tbf93V4k9fY | Duration: 59:06 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This Steel Joist Institute (SJI) webinar introduces the then-new consensus standard for composite steel joists, the CJ series, presented by Robert Hackworth, David Samuelson, and Perry Green [00:00]. Before this spec each joist manufacturer used its own proprietary composite-joist design, so SJI spent roughly five years writing a single ANSI-approved load and resistance factor design (LRFD) standard, SJI CJ 1.0, ANSI approved in 2006 and published in the 2007 catalog [05:45][06:16]. The system is an open-web steel joist with a concrete slab attached to the top chord by headed shear studs welded through the metal deck, the top chord acting as the compression element and developing composite action by horizontal shear transfer [09:21][09:51]. The joists are treated as simply supported members and are not part of the lateral load resisting system unless the engineer coordinates directly with the joist manufacturer [09:21].
### Spec References
The standard cited verbatim is SJI CJ 1.0, the ANSI-approved Composite Steel Joist Standard, published in the SJI 42nd edition catalog with weight tables and bridging tables for both normal-weight and lightweight concrete [05:45][08:21]. An ANSI-approved Code of Standard Practice for composite steel joists is part of the same package, with sections covering general definitions and responsibilities, composite joists and accessories, materials, inspection, estimating (section 5), plans and specifications (section 6), handling and erection, shear-stud installation and inspection, concrete placing, and business relations [36:42][37:14][39:20]. The speakers reference AWS D1.1 for shear-stud installation and inspection, stating the SJI guidelines are very similar if not identical [38:16]. They cite the 13th edition of the AISC steel code (steel manual / composite spec) for comparison of stud strength rules, noting the joist stud-diameter-to-top-chord-thickness ratio limit of 2.7 versus 2.5 in the AISC composite-beam provisions [25:52][28:58]. The SJI Technical Digest TD9 on handling and erection of steel joists and joist girders is recommended [37:14].
### Technical Details
A CJ joist is designated by nominal depth, series, then three factored loads in PLF, for example 30CJ2188/1168/420 where 30 is depth, 2188 is total factored composite design load, 1168 is total factored composite live load, and 420 is total factored composite dead load, because the manufacturer must check three load stages [10:52]. The top chord is designed for compression from non-composite dead plus construction live load, then a total composite check; the bottom chord is designed for tension from composite dead and live loads, with the target failure mode being ductile tension yielding of the bottom chord [19:08][19:40]. Design limit states include bottom-chord tensile yielding and rupture, concrete crushing, and shear-connector strength, with the slab analyzed by the transformed-area method and deflection by the composite moment of inertia [22:43][23:14]. Top-chord area runs about 50 to 70 percent of bottom-chord area, top-chord end panels are conservatively assumed non-composite, and joists assume a minimum yield of 50 ksi for chord and web members [23:48][35:40]. Chord angle sizes range roughly 2.5 to 6 inches, far more selection than the AISC manual, and studs run 3/8 to 3/4 inch over four deck heights from 1 to 3 inches [09:51][29:59].
### Fabrication Notes
The joist manufacturer carries full design responsibility once a CJ designation is specified, the same as for K, LH, or joist-girder series [19:40][20:10]. Composite joists are standardly not painted; when a customer requests paint it must be kept off the top surface of the top chord so it does not impede shear-stud welding [36:12]. Top-chord leg thickness is set as a design minimum so the stud weld does not burn through the angle, with minimum leg thicknesses from a nominal 1/8 inch to 1/4 inch and minimum horizontal flat leg width from 1.5 to 2.5 inches matched to stud size [24:49][25:20]. Joists are cambered by the manufacturer so the floor comes out level under wet concrete weight, typically 1 to 1.5 inches of camber for 30 to 60 foot joists, and because of pin-pin bearing the full camber comes out under load [32:35][33:07][34:38].
### Erection Notes
Composite joist erection and handling is described as no different from non-composite steel joist work, governed by SJI TD9 [37:14]. In the field the deck hides the joists, so crews tap the deck with a hammer at the joist span end, locate the chord, and snap a chalk line over each top-chord angle [39:51][40:57]. The deck must be drawn down tight against the top chord, ideally within 1/16 inch, to make a sound stud weld [40:22]. Studs are laid out ahead of the welder; one observed crew on a large project placed about 250 studs per hour, roughly one every 15 seconds [40:57][41:29]. Two bridging load cases must be checked during erection: the erector standing on the joist before cables are released, and deck bundles landed on the joist, since composite action is not yet available at those stages [58:32].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The named failure observed in testing is the shear stud placed in the weak position tearing out through the metal deck because little concrete sits in front of it; the standard conservatively assumes all studs are in the weak position rather than mandating placement [25:52][26:23][26:54]. A burn-through of a too-thin top-chord angle during stud welding is the risk the minimum-thickness rule prevents [24:49]. Inspection per the Code of Standard Practice requires verifying concrete thickness, testing concrete compressive strength, and inspecting welded studs for quantity and weld quality, with a start-of-shift bend test of a welded stud to a minimum 15 degrees from horizontal and a suggested one bend test per 100 studs [36:42][38:16][38:48]. A non-uniform or locally thin slab is flagged as a defect because it degrades deflection prediction, the UL fire rating, and stud cover [33:37][34:08].
### Bid / Cost Implications
The Code of Standard Practice section 5 covers estimating and lists the items that must appear on the plans for the manufacturer to prepare an accurate bid; a design parameters checklist in the catalog is faxed to the manufacturer with depth, span, spacing, slab data, and loads [37:14][43:34][44:05]. The headline economics: a worked 30-inch, 50-foot joist at about 37 to 39 PLF compared against a non-composite joist at about 56 PLF, roughly a 35 percent weight reduction, and field reports of 20 to 30 percent savings [46:40][47:11][50:20]. Spacing joists wider, on the order of 6 to 10 feet rather than 2 feet, yields larger top chords that speed stud installation and improve economy [41:29][52:26]. Secondary savings come from reduced floor-to-floor height (helpful under municipal height limits), lighter building weight cutting foundation cost, column-free spans, and faster erection [50:20][54:58][55:28].
### Your Company Application
For Ivan, the CJ designation string (depth/series/three factored loads) and the SJI catalog weight tables are the takeoff inputs for any composite-joist floor; these are SJI joist weights, not AISC shape weights, so they fall outside aisc_validator.py and must be sourced from the SJI CJ tables with a confidence tag, never LLM math. For Mario, shear-stud welding through deck to the top chord is the controlling shop and field welding operation: deck tight within 1/16 inch, keep paint off the top chord, run the start-of-shift bend test to 15 degrees and one per 100, all consistent with AWS D1.1, which aligns with his D1.1 lead role. For Paul, the erection-stage bridging cases (erector on joist before cable release, deck bundles landed) are the safety-critical non-composite conditions to brief before the slab cures. For Tekla detailing and the in-house PE stamp, remember the joist manufacturer owns the CJ member design; our model and stamp coordinate loads, layout, stud placement, and the engineer-of-record reinforcing over girders, not the joist internals. Joists are simply supported and not part of the lateral system, so do not assume composite-joist framing carries diaphragm or brace forces without manufacturer coordination. Doctrine conflict: NONE. One caution for outward copy: the transcript names manufacturer-affiliated parties and a "Vulcraft district office" [51:22]; keep any supplier name out of Your Company proposals and capability sheets per Tier 1, and screen framing type internally only.

## Quality Assurance for Structural Engineering Firms
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ofkHTRSZDPU | Duration: 1:00:59 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
Clifford Swinger, full-time QA manager at The Harmon Group (a 50-person, 40-engineer firm with offices in Las Vegas, Philadelphia, and Pittsburgh), describes a 20-year-old in-house quality-assurance program for the engineer-of-record side of structural work [00:00][46:49]. The program rests on six components: training for young engineers, design standards, drafting and CAD standards, a project delivery system, a server-based knowledge base, and involvement of a QA manager who performs reviews [09:14]. The driving thesis is that fast-track and "hyper-track" scheduling, complex codes, and over-reliance on computer software have eroded document quality, so QA must be ongoing across the whole design rather than a single end-of-job check [03:35][18:59].
### Spec References
This is a firm-management and document-quality webinar, not a code clause walk-through, so it cites very few standards. The one document repeatedly recommended as a template for a QA program is the CASE publication "962D, a guideline addressing coordination and completeness of structural construction documents" [07:09]. The speaker also recommends a trade book called "the contractor's guide to change orders" for understanding how contractors mine documents for change orders [07:42]. AISC is credited generally for two decades of guidance to show beam reactions on framing plans for connection economy, but no AISC 360 section, table, or Design Guide number is cited [33:29]. ASD and LRFD are named as the two acceptable design methods [10:46]. No AISC 341, AWS D1.1, or RCSC sections are cited.
### Technical Details
Lateral-system and computer-model judgment dominate the technical content. The speaker warns against trusting infinitely rigid diaphragm outputs that funnel 95 percent of lateral load into one shear wall when a flexible precast diaphragm cannot deliver it, and his rule is to never put less than the tributary load on any brace frame or moment frame and to envelope the rigid-diaphragm result [26:46][27:48]. For low-seismicity regions he insists on a seismic response coefficient R factor of three, noting engineers who used three-and-a-half or six drove unnecessary cost into connections without understanding the connection-design consequence [20:35]. He flags drag-strut load paths that rigid diaphragms ignore when a brace frame shifts bays, requiring an explicit drag strut and drag-strut connections sized for the real force, for example 150 kips [28:49][29:20]. He checks framing by hand-designing one typical beam, girder, and column and comparing to the model, then scanning all member sizes for consistency, and he runs quick wind and seismic hand checks (average wind pressure times sail area for base shear; approximate versus exact building period for seismic) [30:23][31:55].
### Fabrication Notes
The detailability of connections is treated as a QA gate. He cites a W40x593 framing into another W40x593 at a steep skew with a roughly 760 kip reaction that was virtually impossible to detail and had to be reconfigured for constructability [36:34][47:53]. For roof joists, where W shapes on the roof can be shallow, he requires at least a W14 framing into the girder so two rows of bolts fit at the connection [37:34]. He argues that clean, simple drawings using dittos for repeated members lower the fabricated cost per ton, and that small unintended variations (different cambers, 35 versus 37 kip reactions on otherwise identical W18x35 beams) should be enveloped to a single repeated mark [42:13][42:43].
### Erection Notes
The webinar does not cover field erection sequencing, crane, rigging, or bracing procedures. Its construction-phase content is shop-drawing review during construction administration and coordinating late loads (rooftop mechanical, hung piping, theater rigging, catwalks) that are not known until end of design [33:29][35:33]. Field topics such as column splices appear only as design-document subtleties: a splice four feet above a mezzanine floor that does not brace the column effectively doubles the unbraced height [39:07].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Named recurring errors include self-weight entered twice (analysis switch left on while dead load was also added by hand), the wrong R factor, missing or improper expansion-joint layouts that lock up the structure, unbraced columns sized off an unrealistic rigid diaphragm (W12x65 modeled where W14x211 was actually required for an 80-foot theater column), and a girder moved off a column line at the last minute raising a reaction from 36 to 100 kips into an unrevised beam [25:13][40:39][38:06]. He stresses drafting errors that cause structural problems, citing a 111 kip reaction that read as 11 kips and a decimal slip that hid a 155 kip reaction [44:17][44:47]. Missing items (reactions, sections, details, dimensions, member sizes, even an entirely omitted infill beam at a 15-to-16-foot gap) are called the hardest defects to catch, along with architectural-coordination misses such as a slab opening cutting a column free of its two-way slab [43:15][45:18].
### Bid / Cost Implications
The economic case for QA is fewer RFIs and change orders on increasingly adversarial fast-track jobs, where any missing information quickly becomes a change order [03:05][06:39]. Showing actual reactions on framing plans lets fabricators detail connections for real loads instead of a fictitious percentage of member capacity, which the speaker ties directly to lower structural cost [33:29][34:30]. Clean repetitive drawings with dittos are described as a way to lower a fabricator's quoted cost per ton [42:43]. The firm reports an insurance premium reduction for carrying a formal written QA program, and the program's cost is roughly one senior engineer's salary out of fifty staff [50:29][53:33].
### Your Company Application
This is fabricator-relevant from the buy side: when Ivan reviews an incoming EOR set for takeoff, the recurring defects named here (missing reactions, skewed or overloaded connections that cannot be detailed, omitted infill beams, decimal-slipped reactions, late architectural openings) are exactly the drawing-completeness flags our verify-don't-generate gate and the drawing-completeness check should raise before pricing an incomplete or review-only set. The speaker's rule that shown reactions let the fabricator detail for actual loads supports Ivan querying the GC for reactions when a framing plan omits them, and his W14-minimum-for-two-bolt-rows joist note is a concrete Tekla detailing constraint for Mario's shop and our in-house PE on joist-to-girder connections. The skewed W40x593 example reinforces our position to flag undetailable connection geometry early rather than absorb it in the bid. The drag-strut and rigid-diaphragm cautions are an in-house PE design-review checklist item, not a takeoff input, and the seismic R-of-three discipline aligns with conventional structural steel work in low-seismicity Houston. Doctrine flags: NONE. No PEMB language, no supplier names, and nothing here conflicts with using bridge/aisc_validator.py as the sole AISC weight source or with the locked BID_RATES.

## Non-Destructive Examination and Special Inspection of Seismic Welding
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gIBim_sQXUk | Duration: 50:30 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
Mike Mays, a welding engineer and SNT level 3 with 30-plus years in materials testing, walks through visual inspection, NDE method selection, and the special-inspection regime for welded structural steel, then narrows to the post-Northridge seismic welding rules [00:00][01:35]. The central message is that quality control is the fabricator's and erector's job while quality assurance is the owner's special inspector, and the two roles must agree the NDE scope before work starts rather than after welds are made [02:05][10:59][39:02]. He repeatedly stresses that NDE has no inherent code requirement in the IBC or the welding code; it applies only when the contract documents or the seismic provisions call for it [07:50][08:20].

### Spec References
The speaker cites the AWS D1.1 welding code as assigning QC to the fabricator and erector [02:05], and AWS D1.8 as the seismic supplement to D1.1 that governs seismic-critical welds, including Annex (referred to as the D1.8 annex) requirements that UT technicians be tested on real flaw samples [32:46][50:00][23:53]. For seismic design and inspection he points to the AISC seismic provisions and specifically "appendix Q" as the quality-assurance-plan source [32:46][33:18][38:32]. He references the international building code requiring 100 percent visual inspection in shop and field with continuous versus periodic inspection categories [05:43][06:14], and notes the code provision that NDE cannot be imposed after the fact unless there is intent to defraud or gross non-performance [09:23]. He mentions the older FEMA "yellow books" as superseded by the AISC seismic provisions for inspection [32:46]. Counting distinct citations: AWS D1.1, AWS D1.8 (seismic supplement + flaw-sample annex), AISC seismic provisions Appendix Q, IBC visual/continuous-periodic, IBC no-after-the-fact-NDE provision, FEMA yellow books.

### Technical Details
Four NDE methods apply to structural welds: radiography (good for bridge girders, poor for building T-joints, continuity plates, and stiffeners where film and source cannot be oriented), ultrasonic testing (the workhorse for looking inside CJP welds via sound-path trigonometry), magnetic particle testing (surface and near-surface, with dry, wet, and fluorescent sensitivity levels), and dye penetrant (only for ground-smooth surfaces such as cope access holes) [11:29][12:00][14:03][22:19][33:49]. He warns against re-checking a UT or RT finding with the other method because the two see different things [12:31]. Backing bars complicate UT because the unfused backing-bar corner mimics lack-of-fusion, and the beam web-to-flange curve creates a blind "gimme zone" at the lower flange, which is why backing bars come off seismic lower-flange joints [19:13][20:46][21:16]. UT is not appropriate for partial-penetration welds or fillet welds under 5/16 inch; use visual or MT instead [21:46][22:19]. Phased array is emerging for flaw location and sizing via tip diffraction, but the AWS code still compares to side-drilled-hole references and has no adopted criteria for the richer data [25:31][41:50].

### Fabrication Notes
The fabricator should run a well-defined QC program with knowledgeable people, because the speaker observes that those shops run far smoother for all parties [02:35]. Key seismic-fab requirements named: weld access holes (beam cope holes) ground smooth and inspected by MT or PT, since dye penetrant works there [33:49]; the K-area between web and flange flagged as a crack-prone zone of poor material properties that can crack even without welds [36:59][37:31]; and backing-bar handling where the steel backing typically comes off the bottom flange, the root is back-gouged, MT'd, and a reinforcing fillet added, while the top-flange backing is left and seal-welded to the column [33:49][34:52]. He notes that removing steel backing is time-consuming and messy, so some shops use ceramic or copper backing, each of which forces a fit-up root-gap qualification and a separate welder qualification, and melting copper ruins the bar and requires back-gouging the root pass [34:52][35:26]. Mocking up difficult tubular and skewed joints with deliberate flaws lets both QC and QA UT technicians prove they can find them [30:39][31:09].

### Erection Notes
The protected zone is one of the biggest field problems, and it varies by connection type [35:57]. He gives concrete violations the inspector caught and had to have cut off and redone: a curtain-wall subcontractor welding angles across RBS dog-bone flanges, light-gauge framing pins shot into the protected zone, and safety-cable holes drilled into protected flange areas, with the fix being to relocate the holes outside the zone while still serving the erector [35:57][36:28][36:59]. For lower-flange seismic welds the inspector confirms the welder pushes the electrode through the access hole and moves side to side, which takes longer; "angel wing" weld tabs give the welder a place to stand and access both sides [37:31][38:02]. He recommends raising the inspection plan and protected-zone constraints at the pre-fabrication and pre-erection meeting [46:38].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The worst case named is work accepted in the shop and then rejected in the field by a different inspector, which he calls a horrible situation [07:19]. Other failures: arbitrary inspector discretion in S-notes ("do whatever he wants") leading to disputes [10:27][11:29]; re-testing a flaw with a second method and getting conflicting calls [12:31]; misreading a backing-bar corner as lack of fusion [19:45]; the lower-flange "gimme zone" blind spot tied to many Northridge fractures [21:16]; slag left where a welder ran one side then the other without proper access-hole technique [37:31]; UT technicians who never find flaws being a red flag rather than good news [23:23]; and the industry-wide weakness that the post-Northridge round-robin showed most technicians scored poorly on real flaws, which drove the real-sample testing requirement now in D1.8 [26:33][27:04][23:53].

### Bid / Cost Implications
NDE scope drives cost and must be priced from the contract, not assumed; the speaker warns the big surprise is welding without expecting NDE and then having someone X-ray the work later, with the code forbidding owners from imposing UT or RT not in the documents [08:51][09:23][09:56]. Continuous inspection for seismic and CJP welds means the inspector stands at the weld, which is a real burden when the shop runs double shifts [06:14][06:47]. An approved-fabricator or AISC-certified-fabricator status can drop shop welds from continuous to periodic inspection, saving owner money, though seismic provisions still mandate continuous inspection and the fabricator must still negotiate who performs the NDT since AISC-certified shops generally do not run their own [06:47][27:34][29:06][47:11]. Some engineers allow a UT reduction from 100 percent to 25 percent on welders with a low reject history (roughly 40 welds under about 5 percent rejects), which is a documented schedule and cost lever [48:12]. Repairing a flaw that fails the AWS quality code is usually cheaper than the fracture-mechanics flaw-sizing analysis route, which only about five technicians nationwide can do accurately [25:31].

### Your Company Application
This webinar maps directly onto Mario Gutierrez as AWS D1.1 welding lead: if Your Company ever takes seismic moment-frame work, his welders need separate D1.8 procedure and welder qualifications for ceramic or copper backing, K-area awareness, and access-hole technique, and the shop should mock up hard tubular and skewed joints with deliberate flaws to prove both QC and any third-party QA can find them. Ivan's takeoff and bid should price NDE from the S-notes and Division 05 spec rather than assuming it, flag continuous-inspection labor for any seismic or CJP scope, and treat the 100-to-25-percent UT reduction and approved-fabricator periodic-inspection status as explicit estimating levers; this reinforces our verify-don't-generate posture since the NDE line item costs real money if missed. Tekla detailing should carry the protected zone on the model so safety-cable holes, pins, and attachments stay clear, and Paul Guerrero should coordinate the safety-cable and access scope against the protected-zone rule at the pre-erection meeting. For anchor rods and base connections the speaker only touches base-of-pole joints briefly [40:18], so no specific anchor guidance here. DOCTRINE FLAG: NONE. The content is conventional structural steel inspection with no PEMB language; it is consistent with Hard Rule 5 (trust validated weights, not LLM math) by analogy, since it insists on tested inspectors and documented procedures over discretion.

## Design of Lateral Load Resisting Frames Using Steel Joists and Joist Girders
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OvNSy0Zz5iE | Duration: 52:13 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
Dr. James Fisher (SJI consulting engineer) presents the SJI Technical Digest on designing single-story moment-resisting frames where steel joists and joist girders carry lateral wind and seismic load. The central idea is that joists, joist girders, and roof trusses are far stiffer and stronger than the columns, so the usual strong-column weak-beam rule cannot be met; instead these frames run strong-beam weak-column, which the code permits only for one-story buildings [05:09][08:42][41:55]. In seismic terms the system is an Ordinary Moment Frame (OMF) with R = 3.5, and the column is the designated fuse that develops its plastic moment Mp while the joist girder is kept fully elastic [10:48][19:36][40:00]. Fisher repeatedly stresses that a moment frame is the least cost-effective lateral system and should be the last choice after a roof-diaphragm-plus-wall-bracing scheme, which only fails when the length-to-width ratio exceeds roughly 4 to 1 [08:07].

### Spec References
On-slide and spoken citations captured: 2005 AISC Specification (adopted by 2006 IBC) requiring second-order analysis on all steel structures [12:37]; 2005 AISC Seismic Provisions Section 5.1 for engineer-of-record drawing obligations (designate the seismic load resisting system, members and connections, connection configuration, connection material specs and sizes, locations of demand-critical welds, locations and dimensions of protected zones, welding per Appendix W Section W2.1) [39:03, frame 32]; AISC Seismic Provisions Section 7, with Section 7.3 Welded Joints and Section 7.3a General Requirements, governing chord splices and joist-to-column connections for SDC D/E/F and when R>3 in SDC B/C [40:30, frame 33]; chord splice requirement stated verbally as "appendix W or D1 point eight" (AISC Seismic Appendix W / AWS D1.8) [40:32]; bracing per the 2005 AISC Specification Appendix 6 ("appendix six") for joist chord lateral bracing [42:54]; ASCE 7-05 for wind and seismic loads [04:21][51:06]; IBC 2006 minimum roof slope of 1/4 in 12 [45:12]. The system R-value is OMF R = 3.5, with R = 3 recommended in SDC B and C to avoid special inspection and special connection requirements [10:48][41:00]. A forthcoming AISC Design Guide on second-order effects is mentioned by topic, no number given [13:21].

### Technical Details
The frame is modeled two ways. Model 1 takes the structure to mid-height of the joist or joist girder as a prismatic member with an equivalent moment of inertia and area for drift and initial sizing [14:46]; trial joist-girder stiffness comes from the SJI catalog equations (n panel points, P panel-point load, L length, D depth) with the moment of inertia reduced about 15 percent for web distortion [15:36]. Model 2 is the seismic fuse model: each column develops Mp, the connection demand is 1.1 x Ry x Mp extrapolated from bottom chord up to mid-height, applied to a continuous-beam model so end-span girders take the full moment and the center girder splits roughly half-Mp each way [19:36][20:54]. Fisher emphasizes leaning columns and P-Delta: every leaning column needs a brace, brace forces accumulate, and a 2D model uses a pseudo-column carrying the interior gravity and heavy-wall seismic loads [22:54][25:25]. Tilt-up and precast walls drive seismic forces up sharply, pushing designers toward lighter wall systems [26:09]. Worked seismic criteria from frame 27: R = 3.5 for OMF, SDS = 0.9297g, SD1 = 0.39g, rho = 1.0, QE = 49 kips, with Imin = 6790 in^4 exterior girders and 4570 in^4 interior girder, and minimum top-chord width 7.0 in for weld access.

### Fabrication Notes
The joist manufacturer designs the joists and joist girders in conformance with SJI specifications once the engineer of record supplies loads, load combinations (each combination separately because second-order analysis is nonlinear), stiffness data, minimum moment of inertia, and minimum top-chord width [13:53][32:38]. SJI has taken the position that it will design the entire girder, not just the connection, for 1.1 Ry Mp to guarantee the girder stays elastic [40:00]. A specified minimum 7.0 in top-chord width is a fabrication requirement so a downhand fillet weld of the connection plate is possible [34:31]. If the manufacturer returns a moment of inertia larger than the specified minimum, the columns still see no more than Mp, so the analysis usually needs no rerun; among friends, hold the delivered I to within about 10 percent of the specified value [33:00][36:00]. Web members are designed per SJI specifications, and chord splices meet AISC Seismic Section 7 / Appendix W [40:30].

### Erection Notes
The frames erect with no more difficulty than wide-flange beam-and-column systems; the one added requirement is heavy communication and information exchange between the engineer of record and the joist supplier [07:03]. The basic connection (frame 20) sets the joist girder on top of the column with a stabilizer plate, joist bolted to girder using (2) 3/4 in dia A325 bolts, with a 3/4 in stabilizer plate and an explicit "DO NOT WELD" note on the secondary seat. Bases are generally taken as pinned for one-story frames, occasionally fixed to control drift, though fixed exterior bases on piers cause moment-development problems [11:24]. Roof slope and ponding are handled with tapered insulation or camber plus crickets at drains to meet the 1/4 in 12 minimum [45:12].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The named failure modes are conceptual rather than weld-defect photos. Using the standard SJI seat connection in a moment frame is a mistake because it cannot develop meaningful moment capacity and is not recommended for these frames [27:00]. An eccentric force P at the seat creates a P x e moment the two-angle top chord cannot carry, so the eccentricity must be eliminated by welding a plate from the column cap to the top chord [28:17][30:28]. Slender chord elements (width-thickness near the slender limit) cannot reach yield in compression, so inelastic behavior cannot be relied on; the answer is to keep the girder elastic and let the column fuse [41:24]. Specifying R = 3.5 in SDC B or C needlessly triggers special inspection and special connection requirements, so R = 3 is recommended there [41:00]. Pin-base assumptions are acknowledged as rougher than the analysis precision being chased [36:37].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Seismic criteria dominate cost on identical buildings. In the worked comparison (frame 42), Charleston SC (SDC D, R=3.5) gave a seismic base shear of 49.0 kips per frame line versus a wind base shear of 22.9 kips per frame line, while the same building in Jackson MS (SDC B, R=3.0) gave only 14.3 kips seismic [48:01][50:02]. The Charleston seismic moments were nearly three times larger, forcing the interior columns into the moment frames, larger columns, more connections, and bigger girders: exterior columns W18x86, interior W18x97, total column weight 12,000 lb and girder weight 6,300 lb for about 18,500 lb per bay, versus roughly 12,000 lb per bay for the low-seismic case [49:02][50:16]. The estimating takeaway is that seismic design category and R-value, not span, set the steel tonnage on these frames, and a moment frame is the most expensive lateral choice to begin with.

### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, this frames a hard rule: on a single-story joist-girder moment frame the seismic design category and chosen R-value (3.5 OMF vs 3.0) can swing per-bay tonnage by 50 percent or more, so SDC and R must be read off the structural general notes before any tonnage rolls into a price, consistent with the SF-is-controlling and verify-don't-generate doctrine; the W18x86 / W18x97 and per-bay weights here are the speaker's example, not a Your Company number, and must come through aisc_validator.py on a real set. For Mario and welding, the column-cap-to-top-chord plate weld is the load path on these frames, and AISC Seismic Section 7.3 / 7.3a plus a 7.0 in minimum top-chord width for a downhand fillet weld are the constraints to flag to Tekla detailing and to confirm on the WPS; on R>3 seismic jobs the joist-to-column welds become Section 7 connections. For field bolting, the standard joist-to-girder seat uses (2) 3/4 in A325 bolts with a "DO NOT WELD" stabilizer, which Paul and the erection crew should hold as drawn. The biggest operational lesson is the engineer-of-record-to-joist-manufacturer communication loop (loads per combination, minimum I, top-chord width, splice and weld requirements), which maps directly to how Your Company coordinates joist packages on jobs like ACP. No conflict with Your Company doctrine; the video is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language, and the one metal-building reference is the speaker crediting that industry's perimeter-moment-frame economy as methodology, not branding.

## Seismic Design of Ductile Special Concentrically Braced Frames
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NU-GmACmynY | Duration: 1:38:02 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
This University of Toronto webinar (Constantine Christopoulos and Jeff Packer) teaches capacity-based seismic design of Special Concentrically Braced Frames (SCBF). The governing idea is the ductile fuse: the brace yields in tension and buckles inelastically in compression as the energy-dissipating element, and every other element (beams, columns, gusset connections, foundations) is sized to remain elastic against the brace's true developed force [13:19][41:02]. The system uses an R factor of 6, an overstrength factor Omega of 2, and a deflection amplification CD of 5, so the structure is designed for forces roughly six times smaller than the elastic demand and must supply ductility on the order of six in return [20:31][44:36]. Two parallel worked designs anchor the talk, an SCBF in Los Angeles (high seismicity, two braced bays) and one in Boston (lower seismicity, single bay, wind-governed) [18:28].

### Spec References
Speakers cited the following by name: ASCE 7 for the seismic loading, response spectrum, base shear distribution, the accidental 5 percent eccentricity, and the P-Delta stability ratio Theta with a 0.10 threshold [29:15][31:47]; AISC 341 (referred to as the AISC seismic spec, 2005 edition) for the SCBF system, the Ry/Rt overstrength tables, the KL/r upper limit of 200, and the D/t and b/t section-slenderness limits [14:51][52:51]; AISC 360 / LRFD ("AISC 05") for member design [33:19][35:23]; AWS D1.1 for the allowance to overlook a 1/16 inch root gap when sizing a fillet weld [70:01]. Material specs named: ASTM A500 Grade B and C (Ry 1.4, same for both grades), ASTM A501 hot-formed, the proposed new ASTM A1085-type tube spec ("A1000-something") with Fy 50 to 65 ksi and CVN 20 ft-lb at 0 F, ASTM A36 gusset plate, E70 electrodes, and ASTM A958 Class 8050 cast steel (composition near A514) for the cast connector [52:51][84:30][94:08]. Brace force for capacity design is the AgRyFy expected-yield force [51:18].

### Technical Details
Brace ductility is controlled by two parameters: global slenderness KL/r (kept below 200, with a useful range cited as roughly 70 to 200, and ongoing research possibly adding a lower bound) and section slenderness via b/t and D/t limits to prevent local buckling and early fracture [14:20][15:22]. Round HSS (A500 Grade B) is preferred over square or rectangular because square cold-formed corners have heavy cold work, raising Fy near Fu and cutting cyclic life [75:17][76:19]. The Chevron / inverted-V configuration requires the beam to be designed for the unbalanced force between the tension brace at AgRyFy and the compression brace at its post-buckling (lower-bound) capacity [21:03][43:36]. The expected-strength factors Ry and Rt account for delivered steel exceeding minimum specified Fy and Fu; designing a connection to the nominal force when the brace arrives over-strong is what fractures the connection [42:36].

### Fabrication Notes
The standard slotted detail puts a slot in the round tube end, inserts the gusset plate, and fillet welds it. Over-slotting (slot longer than the plate insertion) leaves an open gap at the most critical net section, where shear lag concentrates and fracture starts [54:24][55:24]. Because that reduced net section, after the 0.8 shear-lag U-factor, falls below the gross area, the connection must be reinforced: quarter-sections cut from the same HSS are stretched and patch-welded 90 degrees off the slot to add net area, raising effective area to 4.55 sq in against a 4.03 sq in requirement [65:27][72:08]. Fabricators like to burn the slot rough; under seismic (cyclic fatigue) loading the slot ends must be cut smooth because cracking initiates at the weld termination [56:28]. A500 round HSS must use the 0.93 design thickness, not nominal, when sizing welds [72:38]. The cast-steel connector (marketed as Cast ConneX) welds to the gross tube with a single CJP weld and removes most of this detailing skill [79:24][80:25].

### Erection Notes
The connection is detailed as a field-welded slotted HSS-to-gusset joint: plumb the frame with gusset plates pre-attached to the building frame, bring the bracing member in, set it, then fillet weld it as the final field operation [57:28]. The 2tp gap (about a two-plate-thickness setback) is left so the plastic hinge forms inside the gusset plate rather than in the brace, which gives a stable, repeatable hinge and shortens the brace working-point length for design [37:25][74:14]. The talk centers on connection and member behavior; broader crane, rigging, and sequencing topics are not covered.

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Named failure and error modes: circumferential fracture of the tube driven by shear lag at the open slot end (the dominant brittle mode the design must outrank) [59:00]; shear/tear-out rupture along the weld lines when plate insertion length is too short [59:31]; connection fracture from designing to nominal Fy when delivered Fy is higher [42:36]; rough-burned slot ends seeding cracks under cyclic load [56:28]; square-HSS corner low-cycle fatigue fracture after few cycles from cold-work embrittlement [76:19]; beam yielding under the Chevron unbalanced load if not capacity-designed [21:03]; and forgetting non-seismic load cases (wind governed every Boston brace, and a heavy point load can govern a brace) [34:53].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Using the ductile R=6 SCBF instead of an R=3 ordinary frame roughly halves design seismic forces, so every non-yielding element (diaphragms, foundations, columns, beams) is sized for far less load, often the cheaper path overall despite the detailing cost [91:29][93:03]. Large brace tension forces drive foundation cost, which can dominate seismic economics, so brace sizing has a downstream foundation-price effect [18:59]. Reinforced slotted HSS connections add significant shop labor (cutting and patch-welding quarter-tubes, especially on round sections), which is exactly the skilled work the cast connector replaces with a known, fixed connector cost and one CJP weld [80:25][81:25]. Square HSS is chosen in practice mainly because the flat-face patch plate is cheaper to fabricate, a fabrication-economics tradeoff against worse seismic ductility [67:27].

### Your Company Application
For Ivan takeoff, seismic SCBF jobs are HSS-brace heavy (round A500 Grade B here) and the connection reinforcement (patch quarter-tubes, thick gussets) is real added tonnage and shop hours that pure member takeoff misses; flag any braced-frame seismic set so the estimate captures reinforced-connection labor, not just brace weight, and route all HSS weights through aisc_validator.py rather than trusting the talk's example sizes. For Mario, the welding scope is E70 fillet welds on the slotted joint plus CJP if the cast connector is used, with the seismic-specific requirement that slot ends be cut smooth and welds terminate cleanly; this is AWS D1.1 demand-critical territory and his D1.1 qualification covers it. For Tekla detailing and the in-house PE stamp, the 2tp hinge setback, the 0.93 design thickness rule, the Ry/Rt expected-strength force AgRyFy, and the shear-lag reinforcement check are exact modeling and calc inputs. This is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language, consistent with Your Company doctrine. DOCTRINE FLAG: NONE. Note that all section numbers, factors, and member sizes above are the speakers' stated values for a 2005-era example and must be checked against current AISC 341/360 and a project's controlling code before use on a live ACP-type bid.

## Basic Concepts in Ductile Detailing of Steel Structures
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sldnnd08l-c | Duration: 1:22:08 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
This is a fundamentals lecture on ductility, defined as the ability to sustain large inelastic deformations without significant loss of strength, or simply inelastic deformation capacity [02:04]. The central argument is that ductility is not mainly about warning of failure but about permitting redistribution of internal stresses and forces, which actually increases the strength of members, connections, and structures [17:58][24:40]. Ductility comes from yielding of steel; a steel structure is only brought down when something buckles or something fractures, and both buckling and fracture are non-ductile [14:25][15:57]. The governing detailing rule is that ductile limit states must precede brittle limit states, meaning the ductile element has to be the weakest element in the load path [62:18][80:45].

### Spec References
The speaker cited the AISC Seismic Provisions for Structural Steel Buildings (AISC 341) by name at the close as the document devoted to putting ductility into structures [81:15]. He referenced the seismic expected-yield concept R-y, the ratio applied to minimum specified yield to get expected yield stress [69:30]. He cited ASCE 7 as the source of code earthquake loads, noting those loads are an arbitrary strength target, not real earthquake forces [60:45]. He named A992 steel and its mill-guaranteed upper-bound yield ratio of 0.85 [70:33], and used A36, Grade 50, and A514 stress-strain curves from the Salmon and Johnson textbook [73:36]. He referenced the AISC main specification width-thickness (B/T) limits for compact, non-compact, and slender sections and the plastic-design lateral-bracing rules now in the spec appendix [76:07][79:13]. Bolt nominal shear was cited as 0.4 Fu or 0.5 Fu of the bolt for threads included or excluded "out of the AISC spec" [66:24], though the speaker did not state the specific section number. He named a 3/4 in A325-X bolt and A36 double-angle example [67:26]. No specific AISC 360 chapter/section numbers, table numbers, AWS D1.1 clauses, or RCSC sections were spoken; the seismic plastic-rotation target of 0.03 radians was stated as a design target without a section number [08:16].

### Technical Details
The talk works three idealized examples to prove the strength benefit of ductility. A 1/2 in by 6 in plate with a 1 in hole has an elastic stress concentration of 2.57 times the average net-area stress; brittle material fails at 49 kips while ductile material, which lets stress redistribute and even out, carries 125 kips, about 2.5 times more [22:04][24:08]. A 4 in by 12 in rectangular section (S = 96 in cubed, Z giving 7,200 kip-in) carries 4,800 kip-in brittle versus 7,200 kip-in ductile [27:18]. A fixed-fixed 30 ft beam of 500 kip-ft capacity carries 6.67 kips/ft elastic versus 8.89 kips/ft after moment redistribution [30:54][32:26]. The lower-bound theorem of plastic analysis is presented as the most important concept: any assumed force distribution in equilibrium with the applied load that nowhere exceeds member capacity gives a safe design, so the designer only needs equilibrium and a load path, not the true stress state [34:31][37:09]. Earthquake design trades strength for ductility because a pulse lasts a fraction of a second; the structure reaches the same deformation regardless of strength, so weak plus ductile is economical [56:09][60:14]. The double-angle braced example contrasts the ductile limit state of gross-section yielding over a 20 ft member against the non-ductile modes of net-section fracture, block shear, bolt shear, and plate bearing [62:48].

### Fabrication Notes
The lecture is design and behavior focused and does not cover shop cutting, fit-up, or QC procedures directly. The fabrication-relevant point is material certification and over-strength: A36 steel statistically yields near 54 ksi, not the specified 36 ksi, so a ductile element sized at minimum yield can become stronger than the bolts meant to outlast it, killing ductility [68:27][68:58]. This is why A992 carries a guaranteed maximum yield ratio of 0.85 [70:33]. Section geometry from the mill or from built-up fabrication matters: compact and seismically compact sections with low B/T ratios deliver ductility, while slender flanges and webs invite local buckling [74:36][76:37].

### Erection Notes
Erection appears as a robustness illustration rather than a procedure. The classic lack-of-fit case is named directly: when a beam does not quite reach its connection and is forced into place during erection, a ductile structure redistributes the locked-in stress and carries the same load as if the misfit never happened, while a brittle structure can be killed by it [49:26][49:56]. Support settlement is given the same treatment, with a ductile frame insensitive to one column moving down [49:26]. No crane, rigging, bracing-sequence, or site-coordination detail is given.

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The named failures are all brittle modes that end ductility. Moment-connection bottom-flange weld fracture is shown repeatedly as the classic Northridge failure [71:34][72:04]. A link-to-column flange fracture in an eccentrically braced frame, a fractured column base plate from the Northridge earthquake, and brace-connection net-section fracture occurring before gross-section yielding are all shown as non-ductile failures [72:04][72:34][73:04]. Local buckling of slender and non-compact sections is shown collapsing a building that could not redistribute load [77:08], and column buckling (a W6x20 A36 strut dropping from about 200 kips) is called the ultimate non-ductile failure mode [80:15]. The root error named is unaccounted over-strength in the ductile element, the lesson learned the hard way in Northridge: stronger is not better when the extra strength lands in the element you wanted to yield [68:27][80:45].

### Bid / Cost Implications
The speaker frames a direct cost argument: you should be willing to pay more for ductile material because the same plate carries 49 kips brittle versus 125 kips ductile, so ductility buys load capacity per dollar [24:08]. He calls out the fallacy of high-strength materials, since Grade 100 steel is intrinsically more brittle and a beam made from it will often carry less load than one made from Grade 50, so high strength is not high performance [32:58][74:06]. Ductility also lowers engineering cost: the ductile plate is a ten-second P-over-A check while the brittle one demands two days of finite-element work to find the peak stress [25:10]. For earthquake work, deliberately weak plus ductile structures are the economical choice over keeping the frame elastic [60:45].

### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff and the in-house PE stamp, the controlling design check is the capacity hierarchy: size bolts and welds (the brittle elements) off the expected yield capacity of the connected member using R-y, not off the external load, and confirm the ductile member is the weakest link in the load path [64:50][70:02]. This pairs with our aisc_validator.py member weights and supports flagging slender or non-compact shapes (high B/T) during takeoff since those carry a ductility penalty [76:37]. For Mario and AWS D1.1 welding, the bottom-flange weld fracture lesson reinforces that CJP moment-connection welds are demand-critical and that a weld failure is a non-ductile mode that ends the connection [71:34]. For anchor rods and base plates, the fractured base plate example argues the plate and rods should be stronger than the column so yielding stays in the member [72:34]; this matches our anchor-rod design and tolerance discipline. For Tekla detailing, the brace-connection net-section-before-gross-yield failures argue for checking effective net area against gross area (An/Ag greater than Fy/Fu) on every braced-frame connection [73:04][64:20]. The lack-of-fit point validates our erection tolerance and fit-up handling on ACP controls, since a ductile frame tolerates the misfit but a brittle detail does not [49:56]. DOCTRINE FLAGS: NONE. The content is conventional structural-steel behavior with no PEMB language, no supplier names, and no rate or material-cost data, consistent with Your Company doctrine.

## Seismic Design and Behavior of Composite RCS Frames
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m11ht5_8SNM | Duration: 1:06:14 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
This is a research and practice webinar on composite RCS frames, meaning moment frames built from reinforced concrete columns and structural steel beams, with the steel beam running continuous through the column [09:11]. The central technical problem is moment and shear transfer between the concrete column and the steel beam at the joint [00:31], solved with face bearing plates that mobilize a diagonal compression strut in the concrete, a steel band plate on top, and vertical joint reinforcement [03:32][13:44]. The speaker frames the seismic advantage directly against the Northridge experience: because the steel beam and the column rebar are continuous through the joint, you avoid splicing either member at the location of maximum force, so the field connection is moved away from the column and you avoid welding at the most critical point [09:11][13:13]. The talk centers on a full-scale three-story pseudodynamic frame test done with the National Center for Research on Earthquake Engineering in Taipei to validate the system under design and maximum-considered earthquakes [21:23].

### Spec References
The speaker cites documents by name but rarely by section number. Named: AISC Seismic Provisions "Part Two on composite," which sets strong-column-weak-beam ratios and detailing requirements and points to ACI and AISC for member detailing [10:43][10:12]; the IBC seismic provisions built on ASCE 7 and its R factors, with composite moment frames "first introduced in 1994" in the NEHRP provisions as the ASCE 7 source document [09:41][10:12]; the ASCE design guidelines for these connections, "originally in 1994," being updated "this spring" [11:13][20:22]; ACI for concrete column detailing; the 2003 IBC provisions used to design the test frame [23:25]. Seismic design quantities stated: response modification factor R of 8 [12:13][24:26], strong-column-weak-beam column-to-beam strength ratio target of at least 1.2 [37:41], and a beam splice capacity-design demand of 1.4 times expected plastic moment [36:38]. No specific AISC 360 chapter, AISC 341 section, AWS D1.1 clause, or RCSC table number is stated aloud, so those are not cited here.

### Technical Details
The joint is dissected into an inner panel (the steel beam plus the concrete held captive behind the face bearing plates) and an outer panel (the surrounding concrete), with force transfer between them [18:20]. Two inner-panel failure modes govern: a bearing failure where a strong beam crushes and rocks against the concrete, and a panel shear failure where the steel web yields but the concrete compression strut assists, so doublers or diagonal stiffeners that a bare-steel joint would need are often unnecessary [18:51][19:22]. For seismic design the joint is proportioned stronger than the beam to force plastic hinging into the beam [16:19]. The validation frame used 4 meter story heights, reinforced concrete columns roughly 30 by 30 to 30 by 35, and W-shape beams; a 20-story design example averaged about 3 psf of steel in the moment-frame beams versus 4.8 psf if W24 steel columns were used instead [12:43][13:13]. Even compact, code-conforming seismic sections developed large local flange buckles at 5 to 6 percent drift, and an unexpected story mechanism formed with hinging below the joint in the column because composite beam action raised beam strength, a point the speaker stresses for the strong-column-weak-beam check [33:35][37:10][37:41].

### Fabrication Notes
The fabrication content is the framing of rebar cages and precast columns as steel-shop-type work rather than detailed shop tolerances. The speaker repeatedly tells fabricators these systems look more like a steel shop than a precaster and that engineered rebar cages can serve as erection columns [07:39][26:27][26:58]. The continuous steel beam passes through the column, so the shop builds a beam with welded face bearing plates and a top band plate sized per the ASCE guidelines, plus joint ties [13:44][14:15]. The band plate is noted to let the detailer eliminate the vertical rebar congestion in the joint region, which eases both rebar placement and concrete placement [19:52]. The vertical joint reinforcement connects to the flange through a mechanical coupler that may be welded or welded-screwed [04:03]. No weld procedure, electrode, preheat, or NDE detail and no dimensional fit-up tolerance is stated.

### Erection Notes
The Taipei specimen used precast construction: precast RCS units set with temporary bracing, column splices made with grouted couplers, and steel beams brought in and field-bolted with bolted moment splices [24:26][26:58][27:28]. Splices were deliberately placed at the most daring locations, close to the column but just outside the plastic-hinge region, to make precast units small while testing a worst case [23:55][24:26]. The speaker contrasts a grouted precast column splice against a welded steel column splice and says it is not obvious which is easier [27:28]. The US tall-building practice he describes stages steel erection columns over roughly 10 stories and later encases them in concrete, which he notes effectively buys two columns, one steel and one concrete [07:07][07:39]. Out-of-plane bracing and three sets of large actuators at each floor were used in the lab, not a field condition.

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
This is a research talk, so it names behavioral failure modes rather than shop or field inspection rejections. The motivating failure is the Northridge fracture pattern where steel beams fractured at the welded beam-to-column connection, which RCS avoids by keeping members continuous through the joint [09:11]. Observed test failures: joint panel-shear failure with pinching but stable hysteresis, joint bearing failure, large local flange buckling at 5 to 6 percent drift leading eventually to ductile fracture, concrete spalling and loss of shear transfer at column bases, and final ductile rupture of the bolted beam splice plates past 10 percent drift even though they were designed to 1.4 times expected plastic moment [16:49][17:20][33:35][34:35][36:38]. A modeling caution is flagged: fiber-element analyses missed local buckling and underpredicted drift by roughly 60 to 65 percent at the maximum earthquake, so a nonlinear model is only as good as the failure modes it captures [45:21][45:51].

### Bid / Cost Implications
The economic case is explicit. RCS substitutes reinforced concrete columns for heavy steel columns that carry lead-time risk, putting concrete where it does the most good in compression and reserving steel for the long-span flexible floor [05:05][13:13]. The 20-story comparison quantifies the steel content: about 3 psf in the moment-frame beams versus a heavier all-steel column scheme, with column shapes replaced by 30 by 30 to 30 by 35 concrete columns [12:43]. Staged steel-then-concrete construction speeds the schedule and is called integral to making the system economical [05:05]. The standing caveat is the disadvantage of mixing construction trades and the historical lack of design standards, which is why the systems took hold in newer markets such as 1970s Houston where trade traditions were looser [05:36][06:07]. There is no Your Company rate, tonnage, or dollar figure here.

### Your Company Application
This is academic background, not a fabrication standard Your Company would bid against today, and Houston is a low-seismic market, so RCS seismic detailing is not a near-term workstream. The transferable point for Ivan is the strong-column-weak-beam ratio behavior: composite beam action raises effective beam strength, so a takeoff or check that ignores composite action can misjudge the column demand, which matters whenever a composite floor is in scope. For Mario the relevant note is that the joint relies on welded face bearing plates, a welded top band plate, and welded or welded-screwed rebar couplers, all CJP-grade load-path welds that would need a qualified WPS if such a job ever came in. For Tekla detailing, the continuous-beam-through-column geometry with face bearing plates and band plate is a distinctive connection family worth a template if pursued. The speaker's broader pitch, that fabricators can treat engineered rebar cages and embedded steel as shop work, is a market-expansion idea, not a doctrine change. Doctrine flag: NONE. Nothing here conflicts with Your Company positioning, and the conventional structural-steel framing fits cleanly with no PEMB language involved.

## Bolting & Welding Primer - Part 12
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lbV0VkrOfwU | Duration: 23:26 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This closing session of a bolting and welding seminar covers three linked topics: combined bolts-and-welds load sharing, seismic connection design philosophy, and a full worked design example of a bolted brace gusset plate that finishes on gusset-plate buckling. The recurring theme is checking strength components successively (transverse weld, then longitudinal weld, then bolts) and designing connections by tracking real deformations rather than assuming uniform stress [01:02]. The example ends with the buckling check that controlled the tested specimen, comparing three published methods against a measured ultimate load of 164 Kips [08:17][21:36].
### Spec References
The speaker cites the AISC Code of Standard Practice (referred to as "AIS CPC") as the basis for the combined bolt-and-weld rule and says he prefers a method from the AISC Engineering Journal for upgrading existing structures [00:31][01:02]. He references the net-section / shear-lag relation U = 1 minus (eccentricity / length) with net area S^2/4G times Fu for tension members [02:38], FEMA 350 plus AISC seismic design for connection forces [04:09], and a current AISC Engineering Journal paper on gusset-plate design [19:34]. No AISC 360 chapter, table number, AISC 341 section, or Design Guide number is stated verbatim, so those are general principles, no section cited.
### Technical Details
Transverse welds are effectively ineffective in shear because they fracture early and lack ductility, so the combined rule gives roughly 25% of the slip load (with pretensioned bolts) plus about 50% of the bolt ultimate shear [00:01][00:31]. Frames are classified as ordinary, intermediate, or special moment frames, with design based on achieving a target rotation or story drift [03:38]. High-strength bolt shear strength does not depend on rate of loading, so the static capacities apply directly to seismic conditions [04:09]. The brace-gusset example tracks slip load, bolt shear, plate bearing, block shear, and gusset buckling [08:17].
### Fabrication Notes
The discussion is connection-design and analysis oriented, not shop-process oriented, so explicit fit-up and shop-QC steps are not covered. The one fabrication-adjacent point is that you usually cannot connect the whole cross-section and typically only connect the flanges, which disturbs uniform stress and forces the shear-lag accommodation in the net-section calculation [01:34][02:06]. Bolt holes in the example are standard holes with no oversize-hole discount applied [09:49].
### Erection Notes
This session does not cover field erection sequencing, bracing, or rigging. The closest field-relevant content is the seismic-slip philosophy: connections are detailed so a moderate earthquake produces no slip and a major earthquake allows slip into bearing without catastrophic collapse, which governs how the installed connection behaves [05:43][06:13].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The speaker flags a conceptual error rather than an inspection rejection: assuming the historical Whitmore method checks buckling when it only checks yielding, and using a P/A plus or minus My/I beam-type stress check on a gusset that does not predict ultimate capacity and is sometimes non-conservative [16:29][17:31][18:03]. He warns that mixing bolts and welds in the same faying surface is undesirable because the welds do not deliver enough ductility, and that seismic connections give the designer no choice but to pretension all bolts and prepare faying surfaces as slip-critical [06:44][05:43].
### Bid / Cost Implications
The example is deliberately an unbalanced design set up to force a buckling failure, so bolt, bearing, and block-shear capacities are far higher than needed, which the speaker notes invites the reaction "I could take two bolts out" [13:24][14:26]. The practical cost guidance is engineering-effort scaled to volume: predicted-to-test ratios near 1.23 mean a single connection can be left conservative and shipped, while designing many identical connections justifies refining the buckling method to recover capacity [22:09]. This maps to a fabricator deciding how much detailing time a repeated detail warrants.
### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff and the in-house PE stamp, this reinforces that braced-frame gusset plates need a buckling check (Thornton or modified Thornton), not just the Whitmore yield check, before a connection design is stamped, and that braced-frame and SCBF-type gussets carry that hidden buckling demand into the estimate. For Mario, the rule that transverse welds fracture early and that bolts and welds should not share a faying surface guides weld-detail decisions on combined connections. For field bolting, the seismic requirement to fully pretension and treat faying surfaces as slip-critical sets the installation method on moment and braced frames; pretension plus shear-lag net-section checks tie to ACP project controls on connection submittals. Conflict with Your Company doctrine: NONE.

## Bolting & Welding Primer - Part 11
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SLDVZ_QSjRo | Duration: 28:34 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This segment teaches how high-strength bolts develop and retain pretension through installation, and how inspection should match the load case rather than chase a number that cannot be measured after the fact. The central idea is that turn-of-nut and similar methods deliberately drive the bolt into the inelastic flat region of its load-elongation curve, so that very different snug elongations still converge on nearly the same pretension [02:36][03:38]. The speaker also covers when pretension is and is not actually required, the three main proprietary fastener systems, washer requirements, and a combined bolt-plus-weld joint example.

### Spec References
The speaker cites the Research Council on Structural Connections (RCSC) specification by name as the governing bolting resource with extensive commentary and a free download [22:18][22:48]. He references the "Guide to Design Criteria for Bolted and Riveted Joints," last published 1987, and AISC Design Guide 17 as the source for all the bolting material discussed (noted as not yet updated to the 2005 spec) [22:48][23:48]. ASTM fastener and washer specs cited verbatim: tension-control bolts to ASTM 1852 and load-indicating washers to F959 [16:08]. Bolt grades named are A325 and A490. No AISC 360 J-series section number or table number is spoken aloud, so those are not captured here.

### Technical Details
Turn-of-nut runs the nut down to snug (full effort on a spud wrench or the first impact of an impact wrench, which sounds different), then applies an additional one-half, one-third, or two-thirds turn by bolt length, with one-half turn the usual case [00:01]. Snug elongations vary widely (roughly 0.03 to 0.05 in the example) yet pretensions land within a fraction of each other because the bolt is taken past yield into the flat portion [02:36][03:38]. Rotational tolerance past the half-turn mark is large: A325 can go nearly two more turns, A490 about one and a quarter, before failure [04:09]. Field measurements show actual pretension above specified: turn-of-nut A325 about 35% over, A490 about 26% over, and calibrated wrench about 13% over, and these margins are already built into the rules rather than available as extra capacity [15:07][15:37].

### Fabrication Notes
Rotation (rotational-capacity) tests are required for galvanized A325 bolts and are good insurance for any short-grip bolt (around an inch and a half where a half-turn becomes a third-turn), because short bolts may fracture during installation; A490 cannot be galvanized so the issue does not arise there [12:28][12:58]. Calibration of any installation method must be replicated on the job site, not done for convenience in the shop, to match field conditions [09:50]. For TC bolts and load-indicating washers the friction-controlling lubricant is proprietary and manufacturer-supplied, so the fabricator and installer may not clean or re-lubricate them and must use them in the as-delivered condition [18:12][18:42].

### Erection Notes
Pre-installation verification with a bolt calibrator (load cell) is required once per day and again whenever conditions change, for every method; you cannot return three weeks later and inspect seriously [08:46][09:19]. Work proceeds from the stiffer regions toward the edges to establish snug across the joint [00:01]. A bolt taken through installation rotation without fracture is highly likely satisfactory, and a later quarter-turn rarely causes failure except in exposed structures vulnerable to vandalism, such as towers [04:40][05:12]. TC bolts install from one side with a single operator using a quiet electric wrench, reducing crew and equipment on site [20:44].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The named failure mode for TC bolts is trusting the twist-off tip alone: very high friction (bolt dropped in sand) twists the spline off before adequate elongation, giving no pretension, while a super lubricant prevents twist-off yet over-elongates and does develop pretension. Tip twist-off does not by itself prove pretension; only calibration does [19:12][19:44][20:14]. Pretensions greater than specified are explicitly not cause for rejection [11:56][12:28]. Determining pretension after installation is essentially impractical; an ultrasonic bolt-load indicator costs about 25,000 to 30,000 dollars and is a research tool, not a production tool [05:12][05:42]. Snug-tight joints should not show baked-on gaps that invite corrosion in exposed structures [08:15].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Matching inspection to the load case controls cost: if pretension is not required (snug-tight bearing connections, A325 only, no fatigue or vibration), do not inspect for it; verify the right bolts, nuts, washers, and hole condition [06:44][07:14][07:44]. TC bolts are generally more expensive than standard assemblies but cut labor to a single-side, single-operator install [20:44]. Every method carries the same daily calibration overhead, so that cost is not a differentiator [20:44]. RCSC and the bolted-joint guide are free downloads, and AISC FAQ resources are free, which lowers the engineering-research cost on interpretation questions [22:18][24:20].

### Bolting / Welding Methods
Bolting methods named: turn-of-nut, calibrated wrench, tension-control (TC) bolts to ASTM 1852, and load-indicating washers (direct tension indicators) to F959. TC bolts are torque-dependent and shear off the spline at about 1.05 times the specified minimum pretension when correctly calibrated; load-indicating washers are elongation-dependent and read with a go/no-go feeler gauge on the flattened protrusions [16:08][17:41][21:14][21:46]. Washer rules: hardened washers are required for torque-based methods (calibrated wrench, TC bolts) and for DTIs, but not for turn-of-nut or snug-tight; special washers are needed for slip surfaces, for A490 on steels with yield below 40 ksi to prevent galling, and bar washers for some slotted or oversized holes [25:22][25:52][26:23]. The closing combined-joint example pairs bolts in shear with longitudinal and transverse fillet welds on a renovation, solved by aligning the load-deformation curves (transverse weld near ultimate, longitudinal at about 80%, bolt at about 40% of that deformation) [26:23][27:26][27:56].

### Your Company Application
Mario Gutierrez should run pre-installation verification with a bolt calibrator daily and on any condition change for the ACP field-bolting crews, and should treat TC-bolt twist-off and DTI gap closure as indicators that still require calibration, not as standalone acceptance. Paul Guerrero gets a clear safety and QC line: short-grip and galvanized A325 bolts get rotation tests before they reach the field, and exposed-structure bolts (towers, exposed frames) carry vandalism risk. Ivan should price inspection to the actual load case, snug-tight bearing connections do not need pretension verification, which avoids over-scoping inspection labor, and should note TC bolts trade higher fastener cost for single-operator install when sizing field-bolting hours. For Tekla detailing and the in-house PE stamp, washer callouts must follow the rules here (hardened washers for torque-based and DTI methods, special washers for slip-critical, A490-on-low-yield-steel, and slotted-hole cases). The combined bolt-and-weld renovation method is directly useful where ACP retrofits lack room for added bolts. Doctrine conflict: NONE. Verify-don't-generate is honored; no AISC 360 section or table number was spoken, so none is invented here.

## Bolting & Welding Primer - Part 10
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mvK2YFOp1kk | Duration: 26:50 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This segment teaches the mechanics behind the AISC bolt-design rules for bolts loaded in tension, then transitions into connected-material limit states (bearing, tear-out, block shear) and bolt-installation methods. The instructor derives why an externally applied tension load adds only a small increment to a pretensioned bolt, why the nominal tensile stress provision uses a 0.75 factor on the area rather than a strength reduction, and how installation torque is resisted by friction and disappears at ultimate so the bolt can be designed on pure tensile fracture [00:00] to [12:26].
### Spec References
The speaker works from AISC bolt provisions but mostly names the rule form rather than the section number. Cited or directly quoted items: the tensile-strength rule F_nt = 0.75 F_u (design tensile stress, with the 0.75 stated as an area adjustment, not a strength reduction) [11:25] to [12:26]; bearing/tear-out rules expressed as 1.5 F_u L_c t for tear-out and 3.0 d t F_u as the yielding/bearing upper bound, with the deformation-considered alternates 1.2 and 2.4 [16:03] to [17:35]; block shear written as tension fracture (F_u net area) plus gross shear yield using 0.6 F_y on the gross shear area [21:43] to [22:43]; and the calibrated-wrench install set to 1.05 times the minimum pretension with a 3-bolt minimum daily calibration [25:16] to [26:17]. No explicit AISC 360 section, table, AWS D1.1 clause, or Design Guide number is spoken aloud, so those are general principles, no section cited.
### Technical Details
For a pretensioned bolt with external tension applied, the final bolt force equals the initial pretension plus a fraction of the applied external load, derived by adding a deformation-compatibility equation (PL/AE for bolt and plate) to the single available equilibrium equation; using a plate-to-bolt area ratio of about nine gives roughly a 10% increase, while physical tests show 7 to 8%, small enough to bury in the design expression [03:07] to [09:54]. The tensile stress area is about 0.75 of pi d squared over 4 because the threaded section governs, which is the true origin of the 0.75 factor [10:54] to [12:26]. Installation torque introduces torsional stress that is resisted by friction at the faying surface; as the plates separate that torsion incrementally vanishes, so at fracture the bolt is in pure tension [01:33] to [03:07].
### Fabrication Notes
The shop-relevant content is bolt installation control. Bearing-type connections that are not slip-critical may be installed to snug-tight only, defined as the ordinary effort of a worker on a spud wrench or the first impact of an impact wrench [23:13] to [23:43]. The speaker states a torque-to-pretension formula is too variable (off by about 40%) and is therefore not permitted as a calculated install method [24:15] to [24:45]. Calibrated-wrench installation uses a Skidmore-Wilhelm hydraulic load cell to set the wrench to stall at 1.05 times the minimum required pretension, requires a minimum of three bolts per calibration, must be re-run whenever lot, length, or diameter changes (a 3-inch versus 4-inch A325 of the same diameter needs separate calibration), and must be recalibrated at least once per day, with washers used to set a baseline friction condition [24:45] to [26:50].
### Erection Notes
Field bolting practice is the erection content. The instructor distinguishes the worker effort that produces snug-tight in the field from the controlled calibrated-wrench pretension procedure, and notes the practical reality that calibration must follow any change in field conditions across a shift [23:13] to [26:50]. No crane, rigging, bracing, or sequencing guidance is given in this segment.
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The recurring failure category named is bolts in tension combined with prying action and sometimes fatigue, which the speaker calls where most real bolted-connection problems fall [00:00] to [00:30]. He advises avoiding joints that put bolts in tension and preferring bolts in shear because shear fatigue life is far longer, and prefers A325 over A490 in tension for greater ductility [00:30] to [01:01]. Test specimens are used to show that block shear at ultimate is shear fracture across a small ligament plus tension fracture through the holes, not the pulled-apart appearance seen after the test, which is the basis for a corrected block-shear rule [18:08] to [23:13].
### Bid / Cost Implications
No direct pricing, schedule, or estimating figures are discussed. The cost-relevant takeaway is procedural: calibrated-wrench installation carries real labor overhead because every change in bolt lot, length, or diameter forces a fresh three-bolt calibration plus a mandatory daily recalibration, which an estimator should account for when a job specifies controlled pretension versus snug-tight bearing connections [24:45] to [26:50].
### Your Company Application
For Mario as welding and shop lead, this confirms the install hierarchy our field crews already follow: snug-tight is acceptable for bearing-type non-slip-critical joints, while pretensioned joints need a verified method, and the calibrated-wrench path obligates the Skidmore re-calibration on every lot/length/diameter change and at least once daily, which Paul should track as a documented QC step on field bolting. For Ivan, the design-side point is that AISC bolt tension capacity uses F_nt = 0.75 F_u as an area adjustment, and that prying-governed tension joints are the high-risk category, so takeoff and connection assumptions should favor shear-loaded bolts where the design allows. The block-shear correction and bearing/tear-out limit states (1.5 F_u L_c t and 3.0 d t F_u) are connection checks our in-house PE stamp covers and should be reflected in Tekla connection detailing edge distances. None of this conflicts with Your Company doctrine; capture A325 versus A490 ductility preference as a design note, not outward PEMB language. Doctrine conflict: NONE.
