## Field Fixes - Part 9
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mIViHNf-5ew | Duration: 32:00 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This webinar segment is a field-diagnostics walkthrough of recurring failures in industrial crane buildings and joist framing, drawn from the presenter's career as a forensic structural engineer. The controlling theme is that small, unconsidered details (a stiff tieback, an off-center rail, a diaphragm plate, an out-of-position anchor rod) turn into expensive field failures under repeated crane loading because the original detail did not account for movement, fatigue, or thermal expansion. The opening also covers joist serviceability around folding partitions and joist seat-depth coordination [00:01-02:35].

### Spec References
The presenter cites AISC Design Guide 7 for crane building design [03:38-04:08]. He references AISC member-supplied crane lateral and longitudinal load provisions that "used to be in the spec" and are now in ASCE 7 [07:16], noting the 20 percent lateral-load fraction historically used and 100 percent for mill/scrapyard cranes per the AISE mill-crane document. He cites AISC fabrication and rail-centering tolerances generally rather than as a numbered table [14:38, 16:12-16:43], and contrasts them with ASTM A6 mill tolerances. He states A325 bolts for rail joints [05:11] and references AWS welding only in passing for a field repair [09:54]. No AISC 360 section, 341 section, RCSC clause, or specific AWS D1.1 clause number is stated aloud.

### Technical Details
Long DLH and DH joists carry built-in camber (he cites 8 inches of camber on a 120-foot DLH joist) and details must accommodate it; a roof-deck diaphragm tie-in failed because the cambered joists rose above the wall [01:32-02:03]. Joist seat depths differ by series (a K-series 2.5-inch seat versus an LH 5-inch seat) and must be matched end to end or the floor steps [02:03-02:35]. Unequal joist or joist-girder reactions twist a supporting beam, requiring bottom-chord extensions or torsion design [02:35-03:06]. Crane fatigue is keyed to duty class: classes A, B, C are treated as no-fatigue-concern, while D, E, and F (mill) cranes require fatigue design [06:13-06:46]. AISC tolerance cited: rail eccentricity shall not exceed three-quarters of the girder web thickness, and a quoted runway alignment value of about a quarter inch in 50 feet maximum [15:41-16:43].

### Fabrication Notes
For crane runway plate girders, the recommended built-up detail is a complete-joint-penetration weld of the web to the top flange with a fillet-weld reinforcement (the mill-people detail); a fillet-only web-to-top-flange weld cracks under repeated wheel loads, especially when the section is out of square [13:04-14:07]. Rail joints should be specified as milled joints for a tight fit and bolted with A325 bolts, or welded for high-cycle service [04:40-05:11]. ASTM A6 sweep tolerance is an eighth inch per 10 feet, which over a 40-foot runway beam allows up to a half-inch offset, and the web can be up to 3/16 inch off the flange centerline, so a drawing note should require the fabricator to straighten the beam before shipping if it would leave the rail too far off the web [15:10-16:12].

### Erection Notes
The cautionary case is a 280-foot box-truss runway girder that erected with an S-kink because the column anchor rods at one end were set 6 inches out of straight; the girder was forced down onto them and permanently deformed, and the fix was to realign the crane aisles to the kink rather than rebuild [16:43-22:00]. Rail clips must provide positive lateral restraint while allowing longitudinal thermal movement, and a crane stop should sit about 2 inches off the rail end so thermal growth does not buckle the runway girder laterally [22:30-23:30]. Diaphragm plates added between runway girders make a simple span act continuous, generating unintended negative moment that shears bolts and elongates plates; the field fix is to remove them and reroute the loads [05:41-09:22].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Named failures include cracked rivets in an old mill building that broke clapboard-sash windows [08:18-09:22], cracked and field-welded tiebacks that were too rigid and pulled until something broke [09:22-12:02], rattled-loose bolts in tieback connections that led to slotted holes and a switch to welding [11:30-12:02], fillet-welded crane-girder web-to-flange cracks from out-of-square fabrication [13:04-13:36], rail clip failures and rail gouging from misalignment or excessive building movement [22:30-24:32], loosened bolted rail butt joints that chip the rail and wear crane bearings [04:08-04:40], and joist deflection exceeding the 3/4-inch dust-skirt clearance of folding partitions so the partition cannot open [00:01-00:31].

### Bid / Cost Implications
The presenter flags that gantry-type patented tiebacks with spherical bearings are expensive but worth it on heavy high-cycle cranes because the failure becomes the manufacturer's problem, while welded maintenance-free rail joints are costly and not justified on light, infrequent-use buildings [05:11-05:41, 12:02-12:33]. He warns against accepting crane-supplier demands for eighth-inch tolerances that are not achievable, since agreeing to an impossible tolerance shifts every later crane problem onto the engineer [14:38-15:10]. The segment closes by previewing the partner's talk on fabricators complaining that design drawings lack information yet they are expected to do the work for "$1.98" [25:03-25:33].

### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, crane-building runway girders and fatigue-class D/E/F cranes are not standard $/SF work; they need AISC Design Guide 7 design effort, milled rail joints, and A325 rail-joint bolts priced as line items, and the crane-supplier tolerance demand should be flagged before any bid commitment. Mario's shop should hold the CJP-plus-fillet web-to-top-flange detail and square fit-up on any crane girder, and Paul should note the falling-object and rail-walking hazards the presenter describes. The anchor-rod kink story is the load-bearing lesson for our anchor-rod work: a 6-inch setting error at one runway end propagated into an unfixable 280-foot girder, which reinforces our anchor-rod tolerance discipline and the Tekla detailing of camber and matched joist seat depths. The joist camber and seat-depth coordination map directly to our joist and Tekla workstreams. No conflict with Your Company doctrine; all crane content is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language.

## Field Fixes - Part 8
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Htk2torwoAs | Duration: 29:44 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This session is a practical clinic on reinforcing, modifying, and field-fixing existing steel joists (SJI K-series and similar bar joists), not wide-flange framing. The speaker's central method is to first identify exactly what you are dealing with before touching anything: the web configuration (rod webs, crimped single angles, double angles, or cold-formed channels), the chord type (hot-rolled angles, cold-formed angles, or hat sections), and interferences such as deck above and walls behind [00:02][00:32][01:35]. He stresses that the right field fix is governed as much by access geometry and weld reach as by the calculated forces, and that material is cheap so the conservative reinforcement is usually the economical one [10:56][11:28].

### Spec References
The speaker cites SJI load tables for existing joist capacity [05:13], the SJI "75-year digest" printed in 2003 that compiles specifications and load tables for joists made over the prior 75 years (used to back out steel grade, often 36 ksi for chords and webs, when only the year is known) [05:13][06:15], and a forthcoming SJI technical/joist digest that will give reinforcement details and design procedures [18:10][20:53]. He references the joist tag now mandated by SJI to carry the manufacturer name [06:45], the 2005 AISC manual introduction of HSS design thickness versus nominal thickness (HSS supplied at about 0.90 of nominal wall) [09:20][09:51], the AISI deck thickness allowance of 95 percent of design thickness [08:50], ASCE 7 load combinations (he singles out the load-side complexity, not a specific section) [02:39], and OSHA bridging-termination requirements [28:37]. No AISC 360 chapter, 341 seismic section, AWS D1.1 clause, or RCSC bolting section is cited by number.

### Technical Details
Joist web members migrated from all-rod webs (old practice, roughly pre-1990s) to crimped single angles over the last 20 years, with the transition generally near a 20-inch depth and crimped webs typical by 30-inch K-series, though no exact cutoff exists [00:32][01:02]. Some makers now use cold-formed channel webs, and older bottom chords were occasionally rod, abandoned partly due to wind-uplift demands [01:35][02:08]. Joist members are ordered to thousandths of an inch (for example a 1-3/4 by 1-3/4 by 0.109 or 0.232 angle) and are not standard stock sections, so field measurement requires a micrometer, never a tape [07:46][08:19]. Bridging carries real in-service force: it laterally braces the bottom chord against wind uplift and stabilizes the web system, and bracing demands both strength and stiffness, which is why the end compression diagonal matters most [23:29][24:29][25:32].

### Fabrication Notes
Reinforcement design favors brute simplicity: for web reinforcing, design added angles or rods to carry the entire shear at that panel and weld them for the full load rather than apportioning between old and new members, which removes any dependence on existing weld quality [10:56][11:28]. Chord reinforcing is the exception where the speaker proportions load between chord and reinforcement for economy [11:58]. Welds on joist members must develop the strength of the member, an SJI principle that gives a minimum known weld capacity even when field welds cannot be measured [07:15][10:23]. Reinforcing rods are stuffed alongside chords and tied with flare-bevel welds; double-angle webs that nearly touch the top chord block rod insertion, so the diagonal end is sometimes cropped to make room [13:02][14:04][14:35].

### Erection Notes
Field work on roof joists is done from underneath because deck sits on top, so downhand fillet welds are easy on bottom chords but top-side access is constrained [13:33][15:36]. Reinforcing angles or plates must keep the work point so eccentricity is not thrown into the top chord [16:08][17:08]. For length errors, look past the joist itself: a joist a few inches too long or short may be cheaper to fix by moving the support beam at its column framing, or even shoving a footing, than by modifying many joists [18:44][19:16]. Bridging may be cut for duct penetrations only if X-bridging is added on either side of the cut, and bridging into a wall must terminate with two horizontals to the wall (which bend rather than break) rather than the X-termination OSHA shows, to avoid pulling joists out of the wall under uplift or snow [23:29][28:37][29:08].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Named field failures include framing a joist into a beam at an angle of 30 degrees or less, which guarantees a bearing fit problem [21:55][22:27]; joists badly corroded over a chlorinated pool that were past reinforcing and had to be replaced [03:41][04:11]; and a Houston job where a contractor cut the end diagonals out of 20 joists to fit HVAC duct, destroying the most critical compression member, later patched by torching the duct and welding the diagonals back in [26:33][27:36]. He also cites bottom-bearing joists installed upside down [28:06]. Shoring during reinforcement is driven by safety, since heavy weld heat across a chord can sag the joist, not purely by stress [11:58][12:31].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Cost judgment runs through the talk: replacing severely degraded joists is often cheaper than reinforcing them, and ordering new joists when schedule allows beats reinforcing many in place [04:11][19:48]. Conservative full-load reinforcement saves design and inspection time because material is cheap relative to engineering hours and weld-quality risk [10:56][11:28]. Elaborate fixes (beveling outstanding legs, custom notched plates) are flagged as terribly expensive and to be avoided unless forced [14:35][15:06]. Cutting at joist center versus ends is partly an economic and ownership argument, since the party paying the bill usually drives the detail [19:48][20:53].

### Your Company Application
This maps directly to Your Company joist scope and any renovation or tenant-fit bid touching existing bar joists. For Ivan's takeoff, an existing-joist reinforcement scope cannot be priced from SF; it requires field identification of web type and chord type plus SJI load-table capacity back-calculation, and any joist job lacking that data is a LOW-confidence ROM with an SF-style RFI to confirm members. Mario's shop and field crews should treat the full-load reinforcement rule and flare-bevel/full-strength weld principle as the default, and Paul's safety scope picks up the shoring-for-heat and bridging-cut hazards. Tekla detailing and the in-house PE stamp should hold the work-point and eccentricity discipline on any reinforcement detail, and the bridging-into-wall termination correction is a stamp-level call that overrides the OSHA-shown X detail. No conflict with Your Company doctrine: the speaker names manufacturers generically as joist-tag examples, which is reportage of an SJI tagging rule, not a Your Company outward reference, so we keep those out of any client document.

## Field Fixes - Part 7
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KRhUCvehegQ | Duration: 28:21 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This session covers field remediation for rooftop-unit (RTU) loads on steel framing and steel joists, with most attention on the recurring problem of HVAC units that arrive late, vibrate, or land in the wrong location relative to the framing the structural engineer designed [00:01], [03:34]. The teaching thread is how to support, reinforce, or pre-engineer joist and beam framing so a misplaced or heavier-than-planned RTU does not require destructive after-the-fact fixes [09:42]. The presenter, a steel joist authority, also previews a Steel Joist Institute technical digest he is writing on joist reinforcement [05:36].
### Spec References
The only code citation stated is the AISC 2005 specification, named twice: once for new provisions on single-angle design using an equivalent slenderness ratio that lets you go directly to the column table [07:41], and once for the basic-assumption reminder that the beam design equations assume torsional restraint at the beam ends [17:24], [17:56]. Steel Joist Institute (SJI) is named as the governing body for the K, KCS, and historic H series joists and for the forthcoming reinforcement design guide [05:36], [12:47]. No AISC 360 section number, table number, AWS clause, or RCSC provision was spoken; treat all other guidance here as general principles, no section cited.
### Technical Details
For RTU vibration the rule of thumb given is that supporting beams or joists should have a natural frequency either 50 percent above or 50 percent below the unit operating frequency [01:33]. Two textbook frequency equations were stated in cycles per minute, not cycles per second: 188 divided by the square root of the deflection for a concentrated load at midspan, and 213 divided by the square root of the deflection for uniform load [02:33], [03:04]. K series joists are designed to the exact tabulated load with no spare capacity, the older H series carried an extra 300 lb concentrated load anywhere, and the KCS series carries a constant moment and constant shear capacity along its full length with all diagonals except the end diagonal designed for stress reversal (the end diagonal is 100 percent tension only unless uplift is specified) [06:38], [12:47], [13:48]. A concentrated load that does not land at a top-cord panel point cannot be carried by the top cord and must be transferred to a panel point, typically via an inverted channel across the deck ribs plus an angle web member down to the panel point [06:06].
### Fabrication Notes
The classic fabrication detail for slipping a reinforcing beam under an existing K series joist is to make the beam seat shallower than the 2-1/2 inch joist seat, about 2 inches deep, then shim about 1/2 inch to set it [08:11], [26:11]. A web stiffener is added at that shortened seat so the thin remaining web is not overstressed in shear and bending [08:41]. Using all 50 ksi yield steel gives better web shear strength, sometimes requiring only a slightly thicker web than otherwise [09:12]. For a special reinforcing joist, order it with no camber and a 2 inch deep seat, since every manufacturer cambers joists by default and a cambered joist will not stuff into an existing facility where the surrounding deflection is already locked in [25:08], [25:39].
### Erection Notes
Field installation of reinforcement is driven by access and interference. Before adding a joist or beam, identify existing piping, mechanical, electrical, and gas interference, because the cost of relocating it can make the in-fill solution prohibitive [24:37], [25:08]. A no-camber, shallow-seat member is what lets the erector shove the new piece into place and shim it [26:11]. The presenter's preferred field trick is to specify a joist with no end seat so the bare joist is short enough to lift and set, then field-weld a two-angle seat back to the main panel point, with the seat designed to carry the moment from the offset vertical load [27:13], [28:14]. Lateral support is mandatory: a joist is designed assuming top-cord lateral support every 36 inches normally provided by the deck and its welds, screws, or pins, so any added joist needs equivalent bracing, and you must not shoot nails vertically through the roof membrane to get it [26:42], [27:13].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Field damage examples shown include a plumber who cut most of a joist top cord (stopping only because he ran out of drill) and a tension cord with a large hump from an erector dropping the joist and re-erecting it without flagging it [18:26], [18:59]. A flagged unstable condition: a joist bearing on an HSS column with a beam on top and no stiffener, joist extension, or other stabilizer, which leaves a thin-web column with a poor L over R [16:53], [17:24]. Sprinkler mains, the 8 inch main specifically, must be hung from more than one joist or they overstress a single joist [22:03]. The curb and support-frame weight is frequently omitted from the unit weight the mechanical engineer gives you [16:23].
### Bid / Cost Implications
The cheapest prevention named is providing two extra joists in a bay (roughly 500 dollars each) so a heavier or relocated unit can be accommodated without later reinforcing, though owners resist paying for spare joists on a large job and then pay more for field rework [10:12]. Adding a new joist is generally the most cost-effective fix when schedule allows, but joist-manufacturer lead time often forces a faster beam-with-special-seat solution instead [19:29]. Load redistribution with a stiff spreader beam can carry a concentrated load across multiple joists and avoid reinforcement entirely; a 10 to 15 percent joist overstress is small enough that this often works [22:34], [23:35]. The presenter endorses modest overdesign for mechanical equipment and collateral loads when you already hold the job, and notes simplifying RTU reactions by taking total weight divided by two saves significant engineering time at no material cost [16:23], [20:30].
### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff and estimating, the spare-joist and RTU-zoning guidance is a bid-contingency item: where an RTU bay is shown but the unit weight or location is not fixed, price a KCS-series or extra-joist allowance rather than absorb later reinforcement, and confirm curb plus support-frame weight is in the load (member weights still come from aisc_validator.py, never invented here) [10:12], [16:23]. For Mario's shop crew, the 2 inch shallow seat, no-camber order, web stiffener, and bolt-on or field-welded angle seat are concrete shop and field details, and the field-welded panel-point seat is AWS D1.1 welding scope to plan and qualify [08:11], [27:13]. For Tekla detailing and the in-house PE stamp, model RTU support framing to land concentrated loads at joist panel points or detail the inverted-channel transfer, and carry the AISC 2005 reminder forward that beam equations assume end torsional restraint [06:06], [17:56]. Paul should flag the unstable joist-on-HSS-column condition and the no-nails-through-membrane lateral-support rule during erection-safety review [16:53], [26:42]. Doctrine conflict: NONE; nothing here touches BID_RATES, supplier naming, or PEMB positioning.

## Field Fixes - Part 6
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wBczYp9NRno | Duration: 37:14 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This webinar segment covers field fixes for connection problems: bolt and weld load sharing, mislocated or missing holes, gusset and bracing connection misfits, hole reaming and filling, weldability of steel, weld inspection, welding procedure specifications, and weld crack repair. The unifying theme is verifying a problem against the spec and the actual demand before forcing a costly repair, and detailing connections up front to absorb field variation. The speaker repeatedly contrasts the pre-2005 and 2005 AISC rules on bolts sharing load with welds [00:01].
### Spec References
The major cited change is the AISC 2005 specification rule that bolts shall not be considered to share load with welds, with the shear-connection exception that any permitted bolt grade in standard holes or short slots transverse to the load may share load with longitudinally loaded fillet welds, and that the bolt available strength in such connections is limited to 50% of bearing-type bolt strength [00:34][01:04]. Also cited: AWS D1.1 preheat tables and the AWS D1.1 annex for high-carbon steels [18:08]; ASTM A6 / A992 requiring the carbon equivalent on the mill cert [17:06]; the differing carbon-equivalent formulas between ASTM and AWS [17:38]; the 6G / 6GR welder certification for unbacked HSS CJP welds [22:45][23:15]; and AWS D1.1 Section 6.8, engineer-of-record approval for alternate acceptance criteria [33:30].
### Technical Details
The 50% load-sharing logic comes from University of Alberta research: slip-critical bolts will have slipped before welds deform enough to pick up load, but longitudinally loaded fillet welds have enough deformation capacity to combine with bearing bolts in standard holes; oversized holes force welding the full connection strength [01:35][02:06]. For a missing bolt row, reduce remaining bolts to 50% capacity and design the weld for the difference rather than welding only the missing-bolt portion [03:08][03:38]. The uniform force method allows alternate load paths: analyzing a moment on the gusset surface can remove the horizontal force from angle outstanding legs so the angles need only be welded for vertical shear [07:18][08:20]. The speaker notes A992 carbon equivalents typically land in the low 0.30s and are very weldable, while plate is the commodity item most likely to carry high carbon and govern preheat [18:39][19:09].
### Fabrication Notes
Preferred detailing replaces clip angles with an end plate or a continuous coped member to control the brace-connection dimension in the shop, even though SDS2 defaults to angles and the detailer must be told to change it manually [06:15][06:47]. Hole misfits are fixed by reaming (typically an eighth inch larger to the next bolt size, with edge distance rechecked), field welding, or filling and drilling as the least desirable option since AWS has no general hole-restoration procedure outside fatigue cases [08:52][09:23]. The shop rule is to run the same-size reamer through a couple of off holes and clean them if removal stays within a sixteenth to an eighth of an inch [11:26]. Weldability checks include the mill cert carbon equivalent, wet chemistry (last cost under $300), and the ironworker fillet-break test where a break through the weld is good and a break off the base metal indicates a carbon problem [19:39][20:10].
### Erection Notes
Short-slotted one-sided single-plate or single-angle connections absorb end-slope variation from camber, which can reach three-eighths of an inch [10:25]. Columns tied with precast plank historically walked out of plumb when the precast crew slammed planks in, so the fix is to provide steel tie beams (struts) at one per tier to hold column spacing and alignment, which is cheaper than arguing over plumb responsibility [13:32][14:33]. The erector determines what erection aids are needed but the fabricator details and furnishes them, so the two must coordinate, especially with architecturally exposed HSS where any aid must be cut, ground, and finished [16:05][16:35].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Visual inspection is the primary method: no cracks, base-to-weld-metal fusion, filled craters and intermittent fillets, correct weld profile (slight crown, not concave), allowable weld size, undercut limits, and porosity limits [20:42][21:13]. Named failures include cracks from joint restraint, insufficient preheat, excess carbon, wrong procedure, wrong joint, moisture contamination, or out-of-spec material, illustrated by a plate that arrived as abrasion-resistant material with Brinell over 400 [29:21][30:23]. A Casa Grande moment-connection joint cracked three times from thermal stress on an end wall until the joint was redesigned [30:54][31:25]. Banging bolts traced to column settlement forcing bolts into bearing [32:26]. Post-Northridge inspectors found seismic demand-critical welds with passes two or three times the WPS maximum [25:15].
### Bid / Cost Implications
The recurring cost message is to weigh a field repair against the real demand rather than reflexively fixing. Changing the SDS2 default to an end plate saves shop labor but costs engineering time, an explicit trade-off [06:47]. The owner must specify NDT (mag particle, UT) in the contract documents; an owner who requires it after the fact owns all associated costs including rework unless gross negligence is proven [28:20][28:51]. AWS D1.1 Section 6.8 lets the engineer accept an undersize weld that still carries the shear, avoiding an unneeded repair pass; one example accepts a quarter-inch weld where a five-sixteenth was called out [33:30][34:33]. A fabricator keeps roughly a dozen WPS in a book that cover most structural welds, adding special ones as they arise [27:19].
### Your Company Application
For Mario as AWS D1.1 welding lead, this maps directly: keep WPS coverage current, verify electrode care and joint prep, run the ironworker break test when tacks crack, and check the mill-cert carbon equivalent and AWS preheat tables before welding plate, which governs preheat more often than the wide-flange. The 50% bolt-weld sharing rule and the missing-row repair math belong in Tekla connection detailing and the in-house PE stamp workflow, and the preference for end plates or continuous coped members over SDS2 default angles is a standing detailing instruction. For field bolting, avoid mixing A325 and A490 in the same diameter without a tracking program, and detail extra edge distance so a reamed hole still passes. Anchor-rod and precast-tie lessons (tie beams one per tier to hold plumb) apply to ACP erection sequencing and to Paul on plumb and OSHA bracing exposure. NONE of this conflicts with Your Company doctrine; it reinforces verify-don't-generate, conventional structural steel positioning, and AISC-sourced weights through aisc_validator.py.

## Field Fixes - Part 5
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oiDBL0ZfqGE | Duration: 31:51 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This webinar covers field and shop problems on composite floor systems and their fixes, organized around three themes: beam camber and its interaction with deck and concrete, shear stud welding and inspection, and shop paint defects. The unifying lesson is that camber tolerances are workmanship guidelines, not absolutes, and that uncontrolled deflection, camber mismatch, and coating errors all produce expensive field rework. The speaker draws repeatedly on real composite-floor jobs (hospitals, Class A office midrises, parking ramps) to show how small misjudgments at fab become change orders in the field.
### Spec References
The speaker cites the AISC Code of Standard Practice as the document that first added camber tolerances in its prior edition (he names "not the current 2005 Edition but the previous Edition," roughly 2000 or 2001), where camber was previously only in the manual [01:34]. He gives the camber tolerance as minus 0, plus 1/2 inch for most beams, with an additional increase over 50 feet, measured in the unstressed shop position [01:34][03:37]. He cites AWS D1.1 for stud qualification (manufacturer qualifies the stud for the deck) and for the fillet-welding-studs procedure and minimum weld size [13:22][15:58][18:31]; he notes he sits on an AWS D1.1 subcommittee. On stud cover he contrasts the old ASD requirement of 3/4 inch cover over the stud top against the 2005 specification requirement, which he states as cover over the stud top (he misspeaks the LRFD value but cites the 2005 spec change) [19:01][19:34]. Paint cleanliness is cited by SSPC surface-prep grades by their shop shorthand: SP2 hand-tool, SP3 power-tool, and SPC1 solvent clean [22:37][23:39][26:15].
### Technical Details
Camber is induced mechanically by running the beam through a machine past yield, backing off, and measuring set; uniformity across like beams is approximate and verified by a string line and mid-ordinate tape measurement [02:05][02:36]. Camber loss in shipping was studied historically (a Bethlehem Steel study, attributed to "Larson") but was never conclusively resolved, and the speaker reports no significant field loss except possibly on very light members under 100 percent composite with heavy stud counts [04:08][05:09]. Shear studs are checked for a full 360-degree weld flash at the base, then bend-tested or ring-tested; a few bad studs change composite strength so little they are not worth losing sleep over [15:28][15:58]. He points to an Engineering Journal article by John Ruddy on level floors and ponding as the reference for floor-levelness practice [10:17].
### Fabrication Notes
The shop target is minus 0, plus 1/2 inch camber, but the speaker treats it as a workmanship band: a beam coming in at minus 1/4 inch on a 2.5 inch specified camber will not be sent back through the machine [03:07]. Fillet-welded studs require grinding off the protrusion on the stud base so it seats tight with no gap before welding [15:58]. Paint defects are diagnosed by cause: mill-scale lifting traces to incomplete loose-scale removal under SP2/SP3; paint lifting traces to surface contamination, notably forming lubricant on HSS, which needs an SPC1 solvent clean; runs and sags from too-thick a coat or wrong vehicle; mud cracks from overbuilding the coating in the flange-to-web fillet; pin holes and chipping from top-coating inorganic zinc before full cure [23:08][26:15][29:23][30:24]. He recommends staying inside the paint manufacturer's mil thickness and matching vehicle to substrate (high-solids on smooth HSS, more vehicle on mill-scaled wide flange), and prefers epoxy zinc over inorganic zinc when a shop top coat is required because inorganic zinc needs high humidity and long cure [27:19][28:23][31:26].
### Erection Notes
Cambered beams or joists adjacent to non-cambered supports (moment frames, end walls, bearing walls on concrete or masonry) create deck-bearing problems where the deck will not seat on the adjacent support [01:03][05:09]. On a Rosemont/Chicago job with moment frames parallel to fill-in beams and cellular deck, the field fix was to saw-cut the deck so it acts as a simple span rather than continuous, which is acceptable if strength and deflection still satisfy [05:40][06:13]. After-the-fact floor openings during tenant build-outs can convert deck to a single-span condition that was not designed for it; one job deflected 2 to 3 inches and was saved only because the GC shored it [06:43][07:15]. Heat straightening to remove field camber is possible but rarely done by erectors and needs a specialist or a fabricator-written detailed procedure with supervision [18:31].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Over-cambering: on a hospital floor with an operating-theater opening, members at the unloaded opening edge ended up about 2.5 inches high so studs protruded above the concrete and had to be cut off [00:01][00:31]. Excess concrete from beam deflection when chasing a level pour: a medical facility using 7-inch normal-weight concrete (chosen for vibration) on near-zero-camber beams accumulated 3 to 3.5 inches of extra concrete mid-span and required field-welded cover plates as a change order [07:45][09:16]. Laser-screed level floors thinned slabs below fire-rating cover because camber did not come out as calculated, forcing sprayed fireproofing on the deck underside [12:19][12:51]. The catastrophic case: a parking-ramp cover by a miscellaneous-metals subcontractor without a stud machine fillet-welded studs on embedded plates that also carried moment, and the structure collapsed six floors straight down [16:59][17:59].
### Bid / Cost Implications
Several failures here landed as change orders: cover plates welded in the field to deflected beams, sprayed fireproofing added when laser-screed slabs ran thin, and shoring to rescue an over-deflected single-span deck. The speaker notes that some GCs historically figured concrete volume on theoretical slab thickness and then back-charged for the extra concrete that deck and beam deflection demanded, so drawings should carry a note about extra concrete for deflection [09:16][09:46]. Paint scope is a cost lever: most steel that is enclosed in finish or fireproofed should ship bare or with only an SP2 hand-tool clean and standard primer, avoiding unnecessary paint cost and rework [21:36][22:37].
### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff and estimating, the recurring lesson is to price camber and level-floor coordination as real scope on composite floors and to carry a deflection/extra-concrete note so the GC cannot back-charge concrete to Your Company; over-camber and laser-screed thinning both create fire-rating cover problems that touch fireproofing scope. Mario's shop crew should hold the minus 0 plus 1/2 inch camber band per the Code of Standard Practice as a workmanship guideline, verify it by string line and mid-ordinate, and follow AWS D1.1 for stud welding (360-degree flash, bend/ring test) and the fillet-weld-stud grind-and-seat step; the paint-defect diagnostics (SP2/SP3, SPC1 solvent clean on HSS, epoxy-zinc over inorganic when a shop top coat is needed) map directly to our shop coating QC. Paul's safety brief should carry the parking-ramp collapse as the case for never letting a non-fabricator fillet-weld studs on plates that also see moment. Tekla detailing should flag cambered members adjacent to non-cambered moment frames or end walls and call out deck-splice or camber-transition details, and the in-house PE stamp should design for the single-span deck condition created by any after-the-fact opening. No conflict with Your Company doctrine: NONE.

## Field Fixes - Part 4
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=beLLNbBIG64 | Duration: 30:34 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This Lawrence Kloiber (Clober) session covers field fixes for column-erection problems and the economics and rules of beam camber. The first half walks through column-splice gaps, columns set too short or too long, and out-of-plumb columns, with the recurring theme that the erector must give the fabricator and engineer of record early notice the moment something hangs up on fit-up [05:41][06:13]. The second half is a detailed treatment of when to camber, when not to, and how camber is physically produced and checked.
### Spec References
The speaker cites the AISC splice-gap rule by value: a gap of one sixteenth inch or less needs no action, and a gap over one sixteenth up to roughly a quarter inch may be shimmed with flat mild-steel shims [01:34][02:06]. He cites the AISC column out-of-plumb tolerance of L/500 from the AISC Code of Standard Practice [12:21][12:51], and returns to the Code of Standard Practice for the rule that camber shall be checked in the shop in the unstressed condition [29:45]. He cites AWS D1.1 for moment-weld buildout, prequalified joint configurations, root-dimension limits, and the EOR-accepted larger correction with a developed procedure [14:22][16:24][17:25]. He references an American Iron and Steel Engineers recommendation for cambering crane girders over 75 feet [20:30]. No table numbers or Design Guide numbers were stated.
### Technical Details
Column splices should sit at least 48 inches above top of concrete so a shop-punched hole can serve as both the lifting hole (pin and shackle, lanyard to pull the pin from the ground) and the OSHA perimeter safety-cable hole at 42 inches above floor [03:39][04:09][04:39]. Splice gaps arise from band-saw drift on heavy columns, slight out-of-square ends, or joints opening during plumbing [05:10]. Out-of-plumb causes to diagnose first are misplaced anchor rods or mis-detailed framing beams [11:50][12:21]; a column is a compression member and tolerates more than L/500 if braced for the eccentricity and there is no cladding or fit-up conflict [12:51]. Welded CJP moment joints shrink roughly an eighth inch each; AWS requires a buildout pass when the root exceeds about three eighths inch so a single pass does not crack [14:22][16:54].
### Fabrication Notes
Fabricators prefer bolted-bolted splice details made on CNC punches and drill lines because holes are cheap and a loose bolted upper shaft adjusts more easily on fit-up [02:37][03:08]. Base-plate elevations should be uniform with exceptions clearly flagged, and top-of-column elevations and roof slopes clearly shown, with shop QC verifying column dimensions [07:14][07:44]. Camber is produced in a mechanical press with reaction points about 25 feet apart and rams about 6 to 8 feet apart that push the beam past yield to a permanent set, so beams under 25 feet will not fit the machine [23:40][24:11]. Members are sawn, squared, and punched uncambered, then cambered last, which leaves an end slope; webs of a quarter inch or less can buckle when forced to yield, and heat cambering costs four to five times mechanical cambering [24:41][25:11][25:41].
### Erection Notes
The dominant erection lesson is timely notice: examples include 50 columns decked and ready for concrete before a splice gap was reported [05:41], a brace bent poured into concrete with diagonals that would not fit because one column was an inch low [10:18], and a 165-foot welded moment line drawn 2.5 inches short because the crew did not compensate for weld shrinkage [15:23][16:24]. The fix posture is to plumb the center column and lean columns outward as welds shrink, or to plan shrinkage if starting from one end [17:25]. Big-box joist and joist-girder jobs with slotted end connections can run several inches out of plumb across five or six bays, so OSHA requires bracing and plumbing every couple of days as erection proceeds [13:22][13:52].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Named failures are column splices hanging up on splice plates with unreported gaps [06:13], columns erected an inch too short or too long [06:43][11:19], six columns set an inch low from a base-plate grout-thickness detail error [09:48], out-of-plumb beyond L/500 [12:21], welded and end-plated beam lines running too short from uncompensated weld shrinkage [14:22][16:24], and AWS root dimensions exceeded leading to single-pass cracking [16:54]. Detailing too-light beams from RAM-Steel output and then cambering them is flagged as a buckling failure [25:11].
### Bid / Cost Implications
End-plated and welded moment connections should be detailed short (an eighth inch each end on end plates) so finger shims absorb error, because a too-long member goes back to the shop for a cut-off and new end plate [18:26][18:58]. Camber only what pays: skip camber under 1 inch, under 25 feet, and on stiff girders loaded at third points, and camber filler beams rather than girders for real savings [25:41][26:11][26:41]. Heat cambering costs four to five times mechanical cambering, so upsizing a beam a size or two can be cheaper than a heat-camber requirement [24:41]. The cost of a field fix scales with bay count and end tolerance: a one- or two-bay job tolerates being slightly short or long, but multi-bay or tight-tolerance lines need designed-in adjustment [18:58].
### Your Company Application
For Tekla detailing, set column splices a minimum 48 inches above top of concrete with a shop-punched dual lifting and safety-cable hole, and detail end-plate and welded moment connections short with finger-shim allowance, which Ivan should carry as a takeoff and labor assumption. Mario's shop work covers the mechanical camber press limits (no camber under 25 feet, watch quarter-inch webs, square-and-cut ends after cambering for flange connections) and AWS D1.1 buildout passes when CJP roots exceed about three eighths inch, with camber checked in the shop unstressed per the Code of Standard Practice. Paul should hold the every-couple-of-days brace-and-plumb OSHA cadence, critical on any ACP joist and joist-girder framing with slotted ends. Anchor-rod practice from the in-house PE should keep an extra inch of rod length on first-tier columns for height adjustment. No conflict with Your Company doctrine: NONE.

## Field Fixes - Part 3
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=q8ImUuJ0gww | Duration: 34:29 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This webinar is a practitioner walkthrough of common field-fix situations on structural steel jobs and how to repair or design around them, presented by an engineer (Jim, with co-author Larry) drawing on roughly 40 years of practice. The recurring theme is that most field problems trace to detailing, mill tolerances, and concrete-to-steel coordination rather than bad steel, and that material is cheap while labor is expensive, so reinforce or adjust rather than scrap [22:57]. A second theme: design connections for the completed structure, and visit the job site because, in the speaker's words, he has never gone to a site in 40 years without finding something wrong [22:25].
### Spec References
The speaker cites the 2005 AISC Specification, specifically Section F13 covering holes in beams, noting those requirements were liberalized versus the prior spec [01:31]. He references ASTM A6 for mill tolerances on rolled shapes (web off-center, tilted flanges, depth variation) [06:46]. He cites ASTM A992 (50 ksi yield, flange-sampled mill reports) versus legacy A36 [03:35, 04:39], ACI 117 for concrete vertical and lateral alignment tolerances [12:33], OSHA four-anchor-rod erection-stability rules [27:34], and AWS for column-to-base-plate welding [31:15]. He also mentions the 2005 spec contains new combined bolt-plus-weld strength requirements [25:32].
### Technical Details
Mill reports can hint at higher actual yield (old A36 often ran 42 to 44 ksi) but should not be used directly to justify added capacity; legacy reports were sampled from the stronger web, and A992 now mandates flange sampling, so an old web-based report overstates flange strength [03:02, 04:39]. Steel is not homogeneous or isotropic; webs can run 10 percent higher yield than flanges due to more rolling [04:06]. A6 tolerances (off-center webs, tilted flanges, depth deviation) accumulate and can make a beam-to-column-web weld impossible to land [06:46]. Continuity plates must match the A992 50 ksi material; a real project used 36 ksi plates against A992 members and the moment connections were invalid until field-welded new plates and beam stubs fixed them [07:49, 08:20].
### Fabrication Notes
Oversize embeds and weld plates because they will not land where the form drawings show; make a wall weld plate roughly the size of the wall, and provide nail holes in embeds so the concrete crew can set them [16:08, 13:34]. Use generously oversized continuity plates so a backup bar and full-penetration weld can still be made despite tolerance stackup [07:17]. For bolted flange-plate connections, leave plenty of shim room (at least a 3/8 inch shim stack on the bottom) and consider weld detail and sequence to control distortion, with heat straightening after fab if needed [11:01, 11:31]. Deck does not seat over bolted moment connections where nuts stick up an inch; fix the detail ahead of time so the deck bears and the required concrete cover is achieved [00:01].
### Erection Notes
Field-fit problems are routine: beams too long or short at concrete walls get cut and rewelded, caught on larger angles, or field-measured and replaced, with adjustable and slotted connections designed in to absorb concrete tolerance [11:31, 14:35]. Bolted flange-plate beams can often be jacked into place and the bolts snugged to pull them in, but a mismatched two-fabricator job required air-arcing out all the top-plate CJP welds and repositioning, which was very expensive [09:57, 10:30]. OSHA requires four anchor rods per column for erection stability with limited exceptions (light posts around 300 lb); fewer than four needs special guided-erection procedures [27:34, 28:05]. Avoid weak-axis moment connections entirely where possible; rotate columns or add bracing to frame into the strong axis [05:45].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Named failures include 36 ksi continuity plates installed in A992 moment frames (connection invalid) [08:20], two-fabricator beam-and-column splits that did not fit despite shim allowance [10:30], a torched beam hole oversized past the recommended limit in a building that partially collapsed under snow load when the flanges buckled [20:17], and a crew cutting girt flanges out at midspan to thread bracing rod instead of drilling the web, hidden behind liner panel [21:22]. Epoxy field-fix bolts melt above 200 degrees, so they fail in a fire unless fire-protected [17:12]. Welding to embeds risks concrete spalling, mitigated with small fillet welds, controlled sequence, and thick enough embed heat sinks (1/2 inch for deck bearing, 3/4 inch for beam bearing) [18:13, 18:45].
### Bid / Cost Implications
The standing cost rule stated is material is cheap and labor is expensive, so reinforce existing members (cover plates, bent plates, added members below, boxing with channels) rather than replace when analysis supports it [22:57, 23:28]. The two-fabricator flange-plate mismatch is a cautionary cost case: splitting columns and beams between fabricators removed any shop fit check and forced full-penetration weld removal and rework in the field, described as very expensive [10:30, 11:01]. Job-site visits are framed as cheap insurance; a half-hour walk catches problems, and the speaker urges negotiating a site-visit fee or going anyway [21:52, 22:25].
### Your Company Application
For Tekla detailing and the in-house PE stamp, enforce the continuity-plate material match (50 ksi to A992 members) as a hard detailing check, since the cited failure invalidated an entire moment frame; flag any 36 ksi continuity or stiffener plate in a 50 ksi frame. Mario's shop and welding crew should carry the embed and weld-plate oversizing rule, the 1/2 and 3/4 inch embed thicknesses, small-fillet weld-to-embed practice, and the 3/8 inch minimum shim stack on bolted flange plates. For anchor rods, the four-rod OSHA erection rule and the threaded-nut-over-hooked-rod pullout preference belong in Paul's erection-stability and Ivan's base-plate detailing checks [31:45, 27:34]. On ACP controls, treat single-fabricator scope and a mandatory pre-erection fit verification as a coordination gate, and build a concrete-to-steel tolerance reconciliation step per ACI 117 into the schedule. The mill-report-cannot-add-capacity rule reinforces our verify-do-not-generate doctrine: AISC weights and yields come from aisc_validator.py, never from a mill cert. Doctrine conflict: NONE.

## Field Fixes - Part 2
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RD-lPTNaH9s | Duration: 31:18 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This webinar by Jim Fisher (with co-author Larry) catalogs real field problems on steel-frame jobs and the engineered fixes for them, organized around anchor rods, base plates, spandrel and curtain-wall support, and bolted-connection behavior. The recurring theme is that most field fixes trace back to a foundation or detailing miss that is correctable, but the correct repair must be analyzed, not improvised. The presenter stresses that a "quick weld" type fix is often invalid and that the engineer should pre-draw standard correction details so they can be issued to the field without redrawing each time [09:17].

### Spec References
The speaker explicitly cites AISC Design Guide 1 by topic, naming it as "design guide number three" by mistake but identifying it as the base-plate and anchor-rod guide he co-wrote with Mike West [18:34]. He references "design guide 3" for serviceability of buildings up to five stories, with spandrel deflection criteria such as span over 480 and span over 600 [19:36][20:07]. He cites the RCSC specification as having "three pages on arbitration" for resolving bolt-tension disputes [29:00], and the AISC snug-tight definition of all plies in firm contact [29:32]. He references ASTM F1554 anchor-rod material (A36 / 36 ksi grade) and Grade 55 implications [07:12][07:45], the AISC steel manual standard detail for slab-edge plates [15:58], and an OSHA tripping-hazard rule for anchors projecting over a beam [30:07]. AWS qualified-weld requirements are named generally without a clause number [00:02].

### Technical Details
A fully-threaded nut on an anchor rod develops the full rod strength so the rod breaks before the threads strip, and strength is roughly linear in thread engagement, so half the threads engaged gives about half the strength, allowing a thread-engagement capacity calculation [01:02][01:32]. Buried-nut anchor rods give a significant strength increase for overturning and uplift versus bent (hooked) rods, which can straighten in the concrete and pull out [05:09]. An A36 / 36 ksi rod bent no more than 45 degrees can generally be cold-bent or heat-straightened back; high-strength rods cannot be bent or welded and must be replaced [07:12][08:17]. Tolerance accumulation between steel, concrete, and curtain-wall trades can force tighter-than-normal adjustment provisions [20:38].

### Fabrication Notes
The fix for short anchor rods is to extend with a threaded rod and coupling nut, weld the base plate to the rods, or use epoxy anchors, and the engineer should draw these as standard AutoCAD details for reuse [00:32][09:17]. A clean weld-on extension uses a fabricated runoff-tab plate sized 11/16 inch larger than the rod, slipped over and tacked, with the extension rod beveled for a legitimate weld; flare-bevel welds with side plates are an alternative [02:36][03:08]. Do not specify high-strength anchor rods unless required, since a field weld repair may be needed [02:04]. With threaded studs the weld flash requires holes at least 3/16 inch larger or shims to seat a mating plate, and a reduced-base stud keeps flash within the base diameter to avoid back-charges [24:51][25:23].

### Erection Notes
A collapse during erection is described where bent anchor rods were set with the hook about 4 inches too high (in dirt below the footing), so wind lifted the frame and P-Delta tipped it, a reminder that embedment must be verified against the shop drawing [04:39][06:10]. Leveling nuts must be tacked so workers cannot lower them, and heavy columns favor shim stock over leveling nuts [10:48][12:22]. Spandrels and facades need adjustable connections, plumbness checks as the structure rises, and adequate bracing; sweep can be heat-straightened or jacked into position [13:56][15:28]. Curtain wall is best foundation-supported, next best off columns, and worst off a deflecting, twisting spandrel beam, so spandrels must be detailed stiff [12:53][13:25].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Named failures include welding a nut to a tensioned anchor rod (cannot produce an AWS-qualified weld) [00:02], anchor rods set too short or too long, too-long usually meaning insufficient embedment [04:08][04:39], base plates punching through leveling nuts when only a regular washer is used instead of a thick plate washer [10:48][11:51], and a metric-to-inch drafting error that misplaced 8-inch anchor rods buried 12 feet deep [22:14][23:17]. Banging bolts are detailed at length: a snug or pretensioned bolt slips into bearing after loading with a gunshot-loud report, all known cases occurred in shear-tab connections lacking flexibility, and the fix is snug-tight bolts or single-angle connections that deform [26:24][28:27]. Anchors projecting over a beam are an OSHA tripping hazard and iron workers will refuse to erect [30:07].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Pre-cast curtain-wall engineers in the speaker's office bid steel-supported projects higher than concrete-supported ones because steel spandrels deflect and create erection problems, a direct precedent that flexible support structures carry an erection-risk premium [14:27]. Coupling-nut and weld-on anchor-rod extensions add the cost of torching out the base plate to clear the extra material, so anchor-rod placement near the web or flange affects feasibility and cost [03:38]. Specifying ample thread length and not requiring full bolt torque where snug-tight is acceptable avoids inspection and rework cost [05:40][29:00]. Reduced-base studs and correctly oversized holes avoid back-charges [25:23].

### Your Company Application
This entry is direct reference material for anchor-rod design, setting, and tolerance work: the buried-nut-over-bent-rod rule, the 45-degree A36 cold-bend allowance, the thread-engagement capacity check, and the runoff-tab and coupling-nut extension details should be drawn as standard Tekla and AutoCAD repair details under the in-house PE stamp so Mario's crew can apply them in the field without a new RFI each time. The leveling-nut versus shim-stock guidance and thick plate-washer rule belong in Paul's erection-safety checklist alongside the OSHA anchor-projection tripping-hazard item. The banging-bolt single-angle-versus-shear-tab note informs field bolting and connection-detailing choices, and the spandrel-deflection bid premium is a concrete estimating input for Ivan when an ACP or similar facade is steel-supported. DOCTRINE FLAGS: NONE. The content is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language, and the speaker cites Design Guide 1 (he mis-states the number as 3 on the base-plate guide), so any internal use of that citation should be verified against the actual Design Guide before quoting a number.

## Field Fixes - Part 1
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FZMNk0mTEi8 | Duration: 29:21 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is a two-speaker AISC seminar on diagnosing and fixing structural steel problems found in the field, with the structural engineer and the fabricator presenting as a team because the designer creates the problem and the fabricator has to fix it [02:01]. Part 1 covers a decision process for any field problem followed by a deep section on footings and anchor rods, which the speaker says cause some sort of trouble on almost every project [02:30]. The governing theme is that a field fix is a money and schedule event before it is an engineering event, so the engineer must act fast, verify the proposed fix, and document and price the work.
### Spec References
ASTM F1554 named as the current proper anchor-rod specification, explicitly replacing the older ASTM A307 [16:21] (slide 8). F1554 three grades cited: 36 ksi, 55 ksi, and 105 ksi (slide 9), with Supplement S1 to obtain weldable 55 ksi material [17:53]. Product-marking color code stated verbatim from the slide: 36 ksi blue, 55 ksi yellow, 105 ksi red. OSHA erection rules cited generally: minimum four anchor rods per column except minor posts, and anchor rods designed for a 300 lb person at 18 in eccentricity from the column face [19:03]; OSHA also requires SER approval before any anchor rod is repaired or replaced [19:51]. AISC recommended anchor-rod hole sizes referenced as being in the then-new 13th edition manual and the prior LRFD manual [27:37]. IBC cited generally for special inspection of adhesive anchors (slide 15). No AISC 360 section, no AWS D1.1 clause, and no RCSC reference were cited.
### Technical Details
F1554 grades carry distinct yield strengths and dimensional limits: 36 ksi and 55 ksi rods are available up to 4 in diameter, 105 ksi up to 3 in diameter (slide 9). The speaker's standing recommendation is to use fewer, larger, lower-strength rods rather than many small high-strength rods, because four rods are far easier to place accurately than eight, ten, or twelve [18:44]. A worked anchor-rod strength comparison from slide 15: a 3/4 in F1554 Grade 36 rod has a design tensile strength of 14,310 lb, and a 3/4 in adhesive anchor at 5.25 in embedment in 4000 psi concrete reaches 12,630 lb, nearly matching it, which is why cutting bad cast-in rods and re-drilling adhesive anchors is a viable fix. The term anchor rod, not anchor bolt, is deliberate AISC usage because treating them as bolts led to rods too short and base-plate holes sized as bolt holes with too little clearance [14:21].
### Fabrication Notes
The classic fabrication-side error shown is a template made wrong: the engineer dimensioned center-of-template to anchor-rod as 8 in, the template maker read it as 8 in center-to-center of rods, and the pattern was built to the wrong spacing [22:52]. Fixes that land in the shop include cutting the column off its base plate and fabricating a new base plate sized to the as-built rod pattern, then rewelding it to the column, or relocating the column on the base plate [24:05] (slide 14). The speaker calls survey-before-column-fabrication "baloney" in practice because columns are already being fabricated by the time rods go in [26:37], so the realistic shop posture is to expect some rework. He also flags that base plates can be re-fabricated with long thread length on the rods to absorb position tolerance [29:12].
### Erection Notes
The headline erection-safety lesson is a Boise collapse: an erector tied two roughly 45 ft columns with a beam, went to lunch, a 30 mph wind came up, one beam was not tied off, it slipped, and it pulled the building down [13:14]. Anchor rods commonly break in an erection collapse and crews blame "green concrete," but here the rods held and the footing tipped over [15:24]. The core point is that structures are designed for the completed state, not for erection forces or a falling beam, so erection stability is the erector's responsibility. The four-rod-plus-300 lb OSHA rule was meant to let a worker stand 18 in off the column face safely but gave erectors a false sense of column stability [19:34]. Field layout should use a qualified field engineer or qualified surveyor, symmetric rod patterns such as 8x8 or 12x12 rather than 6x8, and wood or steel templates firmly fastened to the footing or pier so they do not move during the pour [26:51] (slide 16).
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Anchor rods cast in the wrong position is called the recurring problem the industry will never fully eliminate [23:43] (slide 11). Named failures include the wrong template-dimension reading that put 1,300 anchor rods out of place and forced a re-drill to adhesive anchors with a back charge [22:57], anchorage poured roughly 12 ft off location, and a 30 by 40 by 8 ft monster mill footing poured in the wrong spot that had to be blown out [22:25]. Field torching and slotting of base-plate holes to force rods to fit is shown as a common field expedient, sometimes accepted after evaluation using plate washers over the enlarged holes [20:11] (slide 11). A footing-tipping case led to the engineer being sued for an undersized footing even after an erector substituted larger 1-1/2 in rods for the specified four 3/4 in rods on his own [15:00].
### Bid / Cost Implications
The dominant cost in any field fix is field labor, not material; material is described as almost free by comparison, and the erector charges large dollars for any field work [08:20]. Delay charges drive the urgency: a crane sitting idle can cost thousands of dollars a day, so acting immediately is the lever that controls total cost [06:22]. The speaker repeatedly tells the engineer to discuss fee up front, get a PO, and not absorb the 4,000 to 5,000 dollars of calculation effort silently when costs are divvied up [10:16]. A fix proposed by the erector or fabricator usually prices lower than an engineer-originated alternative, because the party whose idea it is prices it as they see fit and someone else's idea almost always costs more [12:30]. Sometimes the cheapest answer is no fix at all: if no money is spent on a fix there is no argument over who pays [07:30].
### Your Company Application
This entry is a direct checklist for Your Company's anchor-rod workstream. Ivan's takeoff and the in-house PE stamp should standardize on F1554 with grade and S1 weldable supplement called out, not A307, and the PE should default to fewer larger Grade 36 rods over many small high-strength rods for placement tolerance, with the F1554 color marking (36 blue, 55 yellow, 105 red) used as a receiving QC check. Tekla detailing should dimension anchor-rod templates center-to-center explicitly to avoid the 8 in misread, and should carry AISC oversized anchor-rod hole sizes and plate washers by default so field torching is not the first resort. Paul Guerrero's safety program maps to the OSHA four-rod and 300 lb at 18 in column-stability rule plus the requirement that no rod is cut or replaced without SER approval, and the Boise collapse is a tie-off briefing for the erection crew. Mario's shop should keep the column-off, new-base-plate refit and the cut-and-epoxy procedures as known field-fix playbooks. For ACP controls, a pre-pour anchor-rod survey by a qualified field engineer with firmly fastened templates is a hold point, and any wrong-position fix needs a stamped sketch, a PO, and a logged back charge. DOCTRINE FLAG: NONE. Nothing here conflicts with Your Company doctrine; the verify-the-fix and document-the-fee posture reinforces the verify-do-not-generate rule, and the conventional structural-steel framing carries no PEMB language.

## Bolting & Welding Primer - Part 1
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1-MhHhODqik | Duration: 35:53 | Upload: NA | Tier: 1 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
This is the opening welding session of a two-part AISC 2006 educational seminar (the bolting session by Dr. Kulak follows). The speaker frames the entire welding subject around two physical requirements that must be met for any weld to form: atomic cleanliness and atomic closeness [16:33]. Heat is not on that list; it is only the common means to achieve the two requirements [17:08]. He separates fusion (the molecular bond between weld metal and base metal, always required) from penetration (arc energy melting into the base metal, desirable but not always necessary) using a copper-pipe soldering analogy where solder fuses with zero penetration [12:41, 14:00]. The back half walks through the arc-welding processes used on structural steel and how each one shields the molten pool from nitrogen and oxygen [20:43].

### Spec References
Cited in the talk or shown on slides: the AISC 2005 combined ASD/LRFD Specification [03:39]; AWS D1.1 Structural Welding Code Steel, invoked by reference from AISC so any AISC-governed project is automatically governed by D1.1 [04:01], for material 1/8 inch and thicker [04:46]; AWS D1.3 sheet steel code for decking welded to supports and sheet steel under 3/16 inch [04:32]; AASHTO/AWS D1.5 Bridge Welding Code (slide shows the cover), covering redundant and fracture-critical highway bridges [05:16]; AREMA, which cites D1.5 with exceptions for railway bridges [05:47]; AWS D1.6 for duplex, precipitation-hardened and stainless steels [06:19]; AWS D1.8 seismic welding supplement that sits on top of D1.1 and carries forward FEMA recommendations [06:48, 07:27]; the AISC 2005 Seismic Provisions [08:52]; the AISC Connection Prequalification document, the CPRP committee output, prequalifying the reduced beam section (dog-bone) and the bolted flange plate connection [09:00, 09:56] (slide cover shown); FEMA 353 as the retired default standard [07:50] (slide cover shown); and AISC Design Guide 21, Welded Connections - A Primer for Engineers, which captures this program content [10:53] (slide cover shown). Electrode strength figures are stated below.

### Technical Details
The five arc processes covered are SMAW, FCAW, GMAW, SAW, and GTAW [21:05]. SMAW uses a 12 to 14 inch flux-coated stick electrode with a core wire of about 1/8 to 3/16 inch [22:25]; the arc runs roughly 6,000 to 8,000 degrees F against steel that melts near 3,000 degrees F [22:01]. FCAW reverses the stick by putting flux inside a steel tube fed from a spool or barrel, in gas-shielded (-G) and self-shielded (-S) variants [27:01, 28:14]. GMAW (MIG) uses a solid or metal-cored wire with no flux, so it demands cleaner surfaces and heavily scaled material is shot-blasted first [30:55, 31:23]. SAW runs the arc submerged under a granular flux blanket, limited to flat and horizontal positions because the flux must stay in place [33:09, 34:35]. The AWS electrode numbering was on screen as E7018: E is electrode, 70 is the 70 ksi minimum specified tensile of the deposited metal, the third digit is welding position, and the final digits give coating type and current [24:40, slide]. The slide shows the low-hydrogen E7018; the speaker generically referenced "E70...1" all-position electrodes [24:56].

### Fabrication Notes
Shop process selection ties directly to shielding method and position. SAW is the bridge-fabrication workhorse and is shown mechanized on a buggy with a preheat torch ahead of the arc [35:13, 35:17]; the slide labels a "Mechanized SAW" track laying granular flux. SAW was chosen on a shopping-mall column job specifically for weld appearance because it deposits cosmetically clean welds [34:42, 35:01]. Gas-shielded FCAW is favored in closed northern shops; self-shielded FCAW is common in open warm southern shops even indoors [30:13, 30:24]. GMAW suits clean tubular (HSS) stock and avoids slag cleanup, which is why automotive and robotic lines use it [31:37, 31:52]. SMAW carries a built-in interruption: burn the stub, eject it, chip slag, restrike [24:53].

### Erection Notes
Most field welding today uses self-shielded FCAW because the gasless process is not disturbed by wind, whereas a gas shield blown off the puddle stops protecting it [29:53, 30:02]. The opening field photo is labeled SMAW, a welder running a stick electrode on an open steel frame [frame, SMAW]. Field welders carry a face shield against arc UV, protective clothing against sparks, and require adequate ventilation for fumes [23:02, 23:18]. The talk is process-focused and does not cover erection sequencing, bracing, crane, or rigging.

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The failure mechanisms are metallurgical, not workmanship lists. Nitrogen is highly soluble in hot liquid metal; as the weld solidifies, solubility drops, dissolved gas congeals into bubbles, and trapped voids become porosity while residual nitrogen embrittles the weld metal [18:23, 19:00]. Oxygen oxidizes alloy elements such as chromium into the slag so they are no longer present to do the job the electrode was designed for [19:02, 19:28]. Dirty or oxidized surfaces defeat atomic cleanliness and prevent a sound bond [14:40, 15:30]. The talk also notes the implementation failure of writing "comply with FEMA 353" into contract documents when that guideline left many engineer decisions open [07:53, 08:24].

### Bid / Cost Implications
A planned cost-reduction section and distortion-control content were flagged as likely to be cut for time, so this part stays at fundamentals [02:52, 03:07]. The practical cost levers stated are process choice and prep: SMAW's stub-and-restrike cycle is slower than continuous FCAW spool or barrel feed [24:53, 27:19], GMAW adds surface-prep cost (shot blasting scaled stock) but removes slag cleanup [31:23, 31:48], and SAW buys weld appearance and high deposition at the price of mechanization and flat/horizontal-only positioning [34:42]. No dollar rates, durations, or estimating tables are given.

### Your Company Application
This is core training for Mario as AWS D1.1 welding lead: it sets the process map (self-shielded FCAW for field welds, gas-shielded FCAW or GMAW in the shop on clean HSS, SMAW for access-restricted spots) and grounds WPS and electrode-classification reading, with E7018 as the low-hydrogen reference. Paul gets the safety basics directly: face shield, UV, sparks, fume ventilation. For Ivan and the in-house PE, the 70 ksi (E70) electrode strength is the number that drives weld-metal allowable shear, and the spec map (D1.1 invoked by AISC, D1.5 for bridges, D1.8 plus the Seismic Provisions and Connection Prequalification for moment frames) tells the estimate which code family a job triggers; D1.8 and CPRP only attach to seismic moment-frame scope, which is rare on Houston conventional work and should not be priced into a standard bid by default. Tekla detailers should note the SAW flat/horizontal restriction when calling out shop weld positions. Doctrine flags: NONE. The video predates the AISC 360 chapter/J-section and RCSC turn-of-nut/DTI vocabulary the count-gap and aisc_validator workstreams use; treat its citations as the 2005/2006 edition baseline, not current section numbers.

# TIER 2 ENTRIES - Design and Analysis Fundamentals

## Days of Steel: [3] Direct Analysis Method
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RAlRCw0Ba_w | Duration: 5:43 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
This video teaches the Direct Analysis Method (DAM) for stability design of steel frames, presented as five required criteria a structural analysis must satisfy [00:31]. Dr. Batts states the method lives in AISC Chapter C and lists the five things the analysis must capture, then two students walk through how each was actually handled in their analysis software [01:03]. The central teaching point is that DAM relies on a second-order analysis (capturing both P-delta and P-little-delta effects) combined with reduced stiffness and modeled imperfections, rather than the older effective-length (K-factor) approach. It is a design-engineer stability topic, not a fabrication or erection procedure.

### Spec References
The speakers cite AISC Specification Chapter C for the Direct Analysis Method [01:03], "AISC Chapter 2.2" for notional loads as the alternative to modeling out-of-plumbness [04:15], "Chapter 2.3" for the tau (stiffness reduction) factor [04:48], and Chapter E for the column curve that captures member-level imperfections in member design selection [04:15]. The spoken "Chapter 2.2" and "Chapter 2.3" references are the student's shorthand and appear to point to the Chapter C subsections on notional loads and the stiffness reduction (tau-b) factor; the only formal chapter letters the speaker names aloud are Chapter C and Chapter E. No AISC table number, Design Guide number, AISC 341 seismic section, AWS D1.1 clause, or RCSC reference is cited in this video.

### Technical Details
The five DAM criteria as stated are: (a) include flexural, shear, axial, and all other deformations in the analysis [01:03]; (b) perform equilibrium on the deformed structure, applying load in increments (for example 5 percent at a time) and re-solving on the deformed shape to capture P-Delta at the structure level and P-little-delta at the member level [03:11]; (c) account for imperfections, modeled either as an initial out-of-plumbness of L/500 on the columns or as equivalent notional loads [03:45]; (d) reduce stiffness using 0.8 times the modulus of elasticity plus the tau factor, achievable directly, via an added notional load, or through a nonlinear material option that softens stiffness as stress approaches Fy [04:48]; and (e) account for uncertainty, which is satisfied by using LRFD load combinations [05:19]. The students note member-level imperfections are also captured through the AISC column curve in Chapter E [04:15], and that a true second-order run produces higher bending moments and deflections than a first-order run [02:39].

### Fabrication Notes
No fabrication content. This is an analysis and design-engineering topic with no shop process, tolerance, fit-up, or QC discussion.

### Erection Notes
No direct erection procedure is taught, though one item is erection-adjacent: the L/500 column out-of-plumbness modeled in DAM [03:45] is the analytical companion to the erection plumbness tolerance, so the design assumes columns are set within that bound. The video does not state field bracing, sequencing, crane, or rigging requirements.

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The video frames one recurring student mistake as a design error rather than an inspection failure: running the same first-order (linear) analysis twice and expecting a second-order result, which yields identical answers instead of the higher moments and deflections a true P-Delta run gives [03:11]. It also warns that the deformation-capture criterion can break down with a "funky or flimsy connection," implying flexible or improperly characterized connections can invalidate the displacement results [04:48]. No bolting or welding inspection failures are named.

### Bid / Cost Implications
No direct cost, schedule, bid, or estimating content appears in this video. The only indirect implication is that DAM is the analysis basis behind member sizes; if the design EOR used DAM, the member weights flowing into a takeoff already reflect second-order stability demands, so the tonnage is what it is and is not a place to find savings.

### Your Company Application
This is EOR/design-side stability theory and sits upstream of Your Company's fabrication and erection scope, so its direct application to Ivan's takeoff, Mario's shop, or Paul's safety is limited. The most useful tie-in is for the in-house PE stamp: when Your Company's PE designs or checks connections and frames (for example on ACP), DAM per AISC Chapter C is the expected stability framework, including the L/500 out-of-plumbness assumption, the 0.8E plus tau stiffness reduction, and notional loads. For Ivan, the takeaway is that DAM only governs how member forces are derived; it does not change AISC member weights, which still come from bridge/aisc_validator.py, so nothing here alters validated tonnage. The L/500 out-of-plumbness assumption is worth flagging to erection as the plumbness the design relies on for columns. Doctrine conflicts: NONE.
