## Days of Steel: [10] AISC Manual Challenge
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5-U2WTGwIB8 | Duration: 6:42 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is a classroom escape-room style exercise teaching students how to navigate the AISC Steel Construction Manual efficiently to find code answers, with the framing that knowing where data lives in the Manual is the real skill. The lesson is procedural, not theoretical: use the pre-tabulated chapters and table of contents rather than randomly flipping pages [01:20]. It walks four worked lookups: axial compression strength of a column, economical beam selection, HSS width-to-thickness slenderness limits, and beam deflection, and emphasizes verifying an answer rather than guessing [02:22].
### Spec References
The exercise names specific Manual locations verbatim: Table 3-10 for beam design (the moment vs unbraced-length plots) [02:52], Chapter B and Table B4.1a for width-to-thickness ratios with the limit 1.4 times the square root of E over Fy [04:58], and Table 3-23 Case 7 for the simply supported beam deflection equation PL cubed over 48EI [05:54]. LRFD is the design basis stated for the column problem [00:50]. No AISC 341 seismic section, AWS D1.1 clause, RCSC provision, or numbered Design Guide is cited; this is a Manual-navigation drill, not a connection or welding lesson.
### Technical Details
Problem 1 finds the available axial compression strength by LRFD of a 14 ft long pinned W14x90 column with Fy equal to 50 ksi [00:50]. Problem 2 selects the most economical beam for an 18 ft braced length carrying a uniform distributed load of 26 kip per foot, simply supported, using Table 3-10 [02:22]. The instructor explains the dashed versus solid lines: plot the required moment against the unbraced length, then move up or to the right to the nearest solid line, which gives the lightest-weight-per-foot section that still works [03:25]. The class first proposes W18x130 (works but not economical) and corrects to W30x108, where 108 denotes 108 pounds per foot, lighter than the 114 figure mentioned [03:55]. Problem 3 finds the limiting width-to-thickness ratio (slender or nonslender) for a rectangular HSS via Chapter B and Table B4.1a [04:28]. Problem 4 computes maximum deflection of a center-loaded simply supported beam from Table 3-23 Case 7, PL cubed over 48EI [05:30].
### Fabrication Notes
No fabrication, fit-up, shop process, or shop QC content appears. The video covers design-side Manual lookups only.
### Erection Notes
No erection, field sequencing, bracing, or rigging content appears.
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The named error is selecting a beam that satisfies the load but is not the most economical section: a student answers W18x130 when W30x108 is lighter and therefore the correct economical pick off Table 3-10 [03:25]. The instructor also flags the recurring confusion over dashed versus solid lines in Table 3-10 [03:25] and stresses verifying a computed answer rather than guessing at it [02:22]. A second mistake shown is random page-flipping instead of using the tabulated chapters and table of contents [01:20].
### Bid / Cost Implications
The most-economical-beam method maps directly to material cost: the lightest section that satisfies moment and unbraced length carries the least weight per foot, and structural steel prices by weight, so picking the correct solid line off Table 3-10 minimizes tonnage and dollars [03:25]. Choosing W30x108 over W18x130 is a direct weight, and therefore cost, reduction on every line of similar beams in a takeoff.
### Your Company Application
For Ivan in takeoff, this is the rule that justifies driving member selection to the lightest qualifying section before tonnage rolls into the bid; the Table 3-10 solid-line method is exactly what aisc_validator.py should reflect when it confirms member weights, and the W18x130-versus-W30x108 example shows why weight, not just adequacy, controls the priced quantity. For the in-house PE stamp, the four lookups (compression Table 3-10/column, beam selection, HSS Table B4.1a slenderness, Table 3-23 deflection) are routine Manual references the stamping engineer relies on, and the deflection equation supports serviceability checks. No conflict with Your Company doctrine: the video reinforces verify-do-not-generate and lightest-economical sizing, and cites no PEMB language. NONE.

## Introduction to Basic Steel Design
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OoSAgbPhnzc | Duration: 1:29:45 | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is a principles review of structural steel design under the current AISC 360-16 specification, presented by Louis F. Geschwindner (former AISC VP of engineering and research, chair of the member design technical committee). The unifying idea is the safety equation "required strength less than or equal to available strength" [14:57], where required strength (load effect) comes from structural analysis and available strength (resistance) comes from the specification's limit-state equations [15:58]. He builds the statistical basis for both LRFD and ASD, including the reliability index beta and the calibration of ASD to LRFD at a live-to-dead ratio of three [38:46]. The session closes on the available steel shapes, materials, and a worked demonstration that second-order effects are real and cannot be ignored [69:29].

### Spec References
The session cites AISC 360-16 (ANSI/AISC 360-16, "Specification for Structural Steel Buildings," dated July 7 2016) [08:43]; AISC 341 seismic provisions and the Code of Standard Practice as the contractual provisions [09:14]; the Steel Construction Manual 15th edition [09:45]. Chapter map stated aloud: Chapter A general provisions, Chapter B design requirements, Chapter C stability, Chapter D tension, Chapter E compression, Chapter F flexure, Chapter G shear, Chapter H combined forces and torsion, Chapter I composite, Chapter J connections, Chapter K HSS/box connections, Chapter L serviceability, Chapter M fabrication and erection, Chapter N quality control and quality assurance [11:20-12:55]. Specific sections named: Section A3.1a (approved materials) [61:42], Section B3.1 LRFD design basis and B3.2 ASD design basis [50:13], and torsion sections H3.1 (round and rectangular HSS in torsion), H3.2 (HSS combined torsion, shear, flexure, axial), H3.3 (non-HSS torsion and combined stress) [83:52]. Appendices 1 through 8 listed (advanced analysis, ponding, fatigue, fire, existing structures, member stability bracing, alternative stability methods, approximate second-order analysis) [12:55]. Material standards cited: ASTM A6 (rolled shapes, 2014 version in the 15th ed.) [53:51], A36, A992, A572 Gr 50, A53 Gr B, A500 Gr C, and the HSS standards A500/A501/A618/A847/A1065/A1085 [54:22-65:19]. Load standard cited: ASCE 7-16 load combinations [37:45]. The torsion Design Guide was referenced but its number was not recalled by the speaker [84:23].

### Technical Details
Resistance is built on three strength limit states (yielding, buckling, rupture) plus serviceability limit states in Chapter L (deflection, drift, vibration, connection slip) [31:59]. Resistance factors given verbatim: phi 0.9 for yielding, 0.75 for rupture, 0.7 for connection slip, 0.65 for composite components with shear studs [36:13]. The tension yielding example is Pn = Fy times Ag with phi 0.9 (LRFD) and omega 1.67 (ASD) [51:16]. Shape counts from the manual: 283 W shapes, 18 M, 28 S, 22 HP, 137 angles, 281 rectangular HSS, 107 square HSS, 128 round HSS, 51 pipe, for 1,452 total; heaviest is a W36 at 925 lb/ft, lightest a half-inch pipe at 0.85 lb/ft [55:58-60:09]. A992 preferred for W shapes (Fy 50, Fu 65), A36 for M/S/C/MC/L, A572 Gr 50 for HP, A500 Gr C for HSS, A53 Gr B pipe (Fy 35, Fu 60) [64:17]. The worked second-order examples (W12x96 columns under 400 kip axial and 200 ft-kip moment) show amplification of roughly 1.14 for uniform moment, 1.11 for the beam-column gravity case, and 1.42-plus for the flagpole cantilever [71:05-76:19].

### Fabrication Notes
Chapter M of AISC 360 covers fabrication and erection, named in the chapter map but not detailed in this introductory session [12:22]. The speaker noted that fabrication variability (actual versus published plastic section modulus when every piece of a section is measured) is one of the three factors, with modeling and material, that the resistance factor accounts for [35:42]. He also flagged that building a custom built-up shape from plates and bars carries significant added cost versus using a rolled shape [60:39]. No tolerances, fit-up, or shop QC procedures were covered.

### Erection Notes
Erection is acknowledged only as the subject of Chapter M and as part of the Code of Standard Practice contractual provisions [09:14]. No field procedures, sequencing, bracing, crane, or rigging content appears in this session, which is scoped to design principles.

### Bolting and Welding
This session names connection limit states and the connection chapters (J, K) but does not cover bolt grades, pretension methods, electrodes, preheat, or NDE. The only welding-adjacent content is metallurgical: manganese improves notch toughness but harms weldability, carbon and manganese both raise strength while reducing ductility, vanadium raises strength without harming weldability, and columbium raises strength with a significant negative impact on notch toughness [65:51]. RCSC, AWS D1.1, and specific bolting or welding installation methods are not addressed here.

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
No inspection failures or rejection modes are named, consistent with a design-principles introduction rather than a shop or field session. The closest cautions are conceptual: ignoring second-order effects underestimates real moments (the flagpole case showed at least a 32 percent and likely larger increase) [76:19], and assuming a simple beam when an end connection induces moment restraint introduces model error [22:38]. The speaker also warned that being listed in A6 does not guarantee a shape is commercially available, so specifying an unavailable or offshore-only shape is a practical design error to avoid [85:26].

### Bid / Cost Implications
The explicit cost lesson is that custom built-up members cost significantly more to make than standard rolled shapes, so the designer should favor rolled sections unless a built-up shape is justified [60:39]. The W36x925 at 925 lb/ft is flagged as a member to specify carefully given its weight and cost [60:39]. The reminder that listed A6 shapes may not be procurable (some produced only offshore, some never produced) is a direct sourcing and lead-time risk; the speaker pointed to an AISC website resource for checking shape availability [85:26].

### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, the shape inventory and per-foot weights here are exactly the data domain that bridge/aisc_validator.py wraps; this session reinforces that member weights come from the AISC shape database, not LLM math, and that W-shape designations encode nominal depth and lb/ft (W16x26 is roughly 16 in deep at 26 lb/ft) [55:58]. The availability caveat supports our verify-do-not-generate posture: a member can be valid in the database yet not procurable, so a takeoff that lists an exotic shape should carry a sourcing-confirmation flag rather than a silent price. The material defaults (A992 for wide flange, A500 Gr C for HSS, A572 Gr 50 for HP, A36 for channels and angles) are a useful default-grade reference for estimate notes, with the speaker's caveat that channels are now also available in Gr 50, so confirm with the supplier. The second-order-effects demonstration is a design-engineer responsibility that belongs to our in-house PE stamp scope, not to estimating, and the torsion Design Guide reference is a follow-up item for the PE rather than the bid pipeline. This is an introductory design webinar with no connection, anchor-rod, joist, or field-bolting content, so it does not touch Mario's shop welding, Paul's safety scope, Tekla detailing, or ACP project controls. Doctrine conflict: NONE. All positioning here is conventional structural steel design, no PEMB language, and no supplier names were introduced.

## Recent Developments in Design for Ponding
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lMeX1Ogym4k | Duration: 1:24:23 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
Ponding is the progressive accumulation of rainwater on a flat, flexible roof where initial deflection traps water, the added water weight deflects the framing further, and the cycle either converges to equilibrium or runs away to collapse [03:42][04:13]. AISC defines it as retention of water solely due to roof deflection [03:08]. The talk distinguishes mitigation (provide enough slope so water drains and never accumulates), stiffness adequacy (keep actual member stiffness above a critical stiffness so deflections do not diverge), and strength adequacy (the framing can carry the ponded load) [07:46][08:16]. The governing physical quantity is critical stiffness, expressed as gamma times L to the fourth power over pi to the fourth, where gamma is the unit weight of water; when actual EI approaches that value the deflection amplifier runs to infinity [11:20][37:37][38:09].

### Spec References
Speakers cited a historical chain of AISC and load specs verbatim: the 1961 spec commentary (span-to-depth limit of FY over 1,000,000 and the 3-in-12 slope rule) [08:47][09:17]; the 1963 spec (FB over 600,000) [10:17]; the 1969 spec, which introduced the still-current Cp + 0.9 Cs less than 0.25 stiffness check and the 0.8 FY bending-stress limit, with a stated factor of safety of four against ponding instability [12:24][13:26][13:58]; the 1986 LRFD spec (Marino graphical aid moved into the main spec) [19:37]; the 1989 spec; the 1993 and 1999 specs (FY minus F0 change) [22:51]. Current provisions are AISC 360-05 and 360-10, Appendix 2, holding the simplified Cp + 0.9 Cs check and the Marino improved (graphical) method [28:14][29:17][59:45]. Load specs cited: ANSI A58.1 and its 1982 version, UBC 1994 (quarter-inch-per-foot safe harbor into main spec), ASCE 7-95, ASCE 7-10, IBC 2000 through IBC 2012 (susceptible bay), IBC 2015, and pending changes in AISC 360-16 and ASCE 7-16 [23:24][26:38][55:34]. Stability mandate references: Chapter C and Appendix 8 (second-order B1/B2 amplifiers), with member capacity taken from Chapter F [69:02][74:14]. SJI Technical Digest 3 was cited for camber and open-web steel joists, which Appendix 2 also addresses [02:38][63:23].

### Technical Details
The Appendix 2 math is a numerical solution of one specific geometry, not a general method: a simply supported beam with deflection described by a half-sine function (under 2 percent error versus the Euler-Bernoulli curve), framing into a girder that carries equal beams on both sides [35:33][41:13][42:16]. Cp and Cs are flexibility coefficients; the 0.25 limit derives algebraically from keeping the deflection amplifier from running to infinity with a factor of safety of four [48:22][49:23]. The pre-computer simplification stripped constants (pi to the fourth, 29,000 ksi E, water unit weight) into the lumped Cp/Cs constants, which is why those coefficients look non-intuitive [46:20][46:50]. The presenters could not derive the second strength equation in the spec and "banged our heads for about 10 days over it"; it ties deflection to stress through the elastic proportionality of stress, moment, and deflection, using 0.8 FY as the allowable stress whose source is also undocumented [50:24][51:26]. The cleaner modern path is to treat ponding as moment amplification (an alpha amplifier like B1/B2) using LRFD-factored loads, or an iterative first-order elastic analysis that accumulates beam-plus-girder deflections cycle to cycle [68:31][78:51][79:21].

### Fabrication Notes
This webinar is an analysis and code-history topic and names no shop fabrication, fit-up, or QC processes; member camber is the only shop-relevant variable mentioned, and the base Appendix 2 method assumes no camber, with camber handled separately via SJI Digest 3 guidance [54:32][63:23]. No fabrication content beyond that.

### Erection Notes
No erection sequencing, bracing, crane, rigging, or field-coordination content was presented. The relevant geometric assumptions are design conditions the erected frame must match: all framing perfectly flat and plumb, all members prismatic and pin-connected, girders framing into non-deformable supports (a column, never girder-into-girder), and the deck direction never reversing so a girder never acts as a beam [53:29][54:32][55:34][56:06].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The recurring real-world error is treating the quarter-inch-per-foot slope as a guaranteed safe harbor; the speakers showed examples where a quarter inch per foot does NOT preclude ponding, especially where secondary members run parallel to the free-draining edge and there is a chain of stiffness toward an unyielding wall [27:09][29:17][32:58][67:30]. A second flagged error is engineers not accounting for the second-order added load: the rain load (5.2 times drain head per the cited formula) grows with roof-framing flexibility, and many designs ignore that increase [33:30]. The closing observation is that a pure ponding failure is rare; ponding usually acts as a contributing factor on top of another underlying deficiency rather than the sole cause [80:55][81:26].

### Bid / Cost Implications
No pricing, schedule, or estimating numbers were discussed. The practical cost lever is indirect: most economical real roofs fail the Cp + 0.9 Cs less than 0.25 check, so satisfying ponding stiffness can drive heavier members or added drainage, which affects tonnage [16:31]. The simplest fielded check is Hossler's rule of thumb cited at [64:23]: apply 5 psf and if deflection is under half an inch the roof is probably fine, over one inch it is probably unstable.

### Your Company Application
On any low-slope or flat-roof structural bid, Ivan's takeoff should flag a ponding check rather than assume the quarter-inch-per-foot slope clears it, and the in-house PE stamp work should run the Appendix 2 Cp + 0.9 Cs less than 0.25 stiffness check (or the iterative amplifier approach) before sizing roof beams and girders, watching specifically for secondary members parallel to a free edge or running into an unyielding wall [29:17][67:30]. Because most economical roofs fail the stiffness check, the estimate model should not silently price minimum-weight roof framing on flat roofs; treat ponding-driven upsizing or added drains as a real tonnage and cost risk and tag it for the PE to confirm. This maps cleanly to count-gap and verify-don't-generate doctrine: the rain load is not a fixed psf, it amplifies with flexibility, so AISC member weights from aisc_validator.py feed a stiffness check that must be verified, never assumed. Joist roofs are in scope per SJI Digest 3 and AISC Appendix 2 [63:23]. DOCTRINE FLAGS: NONE.

## Corrosion Protection Strategies for Bridges
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KQMeNa_VMzo | Duration: 1:35:33 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is an AASHTO/NSBA bridge workshop with three presenters (Jeff Carlson of NSBA, Dr. Jennifer McConnell of the University of Delaware, and Ronnie Medlock of High Steel) covering the four corrosion-protection systems for steel bridges: paint, weathering steel, hot-dip galvanizing, and thermal-spray metallizing. The unifying idea is that corrosion protection is almost entirely about getting zinc onto the steel, the only exception being weathering steel which relies on a self-limiting patina [02:03]. Environment severity drives the choice: marine/salt is most severe, deicing-salt regions are moderate, and arid/rural is mild, with measured loss rates from 0.26 mils/year in Phoenix to 28 at Kure Beach NC [03:34]. The talk is bridge-DOT focused, not building structural steel, so AISC member-design content is absent.

### Spec References
The cited standards are bridge and coating standards, not AISC structural codes: FHWA Steel Bridge Design Handbook corrosion section [03:04][21:29]; AASHTO/NSBA Collaboration guide spec S8.1 for application of zinc-rich primers to steel bridges [12:17]; the new AASHTO/NSBA metallizing guide spec on the AASHTO SCOBS ballot for the June Spokane meeting, written as a supplement to SSPC/AWS/NACE CS 23 [22:00][24:33][49:00]; ISO 2063 as the international metallizing basis [24:03]; AASHTO NEPCOAT qualified-coating menu (ABC list, C = field) [08:42][66:04]; AASHTO 2013 Manual for Bridge Element Inspection condition-state scale 1 to 4 [43:23]; the FHWA 1989 Technical Advisory on uncoated weathering steel [35:43][57:52]; SSPC SP6 surface prep cited in an Iowa DOT spec [14:22]; ASTM A1010 high-chrome (about 11 percent) stainless bridge steel and ASTM A709 Grade 50W weathering steel [20:59][77:28]. No AISC 360, AISC 341, AWS D1.1, RCSC, or AISC Design Guide section was cited; these are bridge coating specs.

### Technical Details
Three-coat paint is an organic or inorganic zinc-rich primer, an epoxy moisture-barrier midcoat, and a polyurethane UV topcoat, with organic zinc preferred for fast cure (hours versus up to 24 hours or even a 3-month hold for inorganic, which needs ambient moisture to cure) [07:41][09:12][80:30]. Two-coat alternatives are a polyaspartic urethane over zinc (Sherwin-Williams Envirolastic 980 named, NEPCOAT approved) and a polysiloxane topcoat [09:43][82:34]. Metallizing is zinc/aluminum wire arc-sprayed onto cold steel (no preheat, no tank distortion), with material options of 99 percent zinc, 85/15 zinc-aluminum, or 99 percent aluminum, building 2 to 3 mils per pass to specs commonly 8 to 15 mils [18:56][26:05][76:58]. McConnell's research quantified weathering-steel performance using packing-tape particle samples scanned and analyzed by image recognition, correlating large-particle percentage to condition state, with worst corrosion on the top of the bottom flange of the first interior fascia girder [46:59][49:33].

### Fabrication Notes
The recurring fabricator message is that surface preparation governs every coated system: paint and metallizing both depend on cleanliness and an angular surface profile, and metallizing specifically requires hand blasting because the automated wheel blasters fabricators use for paint cannot produce the deep angular anchor pattern metallizing needs [19:26][76:27]. Metallizing is dusty and slow, demands dust collection, and is verified with pull-off adhesion tabs whose required pullout values and anchor patterns vary by state spec [25:34][85:37]. Carlson recommends applying all three paint coats in the shop for environmental control, accepting field touch-up of handling damage [06:39]. For weathering steel, run the steel through three wet-dry cycles in the yard (a hose, low skill) before shipping so the patina starts uniformly and most staining bleeds out before the steel reaches the piers [14:22]. Galvanizing thin-web large-flange plate girders risks distortion, and double-dipping long girders adds major cost [17:55][40:00].

### Erection Notes
Field-side content is limited. Metallizing can be done in the field by a third-party metallizer to convert an existing painted bridge, with the same surface-profile and thickness requirements as shop work [31:09][28:06]. The dominant field/detailing lesson is that leaking expansion joints are the single biggest cause of weathering-steel corrosion: 23 of 70 cluster-study bridges had worst corrosion at the joint, and water then travels longitudinally down the girder, so joint maintenance is the cheap fix for an expensive problem [58:22][59:24][61:58]. Detailing for water shedding matters, with wider overhangs acting as a roof and arch/frame geometries needing a planned drainage path to avoid ponding at bearings [60:26][61:27].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Named failure modes: pre-1970 paint failures from ignoring surface prep, which created the lasting bad reputation of paint [05:37]; weathering-steel staining/bleeding onto piers and abutments and non-uniform patina in arid climates (Arizona, West Texas, Southern California) [13:20]; patina washing off in high-rainfall rural settings and streaking glass and walkways [62:28]; galvanizing distortion of flimsy plate girders [18:26]; metallizing inability to coat behind copes, crevices, and double-angle cross frames, where Carlson and Medlock both recommend hot-dip galvanizing the cross frames instead and Medlock recommends an RFI when a job calls for metallized frames [27:36][86:37][87:39]. Inspection ambiguity is itself a failure point: steel that fits none of the four condition states cleanly, which the tape-sample method was developed to resolve [46:28].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Medlock gave percent cost increases over a base weathering-steel grade-separation bridge: three-coat paint adds 24 percent, galvanizing 41 percent, metallizing 42 percent (galvanized cross frames assumed), and A1010 stainless 130 percent [74:54][84:04][90:42]. Adders: two-coat paint 19 percent, end paint 8 percent, end-plus-fascia paint 10 percent, paint-over-weathering 27 percent, galvanize-plus-fascia-paint 54 percent, metallize-plus-seal about 49 percent, metallized cross frames 54 percent [78:28][83:34][84:04]. On a more complicated bridge the metallize-and-galvanize premium dropped to 18 percent, so coating premium shrinks as base fabrication complexity rises [90:10]. Cure-wait drives schedule and shop capacity: inorganic zinc with a mandated 3-month cure forces girders outside and can make a job non-biddable on a tight schedule [80:30][81:31]. The key cost drivers a fabricator prices are cleaning, masking, coating application, and especially handling/girder moves [71:49].

### Your Company Application
This is bridge DOT work; Your Company is a conventional building structural steel fabricator and erector, so most content is reference rather than directly bid-applicable, and none of it touches AISC member takeoff, joists, anchor rods, field bolting, or AWS D1.1 weld procedures. The transferable items for Ivan's takeoff and estimating are the coating-cost structure (cleaning plus masking plus application plus handling moves) and the cure-wait-versus-shop-capacity tradeoff, which mirror how Your Company should think about galvanizing or shop-paint scope on building steel rather than line-iteming it. For Mario's shop crew, the surface-profile point is the durable lesson: paint and metallizing fail without correct blast cleanliness and an angular anchor pattern, and automated wheel blasting does not satisfy metallizing. For Paul's safety file, metallizing is a heavy dust process needing collection. The galvanizing distortion caution (thin web, large flange, width-to-thickness) is worth flagging on any galvanized building member through Tekla detailing and the in-house PE review. Doctrine flag: NONE. The talk names paint and steel manufacturers (Sherwin-Williams Envirolastic 980, ASTM A1010) only as generic product references spoken by the presenter, consistent with the verify-don't-generate rule; no Your Company supplier names appear and no AISC weights or rates are implicated.

## NS24: Structural Stability - From Behavior to Practice, Session 1: Behavior of Compression Members
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6xG592hLKYs | Duration: 1:33:44 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
This is a behavior-and-theory lecture on why steel compression members buckle and how the AISC column curve is built up from Euler's 1750 solution by removing his idealizing assumptions one at a time [17:20]. Ron Ziemann (Bucknell, AISC Committee on Specifications, chairs TC3 Loads Analysis and Stability) walks from full yielding through Euler elastic buckling to the real-world inelastic column, adding initial out-of-straightness, non-concentric load eccentricity, partial yielding, residual stresses, and end restraint [78:48]. The unifying message is that steel is slender because it has excellent strength-to-weight and stiffness-to-weight but must be priced competitively, so slender members in compression have a real possibility of buckling and must be designed for stability [04:40]. The distinction drawn is bifurcation theory (instantaneous, binary buckled or not) versus instability theory (a perfect-real column with imperfection that gradually loses stiffness and grows deflection until it cannot reach equilibrium) [06:42][07:44].

### Spec References
The named citations are: AISC Specification Chapter C, Direct Analysis Method, where the tau (stiffness reduction) factor with the 0.8 on top appears, developed around 2003 and printed in 2005 [53:40]; the AISC column-curve constants 0.658 for inelastic (lower slenderness) and 0.877 for elastic (higher slenderness) buckling [64:56][65:27]; notional loads tied to the Direct Analysis Method, flagged for a later session [53:40]; the AISC Commentary table of end-restraint cases and effective length (K) factors [67:28]; alignment charts for K, with a caution to be careful using them [77:11]; the AISC Code of Standard Practice as the straightness tolerance the mill must meet before rotary straightening [54:10]; and Euler's elastic buckling stress pi-squared E over (L/r)-squared as it still appears in the AISC Specification [65:27][69:01]. Eurocode is cited as using five column curves selected by section, bending axis, and depth-to-width ratio [66:28]. No AWS D1.1, RCSC, AISC 341 seismic, or numbered Design Guide references appear; this is a behavior lecture, not a connection or welding lecture.

### Technical Details
Euler's assumptions are stated explicitly: prismatic member, fixed moment of inertia, small deflections, no bending prior to bifurcation, perfectly straight, concentrically loaded, elastic material with constant E, and pin-roller boundary conditions [40:10][41:22]. The buckling limit states for compression members are full yielding (squash load Py = Fy times A), flexural buckling (the focus), torsional buckling (cruciform sections), flexural-torsional buckling (singly symmetric sections where centroid and shear center differ), and local buckling of slender sections [12:15][15:49]. The moment amplification factor 1/(1 - P/Pe) is derived as the exact amplifier on an initial sine-wave imperfection of amplitude L/1000 [37:16][37:46]. Residual stresses from differential cooling of rolled shapes run 30 to 50 percent of yield, are largely independent of yield strength, and trigger early partial yielding; rotary straightening yields and unloads the section and relieves much of that residual stress [50:37][51:38][54:41]. The worked W14x145 example (Fy = 50 ksi, A = 42.7 in2, Py = 21.35) compared L/r of 50 and 150 across linear buckling, geometric nonlinear, material nonlinear, and full GMNIA analyses in MASTAN, landing the full inelastic strength near 40 ksi at L/r 50 and about 11 ksi at L/r 150 [53:33][60:50]. K factors derived: 0.7 for fixed-pinned, 0.5 for fixed-fixed (four times Euler strength), 1.0 for pin-pin, 2.0 for cantilever [68:30][76:41].

### Fabrication Notes
The fabrication-relevant content is about the rolled product, not shop work. Rolled wide-flange shapes cool non-uniformly off the mill, flange tips set first and lock in residual stress when the web-flange intersection later contracts, producing compression-tension self-equilibrating patterns [50:37][51:07]. Mills increasingly use near-net-section rolling, which reduces residual stress because less rolling is needed, and then rotary-straighten members that do not meet the Code of Standard Practice straightness tolerance [50:04][54:10]. The practical takeaway for a fabricator is that the member you receive is neither perfectly straight nor stress-free, and rotary-straightened material carries lower residual stress [51:38].

### Erection Notes
No erection, sequencing, bracing, crane, or rigging procedure is taught. The only field-adjacent point is rhetorical: even a perfectly straight column, set by workers in white gloves, will see eccentricity the instant it is loaded, so some bending always exists in a real installed column [35:14].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
No connection rejections or NDE failures are named since this lecture covers no connections. The conceptual error corrected by the poll is that residual stresses cause the bending in a compression member; they do not, they accentuate partial yielding, while bending comes from initial out-of-straightness and non-concentric axial load, the answer 83 percent of attendees got right [82:51][84:26]. A second cautioned error is over-trusting K-factor alignment charts and assuming a pin-roller idealization that almost never exists in a real frame [67:28][77:11]. The unconservatism question (is the single AISC column curve unconservative in some cases) was deferred to a later session [80:48].

### Bid / Cost Implications
No estimating numbers, tonnage rates, or schedule figures are given. The single cost-linked statement is structural-economics framing: steel members are slender precisely because the material must come in at a competitive price, which is why stability governs member sizing [04:40]. There is no $/SF, no tonnage, and no labor content in this session.

### Your Company Application
This is a methodology backstop for Ivan's takeoff, not a source of new numbers. It explains why the compression-member capacities behind any column or brace size depend on unbraced length, K factor, and slenderness rather than gross area alone, which reinforces the doctrine that bid-grade tonnage comes from a measured member takeoff through bridge/aisc_validator.py, never SF times psf. For the in-house PE stamp, the lecture is a clean reference on where the 0.877 and 0.658 column-curve constants, the tau stiffness-reduction factor in Chapter C Direct Analysis Method, and the standard K factors (0.5, 0.7, 1.0, 2.0) originate, useful when the PE reviews column capacities or unbraced-length assumptions. For Tekla detailing, the residual-stress and straightness discussion supports treating mill-supplied members as imperfect and confirms why Code of Standard Practice straightness matters. Nothing here touches Mario's welding, Paul's safety program, anchor rods, joists, field bolting, or ACP controls, and there is no AWS, RCSC, or seismic content to apply. Doctrine conflict: NONE.

## That's Not Fracture Critical: Classifying System Redundant Members
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fDcX9uopcRs | Duration: 1:32:15 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
This is a highway bridge webinar (FHWA, TxDOT, WisDOT) on reclassifying steel members that look fracture critical (FCM) as System Redundant Members (SRM), not a building-steel fabrication talk. An FCM is defined as a steel member in tension or with a tension element whose failure would probably cause collapse of a portion or all of the bridge [07:50][08:23]. The 2012 FHWA FCM memo created a path where a member without load-path redundancy can be deemed redundant through demonstrated system behavior, removing the requirement for hands-on FCM inspection every two years [08:23][20:17]. The whole case study is steel twin tub (box) girder bridges whose bottom flanges and webs are fracture critical in the positive moment region [14:37][15:07].

### Spec References
No AISC 360, AISC 341, AWS D1.1, or RCSC building-code sections are cited; this is an AASHTO LRFD and FHWA regulatory talk. Concrete references named aloud: the FHWA 2012 FCM memo [07:50][20:17]; 23 CFR and the National Bridge Inspection Standards (NBIS) as the legal basis [02:09][05:17]; the 1978 AASHTO non-redundant FCM guide specification and AWS the welding fracture-control plan referenced as "AWS C15 class 12" [05:17] (transcript audio, treat the clause label as approximate); AASHTO Strength I and the Extreme Event limit state, with TxDOT adding "Extreme Event 3" for member failure [27:02][29:35]; AASHTO Article 5.7 for deck shear and Article 6.16 for shear connectors [32:40][33:41]; TxDOT Bridge Design Manual Chapter 3 Section 17 plus its Appendix C guide [38:53][37:20]; NCHRP Project 12-87A and NCHRP Report 883 from Dr. Connor at Purdue [53:25][53:55]; and the 2018 AASHTO Guide Specification for analysis and identification of fracture critical and system redundant members [53:55].

### Technical Details
The TxDOT method assumes a full-depth fracture of the bottom flange and attached webs of one girder at the location of maximum factored tensile stress under Strength I, then checks the intact girder under Extreme Event 3 with all fracture-event load effects amplified by 1.2 for dynamic effect [27:32][29:35]. Two analysis routes exist: an approximate method assuming the intact girder alone carries the full self weight and live load (valid for spans under 250 ft, skew under 20 degrees, radius over 700 ft) [35:46][36:17], and a refined nonlinear 3D finite element model with shell-element girders, solid-element deck, and two-node truss deck reinforcement [38:23][38:53]. WisDOT used Purdue nonlinear FEA benchmarked to full-scale UT Austin testing, with strain acceptance limits (average strain under the lesser of 5x yield strain or 0.01, max strain under 0.05, concrete strain near 0.003) plus a 15 percent reserve margin [55:58][59:31][60:36]. UT Austin research project 0-5498 included explosive linear-shaped-charge fracture of a real out-of-service Houston box girder; the cut bridge deflected under one inch after flange cut, seven inches after full web cut, and held 363,000 lb statically (over four times legal load) [16:08][18:13][19:14].

### Fabrication Notes
The webinar keeps the Fracture Control Plan in force during fabrication even for SRM-reclassified bridges: members are still fabricated to FCP standards (higher steel toughness, fine grain, higher shop welding and inspection standards) and only the in-service hands-on inspection relief changes [05:17][52:54][53:25]. Shear stud connectors must be detailed to extend above the bottom mat of deck reinforcement so they can develop the plastic deck mechanism after fracture [33:41][34:46]. No building-shop fit-up, camber, or AWS WPS detail is given.

### Erection Notes
Erection-side content is limited and bridge-specific. The design requires at least two permanent external and intermediate full-depth diaphragms on each side of the assumed fracture location, composite with the slab, to provide alternate load paths [30:36][31:39]. WisDOT stressed that full-depth solid-plate external diaphragms composite with the deck (located about third-span) are left permanently in place and not removed for aesthetics, since their stiffness is what prevents shear-stud failure in the faulted state [48:46][73:22]. Diaphragms should be as deep as practicable, at minimum 0.75 times the tub girder depth [86:39].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The failure modes named are the reasons four WisDOT bridges stayed fracture critical after analysis: bottom flange buckling over the pier on a straight tub with no shear studs over the piers and weak angle cross frames [71:50][71:50]; bottom flange buckling on a Mississippi River structure with no intermediate diaphragms [72:20]; local flange buckling on a long unbalanced end span [72:51]; and shear stud failure on a single long span lacking solid mid diaphragms [73:22]. The historical driver is brittle fracture: Point Pleasant 1967 (eyebar, low fracture toughness, inaccessible detail, 46 deaths), Mianus River 1983 (pin-and-hanger), and Hoan Bridge constraint-induced fracture without prior fatigue crack growth [03:11][04:15].

### Bid / Cost Implications
The economic argument is the entire point. TxDOT spends about 2.3 million dollars every two years inspecting over 480 existing twin tub girder spans, not counting traffic control [15:38]. WisDOT puts a single fracture critical inspection at roughly 36,000 to 66,000 dollars per bridge per biennium, about one million dollars every two years across 17 bridges, each inspection taking 10 to 24 hours over several nights with snooper trucks, four to six operators, lane closures, and law enforcement [50:19][51:21]. Reclassifying members as SRM removes that recurring biennial cost for the life of the structure, and WisDOT removed 17 structures from the FCM list [66:10][73:52].

### Your Company Application
Direct application is low: this is AASHTO highway-bridge fracture control, not AISC 360/341 building steel, and Your Company does not fabricate twin tub girder bridges, so most of the content is out of our lane. The transferable idea for Ivan and the estimating workstream is that a member's redundancy classification, not just its tonnage, can drive lifecycle cost and inspection scope, which matters if Your Company ever bids DOT or pedestrian-bridge work where FCM designation triggers AWS fracture-control fabrication premiums. For Mario, the takeaway is that fracture-critical fabrication means tighter toughness, welding, and NDE standards than ordinary structural work, so any tension-critical or non-redundant member flagged on a drawing set should raise the welding and inspection scope before bid. For our in-house PE stamp, the recurring lesson across all three speakers is verify by analysis against a tested benchmark and submit to the reviewing authority, which aligns with our verify-do-not-generate doctrine. No conflict with Your Company doctrine, but flag the scope mismatch so this entry is not mistaken for building-code guidance. DOCTRINE FLAG: NONE (scope is bridge/AASHTO, not AISC building steel).

## Structural Stability -- Letting the Fundamentals Guide Your Judgement
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AJ85TLthJDA | Duration: 1:36:31 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is the 2020 TR Higgins lecture by Dr. Ronald Ziemian on structural stability theory, framed as fundamentals guiding engineering judgment rather than a shop or field procedure. The spine is the distinction between bifurcation buckling (a perfectly straight member holds load with no lateral movement until it suddenly buckles at the Euler load) and instability theory (a small initial imperfection grows gradually into a large deflection and failure) [19:10][32:01]. He frames the AISC stability provisions around what he calls the "Big Five" effects a stability analysis must account for: pertinent deformations, second-order effects, geometric imperfections, stiffness loss from partial yielding with or without residual stresses, and uncertainty [23:50][82:37]. Two recurring stiffness lessons drive the talk: members in series give a system stiffness smaller than the smallest component, while members in parallel add up and build redundancy and stiffness [06:21][07:22].

### Spec References
This is a theory and methodology lecture, so most references are to specification chapters and methods by name rather than verbatim clause numbers. Cited: AISC 360 Chapter C, Design for Stability (the "Big Five" effects, revised for the 2005 edition and called "Chapter C Big Five") [23:50][30:56]; Chapter E for compression members [30:56]; the column slenderness formula PI squared EI over L squared, which Ziemann states "finds its way all the way into our specification in Chapter E point eight" (spoken; treat the exact subsection as approximate) [11:59]; the Effective Length (K-factor) Method and the Direct Analysis Method as the two general approaches Chapter C permits [31:30][43:50]; the Direct Analysis Method moved from an appendix into the main body in 2010 [46:22]; Appendix 1 inelastic analysis / design by advanced inelastic analysis, approved into the 2010 specification [60:51][53:38]; Appendix 6 member bracing provisions [66:32]; the B1 and B2 second-order amplification factors introduced with the first LRFD specification in 1986 [36:41]; the 0.8 stiffness-reduction (tau-b) knockdown used in the Direct Analysis Method [47:25]. He also cites the SSRC Guide to Stability Design Criteria and the AISC Direct Analysis Method design guide by Griffis and White [65:31][88:21].

### Technical Details
The Direct Analysis Method trade is "the more you directly model, the more simplification you get on the resistance side" [44:20]. Version 1.0 (2005) models system out-of-plumb imperfections plus a 0.8 stiffness reduction and lets you use K equal to 1 (capacity Lc from the actual unbraced length) [46:52]. The Appendix variant (2016) additionally models member imperfections, so the engineer can compute compressive strength from the cross-section alone without knowing the unbraced length [47:25]. Across methods this nets out: raising compressive strength also raises the moment demands, so the effective length, Direct Analysis, and advanced approaches converge on similar designs [49:30]. Ziemann gives a stability screen: run an eigenvalue buckling analysis and read the buckling load factor; below 3 the structure is stability-sensitive and needs a rigorous second-order analysis (roughly B2 above 1.5), 3 to 10 allows approximate methods, above 10 is not stability-sensitive [39:13]. The Higgins-paper contribution covers bracing stiffness for systems of columns in series: ten parallel columns braced by braces in series needed about 45 times the ideal brace stiffness, fit by A equals 0.4 n squared plus 0.4 n plus 2 to within 1 percent against eigenvalue runs [69:39][70:41].

### Fabrication Notes
The lecture does not address shop fabrication, fit-up, cut-list, or QC processes. The nearest fabrication-adjacent point is that initial geometric imperfections (out-of-straightness of members and out-of-plumb of stories) are real and are what the analysis methods explicitly model, which connects to mill and shop tolerances even though no AISC fabrication tolerance is cited [46:52][47:25]. No welding, bolting, or NDE fabrication content appears.

### Erection Notes
No erection sequencing, crane, rigging, or field-procedure content is presented. The closest practical thread is bracing during the standing structure's life: column and system bracing must be stiff enough (the ideal brace stiffness) or the column buckles by lurching before reaching full strength, with design typically using two to three times ideal [67:33][68:05]. Joists are flagged as very slender and unstable out of plane until bridging and deck are in place, demonstrated by a student loading a joist to buckling, which is a real erection-stability reminder even though the talk frames it as theory [73:17][74:20].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
No inspection rejections or weld and bolt failures are named. The errors discussed are analysis and judgment mistakes. Adding a member to a series chain to "fix" a flexible system makes it worse because the added member's flexibility still degrades total stiffness [06:51]. Adding a stiff brace frame in parallel to a too-flexible moment frame pulled almost all force into the stiffer truss and nearly fractured the brace-frame connections, because load follows the path of greatest stiffness [08:24]. Misusing the alignment-chart K factors by ignoring their built-in assumptions, and back-calculating huge K factors from eigenvalue runs where low member forces sit in the denominator, are both flagged [42:17]. He also warns against applying superposition once a structure goes inelastic or unstable [13:31].

### Bid / Cost Implications
No bid pricing, estimating workflow, or schedule content appears. The economic theme is indirect: steel's high strength-to-weight plus competitive pricing pressure produces slender members and cross-sections that want to buckle, so the steel designer's two real jobs are connections and compression stability [18:08]. Choosing the right stability method is an effort-versus-conservatism trade, with the Direct Analysis Method front-loading modeling effort to recover member capacity and avoid hand-calculated K factors [44:20]. Inelastic and advanced analysis can unlock members the standard column curve would reject (the example of large columns turned sideways with webs cut out for a column-free atrium) [54:08].

### Your Company Application
This is doctrine-aligned background for the in-house PE stamp and Tekla detailing rather than a takeoff or shop input. It reinforces verify-do-not-generate: the lecture's core warning is to not let analysis software dominate judgment, to plot the deformed shape and moment diagrams, and to run a buckling-load-factor screen (below 3 means stability-sensitive) before trusting a frame model, which our PE should apply to any moment-frame or slender-truss design we stamp [26:24][39:13]. For joists, the point that they are unstable out of plane until bridging and deck are set is a direct safety and erection-stability note Paul Guerrero and the field crew already live by, and a reason deck and bridging stay in Your Company scope rather than being treated as optional [73:17]. For Ivan's takeoff the content is methodology, not member weights, so it changes nothing in aisc_validator.py. Conflict with Your Company doctrine: NONE. The lecture is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language, and it names no suppliers.

## Design of Facade Attachments, Session L3: Lateral Drifts and Facade Attachments
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i26hOfUImi0 | Duration: 1:27:53 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is the fourth and final session of the AISC facade-attachments series presented by Alex Zimmer of Simpson Gumpertz and Heger, a co-author of AISC Design Guide 22 on facade attachments to steel-framed buildings [00:35]. The controlling idea is that in modern skinned construction the steel frame carries all gravity and lateral load while the facade is decoupled and goes along for the ride, so connections must allow relative movement between frame and skin or the facade picks up unintended loads and can fall off the building [05:11][07:14]. The session focuses on accommodating inter-storey drift, meaning how much one floor displaces relative to its upper and lower neighbors, both in-plane and out-of-plane, plus corners and designing facade joints for less than full code-level drift using mean recurrence intervals [01:36][14:27].

### Spec References
The speaker cites ASCE 7-16 throughout: components and cladding wind loads versus main-lateral-force-resisting-system loads [42:06]; the ASCE 7-16 commentary wind-drift load combination D + 0.5L + W_a where W_a varies by mean recurrence interval [45:13]; Chapter 13 for facade element and facade attachment seismic strengths and the F_p / a_p / R_p / I_p parameters [49:17][51:19][55:24]; Chapter 12 for strength-level lateral-system drifts and the Delta_x = C_d times Delta_xe / I inelastic-drift formula [49:47][61:06]; and Table 12.12-1 for maximum allowable story drifts by risk category [58:32]. Other named references: IBC 2015 Table 1604 out-of-plane wind deflection limits with footnote F allowing 0.42 times C and C loads (0.7 service factor times 0.6 MRI factor) [46:15][47:45]; AAMA Test 501.6 for glazing fallout / drift [56:56]; FEMA P-58 for the drift-versus-damage curves [64:41]; and a Larry Griffiths (Walter P Moore) paper on frame distortion effects on facade panels [25:56]. AISC Design Guide 22 is the underlying source document for the series [00:35].

### Technical Details
Three mechanisms accommodate inter-storey drift for both out-of-plane and in-plane movement: rigid body translation, rigid body rotation, and distortion / racking [14:59][17:34]. Rigid body rotation is generally preferred for rigid facade systems; distortion is rarely done intentionally because it can damage brittle cladding and is mainly seen in aluminum glass curtain wall that racks into a parallelogram [16:33][19:08]. For metal stud and precast back-up the recommendation is rigid body translation: restrain in-plane horizontal, vertical, and out-of-plane at the bottom gravity connection, but allow sliding at the top so the floor above moves freely [21:11][22:16]. Precast panels restrain in-plane motion at only one of two anchors to allow for shrinkage [22:50]. Inter-storey deformation combines frame shear racking and flexural cantilever bending; shear deformation governs joint movement far more than flexure, and for buildings under about 10 storeys all drift is treated as shear [25:56][26:56]. Typical drift limit used in practice is storey height over 400 or 450 [44:12].

### Fabrication Notes
This webinar is about facade-to-frame connection detailing, not steel shop fabrication, so there are no welding, bolting, fit-up, or shop-QC procedures stated. The relevant fabrication-adjacent point is that tie-back anchors restraining out-of-plane motion at corners are often made as rods or relatively light sections so they can flex perpendicular to their axis without permanent deformation, and code language governs the diameter-to-length ratio of those rods so they stay flexible parallel to the panel plane [36:55][54:54]. Panelized facades assembled in a fabricator shop (precast) are contrasted with field-built back-up walls, which can take wider waterproofing joints [80:15].

### Erection Notes
Field coordination items dominate over erection sequencing. The back-up wall position relative to columns must be detailed so a swaying column does not hang up on the back-up; where the slab edge is narrow the back-up depth is reduced locally at the column [29:04][29:34]. Masonry or stud back-up built tight to the frame inadvertently behaves as an unintended shear wall and gets damaged [30:06]. Top-of-wall connections use clips or a slip track that capture the wall for out-of-plane load but let the spandrel beam deflect vertically and slide horizontally with no through-bolts or anchors restraining in-plane motion [31:44][32:15]. The structural engineer of record must communicate inter-storey lateral drifts to the specialty engineer who designs curtain wall or metal panel, usually through the architect's performance specification [52:23][53:24].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Named failures: precast facade panels falling off a building because stiff connections did not allow the frame to drift relative to the panels, creating a life-safety hazard to people below [07:14][07:45]. Gypsum-sheathed metal stud back-up forced to rack acts as a mini shear wall, damaging screws, board, and the air and water barrier behind the veneer where it cannot be seen [19:39][20:41]. Brick built tight to the steel frame on transitional buildings (1890s through about 1950) traps moisture against the steel, corroding embedded items whose rust expands eight to ten times original volume and dislodges the masonry [75:37][76:39]. Corner joints are the most overlooked condition, where one facade moves perpendicular to its neighbor and can break off panel corners or rupture concealed air and water barriers [37:25][83:28]. Brittle finishes like stucco show moderate to extensive damage near 1 percent drift while curtain wall tolerates about 0.5 percent with only gasket damage [63:39][64:10].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Designing for tighter seismic drift than code limits reduces facade damage but requires a heavier, more expensive building frame, so there is a direct trade-off between frame steel tonnage and facade repair risk [59:03][59:33]. Choosing a shorter mean recurrence interval for serviceability drift (for example 25 years for a low-risk warehouse versus 100 years for a hospital) lowers the design wind speed and pressure and can save steel tonnage in the frame [67:46][85:03][85:33]. Designing facade joints for a reduced MRI yields a 30 to 50 percent reduction in design force (69 percent of strength wind at 100-year, 58 percent at 50-year, 50 percent at 25-year for the Boston example) [45:44][46:15]. The owner discussion about repair tolerance directly sizes the frame.

### Your Company Application
Your Company's scope is the structural steel frame, so the bid takeaway is that any facade-performance drift requirement the architect specifies feeds back into frame stiffness and therefore tonnage, which Ivan should flag during takeoff when a spec calls out a tight drift limit such as H/400 or H/450 or a stated inter-storey drift the frame must hold. The H/400 to H/450 service drift limit and the C_d times Delta / I inelastic-drift method are reference points for the in-house PE when reviewing whether a framing scheme satisfies a facade attachment performance spec, and the SEOR-to-specialty-engineer drift communication duty is a coordination item to capture on jobs with delegated curtain wall or precast cladding. Anchor-rod and tie-back detailing guidance (light flexible rods sized by diameter-to-length so they bend without yielding) maps to Your Company's anchor-rod and miscellaneous steel work where loose lateral tie-backs to cladding are in scope. On ACP controls, a facade drift requirement in the architectural spec is the kind of cross-trade interface that belongs in the project register so the frame design is not finalized before that number is confirmed. DOCTRINE FLAGS: NONE. Verify-don't-generate holds because every spec citation above was spoken on the recording; do not let LLM math invent the drift formula constants, and route any member sizing through aisc_validator.py rather than the rules of thumb in this webinar.

## Design of Facade Attachments, Session L2: Facade Attachments, Part 2
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tjFrsfUyXiQ | Duration: 1:27:14 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
Alex Zimmer of Simpson Gumpertz and Heger, co-author of AISC Design Guide 22, teaches how to design the slab edge, the spandrel beam, and the steel hardware that carries a building facade into the steel frame [01:01][02:02]. The central theme is that minor architectural or structural differences at the slab edge drive large construction cost differences, and that spandrel-beam design is governed by serviceability (vertical deflection plus torsional rotation that opens or closes facade joints), not by flexural or shear strength [02:02][33:52][40:38]. Two slab-edge approaches frame the session: approach one lets the slab or deck cantilever past the spandrel beam and resolve the facade eccentricity as a beam, and approach two transfers all facade load through a bent plate as both vertical force and torsion onto the spandrel beam [03:03][09:37].

### Spec References
AISC Design Guide 22 (Facade Attachments to Steel-Framed Buildings), cited repeatedly as the source of the figures, design aids, and worked examples 5.6 and 6.1 [01:01][08:07][22:33][57:01]. AISC Design Guide 9 (torsion), cited for the rigid-support versus torsionally-pinned end conditions at figure 3.3, for warping normal stress and torsional shear stress, and as the basis of the "modified Design Guide 9 method" [30:15][30:46][45:48][50:22]. ACI 318-05 underlies the Design Guide 22 slab-reinforcement design aids, stated to remain valid for ACI 318-14 [08:37]. The Steel Deck Institute pour-stop selection guide is reprinted in Design Guide 22 with SDI permission [12:42]. Brick Institute of America span/600 vertical-deflection limit for brick veneer [34:54]. Material grades named: A36 for the bent plate [24:07], A992 grade 50 for spandrel beams [58:33]. Weld capacity stated as 1.392 kips per inch per sixteenth for 70 ksi weld metal [27:10].

### Technical Details
Slab flexure must address negative moment over the spandrel beam from the cantilever, so top reinforcement is required well into the span, and deformed bar or bar mats are preferred over welded wire fabric because WWF gets walked down toward the deck during construction [05:34][08:37]. Effective compression-block width depends on deck orientation: deck perpendicular to the spandrel gives full slab depth but only the concrete width between flutes, while deck parallel gives full width but reduced effective depth [06:36]. Facade point loads are spread at a non-codified 1:1 (45 degree) slope to set effective width for shear and flexure [07:37]. Worked example 5.6 used FV 1.8 kips at 5 in eccentricity, FH 1.8 kips, a 9 in bent-plate cantilever, a 7/16 in A36 plate, and 1.5 in fillet welds at 12 in on center, dragging roughly 5.8 kips into each threaded bar coupler [23:36][27:10][28:10]. For spandrel torsion the beam is correctly idealized as rotating about a pin at the top flange (restrained by the slab), not about its centroid; Design Guide 22 introduces the "modified Design Guide 9 method" and "modified flexural analogy method" for this, with flexural analogy accurate for short torsional spans near 10 ft and Design Guide 9 closer to FE results at 30 ft spans [48:50][50:22][53:28][54:29].

### Fabrication Notes
Bent-plate attachment has three fabrication options: shop welded (option A, most economical, no field adjustment), shipped with an erection bolt then field welded (option B), or short-slotted-hole slip-critical (option C); the speaker prefers B or C for field adjustability [19:27][19:57]. Light-gauge pour stops are 12 to 20 gauge stay-in-place forms, sized only for wet concrete plus construction live load and not for facade loads [11:41][12:42]. Headed studs or deformed-bar anchors with female couplers are welded to the bent-plate vertical leg to drag facade force into the slab, and the deformed-bar coupler is now preferred because studs on the leg are a tripping hazard for ironworkers; these are often field installed rather than shop installed [16:15][18:23]. Hot-rolled bent plates were limited to 3/8 in in the Design Guide 22 selection tables [15:13]. Stud placement near the web can cause burn-through, so flange thickness may need to increase when the slab edge is left/right adjustable [20:59].

### Erection Notes
Adjustability is the dominant field theme: a long slotted hole, as much as a 3 in slot, lets the erector set the bent plate in or out, after which the plate is field welded to the top flange and the erection bolt is no longer load bearing [18:55][76:10]. Pour stops are field welded to the spandrel beam to absorb spandrel-location tolerance [11:41]. Kicker braces are time-consuming and uneconomical to erect at every hanger, so the speaker installs them only every 10 to 15 ft, or more often uses roll beams [42:41][43:13][85:24]. Roll beams are depressed below the spandrel top flange to avoid coping, connected through a full-depth fitted web stiffener with bolts designed to take the twist as a moment couple [44:44]. The speaker prefers roll beams on roof decks because they also brace the spandrel bottom flange against lateral-torsional buckling under wind uplift [85:56].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
A real-project failure was shown where the erector welded the shear-stud connector to the horizontal leg of the bent plate instead of to the beam top flange; the engineer caught it on site and required supplemental top-flange and underside welds to mobilize the studs [21:30]. Welded wire fabric being trampled down to the deck, where it no longer resists the negative moment over the spandrel, is named as a recurring construction problem driving the preference for deformed bar [08:37]. The presenter also corrected his own slide errors live (deck orientation labeled wrong, and wet concrete weight omitted from the example 5.6 bent-plate and weld check), noting both would be fixed in the next revision [37:31][77:42]. Stud-to-web burn-through is flagged as a fabrication defect when studs sit too close to the web [20:59].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Slab-edge details carry substantial construction cost, and consistent slab-edge conditions around the perimeter lower both cost and inspection effort, while a variety of conditions makes everyone's life expensive [02:02][03:03]. Serviceability, not strength, sets spandrel size, and the cost swing is large: a brick-on-CMU 30 ft spandrel that needs only a W16x26 for strength jumps to a W21x62 to hold a 3/16 in soft-joint deflection, more than double the weight per foot; brick-on-metal-stud likewise goes from W12x19 (strength) to W21x62 (service) [38:01][39:04][39:37]. The speaker warns that chasing minimum tonnage with many different spandrel sizes can cost more in facade-support engineering and field complication than the steel saved, so standardizing sections is often the cheaper total outcome [32:51][33:22]. Option A shop welding is cheapest but option B/C field-adjustable hardware is usually worth the added cost to absorb tolerance [19:27].

### Your Company Application
This session maps directly to Your Company spandrel and facade-attachment scope and supports the in-house PE stamp on connection design. For Ivan's takeoff, the key lesson is that spandrel-beam weight is set by facade deflection and torsion criteria, not by the analysis-software member size, so a facade-bearing perimeter must be priced on the serviceability section (the W21x62-class member), not the strength section, or the bid will be light. For Mario's shop and welding crew, the bent-plate, pour-stop, stud, and deformed-bar-coupler details are conventional fillet and stud welds (70 ksi metal, 1.392 kips/in/sixteenth) that Tekla should detail with field-weld and slotted-hole adjustability per options B and C rather than fully shop-welded plates. For Paul, the named ironworker tripping hazard from studs on the bent-plate vertical leg is a real field-safety item, and the on-site weld-correction story shows why erection welds need inspection. Anchor-rod and bolting parallels are the long-slotted-hole adjust-then-weld workflow and slip-critical option. No supplier names appear and the content is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language. Conflict with Your Company doctrine: NONE.

## Design of Facade Attachments, Session L1: Facade Attachments, Part 1
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jc8XQsMvmiE | Duration: 1:33:34 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This webinar by Alec Zimmer of Simpson Gumpertz and Heger teaches how the structural steel frame supports building facades and how the joints between the facade and the frame are sized to absorb structural deflection, thermal change, and moisture growth [00:34][01:35]. It walks three facade families: hand-laid masonry cavity walls, panelized systems including precast, and aluminum glass curtain walls, then closes with a method for sizing vertical movement joints [02:06]. The controlling idea is that the steel spandrel beam carries the facade eccentrically, so it both deflects and rotates as a rigid body about its top flange, and that rotation drives both a vertical drop and a horizontal translation at the shelf-angle tip that the joints must accommodate [13:47][65:44].

### Spec References
The single document cited repeatedly is AISC Design Guide 22, Facade Attachments to Steel-Frame Buildings, including its shelf-angle deflection tables and worked Example 7-1 [01:05][19:28][71:57][72:28]. Two research papers behind the DG 22 shelf-angle tables are named: Grimm and Yura, and Tide and Krogstad, the speaker preferring the Tide and Krogstad approach for fewer designer limitations [19:28]. For load combinations on joints he cites ASCE 7-16 commentary, specifically dead plus half live plus a reduced-return-period wind Wa [71:24]. No AISC 360 section, AISC 341 seismic provision, AWS D1.1 clause, or RCSC bolting reference is stated in this session; those are general principles, no section cited.

### Technical Details
Shelf-angle sizing targets roughly two-thirds of the masonry veneer bearing on the angle so the resultant stays over the angle [10:13]. Hot-rolled angles are preferred over bent plate for less variability in the horizontal-leg position, with shims behind the vertical leg used to tune the long horizontal leg now driven longer by thicker mineral-wool insulation [10:44][11:15]. Curtain wall out-of-plane deflection is typically span over 175, tightened to span over 360 with brittle finishes and capped near 3/4 inch, with in-plane drift commonly span over 360, 3/4 inch max, and as tight as 3/8 inch on recent jobs [55:33][56:34]. Aluminum mullions expand about twice the rate of steel framing, so horizontal mullion joints must absorb that movement [55:02]. Brick growth is irreversible moisture expansion of as much as 0.07 percent, and sealants typically compress 30 percent, up to 50 percent for high-performance products [69:53][14:52][70:23]. Panel gravity load must bear at exactly two points per panel to keep the load path statically determinate [34:57].

### Fabrication Notes
Shelf angles are galvanized in the shop as standard, with stainless steel used on some projects partly to mitigate thermal bridging, because concealed angles can corrode undetected if flashing joints leak [18:58][19:28]. Threaded studs that carry the shelf-angle-to-hanger connection are shop-welded into the hanger angle, and the designer is warned those studs see flexure as well as shear through the thickness of the thermal isolation pad [50:50][24:07]. Any bolt holes that must be drilled in the curtain-wall hardware should be done in the shop and coordinated with the primary structure [61:39]. Bent-plate pour stops, gussets welded to the spandrel web, and full-depth web stiffeners for local bending are the recurring fabricated steel pieces [57:34][58:05].

### Erection Notes
The shelf angle is first erection-bolted to the hanger angle, set to its final field location, then field welded, and the weld is touched up with zinc-rich coating where galvanizing burned off [22:04]. The hanger angle is then fillet welded to the gusset on the spandrel beam [22:36]. The slab edge is set by the steel erector and poured long before the veneer goes on, so in-and-out adjustment of the shelf angle is made with steel shims [30:52][64:00]. Curtain-wall erectors prefer field-welded connections for adjustability, using a self-drilling erection fastener to set position before the structural fasteners go in, after which the erection fastener is abandoned or removed [52:58][57:04]. Spray fireproofing applied before the curtain wall requires block-outs at anchor locations, patched after anchors are installed [52:27]. Spandrel-beam rotation from the eccentric veneer is restrained with double-angle kickers or small roll beams perpendicular to the spandrel [22:36][23:06].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Sealant joints over-compress and bulge or the brick cracks when joints are not sized for the full set of movements [05:08][84:24]. A shelf angle set out of tolerance can leave less than two-thirds bearing, forcing a field-welded extension [31:55]. The most cited field failure is missed embeds, brackets, block-outs, and recesses in a complicated panel erection sequence, described as a daily struggle on a live project [48:24]. Other named problems are joints in the architectural panel layout not coordinated with load-application points on the primary frame, slotted holes too short to absorb slab-edge or spandrel-sweep variability, and crushing of the thermal isolation pad if compression stress is not kept near one fifth of the pad ultimate strength [49:25][61:39][85:27].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Tight architectural joints drive cost into the steel: a 3/8 inch mortar-matched sealant joint forces very tight spandrel-beam deflection limits, which can mean heavier beams or shorter spans [83:20][56:34]. Galvanized or stainless shelf angles, thermal isolation pads, kickers, roll beams, gusset plates, and field welding all add per-floor connection labor and material beyond a plain spandrel [18:58][22:36]. Long hangers driven by thicker insulation add flexural rotation and may upsize members [25:11][10:44]. The division of design responsibility between the engineer of record and the panel or curtain-wall specialty engineer is a coordination cost that, if mishandled, surfaces as field rework and missed embeds [43:17][49:25].

### Your Company Application
This session frames the facade-support steel that Ivan would take off: shelf angles, hangers, gussets, kickers, roll beams, stiffeners, bent-plate pour stops, and the embeds for panel and curtain-wall anchors, all real members that belong in an AISC takeoff through aisc_validator.py rather than buried in a per-SF allowance. Mario owns the shop and field welding that this work centers on, the gusset-to-web fillet welds and the field shelf-angle welds with zinc-rich touch-up, plus the shop-welded threaded studs into hanger angles, which is squarely AWS D1.1 fillet-weld and stud-weld work even though no clause is cited here. Tekla detailing must carry the shim packs, slotted holes, and block-out coordination this video stresses, and the in-house PE stamp covers the engineer-of-record side that defines deflection limits and the loads delivered to the specialty panel engineer. For ACP controls, the embed and block-out coordination called out as the top field failure is a register item to track per floor against the concrete pour. Doctrine flag: NONE. The content is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language, no supplier names, and no conflict with bid_rates.py or AISC-weight rules.
