## Design of Facade Attachments, Session R1: Facade Fundamentals
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fNdh-oHrtaI | Duration: 1:28:55 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is AISC Night School 17, Session 5, the first session on facade attachments to steel-framed buildings, presented by Alex Zimmer of Simpson Gumpertz and Heger, a co-developer of AISC Design Guide 22 [00:03][01:04]. The core teaching is how the steel frame supports a non-bearing curtain wall facade through attachments that must carry gravity, wind, seismic, and thermal loads while accommodating differential movement between the frame and the cladding [10:44][13:17]. The central problem stated is that poorly coordinated facade attachments drive excess RFIs, shop-drawing delays, out-of-tolerance erection, and envelope failures [03:36]. The session covers facade performance fundamentals, design criteria, roles and responsibilities, thermal bridging, and accommodating construction tolerances and clearances [04:39].
### Spec References
AISC Design Guide 22 (facade attachments to steel-framed buildings, published 2008), table 2.1 of DG 22 for facade assembly weights [03:36][04:06][38:01]. AISC Code of Standard Practice for frame fabrication and erection tolerances, with DG 22 summarizing those tolerances [42:01][62:50][63:51]. ASCE 7-16 for components-and-cladding wind pressures and seismic component force equation, including its commentary load combinations [19:01][22:08][24:11]. IBC 2015 wind serviceability reductions (multiply C and C pressures by 0.42 for cladding, 0.6 for glass) and seismic drift limit 0.025H [25:13][30:21]. ASTM C1472 for calculating joint widths and movements [70:30]. ASTM F593 stainless steel bolts named for thermal-break connections [53:11]. Other cited references: ACI 530 (0.31 in deflection), Brick Institute of America (L/600 to L/720), AAMA (3/4 in curtain-wall guidance), PCI Design Handbook (panel tolerances), and the Northeastern University / Charles Pankow Foundation thermal-break study [28:18][50:08].
### Technical Details
Facade loads to design for are dead load (the predominant gravity load, mostly no live load except for projections that can carry maintenance access), seismic perpendicular and parallel to the wall, wind primarily perpendicular plus joint racking, and thermal expansion-contraction [16:23]. The designer must locate the gravity hinge between panel and frame, since hinge position drives spandrel-beam moment and slab-edge demand significantly [17:59][18:30]. Stiffness governs by rule of thumb (L/360, brick L/600 to L/720, 0.31 in per ACI 530, 3/4 in per AAMA), but sealant compressibility often controls: a 3/4 in joint compressed to 50 percent leaving 1/8 in for tolerance and thermal limits a 30 ft spandrel to about 1/4 in, roughly L/1440 [28:18][29:50]. Interstory drift is handled at H/400 to H/500 for wind, with ASCE 7-16 requiring connections to accommodate at least 1/2 in of interstory movement [30:21][30:52]. Thermal-break design must account for bolt flexure, shear deformation, shim compression, and oversized holes that defeat slip-critical clamping; the Pankow study recommends treating bolts as single-curvature cantilevers and limiting FRP compressive stress to about 30 to 35 percent of ultimate to prevent creep [55:43][58:17][59:48].
### Fabrication Notes
The speaker repeatedly stresses that the steel fabricator and erector cannot reasonably beat AISC Code of Standard Practice tolerances, and specifying tighter frame tolerances should be exceptional and only after consulting local fabricators and erectors [62:50][63:20]. Thermal-break assemblies are built up in the shop using carbon steel plate (left unprotected behind the moisture barrier), galvanized plate outboard of the barrier, thermal isolation pads aligned to the insulation plane, isolation bushings or washers, and ASTM F593 stainless bolts; carbon-steel studs can be shop-welded to a hanger angle to pass through the pad [52:10][53:11][53:42]. Hot-dip galvanized fasteners are cheaper and more available, and field welding of galvanized connections uses common procedures but requires removing the galvanizing locally and touching up the weld-affected area after [34:56][35:27]. Material production tolerances such as beam camber sweep and panel thickness stack with fabrication and erection tolerances into accumulated tolerance that the design must absorb [63:51][64:21].
### Erection Notes
Erection tolerances include column plumbness (Code of Standard Practice allows 2 in inward or 1 in outward at the 10th story in the worked example), spandrel-beam sweep of 1/2 in, panel plan location plus or minus 1/2 in per PCI, and panel bow up to L/360 or 1.33 in [63:51][65:22]. These aggregate so a column gap could open 2.5 in or close 1.5 in, and a mid-span gap could open 4.33 in or close 3.33 in; a square-root-sum-of-squares approach gives a more realistic range of roughly minus 1.8 to plus 2.5 in [66:54][68:56]. Out-of-tolerance erection is corrected through slotted-hole adjustability, and when that is exceeded, hanger angles are unbolted and field welded or a longer shelf-angle leg is installed [86:03][86:34]. A cautionary case showed an aluminum-glass curtain wall erected before the steel sunshade because the building had to be enclosed early, forcing heavy field welding next to installed glass with large deviations [73:33][74:35]. Attachments are also at the confluence of structural erectors, waterproofers, carpenters, and masons, so barrier damage during installation is a recurring erection risk [36:28][36:58].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Named failures include the Christchurch 2001 earthquake where unanchored brick veneer peeled off the entire frame, and a precast panel that fell when a slotted-insert bolt at a building expansion joint was torqued down too far and broke under cyclic movement [20:33][32:23][33:24]. Durability failures center on concealed attachments that corrode unseen: corrugated brick ties accumulated water and rusted out with no inspection access until brick fell, and thin or unprotected steel fasteners penetrating the water barrier are flagged as high risk [33:56][34:26]. Other problems are anchors that block wall drainage, anchors too flexible to prevent differential movement that then tears waterproofing and air barriers, and details that are simply not constructible in the field [35:58][36:28]. Restraint of thermal and structural movement is called out as a condition to avoid entirely because the resulting forces are very hard to predict [32:23].
### Bid / Cost Implications
Wind tunnel testing on larger buildings frequently shows design pressures below ASCE 7 values, which can reduce both cladding cost and the main wind force resisting system forces [19:01]. Thermal-break connections are expensive and the speaker repeatedly weighs whether the cost is justified, recommending them on continuous facade lines with real thermal impact but not on one-off back-of-house connections [37:28][61:18]. Stainless steel fasteners cost more than hot-dip galvanized but last longer on buildings unlikely to be reskinned, and the Northeastern study finding that thermally improved bushings add little benefit lets the designer drop bushings and just use stainless bolts [34:56][60:18]. Tighter-than-code frame tolerances raise fabrication and erection cost and should be avoided, and the team should set the adjustability budget up front rather than absorbing rework later [62:50][70:30].
### Your Company Application
This session is squarely about the structural-engineer-of-record and detailing interface, which maps to Tekla detailing and the in-house PE stamp: Your Company must clearly note on the structural documents which connections are field-adjustable, state facade load assumptions, and flag any frame tolerances that differ from the Code of Standard Practice [41:31][63:51]. For Ivan takeoff, shelf angles, kicker bracing angles, hangers, relieving angles, and embed plates that support a veneer are SEOR scope and should be counted and priced, while panel connections delegated to a specialty engineer are not, so the bid must draw that scope line cleanly [44:33][45:34]. For Mario shop and welding, the galvanized field-weld touch-up rule and shop-welded studs through thermal pads are concrete WPS and finishing items, and field welding adjacent to installed glass is a real condition to plan around. For Paul safety, the falling-veneer failures (Christchurch, the dropped precast panel) underline why positive anchorage and torque control matter. Anchor-rod and slotted-hole adjustability tie directly to Your Company's anchor-setting tolerance discipline. No conflict with Your Company doctrine; this is conventional structural steel with no PEMB framing, and all spec numbers are quoted only as the speaker stated them.

## Column Design: Past, Present, and Future
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L62qt8KcTcI | Duration: 1:28:53 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is a historical and theoretical lecture by Dr. Joseph Yura (UT Austin, 32 years on the AISC specification committee) tracing how steel column strength has been predicted from Greek stone columns to the current AISC formulas [00:31][01:34]. The two through-lines are the axially loaded column curve and the beam-column interaction equation, which Yura presents in the order they evolved because that order predicts where design is heading [01:34][02:05]. The central modern idea is that the column curve is governed by residual stresses (locked-in stresses from rolling) and initial out-of-straightness, not by load eccentricity as the 1800s methods assumed [40:15][57:22][72:31].

### Spec References
The talk is conceptual and names few section numbers, but it does cite specific AISC documents and editions by year. AISC was established in 1921, the first specification in 1923, the Code of Practice in 1924, and the first manual in 1925 [33:25]. AISC switched from a Rankine-type to a parabolic column equation in 1936, used parabolic equations through 1985, adopted the single Galambos-based column curve in the 1985 LRFD spec [35:30][59:58][60:03], and the Johnson parabola of the late 1800s became the AISC column curve adopted in 1961 [23:36][46:55]. The current code uses the direct analysis method in the main body of the AISC specification with the effective-length (K-factor) method moved to an appendix [69:58]. The Eurocode multiple-column-curve approach (1978, table from the 1993 Eurocode) is cited for contrast; AISC rejected it [58:27][58:58]. The SSRC guide to stability design chapter 15 and the AISC ninth edition are named by an audience questioner [80:59]. No AISC 360 J or F section, AISC 341, AWS D1.1, or RCSC clause is cited; general principles otherwise.

### Technical Details
Residual stresses of roughly 0.3 Fy compression at the flange tips (the Ketter distribution) cause the tips to yield first under axial load, shrinking the effective elastic cross-section and reducing stiffness, which is why a stiffness reduction factor (tau) appears in the tables [41:15][44:21][91:00]. Because weak-axis moment of inertia depends on the cube of the elastic-section depth while strong-axis is linear, residual stress hurts weak-axis buckling far more, so weak-axis controls [45:25][62:40]. Yura's key forward-looking finding: modern cold rotary straightening of rolled shapes (now up to 370 lb/ft sections) leaves virtually no compressive tip stress and often slight tension at the tips, which would raise the column curve roughly 10 to 15 percent and would let designers use P/PY in the first interaction term with a plain second-order elastic analysis [72:31][73:33][76:45][77:15]. The direct analysis method reduces elastic stiffness via tau to mimic an inelastic second-order analysis so K can be set to 1 [68:55][70:29].

### Fabrication Notes
The fabrication content is about rolled-shape production, not shop fit-up. Yura explains that continuous casting, continuous rolling, and standard cold rotary straightening now plastify members as they pass through a series of rolls to come out straight, which changes the residual-stress pattern from the 1960s assumption [72:31][73:03]. A visible diagnostic he shows on a W12x65: mill scale flakes off where the cold straightening reached yield, and light surface corrosion (rust marks) then appears across that flange width, indicating the section was rotary straightened [73:33][74:35]. No shop QC, fit-up tolerance, or weld-process fabrication procedure is covered.

### Erection Notes
No erection content. The lecture does not address field procedures, sequencing, bracing, crane or rigging, or site coordination. It is a member-strength theory webinar.

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The errors discussed are historical design and analysis errors, not shop or field rejections. Tredgold's 1822 first metal column formula wrongly assumed the axial-load deflection shape was the same parabola as the end-moment shape [11:30]. Two named structural failures illustrate the cost of weak or isolated specifications: railroad bridges failed at about one per week averaged over a decade partly because individual engineers each used their own column curves, and the 1907 Quebec Bridge collapsed from a compression-member failure under one engineer's unusually liberal specification, which triggered the move to consensus design specs [22:00][30:21][30:53]. A common modern oversight named is that first-order analysis ignores how axial load changes frame moments [48:01].

### Bid / Cost Implications
There is no direct bid, cost, or estimating content. The only indirect implication is methodological: the current single AISC column curve is conservative for modern rotary-straightened rolled shapes by about 10 to 15 percent [76:45], meaning the code already builds in margin on column capacity rather than leaving it to the estimator. The historical safety factor of four on wrought-iron columns is mentioned only as context [14:41].

### Your Company Application
This is reference knowledge for the in-house PE stamp and for Ivan's takeoff, not a procedural change. The practical takeaway for the PE work is that AISC column strength comes from a residual-stress-plus-out-of-straightness model and that the direct analysis method (K=1, reduced stiffness via tau, second-order analysis) is the current main-body approach, with the K-factor method in the appendix [69:58]; any column or frame check should follow that, with weak-axis controlling on W shapes [62:40]. For Ivan, column weights still come only from bridge/aisc_validator.py against the v16.0 database; this video gives zero shape weights and must never be a source for member math, consistent with Hard Rule 5. The welding aside is the one item touching Mario's shop: Yura confirms welded built-up sections carry high tensile residual stress near the weld balanced by compression elsewhere, a column-strength consideration distinct from rolled shapes [83:01][83:32], relevant if Your Company ever fabricates welded built-up columns. Doctrine flags: NONE. The talk is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language and no supplier names.

## Buyer Beware:  Choosin the Right Architecturally Exposed Structural Steel Category
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oPdPXEAxBkU | Duration: 1:00:17 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
This webinar by Jacinda Collins (AISC structural steel specialist) and David Weaver (Moltech Technologies, detailing) teaches the AESS category system introduced in the 2016 Code of Standard Practice and the cost that rides with each step up [00:00][01:01]. The pre-2016 world had only two buckets, standard steel and "AESS," so a small bathroom application and a glass-house atrium were specified identically and priced unpredictably [02:33][03:03]. The new system defines AESS 1, 2, 3, 4, and AESS-C custom, escalating workmanship and labor with each level, and the central message is that buyers should specify the lowest category that meets the visual intent rather than defaulting to the top [06:05][52:08]. A 10-step selection program (understand levels, decide if standard steel works, visual map, budget map, think like an ironworker, address connections, finalize finishes) frames the buyer decision [05:35].

### Spec References
2016 AISC Code of Standard Practice, Section 10 (the AESS provisions and category definitions) [01:01][06:35]. AESS categories 1, 2, 3, 4, and AESS-C custom [06:35]. Surface prep is cited by SSPC number: SP6 commercial blast clean (the default AESS surface prep), SP2 (a lesser hand-tool prep used when an intumescent primer governed), and SP10 near-white blast (more stringent than SP6, called for in wet marine environments) [08:06][38:24][40:25]. The 15th edition AISC Manual is referenced as the edition that carried the expanded AESS language [22:30]. No AISC 360, AISC 341, AWS D1.1 clause, or RCSC section was cited by number in this presentation.

### Technical Details
Category 1 (basic elements) exceeds standard workmanship: ground sharp edges, weld spatter removed, continuous weld appearance (welds not ground), and SP6 surface prep [07:36][08:06]. Category 2 (feature elements over 20 ft away) cuts standard fabrication tolerances in half, removes markings, and requires uniform smooth welds that are still not ground or contoured [09:07][09:37]. Category 3 (feature elements within 20 ft) requires a mock-up, removes all mill marks, grinds and fills button/plug welds, orients and hides HSS weld seams, abuts cross sections, and minimizes open-gap tolerances [10:38][11:08]. Category 4 (showcase elements) contours and blends welds, fills and sands surface imperfections, minimizes weld show-through, and grinds the HSS coil seam smooth so it disappears under paint [12:09][12:41]. AESS-C custom uses the matrix to tick individual requirements line by line, ideal for mixed materials (steel with reclaimed wood), weathering steel, or historic-repair blending [14:12][14:43].

### Fabrication Notes
The cost driver is labor per ton, not material: material is under one third of a complete package, more than two thirds is labor [27:38][28:10]. Weaver's 30-ft beam versus 3-ft beam example shows the same handling, cutting, drilling, inspecting, and loading hours apply regardless of length, so a short heavy member carries vastly higher hours per ton [26:37][27:08]. A full-size visual sample is not a clean 10 percent add because economy of scale is lost when one column must be fabricated ahead of the batch; with 10 identical columns the sample exceeds 10 percent, with 100 columns it approaches 1 percent [30:45][31:15]. Web/beam penetrations are a hidden labor and machine-time cost the fabricator must be asked about [25:33]. Curved-member tolerances could not be priced at all (light angle in-house versus heavy wide flange rolled out of state, easy-way versus hard-way HSS radius) and were left as red zeros in the matrix [32:16][32:46].

### Erection Notes
Field work is harder than shop work, so the standing advice is to do as much as possible in the shop and ship assemblies to the erector [45:32]. The firefighter memorial with over 50 columns used prefabricated modular pieces so the fabricator welded at ground level and the field crew only set two pieces together, avoiding holding a crane in place during column welding [45:32][46:03]. Use bolting instead of welding in the field where possible, because field welding at awkward angles forces preheat, equipment handling, and overhead grinding that drive labor up [46:33][45:02]. On the galvanized walkway truss example, trusses were shop-welded as assemblies and galvanized while the horizontal infill was field bolted, since the design team did not want to field weld on galvanizing [34:48][35:18].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The recurring error is specifying a higher AESS category than the viewing distance or budget warrants, and assuming exposed steel automatically equals AESS [06:05][41:25]. A real conflict shown was a galvanized member spec calling for an SP6 blast clean, which cannot be performed after galvanizing and is wasted money before galvanizing since the galvanizer blast-cleans anyway [36:19][36:50]. Another was an AESS SP6 requirement colliding with an intumescent-primer SP2 requirement on the same 300 tons, resolved only by two mock-ups plus cost and schedule comparison [38:24][38:54]. Assuming a condition is covered by the Code of Standard Practice when it is not is a frequent specification gap flagged by the Steel Solutions Center [50:07]. On inspection: the Code of Standard Practice itself imposes no special AESS inspection or certification, so any inspection must be explicitly called out by the architect or engineer [53:39][54:09].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Category ranges are increases over non-AESS, not cumulative across categories: category 2 lands roughly 25 to 35 percent over non-AESS, with individual line items carrying ranges (for example 5 to 25 percent for a visual sample) [29:12][31:45][66:05]. The matrix is explicitly a conceptual budgeting tool and must NOT be put in contract documents or held against the fabricator; include the AESS matrix but exclude the relative cost matrix [05:05][50:38]. Least weight does not equal least cost, because lighter steel can introduce more craftsmanship and labor [43:27]. The strongest cost lever is mapping category by location on a single member: Bill Zimmerman's line is "the money isn't in the middle of the beam, it's at the ends, in the connections," so keeping connections at a lower AESS while the column shaft runs higher saves real money [58:32][59:02]. Bring a fabricator on board as early as possible, and if difficult work comes back cheap, ask questions because an assumption is probably buried [51:08].

### Your Company Application
For Ivan, this is a takeoff modifier that sits on top of aisc_validator member weights: an AESS scope means hours-per-ton, not tonnage, drives the price, so a count-gap takeoff must capture penetrations, connection welds, mock-up columns, and the SP6/SP10 prep before a $/SF gate means anything. The matrix is a budgeting tool only and must never reach a client proposal or contract, which aligns with our no-internal-cost-data doctrine. For Mario, the category dictates weld finish (continuous appearance at 1, smooth and ground at 3, contoured and blended at 4) and HSS seam grinding, all of which are AWS D1.1 visual-acceptance work that should be scoped into his shop hours, with field bolting preferred over field welding to cut erection labor; this reinforces shop-first sequencing on field bolting. For Paul, the ironworker ergonomics point (overhead grinding, awkward-angle welding) is a safety and fatigue input on AESS erection. For Tekla detailing, category-by-elevation zoning on a single column must be modeled and noted on the drawings exactly as the design documents state, and galvanizing-tank fit governs whether an assembly is shop-welded or field-bolted. PE stamp and joists are not addressed here. CONFLICT WITH DOCTRINE: NONE. The verify-don't-generate posture holds, since this content reinforces that AESS labor cost must be sourced from a fabricator and member-level takeoff, never assumed or generated.

## General Information on Curved Members
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5QCZC7ng4r0 | Duration: 1:31:57 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
This is Session 1 of AISC Night School 17, presented by Bo Dowswell of ARC International, the author of AISC Design Guide 33 (Curved Member Design) [00:00, 01:05]. The session is a general orientation to curved steel members. Dowswell splits curved members into vertically curved and horizontally curved, where the controlling distinction is structural behavior, not just the geometric plane of curvature [02:06, 03:09]. Curving steel is a specialty operation performed by a bender roller company that normally works as a subcontractor to the steel fabricator, because a typical fab shop does not own the bending equipment [06:56, 07:27]. The session walks the Design Guide 33 table of contents, curve geometries, bending processes, and the curving mechanics (strain ratio alpha) that govern fracture and distortion risk [06:26].

### Spec References
Cited verbatim by the speaker or slides: AISC Design Guide 33, Curved Member Design (chapters 1 through 8, glossary, bender-roller company list) [09:03, 11:38]; AISC Design Guide 1, base plates, referenced for its practical content model [10:07]; AISC Specification (360) Section B4.1, compact element limit lambda less than lambda-P [77:01]; a Specification Chapter F flush-style equation form for the tension-flange hole-elongation check, F-u times A-fn greater than or equal to 1.1 times F-y times the gross flange area [65:04, 65:34]; the AISC Seismic Provisions (341) Section B1.1b, lambda-HD for highly ductile elements [78:06]; and an AISC Engineering Journal 2006 research paper (Hubday) that set the alpha = 12 trigger for involving a bender roller [58:51]. No ASTM number was stated, though ASTM mill tolerances on initial imperfection were referenced generically [70:15].

### Technical Details
A standard bend is single-radius curvature about a principal or geometric axis; strong-axis bending is called hard-way and weak-axis is easy-way by bender rollers [18:10, 18:40]. Specialty bends covered: off-axis (conical rolling), compound (two arcs, same direction, optional straight tangent segment), reverse compound (S-curve), multi-axis (multi-plane, any 3D shape from a CAD file), variable-radius (parabolic, elliptical), and spiral or helical (sloped/pitched rolling) [22:53 through 31:06]. The governing mechanics are the maximum bending strain epsilon = y-o / R, simplified to D / 2R for symmetric shapes, expressed through the strain ratio alpha (max strain divided by yield strain F-y/E) [56:51, 57:21, 57:51]. Alpha at 12 is the threshold to contact a bender roller, with roughly 17 still safe; 3 percent strain is a practical upper bound and strain-hardening for 50 ksi steel begins near alpha 8.7 [58:51, 60:24, 61:25]. Detailed radius dimensions go to the inside of the flange for hard-way wide flange, to the centroid for easy-way, and to the HSS center or inside compression face per shape [19:41, 20:12].

### Fabrication Notes
Two temperature classes: cold bending (shop temperature) and hot bending (heat lowers yield, easier to bend) [32:37, 33:08]. Three structural processes: pyramid roll bending (three rolls, most common, cold, multiple passes with rolls drawn closer each pass, supplementary rolls tension the tension flange to control web distortion), incremental step bending (proprietary cantilever pull-and-feed, cold), and induction bending (the only common hot method, a narrow heated ring around the perimeter with immediate water cooling, pivoted on a radius arm) [33:42 through 46:21]. Contour rolls, grooved/special rolls, and internal mandrels brace slender elements against cross-sectional distortion; tooling cost is justified by quantity, not a single member [37:27, 38:27, 71:16]. Tension-flange bolt holes should be punched before bending only for large-radius bends or when the F-u A-fn check passes; small-radius bends should be drilled after bending, which is more expensive because the beam line cannot be used [63:29, 64:01, 65:04]. Holes, cuts, copes, and pre-bend welded fittings all reduce ductility; never cut a diamond-shaped hole before bending [62:29, 63:09].

### Erection Notes
Erection-specific procedure is light in this session. The main field-relevant point is shipping: a curved member held to a tight radius can relax from truck vibration, similar to documented camber loss, although the bender-roller committee did not agree it is real and had no proof [86:30, 87:02, 87:32]. Bender rollers add bracing on long slender curved members for the truck ride to prevent distortion or loss of radius in transit [88:33]. Induction-bent members may hold radius better in shipping because their residual stresses are lower, though this is unproven [88:02].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Distortion is any deviation from the original cross-section and occurs to some degree on every bend because initial mill imperfections are amplified [66:08, 66:39]. Named failure modes: flange or web local buckling under flexural compression, shear buckling between pyramid rolls, contact-force web crippling under the roll, and flange bending when supplementary-roll force is set too high [66:39, 67:11, 67:41, 68:12]. For square and rectangular HSS, distortion is quantified by rho-W (web bow B1/B) and rho-F (compression-flange inward bow E/D); round HSS uses ovalization rho [72:18, 72:49, 74:53]. A real 1988 case showed an HSS spiral stair stringer scrapped because only two internal support HSS were tacked in instead of three, leaving visible sidewall bowing [73:50, 74:21]. Fracture risk rises with alpha and with pre-bend holes, cuts, copes, and welds [61:25, 62:29].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Curving is a subcontracted line item to a bender roller, so the estimate must carry that scope rather than absorb it as in-house fab [07:27]. Cold bending is cheaper than induction (hot) bending; induction costs more but achieves tight radii with low distortion [47:27]. Contour and special rolls or mandrels carry tooling cost that only amortizes over quantity, so one-off curved members are disproportionately expensive [38:27, 76:08]. Drilling holes after bending breaks the beam-line flow and adds cost on small-radius work [64:01]. Bender-roller capability varies widely by shop (heavy strong-axis, spirals, induction), so the bender roller should be engaged in the conceptual stage when a tight radius is involved to avoid late rework [49:33, 50:04]. Galvanizing after bending can shift the radius from residual-stress release and force a re-roll that damages the coating, a schedule risk to flag [89:33, 90:05].

### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, any curved member is a flag, not a standard line: it routes to a bender-roller sub quote, and the estimate should tag confidence LOW until the bender roller confirms the radius is achievable, since "minimum radius for a W14x90" has no table answer and must be asked [50:49, 51:21]. Ivan can pre-screen feasibility with the alpha = D/2R over (F-y/E) check and the B4.1 lambda-P / 341 B1.1b lambda-HD shortcuts: alpha under 12 (or lambda under lambda-P) is routine, above 12 means call the bender roller [58:51, 77:01, 78:06]. Tekla detailing must dimension radii to the correct reference (inside flange hard-way, centroid easy-way) and decide hole timing, because Mario's shop cannot beam-line punch small-radius curved members and would drill after bending [19:41, 64:01]. Mario should not weld fittings, cope, or cut diamond holes before a member ships to the roller [62:29]. For Paul, the field item is shipping bracing and verifying radius on receipt, since tight-radius members can relax in transit [88:33]. No conflict with Your Company doctrine: this is conventional structural steel methodology with no PEMB language, AISC weights still come from aisc_validator.py, and rates stay CEO-locked. DOCTRINE_FLAG: NONE.

## Design of Curved Members with the new AISC Design Guide
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9K_UM8WwtQg | Duration: 1:31:19 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
The webinar walks through AISC Design Guide 33, Curved Member Design, presented by Bo Dowswell of ARC International ahead of the guide's release [02:08]. The central method is that curved members are not equal to straight members, but with three modifications you can design them as equivalent straight members using the standard specification [13:33], [53:22]. The guide covers vertically curved members (arches and beam-like curves), horizontally curved members (flexure plus torsion), and connections, with two design chapters plus an examples chapter [23:31], [30:20]. Vertically curved members get the deep treatment with full equations; horizontally curved get an overview because their behavior is governed by serviceability and deformation rather than closed-form strength [39:17], [80:05].

### Spec References
Cited by the speaker: AISC Design Guide 33 (the subject guide) [02:08]; AISC Design Guide 1 (referenced as the model for practical content, baseplate and anchor-rod washer-plate guidance) [23:01]; specification Section E3 for column strength, used for both in-plane and out-of-plane axial design of the equivalent straight column [56:57], [60:32]; specification Chapter H for combined axial and flexural interaction [70:16]; specification Chapter F, with the Cb modification factor recast as Cb,i, and the equivalent-straight elastic LTB term Mes drawn from the user note to the 2016 specification Chapter F [64:55], [68:08]; and the AISC Code of Standard Practice, with the speaker noting the 2016 edition explicitly added straightness tolerances for curved members equal to the straight-member tolerance [41:54]. A 2001 British publication from the Steel Construction Institute is credited as a source but is not an AISC standard [36:14], [75:23].

### Technical Details
For axial in-plane strength the developed (arc) length Ld replaces the straight column length, an effective length factor Ki from a Design Guide table replaces K (for example parabolic pinned arches use Ki = 0.5 for all rise-to-span ratios, treating the member as braced at midspan), and the maximum load anywhere along Ld is run through Section E3 [53:52], [55:56], [56:57]. Snap-through buckling must be screened out first: if H/Ls is greater than 0.2 it is not a concern, otherwise a table of Ls/r ratios versus rise-to-span and end fixity must be satisfied, where the slenderness must EXCEED the tabulated value (for H/Ls = 0.15 pinned, Ls/r greater than 36) because snap-through is governed by axial stiffness while the preferred buckling mode is governed by slenderness [49:15], [51:19], [52:19]. Out-of-plane axial design uses developed length between braces Ldb, a Ko effective length factor derived from setting the flexural-torsional buckling equal to flexural buckling, with a Co coefficient carrying the St. Venant torsion, warping constant, and out-of-plane moment of inertia [60:02], [61:40]. Flexural strength uses Cb,i in place of Cb and distinguishes opening moments (compression in the outer flange, use the negative root, lower capacity than a straight beam) from closing moments (compression in the inner flange, use the positive root, may conservatively be taken as a straight beam) [64:24], [66:34]. A flange-bending check applies only at small radius and high flange width-to-thickness (example: 15 ft radius on a thin W21 flange) and a web-buckling check applies only at very tight radius (example: 5 ft radius, 20 in deep, 3/8 in web) [19:48], [20:18].

### Fabrication Notes
Chapter 2 of the guide covers three primary bending processes: pyramid roll bending (cold, the most common, three rolls in a pyramid with a supplementary roll to limit tension-flange distortion, multiple passes with roll adjustment between each), incremental step bending (cold, cantilever bending applied as the member is fed through), and induction bending (the only hot method, a heated band cooled immediately while the member pivots around a radius arm) [31:33], [33:07], [35:44]. Fabricators typically do not bend to these radii in-house; their own equipment is generally limited to camber bending, so they sub the work to specialized bender-roller companies whose equipment, personnel, and shop layout differ by shop [27:42], [38:14]. Detailers must add geometry the bender needs, including the rotation or twist dimension on an off-axis curve and a section view showing the rotation angle, before the member can be bent [10:59], [28:13]. Wall thickness can be increased on an HSS to limit distortion when an architecturally exposed (AESS) finish is wanted, and the guide gives arc-length (developed-length) equations for parabolic and elliptical curves so quantities can be computed [26:09], [25:38].

### Erection Notes
The webinar is a design and detailing session and gives little field erection content. The closest field-relevant items are support spreading at arch springing points, which causes large apex deflection and can trigger snap-through, addressed by a tension tie or a vertical truss to reduce spreading [43:30], [45:05]. Out-of-plane bracing of arches is normal and each braced segment must be checked, which implies the erected bracing scheme drives the design segments [59:32], [60:02]. No crane, rigging, or sequencing guidance is given.

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The speaker frames failure modes rather than shop rejections. Snap-through (oil-canning) collapse is the catastrophic case, sensitive to second-order effects and support spreading, and is screened by the H/Ls and slenderness rules [44:33], [49:15]. Excessive deformation and torsional rotation govern horizontally curved members, which often cannot reach their full plastic strength because of deformation, and there are no rotation limits in the building codes, so the engineer must set one (the British guide's 2 degrees is widely borrowed but must not be applied where it does not fit) [74:53], [80:35], [82:09]. Bending defects such as fracture at very tight radius, flange or web distortion, and section instability during rolling are noted as real but generally controllable by the bender roller [27:42], [34:10]. Material-property and brittle-fracture concerns from cold work only arise for tight radius combined with galvanizing and low service temperature; for normal building radii the cold-work effect actually reduces residual stresses and ductility loss is less than from typical punching or torch cutting of a straight member [29:47], [88:02], [89:33].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Curved work is a sub-out cost item: the fabricator routes bending to a specialized bender-roller company, so a curved-member scope should carry that vendor cost and lead time rather than assuming in-house bending [27:42], [38:14]. Calling the bender roller early in design, before sizing is locked, avoids redesign loops and lets them recommend a thicker HSS wall to control distortion for an exposed finish, which is a member-cost and quantity input [26:09]. Developed (arc) length, not span, is the controlling length for both quantity takeoff and design, so weights and lengths must be computed on the curve [25:06], [54:25]. Horizontally curved members are usually serviceability-controlled, meaning member size is set by deflection and rotation limits the engineer chooses, not by strength, which can push sizes up beyond what a strength check alone would suggest [80:05], [83:41].

### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, any curved member must be quantified on developed (arc) length, not chord span, and aisc_validator.py weights then apply per unit length; flag curved scope as a bender-roller sub-out line with separate cost and lead time. For Mario's shop, in-house bending is camber only; curved members go to a specialty bender, and detailing must carry the twist or rotation dimension and a section view so the bend is correct the first time, which is Tekla detailing work to set up before release. For the in-house PE stamp, the design path is the equivalent-straight-member method using Section E3, Chapter F with Cb,i, and Chapter H, with a snap-through screen (H/Ls greater than 0.2 or the Ls/r table) run first, and a documented rotation limit on any horizontally curved member since the codes set none. Connections on horizontally curved members must restrain torsion by attaching to both flanges of the curved member, with a double bolt row sized for the induced flexure, which is a field-bolting and detailing detail for Mario and Tekla. No anchor-rod, joist, or ACP-controls content appears here. Doctrine flags: NONE. The content aligns with verify-don't-generate (weights from the validator, design from cited sections) and is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language.

## SpeedCore:  Rainier Square -- A Project Case Study
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IZVNHlWixhg | Duration: 1:00:18 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
The webinar is a case study of the SpeedCore composite plate shear wall, concrete-filled (CPSW-CF) system used on the Rainier Square tower in Seattle, an 850-foot, ~58-story office and residential building, presented by Brian Morgan of Magnusson Klemencic Associates [00:33][06:50]. SpeedCore replaces a traditional reinforced concrete core with prefabricated steel sandwich panels, two outer steel face plates tied together with cross ties, that are erected in sequence with the steel floor framing and then filled with self-consolidating concrete as a trailing operation several levels below the active erection deck [02:37][14:29][15:01]. The face plates serve as the formwork, eliminating rebar and forming, and the whole tower erects under one trade tolerance instead of separate concrete (ACI) and steel (AISC) standards of practice [04:13][04:44]. The driving benefit was schedule: the core dropped off the critical path, since a reinforced concrete core takes roughly twice as long per floor as the trailing steel framing [10:55][11:27].
### Spec References
The speaker cited AISC 341-2016 as the standard housing the CPSW-CF system [02:37], ASCE 7-16 for the seismic R factor classification as a steel-and-composite plate shear wall [03:10], and ASCE 7-22 Chapter 14 as the target for incorporating new provisions [46:19][46:49]. He referenced the AISC 341 requirement that cross-tie connections develop the yield strength of the bar [18:08], AISC 341 recommendations on effective stiffness of a composite section [48:51], AISC 360 effective stiffness equations for filled composite members for elastic flexural stiffness [45:47], FEMA P695 confirming an R of 8 for the coupled system [46:19], and ASTM A572 grade 50/55 plate (stated as A592 in the auto-caption, almost certainly A572) specified at 55 ksi yield with a 5 ksi tolerance each way [17:07]. Proposed updates to AISC 341 Section H7 plus a new section for coupled CPSW were noted as in the balloting pipeline [46:19].
### Technical Details
Wall face plates were nominally half-inch steel on each face, comprising 75 to 80 percent of the core, increasing to three-quarter inch at high-demand zones and up to two inch where BRB outrigger gussets enter [16:36]. Wall thicknesses ran 21 to 45 inches (two to four feet), thickest at the base and tapering up [16:36]. Cross ties were 1-inch-diameter, grade 55 rod, spaced 12 inches on center both ways on all faces; at Rainier Square this gave about 240,000 cross ties and 480,000 welds [17:07][18:38][19:09]. Concrete infill was a 10 ksi self-consolidating mix requiring no vibration [17:07][30:55]. Coupling beams (the H or dog-bone panels at door openings) were built-up concrete-filled box tubes with cross ties both ways [21:11]. The lateral system was a CPSW-CF core plus buckling-restrained-brace outrigger and belt trusses at the two-thirds height; no dual moment-frame backup, no SMF or IMF, designed by performance-based seismic design [08:21][49:53][50:23]. Wind controlled overturning by a factor of 3 to 4 over seismic, so walls could not be thinned [49:21].
### Fabrication Notes
Panels were fully prefabricated in the shop with cross ties, deck ledger angles, shear tabs for incoming beams, and MEP penetrations all pre-installed, so a panel could be lifted and have steel hung off it immediately [14:29][33:30]. The fabricator was free to choose the cross-tie connection so long as it developed the bar yield; Rainier Square used unthreaded grade 55 rods passed about three-quarters of an inch through the plate and fillet welded each side [17:38][18:38]. Plate width drove sourcing: domestic mills roll to about 10 feet, so below-grade plate (10-foot floor heights) was domestic, but the 13-foot-9 typical floors required 14-foot-wide plate ordered from Korean mills to avoid a shop splice [34:31][35:02]. Plate was cut on a burn table to specification and moved down an assembly line; the fabricator voluntarily added small angle-iron lattice bracing so panels would not rack during handling [32:27]. Mock-ups were built first: a plywood replica of the worst congestion to prove the concrete fill technique and mix, and a steel corner-section mock-up to shake out run-off tabs, backer bars, and fit-up issues before approving shop drawings [29:22][31:26].
### Erection Notes
The first core lift was set on stanchions that delivered full core capacity into the mat foundation; rebar and concrete for the mat were then built around it [36:34]. Corner box columns were erected first, plumbed and welded, then face panels flew in between and were field spliced [19:39][37:36]. Concrete was a fully trailing operation roughly four to six (and up to four to eight) levels below the active erection deck, pumped at 100 to 120 cubic yards per hour through blind access ports using telltale and vent holes for visual confirmation [15:01][26:20][30:25][38:38]. As many as four stories could be unconcreted at once, with the young, unconcreted core carrying the weight of erected floors; the cross ties provided stability during erection, shipping, and the unconcreted condition, then acted as form ties against hydrostatic pressure and finally as composite shear connectors [25:48][26:50]. Concrete placed floor by floor meant only about a 14-foot hydrostatic head [56:29]. Steel went vertical October 15, 2018 and topped out exactly 10 months later on August 15 [37:05][39:39].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The field weld was a full-depth PJP with a reinforcing fillet, chosen over a CJP specifically because there is no way to reach the inside of the wall to repair a CJP, so inspection and repair access drove the joint selection [20:40]. The weld was prequalified by testing to confirm it was a capacity joint that yields the plate outside the weld rather than failing the weld [20:10]. Automated field welding was tried in mock-up but rejected because it could not adjust to the variable root gap; the quarter-inch designed root gap could vary from zero to a quarter inch across a 35-to-40-foot panel due to plumb tolerance, so all 36 miles of field weld were hand welded [54:28][55:29]. Concrete voids were the main quality-control fear, addressed with interior-plate flow holes ("Swiss cheese"), coupling-beam vent holes, and telltale holes to confirm fill [50:53][51:23]. No observed panel distortion or out-of-plumb occurred at the 12-inch cross-tie spacing; distortion risk rises if spacing widens toward 18 inches [56:59][57:32].
### Bid / Cost Implications
Schedule was the entire business case. The paper estimate was 21 months for a concrete core versus 12 for SpeedCore; the realized result was a core topping out in 10 months and concrete finished at 11, a roughly 10-month schedule savings against the contractor's estimated 91 weeks versus 50 weeks for the two approaches [22:45][24:17][24:47]. Faster delivery cut construction cost, reduced owner financing cost, and brought rental income sooner [04:44][05:14]. The 480,000 welds make weld-cycle time the dominant labor variable: every minute saved per weld multiplies across the count, which is why cross-tie spacing and weld automation were targets even though automation failed here [19:09]. Sourcing 14-foot Korean plate to avoid shop splices, and the conservative full cross-tie population, were deliberate cost-versus-risk choices made because this was a world-first in high seismic at great height under difficult peer review [27:51][35:02][58:21].
### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, this system is a count-and-weld-quantity problem more than a tonnage problem: the controlling cost drivers are face-plate area by thickness band, the cross-tie count (spacing times wall area), the resulting weld length and weld count, and field-weld miles, all of which aisc_validator.py member weights do not capture, so a SpeedCore-style scope needs a supplemental weld-and-tie line item with confidence tagging. Mario's shop and welding lead role maps directly to the PJP-with-reinforcing-fillet joint, the prequalified capacity-weld concept, and the hand-welding-over-automation finding, all backed by AWS qualification even though the speaker cited the joint by AISC capacity logic rather than a specific AWS D1.1 clause. Paul's safety scope is engaged by the unconcreted-core stability window (up to four unconcreted stories hanging load) and blind-pour pumping at height. Tekla detailing is explicitly the controlling model: the speaker said the engineer's BIM was rudimentary and the contractor/fabricator detailing model (described as likely Tekla) carried splice locations, pick weights, and shipping limits. In-house PE stamp work would mirror the transformed-section elastic plus fiber-hinge nonlinear modeling and the develop-the-bar-yield cross-tie rule. Anchor-rod relevance is the stanchion-to-mat detail delivering full core capacity into the foundation. No conflict with Your Company doctrine: this is conventional structural steel, no PEMB language, and the schedule-savings story reinforces verify-don't-generate since the realized numbers differed materially from the paper estimate. DOCTRINE FLAGS: NONE.

## To 3 or Not To 3
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hJVsZLSvfTA | Duration: 1:23:00 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
The session, presented by Pat Fortney and John Hooper, examines the decision to use a high-R seismic system (anything above the R equal 3 "steel system not specifically detailed for seismic resistance") versus staying at R equal 3 in low and moderate seismicity. The central message is that choosing a high R factor to cut base shear is not free: once you claim a high R you must satisfy every strength and detailing requirement that comes with it, in both AISC 341 and ASCE 7 [03:08]. Fortney covers what the system seismic factors (R, over-strength Omega0, deflection amplification Cd, and his own ductility reduction factor Rd) physically mean and which systems are permitted by seismic design category and height [03:41]. Hooper then runs two real cost-benefit case studies (Oklahoma City and the Javits Center) showing when the R equal 6 trade actually saves money [46:08].

### Spec References
ASCE 7-16 Table 12.2-1 (system factors, height limits by SDC) [10:58][20:41]; ASCE 7 Chapter 15 (non-building structures with R equal 3) [23:14]; ASCE 7 rule that two systems in the same direction use the lesser R [54:52]; AISC 341 (seismic provisions, F2 for buckling-restrained braces, the 2010 and 2016 editions referenced for shear-stud exceptions and gusset weld changes) [02:36][27:23][31:01]; AISC 358 (prequalified connections for IMF and SMF, RBS, bolted flange plate, Welded Unreinforced Flange-Welded, with a Connection Prequalification Review committee) [08:18][37:42][42:55]; AISC 360 (the basis for R equal 3 design) [23:45]; AWS D1.1 (general welds), AWS D1.8 (seismic supplemental welder certification and demand-critical weld requirements) [07:16][39:48]; ACI 318 (special concrete shear wall detailing, boundary elements) [55:24].

### Technical Details
Systems compared by R, Omega0, Cd, and base-shear reduction versus R equal 3: ordinary concentric braced frame R 3.25 (about 7.7 percent reduction) [15:01]; special concentric braced frame (SCBF) R 6 (50 percent reduction, Cd 5) [16:01][27:53]; eccentrically braced frame (EBF) R 8, Omega0 2 (about 62.5 percent reduction, link yields in shear or flexure) [16:32][24:48]; buckling-restrained braced frame (BRBF) R 8, proprietary brace to AISC 341 F2, Rd of 4 [35:08][72:00]; ordinary moment frame R 3.5 (14 percent reduction); intermediate moment frame R 4.5 (33 percent reduction); special moment frame (SMF) R 8 (62.5 percent reduction) requiring strong-column weak-beam [17:35][36:09]. Fortney stressed that "ordinary" carries a seismic meaning (R above 3) and must not be used loosely on design criteria [17:35]. For SCBF the net area at a slotted HSS-over-gusset connection must be at least the gross area of the brace, so reinforcement is usually needed at the transition [32:32]. Connections are sized for the expected tension strength of the brace under both expected-buckling and post-buckling compression load cases [31:31].

### Fabrication Notes
Protected zones must be marked on the shop and erection drawings by the fabricator; for an EBF the entire link is protected, for an SCBF the center quarter of the brace plus the full gusset and any part of the connection touching the column or frame are protected [26:51][29:28]. Only "approved work" is allowed in a protected zone: welding HSS to the gusset and an erection hole in the brace end are approved, but welding a stray clip angle to the gusset face for lifting is not [29:28]. Gusset-to-beam (and west-coast gusset-to-column) welds are demand-critical and as of AISC 341-2016 must develop the contact shear strength of the gusset, which typically forces large CJP welds [31:01]. Demand-critical welds raise filler-metal and consumable cost and require additional testing [39:16]. Continuity-plate thickness rules relaxed in 2016 (one-sided can be 50 percent of beam flange, two-sided 75 percent), and thinner plates make the CJP to the column flange easier to pass ultrasonic test [41:53].

### Erection Notes
For SMF bottom-flange-to-column welds there is restricted access: the first weld pass must be completed before the second, made in halves on each side of the web and tied together, which AWS D1.8 covers with a supplemental welder certification that the erector must hold [06:46]. Stability bracing is required at the expected plastic-hinge location in an SMF beam plus supplemental points so the beam can reach its plastic moment, adding infill-beam connections [40:52]. The presenters warn to confirm the erector and fabricator have genuine seismic experience before selecting a high-R system in a low-seismic region, since local crews in low-seismic areas often have not built, fabricated, or erected seismic systems [05:15][46:08]. Fire-watch-heavy jurisdictions like Manhattan push the choice toward shop welding over field welding to avoid escalated field-welding fire-watch cost [07:47].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The recurring real-world error: an engineer of record uses a high R to cut base shear but then detailes and fabricates the frame as if it were not seismic, which is incorrect [02:36]. AISC 358 non-proprietary prequalified connections are prequalified only for the beam framing to the column strong-axis flange, not to the column web (weak axis); the presenters have seen weak-axis framing wrongly assumed prequalified on jobs [38:46]. Loose use of the word "ordinary" on design criteria is flagged as a trap [17:35]. ASCE 7 footnotes and exceptions throughout (not only Table 12.2-1) are described as routinely missed and important for both design and the PE/SE exam [21:43][46:40]. A slide typo claiming 62.5 percent reduction for SCBF was corrected to 50 percent live [27:53].

### Bid / Cost Implications
The connection-force factor is the key estimating lever: an SCBF connection is sized on brace tension while the brace member is sized on compression, so the connection demand runs roughly 1.5 to 2.5 times the R equal 3 demand, making every plate bigger [57:27][59:00]. A BRBF cuts that factor to about 1.25 to 1.5 because its tension and compression capacities are closer, a cheaper connection if the whole system is R 8 [59:32][78:28]. The cost-benefit weighs steel-connection premium against savings in base shear, foundations (deep drilled shafts and caissons scale directly with base shear and overturning), and diaphragms (collectors amplified by Omega0 in SDC C). Oklahoma City: going R equal 6 over R equal 3 saved an estimated 0.5 to 0.75 million dollars all-in [63:41]; Javits: 1 to 1.5 million dollars [76:56]. These quick studies were done in roughly one to six weeks of front-end analysis, and having the fabricator and erector on a design-build team to confirm the connection premium made the decision much easier [73:22].

### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff and estimating, the load-bearing lesson is the connection-force multiplier: a high-R braced frame is not a tonnage line item, it is a connection-fabrication premium of 1.5 to 2.5 times that must be priced separately from member weight, with member weights still validated through aisc_validator.py and never inferred from R factor. Mario's shop work and welding lead role map directly to demand-critical CJP gusset welds (AWS D1.8, extra consumables and testing) and protected-zone marking on shop and erection drawings; the AWS D1.8 supplemental welder certification for restricted-access SMF bottom-flange welds is a real crew-qualification gate Mario and any field crew must clear before bidding seismic moment work. Paul's safety scope intersects the fire-watch and field-welding trade discussed for dense urban sites. Tekla detailing must carry the protected zones and approved-work limits, and the in-house PE stamp can either delegate or self-perform the seismic connection design (Hooper's team self-detailed Oklahoma City to keep control on a region new to the system). Anchor rods, joists, and ACP controls are not directly addressed here. Doctrine conflict: NONE; this reinforces verify-don't-generate (never trust an R factor to set tonnage or connection size, run the takeoff and the validator).

## Pedestrian Bridges: Unique Analysis and Design
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ji--4gyfxag | Duration: 1:01:22 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This webinar (session B2) presents two long-span steel pedestrian bridges and centers on pedestrian-induced vibration as the controlling design problem rather than strength. The Fanny Appleton Bridge in Boston is a jointless 550 ft elevated steel structure with a 220 ft divergent pipe arch and a Vierendeel-truss main span, where the team had to push the frequency and acceleration response into a comfortable range [02:01][04:35][12:50]. The 41st Street Pedestrian Bridge in Chicago is a pair of 240 ft inclined steel pipe arches with an S-curved deck hung on cables, where torsion from single-side support and low natural frequency drove the design [38:13][43:18][45:25]. The recurring lesson is that for slender pedestrian spans the natural frequency falls near human walking pace, so designers tune stiffness, mass, and damping and then physically test the finished bridge to confirm acceleration [12:50][18:52].

### Spec References
Referenced standards, stated aloud: AASHTO LRFD pedestrian guide vibration limits of 1.3 Hz horizontal and 3 Hz vertical, with an alternate mass/weight criterion [13:20]; SETRA, the French pedestrian-bridge time-history method, noted as referenced by AASHTO [13:50]; British Standard 5400 used for a code comparison [28:37]; Eurocode used for arch unsupported-length and buckling parameters [50:38][51:08]; AISC cited for the torsion design formula on the deck rib [52:09]; CIDECT cited for tubular connection design [53:42]; ASTM A586 structural strand for the 2 in diameter hangers [52:39]. No AISC 360 chapter, AISC 341 seismic section, AWS D1.1 clause, RCSC provision, or AISC Design Guide number was stated; this is an AASHTO bridge webinar, not a building-code talk.

### Technical Details
Fanny Appleton uses a divergent pipe arch with HSS spandrel columns forming a Vierendeel truss, paired continuous box (tub) girders running end to end, floor beams, and a cantilever bracket carrying a continuously curved steel fascia plate [04:35][05:05]. The Y-piers are built-up sections at the base transitioning to HSS arms, joined at the Y with a steel casting fabricated by CastConnex and co-designed by the engineer [05:36][06:08]. To fix vibration, the team changed the deck from 4,000 psi normal-weight to 5,000 psi lightweight foam-filled stay-in-place forms, increased spandrel-column offset from 7 to 15 degrees from plumb, stiffened selected pier foundations from a two-pile to a three-pile battered configuration, and added internal stiffeners through the column base plates [16:21][17:22]. The Chicago bridge models all steel as frame elements and hangers as cable elements in CSI Bridge, with the inclined hangers producing very large torsion and lateral force in the deck (lateral about 70 percent of vertical at the end transverse girder), addressed with hold-down devices, a special high-lateral bearing, and a permanent jacking device for redundancy and maintenance [45:25][52:09][53:42][54:13].

### Fabrication Notes
The continuously curving fascia plate on Fanny Appleton required tolerances comparable to architecturally exposed structural steel, and those tolerances propagated back into the box-girder fabrication because the girders carry the fascia through cantilever brackets and had to match for fit-up [07:40]. Bolted splices on the tub girders were kept unobtrusive by putting splice plates internal to the tub and nuts on the inside, and splice locations were positioned to be least visible [07:08]. Short spandrel columns were shop-welded to the arch sections, but longer spandrel columns could not be shop-welded due to shipping limits, so alignment studs were added to help field setting of the skewed, non-square geometry [10:46][11:17]. Arch sections shipped in two pieces and were spliced on site; the stair fascia was upsized after the original detail proved poor for fabrication [10:15][17:52]. On the Chicago tubular sections it was difficult to place internal stiffeners inside the pipes and boxes, so the hanger plate itself acts as the stiffener, and internal stiffening was used only at the high-concentrated-force deck connection [50:08][55:43].

### Erection Notes
Fanny Appleton main deck framing was fabricated in three sections and the center section was lifted onto the shorter spandrel columns atop the arch [11:48]. Erection tabs on the spandrel columns held pieces in place and were then field welded, field metallized, and field painted, and cap plates were field-welded to the tub girders [11:48][12:20]. The defining erection problem on the Chicago bridge was railroad access: six active tracks carrying about 270 trains a day, with only a 1 to 3 a.m. work window, so the team designed a temporary bridge threaded into roughly 5.5 ft of clear space between the proposed deck and the overhead catenary lines, giving the contractor 6 to 9 months of nearly uninterrupted work [34:37][39:14][40:16]. Two temporary-support options (spanning all six tracks or using a mid shoring tower within 25 ft of the clear zone) were left on the plans because the railroad would not commit, and the contractor chose the no-middle-support scheme [40:46]. The contractor built the Lake Shore Drive span first and the railroad span second to work out problems before the high-risk railroad area [58:52].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
No bolt rejections, weld-inspection failures, or NDE findings are named; this is a design-and-analysis webinar, not an inspection talk. The closest analog to a defect is the original architect-handed 45-degree arch geometry, which produced an incorrect and uncomfortable natural frequency and would have required an over-robust pipe to carry the curving deck, forcing a redesign to a 30-degree arch with added basket-handle kickers and hangers [36:10][37:11]. On Fanny Appleton the only condition that failed the maximum-comfort acceleration target was deliberate vandalism with people jumping on the structure, not normal pedestrian loading [23:27].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Both projects were design-build with fixed budgets, which directly shaped technical choices: Fanny Appleton carried a budget line for tuned mass dampers and then spent that money on physical structural improvements instead, because the owner preferred to avoid recurring TMD maintenance and retuning every couple of years [27:36][28:07]. The same fixed design-build budget is why no long-term vibration monitoring was funded after opening [26:33]. The Chicago temporary bridge was a high-ticket item that the team said paid its premium back many times over by avoiding years of railroad flagging cost and coordination [39:45]. A repeated estimating point is that engineering a detailed, constructible, biddable plan set, vetted by talking to multiple fabricators and suppliers on a level platform, let the contractor follow the planned erection sequence almost exactly and cut field guesswork and RFIs [56:51][57:21].

### Your Company Application
This is bridge and AASHTO work, outside Your Company's conventional building-steel lane, so treat it as method transfer rather than a directly biddable scope. The strongest carryover for Ivan's takeoff and estimating is that tight, continuously-curved geometry forces AESS-grade tolerances that propagate across connected members and must be priced as added shop hours, not assumed at standard tolerance [07:40]. For Mario's shop and welding crew the relevant pattern is shop-weld what fits the truck and shift the rest to field welds with alignment aids: short members shop-welded, long skewed members set in the field on alignment studs and erection tabs, then field welded and field finished [10:46][11:48]. For Tekla detailing, the value is modeling skewed, non-perpendicular geometry up front and detailing internal access for stiffeners and bolted splices, including hidden-nut splices for appearance-sensitive surfaces [07:08][50:08]. Paul's safety scope maps to the active-rail and overhead-power constraint: a narrow work window and tight clearance to live catenary lines argue for temporary structures and pre-planned, contractor-followed erection sequencing rather than field improvisation [39:14][57:21]. Anchor-rod, joist, and field-bolting specifics and ACP project controls are not addressed by this video. Doctrine conflict: NONE. The talk uses no PEMB language, names no prohibited suppliers (CastConnex and CIDECT are named generically by the speakers), and nothing here touches BID_RATES or AISC weight data.

## Designing for Membrane Architecture
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Br7_uNmmahI | Duration: 1:02:05 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This session, presented by Marko Kino, PE, covers the analysis, design, and fabrication of tensile membrane and pneumatic structures, not conventional building steel. The core idea is that a membrane structure must have three traits: Gaussian (double) curvature, elastic material that only reaches final shape after stretching, and tension-only loading where any compression, shear, or bending is treated as a failure [06:39][07:41][08:11]. The design workflow is a cyclical loop of form finding, loading, analysis, patterning, and detailing, where any downstream change in material or shape forces a return to an earlier step [08:42][09:46][32:29]. The two basic geometries taught are the cone (radial plus circumferential curvature) and the sail (a saddle that curves in two directions between high and low points) [04:38][06:39].
### Spec References
General principles, no AISC section cited. The speaker referenced ASTM-grade steel only by analogy, stating membrane materials are not ASTM materials and are driven by individual manufacturer catalogs rather than a unified code [23:09][53:21]. The only standards-adjacent items named were a European Union design guide for membrane structures that is not yet part of the Eurocode [23:41], "A36" 36 ksi steel cited as a contrast to non-codified membranes [23:09], and a National Institute of Standards and Technology report on the Dallas Cowboys practice facility fabric-roof collapse [25:47][26:17]. No AISC 360, AISC 341, AWS D1.1, RCSC, or Design Guide numbers were stated.
### Technical Details
Form finding uses software to find a minimal surface, the shape of least area between fixed boundary conditions, analogous to a soap film where stresses are equal in all directions [13:56][14:28]. The free tool "Form Finder" was named as an example [15:32]. Pre-stress magnitude controls final curvature: relaxing radial and circumferential stresses gives a subtle shape, increasing them gives a dramatic one [18:28][18:59]. Materials such as PTFE behave orthotropically (a woven cloth bonded between plastic layers), so an isotropic design assumption can produce wrinkles or failure, forcing a second analysis that decomposes stresses into orthogonal weave directions [30:57][31:29][31:59]. Manufacturers supply two values, a modulus of elasticity and an "apparent modulus of elasticity" that accounts for weave slack taken up before the material goes taut [34:35][35:06]. Theory of large deformations applies because deflections of six to twelve inches are normal, unlike steel where original and deformed geometry are assumed close [51:39][52:19].
### Fabrication Notes
Patterning converts a 3D curved surface into 2D strips, typically one meter (about three feet) wide because that is the standard roll width [27:50][30:27][55:56]. Cutting more material out of the gaps between strips produces more curvature but requires higher installation force [29:25][29:56]. Strips are joined by heat or infrared welding with a typical overlap of four to six inches sized to the force through the seam; epoxy and mechanical methods were tried but epoxies dissolved the membrane base material [36:08][38:11][38:41]. ETFE in particular must be welded in a dust-free sterile shop environment because it is clear, then folded and crated for shipment [48:55][49:26]. One Qatar stadium project requested a two-meter roll width to cut the number of seams and the welding labor [55:56][56:27].
### Erection Notes
The membrane is pre-stressed and tensioned into final shape in the field using cables threaded through fabricated edge pockets, interior or flying masts, or clamped steel edge plates pulled with jacks where pocket tearing is a risk [37:09][37:41][39:44][40:16]. Lifting is engineered like a tilt-wall panel: a lifting analysis confirms the pick points, and if reinforcement is needed a strong exterior patch is welded on and cut away after placement, never an interior reinforcement that would alter the designed cutting-pattern behavior [49:26][50:07][50:39]. Rain during installation is a major hazard because an untensioned membrane ponds water progressively, deforming further and accumulating more until it can fail before pumps clear it [20:00][20:30][21:01]. Pneumatic ETFE cushions hold shape by continuous internal air pressure with per-cushion pressure sensors and compressors that top up pressure as temperature and volume change [44:16][44:48].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The dominant named failure is wrongly assuming the membrane braces the supporting steel. The Dallas Cowboys practice facility fabric roof was analyzed assuming the fabric braced the compression chords of light trusses on a light portal frame; with that assumed bracing everything passed, but removing it left members overstressed by 500 percent, and the collapse killed two people [25:13][26:17][26:48]. The fabricator had three or four similar failures and posted a website letter conceding its structures were designed incorrectly without the resources to fix them all [26:48][27:20]. Other errors named are isotropic assumptions on orthotropic woven material causing wrinkles or tearing [31:29], ponding during erection [20:30], and bird strikes or acid rain puncturing or degrading ETFE panels [57:00][57:30].
### Bid / Cost Implications
The speaker can estimate support-structure weight early for a minimal-surface shape, but a more dramatic architect-driven shape makes membrane stresses and therefore the steel support weight shoot up quickly [59:17][59:48]. Cost is also driven by material shelf life chosen up front, ranging from two-year temporary fabrics to materials rated 75 to 80 years that cost much more [52:19][58:37]. Specifying wider rolls trades higher material cost against far less welding labor and fewer seams [56:27]. Wind-tunnel testing is used only when a project is large enough to merit it, otherwise the engineer extrapolates conservatively from existing codes [19:30][20:00].
### Your Company Application
This is membrane and tensile-fabric engineering, which sits outside Your Company's conventional structural-steel scope, so direct fabrication transfer is limited. The transferable lesson for Ivan's takeoff and Mario's shop is the bracing-assumption discipline: the Cowboys collapse is a concrete case of why deck or any sheathing should only be credited as bracing when the connection is real and welded, which reinforces our verify-do-not-generate posture and the rule that validated tonnage comes from a measured member takeoff, not from an unverified bracing or area assumption. For Tekla detailing and the in-house PE stamp, the relevant takeaway is that any tension membrane element on a future ACP-type canopy would need a manufacturer-driven material catalog and a separate specialty engineer, since these materials are not ASTM or AISC codified. No supplier names appear in this entry. Doctrine flag: NONE, with the caveat that membrane work would be a specialty subcontract, not in-house steel scope, and must not adopt PEMB language.
