## Fatigue and Fracture Design
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AoF-PwE4DQo | Duration: 1:29:11 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is AASHTO bridge session L4, presented by Dr. Robert Connor of Purdue, covering the limit state of fatigue and fracture for highway steel bridges [00:02]. The central distinction is that fatigue is a slow, stable, cyclic-load process that progressively cracks the steel by loss of section while the material strength itself never changes [03:39], whereas brittle fracture is a sudden catastrophic failure that runs through material faster than the speed of sound with no plastic-deformation warning [22:13]. Fatigue life is governed by stress range, number of cycles, and the detail category, and is cubed-sensitive to stress range: doubling the stress range cuts life by a factor of eight [09:20]. The design curve uses a safe-life basis of mean minus two standard deviations, a 2.5 percent probability of cracking [13:30].
### Spec References
The standard cited throughout is AASHTO LRFD bridge design, the eighth edition discussed as forthcoming [48:59]. Named provisions: the detail-category fatigue tables titled "detail categories for load-induced fatigue" [57:48]; fatigue load combinations Fatigue I (infinite life) and Fatigue II (finite life) [54:40]; the load factor change from 0.75 to 0.8 on HS-20 for the fatigue truck and from 1.5 to 1.75 (Fatigue I shown as 2x effective range becoming about 2.2) [74:43]; fatigue-adjusted single-lane load distribution factors [55:46]; the constant-amplitude fatigue limit (CAFL) [07:47]; and the provision allowing fatigue to be ignored where compression dead-load stress exceeds the fatigue-limit-state stress range [82:25]. Fracture-critical inspection at 24-month arm's-length intervals is set by the CFR Code of Federal Regulations, with special AASHTO/AWS fabrication requirements [67:33]. An NCHRP report from about 1990 underlies the fatigue truck [45:21]. No AISC 360 chapter, AISC 341 section, or numbered Design Guide was cited; this is a bridge (AASHTO) talk, not a building-code talk.
### Technical Details
Detail categories run A through E-prime: category A is base metal as it comes from the mill with a 24 ksi fatigue limit, while E-prime is the worst at about 2.6 ksi, nearly an order of magnitude lower [11:22]. The categorization, developed by John Fisher at Lehigh, bundles three effects that resist numerical analysis: weld discontinuities, weld-toe stress concentrations, and residual stresses [16:34]. Finite-life equation is N = A divided by stress range cubed, where A is the detail constant from the AASHTO table [08:50]. Stress flows like water, so concentrations occur at attachment terminations, and a smooth radius can upgrade a detail from E-prime to category B while a blunt square end stays poor [35:34]. Residual tensile stresses at a weld toe approach yield (taken as 50 ksi), which shifts the real mean stress so the full stress range, including the nominal compression portion, drives crack growth [40:09]. Fracture toughness is measured directly by compact-tension or single-edge-bend tests, or indirectly by the Charpy V-notch impact test (10mm by 10mm by 50mm specimen) and inferred across a temperature transition curve; zone 3 bridge service is minus 60 degrees [27:50].
### Fabrication Notes
The talk shows residual stress directly in the shop: a CJP complete-joint-penetration weld joining a flange to a girder web requires the fabricator to first pre-bend the plate with V-bevels, then the cooling weld metal pulls the plate flat, locking in stresses near yield strength; this is correct fabrication, not a defect [37:36]. Welds are assumed fabricated to normal quality with members in good condition for the categories to apply; severe corrosion, impact damage, or any existing crack voids the category and forces a fracture-mechanics analysis instead [59:20]. Weld-toe cracking is the dominant fatigue mode when welds are left in place and not ground; grinding a weld toe smooth, as on a CJP butt weld, improves the category but the longitudinal portion is still always checked [62:26]. Fracture is controlled through material selection, welding consumables, and detailing rather than any fracture calculation [31:24].
### Erection Notes
This webinar is bridge design and inspection focused and does not cover field erection sequencing, crane or rigging, or bracing. The closest field content is in-service inspection: fracture-susceptible details cannot be made safe by inspection because the failure is sudden, so the risk must be designed out ahead of time [23:14]. Fracture-critical members are subject to hands-on inspection every 24 months [67:33].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The recurring failure named is weld-toe cracking at attachment and cover-plate terminations, perpendicular to the primary stress range, growing into the base metal where the stress concentration peaks [56:46]. Abrupt or square cover-plate and attachment terminations are flagged as E-prime poor details to avoid [64:28]. Two design misuses are corrected: you cannot treat an already-cracked member as merely a worse category (the categories assume no pre-existing crack) [59:50], and you cannot use the fatigue truck (0.8 HS-20) for an infinite-life check because many real trucks exceed it, which would falsely predict infinite life; Fatigue I with HS-20 at 1.75 is required for that [50:36]. Quiz answers clarify that tensile strength and yield strength do not influence fabricated-bridge fatigue life because welding, cutting, and drilling erase any strength benefit [76:50].
### Bid / Cost Implications
Designing for infinite life is described as economical: because stress is linear, lowering stress by 10 to 15 percent often just means a slightly deeper girder or a more fatigue-resistant detail rather than a large steel increase [54:10]. The speaker recommends infinite-life design as the default for permanent structures, reserving finite-life design for temporary bridges with a known short service window [79:52]. A practical cost point on inspection: the large sums spent inspecting fracture-critical members may not improve safety, and lane closures for inspection create real traffic-fatality risk, motivating a move to risk-based inspection [71:38].
### Your Company Application
The transferable principle for Tekla detailing and Ivan's takeoff is that connection geometry, not steel grade, governs fatigue and stress concentration: terminations and abrupt section changes are where cracks start, so smooth transitions and ground welds matter when a member sees cyclic load. For Mario as AWS D1.1 welding lead, the residual-stress and weld-toe discussion reinforces why CJP weld quality, grinding where specified, and toe condition are inspection-critical, and why a cooling CJP weld can distort or pre-stress a plate. For an in-house PE stamp, the doctrine note is that this is AASHTO bridge methodology: the detail categories, the fatigue truck, and the 0.8/1.75 load factors apply to highway bridges, not to AISC 360 building work, so they should not be carried into a building bid. DOCTRINE FLAG: none, but a usage caution: do not let any AASHTO fatigue category, fatigue-limit value, or load factor from this talk be cited as an AISC 360 or aisc_validator.py number; Your Company's validated weights and building-code basis are separate. Most Your Company conventional building steel is strength-governed and not fatigue-governed, so this content is a knowledge reference rather than a routine takeoff input.

## Effects of Curvature and Skew
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jmOn5TrDhQI | Duration: 1:29:39 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
This is session L3 of AISC's Introduction to Steel Bridge Design series, presented by Dominic Coletti (HDR) and Ronnie Medlock (High Steel Structures), covering how horizontal curvature and support skew change the behavior, analysis, and erection of steel plate girder bridges [00:00]. The central physics is torsion: curved girders carry torsion in nearly every case because the load center of gravity is offset from the chord line between supports, producing an eccentricity times vertical force [09:19][24:15], while straight skewed bridges develop torsion from differential deflection between girder ends that a cross frame connects at points of unequal vertical movement [18:04]. The second half, led by Medlock, is about cross frame fit: as a bridge deflects, the relationship of its parts changes, so the detailer must choose which load state the cross frames are built to fit [50:06][51:40].

### Spec References
This is an AASHTO bridge webinar, so the cited authorities are bridge-side, not the AISC 360/341/AWS/RCSC building specs. Stated references: AASHTO LRFD Bridge Design Specifications (the 8th edition is named as adding fit-up provisions from Task 355 research) [87:30]; AASHTO/NSBA Steel Bridge Collaboration guideline G13.1, Guidelines for Steel Girder Bridge Analysis [38:45][50:06]; NCHRP Report 725 (70 bridges analyzed by 1D/2D/3D, with an accuracy scorecard) [38:13]; FHWA manual on Refined Analysis [39:16]; NSBA "Skewed and Curved Steel I-Girder Bridge Fit" document, August 2014, Medlock co-author [72:11]; NCHRP Project 12-79 / Task 355 research on fit-up forces [84:53][87:30]; and the FHWA Curved Girder Workshop manual from 1976 for the line-girder-plus-factors charts [30:31]. No AISC 360 section, AISC 341 section, AWS D1.1 clause, or RCSC provision is cited in this video.

### Technical Details
I-girders are open cross sections with low St. Venant torsional stiffness, so they resist torsion mainly through warping, which equates to lateral bending of the flanges; box girders are closed sections that resist torsion through circumferential shear flow with large moment arms [05:39][07:48]. The radial flange force is quantified by statics as Q = M / (R x H), where M is vertical moment, R is radius of curvature, and H is the distance between flanges [12:25][13:25]. In curved spans the top and bottom flanges act as beams spanning between cross frames and undergo flange lateral bending that must be designed for, while cross frames pick up horizontal and vertical forces transferring load between adjacent girders [13:25][14:26]. Skew effects scale with skew magnitude and framing layout: skew under 20 degrees with parallel cross frames is generally negligible, but larger skews create a transverse "nuisance stiffness" load path through the cross frames that can be softened by selectively omitting diagonals (lean-on bracing) [16:30][22:38]. Three analysis tiers exist, 1D approximate (V-load, M/R, line-girder-plus-factors), 2D refined (grid, and plate-and-eccentric-beam), and 3D finite element; a common 2D weakness is modeling only St. Venant stiffness and ignoring warping, which misstates I-girder torsion [30:00][34:35].

### Fabrication Notes
The fabricator builds the chosen fit into the geometry of the cross frames and their connections to the girders, laying out to the camber values shown on the plans, since the shop cannot independently know how the bridge will deflect [62:54][64:26]. Three named fit conditions exist: no-load (fully cambered) fit, steel dead load fit, and total (full) dead load / final fit; the cross frames are detailed to close up in whichever girder load state is specified [65:28][66:28]. For total dead load fit the frames are fabricated to match the fully loaded geometry, so the assembled steel will not naturally close under self weight alone and the girders sit laid over before the deck goes on [62:54][57:18]. Medlock urges that the fit be communicated by naming the load condition, not by saying when the girder should be "plumb," because plumb is ambiguous [66:59].

### Erection Notes
With steel dead load fit the bare steel goes together readily because the cross frames are detailed for the self-weight geometry, and skewed girders stand plumb at erection but then lay over as the deck is cast [74:46][75:16]. With total dead load fit on a skewed bridge the crew must force the girders together, typically with a come-along (the example notes it does not take much force), accepting an initial lay-over that resolves out as dead load is applied [57:18][75:16]. AASHTO requires the engineer of record to designate the fit condition, and some owners prescribe practices by bridge type [70:07]. Curved bridges are stiffer and twist less, so they are almost always built to steel dead load fit; total dead load fit is to be avoided on curved bridges because the geometry only closes when all loads are present, which is impossible during erection and locks in additive force effects on long or sharp-radius spans [59:50][76:16][77:19]. The recommended thresholds: skewed bridges over 200 ft or with stiffness factor I_s greater than 0.3 should use steel dead load fit; curved spans over 250 ft move to no-load fit [73:44][77:19].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The video does not catalog weld or bolt rejections; its failure mode is fit and analysis error. A field example is shown where an erector had fewer cross frames than needed and the released girders laid over dramatically along their length, which was corrected by craning a worker up to add frames, after which the welds were inspected and passed [58:19]. A recurring conceptual error named is attributing skew lay-over to loose connections or oversized holes when it actually comes from girder flexibility, so leaving bolts loose or enlarging holes between frame and girder is the wrong fix [59:19]. An analysis-side failure is using a 2D package that ignores warping stiffness and so mismodels I-girder torsion on bridges with significant curvature, skew, deep girders, or long or variable-depth spans [34:35][35:35]. A construction sequencing trap is pouring part of a heavily skewed span and letting the concrete set, which locks in an intermediate deflected condition [75:46].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Analysis method choice is a direct effort and budget trade: moving from 1D to 2D to 3D raises modeling effort and the volume of output to process, and the answer to which to use is "it depends" on bridge complexity, schedule, and budget [27:55][38:13]. Selectively omitting cross frame diagonals (lean-on bracing) on a skewed bridge reduced loads in all the cross frames and produced a more economical design than repeatedly strengthening frames that then attract still more load [22:38][23:41]. Boundary-condition modeling carries real cost sensitivity: changing end bearings from fixed to guided on a 2-span 225 ft curved bridge shifted composite live load deflections by as much as 31 percent and composite moments and dead load deflections by about 5 percent [48:04]. Choosing the wrong fit condition forces field rework (forcing girders, adding frames, re-inspecting welds) or locks in unintended dead load forces, both of which cost erection time [58:19][77:19].

### Your Company Application
This is bridge content (AASHTO plate girders), not Your Company's conventional building structural steel, so the direct overlap is partial. The transferable lessons for Mario's shop crew and Tekla detailing are the fit-condition discipline (detail to a named load state, lay out cross frames and bracing to the plan camber, never communicate fit by "plumb") and the recognition that bracing stiffness redistributes load, which mirrors how lean-on or omitted bracing changes member demand. For Ivan's takeoff and any in-house PE stamp work, the warning that 2D analysis can mis-handle torsion and warping is a reminder to verify analysis assumptions rather than trust software output, consistent with the verify-don't-generate rule. Paul Guerrero's safety relevance is the lay-over demonstration: a released girder with too few frames twists and moves significantly, so erection bracing and sequencing are a fall and stability hazard to manage. No conflict with Your Company doctrine, and the brand rule holds since all material here is conventional welded plate girder steel with no PEMB language; doctrine_flag NONE.

## Plate Girder Design and Stability
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1-vGIfI_wS0 | Duration: 1:29:28 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
This is session 2 of AISC's "Introduction to Steel Bridge Design" series, presented by Todd Helwig (UT Austin), covering plate-girder design and stability for steel highway bridges [00:01]. The through-line is that built-up plate girders are slender-plate assemblies whose strength is governed by stability limit states in two distinct stages: the non-composite construction stage where the bare steel girder carries the full deck-placement load, and the finished composite stage where the steel girder acts with the concrete deck [02:34, 03:05]. The talk works through local plate buckling (flange and web), lateral-torsional buckling, composite plastic-moment design, preliminary girder sizing, and the system (global) buckling mode of narrow twin- and three-girder units [01:33, 75:23]. Most stability checks control during construction, not in the finished bridge, because the cured composite deck provides continuous lateral and torsional restraint [85:47].

### Spec References
The governing code throughout is AASHTO LRFD (the speaker says "AASHTO," transcribed as "Ashto"), with AISC 360 cited by comparison. Captured AASHTO citations: Chapter 6 for flange and web local buckling limits (lambda-r, lambda-p curves) [13:46, 16:50]; Appendix A6 for the lateral-torsional buckling equation applicable to compact and non-compact and singly symmetric shapes [27:39, 28:10]; Appendix D6 for composite girder strength equations [36:50, 76:50]; Chapter 4 for composite deck effective width [40:27]; and the main-body LTB equation intended for slender-web sections carrying the Rb web load-shedding factor [29:12]. For loading the speaker names the HL-93 truck load [58:57]. On the AISC side he cites the Timoshenko elastic LTB equation, the AISC Cb equation (which AASHTO commentary calls the "more accurate Cb equation") [32:44, 33:46], and notes AISC retains the span/8 shear-lag effective-width limit that AASHTO dropped [40:57]. No AISC 341 seismic, AWS D1.1, RCSC, or numbered Design Guide references appear; this is a bridge-design, not connection-design, webinar.

### Technical Details
All elastic plate-buckling stresses share the form K*pi^2*E / (12*(1-mu^2)*(b/t)^2), with K the plate-buckling coefficient set by stress type (axial, bending, shear) and edge support; mu = 0.3 gives the 0.9 coefficient seen in the web bend-buckling equation [10:11, 19:25]. Flange slenderness is bf/(2*tf): lambda-p ~ 9.2 and lambda-r ~ 16.1 for Grade 50, with the elastic cutoff at 0.7*Fy assuming 30% residual stress [14:17, 15:18]. Web slenderness is 2*Dc/tw with lambda-r ~ 137 and a compact limit ~ 90 for Grade 50; designers target webs near lambda-r, roughly 120 to 137 [16:19, 17:21]. Torsional resistance splits into Saint-Venant (GJ) and warping (Cw = Iy*d^2/4 for doubly symmetric) terms [22:32, 26:07]. Composite plastic-moment design uses a Whitney stress block at 0.85*f'c, locating the plastic neutral axis by comparing C* (max slab compressive resultant = 0.85*f'c*beff*ts), Py (steel area times Fy), and Py-web; the PNA lands in the deck, the top flange, or the web [38:54, 41:58]. Worked examples gave Mp = 5865 kip-ft (PNA in deck) and 5645 kip-ft (PNA in flange, using a modified stress diagram) [46:04, 51:13]. Shear-stud strength is 0.5*Asc*sqrt(f'c*Ec) capped at Asc*Fu; a 3/4-inch stud in 4 ksi concrete carries ~26 kip, and the mid-span example needed 184 total studs at uniform spacing [52:17, 55:23].

### Fabrication Notes
Bridge girders are built-up welded plate sections, not rolled shapes, so the fabricator sets plate thicknesses to standard increments (1 inch, 1-1/16, 1-1/4) and the designer iterates flange and web plates to hit slenderness targets [61:33]. Practical flange proportioning keeps bf/2tf near the compact limit (about 9 for Grade 50, AASHTO allows up to 12) and flange-width-to-depth around 1/4 rather than the slender 1/6 limit; singly symmetric girders typically run the bottom flange area about 1.5 times the top [61:02, 122]. Stay-in-place metal deck forms supported on cold-formed angles are common and stay on the bridge; the angles let the contractor adjust form elevation for flange-thickness variation and differential camber, and Texas permits welding those supports to the girder where some states do not [57:25, 58:25]. Longitudinal web stiffeners are added when web slenderness exceeds 150, with an ideal location at 2*Dc/5 [20:27].

### Erection Notes
Stability during construction is the controlling concern, since the bare non-composite girder carries the full self-weight, wet concrete, formwork, and construction live load before the deck cures [66:39, 67:41]. Lateral-torsional buckling during deck placement is resisted by cross frames or diaphragms spaced along the length; the worked example solved a max unbraced length of ~417 in (~35 ft) and adopted five segments giving 30-ft bracing for a 150-ft span [72:16, 73:16]. AASHTO applies a 1.4 construction load factor to cover contractor-method uncertainty [67:10]. The system buckling mode is the key erection hazard for narrow twin- and three-girder units: it is insensitive to cross-frame spacing because the girders buckle as one half sine-wave unit, and the speaker cites real construction failures (a tub-girder pedestrian bridge in Marcy NY and a twin-girder bridge widening in Houston where a flange moved ~10 in during casting) [75:23, 76:23, 76:53]. AASHTO caps applied moment at 50% (raised to 70% in the newest version) of the system-buckling critical load, else temporary bracing or larger girders are required [77:58].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The named failures are construction-stage stability losses rather than weld or bolt rejections. Two field collapses anchor the system-mode discussion: the Marcy NY tub-girder pedestrian bridge that failed during slab casting because it lacked a top lateral truss and behaved like two close eye-girders, and a Houston twin-girder widening whose flange swept ~10 in laterally during deck placement [75:53, 76:23]. The speaker flags that omitting a top lateral truss on a tub girder, or under-bracing narrow girder units, invites a sudden system buckling failure, and that bracing failures generally are the one buckling case that is sudden and catastrophic rather than gradual [06:38, 76:23]. On cover-plating an existing composite girder he warns the real risk is fatigue at weld terminations, evaluated by AASHTO fatigue categories, not loss of yield capacity [87:18].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Bridge girders use custom built-up plates, so there is no rolled-shape table to price against; the estimator must derive depth from span-to-depth ratios (simple spans 25 to 30, continuous ~35), then size web and flange plates from stability limits before any tonnage is known [56:55, 116]. Cross-frame and diaphragm quantity is driven by the construction-stage LTB check, and the worked example showed that trying to drop one cross frame (going from 30-ft to 37.5-ft spacing) failed the appendix LTB check at 30.5 ksi versus a 32 ksi demand, so the cheaper bracing layout was not buildable [74:51, 75:23]. Shear-stud counts are real material and labor: 184 studs on one 150-ft girder in the example, set at uniform spacing [55:23]. Narrow twin- or three-girder units may need temporary construction bracing, an added cost line when the system-buckling demand exceeds the AASHTO fraction [77:58].

### Your Company Application
This is bridge work governed by AASHTO LRFD, which sits outside Your Company's conventional-building structural-steel lane, so treat it as reference rather than directly applicable doctrine. The transferable lessons map cleanly to our workstreams: for Ivan's takeoff, built-up plate girders carry no AISC-shape weight in aisc_validator.py, so any plate-girder member needs a computed built-up weight (plate volume times density) flagged medium or low confidence, never a database lookup. For Mario's shop, this reinforces that built-up girders are fully welded plate assemblies where flange and web plate thicknesses are set to standard increments and fit-up controls the section properties. For Paul's safety program, the Marcy NY and Houston construction-stage collapses are concrete cautionary cases that erection-stage lateral bracing and cross frames are life-safety items, not optional temporary steel, before a deck or slab is placed. For Tekla detailing and the in-house PE stamp, the controlling design check is the non-composite construction stage with its 1.4 load factor and cross-frame spacing, which our detailers and stamping engineer should hold as the governing case on any deep slender-web member. Doctrine conflict check: NONE. No supplier names, no PEMB language, and no fabricated AISC weights or section numbers appear; AASHTO-specific equations are labeled as AASHTO, not attributed to AISC.

## Loads and Analysis
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jzkLzs0q2Zk | Duration: 1:29:29 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is AISC Night School Session 4 of an introduction to steel BRIDGE design, presented by Dr. John Kulicki of Modjeski and Masters [00:01]. The subject is loads and structural analysis under the AASHTO LRFD Bridge Design Specifications, not the AISC 360 building code [06:09]. It teaches the LRFD limit-state philosophy built around four limit states: service, strength, extreme event, and fatigue/fracture [02:34]. The governing form is the LRFD equation, a sum of factored load effects (eta times gamma-i times Q-i) that must be less than or equal to the factored resistance (phi times R-n) [08:11][22:02]. Safety is expressed as a reliability index rather than a factor of safety, with a target near 3.5 selected to match historically acceptable performance [21:31][23:38].
### Spec References
All citations are to AASHTO LRFD, not AISC building specs. Named items: AASHTO LRFD Section 1 introduction and limit-state function [07:11]; Section 3 loads and load factors [07:41]; Section 4 structural analysis and evaluation [08:11]; the load combination Table 3.4.1-1 plus supplementary Table 3.4.1-2 [52:22]; the HL-93 notional live load (HL-93 truck plus lane load, or HL-93 tandem of 50 kips on two 25-kip axles plus lane) [13:20][29:57]; the legacy HS-20 (1944) and HS-25 loads [11:45][80:26]; dynamic load allowance values of 75% for deck-joint components, 15% for fatigue/fracture, and 33% for strength and service [29:26][29:57]; the AASHTO Manual for Bridge Evaluation (MBE) for rating and posting [72:37]; the federal Bridge Formula B for axle weights [75:15]; and the FHWA refined-analysis manual being written under a Lehigh University IDIQ [64:53]. No AISC 360, AISC 341, AWS D1.1, or RCSC sections are cited; this webinar does not cover them.
### Technical Details
Live load is HL-93, a notional envelope (not a real vehicle) that pairs an axle group with a uniform lane load; for negative moment and interior reactions two trucks 50 feet apart are combined with the lane and factored by 0.90 [25:42][87:26]. Multiple presence factors are 1.2 for one loaded lane, 1.0 for two, and 0.75 declining for more, with the greater-than-one value explained by the limited 10,000-truck Canadian database extrapolated to a 75-year design life [26:50][57:21]. Distribution factors moved from the conservative S/5.5 rule to NCHRP equations incorporating girder-to-slab stiffness ratio (longitudinal vs transverse rigidity), which can differ from S/5.5 by up to roughly 50% and in some geometries is even unconservative [18:29][19:29][20:29]. Permanent loads carry both maximum and minimum factors so light-load cases that reduce stability or eccentricity are captured; transient loads are applied at their maximum or omitted entirely [59:41][61:46]. Refined analysis (grid, plate-with-eccentric-beam, finite element) is required for heavy skew, sharp curvature, or large stiffness variation [62:48].
### Fabrication Notes
This webinar is analysis and load derivation only and contains no shop fabrication, fit-up, tolerance, or QC content. General principles, no fabrication section cited.
### Erection Notes
No erection, sequencing, bracing, crane, or rigging content appears; the talk stays at the design-loads and analysis level. General principles, no erection section cited.
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The speaker frames pitfalls in analysis and load application rather than weld or bolt rejections. Named issues: misapplying S/5.5 distribution factors outside their calibrated variable range, where simple methods do not apply [62:48][63:19]; assuming S/5.5 is always conservative when certain geometries make it unconservative [21:01]; complexity in refined finite-element models obscuring behavior and hiding modeling errors ("blunders") [64:21][66:25]; and down-drag from settling soil that has pulled foundation elements out of footings or driven piles through weak strata when not accounted for [37:20]. No AWS, RCSC, or NDE inspection failures are discussed.
### Bid / Cost Implications
HL-93 produces roughly 34% more moment than HS-20 on a 100-foot span and over 40% more on a 140-foot span, so member sizing and steel weight scale up unless an improved distribution factor offsets it [17:57][24:40]. Where the distribution factor did not change, the heavier HL-93 hits the design directly with no offset; shear sees a proportionally larger change than moment [25:10][25:42]. On existing structures, refined analysis can reveal extra capacity and avoid load-posting, repair, or replacement, which is a direct cost avoidance [64:21]. Strength IV puts a floor on very-high-dead-load spans (over 600 feet) because the low dead-load factor would otherwise drop the reliability index [56:03].
### Your Company Application
Limited direct application: Your Company fabricates conventional building structural steel under AISC 360 and AISC 341, while this webinar is AASHTO LRFD highway-bridge load derivation, so the HL-93, multiple-presence, and bridge distribution-factor content does not map to Ivan's building takeoff through aisc_validator.py, Mario's AWS D1.1 welding, Paul's safety work, Tekla detailing, anchor rods, joists, or ACP controls. The transferable idea is the verify-don't-generate discipline it reinforces: loads and analysis results must be checked against calibrated methods and reliability targets before they drive a number, mirroring our confidence-tagging and SF-sourcing gates. If Your Company is ever asked to fabricate steel for a pedestrian or vehicular bridge, this session flags that bridge work runs on AASHTO LRFD with a separate live-load model and the in-house PE stamp would need bridge-specific scope, which is outside the current building-steel doctrine. Doctrine conflict: NONE, but note this is a scope mismatch (bridge vs building code) so treat its specifics as reference only, not as inputs to a building bid.

## Introduction and History of AASHTO LRFD Steel Bridge Design
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5g7ul4CVhxA | Duration: 1:35:00 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is session 2 of an 8-part AISC Night School introductory course on steel bridge design, presented by Michael Grubb [00:00]. It traces the history and evolution of the AASHTO bridge design specifications from the 1931 first-edition Standard Specifications for Highway Bridges through the present-day AASHTO LRFD Bridge Design Specifications, and walks the three design philosophies in sequence: allowable stress design (ASD), load factor design (LFD), and load and resistance factor design (LRFD) [02:03]. The controlling theme is that LRFD, adopted by AASHTO in 1993 and first published in 1994, is the first calibrated probability-based bridge specification in the US, using a statistical calibration to a target reliability index rather than judgment-based safety factors [52:34][53:39]. This is bridge design under AASHTO, a different code family from the AISC 360 building code Your Company works under, so its direct application to the shop is limited.

### Spec References
The talk cites bridge codes, not building codes. Named references: AASHTO Standard Specifications for Highway Bridges (1st ed 1931, 17th and final ed 2002, sunsetted Oct 1 2007) [05:35][32:27]; AASHTO LRFD Bridge Design Specifications (1st ed 1994, 7th ed 2014, 8th ed due 2017) [25:39][30:51]; AASHTO/AWS D1.5 Bridge Welding Code, which now houses the Fracture Control Plan [18:27]; ASTM A709 and the parallel AASHTO M270 material standard for bridge steels [38:07]; the LRFD resistance factors specified in Article 6.5.4.2 [65:05]; Appendix C2 to Section 6 flowcharts [70:44]; NCHRP Report 368 (calibration) and NCHRP Report/synthesis series, plus NCHRP projects 12-26, 12-33, 12-52, 20-7 task 31 [59:24][62:30]; AISI Bulletin 15 (1969 LFD criteria) [16:23]. The single explicit AISC tie is the note that AASHTO resistance factors were generally set 0.05 higher than the corresponding AISC values [65:05].

### Technical Details
Member behavior is organized by limit state and is broadly consistent in form with AISC 360 building provisions. Flexural sections are classified by web slenderness as compact-web, noncompact-web, or slender-web, using the same limiting lambda relations; AASHTO calls them lambda with Dcp/Dc while AISC uses lambda_p/lambda_r with Hcp/Hc [67:09][68:09]. The speaker stresses that a rolled beam "does not know whether it is in a building or a bridge," so the underlying equations match and only notation and organization differ [69:42][70:13]. Bridges skew toward slender-web composite plate girders, singly symmetric and hybrid sections, and moving-load fatigue, whereas buildings favor compact rolled beams [66:07][66:38]. The four LRFD limit states are service, fatigue and fracture, strength, and extreme event [75:23]. Composite action uses shear-stud connectors to prevent slip and force linear strain through the depth [89:16]. Service-level steel stress limits of 0.95Fy composite and 0.80Fy noncomposite trace to the AASHO Road Test [11:46][63:31].

### Fabrication Notes
Fabrication content is bridge-specific and light. The Fracture Control Plan, adopted 1978 after the 1967 Silver Bridge collapse, governs fracture-critical (nonredundant) members or FCMs and sets controls on material properties, initial flaw sizes, fabricator and NDE personnel qualification and certification, welding procedures, welding repair procedures, and required fracture toughness of steel and weld metal, all now inside AASHTO/AWS D1.5 [17:56][18:27]. Fracture toughness is verified by the Charpy V-notch impact test, reported in foot-pounds [79:30]. Curved-girder fabrication carries added labor and material cost to curve the flanges and fabricate the girders [86:12]. No bolt grades, preheat tables, or fit-up tolerances for building steel are given.

### Erection Notes
Erection notes are general and bridge-oriented. The speaker observes there have been more sudden bridge collapses from stability failures during construction, and from scour, than from fracture [19:00]. Curved-girder erection typically needs more temporary supports and bracing, and incurs greater handling, shipping, and erection cost than straight girders [86:12]. Skewed bridges drive large differential deflections between girders, forcing the girders to twist to stay rotationally continuous with the stiff truss-like cross frames, which complicates cross-frame detailing and field fit-up to reach the target geometry [83:38][84:08]. Narrow units of three or fewer girders are checked for global lateral-torsional buckling of the whole system in the noncomposite deck-placement condition [82:35].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
No shop rejection list or weld-defect catalog is given. The failure modes named are at the structure level: brittle fracture (the Silver Bridge, 1967) that prompted the Fracture Control Plan [17:56], construction-stage stability failures, and scour-induced collapse [19:00]. On the detailing side, distortion-induced fatigue is called out as a common problem: out-of-plane secondary stresses in small gaps at welded details when connection plates supporting transverse members are not positively attached to the flanges. The LRFD code addresses it through prescribed detailing (positive attachment of connection plates to flanges) rather than a calculation [78:29][79:00].

### Bid / Cost Implications
The cost commentary is about bridge type, not shop pricing. Curved girders add cost across the board: extra labor and material to curve flanges and fabricate girders, higher handling, shipping, and erection cost, design time slightly above straight girders, and more temporary supports during erection [86:12]. The historical thread that span-to-depth ratios were relaxed (to 34 for the steel section) once composite multi-stringer framing proved economical shows code change tracking fabrication economy [08:09]. The fabricator-side aside that fabricators would prefer ASTM material specs to govern, since AASHTO M-specs lag ASTM, is a real procurement friction point [90:17].

### Your Company Application
Direct application is limited because Your Company is a conventional building-steel fabricator under AISC 360 and AWS D1.1, while this is AASHTO bridge work under AWS D1.5. The transferable items are conceptual. For Ivan, the reminder that flexural-classification equations (compact, noncompact, slender web) are essentially identical between AISC and AASHTO reinforces that section behavior and member takeoff logic in aisc_validator.py rests on the same physics regardless of code family. For Mario, the Charpy V-notch toughness and fracture-control mindset is a useful reference if a bridge or fracture-critical scope ever appears, though D1.5 qualification differs from his D1.1 certification. The distortion-induced-fatigue detailing rule (positively attach connection plates to flanges) is good Tekla detailing hygiene generally. Your Company should not bid AASHTO bridge work as routine building scope without a D1.5-qualified setup and a PE comfortable with Section 6. Doctrine conflict: NONE. No supplier names, no PEMB language, no rate or AISC-weight claims were introduced.

## Introduction to Bridge Engineering
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MOBX2QZ_wcY | Duration: 1:34:17 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is session 1 of an 8-part NSBA / AISC night school on steel bridge design, presented by Anna Teague, Joann Shaner, and Dominic Coletti of HDR [00:01]. The session is a vocabulary-and-orientation overview: bridge nomenclature, the three main elements (superstructure, substructure, foundation) [02:41], bridge types, the typical superstructure plan-set sheets, framing-plan geometry, and a high-level survey of analysis methods. It teaches no design equations and almost no building-steel content, so its value to Your Company is conceptual literacy for any bridge or bridge-adjacent steel work, not a fabrication or connection standard.
### Spec References
Few codes are cited and none are AISC building specs. Named references: AASHTO LRFD Bridge Design Specifications as the governing highway-bridge code (full coverage deferred to session 2) [01:03][80:22]; AREMA Manual for Railway Engineering, specifically Chapter 15 Steel Structures, for railroad bridges, which follow allowable stress design (ASD) and the Cooper E80 railroad live load [80:52][81:24]; NCHRP Report 725, Guidelines for Analysis Methods and Construction Engineering of Curved and Skewed Steel Girder Bridges [77:16]; AASHTO/NSBA Steel Bridge Collaboration document G13.1, Guidelines for Steel Girder Bridge Analysis [78:17]; and the FHWA Manual for Refined Analysis [78:49]. No AISC 360 section, AISC 341 section, AWS D1.1 clause, RCSC provision, or Design Guide number is stated.
### Technical Details
Superstructure elements named: barrier, median, sidewalk, deck and wearing surface, deck forms, girders, cross frames, diaphragms, lateral bracing, and bearings [04:19]. Girder types: rolled beams (limited rolled sizes, short spans) and built-up plate girders with flanges, webs, and stiffeners for longer spans, plus box girders for torsional resistance on curved structures [24:04][25:07]. Bearing families: elastomeric (steel-shim reinforced), high-load multi-rotational (pot and disc, the disc using a molded urethane elastomer, often guided or non-guided), and mechanical (rocker and roller, now mostly rehab-only) [27:16][29:50]. Framing-plan geometry vocabulary: radial/normal versus skewed supports measured to the local tangent, contiguous versus staggered cross frames (contiguous is the term used in the AASHTO LRFD spec) [64:34][66:06], constant versus variable girder spacing, field splices, bearing and intermediate stiffeners, and girder bifurcation with a transfer beam or bulkhead diaphragm picking up an introduced girder [62:29]. Analysis methods: line-girder (1D), 2D grid, 2D plate-and-eccentric-beam, and 3D finite element, with refinement chosen to match geometric complexity [72:05][74:08].
### Fabrication Notes
Fabrication is touched only indirectly. Cross frames are individually designed built-up assemblies of angles and gusset plates and are described as expensive to fabricate, so designers balance their size and count [25:39][89:51]. Variable-width framing where every cross frame is a different length raises fabrication cost, which is the argument for grouping parallel girders so many cross frames repeat [56:17][57:19]. Girder elevations call out plate-size changes at field splices, for example a bottom flange going from 1-1/4 inch by 20 to 1-3/4 inch by 24 across a splice with a constant 3/16 inch by 62 web, and shear-stud spacing for composite action [37:36]. No fit-up tolerance, camber, or shop QC procedure is stated.
### Erection Notes
Girders are broken into shorter shipping pieces because US highway routes limit length, then erected and field-spliced in the air [43:48]. Stated shipping limits run as low as 130 feet, sometimes 150 feet or longer depending on the route from shop to site, which drove the splice layout on a roughly 200-foot single-span example even though it carries no contraflexure point [88:20]. Photos show curved and skewed girders erected before the deck pour, with overhang falsework and formwork in place and bolted field splices visible as dark bolt clusters at web and flange [47:58][48:28]. Lateral bracing in exterior bays is highlighted as needed for global lateral-torsional stability before the deck cures and acts as a composite shear diaphragm [69:14][92:31].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
No inspection failures, weld rejections, or bolting defects are named. The closest to an error theme is the engineering caution that a poorly laid-out framing plan with bad load paths causes design problems downstream [42:15], and that 3D finite-element models are more susceptible to hidden errors that are hard to detect [76:46]. This is a conceptual session, so treat it as having no inspection-failure content.
### Bid / Cost Implications
Cross frames are called out as expensive to fabricate, so reducing their size and count, and repeating cross-frame lengths through parallel-girder grouping, is a direct cost lever [89:51][57:19]. Field-splice count and location trade fabrication and field-bolting labor against shipping limits: more splices add bolted connections and field labor, fewer splices risk over-length shipping [87:16][88:20]. Analysis-method selection is framed as a time-and-money decision, with 3D FEA costing more effort than line-girder or 2D grid for simple bridges [76:46]. These are bridge-design economics, not Your Company building-bid rates.
### Your Company Application
This is bridge engineering, outside Your Company's conventional building-steel lane, so the transfer is limited and conceptual. The framing-plan-as-load-path message reinforces our Tekla detailing discipline and the verify-don't-generate posture: the drawing is simple but the engineering behind it is not, which mirrors why Ivan's takeoff routes member weights through aisc_validator.py rather than trusting a quick read. The plate-girder build-up callouts (flange and web plate sizes changing at field splices, shear studs for composite action) map cleanly to how Mario's shop reads built-up girder shop drawings, and the shipping-length-driven splice logic (130 to 150 feet) is a real constraint Ivan should carry on any long-member bid regardless of building or bridge. The bolted-field-splice and lateral-bracing-before-deck themes connect to our field-bolting and erection-bracing practice. Doctrine flag: NONE. The webinar uses no PEMB language and names no suppliers; if Your Company ever quotes bridge work, note that AASHTO LRFD and AREMA, not AISC 360, govern, which is outside our in-house PE stamp's normal building scope and would need confirmation before bidding.

## More Opportunities - Design by Inelastic Analysis
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qfPplhy4f2U | Duration: 1:31:45 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
This is the eighth and final lecture of an AISC Night School course on stability design, presented by Dr. Ronald Ziemian of Bucknell with Dr. Donald White, covering design by inelastic analysis under AISC 360 Appendix 1 [02:38]. The method extends the direct analysis method one step further by directly modeling inelastic material yielding rather than running a second-order elastic analysis and then checking member equations [03:08]. The controlling idea is that if the analysis program itself captures a given limit state behavior (flexural buckling, lateral-torsional buckling, partial yielding from residual stress), the engineer does not have to satisfy the corresponding equation in the main body of the specification, because the computer acts as a virtual lab predicting the structure's full limit-state response [38:39][42:48]. Ziemian frames this as economy, simplicity, and rationality, the same three arguments Lynn Beedle made for plastic design in 1956 [16:32].

### Spec References
The talk centers on AISC 360 Appendix 1, "Design by Inelastic Analysis," added in the 2010 specification, described as a five-page appendix with eight pages of commentary structured in three parts: general requirements, ductility requirements, and analysis requirements [41:16]. Speaker cites the main body chapters A through N as the equation set you fall back to, specifically the Chapter E column curve, the Chapter F beam curve, and the Chapter H beam-column interaction equation [37:36][43:18]. Chapter C is referenced as the home of the direct analysis method (DM) for elastic analysis [34:31]. The speaker notes Appendix 1 does not apply to ASD and does not cover seismic, directing seismic inelastic work to AISC 341 [42:48]. The Code of Standard Practice is named as a base for geometric imperfection tolerances [88:51]. Historical references include the 1961 AISC plastic design appendix (Part 2) and a 1967 Engineering Journal paper on a 14-story Binghamton apartment building [17:32][21:05].

### Technical Details
The plastic hinge is the core mechanism: a section yields fully at its plastic moment Mp and must keep resisting that moment through a rotation theta-p while load redistributes [49:57]. Appendix 1 requires a rotation capacity of about 3, meaning Mp is maintained for roughly three times the rotation needed to first form the hinge [50:28]. The appendix is limited to doubly symmetric shapes; singly symmetric or non-symmetric shapes require a program sophisticated enough to capture twist and torsion [65:51]. For members with high axial force and low bending, Appendix 1 caps usage at 75 percent of CPy because ductility for multiple hinges is uncertain past that point [66:21]. Analysis inputs that must be modeled include second-order effects, initial geometric imperfections (out-of-plumb, out-of-straightness, often via notional loads or scaled buckling-mode shapes), partial yielding, and residual stresses, with E and Fy reduced by 0.9 as the phi-factor reduction [51:30][89:30].

### Fabrication Notes
This is an analysis and design webinar, not a shop-process talk, so there are no direct fabrication, fit-up, or shop QC procedures discussed. The closest fabrication-relevant content is the demand for compact sections and adequate ductility, which is a member-selection and detailing constraint rather than a shop instruction [77:43]. Residual stresses from rolling and fabrication are named as a modeled effect, with the profile depending on cross-section geometry and adopting published models such as Galambos-Ketter or the European model [87:48].

### Erection Notes
No conventional erection, sequencing, crane, rigging, or field-bracing procedures are taught here. One real-world example touches construction-stage analysis: SDL in Atlanta used advanced (ANSYS) analysis to study twin girder outrigger beams forming a temporary structure that supported large trusses cantilevering over a historic stone building during the construction sequence [67:22]. That illustrates inelastic analysis applied to a temporary erection support condition rather than a standard erection method.

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
No bolt, weld, or NDE inspection failures are discussed; this is not an inspection webinar. The relevant failure modes are analytical limit states: local buckling at a plastic hinge, lateral-torsional buckling, and loss of stiffness leading to a frame instability mechanism [77:11]. The central caution is that a "frame analysis" line-element program that does not capture partial yielding and residual stress (called "frame analysis 1" in the demo) will overstate strength, so the engineer must fall back and check the Chapter E, F, or H equation [45:21]. The late Theodore Galambos urged a "skull and crossbones" on page one of Appendix 1 because an underqualified engineer who does not understand nonlinear behavior can misuse it [73:35].

### Bid / Cost Implications
The economic case is that inelastic analysis recovers steel weight that elastic methods leave on the table by allowing controlled hinge formation and force redistribution. In one portal-frame example the structure carried about 35 percent more load before reaching its limit state versus the direct analysis method governing at 65 percent [62:47]. The speaker is candid that the savings are not always large: in a more redundant frame the gain was only about 8 percent, since the direct analysis method already recovers most of the available capacity as a "poor man's inelastic analysis" [64:49]. Software cost is a real factor: nonlinear-capable frame programs cost more, and full shell-element programs (Abaqus, ADINA, ANSYS) get very expensive [80:51].

### Your Company Application
For Your Company this is engineering methodology for the in-house PE stamp, not a change to fabrication, erection, or takeoff. It is a niche tool for unusual structures where effective length and unbraced length are undefinable (a freestanding arch bandstand, ladder columns that are a webless stocky W12 with two-inch flanges, twin-girder outriggers over a historic building) [66:51][70:58]. It does not override our verify-don't-generate doctrine on tonnage: Hard Rule 5 still requires AISC weights and member checks through bridge/aisc_validator.py against the schedules and framing-plan marks, and Ivan's member takeoff stays the bid-grade basis. The 8-to-35 percent potential weight savings is a value-engineering note worth flagging to a GC only when a PE-stamped inelastic analysis is actually performed and licensed software exists; do not assume it on a standard conventional steel bid. No conflict with Your Company doctrine, with the standing reminder that seismic inelastic work routes to AISC 341, not this appendix. Doctrine flag: NONE.

## Stability Design - Advanced Applications
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1zMxEqo6NPI | Duration: 1:37:49 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is session seven of an AISC Night School course on stability design taught by Dr. Donald W. White of Georgia Tech, focused on advanced application of the Direct Analysis Method (DM) from the AISC specification [02:35][03:05]. The DM models reduced stiffness (0.8 times tau) and explicit geometric imperfections so member checks can be done at the cross-section level without computing effective length (K) factors [05:41][16:00]. The session works four problem types: in-plane stability of a steel arch, erection stability of a long-span roof truss, stability bracing assessment (relative/panel, nodal, lean-on), and a rigorous inelastic buckling analysis that the speaker frames as a refined effective length method [03:05][03:36]. The controlling lesson for a fabricator is that stability-critical structures do not scale linearly: an arch at a 0.49 unity check reached 1.0 at only 20 percent more load [14:58].

### Spec References
The speaker cites these by name: AISC Design Guide 28 (stability bracing examples, including Appendix E and the lean-on example) [04:39][54:50]; AISC Appendix 6 column bracing provisions, with relative bracing being renamed panel bracing in the 2016 draft [31:53][34:28]; Appendix 6 equations A-6-1 (panel bracing strength, 0.4 percent of axial force) and A-6-2 (required panel bracing stiffness) [44:54][48:36]; Appendix 1 sections 1.1 and 1.2 for second-order analysis, referenced by Section A-6-1 of AISC 2016 (ballot 3 under public review) [36:30]; the AISC Code of Standard Practice out-of-plumb tolerance of 1 in 500 and out-of-straightness 1 in 1000 [20:43][49:37]; the AISC column strength curve equations and the 0.877 / phi=0.9 inelastic factors and tau-a derivation [80:39][82:10]. No AISC 341 seismic, AWS D1.1, or RCSC bolting clauses were cited; this is an analysis-method webinar.

### Technical Details
The arch is a two-hinge parabolic rib, 350 ft span, 80 ft rise, steel box section (50 by 1 inch webs, 20 by 2 inch flanges, Grade 50), checked at factored load Wu = 8.6 kip/ft with a 5 inch (span/1000) imperfection scaled to the buckling mode [04:39][06:43]. The example truss is a 120 ft simple-span roof truss, 11 ft deep, W12x65 top chord, W12x53 bottom chord, W12x45 web members, with chord splices near midspan and self-weight increased 20 percent for miscellaneous steel [16:30][17:34]. Modeling web connections as fully restrained (FR) gave a buckling ratio of 6.56 versus 1.3 if pinned, so the gusset-to-flange detail justified the continuous assumption [22:50][24:55]. The lean-on example ties four-story exterior W14x257 columns to an interior moment-frame core; floor beams were upsized from W18x40 to W21x44 and finally W30x90 to provide the required 56.5 kip/inch bracing stiffness [55:22][68:39]. All analyses ran in the MASTAN-style second-order/buckling tool the speaker calls "mast 10" [07:15].

### Fabrication Notes
The session is analysis, not shop process, so fabrication tolerance enters only as imperfection input. The arch construction tolerance was taken as span/1000 (5 inches), and member out-of-straightness as L/1000 per the Code of Standard Practice [06:43][20:43]. The chord splices near truss midspan are flagged as a fabrication and detailing decision: if they are temporary erection splices ahead of a final field splice, the temporary splice must be sized for the erection-stage forces from the analysis [18:35][19:39]. The 20 percent self-weight add for connection and miscellaneous steel is the kind of takeoff allowance an estimator carries before connection design exists [17:34].

### Erection Notes
Topic 7.2 is explicitly an erection-engineer problem: stability during lifting is usually not the driver, but stability after releasing the crane is [17:34][18:05]. The questions posed are whether the truss can be connected and the crane released, what wind magnitude causes failure, what temporary bracing (deadmen and cables to midspan) is needed, and what temporary splice forces result [18:05][18:35]. For erection imperfection the chords are swept L/1000 out of plane, and sweeping top and bottom chords in opposite directions (a built-in twist) is the conservative worst case for letting the truss off the hook [20:43][21:45]. For this truss the bottom chord unity check at 1.4 times self weight was only 0.07, so releasing the crane under self weight alone was fine, but wind still had to be checked separately [25:56][26:27].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
No bolting or welding inspection failures are named; the errors discussed are analysis and assumption errors. The central one is treating a stability-critical structure as if unity checks scale linearly with load, which the arch disproves (0.49 to 1.0 at only +20 percent) [14:58]. A second is mis-idealizing truss web connections as pins when the flange-to-flange gusset detail behaves as FR, which would wrongly fail a stable truss [22:50][24:25]. A third is using too few elements per member in second-order analysis: two elements per unbraced length on the exterior lean-on columns, three if the program has only P-large-delta capability, versus one for the lightly loaded interior columns [76:25][77:26]. A fourth is choosing an imperfection pattern that matches a buckling mode with no brace displacement, which understates the brace demand [93:34].

### Bid / Cost Implications
The bracing economy theme is the cost message: Appendix 6 hand equations are conservative starting points, and DM or inelastic buckling analysis can reduce brace stiffness and member sizes for partial nodal bracing, unequal brace spacing or stiffness, flexible braces, and tapered members [53:48][54:20]. The base brace strength requirement is 0.4 percent of column axial force at the minimum (2 times ideal) stiffness, dropping toward the 0.2 percent floor as brace stiffness increases, so over-stiffening braces lowers required brace force [48:06][50:41]. The lean-on example shows engineering effort trading against steel weight: beam upsizing from W18x40 through W21x44 to W30x90 was driven entirely by bracing stiffness, a real fabrication cost decided by analysis rigor [56:25][69:42].

### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, the 20 percent self-weight allowance for connections and miscellaneous steel on a truss is a usable rough factor before connection design exists, but it is an analysis input, not a validated tonnage. Mario's shop crew and any erection planning map directly to Topic 7.2: any long-span truss or arch lift on a job like Asian City Plaza needs an erection-stability check on crane release, temporary deadman/cable bracing, and temporary splice forces, which is engineering scope our in-house PE stamp owns, not field judgment. The chord-splice point about sizing temporary erection splices for stage forces is a Tekla detailing and PE-stamp coordination item. Paul's safety scope intersects the wind-during-erection check that gates when the crane can be released. NONE of this conflicts with Your Company doctrine: it is conventional structural steel analysis with no PEMB language, and tonnage and member weights still route through bridge/aisc_validator.py rather than any figure spoken in this webinar.

## Second-Order Elastic Analysis - Getting it Right
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MtjnHpW46-E | Duration: 1:33:40 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
This is session four of AISC's Night School on Stability Design of Steel Structures, presented by Dr. Donald W. White of Georgia Tech [00:02]. The subject is how to get a second-order elastic analysis right, meaning equilibrium taken on the deflected geometry of the structure [03:35]. White separates the two amplification effects that drive every steel building check: P-small-delta, the extra moment from axial load acting through member curvature relative to the chord between member ends [03:35][87:29], and P-large-delta, the sidesway effect from axial load acting through the story drift [21:34]. He builds from the basic B1 and B2 amplifiers, shows where member-by-member hand methods break down on real unsymmetric frames, and closes with how many finite elements a general-purpose analysis needs to stay accurate [55:40]. This is an engineering-analysis lecture, not a fabrication, connection-design, or erection lecture.

### Spec References
The presenter cites AISC 360 Appendix 8 repeatedly as the home of the B1 and B2 amplifiers and the PE1 equation [04:38][20:30][30:22], with the C-sub-M form given in the Appendix 8 commentary [04:38]. He references the K2 effective-length equation as commentary equation C-A7-5 in Appendix 7, noting a wording oversight he expected corrected in the 2016 spec [33:30]. He cites chapter H interaction (unity check) equations for the demand-capacity example [55:40], and chapter F lateral-torsional-buckling design for the warping-stiffness discussion [76:43]. Background and the element-count accuracy criteria come from AISC Design Guides 25 and 28, with the worst-case element-count charts drawn from Design Guide 25 [03:05][66:29][73:11]. He also points to AASHTO provisions for effective GJ on curved and skewed I-girder bridges [76:43]. No bolting, welding, or seismic (AISC 341 / AWS D1.1 / RCSC) sections are cited; this is a pure analysis topic.

### Technical Details
For an end-loaded member the amplifier is C-sub-M over (1 minus P/PE1), and B1 is never taken less than one [40:42][41:12]. White warns that member-by-member B1 cannot catch second-order interaction between adjacent members: in an L-shaped frame the knee moment falls to zero as column axial load reaches its pinned-pinned Euler load, and the beam moment can climb past wL-squared/8 because the beam must brace the column [10:43][12:17]. He recommends switching to a rigorous general-purpose second-order analysis once B1 exceeds 1.2 in members that materially affect the structure [14:50]. For sidesway, B2 is 1 over (1 minus 1/gamma-story), where gamma-story is the load multiple to buckling, and R-sub-M (about 1 minus 0.15 times PMF/P-story, ranging 1.0 to 0.85) accounts for P-small-delta feeding the drift [27:16][29:51]. On element choice he contrasts stability-function, cubic Hermitian, and P-large-delta-only elements, and gives element-count rules: one stability-function element per member suffices, the cubic Hermitian element needs one to two per member (up to eight within an unbraced length for lateral-torsional-buckling work), and a bare P-delta element needs two to three or more [55:40][72:07][73:11].

### Fabrication Notes
No fabrication, shop fit-up, or QC content. This webinar is confined to structural analysis method and software behavior.

### Erection Notes
No erection, sequencing, bracing, or rigging content. The only sidesway-bracing discussion is the analytical idealization of leaning columns leaning on the lateral system [83:53], not a field procedure.

### Bolting and Welding
No bolting or welding requirements are discussed. No bolt grades, electrodes, joint types, preheat, or NDE appear anywhere in the session.

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The named failures here are analysis errors, not shop or field inspection rejections. Using member-level B1 on a frame with large gravity-load sidesway underestimates moments badly: White's market-shed example shows the simplified "multiply total moment by B2" method returning 60 ft-kips against an exact 104, and a separate gravity-plus-lateral shortcut being grossly in error for an unsymmetric frame [42:46][43:48][91:09]. A single P-delta element on a contrived cantilever underestimates sidesway displacement by 34 percent, moment by 24 percent, and the unity check by 9 percent [63:23][64:58]. The subtle software trap is torsion: a 12-degree-of-freedom element carrying only GJ/L (omitting warping/Cw) roughly doubles the computed twist and makes a second-order run "go berserk" with false instability before the design load is reached [76:43][80:20]. White also flags that many programs compute only first-order moments between nodes, silently dropping P-small-delta there [16:23].

### Bid / Cost Implications
No pricing, bid, or schedule numbers appear. The indirect estimating relevance is that analysis rigor governs member sizes: a frame with heavy gravity-load sidesway or a light high-axial column can demand more steel than a quick B1/B2 hand check shows, so an engineer who under-analyzes can hand the fabricator a design that later grows. The element-count guidance is a modeling-effort cost on the design side, not a fabrication cost.

### Your Company Application
This is an engineer-of-record analysis topic that sits with the in-house PE stamp, not with Ivan's takeoff, Mario's shop, Paul's safety, Tekla detailing, or field bolting. Member sizes and connection forces our PE produces come from a properly run second-order analysis, so the practical takeaways are that our stamping engineer should run a general-purpose second-order check rather than lean on B1/B2 once B1 passes 1.2 [14:50], should use enough elements per member when the software uses P-delta-only or cubic elements [73:11], and should watch the GJ-only torsion trap on open W-section members in 3D models [80:20]. For Ivan, the estimating point is indirect: tonnage rides on the design the EOR delivers, so we still take off validated member marks through aisc_validator.py and never back-calc weights from an analysis assumption. Nothing here touches anchor rods, joists, ACP project controls, AISC weight data, or rates. Doctrine conflict: NONE.

## Stability Design of Low- and Medium-Rise Steel Buildings
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hrcunOPP7DA | Duration: 1:34:45 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is AISC Night School Session 6, presented by Dr. Donald W. White of Georgia Tech, teaching stability design of low- and medium-rise steel buildings using modern analysis methods [00:02]. The controlling idea is estimating the sidesway amplifier B2 from serviceability and code drift limits rather than guessing it, then using that B2 in member design [02:06, 37:21]. White works one example building (a 4-story office near Atlantic Station in Atlanta) end to end: braced frames in the north-south direction designed by the effective length method, and moment frames in the east-west direction designed by the direct analysis method [05:48, 22:09, 23:10]. The recurring lesson is that for practically all multi-story buildings under wind and earthquake combinations, the structure comes out stability non-critical with B2 at or below 1.7, so notional loads are not required with the lateral combination [76:28, 78:30].
### Spec References
The speaker cited AISC 360 Appendix 8 for the approximate second-order analysis B1/B2 equations [24:42, 90:00] and AISC Manual tables Table 4-1 (column axial capacity) [62:18], Table 4-4 (HSS compression) [62:18], Table 6-1 (combined axial/flexure preliminary sizing) [81:45], Table 3-2 (W-shape flexural strength) [85:23], and Section 3 Ix tables [90:32]. From AISC 360 he named interaction equation H1-1a [83:50] and equation F1-1 for the Cb factor in Chapter F [85:23], plus the sidesway-uninhibited alignment chart G equations (Chapter C commentary, "equations of 10") [86:57]. From ASCE 7 he cited the seismic P-Delta provision Section 12.8.7 and the stability coefficient theta [42:00, 49:51], effective seismic weight Section 12.7.2 [48:48], and Chapter 12 seismic provisions generally [48:18]. Design loads ran on ASCE 7 with IBC 2012; the building was Seismic Design Category B, Risk Category II [03:42, 04:14].
### Technical Details
The braced frames are vertically cantilevered trusses designed for axial force only, neglecting secondary moments [60:42]. Sidesway amplifier B2 is built from a required minimum story lateral stiffness, taken as the larger demand from three limits: a first-order service wind drift (assumed L/500 at a 10-year MRI wind, which ASCE 7 puts at 0.44 of the strength-level nominal wind) [38:24, 39:27, 79:35]; a seismic drift limit converted to elastic drift through Cd = 3, giving an elastic ratio of 1/120 [40:59, 41:30]; and the ASCE 7 seismic P-Delta limit, which for braced frames with beta = 1 and Cd = 3 yields theta_max = 0.167 and PL_story_min = 6 x Px [42:30, 43:35]. Px uses 1.0 dead + 0.5 live + 0 snow with no individual load factor above 1.0 per 12.8.7 [44:06, 49:51]. For the moment frames he back-calculated a first-order wind drift limit (L/593) needed to hold a target second-order drift of L/400 using Bill LeMessurier's 1977 EJ method [62:48, 68:59, 70:35], used Rm = 0.94 for P-small-delta and the 0.8 stiffness reduction of the direct analysis method [66:27, 73:16]. A live-load-reduction technique applies equivalent upward joint loads so the global second-order analysis is not run "filled to the gills" with unreduced live load, trimming B2 from 1.24 to 1.21 on the braced frame [50:54, 58:07, 59:39].
### Fabrication Notes
This is an analysis and design webinar, so explicit shop fabrication, fit-up, and QC processes were not covered. The only fabrication-relevant outputs are the selected member sizes: a W12x53 braced-frame bottom-story column (W10x54 or W14x61 as alternates) [61:46], a 9x9x1/4 HSS diagonal brace [62:18], a W14x68 moment-frame column [81:45], and W24x62 then W24x68 moment-frame spandrels after a drift-driven upsize [85:23, 90:00]. Column splices occur at the third-story level on both the braced and moment frames [06:49].
### Erection Notes
Field erection procedures, sequencing, crane and rigging, and bracing were not addressed in this design-focused session. The structural idealization assumes rigid diaphragms distributing lateral load to the perimeter braced and moment frames, with all interior gravity ("leaning," "dummy," or "gravity") columns providing no lateral resistance and leaning on the lateral system through the diaphragm [04:45, 13:36, 47:12]. That diaphragm-transfer assumption is the load path an erector and detailer must preserve.
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
No bolting, welding, or NDE inspection failures were named; this session does not touch shop or field QC. The design-side cautions White raised are the analysis equivalents: analyzing the frame with full unreduced live load overstates second-order effects [58:37, 59:39]; the gravity-load B1/B2 shortcut he used "gets you into trouble" if the frame has significant sidesway under gravity (his example was symmetric, so it was safe) [60:42]; and if B2 exceeds 1.7 the frame is stability-critical and you must add a notional lateral load to the seismic combination [74:21]. He also flagged a copy-paste typo on his own stiffness slide as a reminder to check the numbers [87:58, 89:28].
### Bid / Cost Implications
The cost lever in this talk is member weight driven by drift, not strength. White states that braced-frame members are usually governed by strength while a meaningful fraction of moment-frame members are governed by lateral stiffness [23:40], so moment-frame tonnage can grow late in design when a story fails its drift check (his spandrel jumped from W24x62 to W24x68 purely to add stiffness) [89:28, 90:00]. The live-load-reduction-by-equivalent-upward-load method buys a smaller B2, which matters most on flexible moment frames with large amplification and can reduce required member sizes [59:08, 60:09]. His rule of thumb for which member to grow (columns when G is much less than 1, girders when G is much greater than 1, both near G = 1) is a fast way to converge a design without overspending on steel [89:28].
### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, the load shows that medium-rise moment-frame tonnage can be stiffness-governed, so an early member takeoff through aisc_validator.py should not assume strength-sized members are final; flag moment-frame spandrels and columns as drift-sensitive and expect upsizing, which is exactly the verify-don't-generate posture. The member picks here (W-shapes plus a 9x9x1/4 HSS brace) are all standard AISC shapes our validator carries, good for sanity-checking a takeoff against a real design. For the in-house PE stamp, this is a clean reference for the B2 / direct-analysis-vs-effective-length workflow and the ASCE 7 P-Delta limit (12.8.7) and effective seismic weight (12.7.2) citations our calc audit can reference. There is no anchor-rod, joist, field-bolting, welding, Mario-shop, or Paul-safety content to map, and nothing here ties to ACP controls. No conflict with Your Company doctrine: NONE.

## The AISC Direct Analysis Method from Soup to Nuts
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Xm0nn_lm5cg | Duration: 1:36:02 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is Session 5 of an AISC "night school" stability-design series, presented by Dr. Donald White of Georgia Tech on March 2, 2015 [00:01]. The subject is the Direct Analysis Method (DM) for steel stability design, which AISC names as the preferred of the three sanctioned approaches in Chapter C, the others being the Effective Length Method (ELM) and the First-Order Analysis Method [03:36]. The DM assesses overall system stability by carrying geometric imperfections and stiffness reduction directly inside a second-order load-deflection analysis [05:11], which then lets the engineer take K equals 1 and treat all members as braced in the resistance checks [05:42]. The payoff is that the DM gives a more representative picture of the real internal forces and applies uniformly to sway, braced, and combined frames [06:13].
### Spec References
The talk cites these explicitly: AISC Specification Chapter C and Section C1 (general stability requirements) [03:36][06:13]; equation C2-1 for notional load N = 0.002 (or 1/500) times Y_i [42:25][42:55]; equation C2-2b for the 0.8 stiffness reduction and the tau-b column inelastic factor [26:21]; Appendix 8 for the B1 and B2 amplifiers [62:33]; Appendix 1 for distributed-plasticity / inelastic analysis with the 0.9 stiffness reduction [77:03][82:15]; Chapter F for the girder flexural-resistance checks [71:51]; the AISC Code of Standard Practice for the L/1000 out-of-straightness and L/500 (delta-0/L = 0.002) out-of-plumb tolerances [18:40][40:20]; and AISC Design Guides 25 and 28 as companion reading, with DG 25 supplying the K=0 / cross-section-strength extension when alpha-P_r is under 10% of the buckling load [03:05][28:55][33:32]. ASCE 7 is referenced for seismic eccentricity and drift relaxation [51:42][56:20].
### Technical Details
The six stability requirements of Section C1 are component limit states, flexural/axial/shear deformations, second-order P-large-Delta and P-small-Delta effects, geometric imperfections, stiffness reduction, and uncertainty in stiffness and strength [06:44][07:45][08:46]. For ASD the working loads are scaled up by alpha = 1.6 before analysis and divided back afterward [10:20]. Leaning (gravity) columns and walls not in the lateral system must still be carried, often through a pinned "dummy column" strut-connected to each level [11:24]. A structure is "stability critical" when second-order drift over first-order drift exceeds 1.7 for the DM reduced stiffness, or 1.5 for the ELM nominal stiffness [25:20][88:05]. The worked example is a squat single-story, five-bay frame with W12x65 lateral columns and a W24x62 roof girder, where wide footprint plus large gravity load on small lateral stiffness produced a B2 amplifier near 4.8 and a beam-column unity check of about 0.63 [53:46][54:47][63:07][71:21]. White warns that under the DM you cannot read spare capacity off a low unity check because gravity-only stability-critical frames scale nonlinearly [71:21].
### Fabrication Notes
The video is an analysis-and-design webinar and does not address shop fabrication, fit-up, or weld procedures. The only fabrication-adjacent content is the imperfection tolerances the analysis assumes: out-of-straightness L/1000 and out-of-plumb L/500 per the Code of Standard Practice [18:40][40:20], which are the as-built limits a fabricator and erector must hold for the design assumption to remain valid.
### Erection Notes
Erection procedures, sequencing, and rigging are not covered. The relevant link is that the L/500 maximum out-of-plumb erection tolerance from the Code of Standard Practice is the physical basis for the notional load and the modeled lean [40:20][42:55]. White also notes that for an existing structure measured to be out of plumb beyond the code tolerance, the DM lets you model the actual measured out-of-plumbness rather than 0.002 [72:53].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
No shop or field inspection failures are named. The errors discussed are analysis mistakes: forgetting to include gravity/leaning-column loads in the second-order model [11:24]; reducing E inside the specification resistance equations, which is wrong because stiffness reduction is already implicit there [29:56]; assuming a low unity check means large reserve capacity on a stability-critical frame [71:21]; and the common confusion that summed notional loads leave a net foundation shear, when the missing P-Delta shear restored at the foundation brings the gravity-only total back to zero [52:15].
### Bid / Cost Implications
The DM is presented as more analysis work for a payoff in the resistance side, removing the effort and uncertainty of computing K factors for irregular frames with setbacks [16:36][37:06]. The headline economic point is that on the example frame the DM (with the DG 25 extension giving an anchor of phi-P_y = 860 kips versus phi-P_n on KL = 69.2 kips) developed about 46% more column axial strength than the ELM, but that gain costs roughly 133% more required girder moment [80:09][82:47]. That trade, more demand pushed into the girder to unlock column capacity, is exactly the kind of member-sizing consequence that changes tonnage and connection cost.
### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, the DM-versus-ELM choice can move member sizes: the example showed the same column passing far more axial load under DM but only by upsizing girder moment capacity, so a designer's stability method directly affects fabricated tonnage that flows through aisc_validator.py. The L/1000 straightness and L/500 plumb tolerances tie to Mario's shop and the erection crew, since the whole analysis assumes those limits are held, and to anchor-rod setting where base-moment from imperfection lean must be designed for even on a nominally concentric column [18:40][19:10]. For the in-house PE stamp, this session is a clean reference on when the DM is mandatory (drift ratio over 1.7) and how to model notional loads, which is useful when ACP project controls need a documented stability-method basis. The DG 25 K=0 extension and leaning-column "dummy column" technique apply directly to typical low-rise framing with many gravity-only interior columns, which matches Your Company's conventional structural steel work. No conflict with Your Company doctrine: this is general AISC stability methodology with no PEMB language. Doctrine flag: NONE.
