## Introduction to the  Steel Construction Process: The Team Behind the Building
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zZ5P-alBQaI | Duration: 1:29:15 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is session one of AISC Night School 18, presented by Drew Toric of Ruben Associates, an overview of the entire steel construction team from the mill through topping out, organized around the AISC Code of Standard Practice (AISC 303) and who is responsible for what [07:11]. The controlling idea is that every party (owner, EOR, CM, mill, fabricator, detailer, connection designer, erector, erection engineer, QC/QA) has defined responsibilities, and understanding them all is what produces constructability [12:56]. Constructability is defined as the optimum use of construction knowledge in planning, procurement, and field operations, applied throughout design, fabrication, and erection, not as a one-time value-engineering or review session [11:17][12:23].
### Spec References
AISC 303 Code of Standard Practice (the governing document, 2016 edition) with specific sections cited: 2.1 (definition of structural steel) [07:41], 2.2 (what is not structural steel) [08:42], 6.4 (fabrication tolerances) [55:32], Section 7 erection and 7.5.1 (anchor rod setting tolerances) [57:07], and commentary to 7.10.1 (lateral force resisting system statement) [17:35]. AISC 360 Specification Chapter N (QC, QA, and NDT, new in 2010) [71:15]; AISC 341 Seismic Provisions (designation of seismic force resisting system, protected zones, notch toughness) [16:02]. ASCE 37 design loads on structures during construction [64:02]. Material/product specs cited verbatim: ASTM A992, A500 grade C and grade B, A1085, A36, A572 grade 50 [24:49 through 26:22], and ASTM F3125 (which superseded the withdrawn A325/A490, retaining grade A325 and grade A490; bolt Groups A/B/C at 120/150 and 200 ksi) [26:22 through 26:54]. Also AISC Design Guide on constructability, the column base plate and anchor rod and vertical bracing design guides, the clean columns spreadsheet [48:03], IBC special inspection tables, and Blodgett "Design of Welded Structures" [51:46].
### Technical Details
Structural steel per 2.1 is the frame elements shown and sized in the design documents to support design loads (beams, columns, bracing, leveling plates) [07:41]. Connection design has three Code options: option 1 fully shown on the design documents (common on the West Coast and in seismic regions), option 2 selected/completed by an experienced detailer from tables with EOR-provided loads, and option 3 delegated to a licensed engineer (added to the Code in 2010), split into 3A and 3B for member reinforcement [43:52 through 48:03]. Member reinforcement (web openings, bearing stiffeners, doublers) is explicitly NOT connection design and stays with the EOR [47:02]. The lateral force resisting system may combine steel and non-steel elements (metal deck, concrete diaphragm, masonry shear walls, precast, open web joist, cold-formed) and must be identified for construction-stage stability [17:04].
### Fabrication Notes
The fabricator turns stock into assemblies and sources steel plus buyout items like bolts [29:57]. Shop stations walked through: cut to length on a band saw, hole-making by multi-spindle drills (top flange, bottom flange, web at once), mag drill for field holes, punching plus angle shear on an "angle master," coping by manual plasma torch or a multi-axis robotic plasma coper that also burns holes, and plasma tables for plate stiffeners and gussets [30:57 through 34:03]. Layout/assembly joins pieces by bolt or weld; the common shop weld processes are FCAW and GMAW (both wire-fed), plus submerged arc welding (SAW) with a preheater and powdered flux on items like plate-girder web-to-flange [33:32 through 35:04]. Steel need not be painted if it will be enclosed, fireproofed, or encased in concrete [35:39]. Fabrication tolerances live in Code section 6.4 and are coordinated with the erection tolerances [55:32].
### Erection Notes
The erector owns the means, methods, and safety of erecting the steel frame [53:55]. Before the erector starts, the ODRC (GC/CM) must provide access, a dry flat site, laydown/shakeout storage, foundations, setting lines, benchmarks, and installed anchor bolts; grouting under base plates is a separate trade the ODRC coordinates [19:42 through 20:46]. Columns are set on shims or leveling nuts until connected and plumbed. Erection tolerances in Section 7 have been essentially unchanged since 1959 and are tied to the H/500 out-of-plumb limit that yields the 0.002 direct-analysis notional load coefficient; a column may land up to 3 in out / 2 in toward the building exterior at the 36th floor and above [55:32 through 57:07]. The erector furnishes and installs temporary supports (typically wire rope with turnbuckles) sufficient against erection loads but need not consider others' work loads or hurricanes; ASCE 37 governs reduced construction wind, the CF shape factor for square-sided members, and limited shielding (only a 20% reduction past the third beam in a row) [62:29 through 67:07].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Anchor bolt placement tolerance is called out as a frequent field problem, drawing a laugh from the speaker's own office [58:07]. The Code treats moderate reaming, grinding, welding, cutting, and drift-pin drawing as normal erection operations; anything beyond that is a field error to be resolved [58:07]. Chapter N inspection tables flag tasks "observe" (random basis) versus "perform" (every welded joint or bolted connection), analogous to IBC periodic versus continuous; where both QC and QA letters match, coordinated inspection is allowed [73:50 through 74:56]. Bid-time risks named: unidentified member reinforcement quantities, blanket "design all connections for a percentage of UDL" notes (discouraged; provide actual member-end loads), and mismatched bolt groups (a Group A bolt forced into a Group B hole) [45:31][52:48].
### Bid / Cost Implications
The cost-to-influence curve is the central money lesson: the ability to influence cost is highest early and the cost of change grows exponentially once documents, fabrication, and erection begin [11:17]. Mill orders must be timed to the rolling schedule; once a mill order is released the EOR must lock member sizes and lengths because re-rolling can take months, and an accurate advance bill of materials is required [28:26 through 28:56]. A572 grade 50 plate often carries no surcharge over A36, giving 40% stronger connection material for free [25:51]. Member reinforcement is costly, so a heavier clean member can beat a reinforced one (the clean columns spreadsheet) [48:03]. Tight or constrained sites, owner-dictated erection sequences, hurricane-season bracing readiness, critical lifts (two-crane or over 75% capacity), and tighter-than-standard tolerances for AESS all add cost and must be priced and stated at bid time [42:50][56:03][67:38][80:33].
### Your Company Application
This webinar is the role-map for Your Company's own workstreams. Ivan's takeoff/estimating maps to the mill-order discipline: lock member sizes against AISC shape availability and the rolling schedule before committing, and price member reinforcement separately since aisc_validator.py only validates the base shape weight, not added doublers or stiffeners. The Code's three connection-design options frame our in-house PE stamp posture: when we delegate or self-perform under option 3, the EOR still owes member reinforcement (3A/3B), and our stamped substantiating package goes back to the EOR, not on every detailer sheet. Tekla detailing matches the 3D BIM/approval-documents role, CNC/DXF output, and model sharing; Mario's shop crew maps to FCAW/GMAW/SAW, coping, and fit-up; Paul's safety scope aligns with erector means-and-methods, temporary bracing, and critical-lift planning. Anchor-rod work ties directly to Code 7.5.1 tolerances coordinated with base-plate hole sizes (the recurring field-fit problem to watch on ACP controls), and field bolting should follow the Group A/B/F3125 cautions. One doctrine note: the speaker mentions metal building systems and names manufacturers (Nucor, New Core, Butler) generically as industry examples; Your Company positions as conventional structural steel with no PEMB language, so none of that framing carries into our outward copy. Doctrine conflict: NONE.

## Towards an Integrated Fracture-Control Plan for Steel Bridges
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7gG3OTxzOCA | Duration: 1:10:02 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is the 2018 T.R. Higgins lecture by Dr. Robert Connor of Purdue, on rethinking fracture-critical steel bridges as a risk problem rather than a member count [01:01]. The central idea is an integrated fracture-control plan: instead of treating every non-redundant tension member as automatically high-consequence, you engineer the fracture limit state the way you engineer buckling, controlling likelihood through tough material, fatigue-resistant details, and low stress ranges, and controlling consequence through redundancy analysis [23:40][51:19]. Connor argues "fracture critical member" is a misleading name driven by emotion, and that bridges built to the modern fracture-control plan have had no recorded fractures [03:35][48:17]. The payoff is rational inspection intervals in place of mandatory 24-month arms-length inspection.

### Spec References
The talk is bridge-code-centric, not building steel. Cited verbatim: AASHTO LRFD bridge design specifications (illustrative details to prevent constraint-induced fracture, plus temperature zones 1, 2, and 3) [16:29][67:20]; AWS D1.5 bridge welding code, specifically clause 12 as the fracture control plan and its commentary on intended scope [57:34][60:05]; the 2018 AASHTO Guide Specifications for Internal Redundancy of Mechanically Fastened Built-Up Steel Members [39:33]; the AASHTO Guide Specifications for system redundancy evaluation derived from NCHRP Project 12-87A, published as NCHRP Report 883 [44:09]; the Code of Federal Regulations special-inspection provision [40:04]; and the FHWA 2012 memo defining the system redundant member (SRM) [59:05]. Note: this is AWS D1.5 and AASHTO, not the AISC 360, AISC 341, AWS D1.1, or RCSC standards Your Company works under.

### Technical Details
Two redundancy mechanisms are distinguished: internal (member-level) redundancy, where a built-up member of angles, plates, and cover plates lacks a continuous crack path so a fracture cannot jump component to component, and system redundancy, where a composite deck and cross members let the bridge carry load after a full girder or chord fails [26:49][59:35]. The property that fractures do not propagate across riveted or bolted interfaces is named cross-boundary fracture resistance, valid only when the member stays within prescribed proportion and fatigue-life limits [39:03]. Two new evaluation load combinations were introduced, Redundancy I and Redundancy II, with Redundancy II being Strength I at reduced reliability indices of 1.5 or 2.5 on HL-93 loading [62:10]. Probability of detection data showed a 50-percent-detection crack near one inch and 90-percent detection requiring about a 5.5 inch crack, with some veteran inspectors detecting worse as cracks grew [22:38].

### Fabrication Notes
The relevant fabrication content is historical failure causation rather than current shop practice. Named root causes were electroslag repair welds where a spool change left a defect that a repair made worse (Neville Island) [13:56], poor-quality intersecting welds (Lafayette Street, Hoan) [15:29][16:29], and plug-welded filled holes in non-weldable steel that was meant to stay riveted (Delaware River) [17:00]. Connor stated that modern fabricators know not to plug-weld and that repair welds now carry strict procedure and inspection requirements [14:27][17:31]. Test specimens were full-scale 36 and 46 inch deep built-up girders, notched to grow sharp fatigue cracks, then cooled to between minus 60 and minus 120 Fahrenheit to force lower-shelf single-digit foot-pound toughness before loading [30:58].

### Erection Notes
There are no conventional building erection, sequencing, crane, or rigging procedures in this lecture. The nearest content is field demonstration: on the Milton-Madison bridge in Indiana the lower chord was severed in stages with shaped charges to prove internal redundancy, and even with the full chord cut and 300,000 pounds of sand at the panel point the bridge sagged only an additional three-eighths of an inch [28:50][29:23]. The practical erection-adjacent point is safety risk from inspection access: closing interstate lanes for snooper trucks creates queues that Connor cited as 24 times more likely to produce a serious accident after a short queue [20:35].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Several documented bridge failures were attributed to specific defects: the Silver Bridge I-bar with a defect the size of half a pinkie nail, hidden inside near the pin and undetectable by visual inspection [12:52]; the constraint-induced fracture detail with intersecting welds (Hoan three-girder) [16:29]; intersecting welds at a gusset (Lafayette Street) [15:29]; and electroslag repair-weld defects (Neville Island) [13:56]. Connor stressed that most of these were sudden pop-in fractures with no detectable fatigue cracking even under an electron microscope, so field inspection would not have caught them [17:00]. The inspector probability-of-detection study is itself the key inspection-failure finding: detection is highly variable, small cracks are routinely missed, and seniority is no guarantee of performance [22:08][23:10].

### Bid / Cost Implications
The economic thesis is that mandatory 24-month arms-length fracture-critical inspection is very expensive and often low-value [11:49]. Reclassifying a member as internally redundant (IRM) or system redundant (SRM) replaces FCM inspection with a special inspection at an owner-set or calculated interval, where a calculated 18-year faulted-state fatigue life yields a 9-year interval after a safety factor, rounded to 10 [41:36]. For Wisconsin twin-tub-girder bridges this removed the need for nighttime lane closures and inspectors crawling inside the boxes [46:12]. The broader cost argument is that engineering two-girder and tied-arch systems out of the FCM penalty unlocks more efficient, lower-cost structural forms [05:40].

### Your Company Application
Direct application to Your Company is limited because this is AASHTO and AWS D1.5 bridge work, while Your Company fabricates and erects conventional building steel under AISC 360, AWS D1.1, and RCSC. The transferable principles are the verify-don't-generate posture and the fatigue-and-toughness discipline: built-up member behavior, intersecting-weld avoidance, and repair-weld control are relevant to Mario Gutierrez as AWS welding lead even though the governing code differs, and the inspection probability-of-detection data reinforces why visual checks alone are weak, supporting Paul Guerrero's QC framing. For Ivan takeoff and Tekla detailing the practical note is to avoid intersecting welds and uncontrolled plug welds in detailing, a good-practice carryover not a new bid rate. No anchor-rod, joist, field-bolting, in-house PE stamp, or ACP-controls content appears here. Doctrine flag: NONE; nothing conflicts with Your Company doctrine, but this entry should be tagged bridge-domain so its AASHTO and D1.5 citations are never applied to a building-steel bid.

## Challenging Bridge Projects in Steel
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uEmnJDMvLmI | Duration: 1:13:17 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This session pairs two AECOM bridge case studies on highway plate-girder steel, both centered on the idea that erection and pour sequence change the internal forces in a continuous girder grid. The first talk (Shane Eavis) covers the 11th Street river bridge in Washington DC, where five of seven girders were already fabricated and erected when the owner asked to resequence construction, forcing a three-stage deck pour with a full-length longitudinal closure pour [05:40][11:20]. The controlling lesson stated repeatedly is that girders and cross frames connected together share load, so when you build a bridge in a different order it redistributes moments and shear through the grid [14:25][35:24]. The second talk (Chris Stein) covers the I-55 and Lake Shore Drive interchange in Chicago, focused on tight-radius curved girders, joint elimination, and coating selection.

### Spec References
The speakers cite AASHTO design code repeatedly but no AISC section, table, or Design Guide number is stated. Named references: the AASHTO bridge code for cross-frame spacing, with the speaker noting the old code said 25 feet while the new code "leaves it to you based on rational methods" [38:35]; AASHTO development-length and lap provisions that were shortened by analysis in the closure bay [32:21]; the 600-kip crash load to AASHTO for column design [50:39]; the "2012 AASHTO specifications and the 2013 interims" plus the IDOT bridge manual for the Chicago job [57:26]. Member buckling resolution credits "Columbus and Yura" for the principle that all three flanges cannot buckle independently [19:06]. For steel structural design these are bridge (AASHTO) rather than AISC 360/341 citations, so treat this as general principles for building work, no AISC section cited.

### Technical Details
Member and system types: five-span continuous plate-girder bridge, seven I-girder lines about ten feet on center, with inverted-K cross frames with a top chord spaced 17 to 20 feet, the top and bottom chords forming what the speaker calls a "pseudo box" for torsional stability of the grid [04:10][38:35][39:08]. Haunched girders were used over the piers for the DC bridge [05:10]. The lean-on bracing fix added bottom-flange bracing on girder six kicked back to girders five and seven to recover lateral-torsional buckling capacity, relying on the fact that adjacent girders are not loaded to maximum at the same time [18:36][19:06]. The Chicago job ran very tight radii down to a 469-foot innermost girder, 15-foot cross-frame spacing, flanges up to 24 inches wide, and only five plate sizes across 12 units and 40 spans [59:02][58:31]; cross frames were analyzed with MDX in plate-and-eccentric-beam mode, which the speaker says yields cross-frame forces about half those of a standard 2D grid [57:26].

### Fabrication Notes
On the DC resequencing, no changes to the as-fabricated steel were permitted, so camber profiles were already cut into the webs and cross-frame drops already fixed by geometry [07:14][09:18]. Field measurement of actual weld and gusset overlap mattered because shop drawings show a typical weld-all-around length but not how far an angle laps onto a gusset, or how the fabricator blocks out cross frames to reuse a common gusset size; a blank schematic was sent to the field to record real weld lengths [25:44][26:14]. Where a cross frame could not be made to fit, the fix was to remove the members from the gussets, install a blank gusset on the connector plate, then match-mark and field-drill the gusset to the connection plate [23:09]. The fabricator had material certs on site, so actual yield strengths were used in the reanalysis rather than notional code values [25:13]. Coating: the Chicago girders were metallized at about $0.50 per pound because hot-dip galvanizing cannot be done on the curved girders; splice plates, cross frames, and bearings were hot-dip galvanized where possible [62:09][63:40].

### Erection Notes
The DC bridge had five of seven girder lines erected, two cantilevered field pieces left off, over water with the erection barge already demobilized [07:14][12:52]. To resequence, cross-frame bolts in the closure bay were removed on one side and loosened on the other so the cross frame could swing out and avoid a spatial conflict as girders three through seven deflected down under deck while girders one and two stayed up [12:52][13:24]. The grid was then tuned along a thousand-foot length using staged loads: partial sidewalk and barrier placement, plus a 15-ton jack force and 5-to-15-ton counterweights, the jack also providing a resistive couple to keep the curved girders from walking outward off the connection holes [16:00][17:32][29:47][30:18]. Overhang brackets had to be set precisely because one side moved while the other stayed fixed, with constant geometry checks coordinated with the contractor [31:19].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
No code-inspection rejections are named; the failures discussed are analysis and fit-up driven. The central error called out is assuming a bridge built out of sequence carries the same forces as one built monolithically, which overloaded the cross frames in the leading bay near the discontinuous girders [09:48][35:24]. Fit-up risk was the controlling issue: out of 46 cross frames in the closure bay, 34 came in under the 3/8-inch differential the contractor said full-size drift pins could pick up, and 12 exceeded it; of those 12, only three actually needed the blank-gusset field-drill fix [22:38][23:40]. The Chicago job documents the existing 1965 deck reaching full-depth failures from 50 years of salting at simple-span joints [45:31][46:31]. The speaker also corrects the misconception that A490 bolts cannot be field welded or always break, noting good field QC keeps yield strength in the required bracket [27:14][27:44].

### Bid / Cost Implications
The DC resequencing salvaged nearly all of about 1,600 tons of erected steel (close to 1,400 tons of I-girder plus 217 tons of cross-frame steel), costing only a couple of angles for lean-on bracing and a few gusset plates [36:25][36:55]. The DC project was a $260 million design-build, where doing more interchange movements within budget won the work [02:40]. Schedule risk dominated the Chicago job: third-party Metra catenary wires not being removed put the contractor three to five months behind [52:41]. Cost choices included metallizing at roughly $0.50 per pound versus paint and galvanizing, minimizing plate sizes to five, eliminating 45 joints and reducing spans from 85 to 40 for durability, and avoiding fracture-critical straddle bents by holding spans near 180 feet [56:51][63:10][71:55][48:34]. Contracts were deliberately split smaller to attract big contractors busy with tollway work, yet the outbound contract still drew high bids while the inbound matched the engineer's estimate [68:18][68:50].

### Your Company Application
The strongest transferable lesson for Ivan's takeoff and the ACP project controls is that erection and pour sequence change member forces, so a sequence change after steel is fabricated is not free; on a connected frame the cross frames and bracing redistribute load, and refit at the connection holes governs whether the change is cheap or costly. This is the same connection-fit-up and tolerance discipline Your Company applies to anchor rods, and it argues for capturing erection sequence in Tekla detailing and flagging any owner-requested resequence to the in-house PE rather than absorbing it as field labor. The fit-up data point (target 3/8-inch differential picked up by full-size drift pins, blank-gusset match-drill as the fallback) is a concrete field-bolting tolerance Mario's crew can use as a go/no-go before forcing a connection. The field-verify-the-weld-length point reinforces verify-do-not-generate: shop typical weld callouts understate real lap, which matters for both Mario's welding estimate and Ivan's tonnage. The A490 field-weld correction supports good shop and field QC over blanket prohibition. Doctrine note: this is AASHTO bridge work, not AISC 360/341 building steel, and it uses bridge-specific systems (plate girders, cross frames, metallizing, fracture-critical straddle bents) that do not map to Your Company's conventional building-frame scope, so treat the sequencing and fit-up principles as transferable but do not import bridge spec citations into building bids. No conflict with Your Company doctrine; no PEMB language and no supplier names appear.

## ASCE 37: Design Loads on Structures During Construction [E17a]
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vZEKIeGhvJ4 | Duration: 1:25:39 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
The webinar, presented by Dave Ruby and Jeff Gasparot of Ruby and Associates, treats ASCE 37 as a source of construction-period loads but not as a design code. The repeated thesis is that ASCE 37 supplies the loads (dead, live, construction, wind, lateral earth pressure, temporary supports, sequencing effects) but does not say when, where, why, or how to apply them, and assigns no responsible party for field supervision [02:41][11:23][17:31][28:00]. The structure during erection is often controlled by higher wind because the open frame has no siding and no completed lateral load resisting system, so members and connections may need to be stronger than the permanent design required [14:28][15:29][34:00]. The governing idea is stability and load path: the frame must be stable at every stage as it is built one piece at a time, which means the erector runs the model many times, not once [07:17][08:21].
### Spec References
ASCE 37-14 (and prior ASCE 37-02) construction loads; ASCE 7-10 design loads with risk category two wind maps used during erection, given in LRFD and converted to ASD by dividing by 1.26 [50:29][53:35]. ASCE 37 duration reduction factor of 0.8 for a project lasting six weeks to one year [53:03]. Wind force equation F = qz x G x Cf, with gust factor G typically 0.85 and force coefficient Cf from 1.6 to 2.0, usually 1.8 in their practice [48:55][49:28]; velocity pressure 0.00256 x Kz x Kzt x Kd x V squared [49:58]. AISC Code of Standard Practice Section 1.8 was cited from the floor for responsibility of the EOR and erector [39:35]; the Code of Standard Practice requirement that the EOR define the lateral load resisting system in the general notes [20:37][74:34]. AISC Design Guide 10 (erection bracing), AISC Design Guide 23 (constructability of structural steel buildings, authored by Ruby), and AISC Design Guide 28 (stability of steel structures) [31:53]. AISC 360 referenced through IBC; general stability provisions in the AISC 14th edition Code of Standard Practice [19:35]. OSHA four-anchor-bolt requirement for iron workers [10:22].
### Technical Details
Wind pressure scales with velocity squared, so a 100 mph wind is 100 times a 10 mph wind, not 10 times [50:29]. Erection bracing is normally analyzed to about 73 mph: starting from the 115 mph LRFD map, divide by 1.26 to reach 92 mph ASD, then apply the 0.8 duration reduction to land near 73 mph [53:35][54:06]. A worked AISC design example showed permanent base shear of 168 kips rising to roughly 602 to 608 kips on the fully bare frame, because bare beams catch wind that would otherwise pass between decked floors [25:12][40:05]. The rule of thumb for cutting a truss free from the crane is span in inches over flange width (L over B): under 80 is generally fine, 80 to 100 needs a look, over 100 calls for engineering help [76:08]. Real-world reference: a 60 to 65 mph Midwest windstorm equates to about 9 to 13 psf, roughly half of full design and about 65 percent of the 73 mph erection-analysis load [56:41][57:43].
### Fabrication Notes
The webinar is erection-focused and gives little direct shop-fabrication guidance. The one clear fabrication-relevant point is truss top chord geometry: a wide-flange top chord turned so the web is horizontal gives substantially more bending capacity and axial strength than an 8-inch upright flange, which matters for unbraced setting length and weak-axis wind resistance [69:27][72:30]. It also notes that ultra-light framing chosen to minimize tonnage is not necessarily least cost once erection labor and temporary works are added [73:00][74:02].
### Erection Notes
Erection is the heart of the talk. Stability and a continuous load path must exist at every stage, the permanent lateral system may not yet be present, and the actual build sequence is often dictated by site logistics rather than the designer's intent [04:11][08:21]. The lateral load resisting system must be known so the erector can use completed portions as bracing, and special schedules for precast, masonry, or cladding that act as the final lateral system must be communicated since the first 15 to 25 percent of cladding adds wind sail without stability [20:37][23:40][50:00]. Case studies covered an 80-foot column on an undersized 6-foot by 6-foot foundation that would slide under full ASCE 37 wind (factor of safety near one at 60 mph), and a one-mile-long light industrial building where 40-foot joists on the column line and 8-inch truss top chords forced temporary sway frames and wire-rope horizontal bracing until enough deck was placed for diaphragm action [63:19][67:26][70:59]. Hurricane plans are required during the roughly eight-month hurricane season on the coast and must be installable in a day or two, with constant weather monitoring [51:01][104:00].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
A 45-foot freestanding column failed during fit-up: anchors were 3/4-inch A36 threaded rod on leveling nuts with no shims, set in a 6-inch by 6-inch pattern inside a 24-inch by 24-inch base plate [58:43][59:13]. Forcing a girder into the column applied about a 500-pound incidental load, generating roughly 22 kip-feet of moment against an anchor capacity near 19 kip-feet, causing tensile rupture and toppling [60:16][61:49]. The named lessons: push anchor bolts outside the column profile, question a tight anchor pattern inside a large base plate, never rely on leveling nuts to carry dead load, and add shims as cheap insurance [62:19][125:00]. A church roof collapse came from masonry shear walls shown only on architectural drawings and omitted from the structural set, leaving no load path [21:38].
### Bid / Cost Implications
Temporary works (false work, wire-rope bracing, temporary sway frames, added members to shorten unbraced length, hurricane bracing) are real costs that are routinely absent from the bid number, especially on light structures [71:59][73:00]. The explicit warning to erectors is do not base a bid on tonnage alone, because the lightest framing often carries the highest erection cost and you will take it on the chin [74:02]. When the lateral load resisting system is not in the general notes, fire an RFI back at the EOR asking for it in both directions before committing [74:34]. Wind contingency is also seasonal: building off hurricane season lets the erector use the lower 115 mph base, while in season the Miami case could require on the order of 200 times the temporary bracing [51:01][52:02].
### Your Company Application
For Ivan, this confirms the doctrine that tonnage alone is not a bid: light long-span jobs with small foundations and joists on column lines need a temporary-works cost line, and any set missing the lateral load resisting system in the general notes should trigger an RFI before pricing. For Paul Guerrero, the erection-stability, hurricane-plan, and incidental-load failure modes (Gulf Coast wind, the 73 mph bracing baseline, weather monitoring on the red phone) map directly to Houston site safety. For our anchor-rod design, setting, and tolerance work this is the strongest single source: it argues to spread the 3/4-inch (and larger) anchors outside the column profile, never to leave a 6 x 6 pattern inside a 24-inch base plate, to require shims rather than trusting leveling nuts for dead load, and to treat the 500-pound fit-up beating force as a real design case. For the in-house PE stamp, ASCE 37 plus AISC Design Guides 10, 23, and 28 and Code of Standard Practice Section 1.8 are the citation backbone for any erection-engineering or stability deliverable. For Tekla detailing, turning a wide-flange truss top chord web-horizontal and checking the L-over-B (80/100) cut-free rule should be standard. For joists, the warning that 40-foot joists carry only 600 to 1,000 pounds of compression affects how Mario's crew braces and sequences them. For ACP controls, the survey-at-temperature lesson (8 to 12 inches of thermal sway) reinforces tying field survey points to a controlled time of day. Doctrine conflict: NONE. The material is conventional structural steel erection engineering with no PEMB language and no supplier names.

## Entertaining With Steel, From Theatrical Rigging to Concert Touring Stages
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vcguOi022pE | Duration: 58:03 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
Bill Goren of McLaren Engineering Group's entertainment division walks through why structural steel is the controlling material for the heaviest entertainment work: theatrical rigging, concert touring stages, themed sculptures, amusement rides, and animatronic show structures [02:03][03:34]. The recurring theme is that aesthetics, motion ranges, and tight field tolerances drive the geometry, and steel earns its place over aluminum and wood on stiffness, fatigue resistance, ductile failure, impact resistance, weldability with low distortion, and worldwide availability for touring [09:13][09:44][10:16]. Steel is chosen even where it is heavier because it survives being thrown around on trucks and welds with less warping than aluminum [10:49][47:16].
### Spec References
No AISC 360 sections, AISC 341 seismic provisions, AWS D1.1 clauses, RCSC provisions, or numbered Design Guides are cited verbally in this talk. The only named standards are the ASTM amusement-ride standards governing ride engineering responsibility [38:18][38:49] and TUV, the German certifying agency that required several thousand pages of calculations over six months for the Macau dragon gondola towers [21:40]. Bolt and connection types are named generically (A325, A490, slip-critical, pins) but no spec section accompanies them, so treat these as general principles, no section cited.
### Technical Details
Connection and system types span pinned connections favored for speed of erection over A325/A490 bolts [08:11], custom tubular cross sections fabricated from plate cutouts with rolled sides joined tab-in-slot like a jigsaw [26:21], internally sleeved column splices with flat countersunk bolts in tapped holes to hide fasteners under cladding [26:52][28:57], ring (crane) bearings five feet in diameter standardized across four turntables so they could be ordered together [35:41][36:13], and slip-critical A325 bolted moment connections forming a portal frame in a theater [53:33]. Member sizing leans on tubes for the strongest cross section under strange multi-axis and torsional forces, with finite-element modeling of body segments on the dragon and cable-stay vibration analysis tuned with pretension so foe rods would not flutter except in extreme wind [16:30][19:35].
### Fabrication Notes
Tolerances on themed work exceeded architecturally exposed structural steel requirements: the treehouse at Crystals had tighter tolerances than AESS and allowed no exposed bolts, forcing nuts inside beams with access holes and detailer-modeled wrench reach to make up the connections [26:21][28:23][28:57]. The Macau dragon bull-wheel center had to land inside a one-inch-radius sphere 60 feet in the air, met with spherical washers, Teflon alignment pads, longitudinal slots, and Enerpac hydraulic pancake actuators adjusting under load before tie rods locked it off [15:59][17:01][18:04]. Wall sections were replaced with thick local plates welded from both sides to handle concentrated forces, and lift machines were detailed for removal through a hatch with four bolts for service [29:27][36:45].
### Erection Notes
Erection sequencing is brutal on these structures because geometry, balance, and access fight back. The dragon used temporary shores under the neck, then a controlled handoff where releasing a pin and removing a strut confirmed load transfer to the cable stays and bull-wheel rope [18:04][18:34]. Touring practice favors pins over bolts because a pin takes thirty seconds versus three minutes for a bolt, and across many connections that delta makes or breaks a show schedule; U2's tour leapfrogged three claw structures across stadium sites so one was always being finished while shows ran [08:11][08:41]. In a theater no crane can enter, so a mast-mounted arm with a chain motor lifted an aluminum truss assembly and lift crews bolted it to column tops [53:03][53:33].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
No formal rejection categories or inspection-failure types are enumerated. The named risk is loss of quality control on overseas work: the Sentosa crane dance had the engineer of record value-engineered out, leaving the team unsure whether paint and welding QC requirements were followed [44:07]. Aluminum was rejected for the salt-water animatronics because welded aluminum carries fatigue problems, lacks an endurance limit, and demands higher welding QC than fewer qualified Asian fabricators could reliably hit [47:16][47:46]. The fee-estimating caution was to price carefully and conservatively and re-price after schematic design [22:12].
### Bid / Cost Implications
Fees on one-off entertainment structures are estimated conservatively at schematic design and revised once the final design is known, sometimes with a staffed presence through fabrication and installation written into scope [22:12][22:43]. Connection method directly drives the schedule budget: pins over bolts to compress load-in and load-out, since on the Roger Waters tour a million-dollar flying rig added 45 minutes to load-out and got cut because the act could not afford the time [55:35][56:06]. A 30-day temporary-structure limit being exceeded reclassified a Seattle show as a permanent building, triggering higher importance factors and a code fight before fire-treated lumber was allowed [52:02][52:33].
### Your Company Application
This Tier 2 talk is adjacent to Your Company's conventional structural steel work rather than core to it, but several threads transfer. Ivan should note the discipline of conservative schematic-stage fee estimates with re-pricing after design lock, and that connection method (pin versus bolt) is a schedule cost line, not just a detailing choice. Mario's welding leadership maps to the distortion and fatigue arguments for steel over aluminum, and to the overseas-QC failure where unverified weld inspection sank confidence, which reinforces our verify-do-not-generate posture and AWS D1.1 documentation on every joint. Tekla detailing and the in-house PE stamp connect to the AESS-beating tolerances, hidden countersunk bolts, internally sleeved column splices, and detailer-modeled wrench access shown here, all relevant when ACP or any exposed-steel scope demands clean connections; the spherical-washer and slotted-plate alignment tricks are a useful reference for hard anchor-rod and field-fit tolerance cases. Doctrine flags: NONE. No PEMB language, no supplier names, and nothing here conflicts with locked rates or AISC-validator sourcing, since the talk cites no member weights for us to trust.

## ATFP Retrofits for Unconventional Buildings
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p__OuSqnNFk | Duration: 1:00:51 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is a blast and progressive-collapse retrofit webinar by two physical-security engineers from Thornton Tomasetti, covering anti-terrorism force-protection (ATFP) upgrades to two existing steel and concrete buildings that were never designed for those loads [02:12]. The teaching focus is which federal security standard governs (DoD owned versus DoD leased versus other federal agencies), how blast facade hardening and progressive-collapse mitigation interact, and how to develop reactions into an existing structure that has nothing substantial to anchor to. It is a structural-retrofit and detailing webinar, not an AISC member-design course, so steel-spec content is thin and the dominant standards are the security UFCs and ISC documents.

### Spec References
The standards named are mostly federal security criteria, not AISC: UFC 4-010-01 minimum anti-terrorism standards for DoD owned facilities, spoken as "UFC 4-1001" [04:14]; the companion UFC blast and progressive-collapse documents spoken as "4-2001" and "4-1002" [10:35]; the Interagency Security Committee (ISC) standards that govern DoD leased and most non-DoD federal space per a December 2012 DoD memo [07:25]; "PDC TR 06" / "PDC TR 1006", the Protective Design Center technical report for ductility and rotation response limits in single-degree-of-freedom analysis [13:13][13:46]; and the GSA interpretation document for ISC facilities [13:46]. AISC-adjacent references stated once at [17:21] are ASCE 59-11 (spoken "ASC 59 11"), AISC Steel Design Guide 26 (spoken "ASC steel design guide 26"), and the AISC blast and progressive-collapse resource; the speaker notes these are not formally referenced by the UFC or ISC but are useful. No AISC 360 section, AISC 341 seismic provision, AWS D1.1 clause, or RCSC bolting reference was cited.

### Technical Details
Case one is a 130,000 SF three-story steel building, originally a tennis dome with two wings of column-free space framed by three 120-foot trusses carrying bar joists, later infilled with two structurally independent steel-framed office floors on open-web joists and a thin 1.5-inch slab on 9/16-inch rolled deck [17:51][18:55][24:28]. Because that thin slab and the open-web joists gave nothing to anchor to, the facade fix was a three-story cable-catch system: shatter-resistant film on the glass plus half-inch cables (about 20,000 lb break strength each) run from a new ground-floor grade beam up to new tubes on the roof underside, with sacrificial fuse plates (knife plates, slotted holes, Teflon bearing pads that slide) so a half-inch cable could survive 100 psi-msec impulse loads that otherwise demanded inch-plus cables at 50,000 to 60,000 lb [24:58][27:30][28:32]. Case two is a 2013 post-tensioned concrete office with banded and uniform tendons; the facade fix was security film plus an HSS steel-tube backup behind every vertical mullion, connected by discontinuous aluminum extrusions at three points, with bent edge plates that bear on the slab inbound and FRP plus epoxy developing the rebound (outbound) force without drilling anchors into the PT slab [40:21][42:22][46:28][49:38]. Progressive collapse on case two used the GSA-allowed specific-local-resistance method: harden columns for the defined threat rather than do alternate-path column removal, ultimately a four-sided steel jacket on the columns [41:52][57:26].

### Fabrication Notes
The engineer of record detailed all the connections in-house rather than delegating reactions to a steel fabricator, because the multiple loading cases, large eccentricities, and very high blast forces made delegated connection design impractical [32:39]. A steel fabricator was brought on early and worked directly with the engineer on connection layout to fit the fabricator's tolerances and the field tolerances of an existing building [32:39]. On case two, steel tubes were chosen over aluminum backups partly because aluminum extrusions had a long lead time while steel tube was readily available, and tube-plus-knife-plate assemblies were fabricated first so the aluminum extrusions could drop in later [43:54][44:57]. Plates were coped as much as possible to cut weight and material cost, because every piece had to ride the building elevators, and the coping and sequencing of which plate went where was described as quite complicated [52:15].

### Erection Notes
Both retrofits were erected from inside the occupied or finished shell because schedule barred removing the roof, the windows, or the facade [22:58][35:43]. Ring beams and column-pickup assemblies had to be buildable inside and lifted into place; on case one, collars and rods were dropped through the slab to grab columns from above [37:50][38:20]. On case two, all steel moved through the elevators, so weight and plate size were hard erection constraints, and overhead FRP installation made the contractor nervous but went fine [52:15][51:44]. Selective demolition before erection mattered: the drawings showed a three-inch slab-to-curtainwall gap but as-built ranged from zero to three inches due to construction tolerance, so details had to be adjusted in the field [50:09][50:41].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
No formal inspection-failure or rejection categories were named; the warnings are field lessons. Trusting the construction documents was the recurring error: the case-two shop drawings were treated as the as-built and proved conflicting, and the actual slab edge condition forced detail revisions [45:58][50:09]. A demonstrated bad practice from a separate building was cables fished through drilled holes in steel angle and wrapped loosely around members, not pulled tight, which the speaker said will fray off when they scrape the steel and fail because cable systems depend on pretension [30:35][31:07]. Cutting through and failing to restore fire-stopping at the slab edge was flagged as an easy miss, resolved by working with the firestop manufacturer [51:11].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Schedule was the dominant cost driver, not material: case one ran a three-month design and six-month construction window, and the team explicitly said most of these retrofits would not be chosen for ninety percent of buildings if schedule were not forcing the decision [21:26][39:20]. Procurement lead time drove material choice, with long-lead aluminum extrusions losing to readily available steel tube [43:54]. Hidden site costs were large: removing and reinstalling multi-ton precast panels at an urban location required pulling sidewalk and pavers and a special permit, a major cost line [54:22]. Constant on-site presence and tight architect-contractor-subcontractor coordination were repeatedly cited as the price of these short-duration jobs [59:31].

### Your Company Application
This entry maps best to in-house PE stamp and Tekla detailing rather than routine bidding: the take-home is that on a heavily-constrained retrofit, the engineer of record should detail connections in-house rather than delegate reactions to the fabricator when eccentricities and load cases are extreme, which is how a small shop with an in-house PE can keep control of unusual work. For Ivan takeoff, the lesson is that as-built and shop drawings on existing buildings are unreliable, so any retrofit or tie-in bid should carry a field-scan/selective-demo line and a tolerance contingency rather than trusting stated dimensions, consistent with our verify-do-not-generate posture. For anchor-rod and connection work, the FRP-plus-epoxy and bearing-plate approach to developing rebound force without drilling a PT slab is a useful pattern for edge-of-slab tie-ins where embedment is impossible. Mario shop and Paul safety relevance is limited here; overhead work and elevator-constrained piece weights are the only crossover. No conflict with Your Company doctrine: this is conventional structural-steel retrofit content with no PEMB language, and nothing here touches BID_RATES, AISC weights, or supplier lists. NONE.

## Recommendations for Improved Steel Design
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5yR7yjfLqJI | Duration: 54:46 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is a two-part AASHTO LRFD steel I-girder BRIDGE webinar, not a building-code session, so most content maps to bridge superstructure design rather than Your Company's conventional building work. Part one (Dominic Coletti, HDR) covers practical implementation of stability bracing strength and stiffness requirements for cross frames and diaphragms that brace girders against lateral-torsional buckling [00:30][02:03]. Part two (Dennis Galabek, formerly FDOT) covers estimating wind loads on partially constructed I-girder bridges that are erected on substructure supports with no deck yet in place [25:45][28:21]. The shared theme is bracing and stability of bare steel before the composite deck hardens.
### Spec References
Cited verbatim by the speakers: the stability bracing provisions originated in Dr. Joseph Yura's University of Texas at Austin work published in the AISC Engineering Journal in 2001, adopted by AISC for buildings in Appendix 6.3, and reproduced in the FHWA Steel Bridge Design Handbook Volume 13 (bracing system design, first November 2012, updated late 2017) [04:36][05:06]. AASHTO LRFD load combinations and factors are in Chapter 3 [09:10]; construction load factors are in AASHTO LRFD Article 3.4.2 [27:19][36:58]; and the cited steel articles are 6.5.1 (stages of construction), 6.7.4.1 (top-flange stability before deck hardens), 6.10.3 (constructibility / discretely braced flange), and 6.7 third load path for wind distribution [38:29][40:33]. Wind methodology references ASCE 7-10 (three-second gust), with AASHTO adopting the three-second gust in the 2016 interims [27:19][30:23]. No building AISC 360, AISC 341, AWS D1.1, or RCSC sections were cited; this is an AASHTO bridge talk.
### Technical Details
Stability bracing is governed by two Yura equations, one for required cross-frame stiffness and one for required strength expressed as a moment demand, both driven by the factored girder design moment M sub F, span L, unbraced length (cross-frame spacing), girder depth h sub o, and girder stiffness [05:36][06:06]. Provided cross-frame stiffness is the inverse sum of three flexibilities: system stiffness beta-e (conservatively based on two girders), web distortional stiffness beta-sec (taken as infinity for a full-depth cross frame), and in-plane girder stiffness beta-g [12:49][13:51][14:53]. The worked example gave M sub F of 77,000 kip-in (Strength I controlling), required stiffness 225,000 kip-in/rad, provided 272,000 kip-in/rad, so the brace passed [19:59]. Part two ties wind pressure to a spacing-to-depth (s/D) ratio: at s/D less than 3 heavy shielding lets you apply CP 2.2 to the projected superstructure height, while s/D greater than 3 loses shielding and loads interior girders [31:24][36:28].
### Fabrication Notes
No shop fabrication, fit-up, or QC content appears; the talk is design-side bridge engineering and does not address shop processes.
### Erection Notes
The central erection concern is that bare girders standing on substructure before the deck hardens are braced only at discrete cross-frame points, and wind on this partially constructed system can cause large lateral deflection and sway [02:34][38:59]. The presenter showed video of a long-span erection where cantilevers and mid-spans visibly flexed under roughly 50 mph wind, motivating deflection criteria such as L/150 [38:59][39:32]. Wind estimates also size the temporary restraints needed before anchor bolts are set and govern loads handed to the specialty engineer for falsework design [38:29][52:59]. Florida applies a 0.6 velocity modifier for construction periods under a year and a reduced 20 mph case when the contractor is actively on site and can watch the weather [45:12][45:43].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The speaker noted recent steel I-girder bridge construction problems traced back to inadequate cross-frame and diaphragm bracing, which is why the stiffness and strength check matters [23:37]. A flagged design error is over-conservatism, using the maximum negative moment directly over the pier instead of moving out to the first cross-frame line where bearings and anchor bolts provide restraint [11:46]. A second flagged mistake is combining maximum factored construction dead and live load with maximum factored wind, since a deck is not cast during a windstorm [10:14].
### Bid / Cost Implications
The estimating takeaway is that including stability bracing forces on top of wind raised cross-frame design loads only modestly, and the example resolved to routine 5x5x7/16 angles for chords and diagonals, so the check rarely drives steel weight up [21:31][22:02]. The cost warning is on the temporary side: under-shielding or over-estimating wind beefs up falsework members and, more expensively, the temporary foundations under that falsework grow large and costly, so the goal is a reasonable system-level wind estimate, not a padded per-girder number [52:59].
### Your Company Application
This is bridge-specific AASHTO content with limited direct transfer to Your Company's conventional building bids, so Ivan should treat it as reference, not a takeoff basis. The transferable principle is real: bare steel before a deck hardens is braced only at discrete points and is most exposed to wind during erection, which supports flagging temporary bracing, anchor-rod restraint, and falsework loads in erection planning for Mario and Paul rather than assuming the final-condition load path. The anchor-bolt-provides-restraint-at-the-pier note reinforces our anchor-rod setting and tolerance discipline. Confidence is medium since the worked numbers are bridge girders, not building frames. Doctrine flags: NONE. No supplier names, no PEMB language, no invented sections; all citations above are spoken by the presenters.

## Night School 6, Session 1: Basic Principles
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8J0O37WiNzg | Duration: 1:31:15 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
William Thornton, the 1995 TR Higgins lecturer and longtime chair of the AISC Committee on Manuals, teaches the foundation for bracing-connection design: the lower bound theorem of limit analysis and the principle that a connection model must stay true to the main-member design assumptions [27:54], [38:23]. The central claim is that a designer may choose any internal force distribution that satisfies equilibrium and does not exceed any limit state, and provided the steel is ductile enough to redistribute, that distribution yields a safe connection [43:33], [45:04]. The corollary is that the admissible force field which maximizes connection capacity is closest to the true collapse solution, so a smarter load path is both safe and cheaper [47:45]. He frames connection design as the "last bastion of rational design" because complex bracing connections cannot be solved by frame-analysis software and must be built from free-body diagrams and first principles [29:28], [33:03].
### Spec References
AISC 360 (14th edition) chapters cited: Chapter B (local buckling, definition of a simple connection), Chapter D net tension and shear lag with Table D3.1, Chapter J as the principal connections chapter, Chapter K for HSS (noted but not covered), Appendix 3 fatigue (noted not covered), and Chapter M tolerances on column bearing/mating surfaces and shimming [05:10], [06:10], [16:01]. Specific Chapter J sections: J2.4 weld and base-metal rupture (the 14th edition dropped the base-metal yield check that the 13th had) [08:13], [78:35]; J3 bolts; J3.7 and J3.9 bearing-connection and slip-critical shear-tension interaction [09:16]; J3.10 bolt bearing and bolt tear-out [09:47]; J4.1 connecting-element tension yielding/rupture (he prefers "fracture"), J4.2 shear, J4.4 buckling of connecting elements with the slenderness-25-or-less yield-controls note [10:17]. Seismic: AISC 341-10 general provisions and AISC 358-10 prequalified moment connections (noted not covered) [07:11], [08:13]. Section B3.6a is cited for simple/rotational connections [13:23], [13:55]. RCSC is named as the specification for structural joints using high-strength bolts covering A325/A490 and their twist-off variants [16:33], [17:35]. AWS D1.1 is named the structural welding bible, AWS D1.8 the seismic welding supplement [18:06], [18:36]. Design Guides named by number: DG 17 high-strength bolting (Kulak) and DG 21 welded connections (Miller) [20:07]. Manual parts cited: Part 7 eccentric bolts, Part 8 eccentric welds, Part 9 connecting elements and prying with Whitmore, Part 10 simple shear connections, Part 13 bracing connections / uniform force method, and Table 1-7A workable gauges for angle legs [12:53], [40:58]. Code of Standard Practice three connection-design options [22:09].
### Technical Details
The Code of Standard Practice gives three options for who designs connections: option 1, complete connection design shown on the structural drawings by the engineer of record; option 2, an experienced detailer selects from manual tables for simple connections; option 3, connections designed by a licensed engineer working for or hired by the fabricator [22:41], [25:49]. Under option 1 the EOR must show everything: bolt sizes, spacing, edge distances, gauge, pitch, and weld size and type, and a bare CJP symbol no longer means CJP under current AWS D1.1, it only means a weld that develops the strength of the base metal [23:11], [23:43]. The uniform force method gives one of infinitely many statically admissible force distributions for a highly indeterminate bracing connection, defined by the geometric parameter r and four edge forces [36:46], [37:18]. A three-bar tension example shows that every equilibrium-satisfying split is safe but only the compatible split (one third each) reaches the true 100-unit capacity, demonstrating the corollary [49:17], [53:26]. Bolt gauges for angles are placed on the workable gauge line from Table 1-7A, not the gravity axis, and the small resulting eccentricity is ignored for bolted angles by long-standing practice, while welded connections balance to the gravity axis [39:56], [74:21].
### Fabrication Notes
The economic comparison is the fabrication-cost heart of the session. A single bracing connection by the uniform force method ran about $664 versus about $844 by the kiss method, roughly $182 per connection, which on a 40-story building with 32 connections per floor reaches about a quarter million dollars in material and fabrication alone, before erection and shipping [65:23], [65:55]. On a Georgia job the optimized load path saved about $2 million against the owner-engineer budget, with 80 percent savings in column drilling time because fewer columns had to be drilled, 50 percent savings in weld consumables, 60 percent savings in welding labor, and 30 percent material savings from thinner plates [68:36], [71:40]. The optimized detail used 5/16 inch fillet welds instead of 5/8, a 1/2 inch plate instead of 1 inch, and 3/4 inch bolts [70:09]. He notes X-type (threads-excluded) bolts give higher shear value and are warranted once plate thickness near the nut is about 3/4 inch or more, with a thickness table in a "practical connections" reference [69:06].
### Erection Notes
Shear tabs are favored mainly for erection: a beam with a shear-tab/gusset can be brought in laterally and set easily, whereas double-clip angles must be jammed between column flanges or dropped down a column web, which becomes a problem when stiffeners are present [81:43], [82:15]. The tab trades a single-shear bolt pattern (sometimes more bolts) for a faster field set, and the shop bolt cost is more than offset by erection savings [82:15], [82:45]. Double clips have the advantage that the beam can be cut slightly short and the slack taken up in the setback dimension on the clips, while an end plate must be cut nearly exact or the piece is stuck [83:17], [83:49]. He also notes OSHA has had structural-connection erection requirements in place for roughly 15 years that the engineer must respect [21:08].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The recurring failure mode is an inadmissible force field that does not satisfy equilibrium, which voids the lower bound theorem and leaves the connection unverifiable [60:12], [62:14]. Historical American Bridge and Bethlehem practice ignored gusset couples and work-point location, and Thornton warns that detail would be caught today by a building inspector or peer reviewer and rejected [63:48], [64:19]. He cites real consequences of bad detailing: a ferry-terminal ramp connection done by hand outside the frame software failed and killed about half a dozen people, and the Hyatt Regency 1981 walkway collapse is referenced as engineers citing the Code of Standard Practice without knowing its contents [30:29], [22:09]. A named drafting defect is referencing a bare weld symbol without size, or omitting bolt pitch, on an option-1 mandated connection [24:15], [24:45]. A common knowledge gap is engineers who cannot draw a free-body or shear/moment diagram without software [33:03].
### Bid / Cost Implications
Thornton estimates that about 50 percent of the cost of erected steel is tied to connection design once you count design, detailing, shop drawings, fabrication, shipping, erection, and finishing [66:33]. The per-connection and per-building dollar comparisons make method choice a real bid lever: for one or two connections the method barely matters, but across hundreds or thousands of repeated connections the uniform force method's cheaper load path compounds into six- and seven-figure differences [63:48], [65:55]. The Georgia job's $2 million saving came from choosing the admissible force field that minimized welds, plate thickness, and column drilling [68:36], [71:40]. The takeaway for estimating is that a load-path choice, not just member tonnage, drives connection cost and should be considered when comparing bids.
### Your Company Application
This session is directly relevant to Your Company as an option-3 shop that designs its own connections under an in-house PE stamp: the Code of Standard Practice three-option framework defines exactly what the PE must verify when the EOR mandates a connection versus when Your Company selects one [22:41], [25:49]. For Ivan's takeoff and estimating, the 50-percent connection-cost figure and the per-connection method comparison justify treating connection load path as a cost driver, not just feeding tonnage through aisc_validator.py [66:33], [65:55]. Mario's shop crew benefits from the welded-detail economics (smaller fillets, fewer drilled holes, thinner plates) and the X-bolt thread-exclusion threshold near 3/4 inch plate [69:06], [71:40]. Paul's safety scope connects to the OSHA structural-erection requirements and the shear-tab erection advantage that reduces unsafe jamming of members between flanges [21:08], [82:15]. Tekla detailing should follow the Table 1-7A workable angle gauges and show complete bolt and weld data so a mandated connection is not flagged on review [40:58], [24:15]. No conflict with Your Company doctrine: nothing here touches BID_RATES or AISC weights, the content is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language, and all spec section numbers are quoted as the speaker stated them. DOCTRINE_FLAGS: NONE.

## Night School 6, Session 2:  Uniform Force Method
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6OmazwL3dAE | Duration: 1:25:58 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This session, presented by William A. Thornton (Cives Corporation, TR Higgins 1995 and AISC Lifetime Achievement 2003), develops the Uniform Force Method (UFM), the geometric method for distributing forces in a vertical (diagonal) bracing connection gusset [03:01]. The method evolved from AISC-sponsored finite-element research by Ralph Richard at the University of Arizona in the mid 1980s [03:31]. Its core idea is to force the brace force, the gusset-to-beam force, and the gusset-to-column force to intersect at a single concurrent point so the gusset is in equilibrium with no couples [03:31, 04:01]. The controlling constraint is alpha minus beta times tangent theta equals e-sub-B times tangent theta minus e-sub-C, where alpha and beta locate the gusset connection centroids, e-sub-B is the beam half depth, e-sub-C is the column half depth, and theta is measured from vertical [05:38, 11:53]. When the actual connection centroids alpha-bar and beta-bar do not satisfy that constraint, real couples (moments) appear on the gusset edges that must be designed for [06:09].
### Spec References
Thornton cites the AISC Manual Part 13 (the bracing-connection / UFM section) repeatedly as the home of all the UFM formulas, special cases, and the optimization routine, stating it is identical in the 13th and 14th editions and traces back to the 2nd and 3rd edition LRFD manuals [25:17, 30:29, 39:48, 77:06]. The worked example is run to the 14th edition Manual as an ASD problem [15:29]. He references his own 1991 AISC National Steel Construction Conference paper and his 1995 TR Higgins paper [54:47], a forthcoming AISC Design Guide for the non-orthogonal case (number not stated) [58:20], and a book edited by Akbar Tamboli (Claude/Akbar Tamboli, 2nd edition, ~1999) for the non-orthogonal UFM derivation [57:50, 67:07]. No specific AISC 360 section numbers, AISC 341 seismic sections, AWS D1.1 clauses, or RCSC sections are spoken; bolt callouts are given as ASTM A325 (3/4 inch and the example tab at 7/8 inch) [15:29, 47:32].
### Technical Details
The constraint is derived live by writing the three line equations (brace line, gusset-to-beam force line through control point A, gusset-to-column force line through control point B), solving pairs for the common point Q, and equating [09:46, 11:22]. Edge forces are written as P over R times a length term: H-sub-B, H-sub-C, V-sub-B, V-sub-C, where R is the geometric distance from the work point to where a vertical from the gusset-to-beam centroid meets a horizontal from the gusset-to-column centroid [13:26, 14:26]. A critical computational rule: R must be calculated with the constraint-satisfying alpha and beta, never with alpha-bar [19:39, 22:12]. Four special cases are covered: case 1 (non-concentric work point, e.g. at the gusset corner, which always produces couples in the beam and column distributed by an alpha factor of I/L) [32:33, 35:07]; case 2 (transfer some brace vertical V-sub-B to the column via Delta-V to relieve beam shear) [36:08]; case 3 (very shallow or very steep brace connected to only one member, leaving an unavoidable M-sub-EC couple) [41:53]; and the newly named special case 4 (a column-web connection treated like a flange connection by setting e-sub-C equal to the distance out to the first column of bolts rather than zero) [43:29].
### Fabrication Notes
The economic core of the session is special case 4 versus the conventional kiss-method double-clip approach, compared in a force-and-quantity table [48:33]. Using extended and conventional shear tabs in place of double clips eliminated drilling holes in jumbo columns with four-inch flanges [45:32]. The optimized design used 24 standard holes versus 14, one-inch plate versus half-inch, 7/8 inch bolts versus 3/4 inch, giving only 21 percent of the hole-drilling volume, an 80 percent savings in drilling time [48:33, 50:38]. Weld comparison: a 5/8 inch fillet is a six-pass weld, so 30 inches of 5/8 fillet equals 180 inches of single-pass weld, while the optimized 5/16 fillet at 52.3 inches stays single pass, yielding roughly 50 percent or more savings in welding consumables and the optimized tab weighing about 71 percent of the standard [49:34, 50:38]. Thornton notes there is no commercial software for these connections; even his firm calculates each from scratch [65:36].
### Erection Notes
Erection is treated mainly through the connection-type tradeoff and the truss examples rather than sequencing or rigging. He cites a 60 percent (possibly 70 percent) labor savings from the tab approach on the case-4 job [50:38]. The headline jobsite economics: the engineer of record reported the special-case-4 job finished about two million dollars below the estimated cost, in part by replacing traditional double clips at jumbo columns to cut both fabrication and erection cost [45:01, 45:32]. A Boston building example shows a 38-story tower where 30-plus stories sit on main trusses, with a jack-truss gusset slotted through a near-side main-truss gusset to land roughly a 2,000 kip vertical component dead center on the main-truss vertical [59:22, 59:54]. No crane, bracing, or shoring procedures are detailed.
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The repeated error called out is substituting alpha-bar for alpha when computing R, which violates equilibrium and is caught by the check that V-sub-B plus V-sub-C must equal the brace vertical component (P cosine theta) and H-sub-B plus H-sub-C must equal the horizontal component (P sine theta) [22:12, 22:43]. On X-bolts (oversize / bolts in shear plane usage), Thornton notes extra inspection can be avoided if the ply next to the nut is thick enough to keep threads out of the shear plane; for a one-inch bolt with flush nut and no washer the ply needs to be about 13/16 inch, dropping to about 5/8 with a 5/32 washer or 3/8 with a quarter-inch stick-through, otherwise N-type (threads-included) bolts are used on thin webs or plates [44:31, 46:32, 47:02]. The limit-state list validating the UFM against six full-scale tests (University of Alberta tension tests and three NIST tests by John Gross and Geraldine Cheok, ~1989) included bolt fracture, Whitmore buckling, Whitmore yield, block shear with the tearout-versus-bearing distinction, with test-to-predicted ratios near 1.01 to 1.11 [54:47, 55:48, 56:19].
### Bid / Cost Implications
Thornton states connections can account for up to 50 percent of the cost of erected structural steel, though a simple brace connection like the first example is closer to 15 to 20 percent [64:34]. The quantified savings on the case-4 job (about two million dollars under estimate, 80 percent less drilling, ~50 percent less weld consumable, ~60 to 70 percent less labor, ~29 percent lighter tab steel) show that connection-method choice, not just member tonnage, drives erected cost [45:32, 48:33, 50:38]. He warns that specifying beam shear as a percentage of UDL (uniform design load), such as half or three-quarters UDL, inflates the design shear far above real floor loads (he estimates implied loads of 1,000 to 2,000 psf versus a real ~200 psf), forcing special case 2 and expensive doubler plates that real gravity loads would avoid [36:39, 40:51, 41:53]. Because no software exists, every non-standard bracing connection carries real engineering labor that must be priced.
### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff and estimating, this session is direct evidence that connection method, special case 4 with extended shear tabs versus double clips, swings erected cost materially, so a bracing-heavy job warrants a connection-engineering line in the estimate rather than a flat per-ton connection allowance; the UDL-versus-real-load warning is a check on inflated shear specs that drive needless doubler plates. For Mario's shop and welding, the 5/8 fillet equals six-pass insight (30 inches of 5/8 fillet equals 180 inches of single-pass weld) is a consumable and labor planning fact, and the X-bolt ply-thickness rule (keep threads out of the shear plane to avoid extra inspection) ties to AWS D1.1 and RCSC practice for our field bolting. For the in-house PE stamp and Tekla detailing, the controlling takeaway is that R must use constraint-satisfying alpha and beta, the equilibrium cross-check (V components sum to P cosine theta, H components to P sine theta) belongs in our connection-calc QC, and there is no software shortcut, so each UFM connection is a hand calc the stamping PE owns. This maps to anchor-rod and base-plate work only loosely (Thornton flags base plates as a later session), and the truss examples inform any heavy-transfer gusset on ACP. Doctrine conflict: NONE. The content is conventional structural steel bracing design with no PEMB language and no supplier names.

## Modern Methods of Structural Analysis - Pt.I
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lw3fAlQITFY | Duration: 1:33:35 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is session 1 of AISC Night School 7 (Stability Design of Steel Structures), presented by Ronald D. Ziemian of Bucknell on behalf of the Structural Stability Research Council, January 26 2015 [00:01]. The lecture teaches stability design through the lens of an engineer with access to modern computer analysis, contrasting the effective length method (rooted in bifurcation theory, K-factor based) against the direct analysis method (rooted in instability theory, where a small initial imperfection grows under load and approaches the limit state asymptotically) [05:13][09:50][11:22]. The second half explains how a computer actually solves a structure: the direct stiffness method, which combines equilibrium and compatibility equations, translated through F=K*Delta, into a balanced set of equations in unknown displacements [47:37][62:05]. Stability, not strength alone, is framed as the controlling design problem for slender steel members and systems [06:13].

### Spec References
The speaker cites the AISC Specification body where the direct analysis method lives, the word "analysis" entering the spec in the 2005 edition, its move from Appendix 7 (2005) to Chapter C (2010), the inelastic-analysis rules in Appendix 1, and the forthcoming 2016 edition adding a third variant (direct modeling of member imperfections) [04:09][30:46][31:16][22:07]. He names the Chapter C Commentary as the source for the 0.8 stiffness-reduction derivation [38:57], the LRFD beam-column interaction equation as the controlling check [31:46], and references the Code of Standard Practice as the basis for initial out-of-plumb tolerances [20:33][83:06]. For further reading he cites AISC Design Guide 28 (Stability Design of Steel Buildings, White and Griffis) and his own textbook Matrix Structural Analysis [89:49][90:20].

### Technical Details
The direct analysis method reduces all stiffness contributing to stability by a factor of 0.8 times tau, models system out-of-plumb imperfections, and in return lets the engineer use K equal to 1 (the unbraced length) instead of computing K factors [18:00][21:04][33:16]. Tau-b is a stiffness-reduction factor capturing partial yielding from residual stresses, which the speaker explains arise from uneven cooling of a rolled shape: flange tips cool and set first, the web-flange junction last, leaving the flange tips in compression at up to about 30 percent of yield stress, so they yield early under load [85:41][86:41]. The 0.8 value came from averaging study results: minor-axis bending suggested roughly 0.75 to 0.78 and major-axis roughly 0.83, and the committee chose a single averaged number [39:58]. The 0.8 must be applied to every element providing lateral stability, columns, beams that participate in lateral stiffness, and modeled connection stiffness [88:13]. The three direct-analysis tiers trade analysis effort for relaxed design checks: the basic method still uses the column curve, modeling member imperfections lets you check only cross-sectional strength (A times Fy for a compact section), and full inelastic analysis can waive specification design equations entirely [21:37][23:38][24:39].

### Fabrication Notes
This is an analysis and design webinar, so it carries no shop fabrication, fit-up, or QC procedures. The only fabrication-adjacent content is the explanation of residual stresses from uneven cooling of hot-rolled shapes and the contrast with aluminum, which is extruded and then pulled straight in a tension operation that relieves residual stress [85:41][84:41]. No fabrication tolerances or shop processes are specified.

### Erection Notes
Erection is touched only through the out-of-plumb initial imperfection: the building is not built perfectly plumb, and the analysis must include an out-of-plumb at least as large as the Code of Standard Practice erection tolerance, reflecting what is documented in the design agreement [20:33][83:06][83:37]. The speaker notes a popular application of the member-imperfection method is checking a beam or truss being lifted by crane during erection, where the engineer must capture the initial bending or imperfection of the member as it comes off the ground [77:25][37:55]. No sequencing, bracing, or rigging procedures are given.

### Bolting and Welding
No bolting or welding content. The webinar is entirely about global structural analysis and stability theory and does not address bolt grades, pretension, welds, electrodes, preheat, or NDE.

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The central error theme is engineers selecting the wrong effective length (K) factor: if K is wrong, any apparent conservatism is meaningless and the result is unreliable, and the speaker's gut feeling is that correct K factors are not being chosen consistently [36:52][37:24]. A second recurring error is two analysis programs disagreeing, where nine times out of ten one program has shear deformations turned on in the stiffness coefficients and the other does not [63:38]. He warns that treating computer analysis as a black box is itself a failure mode, and that capturing lateral-torsional buckling in a direct-analysis run requires a program sophisticated enough to update geometry and account for member twist, not a routine P-Delta plus P-small-delta analysis [40:58][78:25][79:28].

### Bid / Cost Implications
The methods are presented as a cost-of-effort trade-off rather than a cost number. Effective length and basic direct analysis generally give very similar designs, so neither is reliably cheaper [34:48]. Direct modeling of member imperfections gives the most efficient (least conservative) design and the most steel savings, but at the cost of building an imperfection sweep into every member, which the speaker repeatedly calls tedious and time-consuming, suitable only for special structures like tree columns, arches, or airport-terminal framing, not routine work [22:37][34:17][35:18][75:54]. Full inelastic analysis is described as an expensive analysis that gives near-exact results. The estimating takeaway is that exotic geometry can justify a more efficient (lighter, lower-tonnage) design only if the engineering budget covers the added analysis labor.

### Your Company Application
This is engineering-design background, not a takeoff or shop input, so it does not change Ivan's member takeoff (which still runs measured schedules and framing marks through bridge/aisc_validator.py against the v16.0 database) and it has no direct Mario welding or Paul safety content. Its real value is for the in-house PE stamp: it sharpens how Your Company's engineer justifies the analysis method on a stamped job, the 0.8 tau-b reduction, K equal to 1 under direct analysis, and the Code of Standard Practice out-of-plumb that must be modeled. The crane-lift point [77:25] maps to erection-stress checks on long trusses or joist girders during pick, and to Tekla-modeled geometry feeding an analysis. For ACP project controls, treat any lighter "optimized" tonnage claim as requiring confirmation of which analysis method and imperfection modeling produced it before trusting the number, consistent with verify-do-not-generate. No conflict with Your Company doctrine; this is conventional structural steel, no PEMB language. Doctrine flag: NONE.
