## Modern Methods of Structural Analysis Pt.II
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YtJCiXAhQqU | Duration: 1:33:10 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is AISC Night School session 2, taught by Dr. Ronald Ziemann of Bucknell University, on material and geometric (second-order) nonlinear structural analysis methods [00:31][02:37]. The core idea is that a computer can only capture nonlinear behavior by modifying member stiffness: yielding is modeled by zeroing or reducing the elastic stiffness, and second-order effects are modeled by adding a geometric stiffness term [05:10][50:07]. The lecture builds from the elastic-perfectly-plastic material model and concentrated plastic-hinge concept up through full second-order inelastic analysis and eigenvalue buckling [06:43][60:20]. This is theory and software methodology for structural engineers, not a fabrication or erection topic.

### Spec References
The speaker references the 2005 AISC Specification as the first time the word "analysis" entered the body of the spec [03:07], and notes that the 2016 commentary was to add language permitting a tension diagonal to brace a compression diagonal in X-bracing [65:59]. He cites AISC compactness requirements generally as the limit governing whether a true plastic hinge can form, but states no section, table, or Design Guide number [32:36][33:07]. No specific AISC 360 chapter or section, AISC 341 seismic section, AWS D1.1 clause, or RCSC provision is quoted in this lecture; the content is analysis-method principles, no section cited.

### Technical Details
The material model is elastic-perfectly-plastic: below yield the member uses full E, and once yielded the modulus drops to zero [07:45][08:17]. A plastic hinge forms when an axial member reaches P/Py = 1, a flexural member reaches M/Mp = 1, and a beam-column reaches its yield surface, the interaction curve of axial force versus bending [11:26][24:48]. Axial compression reduces effective lateral and flexural stiffness, so beam-columns hinge at lower load than pure flexural members; the speaker illustrates a W12x50 example where the first hinge moves from 83 percent to 65 percent of load when 400 kips of axial is added [18:40][27:54]. Second-order stiffness equals first-order stiffness reduced by a geometric stiffness term proportional to axial force (P over L in the simple case), and second-order moments ran about 10 percent higher than first-order for his example, with one column case jumping from roughly 14 in-kip to 1831 in-kip [50:38][59:18][84:28]. Eigenvalue buckling analysis finds the load factor at which the structure determinant goes to zero; his single-element example gave 10EI/L squared versus the exact pi-squared EI/L squared, within about 1.3 percent [76:46][77:17]. The MASTAN2 educational software, the McGuire/Gallagher/Ziemann matrix-structural-analysis textbook, plastic-zone (distributed plasticity) and full shell finite-element approaches (ABAQUS, ADINA, ANSYS named generically) are discussed [17:36][18:07].

### Fabrication Notes
No fabrication content. This webinar covers analysis software methodology and contains no shop process, fit-up, tolerance, or QC material.

### Erection Notes
No erection content. The lecture has no field procedure, sequencing, bracing-install, or rigging material; the only "bracing" discussion is the analytical effect of a tension X-brace diagonal stiffening a compression diagonal [64:56].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
No inspection or rejection content. The closest engineering caution is that a plastic-hinge analysis is only valid if the section is compact enough to fully yield and rotate without local buckling, so applying it to a non-compact or slender section is a modeling error [32:36][33:07]. The speaker also warns that element count must be checked by convergence (refine until the answer stops changing), since too few elements misrepresents a tight buckled shape [67:32][88:35].

### Bid / Cost Implications
No direct estimating, bid, or schedule content. The indirect takeaway is engineering cost: rigorous second-order inelastic or buckling analysis is computationally heavy and requires trained judgment, and second-order effects can raise design moments by roughly 10 percent or far more in flexible frames, which the engineer must capture rather than assume away [59:49][84:28].

### Your Company Application
This is reference material for the in-house PE stamp, not for Ivan takeoff, Mario shop, Paul safety, Tekla detailing, anchor rods, joists, field bolting, or ACP controls. It supports the stamping engineer's understanding of why second-order (P-Delta) effects and the direct analysis method matter and why a frame analysis can show meaningfully higher column moments than a first-order run, which is useful background when reviewing a delegated connection-design package or a structural model behind a bid. It also confirms the analytical basis for using a tension diagonal to brace a compression diagonal in X-braced bays, relevant when our PE reviews lateral systems. Doctrine flag: NONE; the entry quotes no fabricated section numbers and the content sits inside engineering analysis, with no PEMB language and no supplier or rate claims.

## Design Guide 32: AISC N690 Appendix N9
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_JJS-gkt6Iw | Duration: 1:25:31 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This webinar by Dr. Amit Varma and Sahas Bardwaj of Purdue presents AISC Design Guide 32, which explains how to apply AISC N690S1 Appendix N9 to design steel-plate composite (SC) walls and their connections for safety-related nuclear facilities [01:32][09:44]. An SC wall is two steel face plates with concrete infill, where the plates act as both stay-in-place formwork and primary and secondary reinforcement, anchored to the concrete by shear studs and tied across by tie bars [04:36][05:06]. The system exists to eliminate rebar congestion (wall reinforcement ratios reach 1 to 2% in nuclear and high-rise work) and to enable modular prefabrication that compresses construction schedule [03:35][06:08]. The talk walks a full design example for a 56-inch wall plus a wall-to-base-mat connection [11:48][15:57].
### Spec References
Cited verbatim by the speakers: AISC N690 and its supplement AISC N690S1 (published August 2015, free download from AISC) [09:44][10:46]; Appendix N9 with its four sections covering design requirements, analysis, wall design, and connection design [10:46]; ACI 349 (used in place of N690S1 for RC design, source of the 1.25 capacity factor, and used for shear-friction design) [09:44][64:01][67:34]; Chapter NB-2 for basic load combinations [37:57]; specification Section I8.3 for steel headed stud anchors [67:34]; Chapter NJ for welds and bolts [67:34]; Section I6.3 for compression transfer by bearing [67:34]; AISC 341 seismic provisions Chapter H7 for wall piers [78:14]; AISC Design Guide 1 for base-plate design (bending and prying) [70:05]. The joint shear strength was given as 12 times root f'c times Ac, drawn from an ACI joint-shear publication [75:10].
### Technical Details
Minimum-requirement gates were checked numerically: SC thickness 56 inches, face plate 0.5 inch, yield stress between 50 and 65 ksi, concrete between 4 and 8 ksi, no lightweight concrete permitted [18:31][19:02]. Three detailing controls govern: face-plate slenderness (largest unsupported length over plate thickness must stay under root E over Fy so the plate yields before it buckles), shear-connector spacing (set by slenderness, by a development length around 3 times the SC thickness for 75 to 90% partial composite action per Zang and Ollgaard, and by an interfacial-shear limit), and tie detailing (spacing under the section thickness, ties classed yielding or non-yielding, with a tensile-strength check against delamination) [19:32][22:36][25:38]. The example used 6-inch stud spacing and 24-inch tie spacing both ways [20:34][26:08]. Analysis uses elastic 3D thick-shell finite elements with element size under twice the section thickness in interiors and under one thickness at connections and openings; two models are run, condition A operating and condition B accident thermal, with calibrated stiffness, modulus, density, and specific heat [28:40][29:10][35:53]. Each element returns eight demands (out-of-plane MX, MY, twist MXY, membrane SX, SY, SRX, and out-of-plane shears) checked through interaction surfaces [39:00][43:34].
### Fabrication Notes
SC modules are shop-fabricated with plates, studs, and tie bars, then shipped and craned into place; the talk shows a 1,100-ton CA20 module built in a dedicated module shop [08:42][09:13]. The steel face plate doubles as stay-in-place formwork, which removes the formwork-set and strip steps of modular RC walls [05:36]. Tie bars hold the form of empty modules during lifting and transport, so detailing serves both structural and handling needs [25:38]. Tie-to-face-plate welds in the example were complete-penetration (the speaker said the weld makes the connection stronger than the tie, so tie rupture governs) [27:08]. Embed plates, attachments, and piping sleeves can be built into the module during fabrication [05:06][16:28]. Fabrication and construction tolerances are specification-mandated and matter because adjacent modules must mate; the example assumed they were met [16:28][16:58].
### Erection Notes
Modules are set onto dowel bars protruding from the concrete foundation and lap-spliced into the SC wall, a detail shown from the Sanmen, China site [08:11][49:44]. Because modules grow very large very fast, crane lifts and field mating dominate erection planning, and tie bars keep empty modules in shape during the lift [07:40][25:38]. The connection region (the transition where stresses equalize between wall and foundation) must be less than twice the wall thickness and preferably about one thickness, both to develop composite action and to avoid cramming so many anchors and ties that the region congests [57:25][58:55]. A Q-and-A point noted that large bars (number 14, roughly 100-inch development length) cannot be developed by bond inside a short connection region, so mechanical anchors or terminators are needed, with the dropped stress picked back up into the steel plate [80:46][81:48].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The speakers named several failure modes the detailing rules are written to prevent: face-plate compression buckling before yield, interfacial (stud) shear failure before out-of-plane shear failure, and section delamination or splaying if ties are absent [19:32][24:08][25:38]. A splice between RC and SC without ties can split open from the eccentricity between the tension force and its reaction, producing a tension field, especially on thick walls [50:45][51:15]. In the worked example two interaction-surface points fell outside the envelope, forcing a redesign with higher-grade steel or demand averaging [44:35][45:06]. A recurring design-process error flagged: an analytical assumption made months earlier (modeling a slab connection as fixed) comes back and forces shear transfer that was never intended, a sign the model and the connection philosophy were not reconciled [83:50].
### Bid / Cost Implications
The whole motivation is schedule: modularity through prefabrication and preassembly cuts construction time versus rebar-cage RC walls [03:05][06:08]. Nuclear walls are routinely over-designed because thickness is set by radiation shielding, not structural demand, so demand-to-capacity ratios can sit at 0.2 or less; this drives the choice between a costlier full-strength connection and a leaner over-strength connection [61:59][62:29]. The closing message was design optimization: the example's first pass ran utility ratios near 0.6 with heavy 6-inch stud spacing and 3-square-inch ties, and a second optimization pass pushed ratios up to 0.9, reducing steel, though the optimization itself is calculation-heavy [84:21][85:22].
### Your Company Application
This is a deep nuclear-specific standard (N690 safety-related facilities) outside Your Company's conventional commercial steel scope, so direct project use is unlikely. The transferable items are concrete: shear-stud development-length and spacing logic ties to Ivan's takeoff and to how stud counts get justified rather than assumed; the complete-penetration tie-to-plate weld classification and the no-bond-as-connector rule reinforce Mario's AWS D1.1 discipline and the verify-don't-generate stance on weld strength; the dowel-bar-to-base anchorage and tolerance-driven module mating map to Your Company anchor-rod setting and tolerance work and to ACP project controls; the 1.25 capacity-design factor (consistent with ACI 349) and the wall-pier-versus-wall distinction in AISC 341 Chapter H7 are useful reference points for the in-house PE stamp on any composite or shear-wall question. Doctrine flag: NONE. The content is general nuclear-engineering education with no supplier names, no PEMB language, and no conflict with Your Company rules.

## Solutions for Vibration Issues-Evaluation and Retrofits
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x5aIywz1XI0 | Duration: 1:26:35 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
This webinar by Dr. Tom Murray (first author of AISC Design Guide 11) and Dr. Brad Davis teaches how to evaluate and retrofit floors and other structures that vibrate excessively under human activity. The controlling distinction is the "low frequency floor" with a natural frequency below about nine Hertz, where an occupant walking at a subharmonic of that frequency drives the floor into resonance and produces the maximum felt response [08:19][08:51]. The retrofit decision rests on the equivalent sinusoidal peak acceleration (ESPA), not the raw peak particle acceleration, compared against the tolerance limits in Design Guide 11 [14:59][16:33]. The repeated message is that retrofit design must begin with field measurements rather than calculation alone, because predictions are only moderately accurate [74:40][75:10].

### Spec References
The speakers cite AISC Design Guide 11, Second Edition (floor vibration, published roughly two years before the talk) and its chapters: Chapter 2 (tolerance limits) [31:36], Chapters 4 and 5 (manual prediction methods, the "gold standard" used over 20 years) [40:17][57:16], Chapter 6 (finite element and sensitive-equipment criteria, including the 1/3 octave velocity limits) [35:42][38:15], and Chapter 7 (the FRF method, with a Version 2 in development) [49:02]. Equation 6-38 of Design Guide 11 is cited by number for the combined resonant-plus-impulse walking response [40:17]. SJI Technical Digest No. 5 is named as an alternate manual method [04:41]. Dunkerley's equation is cited for combining joist and girder frequencies [24:52]. No AISC 360, 341, AWS D1.1, or RCSC sections were stated in this floor-serviceability talk.

### Technical Details
Natural frequency is found in the field by a heel drop (rise on the balls of the feet, strike with the heels), which has frequency content to about 40 Hertz, then processed by FFT to a response spectrum [06:46][07:16]. Walking tests use a metronome set to a step frequency in the 1.6 to 2.2 Hertz range, chosen so an integer multiple equals the floor natural frequency (for a 6 Hz floor, divide by 3 to get a 2 Hz gait) [09:52][10:23]. Records are bandpass filtered between roughly 1 and 15 to 20 Hertz because humans are insensitive outside that band, and 30 or 60 Hz equipment noise is filtered out [13:55]. ESPA is computed by taking the maximum rolling one-second RMS acceleration and multiplying by the square root of 2 [15:30][16:02]. The quiet-environment tolerance is 0.5 percent of gravity; the lab/microscope limit was 4,000 micro-inches per second on a 1/3 octave velocity basis [17:38][35:42]. Humans perceive vertical displacements as small as ten thousandths of an inch, so any retrofit element must be very stiff [19:10].

### Fabrication Notes
The fabricated retrofit members are conventional rolled shapes welded to existing framing. Examples named verbatim: W10x15 welded 20 feet long to joist bottom chords [27:29]; W16x26 placed between joists near midbay with HSS pieces welded between the girder top flange and the deck underside to force composite girder action [40:48][41:19]; and cold-formed channels (the heaviest 12-inch channels available) plus shorter top-chord channels added to light steel trusses for added mass and stiffness [42:50][51:08]. Reinforcement is welded only at the joist panel points [28:32]. Because the elements add both mass and stiffness, mass-only blocks (the owner's 1-foot concrete cubes) changed the response by only about one hundredth of a percent and were a waste [24:21][25:53].

### Erection Notes
Field installation is the hard part. To strain the new member into the load path, the crew jacks up the floor about a half inch, then welds the reinforcement to the bottom chord or bottom flange before releasing the jacks [19:41][29:03]. Joists were stiffened a set of three or four at a time across the whole bay, which required removing the ceiling first [28:32][29:03]. Welding in an occupied building is rarely feasible and is risky around computers, so tenants below were relocated to temporary space during the work [20:12][28:32]. Other field fixes shown were hidden posts disguised as electrical or communication drops (which must run to grade or they only move the problem to the floor below) [21:16][21:46], HSS 3x3 columns at cubicle corners to raise frequency [58:52], and tuned mass dampers installed between a raised access floor and the slab [70:51].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The named diagnostic errors are using peak particle velocity or peak particle acceleration instead of ESPA, which overestimates what a human feels (an 0.875 percent G peak against a 0.531 percent G ESPA) [14:59][30:36]; relying on long-term monitoring without paired video so the cause of each event is unknown [31:36]; and using cell-phone accelerometers, which lack control of sampling rate, voltage range, and bandwidth and are not sensitive enough at the very low floor levels [32:37]. Real design misses included an engineer who eyeballed a hotel crossover (W16x31, 30 ft) as fine, predicting 9.35 Hz and 1 percent G but getting 4.71 Hz and 4.4 percent G [64:34][65:39]; a monumental stair on wire-rope-supported landings where the EOR added a few secondary members without a vibration check and got 3.25 percent G under four people descending [67:11][68:14]; and resonant cross-floor transmission where dancing six floors below shook tenth-floor offices through axial column deformation [61:30][63:02].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Retrofits in occupied buildings carry heavy soft costs: tenant relocation, ceiling removal and reinstatement, jacking, and after-hours welding around live computers, which the speaker repeatedly calls "not cheap" and sometimes infeasible [20:12][28:32]. The cost message for estimating is that mass-only fixes (concrete blocks or cubes) are wasted money because they do not move the response, while the effective fix is stiff welded reinforcement that adds mass, moment of inertia, and transverse stiffness together [20:44][25:53]. Field measurement campaigns (multiple walkers, multiple paths, seismic accelerometers, FE calibration) are an engineering-service line item that should precede any retrofit pricing.

### Your Company Application
This is a serviceability and retrofit topic, not a routine new-build fabrication driver, so it does not change Ivan's AISC member takeoff through aisc_validator.py for a normal bid. Where it matters for Your Company is on long-span open-bay jobs (lobbies, fitness rooms, monumental stairs, pedestrian crossovers, lab or healthcare floors) where a vibration RFI or owner complaint can pull us into a welded retrofit scope. For Mario's shop and field crew, the load-bearing detail is the procedure: jack the floor about a half inch, weld the rolled reinforcement (for example a W10x15 or W16x26) to joist bottom chords at panel points only, all under AWS D1.1 field welding, with Paul Guerrero managing hot-work safety around occupied space and computers. Tekla detailing should carry the jacking and panel-point weld notes when such a scope appears. On Asian City Plaza controls, flag any long-span assembly or monumental stair for a vibration-serviceability check by the in-house PE rather than assuming the gravity design covers it. Doctrine conflict: NONE. This stays conventional structural steel and adds no PEMB language.

## Solutions for Vibration Issues-Evaluation and Retrofits
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2ayxtd9FjzU | Duration: 33:30 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
Dr. Tom Murray (first author of AISC Design Guide 11) and Dr. Brad Davis teach how to evaluate and retrofit floors that occupants report as lively, plus floors whose human-induced vibration exceeds the tolerance of sensitive equipment [02:36][03:07]. The controlling problem is low-frequency floors, defined as floors whose first natural frequency is below about nine Hertz, where occupant footfall at a sub-harmonic of the floor frequency drives resonance and the perceived response [08:51]. The whole method compares a measured equivalent sinusoidal peak acceleration (ESPA) against the Design Guide 11 acceleration limit, and retrofits the floor when that limit is exceeded [14:59][15:30].
### Spec References
AISC Design Guide 11, second edition, published roughly two years before the talk, is the central reference, including its manual method for regular (rectangular) bays, its finite-element method for irregular bays, and its tolerance limits in "Chapter two" [04:41][05:13][05:44][31:36]. SJI Technical Digest Number 5 is cited as the alternate manual method for joist floors [04:41]. Dunkerley's equation is named as the Design Guide 11 way to combine the joist-mode and girder-mode frequencies into a system frequency [24:51]. No AISC 360, AISC 341, AWS D1.1, or RCSC sections were cited; this is a serviceability talk, not a strength or connection-code talk.
### Technical Details
Floor natural frequency is measured fastest by a heel drop (rise on the balls of the feet, strike with the heels), which injects content to about 40 Hertz and is processed by FFT into a response spectrum to read the dominant frequency [06:46][07:16]. Walking tests use a metronome at a step frequency in the normal range of 1.6 to 2.2 Hertz, chosen by dividing the floor's natural frequency by an integer so resonance occurs; for a 5.06 Hertz floor, divide by three to get 1.68 Hertz, about 101 steps per minute [09:52][17:03]. Records are bandpass filtered between roughly 1 and 15 to 20 Hertz, since humans are insensitive below 1 Hertz and above about 15 Hertz, and 30 or 60 Hertz building-equipment noise must be filtered out [13:55][14:25]. ESPA is computed as the maximum one-second rolling RMS acceleration multiplied by the square root of 2 to recover an equivalent sinusoidal peak, compared against the 0.5 percent of gravity quiet-environment limit [15:30][16:33][17:36].
### Fabrication Notes
The shop fabrication relevant to a retrofit is straightforward member supply, since the cited fix welds a wide-flange (a W10x15, 20 feet long in the example) to the bottom chords of composite joists at the panel points only [27:29][28:32][29:03]. Whatever is added must be very stiff because the target is reducing midspan motion from about ten thousandths of an inch to five thousandths, so bolted or turnbuckle-tensioned schemes were tried over the years and rejected as not stiff enough; welding is required [19:10][19:41]. The reinforcing member must also be strained into the structure, which means the floor is jacked up about a quarter to a half inch before the reinforcement is welded so the new steel picks up load [19:41].
### Erection Notes
Field retrofit work is done from below in an occupied building, requiring removal of the ceiling, jacking a set of three or four joists at a time, welding the beams to the bottom chords, then moving across the whole bay rather than only the locally complained area [29:03]. The tenant directly below had to be relocated to a temporary space because hot welding work over a computer-filled occupied floor is risky and usually not feasible [20:12][28:32]. An alternative field fix is installing posts (props) below the lively floor, but they must bear to grade; one job doubled the problem by propping between two suspended floors over a parking garage and the posts were pulled the next day [21:16][21:46].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The talk names several questionable testing and evaluation errors. Reporting peak particle velocity or peak particle acceleration (PPV or PPA) from a record badly overstates what people feel, because a single filtered peak (0.875 percent G in the example) is not representative while the persistent ESPA (0.531 percent G) is [30:36][31:06]. Long-term monitoring without paired video monitoring leaves the cause of each vibration event unknown, and even video can miss excitations like a person's leg jiggling [31:36][32:06]. Using cell-phone accelerometers fails because vibration measurement needs tight control of sampling frequency, input voltage range, and bandwidth that consumer hardware does not provide [32:37]. A field error shown was placing nine one-foot concrete cubes as added mass, which changed the predicted frequency by one hundredth of a percent and was a waste of money [24:21][25:53].
### Bid / Cost Implications
Adding mass is usually ineffective because it takes a large amount of concrete to move the response, and added slab helps only when it also raises moment of inertia and transverse stiffness, so block mass buys little [20:44]. The welded-stiffener retrofit is expensive and disruptive: it requires tenant relocation, ceiling removal, jacking, and field welding in an occupied space, which is the cost driver, not the steel weight itself [20:12][28:32]. The practical lesson for pricing serviceability work is that a cheap-looking fix (mass blocks, props) can fail or backfire, and the defensible fix is engineered stiffening plus measurement, which carries real labor and access cost.
### Your Company Application
This is serviceability and forensic territory rather than core bid work, but it touches several Your Company workstreams. Joist floors are squarely in scope: the example is a 24-inch composite joist (a "24 V C", 300 plf design, 80 inches on center, 40-foot span), so Ivan's takeoff and the in-house PE stamp should flag long-span composite-joist office and healthcare floors as low-frequency vibration risk early, since Design Guide 11 and SJI Technical Digest 5 screening is cheaper than a post-occupancy lawsuit (the example reached litigation). Mario's crew owns the retrofit method, welding a wide-flange to joist bottom chords at panel points after the floor is jacked a quarter to a half inch, and Paul's safety scope covers hot work over an occupied, computer-filled floor with temporary tenant relocation. Tekla detailing can model the added stiffener and the panel-point weld locations. Doctrine flags: NONE. Nothing here conflicts with Your Company doctrine; all member and frequency figures are quoted from the speaker, no AISC weights were generated, and the conventional-structural-steel positioning holds.

## Lateral-Torsional Buckling and its Influence on the Strength of Beams
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QtyGWZDPtCI | Duration: 1:29:46 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This NASCC webinar by Craig Quadrado and Perry Green covers lateral-torsional buckling (LTB) as the limit state that governs the flexural strength of beams, defined at [03:35] as a geometric instability combining lateral translation of the compression flange and twist of the cross section. The presenters frame the AISC beam curve as three regions tied to unbraced length: elastic LTB at long unbraced lengths, inelastic LTB in the middle, and full plastic moment capacity Mp at short unbraced lengths [05:38][06:08]. The controlling design variable for a given cross section is the unbraced length Lb [04:35], where Lb is the distance between points that restrain lateral displacement of the compression flange or restrain twist of the section [08:38]. Green's research half derives rotation capacity and shows that achieving Mp also requires a stocky (compact) flange and effective bracing, not just short Lb [11:45][13:15].

### Spec References
The talk lives in AISC 360-16 Chapter F, primarily Section F2 with reference down into Section F3 for non-compact and slender flange sections [02:35]. Specific citations: Section F3 paragraphs (b) and (c) for reduced strength under flange local buckling [15:19]; the statement that full plastic moment is the optimum use of steel on manual page 16.1-323 [06:38]; the list of shapes susceptible to flange local buckling on manual page 16.1-47 [15:50]; AISC Commentary Appendix 6.3 for bracing design [10:42]; the rotation-capacity and compact-section definitions in the AISC 360-16 Glossary [20:58][31:45]; AISC 341 as the home for seismic and cyclic loading beyond the static basis of 360 [19:57]; Commentary to F1 for alternate Cb formulations including reverse-curvature and uplift cases [71:35][72:36]; and the SSRC Guide to Stability Design Criteria for Metal Structures and the fire/elevated-temperature appendix tables [78:13][35:26]. The compactness limit is given verbatim as 0.38 times the square root of E over Fy [13:15], replacing the legacy 65 over the square root of Fy from the 9th edition ASD [33:53]. The Cb equation is stated as 12.5 Mmax over (2.5 Mmax + 3MA + 4MB + 3MC) using absolute values [68:57].

### Technical Details
Mp equals Z times Fy [65:54]. Lr is set by making the elastic moment equal 0.7 Fy times Sx, where 0.7 accounts for residual stress, then solving for unbraced length [64:53]; Quadrado notes as SSRC Task Group 2 chair that this residual-stress reduction for modern hot-rolled shapes may be revisited [64:53]. Lp is anchored in equations near the plastic range (with GJ set to zero and Me set to Mp) but its final form is experimentally derived to deliver the rotation capacity [65:54][66:24]. Compact sections must develop a rotation capacity of approximately three before onset of local buckling [31:45], a requirement that matters for cyclic/seismic loading, not monotonic [32:48]. Green's 13-specimen program found monotonic tests reach rotation capacities of eight or nine while cyclic moment-gradient loading drops them toward three [38:30][41:34], and higher-yield steels (50, 60, 65, 80, 100 ksi grades discussed) carry less rotation capacity than A36 [38:30]. The open wide-flange torsional constant J equals the sum of (b t cubed over 3) for the three plates, roughly 4 in^4 class versus about 22.95 for a comparable closed tube [53:00][74:40]. Both E and Fy drive slenderness, and elevated temperature (200 to 300 degrees on industrial supports) reduces it as well [34:55].

### Fabrication Notes
The practical fabrication theme is reusing one critical-beam section across many members so the shop runs fewer distinct pieces even when most beams never see full load [42:11]. Producers have nearly eliminated flange local buckling from rolled shapes except the specific list on manual page 16.1-47, and the manual flexural-strength tables already bake in the reduced values for those shapes [15:50]. For built-up plate girders that cannot be looked up, J is computed as the sum of (b t cubed over 3) and flange local buckling is managed by using thicker flange plates rather than changing material [15:19][53:00]. The Q&A discusses variable-cross-section built-up members made from coil/plate where thickness or width is profiled along the length, with the caution that a single Cb cannot be applied across a varying section [85:43][86:52]. The presenters do not state AWS D1.1 weld procedure detail; welding appears only in the lab context of vertical flange-to-flange stiffeners welded to specimen ends to act as end restraint [45:47].

### Erection Notes
The strongest erection message is that bracing controls Lb only if it is effective, meaning it restrains twist, is not connected at the shear center, and is not taken at a point of inflection [10:11][10:42]. Reverse-curvature points of inflection are explicitly not valid brace points [10:11]. During steel erection before the deck is placed, the girder unbraced length is the spacing of cross frames or the distance between the two beams providing twist resistance, not a continuously braced length [09:09][09:40]. A repeated field warning: when re-roofing, removing deck or purlins removes top-flange (compression-flange) lateral support, so contractors must confirm stability before stripping too far [59:44][60:14]. The Edmonton bridge girder failure is attributed not to absence of bracing but to bracing that was too slender to be effective, the braces themselves buckled [11:13][11:45]. Warping-restraint tubes between flanges at girder ends gave a 30 percent class increase (up to about 130 percent more lateral capacity in a W30x90 test) and are most useful during erection while the steel stays elastic, before deck and final bracing are in place [73:39][75:41][81:17].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Named errors: treating points of inflection as brace points [10:11]; designing bracing that is not effective (insufficient brace force, a failed specimen brace rated for only 10 to 15 kips of flange force buckled and lost rotation capacity, forcing a rebuilt test) [28:43][29:13]; computing a nominal moment Mn greater than Mp from a Cb multiplier and using it instead of capping at Mp [70:29][71:35]; and forgetting that Cb uses absolute values of the moments so reverse curvature must not be entered as a negative [69:27]. A material-specific error is using table values valid only for A992 grade-50 steel after the job switches to a different grade or higher yield, which requires recomputing slenderness from the spec rather than the manual tables [17:21][39:00]. Field LTB failures shown include permanently bent bridge girders from overload and elastically buckled girders that recovered when load was removed [05:38][06:08].

### Bid / Cost Implications
The cost logic is to design one governing beam and replicate it so fabrication is simpler and most members pass by inspection, accepting that non-critical beams are under-utilized in exchange for fewer section types [42:11][42:42]. Living with a small strength reduction from a slightly slender flange can be more economical than switching cross sections mid-structure when the lower-strength region is also lightly loaded [15:19]. Higher-strength steels look attractive for weight but the talk warns rotation capacity and slenderness limits degrade with yield strength, so a higher-grade substitution can force added analysis and may not bank the expected savings [38:30][39:30]. Warping-restraint tube devices add elastic capacity cheaply during erection but were not widely adopted in buildings because building members are usually not kept in the elastic range, unlike bridge erection under AASHTO [73:39][74:10].

### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff and estimating, this reinforces the verify-don't-generate posture: member flexural strength must come from AISC 360-16 Chapter F through bridge/aisc_validator.py, never from LLM math, and the unbraced-length region (Lp, Lr, Cb) decides whether a given W-shape is adequate before any tonnage is priced. Tekla detailing must place effective lateral bracing at points that restrain twist and never call out points of inflection as brace points, and any plate-girder J or compactness check uses the sum of (b t cubed over 3) and the 0.38 root(E/Fy) limit. ## Benefits of Steel in Accelerated Bridge Construction
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RDOXPhZXR70 | Duration: 1:32:21 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is an AASHTO/NSBA-oriented highway-bridge webinar by Michael Cuomo of CME Associates, not a building-steel or AISC 360 talk. The thesis is that structural steel is a strong choice for accelerated bridge construction (ABC) because steel beams are lighter than equivalent concrete, accommodate large force and moment reversals during lifting and moving, and fabricate to tight tolerances for fast field fit-up [05:11][07:13]. Two ABC families are covered: full bridge-system moves on self-propelled modular transporters (SPMTs) or lateral slides [08:44], and prefabricated modular deck-beam units (steel girders with a precast deck cast on top) erected span by span [30:18][30:48]. A central design idea is the link slab, a short jointless deck detail that lets simple-span steel beams behave as a continuous-deck bridge without field splices [43:05].

### Spec References
No AISC 360, AISC 341, AWS D1.1, RCSC, or AISC Design Guide section is cited; this is the bridge (AASHTO) world. The speaker names the AASHTO Guide Specifications for Accelerated Bridge Construction developed under NCHRP Project 12-102 [03:38][72:01], and the Guidelines for Dynamic Effects for Bridge Systems plus prefabricated-element tolerance guidelines from NCHRP Project 12-98 / 12-102 [04:10][68:25]. The link-slab theory traces to a 1998 PCI Journal paper, and girder design used the NSBA SIMON program (LRFD, AASHTO) with the NSBA SPLICE program for bolted field splices [44:39][53:29][57:31]. All are AASHTO/NSBA/NCHRP references, general bridge-code citations, no building-steel section number cited.

### Technical Details
SPMT capacity is estimated at roughly 60,000 lb per axle line, with modular six-line, twelve-line, and twelve-line double-wide (24-axle) configurations bolted together [18:31][19:32]. Lift pick points run about 0.15L from the span ends to manage negative bending in girder and deck during the move [17:29][38:31]. A man-made-earthquake hypothesis was validated by physical SPMT testing in a Houston yard (15, 25, and 50 percent load cases, accelerometers, Utah State University), producing vertical and horizontal response-spectrum curves; starting and stopping generated larger lateral forces than vertical bounce, on the order of 5 to 10 percent of bridge mass as a horizontal design force [21:34][24:11][27:16][29:18]. Link-slab design keeps the slab thin, with a debond zone of about 5 percent of span on each side; doubling slab thickness raises the slab moment by a factor of eight (h-cubed), so thicker is worse [44:06][45:39].

### Fabrication Notes
The talk frames fabrication economically rather than by shop procedure. Steel fabricates to much tighter tolerances than precast concrete, which drives better field fit-up on tight ABC schedules [08:14]. In the cost study, fabrication cost was split by part: flanges at about 1.13 dollars per pound, webs at 0.97 dollars per pound, and stiffeners and connection plates at about 2.00 dollars per pound, because fitting and welding a connection plate into a plate girder is labor-intensive handwork [57:31][58:01]. Webs were noted as the cheapest steel on the girder; the SIMON program optimizes flange and web sizes for a cost-effective section [56:31].

### Erection Notes
Modular steel deck-beam units (for example about 85 ft, over 200,000 lb) were set as single-crane picks with roughly a 500-ton hydraulic crane; an equivalent concrete double-T about 25 percent heavier could force a two-crane pick and complicate erection [30:48][31:18]. The I-93 Fast 14 project in Medford MA replaced three- and four-span interstate bridges in 55-hour weekend closures using six-section cross-sections, high-early-strength concrete (about 4,000 psi in four to five hours) for the closure pours, and span-by-span erection that eliminated field splices [37:59][40:32]. Lateral-slide moves use Teflon sliding bearings; tested lubricants included Dawn dish soap, 10W-40 motor oil, and bridge-bearing grease, with oil and grease giving lower friction [70:30]. SPMT moves are typically under 100 to 200 yards but range from 50 ft to over a mile; tire-pressure loads approximate a fully loaded truck, so driving over buried utilities is generally acceptable [89:39][90:10].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The recurring failure named is the leaking bridge deck expansion joint: joints at every pier leak, and the speaker showed beam-end and pier corrosion with a girder web over 75 percent section-loss that crippled because it lacked a bearing stiffener, on bridges only built in the mid-to-late 1970s [34:52][35:57]. Over-conservative link slabs that are made too thick crack more, not less, because slab moment scales with thickness cubed [45:39]. The simple-made-continuous-for-live-load moment connection at the pier (post-tensioning, grouting, bottom-flange bolted splice) was flagged as complex with documented live-load cracking risk at the pier, versus the simpler link slab [42:34].

### Bid / Cost Implications
The headline takeaway for estimating: least weight is not least total cost. A two-span 122 ft by 122 ft continuous girder bridge totaled about 310,635 dollars in steel but added roughly 24,000 dollars of negative-moment deck rebar (about 12,000 lb), ten bolted field splices at near 6,000 dollars each (about 58,000 dollars total), bearings, and roughly 20,000 dollars of shoring towers, for about 419,000 dollars [58:01][62:13][65:20]. The link-slab span-by-span alternative used about 70,000 dollars more steel but eliminated the bolted splices and shoring and cut deck rebar to about 1,000 lb, landing roughly 30,000 dollars cheaper overall and erecting far faster [63:17][66:22]. Bolt cost is driven by hole drilling and field tensioning labor, not the bolt itself; the study used 50 dollars per bolt from a national bridge fabricator, and the speaker stressed costs vary widely by region [54:29][60:40][62:13].

### Your Company Application
This is highway-bridge content and most of it sits outside Your Company's conventional building-steel lane, so treat it as adjacent reference, not a methodology change. The transferable lessons for Ivan's takeoff are real: price by part type, not a single dollar-per-pound, since stiffeners and connection plates cost far more to fab than webs and flanges, and count bolted field splices and shoring as their own line items because hole drilling plus field tensioning labor dominates bolt cost, which maps to our field-bolting and aisc_validator member takeoff. Mario's shop work and the in-house PE stamp connect through the connection-plate fit-up labor point and the warning that over-thickening a detail can hurt performance. Paul's safety angle is the heavy-lift / crane-pick and SPMT braking-force material if Your Company ever rigs a large preassembly. Tekla detailing and anchor-rod tolerance work parallel the talk's tight-tolerance fit-up theme. DOCTRINE FLAGS: NONE. No supplier names appear (Sarens and Dawn are equipment/lubricant mentions by the speaker, not steel suppliers), no AISC weight or rate is asserted, and no building-steel spec number was fabricated; the entry stays inside verify-don't-generate.

## Design of Curved Members with the New AISC Design Guide
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jh9tjTDz4ms | Duration: 1:03:10 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
The session, presented by Bo Dowswell of ARC International (PhD on gusset plates, AISC committee member), previews AISC Design Guide 33, Design of Curved Members, then in development [02:08]. The central teaching is that curved members do not behave like straight members: a curved member under axial compression buckles in a side-sway mode rather than a half sine wave, and a horizontally curved beam under equal end moments develops flexure plus torsion rather than pure flexure [13:33][16:10]. The practical design method, however, converts the curved member back into an equivalent straight column or beam by using the developed (arc) length and tuned effective length factors, then runs it through familiar specification provisions [53:49][54:20].
### Spec References
The speaker cites AISC Design Guide 33 (curved members) and Design Guide 1 (base plates, anchor rods, washer plates, the practical-information model he wanted to copy) [02:38][22:30]. He references AISC Specification Section E3 for column flexural buckling, used for both in-plane and out-of-plane curved-member axial strength [56:58][60:32]. He names the AISC Code of Standard Practice, noting the 2016 edition explicitly adds straightness tolerances for curved members [41:54]. The British source is the Steel Construction Institute publication from 2001 [37:14]. No AISC 341 seismic, AWS D1.1, or RCSC bolting sections are cited in this webinar.
### Technical Details
Curve types named: vertically curved members, horizontally curved members, parabolic and elliptical (variable-radius) curves, off-axis curves, the s-curve (also called a reverse compound bend in roadway transportation), and the spiral or true helical curve [07:48][08:19][12:01]. Snap-through buckling is the governing in-plane concern: if rise-over-span H/L sub s is greater than 0.2, snap-through need not be checked; below 0.2 a design-guide table sets a minimum L/r (for example H/L 0.15 with pinned ends needs L/r greater than 36) [49:15][51:17]. The in-plane effective length factor K sub I depends on rise ratio and on circular-versus-parabolic and pinned-versus-fixed ends; a parabolic fixed arch uses K sub I of 0.5 (full sine wave) for all rise ratios [55:26]. Out-of-plane buckling is flexural-torsional, converted to flexural via a coefficient C sub o that carries the St. Venant torsion, warping constant, and out-of-plane moment of inertia, combined with the brace-segment angle theta sub B [59:02][61:40]. Local effects (flange bending, web buckling) matter only at tight radii, for example a 15-foot radius on a thin W21 flange [19:48].
### Fabrication Notes
Chapter 2 covers three primary bending processes: pyramid roll bending (cold, most common, three pyramid-arranged rolls with a supplementary roll to limit tension-flange distortion, multiple passes), incremental step bending (cold, cantilever force applied step by step), and induction bending (the only hot method, local induction-coil heating with immediate cooling around a pivot arm) [31:33][34:41][35:44]. Most steel fabricators only bend for camber on their own equipment and sub the tighter-radius work to a specialized bender-roller company [28:13]. To control distortion on an architecturally exposed (AESS) bent HSS, the bender roller may recommend a thicker wall, for example stepping up from a quarter-inch wall rather than redesigning later [26:41]. Material-property and brittle-fracture concerns arise only at tight radii combined with galvanizing and low-temperature exposed service [29:47].
### Erection Notes
The webinar is design and fabrication focused and gives little field-erection procedure. The one erection-adjacent point is support spreading: an arch on cantilever columns can spread at the supports, producing large apex deflection and pushing toward snap-through buckling, mitigated by a tension tie or a vertical truss [43:30][45:05]. No crane, rigging, sequencing, or field-bracing procedures are detailed.
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
No inspection-rejection list is given. The named failure modes are engineering buckling modes rather than fabrication defects: snap-through buckling (catastrophic in-plane flip-through, the example drops a 30-foot rise to 60 feet below), out-of-plane flexural-torsional buckling of an unbraced arch, and local flange bending or web buckling at tight radii [48:42][59:32]. Detailing errors are flagged indirectly: an off-axis curved member requires the detailer to dimension the rotation twist for the bender roller, and missing that geometry stops the bend [10:59][28:44].
### Bid / Cost Implications
Bent structural members are almost always subcontracted to a specialized bender-roller firm, which is a procurement and lead-time line distinct from in-house fabrication [28:13]. Each bender roller has different equipment and capability (induction, heavy strong-axis bends, spiral stairs needing wide rolls and large shop layout), so the right vendor must be matched to the curve type early [37:44][38:45]. Engaging the bender roller up front on wall thickness and achievable radius avoids redesign loops and distortion rework on exposed members [26:09]. The guide also gives developed (arc) length equations for parabolic curves so material quantity on a curved member is computed correctly rather than from chord length [25:06].
### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, a curved member must be quantified on its developed arc length, not the straight span, and bent-member work should be priced as a bender-roller subcontract line with its own lead time rather than folded into shop fab hours. For Tekla detailing, any off-axis or s-curve member needs the rotation and twist dimensions placed on the detail so the bender roller can run it, which is a detailing-completeness check to add. The in-house PE stamp work maps directly: design the curved member as an equivalent straight column or beam using developed length, AISC Specification Section E3, the Design Guide 33 K-factor and snap-through tables, and the H/L greater than 0.2 screen. Mario's shop bends only for camber, so tighter radii go out to a specialist, and a thicker HSS wall may be the cleanest distortion fix on an exposed bent tube. This is conventional structural steel content with no PEMB language and no conflict with Your Company doctrine. Doctrine flag: NONE.

## Birth of the Steel Skyscraper
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HOx1gHRdMa0 | Duration: 59:42 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is a Steel Day 2018 history lecture by Dr. Benjamin Schafer of Johns Hopkins on how the steel skeletal skyscraper was born in post-fire Chicago, told through the engineer-architect John Wellborn Root of Burnham and Root. The technical through-line is the transition from exterior load-bearing masonry with cast-iron interior columns to a fully self-supporting steel skeletal frame, and the engineering consequences that transition forced [18:00] to [44:00]. It is structural history and design philosophy, not a code-clause webinar, so it carries no modern spec instruction.
### Spec References
No modern AISC, AWS, or RCSC sections are cited; the lecture predates those standards by design. A question at [52:30] confirms there was no organizationally created standard or design manual for cast-iron columns and beams in the 1800s, only manufacturer-produced guidelines and weekly practitioner club discussion. General principles, no section cited.
### Technical Details
The structural systems described are cast-iron interior columns inside load-bearing masonry (Montauk Block 1882, Rookery 1886, Monadnock), then riveted steel skeletal framing (Rand McNally 1889, the first full steel skeletal skyscraper, and the Reliance Building) [19:00] to [42:00]. Root invented the first concrete-and-rail-grid mat foundation at Montauk Block, an orthogonal grid of railroad rail set in concrete to spread column load across Chicago hardpan over squishy clay [21:30]. Schafer notes a real numerical fact: the design factor of safety on direct stress dropped from 8 for cast-iron columns to 4 for steel riveted columns, which alone roughly halved building self-weight, and removing the masonry halved it again [37:21] to [38:00]. Lateral systems progressed from masonry mass through rod bracing, knee bracing, and portal frames to the early moment frame ("table-leg" rigid connection analogy) detailed by the engineer Shankland on the Reliance Building [40:30] to [43:30].
### Fabrication Notes
The video does not cover modern shop fabrication, tolerances, fit-up, or QC. The only fabrication-adjacent content is historical: the period shift from cast-iron columns to riveted built-up steel columns in the 1870s to 1890s and early terracotta-tile and plaster-arch fireproofing of columns and floors [22:30] to [24:15].
### Erection Notes
No modern erection procedures, sequencing, bracing, or rigging are taught. The lecture references early construction falsework for iron train-shed arches and the general difficulty of building tall on Chicago soils, but only as historical context [11:00], [37:00].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
No modern inspection or rejection content. Two historical structural failures are named: differential settlement of a Chicago post office that sank multiple feet [20:35], and the collapse during construction of a lightweight steel-joist hotel roof in Kansas City that Burnham attempted without fully understanding the system [31:00]. Schafer also quotes the 1893 Engineering Record warning that skeleton buildings fortified only by a lack of failure are "very indifferent engineering," a period reminder that wind resistance must be designed, not assumed [40:00].
### Bid / Cost Implications
Cost appears only as a design-philosophy theme: structural efficiency and economy as the discipline that drove the Chicago school, with the safety-factor and masonry-removal weight reductions cited as the economic driver of the steel switch [38:00]. Schafer contrasts efficient steel expression against buildings whose sculptural form made the steel inefficient and very expensive, such as the HSBC Hong Kong and CCTV examples [47:43] to [48:46]. No modern estimating, takeoff, or pricing method is presented.
### Your Company Application
Value here is cultural and brand, not technical. The lecture reinforces Your Company conventional-structural-steel positioning: skeletal steel frame, moment connections, and braced frames as the honest expression of the structure, with no PEMB language anywhere, which is useful context for capability statements and proposal narrative. The safety-factor history is a good reminder for Ivan that allowable-stress factors and member self-weight are not arbitrary, but no value flows to aisc_validator.py takeoff, Tekla detailing, Mario welding, Paul safety, anchor rods, joists, field bolting, or ACP controls from this video. ## Case Studies in Construction Engineering of New and Existing Complex Steel Bridges
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3tRXaOW1wdE | Duration: 1:26:54 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is a three-part World Steel Bridge Symposium panel on construction engineering for steel bridges, where the controlling discipline is the partially-erected state, not the finished structure. Talk one (Dan, HNTB) covers replacing a fracture-critical pin and link on the 1940 US-84 Mississippi River cantilever truss at Natchez [00:00], built around staged temporary load paths so a single member holding up the bridge can be cut and replaced. Talk two (Bob Cisneros, High Steel Structures) covers metrology and full trial assembly of a skewed, curved, haunched pedestrian bridge, and steel dead-load camber verification [31:49]. Talk three (Andrew Key Shaw, Alfred Benesch) is four erection-engineering case studies on girder stability during the pick, strand jacking, pier brackets, and a shoring tower on a barge [57:31]. The recurring theme is that structures are most vulnerable partially erected and that means-and-methods analysis, not the design code, governs that window [58:01].
### Spec References
This is a bridge-sector panel governed by AASHTO, not AISC building specs, so almost no AISC 360 / 341 / AWS / RCSC section numbers are spoken. The cited references are NCHRP Project Report 725 on curved and skewed bridges [35:27], the AASHTO/NSBA Steel Bridge Collaboration [31:12], and a noted observation that AASHTO devotes "277 pages" to the completed steel section but leaves partially-completed erection in the "you better know what you're doing" category [79:22]. Speakers also reference a University of Texas two-girder buckling paper (Helwig involved) [62:36] and the UT Lift erection-analysis tool [71:17]. No AISC 360 chapter, AISC 341 seismic section, AWS D1.1 clause, RCSC provision, or AISC Design Guide number was stated; for bolting and welding specifics, general principles, no section cited.
### Technical Details
The Natchez truss is a five-span cantilever truss with a suspended span and quasi-suspended spans, the hangers being forged links (a roughly 10 in by 16 in by 7 ft 6 in "dog bone") on 10 in diameter pins, treated as a single fracture-critical pin-and-link system that must be replaced as an assembly [00:31][06:40]. Instrumentation tracked real forces: the diagonal bypass was tensioned to 836 kips against a member dead load of 761 kips, and the link dead load of about 660 kips showed a 655 kip change when bypassed [13:14]. Cutting the pins transferred 20 to 40 kips into the link and 1 to 3 ksi into the splice plate because stiffness tracks force [16:48]. The pedestrian bridge work centers on metrology: a total station accurate to roughly 3 mm at 300 to 600 ft, a 360 prism, horizontal control set from a MicroStation/AutoCAD model exported into the total station, and camber generated from the CAD/CAM single-source model [38:31][42:36]. Erection-engineering details include eigenvalue/geometrically-nonlinear buckling analysis, a two-girder system with factor of safety 1.21 fixed by adding top lateral bracing, quartering-wind control via twin HSS pipe braces, and "good roll" spreader-beam geometry to replumb girders during the pick [62:36][67:11][71:47].
### Fabrication Notes
High Steel's position is that full bridge assembly is rare and not recommended; the norm is unit assembly, and full trial assembly here was a contractual exception that produced near-laboratory data [34:56]. Holding tight fabrication tolerances when drilling full-size holes is a cost decision: the fabricator does not want to "build this bridge twice for free," so full-size holes demand tighter tolerance than sub-size holes that get reamed later [41:04]. A shop catch was a bearing stiffener whose incline had to be truly vertical only after all deflections; the shop welded it full-penetration in the correct skewed orientation rather than matching its tilted neighbors, and catching that in the shop is far cheaper than in the field [50:51]. On the Natchez repair, splice-plate templates were welded over the existing gussets with 300 A490 bolts through the existing steel, then the 1 in splice plates were drilled from those templates and beat to fit [14:15]. New eye bars were bored undersized then line-bored in place over about 30 hours to take a 10 in hole to 10 and 3/4 in, with a 24/7 fab shop turning pins to measured dimensions overnight [19:22][23:29].
### Erection Notes
The Natchez sequence is the model: tension the diagonal bypass first, then upper longitudinal restraints sized to a predicted temperature swing, weld splice-plate templates, install the splice plate as the 100 percent load path, add a top strut plate against locked-up lateral forces, install lower longitudinal restraints as a secondary bypass, then cut the pin (the contractor used a wire saw, about 1.5 hours per pin face) [12:44][16:16]. The bridge was fully closed 11 weeks rather than keeping one lane open, to remove live-load vibration during the cut [11:13]. Across the girder case studies the controlling moves are shoring towers (one released with nearly 20 in of deflection), pier brackets for deep-water spans, strand jacking pre-assembled segments off barges, and a shoring tower mounted on a ballasted barge where the crew pumped roughly 100,000 lb of water out so the tower, not the crane, took the girder [60:34][66:08][81:25]. A consistent lesson is detailed, picture-driven, phone-coordinated release procedures so the crane operator knows exactly when it is safe to lower load [69:46].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The original 1940 detail failed by an unintended mechanism: pins were never meant to rotate, so high bearing stress grooved the pins (the weaker metal) and oblonged the gusset holes, keeper-plate welds sheared, and a prior 1995 contractor failed four times to reset a pin that had effectively seized [02:33][17:49]. Hidden defects only visible after disassembly included an existing pin misaligned 3/16 in per foot and a U29 cantilever gusset buckled out about 2 in from an erection force locked in during the original 1940s closure, which forced added splice plates and a jump from about 200 to about 300 A490 bolts for the eccentricity [22:27][24:31][26:02]. The named failure example is a Tennessee bridge that collapsed over 20 years ago after a cross frame was removed to fix a fit-up problem, increasing the unbraced length [58:01]. Common fit-up trouble on curved girders comes from differential deflection (1.25 in versus 2 in between adjacent girders) when cross frames are hung before the next girder lands, especially erecting inside-out [73:47].
### Bid / Cost Implications
Owners (MDOT plus Louisiana DOT) deliberately bypassed pure low-bid, using an RFQ to shortlist qualified specialty contractors so an unqualified bidder could not win the work, and planned to similarly prequalify painters to avoid finger-pointing [10:43][29:39]. Life-cycle economics drove the whole Natchez program: extending a bridge 75 years instead of replacing a Mississippi River crossing the state cannot afford, with the next phase bundling six remaining pin-and-link replacements into a 9-month painting closure [21:55][29:09]. The fabricator's cost message is that full assembly is expensive and usually unnecessary given modern metrology, and that the operationally efficient design (fewer bolts per partial splice, faster crew release) is what a good contractor actually pays for because crane and ironworker time is the number-one cost [34:56][59:33]. Catching detail errors in the shop versus the field is repeatedly framed as the big cost lever [51:21].
### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, the durable lesson is that bolt counts and splice plate sizes can grow once eccentricity and field reality are known (200 to 300 A490 here), so estimate connection material with margin and flag any partially-supported or staged-erection scope as an engineered line, not a unit rate. For Tekla detailing and the in-house PE stamp, the metrology and "validate with a second method" discipline maps directly: drive camber and geometry from one single-source model, hand-check the model with an independent calc, and remember that ironworkers want a stamp before they lower a crane [42:36][70:46]. For Mario's shop crew, the full-penetration stiffener fix and the "fix it in the shop, not the field" rule reinforce that a flagged fit-up issue is cheaper welded right at the bench. For Paul's safety program, reaming and large drill-bit bind-up are named as bridge-fab hazards and partially-erected stability is the dominant risk, both worth a toolbox-talk analogue even on building steel. Anchor-rod relevance is indirect (pin alignment and line-boring tolerance echo our anchor-tolerance discipline). DOCTRINE FLAGS: NONE; this is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language, and no supplier names were added. Caution that A490 and AASHTO bridge practice cited here do not override our building-side AISC 360 / RCSC defaults, and no AISC weight or section number should be inferred from this bridge-sector content.

## Is It Likely My Design Will Fail?
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=itie93Adetc | Duration: 57:51 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
Ron Hamburger (Simpson Gumpertz and Heger, past Higgins lecturer) teaches a method to estimate the annual probability of failure of a member whose demand-capacity ratio (DCR) exceeds 1.0, instead of just writing "OK" at the bottom of a calc sheet [03:07][05:13]. LRFD separates a log-normal load (demand) distribution from a log-normal resistance distribution; the overlap is the notional failure probability, and a code-conforming DCR of 1.0 already builds in large margins [06:13][18:38]. The procedure: pull the target probability of failure at DCR=1.0 from ASCE 7, estimate the combined dispersion of load and resistance, then use Excel LOGNORM.DIST to back out the failure probability at the actual DCR [21:16][35:39]. This is a design/evaluation engineering lecture, not a fabrication or erection lecture.
### Spec References
The speaker cited specific documents: ASCE 7 (editions 7-05, 7-10, 7-16) Tables 1.3.1 and 1.3.2 for target reliability / probability of failure by risk category and failure mode [20:46]; ASCE 7 Chapter 1 reliability tables and the Chapter 2 commentary on load and resistance factor derivation [10:20][14:03]; NBS Special Publication 577 (Ellingwood, National Bureau of Standards, 1977) for load and resistance dispersions [27:54][28:25]; and a Galambos paper giving bias and coefficient-of-variation values for steel members [28:55][30:58]. No AISC 360 section numbers, AISC 341 seismic provisions, AWS D1.1 clauses, or RCSC bolting sections were cited; this talk stays in reliability theory and ASCE 7 load combinations.
### Technical Details
A code DCR of 1.0 for a simply supported steel beam in flexure (dead plus live) carries an annual failure probability near 3 x 10^-5 [10:50][32:31]. The worked example: a beam at DCR 1.07, 10 percent dead / 90 percent live demand, combines dead dispersion 10 percent, live dispersion 25 percent, and modeling dispersion 9 percent (root-sum-square) to a load variability of 25 percent; resistance variability for an elastic beam is 12 percent; total dispersion 0.28 [33:02][34:04][34:37]. Solving in Excel gives a median DCR near 3.1 and a failure probability of 7 x 10^-5 at DCR 1.07, roughly twice the code target but still low [35:39][36:11]. For seismic, ASCE 7 sets a 10 percent failure probability at maximum considered earthquake (MCE) for risk category II, dispersion 0.60; design-level shaking (two-thirds MCE) then yields about 2.5 percent [40:22][41:53][42:26]. A 50 percent material yield deficiency in an old structure was shown to give a 21 percent failure probability under design shaking [42:57].
### Fabrication Notes
Fabrication is not the subject of this lecture. The one relevant aside is material-strength bias from the mill: A572 Grade 50 steel has a 50 ksi specified minimum yield but actual heats often run 58 to 60 ksi, and there is no upper cap on yield, so the resistance distribution is skewed upward and gives the design 20 to 30 percent of unstated reserve [13:32][25:50]. Mills remelt heats that test below the minimum, which is why the lower tail is controlled and the upper tail is not.
### Erection Notes
No erection content. The talk does not address field procedures, sequencing, bracing, rigging, or site coordination.
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The recurring error named is the reflexive "OK" written next to a DCR of 1.05 or 1.07 without quantifying the actual risk [03:07][05:43]. A second is misreading the Excel LOGNORM.DIST inputs: its "mean" argument wants the log of the median value and its "standard deviation" argument wants the coefficient of variation, not the literal mean and standard deviation [27:24][27:54]. The speaker warns that accepting DCRs of 1.2 to 1.3 routinely is a real failure path: across 100,000 members over a 50 to 100 year life, one or more will fail even at 0.1 percent annual probability each [37:48]. He also flags that building officials will not approve a sub-code DCR even under alternative-means provisions, because it is demonstrably less safe than code [48:13].
### Bid / Cost Implications
The driver is the cost of strengthening a member discovered to be overstressed after fabrication or after finishes are installed [04:43][46:07]. A late beam fix can require demolition, delay building opening, and cost in the tens of thousands; the example cites a roughly 20,000 dollar contractor fix [46:37][47:08]. The reliability method gives the engineer and client a basis to decide whether to spend that money or accept a quantified, low residual risk, and the lecture stresses that the client, not the engineer alone, should own that risk-versus-cost decision [44:30][52:09].
### Your Company Application
This is a design and evaluation lecture, so it touches Your Company's in-house PE stamp far more than the shop floor. If the in-house PE ever signs off on a member running slightly over 1.0 (a late load change, a reused existing frame, or a value-engineering trim), this method is the defensible way to quantify the residual annual and service-life failure probability and to document standard-of-care reasoning rather than scrawling "OK" [40:22][52:40]. For Ivan's takeoff and estimating, the cost lesson is concrete: catching an overstress during detailing or estimate review is cheap, while a fix after fabrication or after the building is finished costs demolition, schedule, and roughly 20,000 dollars per the example, so an early member check pays for itself [46:07]. The A572 Grade 50 actual-versus-specified yield point [13:32] reinforces our doctrine that AISC weights and capacities come from aisc_validator.py and never from LLM math. Doctrine flags: NONE. Nothing here conflicts with Your Company doctrine, and the talk is design-side only, so it does not touch Mario's welding, Paul's safety program, Tekla detailing, anchor rods, joists, field bolting, or ACP controls.

## Efficient Lateral Load Resisting Systems for Low Rise Buildings
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1UQIe4K5aDA | Duration: 1:08:23 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
Jason Perry (Stanley D. Lindsey) and Patrick McManus (Martin/Martin) walk through choosing and economizing lateral systems for low-rise steel buildings, focused on low-seismic R=3 systems where the engineer has freedom to detail braces and frames around architecture [01:07][01:37]. The controlling theme is that least weight is not least cost: structure is only about 18 to 25% of total construction cost, structural steel about 10 to 12%, and that steel cost splits roughly a third material, a third shop labor, a third erection labor, so chasing tonnage rarely moves the project number [38:03][38:35][39:07]. The better levers are constructability, fewer trades, less sequencing, and less time on site [40:38][41:10]. A second thesis is that high-seismic systems (SCBF, EBF, BRBF) can pay off even in low-seismic areas when they cut foundation size on poor soil or spread footings [56:29][68:12].

### Spec References
ASCE 7-10 3-second gust and n-year wind speeds via the ATC wind speed map [14:27]; ASCE 7-05 wind reduction factors roughly 0.74 and 0.84 [14:57]; AISC Design Guide 3 (serviceability design considerations, drift criteria), with Larry Griffis cited as an author [12:55][13:26]; an AISC acoustics design guide produced "last year" (number not stated) [42:12]; Steel Deck Institute Diaphragm Design Manual and the SDI deck catalog [21:07]; ICC-ES / ICBO evaluation reports for deck diaphragm capacity, specifically ESR-1227 for diaphragm flexibility and aspect ratios [25:14]; Factory Mutual Global property loss data sheets for deck wind-uplift spans [22:10]; SJI joist guidance and spreadsheets for joist moment connections to wide-flange strong axis, weak axis, and HSS columns [31:27][31:58]; AISC 341 seismic provisions for composite shear walls and ordinary composite shear walls [45:46][46:17]; ACI 318 reinforcement ratios for ordinary walls referenced through AISC 341 [50:53]; AISC 358 prequalified moment connections for IMF and SMF [58:30]; R-factor values cited (R=3 baseline, OCBF 3.25, IMF higher, EBF 8, SCBF 6, BRBF 8) [58:00][59:32][60:02][61:02].

### Technical Details
Braced frames are almost always cheaper than moment frames, with the tradeoff of bigger uplift-resisting foundations; keep brace angle 30 to 60 degrees, ideally near 45, sometimes held to 35 to 55 for connection economy [02:08][03:11]. For an X-brace in a non-high-ductility R=3 system, the tension brace can be taken to brace the compression brace so an effective length of 0.5L is justified, because tension stiffening offsets P-delta and yields the same stiffness as an eigenbuckling analysis [07:14][08:15]. Single-diagonal frames erect one piece but have no redundancy and larger braces; chevron and V configs drive a heavier collector beam [05:13][08:45]. Moment frames are drift-governed (wind drift on a 10-year wind, a serviceability state so stiffness is not reduced for direct analysis), and the cheapest stiffness gain is a deeper column (W18, W21, W24) rather than more weight [11:52][12:25][17:32][18:02]. Diaphragm starting points: 1.5-inch B deck at 6.5 ft max span, 22 gauge minimum, 5/8 spot welds in a 36/4 pattern give about 335 plf service, while 18 gauge with 36/7 reaches about 943 plf; aspect ratios run 2:1 up to 5:1 by flexibility [22:10][22:40][23:10][24:43]. Continuous-chord joists used as moment frames avoid chord splices and barely hit joist cost; the difficulty is decoupling large gravity chord forces (carried around the column on sandwich plates) from the small lateral component carried into the column [29:24][32:59][35:32].

### Fabrication Notes
The recurring fabrication economy argument is to avoid full-penetration welds: a shop-welded column cap plate with four bolts beats a CJP beam-flange-to-column detail on a roof, even when the bolts grow to 1.25-inch A490 to carry the moment [15:27][15:58]. Single-story cap-plate detail is a cap plate with stated thickness, a stated bolt count and size, one stiffener for an HSS column and two stiffeners for a W10 or W12 column [16:31]. Continuous moment lines extend the connection toward the gravity inflection point so the moment connection need only be a fraction (about 50%) of beam capacity, allowing a PJP top flange (chosen for deck interruptions) and a bolted flange plate or PJP at the bottom [17:01][17:32]. Joist seats should not carry large axial loads because that cranks moment into the joist chord the manufacturer will not design for, so attach to the outstanding legs concentric to the chord [34:31][35:01]. Composite shotcrete walls keep every connection steel-to-steel with vertical deck as the form, so there are no fit-up or form-saver issues [48:49][49:19].

### Erection Notes
Single-diagonal braces save erection because there is one brace to set per bay per floor instead of two [05:13]. Beam lengths are held to about 50 to 60 ft to fit on a truck without a special permit [19:05]. Cast-in-place concrete cores are critical path, must come out of the ground first, and over three stories create sequencing conflicts where you can only build so much wall before steel must go up to brace the next lift, putting trades over each other [43:45][44:15]. Concrete tolerance is far looser than steel, forcing expensive adjustable field-welded connections, and every shear-wall building the speaker has done has had a missed embed [44:45][45:15]. The shotcrete composite wall is built to let steel erection finish and the crew leave site before the shotcreters return to spray [48:49]. Whether shotcrete or deck pours first changes whether the spandrel beam can be light or must carry wet concrete weight [52:55][53:25].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Named pitfalls: missed embeds on cast-in-place shear-wall jobs (the speaker says he has never had one without it) [45:15]; concrete tolerance misfits that drive field welding and delays with disputed fault [44:45][45:46]; loading a joist seat with large axial force that overstresses the chord against the manufacturer's design [34:00]; assuming an X-brace compression effective length of full L when 0.5L is defensible, leaving tonnage on the table [07:44]; treating diaphragms as rigid in software when reality is flexible or semi-rigid, so analysis assumptions do not match behavior [26:45][27:17]; and under-detailing the brace-to-foundation anchorage on capacity-designed SCBF braces, where a brace sized for 100 kips compression forces a connection and anchorage to develop 400 to 500 kips in tension and surprises the GC [60:32][61:02][66:07].

### Bid / Cost Implications
A 5% tonnage saving on a project equals about 0.2% of total project cost, so weight-based value engineering rarely matters; GCs and pre-con estimators price on unit cost ($/ton, $/SF), which reinforces the least-weight habit but is not reality [39:07][39:37][40:07]. Real savings come from schedule and trade reduction since GC time on site always costs money however the bid was priced [41:10]. Concrete cores are partly a GC profit play: one GC told the speaker self-performing cores lifts profit from 2 to 3% up to 8% [43:13]. Two foundation case studies quantify the high-seismic-in-low-seismic argument: an SDC B job dropped base shear from 490 kips at R=3 to far less at R=8, cutting one footing from 46 to 21 cubic yards (54%) for about $12,500 saved against a BRB at roughly $3,000 per brace [62:02][63:33][64:04]; an SDC C job on poor soil used SCBF R=6 to roughly halve foundation loads, where the R=3 footing alone would have run about $51,000 versus $23,000, leaving room to add about 120 plf to every brace and still come out ahead at an in-place steel cost of about $4,000 per ton [64:35][66:07][67:09].

### Your Company Application
For Ivan takeoff, this validates the verify-don't-generate posture: do not let a least-weight assumption drive a bid number, because the $/SF gate and the third-third-third (material, shop, erection) split mean schedule and connection complexity move price more than tonnage, and AISC member weights still come only from aisc_validator.py. For Mario's shop, the cap-plate-with-four-bolts versus CJP point is a direct fabrication-cost flag (1.25-inch A490 bolts can beat full-pen welds on a roof), and the PJP top flange at deck interruptions plus joist seat eccentricity rules are AWS D1.1 and SJI items for WPS planning. For anchor rods, the SCBF brace-anchorage warning is the most load-bearing item: capacity-designed braces force very large tension into the anchor-rod group and foundation, so our anchor-rod design, setting, and tolerance workstream must size for the developed brace strength, not the service load. For joists, the continuous-chord moment-frame detailing and "attach to outstanding legs, not the seat" guidance feed Tekla detailing and any in-house PE stamp on joist-to-column moment connections. For Paul Guerrero, the over-three-story core sequencing with trades stacked vertically and the missed-embed pattern are coordination and inspection hold points. For ACP project controls, the foundation-cost-versus-steel tradeoff and early-GC-involvement message support recording lateral-system decisions and their foundation impact in the register rather than optimizing steel weight in isolation. Doctrine conflict: NONE. The talk references concrete cores and shotcrete composite walls, but only as engineering context for steel-frame coordination, and it uses no PEMB language, so our conventional structural steel positioning holds.
