## AISC Design Guide 31    Castellated and Cellular Beam Design
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5hdwcnP7XLk | Duration: 1:07:27 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This webinar walks through AISC Design Guide 31, which documents US state-of-practice design for castellated beams (hexagonal web openings) and cellular beams (round web openings) and conforms to the 2017 AISC spec [01:34][04:39]. Both are fabricated by splitting a rolled wide-flange along its web, staggering the two halves, and welding them back together to create a deeper section from the same material, increasing depth by about 50 percent so the section gains bending stiffness because depth is cubed in moment of inertia [06:12][07:13]. The presenters (Dave Deinhart, Sam Ferris, John Colson) stress that the single biggest benefit is stiffness, so these members make sense on long spans (about 40 ft and up) and heavier loads, not on short stiff-controlled spans [13:50][15:23].
### Spec References
The speakers cited AISC 360-16 throughout: vertical shear strength per Spec Section G2 [32:28], T-section compressive strength per Chapter E3 [41:12], T-section flexural strength per Section F9.1 (yielding) and Section F9.2 (lateral-torsional buckling) [43:19], and the combined axial-plus-flexure interaction per Equations H1-1a and H1-1b [43:49]. Welded fabrication is per AWS D1.1 [31:57]. Design Guide 31 itself is the governing document. Web-post buckling equations for castellated beams trace to Dr. Redwood's McGill University testing, and the cellular-beam web-post equations to the Steel Construction Institute of England [35:31][37:37].
### Technical Details
Castellated geometry uses a cutting angle phi held between 58 and 62 degrees, with geometric limits E greater than or equal to 3 in, opening height over E less than 8, and E over web thickness less than 30 [23:00][24:00]. Cellular geometric limits are spacing over hole diameter between 1.08 and 1.5, and gross depth over diameter between 1.25 and 1.75, with E at least 3 in [25:34]. Unlike a wide-flange where you check max moment and max shear once, these beams require checking moment-shear interaction at every opening and every web post [27:16]. The full limit-state list is compactness and local buckling, vertical shear at gross and net section, horizontal shear yielding in the web post, web-post buckling, Vierendeel bending of the tees, axial tension and compression in the tees, overall flexural strength, and lateral-torsional buckling if the top flange is unbraced [30:21][31:27]. Composite asymmetric sections converge effective depth over three or four iterations, and full versus partial composite action is checked opening by opening, not once for the whole beam [44:50][48:27]. A castellated section is named like CB30x44 (gross depth x weight) and cellular like LB30x44, with asymmetric forms such as CB30x44/50 [07:44][11:48].
### Fabrication Notes
A castellated beam is made with a single zigzag cut that yields two halves and a little end waste; a cellular beam takes twice the cutting (two passes) and drops a waste sliver from the middle [06:42][10:15]. When split, the tees tend to banana from internal stress and are straightened back flat on the table before staggering and welding [11:18]. Asymmetric composite sections combine a lighter top beam and a heavier bottom beam (rule of thumb roughly 20 percent heavier bottom), so two parent shapes are needed and an odd beam count leaves a spare top or bottom [08:44][14:22]. Cellular depth varies with spacing, so the beam supplier needs a spacing range rather than a single S to fit a profile to the beam length, and the depth call (LB24) is nominal and can run plus or minus [54:39][55:41]. The lone named US fabricator was SteelFab of Charlotte NC, with Arcelor (Belgium) and Westok (UK) named in Europe [56:43].
### Erection Notes
The webinar does not cover field erection sequence, crane, rigging, or bracing in any detail. Its erection-economy point is that long-span castellated framing reduces erection piece count, sometimes by nearly half, which the presenters argue is where the real cost savings sit because piece handling, not weight per square foot, drives erection cost [16:23][16:54].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Failure modes named are web-post yielding, web-post buckling (which carries a twist, distinguishing it from local web crippling), web yielding at the fillet, web crippling, and horizontal weld rupture along the weld line [29:51][30:21]. A design error flagged was specifying a single hole spacing instead of a range, which makes it hard for the supplier to fit a profile [55:41]. The closing research story is a cautionary material failure: a 3-in thick end plate fractured prematurely under cyclic seismic loading because Charpy through-thickness toughness was below 10 ft-lb where 70-plus was expected, traced to thick plate not manufactured properly [65:28][66:29].
### Bid / Cost Implications
There is an up-front fabrication cost premium for cutting and re-welding, so the steel savings have to be large enough to clear it; the rule of thumb is the parent beam should be roughly 40 lb/ft over a roughly 40 ft span before castellating pays, because saving 30 percent on a 14 lb beam is not enough steel to beat the manufacturing cost [15:23][15:53]. The presenters argue against judging these by tonnage per square foot alone and toward total installed cost including reduced piece count [16:23]. A 40 ft beam can require on the order of 350 individual calculations (160 bending, 72 shear, 26 web-post buckling, plus LTB and 100 deflection checks), so design is software-driven via tools such as Bentley RAM SBeam and RAM Steel [53:36][54:07]. Parking structures at 60 ft clear spans are called the single best application, sometimes cheaper than precast [19:59][20:29].
### Your Company Application
Castellated and cellular beams are a specialty product, not a stock takeoff item, so for Ivan the named designations (CBxx and LBxx, asymmetric CB30x44/50) and the supplier-spacing-range requirement must be captured at takeoff; these members carry no AISC database weight, so aisc_validator.py applies only to the parent W-shape, not the fabricated section, and any castellated tonnage stays LOW confidence pending supplier confirmation. Mario's shop note is the AWS D1.1 longitudinal web weld, the banana-then-straighten step, and the partial or full hole fill where a beam frames into a cellular beam at an opening [53:04]. Tekla detailing must model openings, web-post spacing, and connection hole fills explicitly, and the in-house PE stamp work is opening-by-opening per-section checking that is realistically software-driven, not hand calc. The thick-plate Charpy failure is a direct QC flag for any thick connection plate Your Company buys. Doctrine flags: NONE. This is conventional structural steel, no PEMB language, and nothing here conflicts with rate locks or governance; note only that these fabricated sections are outside the 2,299-shape validator and must be priced as a flagged specialty item.

## Steel Castings in Architecture -- Do You Know How to Design Them?
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EswVvIhiSPM | Duration: 1:26:23 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This webinar teaches how to design and specify custom and standardized steel castings as monolithic connection nodes in architecturally exposed and fatigue-critical steel structures. The panel was Raymond Monroe of the Steel Founders Society of America, Carlos de Oliveira of a casting design firm, and design engineer Tom Meyer. The central idea is that pouring molten steel into a complex mold lets you put material exactly where the flow of forces wants it, replacing welded tube-to-tube junctions where stress concentration and weld defects normally cause fatigue failure [32:07][33:08]. A cast node moves the weld away from the geometric stress riser, which can extend fatigue life by an order of magnitude (a factor of 10) and last 10 times longer than a weld-fabricated connection [33:38][69:00]. Cast steel is real steel: all steel is cast, and a typical structural cast carbon steel runs about 30 ksi minimum to 40-plus ksi typical yield with 25 percent elongation, weldable under prequalified procedures with the engineer's approval [25:27][52:00].

### Spec References
The speakers cited very few formal code sections by number. Named references: AWS prequalified weld procedures, usable on cast steel only with the engineer's approval [25:27]; ASME allowable stresses, which Monroe stated match the cast-steel allowables to plate and other materials [28:01]; surface-finish standards MSS SP-55 (visual examination, fire-hydrant-grade finish for far viewing) [80:20] and ASTM A802 with criteria levels 1 through 5 against tactile comparator plates, level 1 being the finest [80:50][81:23]; and surface roughness expressed in RMS, down to about 100 RMS by blast and grind or a mirror buff [82:24]. The forthcoming SFSA-AISC steel-castings design guide was described as in early development, funded by a Department of Defense grant, intended to set design allowables, ET requirements, and prequalified weld procedures [05:17][27:30]. No AISC 360 chapter, AISC 341 section, RCSC clause, or Design Guide number was stated, so those are general principles, no section cited.

### Technical Details
Cast nodes are non-prismatic disturbed-region (D-region) bodies where beam theory does not apply, so finite element analysis is required to find the stresses; the Charlotte airport job ran 1,044 FE cases across 32 cast nodes [50:07][51:08]. Geometry is tuned so wall sections taper to reduce stress at complex joints and so tubes framing into a node can be thinner-walled because the casting absorbs the local connection limit states (for example HSS chord-wall plastification), which reduces overall tonnage in tubular structures [34:40][35:42][54:09]. Castings are heat-treated and austenitized more than once to give equiaxed grains and uniform properties in every direction, unlike rolled product that retains directional sulfide and oxide stringers [83:26][84:28]. Common structural cast steel carries roughly 20 to 30 percent ductility; the firm can reach 180 ksi yield with reduced ductility, and grinding-media castings hit 300 ksi ultimate with essentially no yield [84:59][86:02]. Projects cited include Queen Richmond Centre Toronto (a 35,000 lb cellular cast node carrying about 20 million kip down each Delta frame, 70 ft tall, 40 in diameter, 2 in wall concrete-filled tubes) [41:20][44:26], University of Connecticut V-columns, Charlotte Douglas airport, and the Transbay Transit Center (34 castings, 5,000 to 50,000 lb each, an eccentric braced frame seismic system) [53:00].

### Fabrication Notes
A casting is built in a bonded-sand mold held with organic glue, with a gating (plumbing) system to admit metal, risers to feed shrinkage as steel contracts on solidifying, vents to release air, and a core to form internal passages [21:21][22:23]. Foundries use casting solidification and fluid-flow simulation to place risers and avoid shrinkage pockets, and additive sand printing to skip hard tooling and produce parts in one to two weeks [23:24][24:26]. After FE analysis sets the stresses, the casting designer sets non-destructive examination acceptance criteria zone by zone; any indication larger than the criterion is weld-repaired in process before final stress relief, yielding a sound monolithic part [50:38][51:08]. The team decides which features are as-cast (needing generous radii so detail is not lost) versus machined (counterbores and sharp-cornered reveals were machined at Charlotte for a clean aesthetic) [51:38][52:08]. Surface finish is matched to viewing distance and coating system, from MSS SP-55 for far views up to a machined or buffed mirror finish for close range; San Ysidro castings were galvanized then high-performance painted [54:09][82:55][77:12].

### Erection Notes
Cast nodes simplify field construction because they convert complex tube-to-tube T, Y, and K intersections into simple circumferential welds with good all-around weld access; a tree node would be shop-welded to the lower column and the upper branches field-welded as circumferential joints [37:46][38:16]. The Stuttgart Airport tree and similar structures show the casting taking the geometry so field welds are clean and accessible [37:15]. For the San Ysidro cable-stayed canopy, procurement and lead time were planned early so the custom castings (made overseas and shipped) would not become the critical-path item delaying erection [71:59][72:29]. Cable end fittings (open spelter sockets, conical sockets, head blocks) are themselves castings, connected by reverse-threaded rods for adjustable cable length rather than welding [64:35][65:39].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The recurring failure mode named is fatigue cracking at welded tube junctions, where the weld sits at the peak geometric stress concentration and weld defects add their own stress riser, leading to failure after a number of load cycles [32:07][32:37]. Cast iron failures were described for contrast: graphitization, where acidic soil consumes the steel in gray iron pipe and leaves only continuous graphite that fails under load, plus gray iron's near-zero tensile ductility [13:38][14:09]. Inspection is by foundry NDE plus third-party NDE using radiographic, ultrasonic, magnetic-particle, and visual testing, with acceptance criteria and tensile testing of sample portions written into the spec; the warning is that the engineer of record should not set those criteria alone but with the casting designer [75:39][76:09].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Castings are not a cheap source of steel because the foundry spends as much effort on the shape as on the metal and works in small custom batches, but they are often the cheapest route to the final engineered component [20:48]. The strongest cost lesson is design-for-manufacturing: on Transbay the pre-design casting estimate was 22 million dollars on a 4 billion dollar project, and after a casting designer was engaged at 95 percent CD and redesigned plus added 46 castings across 15 new geometries, the final cost dropped 30 percent to 15.5 million [54:39][55:09]. Standardized off-the-shelf clevis and socket castings cut fabrication labor sharply: a fabricated aesthetic pin connection on a 6-5/8 in pipe needs about 102 linear inches of weld and grinding versus roughly a third of that for a circumferential weld of a clevis, weldable fast on a turning spindle with an automated machine [59:48][60:20]. Lead time spans bid-and-award, design, submittal-and-approval, manufacture, and shipping, so schedule must be planned early [72:00].

### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, the key insight is that cast nodes let tubular members be thinner-walled, so a structure with castings carries less tonnage than the equivalent all-welded tubular frame; do not price a cast-node job at the heavier weld-fabricated wall thickness, and treat custom castings as a delegated-design, performance-spec line with its own long lead time rather than a shop fabrication item. Mario's shop welding ties directly to the standardized-casting workflow: clevis and socket castings weld to HSS with simple circumferential welds (the spindle-plus-automated-welder method), far less deposit and grinding than a fabricated pin, and cast steel is weldable under AWS prequalified procedures only with EOR approval, so any cast-to-steel joint needs a WPS check. Paul's safety scope touches the heavy node picks (a 35,000 lb single casting at Queen Richmond, up to 50,000 lb at Transbay) for rigging and lift planning. Tekla detailing should model the casting as a defined-geometry insert with circumferential field welds and capture out-to-out dimensions and the mating diameter to the steel, since the foundry owns the internal FE-driven shape. The in-house PE stamp role maps to engineer of record here: write a performance spec that delegates final casting design, states the governing load case, and requires shop drawings, FE and calc submittals, and NDE reports (RT, UT, MT, VT). Standardized end-of-member castings are the most realistic near-term fit for our typical conventional-steel work, not exotic cast trees. Doctrine flags: NONE. This is conventional structural steel and AES content with no PEMB language, and nothing here overrides aisc_validator.py weights or bid_rates.py, since cast nodes are delegated-design custom components priced outside the standard $/T member rates.

## Flexural Members:  Is my Cb Factor Correct?
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rNMX962XVsQ | Duration: 58:52 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This SSRC webinar by Todd Helwig (UT Austin) explains the Cb moment-gradient factor used to size laterally unbraced flexural members against lateral-torsional buckling (LTB). A beam under uniform moment is the base case Timoshenko derived [04:34], and Cb amplifies that base LTB curve for any real moment diagram, then the result is capped at the plastic moment Mp [08:11]. The talk teaches how to confirm a Cb value is correct, including back-calculating it from an eigenvalue buckling analysis as the ratio of the moment-gradient critical moment to the uniform-moment critical moment [10:13], and it covers cases the code equation does not cover cleanly: load position, singly symmetric sections, continuous beams with one-flange bracing, roof uplift, cantilevers, and girders during lifting.
### Spec References
The speaker cites the AISC specification Cb equation that has been in place since the mid-1990s, written brace-point to brace-point using M1 and M3 at the quarter points, M2 at centerline, and Mmax in the denominator [14:50]. He references AISC Section F2 for singly symmetric sections, noting the 13th-edition Section F2 modifier caused confusion and was removed so F2 now directs the user to a rational analysis [29:39]. The singly symmetric and special-case Cb expressions (one-flange bracing, gravity and uplift, the rho-top modifier 0.5 + 2(rho_top)^2 capped at 3) now live in the AISC Commentary [25:33][40:27]. He also cites AASHTO's older moment-gradient form and Timoshenko's cantilever buckling equations, plus the SSRC Guide (Nethercot) curve fits for load position [20:58]. The session PDCH code stated aloud is 288874 [00:30].
### Technical Details
The conventional Cb equation gives 1.0 for uniform moment, about 1.32 for a midspan point load with no intermediate bracing (published 1.35), and about 1.14 for a uniform load (published 1.12) [16:52]. It is unconservative only for a fixed-fixed beam with a midspan point load, a rare case [17:23]. Load position matters: top-flange loading lowers Cb, bottom-flange loading raises it, handled by multiplying Cb by 1.4 raised to the 2Y/H power, where H is flange-centroid depth and Y is positive below mid-height [20:58]. Top-flange load can drop effective Cb from 1.35 to about 0.96 [19:56]. Singly symmetric sections use rho = Iyc/Iy; reverse curvature requires the 0.5 + 2(rho_top)^2 modifier and a check of both flanges as potentially critical [25:33][27:36]. Special cases give very large Cb (5.5 and 2.93 in worked examples) because the full twist-prevented length is the unbraced length [38:25][40:58].
### Fabrication Notes
This is a design-stability webinar with no shop fabrication, fit-up, or QC content. The only fabrication-adjacent item is the continuity-plate detail across the column panel zone used to provide warping restraint to a cantilever beam at the column face, which the speaker flags as a costly detail often skipped in favor of conservatively neglecting warping stiffness [45:06].
### Erection Notes
The strongest erection content is girder stability during lifting [45:36]. With a single crane, spreader beam, and beam clamps, no point along the girder reliably stops twist, so the recommended method defines the unbraced length as the total segment length and assigns Cb by pick-point location: Cb = 2 for a/L below 0.225, Cb = 6 between 0.225 and 0.3 (near quarter points), and Cb = 4 above 0.3, using the minimum cross section properties along the length [50:46][51:48]. Picking at midspan is explicitly warned against. Bridge girders 180 to 200 feet need the large Cb values [51:48]. Two-crane or dual-spreader picks spread the moment diagram and help, but pick points are not brace points so the same total-length Cb method still applies [54:53].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The recurring engineering errors named are: trusting the code Cb as exact when it varies roughly 1.25 to 1.4 in reality [11:15]; ignoring top-flange load position when there is no intermediate bracing and no tipping restraint, which is unconservative [33:44]; missing that masonry or stacked loads whose centroid sits above the top flange can cause Cb to plummet [34:16]; and assuming full warping restraint at a cantilever-to-column face, where web distortion can drop capacity from 2.8 kips to about 2 kips [45:06]. There is no welding or bolting inspection-failure content in this talk.
### Bid / Cost Implications
Cost implications are indirect. Over-conservative Cb assumptions add steel weight and tonnage; the warping-restraint cantilever case is framed as a direct trade between an expensive continuity-plate panel-zone detail versus accepting a conservative lower capacity [45:06]. Correctly crediting moment gradient and tipping restraint lets an engineer avoid adding bracing or upsizing members. None of this changes fabrication or erection unit pricing directly, but it drives member sizes that flow into tonnage.
### Your Company Application
This is design-engineer knowledge that lands on the in-house PE stamp workstream, not on Ivan's takeoff or Mario's shop. When Your Company stamps beam designs, the PE must confirm Cb is set correctly for moment gradient, load position, and the special cases here, since a wrong Cb either wastes tonnage Ivan would carry or under-sizes a member. The lifting-stability content is directly relevant to erection planning: long or slender girders picked for setting should use the total-length plus pick-point Cb method before the crane plan is finalized, which ties to crane and rigging coordination that Paul Guerrero reviews for safety. The crane-rail cap-channel example [56:06] is useful if any Your Company project includes a runway beam. No conflict with Your Company doctrine; this is conventional structural steel stability, no PEMB language. Doctrine flag: NONE.

## 04 27 17 Secrets of the Manual
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7JsTSrC16H8 | Duration: 1:34:18 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
Carol Drucker walks the full AISC Steel Construction Manual (14th edition referenced throughout, with the 15th noted as imminent) part by part, showing how to pull strengths and tolerances from the design tables instead of grinding the specification equations by hand [01:34][88:00]. The manual has 17 parts: Part 1 shapes and properties, Part 2 general design info, Parts 3 to 6 main-member design (flexure, compression, tension, combined), Parts 7 to 15 connection design, Part 16 the specifications, and Part 17 miscellaneous [01:34][05:10]. The recurring lesson is to read the brief introduction to each table before using it, because the table description states the controlling assumption, for example that loads above the heavy horizontal line in the UDL tables are shear-limited not flexure-limited [55:25][63:38].
### Spec References
AISC 360-10 specification chapters and sections cited: Chapter E and E5 (single-angle compression, simplified KL/r) [15:54][16:25]; Appendix 6 (bracing strength and stiffness) [10:49]; Chapter F equations F1-1, F2-6, F3-1, F3-2 (flexure, LR, non-compact and slender flanges) [75:40]; Chapter G equation G2-1 and the CV user note in G2 (shear) [40:27][57:58]; concentrated-force equations J10-1, J10-2, J10-3, J10-4, J10-8 (flange bending, web yielding, crippling, web buckling) [44:03][50:20]; Chapter I equation I3-8 for stud strength and commentary equation I3-10 for partial composite [79:46][85:25]. Manual tables and figures: 2-4, 2-6, 3-1, 3-2, 3-21, 3-23, 4-1, 4-9, 4-12, 4-22, 7-15, figures 7-6 and 7-7, 8-4, 9-4, 10-2, 10-3, 10-14, 14-3, 15-4, and manual equation 7-21 for C prime [11:19][86:00]. Also cited: RCSC bolt specification table 6.1 (washer requirements) and the Code of Standard Practice, both in Part 16 [40:27][41:29]; AWS D1.1 prequalified joints (figures reproduced in the manual) [31:30]; Design Guides 4, 6, 16, 24, and 29 [22:00][36:17][92:09].
### Technical Details
Table 3-2 lists plastic flexural strength of wide flanges in descending order with LP and LR, so an unbraced length below LP gives MP directly and a length between LP and LR is interpolated between MP and MR [12:52][74:09]. Table 4-1 carries the PWO, PWI, PWB, and PFB constants that check whether a column needs stiffeners for web yielding, web buckling, and flange bending, though it currently omits crippling constants so Table 9-4 must be used for crippling (Drucker says crippling variables are expected in the 2022 manual) [51:51][53:22]. The instantaneous-center C prime table reduces three pages of elastic bolt-group calculation to three lines and yields a higher connection strength, 384 versus 360 kip-inches in her example [64:14][67:22]. The UDL tables assume full plastic bracing, and she warns the percentage of UDL is a guess on composite jobs, hitting 119 to 190 percent in her examples, so a shear schedule or actual reactions beats a 50 percent UDL assumption [55:25][61:33].
### Fabrication Notes
The maximum single-pass fillet weld is 5/16 inch; a 5/8 fillet takes six passes, so twice the strength costs six times the labor, favoring smaller longer welds [24:34][25:06]. Fabricators prefer a maximum 3/4 inch fillet and switch to a PJP above that [25:37]. Clean column shafts without stiffeners are preferred for both cost and erection, since a beam can slide down a clean shaft [14:23]. The weldable flat width in Part 1 governs reinforcing plate width on an HSS face because corner radii prevent the longitudinal fillet from being placed [08:47]. Bent plates for skewed connections are capped near 1/2 inch thickness by what fabricators can bend [34:10], and many fabricators avoid CJP plates, preferring a PJP with reinforcing fillet [33:06]. Column underrun of up to 1/4 inch should be accounted for when checking connection encroachment into the column [70:31].
### Erection Notes
Beam-bearing connections need rotational stability at the support so the beam does not roll off, covered in Part 2 [10:19]. Stitch plates between double angles must be specified or verified, because without them you have two single angles at reduced strength; Table 4-9 gives the number required [14:54]. Field-fit issues are handled with Table 10-2, which Drucker uses for a quick field-weld size when holes in an outstanding angle leg do not align [35:16]. Clear-distance and encroachment checks (figure 10-3) decide whether a chosen shear connection physically fits a small W8 column [27:39][70:01]. The detail itself should carry all data to support field decisions, including where the design loading came from if it arrived by RFI, email, or phone [42:31][43:01].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Anchor rods misaligned in base plates on every job traced to standard or oversized holes instead of the AISC maximum recommended base-plate hole sizes; switching to the larger holes via an approved RFI eliminated the alignment problems [37:18]. A490 bolts of 1 inch diameter or larger in oversized or slotted holes require thickened washers per RCSC Table 6.1, and an inspector will catch ordinary washers in the field [40:58]. Using a single bolt in a single-angle brace forfeits the simplified E5 procedure and forces eccentricity to be checked about both axes, which can quietly lower strength [16:25][17:26]. Local flange bending is the limit state most likely to control and govern stiffener need, so it is the one to check first [50:50][51:20]. Over-stiff WT or end-plate shear connections can attract moment to a weld line sized only for shear and crack the weld unless rotational ductility is provided per Part 9 [26:07].
### Bid / Cost Implications
Weld-pass economics drive cost directly: a larger fillet multiplies passes faster than strength, so detailing to smaller welds and PJPs over 3/4 inch saves shop hours [24:34][25:37]. Avoiding column stiffeners keeps cost down and speeds erection, so the Table 4-1 stiffener check has a real estimating consequence [14:23]. On smaller or industrial jobs the bid driver is getting tonnage down, which pushes W8 columns and tighter connection fits that the encroachment checks must validate [28:12]. Specifying a flat 50 percent UDL on composite framing is risky and can be grossly unconservative (190 percent in one project), so connection capacity tied to actual reactions protects the bid from rework [61:02].
### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, the lesson to link estimating spreadsheets to the AISC shape database via index-match maps onto Your Company's aisc_validator.py path: pull section properties and member weights from the validated database, never re-key from the book, and keep angle-gauge and splice-gauge data with the shapes [07:13][08:16]. Mario's shop work benefits from the weld-pass cost table and the 3/4 inch fillet-to-PJP threshold for WPS and labor planning, and from the prequalified-joint figures reproduced in the manual since AWS D1.1 is not always on the bench [24:34][31:30]. The anchor-rod base-plate story is a direct fit for Your Company anchor-rod design, setting, and tolerance: use AISC maximum recommended base-plate hole sizes to absorb anchor-rod misalignment, and raise an RFI to the EOR when the contract calls smaller holes [37:18]. For ACP project controls, the detail-completeness rule (spec year, ASD or LRFD, bolt and plate grades, weld sizes, and the documented source of every load) reinforces the verify-don't-generate posture and the requirement to cite where a number came from. Doctrine flags: NONE. The content is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language, and it aligns with the requirement that weights and strengths come from the validated AISC source rather than from hand math.

## SteelDay 2017: Designing in Steel
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dXS980Ed6_I | Duration: 59:23 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
Larry Owner, AISC VP of engineering and research and a former fabricator at Douglas Steel, walks through what changed across the three documents that govern steel buildings: the 2016 Specification (AISC 360-16), the 2016 Code of Standard Practice (AISC 303-16), and the 15th edition Steel Construction Manual [00:31][01:03]. His framing point is the one fabricators most often get wrong: the Manual is a convenience, not law. The 2018 IBC references the Specification, and Chapter A of the Specification in turn references the Code of Standard Practice, so those two documents are the contract-binding ones, not the Manual [02:03][02:33].
### Spec References
Verbatim citations stated by the speaker: AISC 360-16 (the Specification) with Chapter A, Chapter D and Table D3.1 case 4 shear-lag revision, Chapter E (compression, KL replaced by L sub C), Chapter J connections (Sections J1.8 bolts-with-welds, J3 bolting, Table J3.3 hole sizes, J3.3 spacing/block-shear, J10 HSS now folded in from Chapter K), Chapter K retitled to additional HSS/box requirements, Appendix 1 advanced analysis, Appendix 3 fatigue, Appendix 6 member stability bracing, equation H1-1a [02:33 through 09:55, 41:38]. AISC 303-16 Code of Standard Practice, now an ANSI standard, Sections 3.1.1/3.1.2 (stiffening options), 1.10 (no zero tolerance default), 1.11 (protected-zone marking), 7.5.1 and 10 (anchor-rod and AESS tolerances) [15:43 through 30:44]. Referenced external standards: ASCE 7-2016, AWS D1.1-2015, RCSC-2014, ACI 318-14, ACI 117 (anchor-rod holes), ASTM A1065 and A1085 (HSS), ASTM F3125 umbrella bolt standard, ASTM F3043 and F3111 (200 ksi bolts), AWS A5.36 replacing A5.20/A5.29, ASTM F844 washers, ASTM A500 grade C, A572 grade 50 [04:39 through 46:18]. Manual tables named: 1-1, 1-15, 2-4, 2-5, 2-7, 6-2 (the super table), 7-14, 10-1, 10-14C, 14-2.
### Technical Details
Compression design drops KL for L sub C and eliminates the Q slender-element factor; the old K-factor alignment chart still lives in the Appendix 7 commentary if wanted [08:53][10:28]. The flagship Manual addition is the super table 6-2, which combines axial compression and biaxial bending capacity in one place; Owner worked a W14x99 at L sub C = 14 ft, reading 1130 kips compression, 642 kip-ft strong-axis and 311 kip-ft weak-axis, then ran H1-1a to an interaction of 0.928 [38:31 through 42:09]. A500 grade C is now the preferred HSS grade, raising rectangular/square yield to 50 ksi and round to 46 ksi, and 50 ksi is the preferred plate yield up to 4 inches thick [35:24 through 36:57]. Mill rolling-tolerance changes shifted the k, k1 and T detailing dimensions on many W-shapes (Table 1-1) [34:20].
### Fabrication Notes
The Code of Standard Practice now treats digital models as equal to drawings: design documents, fabrication documents and the fabrication model, approval documents, and erection documents replace the old shop/erection drawing terms, with model approval (EOR to detailer and back) recognized as standard practice [16:45 through 21:25]. Hole sizes grew: for one-inch-and-larger bolts the oversize allowance went from 1/16 to 1/8 inch per Table J3.3 because the larger F3125 bolts physically would not seat in the old holes [13:38][53:12]. Anchor-rod hole sizes in Table 14-2 all increased to match ACI 117 field-installation needs, and F844 washers are now permitted in place of fabricated plate washers within stated clearance limits, which removes a shop cost [45:48][46:18]. Washer requirements now point to RCSC rather than being duplicated in the Specification [15:11].
### Erection Notes
Erection coverage is light in this webinar. The relevant items are anchor-rod placement tolerances under Section 7.5.1, revised to align with the AISC Manual and ACI 117, and the protected-zone marking rule under Section 1.11: in high-seismic work the protected zones must be permanently marked (paint or sign) so that nobody welds or hangs attachments in them later once fireproofing hides the field marks [28:08][29:42][30:44].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Owner names practical failure modes rather than rejection statistics. The big one is inconsistent bidding from vague drawings: a moment connection noted "continuity and doubler plates as required" let some bidders carry stiffening and others omit it, producing non-comparable bids, which Sections 3.1.1/3.1.2 now fix [22:28][22:59]. Misreading Section 1.10 as making unlisted tolerances zero-by-default is called out as a long-standing error [29:11]. He warns that the new 200 ksi F3043/F3111 bolts cannot be hot-dip galvanized and must not be used where corrosion is possible [54:49][55:20].
### Bid / Cost Implications
The stiffening-options change directly affects estimating fairness. Under option 3B the EOR who does not show required stiffening must give a bidding quantity, for example 70 percent of connections; if actuals come in lower the owner gets a credit and if higher the owner pays the difference, an equitable mechanism instead of guess-and-pad [23:31][24:33]. AESS now has five graded levels (AESS 1 basic, 2 viewed beyond 20 ft, 3 viewed within 20 ft, 4 showcase, C custom), and cost rises sharply with each step, so over-specifying AESS wastes money [26:34][27:36][28:08]. Preferred grades (A500 grade C, 50 ksi plate) carry no cost premium because mills already dual-certify and supply the stronger material [56:21][57:53]. F844 washers cut anchor-rod cost versus plate washers [46:18].
### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, the stiffening bidding-quantity rule under AISC 303-16 Section 3.1.1/3.1.2 is the actionable item: when a set says "doublers as required" without showing them, carry a stated stiffening percentage rather than zero or a silent allowance, which fits our verify-don't-generate posture and the confidence-tag flow. Ivan should also apply preferred grades (A500 grade C at 50 ksi, 50 ksi plate) since the material is already what mills ship, and should confirm availability of the very heavy W14/W36 and large HSS shapes before pricing them, because rolling once every six months can break a schedule. The model-equality language supports our Tekla detailing and in-house PE stamp workflow, where option 3 (fabricator's licensed engineer completes connection design) is exactly our model and the approval-document exchange describes our EOR review loop. Anchor-rod work maps to Table 14-2, ACI 117 holes, F844 washers, and Section 7.5.1 placement tolerance for our anchor design/setting. For Mario's shop, note AWS A5.36 superseding the old A5.20/A5.29 electrode specs and the F3125 bolt renaming (A325 to F3125 grade A325). For Paul's safety/quality file, Section 1.11 protected-zone permanent marking applies on any seismic job. No conflict with Your Company doctrine; this is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language. NONE.

## Direct Analysis Method Applications and Examples
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dcKQ0SD-rp8 | Duration: 1:28:53 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
This webinar by David Landis of Walter P Moore (recorded December 8, 2016) teaches the Direct Analysis Method (DAM) for steel stability design, a second-order approach that captures both P-big-delta system effects and P-little-delta member effects directly and lets the engineer design with K equal to 1 [01:33], [02:03]. DAM works by accurately modeling frame behavior, factoring all loads even for ASD, including initial frame imperfections through notional lateral loads, reducing member stiffness to account for residual stresses and distributed plasticity, running a second-order analysis, and using K equal to 1 in all member equations [19:03], [36:30]. The recurring lesson is that the effective length method underpredicts the moments needed to stabilize a frame at the strength limit state, which matters for base plates, anchor rods, beams, and connections [16:29], [16:59].

### Spec References
Cited verbatim by the speaker: AISC Specification Appendix 7 (where DAM first appeared in 2005, and where the effective length and first-order methods now live as alternates) [01:33], [02:33]; AISC Specification Chapter C (the primary stability method since 2010) [02:33]; Appendix 8 amplified first-order B1 and B2 factors [08:15]; AISC Design Guide 28 "Stability Design of Steel Buildings" by Larry Griffis and Don White [02:33]; the AISC Code of Standard Practice column out-of-plumbness tolerance of H over 500, consistent with the 0.002 notional factor [24:05]; Chapter H interaction equations, specifically H1-1A [42:04], [43:37]; Chapter F flexural equations F1-1 for Cb and F2-2 for moment capacity [48:09]; Chapter E compression equations including the simplified equation referenced as 3-2 [47:39], [70:36]; Manual Table 3-2 for moment capacity [70:05]; the sidesway-uninhibited alignment chart and the story-buckling method in the Specification commentary for adjusting K for leaning columns [67:33], [68:33]. ASCE 7-05 load combinations and seismic provisions (R equal to 3 for systems not detailed for seismic, Cd equal to 3) are cited for the examples [44:37], [57:18], [62:26].

### Technical Details
Notional lateral loads are 0.002 times alpha times Yi, where alpha is 1.0 for LRFD and 1.6 for ASD, applied at each level per that level's gravity load and in the most destabilizing direction [24:36], [52:35]. Stiffness reduction is 0.8 EA axial and 0.8 tau-b EI flexural, with tau-b equal to 1 when required axial strength is below half the yield load (PR over PY less than 0.5), which is common for moment frames [28:42], [46:38]. A simplification lets you raise notional loads to 0.003 times the gravity loads and then take tau-b equal to 1 without calculating it [29:12]. When the second-order to first-order ratio exceeds 1.7 on reduced stiffness or 1.5 on nominal stiffness, notional loads must be added to all lateral combinations [25:39], [33:54]. Compression members should be meshed, the speaker uses four segments, to capture P-little-delta [31:48]. Serviceability checks, drift, building period, mode shapes, and vibration use the full unreduced stiffness, not the reduced stiffness [35:29], [58:22]. Examples covered a grain-bin frame, an unsymmetrical moment frame with a leaning column carrying 1875 kips, an ASD moment frame, a 10-story dual system, and long-span roof trusses at the KFC Yum Center and the Marlins Park retractable roof.

### Fabrication Notes
The webinar is an analysis and design webinar and does not cover shop fabrication, fit-up, or shop QC. The one fabrication-adjacent point is that out-of-straightness from fabrication tolerance is already built into the column strength curves, so only story out-of-plumbness needs explicit modeling [22:35].

### Erection Notes
Erection process is not covered, but the 0.002 notional factor is tied directly to the erection-stage tolerance: the AISC Code of Standard Practice allows column out-of-plumbness of H over 500, and the notional load reproduces the destabilizing force from that built-in lean [24:05]. If a job specifies and verifies a tighter plumbness tolerance, the factor may be reduced; if tolerances are relaxed or an out-of-tolerance condition must be checked, a larger factor is required [24:05]. This is the link between erection survey results and the design assumption.

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The dominant error named is forgetting leaning columns: gravity columns that are not part of the lateral system still lean on the frame and add P-big-delta, and engineers analyzing isolated 2D models often omit them, which understates the destabilizing demand [20:03], [21:03]. The second named error is K-factor misapplication under the effective length method, especially failing to adjust K for leaning columns; in Example 4 the alignment-chart K of 1.4 had to be raised to 2.52 by the story-buckling method, and software that returns only the 1.4 leaves an unconservative design unless corrected by hand [67:33], [68:33]. A third pitfall is illegitimately superimposing separately run linear load cases, since the second-order response is nonlinear and must be run as a single combined nonlinear case [07:43], [33:24].

### Bid / Cost Implications
DAM produces higher design moments than the effective length method because the frame stiffness is softened, so beams, columns, connections, base plates, and anchor rods carry larger stabilizing moments, which can drive heavier members or beefier connections on flexible frames [18:31], [16:59]. For stiff frames the difference is small and there is little cost impact [82:24]. The iterative cycle (analyze, design-check, rerun for stiffness, recheck, and repeat on any size change) is real engineering labor that an estimate of design or detailing hours should account for on moment-frame and long-span work [30:47], [33:24].

### Your Company Application
The load-bearing takeaway for Your Company is the base-plate and anchor-rod design question at [87:32]: the moments coming out of a DAM analysis are the valid moments for sizing base plates, anchor rods, and foundations, while the notional shears are fictitious and may be subtracted out (moments must be kept, shears are optional). That ties straight to our in-house PE stamp work and anchor-rod design, setting, and tolerance scope: the H over 500 plumbness tolerance from the Code of Standard Practice at [24:05] is the same tolerance our erection crew under Mario and the field survey must hold for the design assumption to be valid, so a survey that comes back worse than H over 500 is not just a field issue, it can invalidate the stability basis and should trigger a check. For Ivan's takeoff and estimating, flag that flexible moment frames and long-span systems analyzed by DAM tend to need heavier members and larger connection moments than a quick K-based check would suggest, so engineering and connection allowances should not be trimmed on those jobs. The content is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language and presents no conflict with Your Company doctrine. Doctrine flag: NONE.

## Blast-Resistant Design of Steel Buildings - Part 1
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oESuH3ed18g | Duration: 1:29:33 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
This is part one of a two-part AISC webinar presented by Kirk Marchand of Protection Engineering Consultants on March 17 2016, scoped to blast loads and their interaction with buildings, with part two (Aldo McKay) covering structural response [01:33]. The core teaching is how to predict the air-blast pressure-time history on a steel structure from a high-explosive event: define the explosion source, convert the charge to a TNT-equivalent weight, compute a scaled standoff Z, and read peak pressure and impulse off empirical curves to build a simplified design load [38:46], [58:18]. It is a loads-prediction primer, not a connection, fabrication, or welding design course, so most of the nine fabricator dimensions are thin here.

### Spec References
The references named are governmental and AISC documents rather than AISC 360 or 341 section numbers. Cited by name: AISC Design Guide 26 (blast-resistant design, Ron Hamburger and others, also covers response) [76:29]; the AISC "Facts for Steel Buildings" document, which also touches progressive collapse [77:00]; UFC 3-340-02 "Structures to Resist the Effects of Accidental Explosions," the unrestricted Department of Defense reference with the pressure and impulse charts [51:38], [77:30]; UFC 3-340-01, the companion restricted weapons-effects document [78:00]; UFC 3-341 for cratering methods [35:05]; and Wilfred Baker's 1983 "Explosion Hazards and Evaluation" [04:38], [78:30]. Software named: CONWEP, BlastX, the Kingery-Bulmash empirical curves (developed 1984), plus CFD codes Air3D, Shamrock, and FEFLO [66:43], [67:43]. No AISC 360, AISC 341, AWS D1.1, or RCSC clause numbers are stated in this part.

### Technical Details
An ideal free-field (side-on) blast wave is an instantaneous rise to peak pressure followed by a Friedlander decay to ambient and then a negative phase [43:22], [44:54]. The controlling design quantities are peak side-on pressure, peak reflected pressure, and specific impulse (the time integral of pressure, a force per unit area) [45:25]. Reflected pressure exceeds incident pressure by a factor of 2 for weak shocks under about 15 psi but can reach a factor near 12 to 13 for very strong shocks around 1000 psi [54:08], [55:11]. Loads are simplified to an equivalent triangular pulse with duration equal to twice the impulse divided by peak pressure [58:49]. Face assignment on a building: the front wall takes reflected pressure with angle-of-incidence reduction, while sides, roof, and back wall take incident (side-on) pressure at progressively longer combined standoffs [60:20], [62:56]. Pressure decays with standoff at roughly an exponent of 2.8 and impulse at roughly 1.25, so every foot of standoff materially reduces the load [57:17].

### Fabrication Notes
No shop fabrication, fit-up, tolerance, or QC content appears in this part. The webinar stays at load prediction and does not reach member sizing, connection detailing, or shop processes; those would fall to Design Guide 26 and part two on response.

### Erection Notes
No erection sequencing, bracing, rigging, or field-procedure content appears. The one site-level point relevant to layout is that increasing standoff between a credible detonation point and the structure is the most efficient design lever, so building siting on the plot is a load-reduction decision [57:47], [63:33].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
No weld or bolt inspection failures are discussed. The conceptual errors flagged are analytical: treating blast as a static or equivalent wind load (it is a transient millisecond dynamic event that does not convert cleanly to an equivalent static or seismic load) [13:22]; assuming TNT-equivalence is accurate at all standoffs when equivalency factors for pressure and impulse differ and vary with atmosphere and standoff [16:59], [39:47]; over-relying on blast walls, since an expanding shock recombines a short distance behind the wall [11:49]; and oversimplifying the load triangle when the structure period is near the load duration [59:50].

### Bid / Cost Implications
No bid pricing, schedule durations, or estimating numbers are given. The cost-relevant takeaway for a fabricator is that blast resistance is a project-specification-driven add scope (antiterrorism requirements for courthouses or government facilities, or industrial vapor-cloud, pressure-vessel, and steam-explosion scenarios) [26:47], [27:47], and that design efficiency, and therefore steel weight, is governed heavily by available standoff [57:47]. Whether negative-phase pressure must be considered is set by the project specifications, not chosen by the contractor [82:38].

### Your Company Application
This is reference-shelf material, not a directly actionable fabrication input for Ivan's takeoff or Mario's welding. If Your Company is ever invited on a blast-resistant or progressive-collapse job (Houston petrochemical control rooms, pulpits, or a federal facility), the controlling documents to obtain are AISC Design Guide 26 and UFC 3-340-02, and the scope premise is that the structural engineer of record (or in-house PE) sizes members and connections for the dynamic demand before Tekla detailing begins; the fabricator does not back into blast loads. Practical hooks: site standoff drives steel tonnage so it belongs in an early scope-qualification note, and any blast spec must flow down to demand-critical detailing the same way a seismic spec would. No conflict with Your Company doctrine: this stays conventional structural steel with no PEMB language, no supplier names, and it reinforces verify-do-not-generate since blast loads come from cited UFC and AISC charts, never from LLM math. DOCTRINE FLAG: NONE.

## Blast-Resistant Design of Steel Buildings - Part 2
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IETfG5Y4SZ4 | Duration: 1:31:44 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This webinar, presented by Aldo McKay of Protection Engineering Consultants on 2016-03-24, covers blast-resistant analysis and design of steel buildings, the second part of a two-part series after Part 1 on blast loads [00:01]. The controlling idea is radical simplification: a building hit by blast responds in compression, tension, and twisting in every direction, but the engineer analyzes it component by component and tracks one dominant mode of response, usually flexure, because bending lets a member absorb large energy cheaply [04:36][19:19]. Design is not stress-based; it is governed by deformation limits expressed as support rotation and ductility ratio, with members pushed into the ultimate plastic capacity region rather than held to first yield [12:39][13:10]. The envelope is the first line of defense, so the engineer concentrates on exposed members, generally the roof, occasional perimeter or spandrel beams, and rarely columns [16:43][17:44].
### Spec References
The speaker named guidance documents rather than AISC 360 connection sections. Cited by number: AISC Design Guide 26 (blast-resistant design, with close-form and single-degree-of-freedom examples) [16:12]; UFC 3-340-01 (DoD minimum standards for all military construction) [13:40]; UFC 3-340-02 and UFC 3-340-01 again as the comprehensive technical references [15:10]; PDC-TR 06-08, the Protective Design Center technical report that supplies the response limits for DoD, VA, and ISC designs [39:27][57:20][60:23]; the ASCE "Design of Blast Resistant Buildings in Petrochemical Facilities" [14:10]; and the SBEDS / ESBEDS methodology manual [15:40][36:21]. For the beam-column interaction equations the speaker cited Chapter H of the AISC Specification for Structural Steel Buildings [54:16][54:48], and noted shear capacity uses the AISC manual form (0.6 Fy) adapted to 0.55 Fy for dynamic web yielding [64:32].
### Technical Details
Blast load arrives as a pressure-impulse pair (triangular pulse, impulse equals half the duration times peak pressure) or as charge weight plus standoff [24:31]. The member is reduced to a single-degree-of-freedom spring-mass system defined by stiffness, ultimate resistance, and mass, with a KLM load-mass transformation factor applied to the mass to keep energy equivalent to the real member [30:46][34:20]. Dynamic moment capacity multiplies the static yield by two factors: the dynamic increase factor (DIF) for strain-rate effects, roughly 20 percent for 50 KSI steel, and the static increase factor (SIF), about 5 percent, to lift the lower-bound spec strength to realistic strength [35:21][36:21]. Energy (close-form) solutions apply only when clearly impulse-controlled (load duration below one third of natural period) or pressure-controlled (duration at least 10 times natural period); the worked roof-beam example landed firmly impulsive and gave 4.6 inch midspan deflection by hand versus about 4 inches in the ESBEDS single-degree tool [47:38][48:40][49:41]. Beam-columns use the Chapter H interaction set to one, solved for reduced moment capacity, and the speaker noted he has not seen a blast column exceed 20 percent of P critical because protected interior columns carry the heavy loads [54:48][55:18].
### Fabrication Notes
The fabrication-relevant rule is the column base plate: the speaker stressed a recessed base plate with grout to keep lateral reactions in shear straight into the floor diaphragm, because a non-recessed plate lets the anchor bolts fail in shear while the column itself bends well into the plastic range [53:15][53:45]. Members must be compact sections only so they can develop full plastic capacity, and the engineer uses the full plastic section modulus Z for beams once ductility passes three, but only the average of elastic and plastic modulus for plates unless ductility exceeds about seven [37:22][38:26][38:57]. Steel grades discussed were 36 and 50 KSI, with 50 KSI (A992 for the W10x100 shear example) more typical [38:26][65:33].
### Erection Notes
The webinar is analysis-focused and gives little on sequencing, cranes, or rigging. The closest erection content is the bracing requirement: the compression flange must be braced, and for roof members the engineer often must brace the bottom flange as well because rebound makes it the compression flange [38:57]. Frames generally need no blast design because their sway natural period is so long relative to the millisecond load that the response approaches zero, which means lateral bracing systems and foundations are usually sized by the equivalent static facade reactions rather than direct blast on the frame [80:00][81:32].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The named failures are connection and base-plate failures. A test column bent deep into the plastic range but its anchor bolts sheared because the base plate was not recessed, the classic weak-point failure [53:45]. A window-retrofit steel frame pulled out of its concrete beam in a concrete breakout because the connection was not designed to stay attached, sending the whole frame into the occupied space [70:09]. The recurring design error theme is rebound: connections sized only for inbound load can fail when the member springs back, so elastic members get equal inbound and outbound connection design and yielding members can use about 50 percent of the inbound for rebound [67:37][68:08]. In the column example the flexural response passed but shear capacity was inadequate for the ultimate moment, forcing a web plate or a heavier member [78:27].
### Bid / Cost Implications
Blast work is best inserted at roughly the 65 percent design stage, after members and geometry are set for conventional and serviceability loads, so the blast engineer tweaks connection capacity, spacing, and member strength rather than starting from zero [20:22][41:28]. Designing components to bend ductilely is the cost lever: keeping members elastic under blast is described as far too expensive, and over-conservative strength assumptions drive heavy sections [19:50][91:23]. Single-degree-of-freedom analysis is favored because it balances accuracy with the speed needed on fast design-build teams, and modern tools make a single-degree run faster than a hand calculation [09:08][50:42].
### Your Company Application
This is a specialized analysis discipline outside Your Company's normal conventional-steel takeoff, but several threads connect. The base-plate and anchor-rod point maps directly to Your Company anchor-rod design, setting, and tolerance: a recessed, grouted base plate transferring lateral shear into the diaphragm is exactly the detailing Tekla and the in-house PE stamp would carry, and the test showing bolts shearing while the column bends reinforces our anchor-setting discipline. Mario's shop crew should note the compact-section and full-flange-bracing requirement, including bottom-flange bracing on roof beams for rebound, since that affects fit-up and added stiffeners or web plates. For Ivan's takeoff, blast scope means heavier members and beefier connections than a conventional bid, and the open-web joist dynamic-reaction note [26:02] ties to our joist work where a weaker supported member can reduce the load on supporting girders. If a Houston petrochemical client ever requests blast design (the ASCE petrochemical document governs there), it would need an outside blast specialist plus the PE stamp; Your Company would fabricate and erect, not perform the SDOF analysis. Doctrine conflict: NONE. Conventional structural steel positioning holds, no PEMB language appears, and all spec citations are spoken by the presenter, not generated.

## Get Fired Up
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K5o3Db4InEs | Duration: 1:03:11 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
Maria Garlock (Princeton, 2016 AISC T.R. Higgins lecturer) teaches what a practicing structural engineer should know about fire design, contrasting the traditional prescriptive approach with structural fire engineering, which is performance-based design that treats fire as a thermal load and analyzes the real structural response to a real fire [00:02][07:17][12:26]. The central message is that designers have choices and do not have to give up efficiency, economy, and elegance for fire protection, because a structure can sometimes be designed to resist a fire rather than be shielded from it [01:36][12:57]. A key teaching point is that the fire-resistive rating is principally a thermal comparative test, not a structural test, so the rating does not imply the time that structural integrity is maintained [10:53][22:00].
### Spec References
ASTM E119 fire qualification test, cited repeatedly as the prescriptive standard fire test with no decay phase [08:49][10:22][29:10]. AISC 360 ("the steel Bible"), which allows two analysis types: qualification testing (prescriptive) and design by analysis (structural fire engineering); load combinations including fire are in AISC 360, and fire need not be combined with wind or seismic [15:34][58:56]. ASCE 7-16 fire appendix (non-mandatory, the "what" document about five pages, with a companion "how" document then in development) [16:06]. NFPA 5000 and IBC (2012 referenced) permit alternatives that meet the intent of the code [14:33][15:04]. NFPA 502 for bridges, requiring critical structural members be protected from collision and high-temperature exposure [42:01]. Bolt grades cited: grade 8.8 equated to A490 and grade 5.6 equated to A325 [33:47]. The AISC effective-width B-sub-e procedure for post-buckling capacity of simply supported plates is referenced as the method modified into an equivalent-length approach for shear [46:08].
### Technical Details
Perimeter columns in a fire develop unexpected behavior because a heated beam expands, pushes against adjacent structure, and induces axial load in the beam plus a moment in the column that was designed for axial load only [18:43]. Thermal gradients through the section matter: the web heats faster than flanges, yield strength drops non-uniformly with depth (around 6 to 7 percent of Fy at roughly 500 C), and the stiffer cooler side shifts the effective centroid, producing a moment reversal that can dominate the column response and push demand outside the assumed plastic interaction envelope [22:27][26:03][26:35]. In the One Meridian Plaza study a W14x314 perimeter column failed at about 41 to 42 minutes by combined axial-load-and-moment full plastic yielding, not lateral buckling, once fire protection was removed for study [20:20][25:32]. Connections fail during the cooling/decay phase, not the heating peak, because the beam buckles its web then flange, hangs in catenary, then contracts on cooling and pulls significant tension into the connection [29:40][30:43]. For bridge girders with slender webs, web shear buckling is the critical limit state, addressed with post-buckling tension-field theory and an equivalent-length column along the plate diagonal calibrated against 60 finite-element models and 84 physical tests [42:33][47:09][49:12].
### Fabrication Notes
The talk is analysis-focused, but connection detailing choices that fabrication controls drive fire performance. Adding a 4 mm web reinforcing plate so the 6 mm web plus plate matches the 10 mm shear-tab thickness eliminated failure across the full heating and cooling cycle, while conversely thinning the shear tab from 10 mm to 6 mm to match the web added roughly 50 minutes of endurance by making the connection more ductile and able to "breathe" with thermal movement [34:49][35:20][35:52]. Increasing the gap between beam end and supporting girder let all four bolts share load more uniformly and extended endurance from 123 to 165 minutes [36:53][37:23]. The lesson for detailing is that connections need flexibility to accommodate expansion and contraction rather than maximum rigidity.
### Erection Notes
No erection sequencing, crane, rigging, or field-bracing content is covered; this webinar is about design analysis and connection behavior under fire, not field procedures.
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The recurring conceptual error is assuming the ASTM E119 rating equals structural integrity time, and assuming an average uniform section temperature when thermal gradients can either overstate or understate capacity in different regions of the section [10:53][24:30]. Garlock notes B. Hopold's analysis of 60-foot university columns found the demand fell in the "red zone" where ignoring thermal gradients would have overestimated capacity [28:07]. In the Cardington full-scale fire tests, lower-grade bolts unexpectedly sheared off, an effect missed in the first test series because no sensors were placed on the connection [59:56][60:27]. Standard oversized and slotted holes were found too small to accommodate the thermal movement, so they made little difference [62:32].
### Bid / Cost Implications
Structural fire engineering is presented as a direct cost-saving alternative to blanket prescriptive fire protection. The 60-foot columns example showed two-hour protection costing about $20,000 per column, and the analysis eliminated protection on many columns for significant savings [28:07]. The Five Broadgate project in the UK used tensile membrane action, leaving interior filler beams unprotected, with a study showing about 40 percent fire-protection cost savings [38:25][39:57]. The Hotel Arts Barcelona exoskeleton needed no fire protection per its analysis [40:29]. The trade-off is engineering effort: this is a specialized analysis (SAFIR software, Abaqus with contact and nonlinear material) more common in the UK than the US, with only a few US firms doing it [56:50][57:54][61:29].
### Your Company Application
This entry's value is conceptual context, not a doctrine change. Your Company does not perform structural fire engineering, and the bid pipeline correctly prices conventional prescriptive fire protection; nothing here alters validated tonnage, AISC weights from aisc_validator.py, or BID_RATES. The transferable insight for Mario's shop and Tekla detailing is that shear-tab thickness, web reinforcing plates, bolt grade, and end gap measurably change connection ductility, which reinforces our standing practice of detailing connections to the engineer's drawings exactly rather than substituting. For Ivan's takeoff, the bolt-grade distinction (A325 vs A490, equated here to grade 5.6 and 8.8) is a reminder that bolt grade is a hard spec input that field bolting must match, not an interchangeable item. For the in-house PE stamp, if a GC or EOR ever raises a fire-engineering or unprotected-steel scope on a job like ACP, that is a specialist analysis outside our normal scope and should trigger a clarifying RFI rather than an assumption. Doctrine flag: NONE.

## Seismology and Earthquake Effects
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uygiMzKwHDE | Duration: 1:26:37 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is session one of AISC Night School 4, Fundamentals of Earthquake Engineering for Building Structures, presented by Raphael Sabelli, SE, on February 24, 2014 [00:01]. It is a foundations lecture on seismology and earthquake effects, not a connection or fabrication session. Sabelli covers plate tectonics, how stored strain energy releases as ground-shaking waves, how earthquakes are measured, and the hazard, risk, and probability framework that drives code design accelerations [09:15]. The central engineering point is that we do not design from a Richter magnitude directly to a force; we design to a target acceleration tied to a probability of exceedence or return period, and the strategies to resist horizontal shaking and overturning are strength, stiffness, displacement capacity, and energy absorption [31:57][46:25].
### Spec References
The talk names documents and code frameworks but cites no chapter, section, or table numbers for steel design. Named references: AISC seismic provisions and the AISC Seismic Design Manual [04:08]; the free AISC publication "Earthquakes and Seismic Design" by Ron Hamburger in the Facts for Steel Buildings series [03:08]; the textbook "Ductile Design of Steel Structures" 2nd ed. by Bruneau, Uang, and Sabelli [03:38]; ASCE 7 and its shift from uniform-hazard to uniform-risk maximum considered earthquake (MCE) [65:25]; IBC seismic design category and SS / S1 parameters raised in a question [30:56]; USGS probabilistic and deterministic ground-motion maps, updated every three years [64:24]. AISC 360 and AISC 341 section numbers, AWS D1.1 clauses, and RCSC bolting provisions are not cited in this session.
### Technical Details
Earthquakes originate where tectonic-plate strain energy ruptures along a fault, radiating primary (pressure), secondary (shear), and surface (Rayleigh and Love) waves; surface waves carry most of the damaging energy to structures [15:22][84:36]. Ground-motion intensity attenuates with distance from the source, but soil controls amplification: soft bay mud acts like a soft spring and amplifies motion far more than bedrock [20:31]. Richter magnitude is logarithmic at roughly 32x energy per unit; Modified Mercalli is a subjective 12-step intensity scale keyed to observed effects on conventional construction [23:08][24:40]. Current ASCE 7 uses a risk-targeted MCE with a 1% chance of collapse in 50 years, replacing the old uniform-hazard 2,475-year (2% in 50-year) return period [65:25][66:28]. Brittle systems are designed for higher forces than ductile systems to keep collapse reliability high [76:52].
### Fabrication Notes
No fabrication, shop-process, fit-up, or QC content is present in this session. It is a seismology and hazard-characterization lecture; member behavior, connections, and shop work are deferred to later sessions of the eight-week course [08:14].
### Erection Notes
No erection, field-sequencing, bracing, or rigging content is present. The only construction-adjacent remark is that a temporary structure such as a construction crane could in principle be designed to a shorter return period, though the building code does not encourage that [74:13].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
No connection rejections, weld defects, or inspection failures are discussed. The failure modes shown are geotechnical and structural-system level: liquefaction of saturated sandy soils causing loss of bearing and rigid buildings tipping over intact [43:54][44:24], lateral spreading and sand boils [44:54], fault-rupture offset under structures, and code prohibitions on building over known active faults or unimproved liquefiable sites [42:20][44:24]. A common conceptual error the speaker corrects is treating "we are due for an earthquake" as fact; risk does rise as strain accumulates, but a magnitude 6 does not meaningfully relieve a magnitude 7 fault [82:02].
### Bid / Cost Implications
Cost here is societal earthquake loss, not bid estimating: Northridge at roughly 20 billion dollars and the Tohoku Japan event as the costliest on record are used to motivate design [38:11]. The design-economics point relevant to estimating is that the seismic design category and ground-motion level vary by site and govern lateral-system demand, and the move to uniform risk gives modest relief (0 to about 15 percent) in low-seismic regions like New York versus high-seismic Los Angeles [71:04]. For a Houston, TX fabricator this signals low seismic demand locally, but any out-of-region or higher-SDC job changes the lateral system, member sizes, and connection demand that drive tonnage and labor.
### Your Company Application
This session is background, not a directly actionable detailing or shop reference, so the application is at the screening level. For Ivan's takeoff and bid screening, the takeaway is that a project's seismic design category and lateral system are inputs that scale tonnage and connection complexity, and a job in a higher-SDC region than Houston cannot be priced off a low-seismic assumption; flag SDC alongside SF on out-of-region bids. The detailed seismic detailing that affects Mario's welding (demand-critical welds, protected zones) and the in-house PE stamp comes from AISC 341 in later sessions, none of which is cited here, so do not infer seismic weld or connection requirements from this video. Anchor rods, joists, field bolting, Tekla detailing, Paul's safety scope, and ACP controls are not addressed. Conflict with Your Company doctrine: NONE.

## Load Paths! The Most Common Source of Engineering Errors
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1jaHSQhGUgA | Duration: 1:24:20 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
Carol Drucker (Drucker Zaidel Structural Engineers, AISC TC6 connections committee) teaches that load applied anywhere on a structure must travel through a complete, continuous path of elements down to the foundation, and every element along the way needs sufficient strength and stiffness [01:31][02:02]. The two governing rules of thumb are that the shortest load path is the best, because it also minimizes piece count and cost, and that force is attracted to stiffness, so members carrying more load get the shorter spans [03:03][04:07][04:39]. The recurring failure mode is a load path that "slips through the cracks," meaning the engineer designs a joint without tracing how force actually crosses it, which is why she calls load path the most common source of engineering errors.

### Spec References
The cited references are: AISC Specification Chapter K, which mandates the thicker and wider HSS member be the continuous member at a welded truss joint [07:42]; AISC Specification Section J1.2, which requires connections to allow simple beam rotation (so welded-up shear tabs should be avoided) [72:33]; AISC Manual figure 7-7, used to uncouple a column moment over a bolt group for KISS-method gusset-to-column-flange connections [78:00]; AISC Design Guide 13, on stiffener welds where the column-flange weld is treated as more rigid than the column-web weld [61:42]; and the 14th Edition Seismic Design Manual plus the AISC website "companion" for Chevron connection examples, which add a shear-through-the-doubler limit state [47:36][48:07]. She also names the Uniform Force Method as the AISC-preferred bracing approach and references Bill Thornton and Pat Fortney's work on adding transfer forces to Hc forces [33:00][36:04].

### Technical Details
The talk works through trusses (top and bottom chords acting as beam flanges, web diagonals as the web), vertical and horizontal bracing, Chevron connections, moment connections to column flanges and webs, sloping columns, kickers, davits, thermal-slip connections, and discontinuous columns carried back on vertical trusses [09:15][25:43][50:13][59:03][65:51]. For bracing she contrasts the Uniform Force Method (Hc, Vb, Delta-Vb forces distributed around the joint, gusset laid out in AutoCAD or Excel) against the KISS method (vertical component to gusset-to-column, horizontal component to gusset-to-beam), noting UFM special case 2 to a column web exactly equals the KISS method [33:29][41:43]. Panel-zone shear is found by assuming an inflection point at column mid-height, and the key insight is that the sum of beam moments cannot exceed the sum of the column moment strength, which can drastically cut the doubler design force [55:53][57:26]. Transfer forces, diaphragm strength, and the equal-transfer-force-on-each-side-of-a-column rule recur throughout [16:56][17:27].

### Fabrication Notes
Welded trusses are favored because they can be fabricated whole in the shop and erected in one piece, and a continuous stiffener directing the chord tension force across a panel zone eliminated the need for stiffeners and doublers on one job [30:22][30:53][31:24]. Drucker stresses that all welds in a stiffener group should be the same size to avoid deformation-compatibility problems, and she believes this is somewhat mandated in the spec [62:45][63:16]. On a price-per-ton Canadian job the EOR spliced members "as soon as they could be spliced" to cut tonnage, and she warns against splicing at joints because material is often ordered before the resulting connection problem is caught [14:23][15:24].

### Erection Notes
"Watch erection" is one of the two stated lessons: a roof-truss plan created a stability loop (T5 through T9, T8, T3 back to T5) because a stub column was placed in the wrong truss, fixed in the field by adding a shoring post and re-sequencing the erection (C5, then T3, T8, T9) [05:11][06:12]. Advanced detailing software (Tekla, SDS) is credited with making field rework less common than the old practice of designing connections for a year then doing three months of field fixes [72:02]. A field fix offered for a shear tab with mis-drilled holes was to add a tab on the backside and drill new holes through the beam, decided jointly with the fabricator [80:18].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Named failures include a pool-deck kicker collapse the day before opening, traced to 5/16-inch clip angles with a few hundred kips of compression that pulled away from the column [11:51][12:21]; the David Lawrence Convention Center 2007 expansion-joint failure where bolted-welded double angles had slots too short for thermal movement, putting a moment across the fillet weld root [69:58][70:29]; and the Hyatt-style hanger-rod change where splitting continuous rods into two nuts overloaded the lower nut [70:29][71:32]. Other rejections covered are coped-beam reactions exceeding the UDL force and the beam shear strength [07:42][08:12], shop drawings returned with an X over a truss-rotation detail because the EOR had braced the column off the bottom chord [28:18][28:48], and Chevron connections missing the shear-through-the-doubler check [48:07].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Shortest load path equals fewer pieces equals lower fabrication and erection cost, which is the through-line of the talk [03:35]. The concrete cost data point: switching an entire job from the Uniform Force Method to the KISS method (because the EOR refused to touch the beam-to-column connection) added 14 percent more bolts and bumped every brace-to-column-flange angle up one size, for example a 5/8-inch angle going to 3/4-inch [38:36][39:08]. She frames the bolts-versus-thicker-angles decision as a trade-off to coordinate with the fabricator, and notes price-per-ton contracts push EORs to minimize tonnage in ways that complicate connections [39:39][14:23].

### Your Company Application
This is direct doctrine support for Your Company's connection and detailing work. For Ivan's takeoff, the shortest-load-path and piece-count points reinforce that framing choices drive tonnage and cost, and the 14-percent-more-bolts KISS penalty is a concrete reason to confirm the design method before pricing a brace-heavy job. For Tekla detailing and the in-house PE stamp, the J1.2 simple-rotation rule, the Chapter K continuous-member rule, figure 7-7, Design Guide 13, and the panel-zone "sum of beam moments cannot exceed column strength" check are reusable verification gates when our PE reviews connection submittals. For Mario's shop, the same-size-weld-in-a-group rule and welded-truss-in-one-piece advantage map to fit-up and erection planning. For field bolting and anchor work, the thermal-slip-connection cautions (long enough slots, threads excluded from shear plane, fingertight bolts not a prequalified install) and the hanger-rod change-of-load-path lesson are field-coordination warnings. For Paul's safety file, the kicker and convention-center collapses are teaching cases that connection load-path errors are life-safety, not paperwork. No conflict with Your Company doctrine: the content is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language. doctrine_flags: NONE.
