## Modules for Learning Structural Stability
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N5hLj6zRhaw | Duration: 1:34:26 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is session three of AISC Night School "Stability Design of Steel Structures," presented by Dr. Ronald Ziemian of Bucknell (chair of AISC TC10 on frame stability) on February 9, 2015 [00:02]. The subject is nonlinear computational analysis as a "virtual laboratory" for understanding structural stability, taught through nine free downloadable learning modules paired with the free MASTAN2 software [03:35][22:27]. The driving idea is that limit-states design targets ultimate strength, where yielding and second-order effects combine, so the behavior lends itself to nonlinear analysis rather than closed-form differential equations [02:05][02:35]. This is a teaching and analysis-method webinar, not a fabrication or connection-design lecture; it does not cover shop or field work.
### Spec References
Citations are sparse and qualitative. Named items: the AISC commentary effective-length-factor (K) table for six idealized end-restraint cases [31:36]; the alignment charts for K factors in framed systems [89:46 approx, 43:16]; Chapter F as the home of the beam (lateral-torsional-buckling) curve and the Cb moment-gradient equation [43:46][51:59]; Chapter H interaction for combined major and minor axis bending [92:04]; the B1 and B2 moment-amplification factors [69:52]; the Direct Analysis Method with the 0.8 tau-b stiffness reduction and notional loads, and an Appendix-1 type second-order inelastic check [74:33][79:42]; AISC's nine-tenths moment-redistribution allowance for inelastic design [68:19]; and an AISC Engineering Journal 2010 paper by Wong and Driver on Cb factors across codes [55:35]. No exact section numbers like J3.6 are spoken; the speaker stays at chapter and method level.
### Technical Details
The modules walk through elastic column buckling versus end restraint (K = 0.5 to 2.0 reproduced from pi-squared-EI over (KL)-squared back-solved from the buckling load) [39:43][40:14]; flexural buckling column curves with imperfections and residual stresses on or off, compared to the AISC curve [42:15][43:16]; lateral-torsional buckling with the Cb factor, where a computed Cb of 2.7 was compared to the AISC equation value of 2.2 (AISC conservative) [54:33]; Saint-Venant (GJ) versus warping (Cw) torsion, showing a uniform-moment beam buckling at 2,265 in-kips with warping off versus 3,600 in-kips with warping on [62:17][66:19]; and second-order P-large-delta effects, where adding gravity load drove a column minor-axis moment from 722 to 1,042, a 44 percent increase [77:37][78:09]. A repeated teaching point is that an inflection point is not a brace point: a mid-span brace cut the unbraced length in half and raised capacity by 7.6x combined with the moment gradient [67:49][68:19]. MASTAN cannot model local buckling or unsymmetric angles; HSS and stocky box girders are fine if Z is input [16:17][47:24][93:09].
### Fabrication Notes
No fabrication content. The lecture is analysis-only and does not address shop processes, fit-up, cutting, or QC. The one tangential fabrication remark is that the first demonstration beam had warping resistance deliberately turned off "so this beam could never be manufactured" because no real wide-flange section lacks warping stiffness [59:12].
### Erection Notes
No erection, sequencing, crane, or rigging content. The only field-adjacent themes are conceptual: bracing reduces unbraced length and sharply raises buckling capacity [66:49], and out-of-plumb frame sway and member out-of-straightness are the two initial-imperfection types a stability model must capture [15:16]. These inform why erection plumb and brace placement matter but are not erection procedures.
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
No inspection or rejection content (this is not a QA/QC lecture). The conceptual error the speaker most wants to correct is treating an inflection point as if it were a brace point, which overstates capacity [68:19]. A secondary modeling caution is using too few finite elements: one element badly under-predicts the buckling load, while eight elements land within a whisker of the exact solution [32:36][33:06].
### Bid / Cost Implications
No direct bid, cost, or estimating content. The indirect economic argument is that competitive steel pricing pushes designs toward slender members and systems, which makes them buckling-governed and forces stability to control the design [04:06]. The software discussed (MASTAN2 and CUFSM) is free, so the cost angle is analysis-tooling access, not fabrication or erection pricing [14:15][81:12].
### Your Company Application
This is a design-engineering-method webinar with low direct relevance to fabrication and erection, but it has value for the in-house PE stamp. The Direct Analysis Method content (notional loads, 0.8 tau-b stiffness reduction, B1/B2 amplification, and the K=1 simplification versus alignment-chart K above 2) is exactly the stability framework our PE should be applying when stamping frame designs [74:33][79:42]; it is reference grounding, not a takeoff or rate input. For Ivan's takeoff there is nothing to change: this material does not touch member weights or quantities, and all AISC weights still come only from aisc_validator.py. For Mario and Paul there is no shop or safety procedure here. The one practical erection-adjacent takeaway worth noting for our crews is the inflection-point-is-not-a-brace-point principle, which reinforces that temporary bracing location during erection is load-path critical [68:19]. No conflict with Your Company doctrine: the lecture is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language. DOCTRINE FLAGS: NONE.

## Design for Stability Using the 2010 AISC Specification
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HzV6aAaww1c | Duration: 1:27:18 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
Louis Geschwindner (former AISC VP of Engineering and Research) teaches the AISC 360-10 stability framework: how to determine the second-order required strengths PR and MR for beam-columns and then check them against available strength using the Chapter H interaction equations [01:36][02:37]. The structure of the spec is that Section B3.5 sends you to Chapter C, where C1 lists the five effects that must be considered, C2 tells you how to get required strength, and C3 tells you how to get available strength, and the method you pick for required strength dictates the method for available strength [06:15][17:36]. The three permitted methods are the direct analysis method (C2/C1.1), the effective length method (Appendix 7.2), and the first-order analysis method, with the direct analysis method as the foundation because it sets the applicability limits on the others [09:51][29:30][62:00].
### Spec References
Cited verbatim by the speaker: Chapter H combined forces, Section H1 and equation H1-1A [01:36][47:34][64:34]; Chapter B, Sections B2, B3.1, B3.5 [05:43][06:15]; Chapter C with C1, C1.1, C1.2, C2, C2.1, C2.1.3, C2.2, C2.3, C3 [06:15][31:31][66:37]; Appendix 7 (effective length method 7.2 and first-order method) [09:51][29:30]; Appendix 8 (approximate second-order, the B1-B2 method) [15:01][16:33]; Appendix 6 (member and frame bracing) [41:51]; ASTM A6 out-of-straightness tolerance [24:22]; the AISC Code of Standard Practice out-of-plumb tolerance [24:22]; 14th Edition Manual tables 4-1, 3-2, 3-4, 3-10, 6-1, 2-1, 2-2 and Part 6 combined-force tables [03:09][03:40][72:18][73:49]; the 2005 and 1989 ASD specifications and the 2nd edition LRFD commentary for leaning-column K adjustment [01:36][20:11][63:33].
### Technical Details
The interaction equations are required-over-available in force-and-moment form, unchanged from the 2005 spec [01:36]. Five effects must be considered per C1: member deformations (flexural, shear, axial), second-order P-big-delta sway and P-little-delta member effects, geometric imperfections, stiffness reduction from inelasticity and residual stress, and uncertainty in stiffness and strength [07:15][08:19]. Out-of-straightness is L/1000 (ASTM A6, already in the strength curves) and out-of-plumbness is L/500 (Code of Standard Practice) [24:22]. The direct analysis method reduces all stiffnesses to 0.8 and applies tau-sub-b only to flexural stiffness, which earns K=1 in design [40:18][41:20]. Loads are run at LRFD level or 1.6 times ASD (alpha = 1.6) so the higher second-order amplification is captured [08:19][34:05]. Notional loads of 0.002-alpha times the gravity load at each level model out-of-plumbness, and B2 thresholds (1.7 with reduced stiffness, 1.5 with nominal) decide whether the direct analysis method is mandatory [38:18][55:49].
### Fabrication Notes
This webinar is design-office analysis, not shop work. The only fabrication-adjacent content is the tolerance basis: column out-of-straightness L/1000 is an ASTM A6 mill tolerance already baked into the column strength curves [24:22]. No fit-up, cut, weld, or shop QC procedures are discussed.
### Erection Notes
The single erection-relevant fact is that the Code of Standard Practice permits a column to be erected out of plumb by L/500, and the stability methods explicitly account for that erected out-of-plumbness through notional loads or direct geometric modeling [24:22][31:31][38:18]. No sequencing, bracing-plan, crane, or rigging guidance is given; Appendix 6 bracing is referenced only to say you model real bracing in the analysis rather than applying the appendix forces [41:51].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
No shop or field inspection failures are covered. The errors named are analysis mistakes: failing to include the right deformations or mis-modeling supports (modeling fixed supports as pins ran one example deflection from 1.79 in to 7.11 in) [12:29][12:59], improperly omitting second-order effects, which the speaker says many engineers were doing [28:28], and the speaker's own live error of applying B1 to a no-translation moment that did not exist, corrected on air [81:04][82:06]. He also warns against faking stiffness reduction with a reduced modulus E, because that corrupts width-to-thickness checks on the design side [86:12].
### Bid / Cost Implications
No direct estimating, schedule, or pricing content. The indirect implication is that the analysis method chosen drives member sizes and therefore tonnage: leaning (gravity-only) columns design at K=1 and are cheap to handle, but in the example 50 percent of the columns carried 64 percent of the load, which raised the moment-frame column K from 1.6 to 2.67 and grew those members [59:24][63:33][64:34]. The direct analysis method, by eliminating the K calculation, removes a source of conservatism and rework on irregular frames [55:19].
### Your Company Application
This is engineering theory for the in-house PE who stamps frame design, not a fabrication or estimating input, so it should not change validated tonnage, AISC weights, or rates. The one operational tie-in for Ivan takeoff and Tekla detailing is the erected out-of-plumb tolerance of L/500 from the Code of Standard Practice, which is the same tolerance our erection and column-survey checks should hold to [24:22], and the L/1000 out-of-straightness from ASTM A6 as the mill basis. For Paul Guerrero and Mario, there is nothing actionable on safety, welding, or shop QC in this video. Doctrine flag: NONE. The content is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language and no supplier names; weights and rates here must still come from aisc_validator.py and bid_rates.py, never from this webinar.

## New Composite Design Provisions in the 2010 AISC Specification
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UBZfrNeIrn0 | Duration: 1:26:27 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
Will Jacobs of Stanley D. Lindsey, vice chair of AISC Task Committee 5 on composite construction, walks through how Chapter I of the 2010 AISC 360 specification was rewritten and expanded [01:36, 08:45]. The mandate was minimal change, so ordinary composite beam design and shear-stud strengths in composite deck did not change [06:43, 22:40], but the chapter grew from five to nine sections and from 12 to 24 pages to cover composite columns, load transfer, composite diaphragms, and a new steel-anchor section [05:42, 08:45]. The big terminology shift is that "shear stud" is replaced by the generic "steel anchor" for ACI 318 Appendix D consistency [09:45].

### Spec References
AISC 360 Chapter I, reorganized into I1 general, I2 axial, I3 flexure, I4 shear, I5 combined forces, I6 load transfer, I7 composite diaphragms and collector beams, I8 steel anchors, and I9 special cases [10:17, 46:08]; load transfer equations I6-1 (force to steel) and I6-2 (force to concrete) [38:00, 74:42]; steel-anchor-in-composite-component provisions in I8.3 [44:04]. External references cited: ACI 318 (rebar and concrete detailing, the 6-inch lateral-support tie rule, 1% minimum longitudinal reinforcement) and ACI 318 Appendix D (concrete breakout) [08:45, 18:03, 78:16]; AISC Design Guide 6 as a fourth combined-force method [31:50]; AISC Design Guide 3 (deflection limits, 10% ponding allowance) [58:20, 62:29]; AISC Design Guide 19 and ASCE 29 for filled-column fire resistance [83:50]; ASCE 37 (25 psf construction live load for hose-placed concrete) [59:21]; ASCE 7-10 load combinations [43:04]; IBC 2009 Table 721 for encased-column fire rating and the L/360 full-live-load deflection rule [83:50, 70:07]; SDI diaphragm design guide [42:01].

### Technical Details
Concrete-filled tubes (CFT) now get compact, non-compact, and slender local-buckling classifications, so a 30-inch round tube can run a wall down to about 3/16 inch [11:48, 12:19]. The confinement factor C2 is 0.85 for rectangular and 0.95 for circular compact sections, dropping to 0.7 for non-compact [20:35, 21:37]. Encased columns use a plastic strength model with minimum encased-shape ratio 1% and minimum longitudinal reinforcement 0.4% (about 1.4% total), with the economical encased ratio at 8 to 12% [15:25, 16:28]. The old "0.009 square inch per inch" tie rule is now plainly stated as a number 3 bar at 12 inches [16:59]. Steel anchors in load-transfer zones need H/D greater than 5 so failure is in the steel shank and the concrete limit state can be ignored, with phi 0.65 [45:06, 45:37]. Bond strength for filled sections is only 60 psi with phi 0.45, the lowest in the spec [41:01]. Composite beams should run 40 to 50% composite action minimum, since 40% already reaches about 80% of full strength [67:34, 68:04].

### Fabrication Notes
Steel headed stud anchors lose length to burn-off when welded: about 3/16 inch welded directly to base metal and about 3/8 inch when welded through deck, so anchor length must be specified to still extend 1.5 inches above the deck after installation [64:31, 65:02]. The 2010 spec wording was corrected so the half-inch concrete cover over studs is a specified value, not a field-reject trigger, and a stud ending at 3/8 inch cover is acceptable for strength as long as it does not protrude through the slab [63:30, 85:22]. For encased columns, two-piece U-ties through holes drilled in the steel section are an option contractors dislike, so bundling rebar in the corners or using weldable rebar or carry bars is preferred [18:34, 19:35, 50:42].

### Erection Notes
This webinar is a design-and-detailing talk and does not cover crane, rigging, sequencing, or field bracing for erection. The nearest field item is unshored composite beam construction, where ponding from beam and girder deflection during the pour adds roughly 10% of slab weight unless the slab is poured to constant thickness, and a 25 psf construction live load is applied for hose-placed concrete [57:50, 58:20, 59:21].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The named pitfalls are the "non-composite composite beam," where a few studs added only for drag-strut force fracture under gravity load, so a minimum 25 to 50% composite action is required [42:34, 51:42]; the unconservative corner near point D-prime-prime in the plastic interaction curve when pushing a column to its limit, avoided by the simplified straight B-C method [29:49, 31:20]; the 13th edition manual CFT tables that listed non-composite flexural capacity, fixed in the 14th edition [28:47]; and field rejection of studs at 3/8 inch cover that was never the spec intent [63:30]. Concrete breakout toward a free edge is not precluded by the H/D and spacing rules and must be checked separately [77:45].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Adding studs beyond about 40 to 50% composite action buys little strength and wastes labor and material, so the takeoff should target that range rather than full composite [68:04]. Choosing a 7.5-inch normal-weight slab on 3-inch deck achieves a 2-hour UL fire rating without sprayed fireproofing on the deck, trading concrete weight for avoided fireproofing scope [57:19]. The load-introduction-length limit (anchors within twice the column transverse dimension above and below the transfer point) can force an extra non-composite floor lift when a high-rise lands on a podium, which is a real material and detailing cost to carry [79:48, 80:48]. The 2010 design examples are free at aisc.org/designexamples, reducing engineering hours on composite checks [55:14].

### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, steel-anchor counts should be sized to 40 to 50% composite action and validated against beam member weights from aisc_validator.py, not pushed to full composite. For Mario's shop and welding crew, stud length must account for 3/16 inch direct burn-off or 3/8 inch through-deck burn-off so the 1.5-inch-above-deck rule is met after welding, and stud welding is steel-anchor work consistent with AWS practice. For our in-house PE stamp, the new Chapter I local-buckling, load-transfer (I6-1, I6-2), and I8.3 steel-anchor provisions apply on any composite-column or transfer-condition job, and Design Guide 3 deflection limits with the IBC 2009 full-live-load L/360 rule govern composite floor checks. For anchor-rod and embedded-plate work, the direct-bearing and yield-line embedded-plate methods map to our connection detailing in Tekla. This is a conventional structural steel composite topic with NO conflict with Your Company doctrine.

## Designing Structural Stainless Steel - Part 1
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-a_Xzty2YK4 | Duration: 1:32:10 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is part one of a two-part AISC webinar on designing structural stainless steel, presented by Katherine Husa of TMR Stainless [00:02]. It covers applications, history, performance, sustainability, the specific stainless families used in structural work, physical and mechanical properties, and a long treatment of corrosion-driven specification [01:33]. The governing reference throughout is AISC Design Guide 27, Structural Stainless Steel, issued September 2013, which covers hot-rolled and welded structural sections 0.125 in thick or greater, including I-beams, channels, angles, and hollow sections, plus fasteners and tension bars [05:07][05:37]. The central engineering message is that stainless is specified first by required corrosion resistance for the actual environment, then by mechanical and physical properties, because the name is stainless not stain-free and the wrong alloy will still pit, stain, or crack [22:42][23:12].

### Spec References
The speaker named these explicitly: AISC Design Guide 27 (structural stainless steel) [05:07]; SEI/ASCE 8 for cold-formed structural stainless [03:36][04:36]; Eurocode 3 (cited as the first global code to include all stainless product forms) [04:36]; AISC 360 by name as the carbon-steel specification that DG 27 parallels [06:08]; AWS D1.6 as the correct structural welding code for stainless, repeatedly contrasted against D1.1 [73:23][75:27]. ASTM/ASME material standards cited verbatim: A240 (plate/sheet/strip chemistry and mechanical properties) [64:18]; A480 (finishes and dimensional tolerances) [64:18]; A666 (cold-rolled higher strength) [64:18]; A276 (bar and hot-rolled/extruded shapes) [65:19]; A484 (dimensional tolerances) [65:19]; A554 (welded austenitic tube to 16 in) [66:22]; A789 (duplex tube interim) [66:22]; A269 (large-OD austenitic tube) [66:55]; A312 (austenitic pipe) [67:25]; A790 (duplex pipe) [67:25]; A351 (austenitic castings) and A890 (duplex castings) [67:58]; F593 (bolts/screws/studs) and F738 (metric) [68:00]; A193 (high-temp/high-pressure bolting) [68:29]; A1082 (high-strength PH and duplex bolting, all sizes, new) [69:00]; A167 (obsolete, replace with A240) [64:48]; A380 (post-fabrication corrosion-resistance restoration) and A967 (chemical passivation) [81:05][81:36]; UNS designations s30400, 32101 (LDX 2101), 2304, 2205, 17-4 PH [08:45][09:18][23:12]. NACE is referenced as the corrosion-engineering literature source [47:34].

### Technical Details
Three families are covered: austenitic (304, 304L, 316, 316L, non-magnetic, strengthened by cold work, easiest to weld) [07:11]; duplex (UNS 32101/LDX 2101, 2304, 2205, magnetic, higher strength) [08:13][08:45]; and precipitation-hardened (17-4 PH, highest strength but least corrosion resistant, tension bars and fasteners only) [09:18]. The L suffix means low carbon, required for welding and weld corrosion integrity [07:41]. Stainless has no defined yield point, so yield is the 2% offset, and the elastic limit runs roughly 40 to 70% of that offset yield [10:21][88:29]. A pitting resistance equivalent number ranks relative corrosion resistance, with 17-4 PH lowest near 15, 304 a step up, 2205 around 35, and 2507 higher [25:15][25:45]. Austenitic grades hold excellent impact toughness to cryogenic temperatures; duplex thermal expansion is close to carbon steel while austenitic expansion is near copper [69:30][70:31]. Chloride stress corrosion cracking is the named failure mode for 304/316 in load-bearing high-chloride service, with six-moly austenitics or super-duplex 2507 recommended instead [46:33].

### Fabrication Notes
Welding is the common method and AWS D1.6 governs, covering all welding methods, all stainless grades, dissimilar stainless joints, and stainless-to-carbon joints, plus stud welding, pre-qualification, welder qualification, inspection, and rejection criteria [73:23][75:57][79:35]. Do not preheat austenitic or duplex stainless or you destroy corrosion resistance; only PH grades sometimes need careful preheat [73:54]. Use a matching, slightly higher-alloy filler so corrosion resistance survives alloy loss in the weld; 304L, 316L, and lean duplex can be welded without filler, while 2205 should almost always use filler [76:28][76:59]. Stainless joints use wider included angles, a smaller root face, an allowed root gap, and more tack welding than carbon steel [78:01]. Heat tint must be removed by pickling paste or abrasion (remove the tint plus a little base metal), with ASTM A380 for restoring corrosion resistance and A967 for passivation; A967 does not restore weld corrosion resistance [80:35][81:05][81:36]. Use experienced stainless fabricators, dedicated stainless work areas, thoroughly cleaned tooling, and never let carbon-steel-contaminated equipment touch stainless [82:43][83:14]. Do not use oxyacetylene welding on stainless [75:57].

### Erection Notes
The webinar states that fabrication and erection costs should be roughly equivalent to carbon steel [17:32], but it gives little field-sequencing, crane, or rigging content. The practical erection-adjacent cautions are galvanic: dissimilar metals in regular contact with moisture must be separated by insulating washers, paint, or a non-conducting barrier, or one metal corrodes rapidly [48:04][48:36]. A field example showed galvanized fasteners in a stainless assembly corroding fast and becoming the structural failure point because of an unfavorable small-anodic to large-cathodic surface-area ratio [49:38][50:46]. Thermal expansion must be accommodated during installation: 316 wall panels installed flat in winter with no expansion room ended permanently oil-canned [69:30].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Named failures include chloride stress corrosion cracking that split a 304 load-bearing deck a third of the way through in a high-snow region [46:01]; a broken 316 ceiling bolt in a load-bearing application [46:01]; carbon-steel framing under a Tokyo cathedral roof corroding away from condensation contact [51:47]; galvanized fasteners corroding catastrophically when paired with stainless or carbon surfaces because of surface-area ratio [49:38][50:46]; crevice corrosion concentrated under washer heads and inside cable strands even when exposed members stayed clean [54:26][54:58]; and accelerated corrosion from rough finishes above Ra 0.5 microns (20 microinches) [56:01][56:34]. Specifying AWS D1.1 instead of D1.6, calling out obsolete ASTM A167, or specifying pressure-rated pipe where structural tube would do are all named specification errors [64:48][66:22][73:23]. Welder certifications for the specific alloy and method should be in the bid package so no one is learning on the job [78:31].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Raw-material premium over carbon steel, before fabrication: rolled angles and channels in 316L run about four to five times; duplex welded structural sections about six times; 316L welded structural sections about eight times [16:32][17:02]. Those figures exclude offsetting savings: no galvanizing or painting, possibly no fireproofing, no coating-reapplication maintenance, and potential section-size reduction with higher-strength duplex [17:02][17:32]. Stainless rebar installed cost runs only 2 to 12% higher than carbon when repair and replacement are counted [18:33]. The recommended bid-time analysis is a life-cycle cost analysis rather than first-cost comparison [16:02]. Stock sizes are more limited (typically only 304/304L/316/316L stocked), so custom fabrication and short runs through specialty sources add lead-time and cost considerations [61:11][61:43].

### Your Company Application
This material is reference, not a current Your Company workstream, since the shop runs conventional carbon structural steel. If a coastal, water-treatment, food/pharma, or architectural-monument job ever specifies stainless, Ivan must read the spec for the exact UNS grade and family before takeoff, because stainless density differs from carbon steel and varies by family, so weight-per-foot cannot be assumed from carbon AISC tables and must come from the stainless material standard, not aisc_validator.py [84:16]. Mario and the welding crew would face a hard process change: AWS D1.6 not D1.1 governs, no preheat on austenitic or duplex, matching higher-alloy filler, mandatory heat-tint removal by pickling, and a dedicated contamination-free stainless work area with current alloy-specific welder certs [73:23][73:54][80:35][83:14]. For anchor rods, field bolting, and any mixed assembly, Paul and the field crew must enforce galvanic separation so galvanized fasteners are never set against stainless [48:36][50:46]. For Tekla detailing and the in-house PE stamp, connection and member design would key off AISC Design Guide 27 plus SEI/ASCE 8 for cold-formed, not AISC 360 alone, and the page-1 cost story is a life-cycle case, not first cost. Doctrine flag: NONE. Nothing here conflicts with Your Company doctrine; it reinforces verify-do-not-generate, since stainless weights and grades must be sourced from the material spec and never from the carbon AISC database.

## Designing Structural Stainless Steel - Part 2
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FtO2g6BEnWg | Duration: 1:32:22 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This webinar, presented by Nancy Baddoo of the Steel Construction Institute (UK), author of AISC Design Guide 27, covers the structural-engineering design rules for stainless steel members and connections [00:33][02:35]. The controlling idea is that stainless steel has a nonlinear (rounded) stress-strain curve with no sharply defined yield point and high strain hardening, unlike carbon steel which has a defined yield plateau [09:53]. Because of this nonlinearity, design uses the 0.2% offset yield strength: travel to 0.2% permanent strain, draw a line parallel to the initial elastic modulus, and read the stress where it intersects the curve [10:23]. The design approach mirrors AISC 360 carbon-steel methods but with modified coefficients, lower width-to-thickness limits, and lower buckling curves [36:08].

### Spec References
AISC Design Guide 27 (structural stainless steel, published roughly 6 months before the webinar, freely downloadable for AISC members or $60 PDF) [02:35][03:11]. AISC 360 cited repeatedly as the carbon-steel baseline, with named equations E3-1, E3-2, E3-3, E3-4, E7-3, E7-4, E7-5, E7-6, F2-2, F2-3, F2-5, F7-4, F7-5; Chapter F (flexure), Chapter G (shear), Chapter J Section J4 (affected elements), Section J10 (concentrated forces), Table J3.2 (bolt nominal strengths), and Appendix 4 plus Appendix C (fire) [40:53][53:15][62:02][76:08]. DG27 internal references: Table 3-2 (width-to-thickness limits), Table 6-1 (secant modulus), Appendix A (Continuous Strength Method), Appendix B (reliability commentary) [80:23][81:58][03:41]. Material/product specs named: ASTM A666 (cold-worked sheet/strip), ASTM A992 (grade 50 carbon comparison), ASTM F593 (stainless bolt tensile strength), ASTM A1082 (duplex fasteners) [15:40][11:59][58:55][59:26]. Also referenced: ASCE/SEI 8 (cold-formed stainless) and Eurocode 3 Part 1.4 [18:48][26:17].

### Technical Details
Initial elastic modulus is 28,000 ksi for austenitic versus 29,000 ksi for carbon and duplex; density runs 485 to 500 lb/ft3 [12:29]. Austenitic 304/316 design strength is generally FY = 30 ksi; duplex runs 58 to 67 ksi; precipitation-hardening grades are very high strength for tension rods and fasteners [37:15][28:22]. Local-buckling limits are lower for stainless: unstiffened I-shape flanges 0.47 vs 0.56 root(E/FY), stiffened webs of W and channel sections 1.24 vs 1.49, round HSS 0.10 vs 0.11 [38:48]. Compression equation coefficient 4.71 is reduced to 3.77 [42:34]. Deflection uses the secant modulus from a Ramberg-Osgood model (n around 5 for austenitic, 7 to 8 for duplex); at a stress ratio of 0.6 the austenitic secant modulus drops about 15% to 23 to 24,000 ksi, duplex only about 5% [49:32][52:11]. Scope excludes flexural angles and tees, slender webs in flexure, unequal-leg angles, round-HSS flexure, tension-field action, composite members, and plastic analysis [30:58][37:48].

### Fabrication Notes
Strain hardening from cold forming, roller leveling, and other fabrication operations can raise the 0.2% offset yield strength by about 50% in the highly worked corner regions of a hollow structural section [15:40]. This is not free: working strain-hardened stainless requires more powerful equipment, stronger tools, and greater forces, and it can reduce ductility (though stainless ductility is high enough that this is rarely a problem) [16:12]. Welding stainless to carbon steel is common and acceptable provided the correct filler metals and welding procedures are used [56:52]. Because stainless has low thermal conductivity and high thermal expansion, weld distortion is a concern; DG27 recommends symmetrical joints, good fit-up, and reducing the extent of welding [73:30]. Scope applies to sections thicker than 0.125 inch [27:19].

### Erection Notes
The webinar is design-focused and does not cover field erection sequencing, crane, rigging, or bracing. The closest erection-adjacent guidance is detailing connections to accommodate the higher thermal expansion of stainless in a restrained frame, since trapped expansion forces can cause premature failure at elevated temperature [72:58]. Galvanic separation between dissimilar metals was addressed in Q&A: a small stainless canopy against a large aluminum standing-seam roof may not have a galvanic issue because relative surface areas govern [89:29].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The headline failure mode for stainless bolting is galling (also called cold welding), a local adhesion and seizure that occurs when underloaded surfaces are in relative motion under high torque; it is distinct from thread stripping and also affects aluminum and other oxide-film alloys [63:32]. DG27 mitigations are lubricating internal or external threads, smoothing the threads, or pairing bolt and nut of different stainless types with different hardness [64:33]. A carbon-steel DTI will not correctly predict tension in a stainless bolt and should not be used [65:05]. Other named pitfalls: time-dependent stress relaxation in pretensioned austenitic and duplex bolts [64:33], using carbon-steel bolts in stainless members [58:25], and the dual-certified penalty where 304/304L material must be designed to the lower FY per ASTM [82:29]. Chloride stress-corrosion cracking is an ambient-temperature risk noted for swimming-pool environments [90:36].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Stainless is specified for corrosion resistance and long, low-maintenance life, plus aesthetic exposed finishes, blast and impact resistance, and hygiene; the payback is in avoided coating and maintenance, not first cost [04:11]. Lean duplex grades are cheaper than standard duplex because they are less highly alloyed, while offering strengths well above austenitic [28:52]. The higher strength of duplex cannot always be fully used when deflection or local buckling governs, which caps the tonnage savings [37:15]. There are no AISC-manual-style member capacity tables for stainless; some producers publish section properties but not full capacity tables, so design effort per member is higher [83:36]. The dual-certification rule (design to the lower yield) is a real cost penalty on material that is physically stronger than its stamp [82:29].

### Your Company Application
Your Company builds conventional carbon structural steel, so DG27 is a reference for any future corrosive or architectural-exposure scope, not a change to current rates. If Ivan ever takes off a stainless job, the FY inputs (austenitic 30 ksi, duplex 58 to 67 ksi) and lower local-buckling and buckling limits would need a separate validator path, since aisc_validator.py wraps the carbon v16.0 database and these are different design curves; flag any stainless line as outside the current validator scope. For Mario, the welding takeaways are matching filler metal when joining stainless to carbon, and distortion control by symmetrical joints and good fit-up given stainless thermal behavior, consistent with his AWS D1.1 discipline. For field bolting, the doctrine note is that stainless bolts must not be pretensioned or inspected with a carbon-steel DTI, and turn-of-nut remains valid; galling and lubrication become real install steps. Anchor rods and joists are not addressed here. DOCTRINE FLAG: NONE. This is reference knowledge for a material Your Company does not currently fabricate, and nothing here alters BID_RATES, AISC weights, or the carbon-steel positioning.

## Facade Attachments for Steel Framed Buildings
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=URmmEJk22xM | Duration: 1:27:58 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This webinar by Alec Zimmer of Simpson Gumpertz and Heger condenses AISC Design Guide 22, Facade Attachments to Steel Framed Buildings, which he co-developed with James Parker [00:32][02:36]. The central message is that the structural engineer of record (SER) owns the strategy for how the facade attaches to the building frame even though the facade and its attachments are usually delegated to a specialty structural engineer working for the contractor [05:11][37:05]. The talk works through facade performance fundamentals, design criteria, roles and responsibilities, accumulated tolerances and clearances, slab edge design, spandrel beam torsion, and masonry cavity walls, all centered on how the chosen attachment strategy drives the slab edge and spandrel beam design [04:08][82:07].
### Spec References
The speaker cites AISC Design Guide 22 (the subject document) [02:36], AISC Design Guide 9 for torsion of members rotating about their center [62:57][66:01], and the AISC Code of Standard Practice for the SER and specialty engineer definitions and for column out-of-plumb tolerances (2 inches in / 1 inch out at the tenth story in his example) [36:01][43:43]. For loads he cites ASCE 7 component-and-cladding provisions including the 0.7 reduction factor on wind for serviceability deflection [18:35], the seismic component equation with Rp and ap factors (connection designed at ap 1.5 / Rp 1.0, panel at ap 1.0 / Rp 2.5, so connections carry more than three times the panel force) [22:42][23:14], ASCE 7 Section 13.1.3 exempting seismic design category B (and SDC C under straight IBC) from facade attachment requirements [20:38][21:10], and the friction-clip prohibition for facade anchorage [21:41]. He also cites ACI 530 brick crack-control limits [28:52], the PCI Design Handbook 6th edition panel tolerances (plus/minus 0.5 inch, bow L/360) [44:15], the Steel Deck Institute pour-stop selection guide [52:05], and ASTM A615 / A706 deformed bar over welded wire fabric in slabs [51:35].
### Technical Details
Connection and system types covered: masonry brick veneer with light-gauge or CMU backup, relieving/shelf angles on hangers, story-tall and column-supported precast concrete panels, and aluminum-and-glass curtain wall with mullions [38:38][41:11]. Facade gravity load is eccentric to the spandrel beam and produces a horizontal component plus torsion; negative wind pressure combines with gravity eccentricity and often controls the attachment [15:59][19:37]. Spandrel torsion is resolved by kickers (double or single angles, or a channel bracing the bottom flange to the next interior beam), by roll beams (a wide-flange on a full-depth stiffener plate), or by plating the back of the wide flange to make a closed tube at atriums and stairwells where kickers cannot fit [54:12][67:33]. Two slab edge approaches: the slab cantilevers past the spandrel as a beam (needs top flexural reinforcement, loads distributed on a 1:1 slope), or the spandrel carries the eccentric load in torsion [48:27][50:32]. Accumulated tolerance is the aggregate of material production, fabrication/assembly, and erection/installation tolerances; his worked example yields a midspan gap range of plus 4.33 to minus 3.33 inches [42:42][45:22].
### Fabrication Notes
Pour stops at exterior slab edges are frequently beyond the 12-inch SDI table limit, so DG22 adds a bent-plate pour-stop table for extensions up to 18 inches from the spandrel beam, and a bent plate is preferred over light-gauge so it can be welded readily [52:05][52:39]. Forces from the vertical slab edge are transferred back into the slab with welded headed studs or deformed bar anchors on the pour stop vertical leg, and headed studs on a spandrel are usually field-applied because shop-applied studs are a tripping hazard during erection unless the bent plate follows after framing [52:39][53:11]. Relieving and shelf angles are always galvanized because water that gets behind the barrier collects on them and rusts them out [79:58]. Slabs use A615 or A706 deformed bar rather than welded wire fabric, which sinks to the deck and does no good in negative moment [51:35].
### Erection Notes
Field fit-up adjustability is built into the hanger detail with vertical slotted holes in the stiffener plate and horizontal slotted holes in the angle, set with erection bolts and then field-welded once the final position is fixed just before the brick goes up [78:22][78:55]. The shelf-angle-to-hanger connection uses a vertical long-slotted hole and an erection bolt, then a field weld at the top of the shelf angle, and the erection bolt is removed so it does not interfere with flashing or waterproofing [78:55][79:27]. Clearances are deliberately provided to absorb the accumulated tolerances and give access during erection, and the speaker notes the cost trade between long slotted holes and a field-welded connection in lieu of bolted [33:26][46:24]. Steel erectors often prefer a slotted hole at the roll-beam-to-spandrel connection, which is acceptable if the faying surfaces are prepared for slip-critical friction and the bolts are pretensioned to resist the moment [55:15].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The recurring field failure is sealant bulging out of soft joints because the joint was sized too small and the brick grew with moisture and temperature [28:52][72:11]. Transitional masonry buildings (late 1800s to mid 1900s) built integrally with the frame crack and bulge as trapped moisture rusts the unprotected steel and the rust expands [08:15][09:16]. Corrugated brick ties are no longer used because they trap water on thin steel [34:27]. A historical defect he has seen is omitting the horizontal soft joint under the shelf angle (a 1962/1966 building), where the brick below jacked up the relieving angle and lifted the parapet [86:16][86:46]. A coordination error is the panel designer and the SER assuming different hinge locations, which mislocates the design moment [17:33]. Friction clips for facade anchorage are not permitted under seismic provisions [21:41].
### Bid / Cost Implications
Slab edge details are finicky and carry a lot of cost, and minor architectural or structural differences strongly affect constructability, so they must be addressed early [46:54]. Keeping perimeter conditions uniform and using similar spandrel sizes throughout makes everyone's life easier and cheaper, and the speaker explicitly warns that a net tonnage saving may not be worth the headache of supporting the facade at two dozen different spandrel beam types [48:27][59:19]. A wind tunnel study on a large project often shows pressures below ASCE 7, reducing cladding cost and main wind-force-resisting-system force [18:35]. Field-welded connections and long slotted holes add adjustability but cost more than plain bolted ones, a trade to price per project and region [34:58][46:24].
### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, the warning that minimizing spandrel tonnage can multiply facade-support detail types is a direct estimating flag: count distinct spandrel/edge conditions, not just tons, and price kickers, roll beams, relieving angles, hangers, and galvanizing as their own scope rather than rolling them into bare beam tonnage. Mario's shop work picks up the bent-plate pour stops, galvanized shelf and relieving angles, welded headed studs and deformed bar anchors, and the slotted-hole adjustability detailing; the field-applied stud note and the trip-hazard reason belong in Paul's erection safety brief. Field bolting maps cleanly to the roll-beam slip-critical pretensioned connection and the RCSC-style faying-surface prep, and field welding of hangers per AWS D1.1 is Mario's. Tekla detailing should carry the vertical and horizontal slotted holes and the erection-bolt-then-field-weld sequence; the in-house PE stamp scope question (SER vs specialty engineer per the Code of Standard Practice) is worth confirming on any job where Your Company is asked to design facade attachments rather than just the frame. This is conventional structural steel work with no anchor-rod or joist content here and no PEMB language, so doctrine flag is NONE.

## SteelDay 2013: The Life of the K-Factor
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=87tf_AwrHOM | Duration: 1:04:42 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
Charlie Carter, AISC vice president and chief structural engineer, traces the column effective length factor K from its empirical origins to its modern role, where current AISC stability methods let the designer set K equal to one [05:13][45:47]. K is the multiplier on actual column length L that gives the buckling length KL: less than one for rotation-restrained ends, one for pinned-pinned, and two for a flagpole or cantilever column [02:37][03:39]. The unifying theme is that any stability method must satisfy "five things": flexural, shear, and axial deformations from first-order displacement; second-order effects (P-big-Delta at connections and P-little-Delta along members); geometric imperfections (initial lean and curvature); stiffness reduction due to inelasticity (residual stresses); and variability in component and system stiffness [05:44][09:51][43:15]. This is a design-engineering and code-history lecture, not a fabrication or erection talk.
### Spec References
Cited explicitly: 2005 and 2010 AISC specifications Section C1.1 for the five stability requirements [05:13]; Chapter C and Appendix 7 as the home of the prescriptive stability methods [36:34]; AISC Code of Standard Practice for tolerances, including Figure C7.5 and the one-in-500 (0.002) column out-of-plumb limit [06:45][07:17][53:29]; AISC Design Guide 28 (Larry Griffis and Don White, stability design) released December 2013 [10:22][39:08]; ASTM A6 for the W-shape straightness basis of about one in 950 versus the code-assumed one in 1000 [08:18]; and the Engineering Journal paper "A Comparison of Frame Stability Analysis Methods in AISC 360," Carter and Geschwindner, third quarter 2008 [49:53]. Historical specification milestones named: the first AISC spec 1923, then 1936, 1961, the 1963 spec where K became explicit, 1969, 1978, 1989 ASD, and the 1986, 1993, and 1999 LRFD specs [04:41][21:40][25:42][28:45].
### Technical Details
The three prescriptive stability methods are the direct analysis method (new in 2005), the effective length method, and the first-order analysis method [37:05]. Direct analysis requires a second-order analysis (or first-order plus a B1-B2 amplification), notional lateral loads of 0.002 times the gravity load at each level or node to model the one-in-500 lean, reduced stiffnesses EA-star and EI-star (generally 0.8 times EA and EI, with a tau-b factor often but not always equal to one), and strength-level (LRFD) load combinations [39:39][40:42][41:45]. For ASD the designer multiplies loads by 1.6, analyzes, then divides results by 1.6; the 1.6 (not 1.5) reflects the nonlinear growth of second-order deformations at strength-level drift [41:45][50:24]. The effective length and first-order methods are limited to structures with calculated B2 less than or equal to 1.5; direct analysis has no such limit and is favored for moment frames, mixed brace-and-moment systems, and irregular industrial or process structures [55:35][56:06]. The 1962 Kavanaugh alignment charts (originally the 1959 Julian-Lawrence charts) gave the graphical K, with separate sway and non-sway cases [22:10].
### Fabrication Notes
No fabrication, fit-up, or shop QC content. The lecture stays on analysis and member-strength theory; the only fabrication-adjacent fact is that residual stresses lock into a W-shape as the section cools (extremities first), with rolling and straightening altering the distribution, and welded shapes showing a different pattern than rolled shapes [08:49][09:20].
### Erection Notes
No erection procedure, sequencing, crane, or bracing-of-record content. The single erection-relevant item is the one-in-500 (0.002) maximum column out-of-plumb tolerance from the Code of Standard Practice that the notional-load and lean assumptions are built on; columns near elevators or the facade carry tighter tolerances, which the code conservatively ignores for stability [07:17][53:29]. If a field survey establishes the actual erected lean, the designer may model that geometry directly or scale the notional load instead of using the 0.002 maximum [53:29][54:32].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
No bolting, welding, or shop-inspection rejections are discussed. The errors named are design and code-history failures of judgment. The 1989 ASD spec omitted stability advances already in the 1986 LRFD spec, fostering the mistaken belief that stability was an LRFD-only concern [26:44]. The John Hancock Tower in Boston is cited as the dramatic case where design outpaced the code: stability was blamed for glass facade panels popping out [28:14]. The deeper point is that few if any of the alignment-chart assumptions behind a hand-calculated K are actually satisfied in real frames, so K was accepted because it did something rather than nothing, and leaning columns can drive K well above one [24:42][59:16].
### Bid / Cost Implications
No direct estimating, schedule, or dollar content. The economic thread is historical: construction-management influence and economic evaluation pushed framing toward lighter sections, longer spans, and limited lateral framing, which raised the demand for rigorous stability analysis [27:14]. The practical takeaway for a design office is that direct analysis with K equal to one simplifies moment-frame design and avoids fragile alignment-chart K calculations, which is an engineering-hours and rework consideration rather than a fabrication cost [42:45][55:03].
### Your Company Application
This is theory for the in-house PE stamp and any moment-frame or mixed-system design Your Company engineers, not for Ivan's takeoff, Mario's shop welding, Paul's safety program, or Tekla detailing, none of which the talk touches. The one concrete crossover is anchor-rod and column work: the one-in-500 column out-of-plumb tolerance from the AISC Code of Standard Practice that underpins the 0.002 notional load is the same erection tolerance band that governs Your Company anchor-rod setting and column plumbing, so it is worth citing by name when defending field plumb tolerances or an anchor-setting RFI. For ACP controls the value is reference-only: stability-method selection (direct analysis with K equal to one) is an EOR design decision that does not change validated tonnage, AISC weights from aisc_validator.py, or locked bid rates. NONE: no conflict with Your Company doctrine, and the conventional-structural-steel framing of the talk aligns with our positioning.

## Fundamentals of Structural Stability for Steel Design - Part 3
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MzT-sNvixWU | Duration: 1:32:09 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
This is session five of AISC Night School, presented by Ron Ziemian of Bucknell University and the Structural Stability Research Council, covering beam-column behavior and the analysis side of system stability [00:02][01:33]. The central teaching is how a structure's required strengths (the P and M forces and moments you design for) must be computed from an analysis that captures four destabilizing effects, and how the resulting forces feed the AISC interaction equation [32:48][33:49]. It walks from cross-section yield surfaces through elastic and inelastic member strength to the two code-permitted stability methods. This is analysis theory and design methodology, not a fabrication or erection lecture.

### Spec References
The talk names specific provisions: the AISC interaction equation form p/py + 8/9 (M/MP) less than 1 when axial is over 20% of yield, and p/(2py) + M/MP less than 1 for light axial [08:45][09:15]; alternative interaction equation H1.D2 for the lateral-torsional buckling case [27:10]; the 0.866 factor on the AISC column curve from lecture one [26:39]; the B1 and B2 amplification factors and the C_m moment-gradient factor [42:32][54:54][61:01]; Appendix 1 for inelastic analysis [03:38][67:11]; Appendix 7 for the effective length method and the first-order method, the effective length method dated to the 1961 specification [66:41][69:13]; the RM factor between 0.85 and 1.0 [64:08]; the direct analysis method 0.8 stiffness factor with the tau-b factor, the notional load of 0.002 times the gravity load, and the 0.001 equivalent notional load [73:19][75:21][76:22]; out-of-plumb tolerance H/500 referenced to the Code of Standard Practice [74:50]; commentary table on page 273 from a Shankar Nair paper and the TC10 committee [81:03]. All quoted because the speaker stated them aloud.

### Technical Details
The lecture builds the yield/interaction surface for combined axial force and major and minor axis bending, showing axial force directly reduces the bending capacity below MP [15:23][17:24]. It derives the exact B1 moment amplification factor as 1/cos of a term in P/PE, then shows the familiar approximate B1 = 1/(1 - P/PE) and notes the approximation underestimates the exact by roughly 10% at 40% of Euler load [49:13][53:20][55:25]. The B2 story factor sums all column axial forces on a story over the story elastic buckling load, approximated through story shear stiffness rather than per-column K factors [61:01][62:33]. The four factors driving system stability are flexural/shear/axial and connection deformations, second-order P-large-Delta and P-small-Delta effects, geometric imperfections (member out-of-straightness and frame out-of-plumbness), and stiffness reduction from partial yielding accentuated by residual stresses [34:50][66:11].

### Fabrication Notes
No shop-floor fabrication, fit-up, or QC content appears in this lecture. The only fabrication-adjacent point is residual stress: the speaker states residual stresses run a low of 20%, an expected 30%, up to 50% in jumbo sections, and that member-straightening methods can nearly remove them [11:18][84:38][85:08]. That is a material-condition input to the stability math, not a shop procedure.

### Erection Notes
No field erection, sequencing, bracing, crane, or rigging procedure is covered. The lecture touches erected geometry only through frame out-of-plumbness, which it ties to the H/500 out-of-straightness from the Code of Standard Practice and handles in analysis by directly modeling the distortion or applying notional loads of 0.002 times the gravity load on a level [74:20][74:50]. Sway versus non-sway framing is discussed analytically: a sway frame carries P-large-Delta plus P-small-Delta, a braced non-sway frame usually only P-small-Delta [56:27][57:28].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
This is a design-analysis lecture, so the errors named are engineering judgment errors, not weld or bolt rejections. The speaker repeatedly warns that practitioners misuse the B1 and B2 amplification factors and would be better served pressing the second-order elastic analysis button after learning nonlinear analysis [41:31][42:02]. He flags the alignment-chart K factors as the scary part: the charts rest on nine idealized assumptions that seldom exist in real structures, and back-calculating K from an eigenvalue analysis on a lightly loaded column produces a misleadingly large effective length [70:46][71:46]. He also notes that with the effective length method the design moment used for beams and connections can differ from the actual moment, a differential that can cause concern [78:25].

### Bid / Cost Implications
No direct cost, schedule, or estimating content. The implication for engineering labor is that the direct analysis method shifts effort into a more rigorous second-order analysis but removes the time and uncertainty of justifying K factors, so KL is simply the unbraced length [72:18][76:22]. The two methods generally yield similar final designs, the effective length method showing more axial strength while the direct analysis method produces larger moments, gaining in one place and losing in the other [80:01][80:32].

### Your Company Application
This lecture sits with the in-house PE stamp workflow, not with Ivan takeoff, Mario shop, Paul safety, Tekla detailing, anchor rods, joists, or field bolting. Its practical value is that whoever runs the analysis behind a stamped Your Company package should use the direct analysis method with the 0.8 and tau-b stiffness reductions and notional loads, since it gets both the axial force and the moments right for sizing beams and connections, rather than wrestling with alignment-chart K factors [76:22][79:29]. The H/500 out-of-plumb tolerance tied to the Code of Standard Practice is the one item that crosses into erection: it is the plumb tolerance our crews must hold and our analysis already assumes, so it belongs in field plumbing checklists on a job like Asian City Plaza. There is no member-weight or AISC-shape data in this video, so nothing here touches aisc_validator.py outputs. No conflict with Your Company doctrine: NONE.

## Fundamentals of Structural Stability for Steel Design - Part 2
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OVDgf70Dl84 | Duration: 1:34:06 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is AISC Night School session three, Behavior of Flexural Members, presented by Ron Ziemian of the Structural Stability Research Council [00:01]. The lecture covers the strength limit states of beams: full cross-section yielding to the plastic moment Mp, and member instability by lateral torsional buckling (LTB), both elastic and inelastic [02:33]. The throughline is that a long-enough unbraced compression flange behaves like a column and buckles laterally while twisting, so beam capacity drops as unbraced length grows. It is theory and behavior, not a fabrication or erection lecture; the design-application companion was deferred to Todd Helwig the following week [84:50].
### Spec References
The talk is built around AISC 360 flexural provisions but the speaker names few exact callouts. The cited items are: AISC Design Guide 9 on torsional analysis for warping coefficients [56:11]; the AISC Manual shape tables that list cross-sectional area, Ix, Iy, the Saint-Venant torsion constant J, and the warping coefficient Cw (sometimes scaled by 10 to the sixth) [56:41]; the AISC 2005/2010 Specification user note giving the simplified elastic LTB moment Me/Mcr for wide flange shapes [88:59]; and the Wong and Driver Cb summary in a 2010 AISC Engineering Journal paper [73:32]. The governing equations discussed are the elastic LTB moment, Lp = 1.76 ry sqrt(E/Fy) [69:28], the Lr transition, the Cb moment-gradient modifier, and Mr at first yield taken near 0.7 Fy Sx with about 30% absorbed by residual stress [80:13]. No AISC 341 seismic, AWS D1.1, or RCSC bolting sections are cited; this lecture does not cover them.
### Technical Details
Yielding moves through the section depth from the flanges inward, and the plastic-to-elastic section modulus ratio (shape factor Z/S) is only about 1.15 to 1.2 for wide flange shapes [09:11]. LTB couples minor-axis bending with twist; the resisting torque is the sum of Saint-Venant torsion (GJ, small for open shapes) and warping torsion (E Cw, the dominant term for wide flanges), with Cw approximated as Iy h squared over 4 [37:43]. The worked comparison of a W8x13 open shape (J = 0.0871) against an equal-area closed tube (J = 22.95) shows closed sections carry roughly 264 times the torsion, which is why HSS rarely governs by LTB [29:36]. Residual stresses from differential cooling run on the order of 30% of Fy and pull first yield below My, driving inelastic LTB [62:48]. The Cb factor scales the uniform-moment solution; AISC is conservative on Cb relative to Eurocode but liberal on the inelastic curve, so the codes wash out to similar capacity once moment gradient is included [83:18].
### Fabrication Notes
No shop fabrication, fit-up, or QC content. The only fabrication-adjacent point is metallurgical: hot-rolled wide flange shapes lock in residual stresses near 30% of Fy because the flange tips cool and set before the web-flange junction, which the section then carries as locked-in compression at the tips and tension at the core [62:48].
### Erection Notes
The one direct field caution is about handling long, deep girders: if a crew releases the hoisting cable before torsionally securing the girder ends, the member can pick up torque under its own self-weight, twist, and tip over [58:44]. The lecture stresses that beam ends must be braced against twist at supports or the section will roll over once it buckles. Detailed bracing design was deferred to lectures 7 and 8 [88:26].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
This is a behavior lecture, so the named failures are design and analysis errors rather than weld or bolt rejections. The headline error is treating an inflection point as a brace point: a 40-ft W24x68 in reverse curvature is far stronger with a real torsional brace at midspan (shorter unbraced length) than if the inflection point is assumed to brace it, even though adding the brace lowers Cb from 2.27 to 1.67 [77:07]. A second error is forgetting that adding a brace creates two unbraced segments that each need a separate Lb and Cb check; the longer span does not automatically govern [75:37]. A third is releasing rigging before securing girder ends against twist [58:44].
### Bid / Cost Implications
No direct pricing, schedule, or estimating content. The implied takeaway for cost is that unbraced length controls beam capacity, so brace spacing decisions in detailing affect required member sizes and therefore tonnage. Using Cb = 1 is always conservative but leaves capacity on the table when moment gradient exists [75:06].
### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff through aisc_validator.py, this reinforces that beam capacity is governed by unbraced length, Lp, Lr, and Cb, not just section weight, so a member size pulled from a schedule already reflects the engineer's brace assumptions; the validator stays the source for J, Cw, Sx, and Zx, never LLM math, which matches our verify-don't-generate posture. For Tekla detailing and the in-house PE stamp, the inflection-point-is-not-a-brace-point rule and the two-segment Lb/Cb check are direct review items when locating beam braces, joist seats, and bridging. For Paul Guerrero's safety program, the concrete erection rule is to torsionally secure long girder ends before releasing the crane hook, since an unbraced deep girder can twist and tip under self-weight. Joist and field-bolting specifics, anchor-rod tolerances, and ACP project controls are not addressed in this lecture. Doctrine conflict: NONE.

## Fundamentals of Structural Stability for Steel Design - Part 1
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WsWjunLKAIU | Duration: 1:30:43 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is the opening session of AISC Night School "Fundamentals of Stability for Steel Design," presented by Ron Ziemian of Bucknell University for the Structural Stability Research Council, covering course introduction and the behavior of compression members [00:01]. The lecture builds the AISC column strength curve from first principles, starting with the 1744 Euler buckling solution and then progressively undoing each of Euler's idealizing assumptions: prismatic member, small post-buckling deflection, no bending before bifurcation, linear-elastic material, and pinned-pinned ends [11:24][24:11]. It distinguishes bifurcation (theoretical critical load) from instability (buckling preceded by growing deflection), and shows that initial out-of-straightness, partial yielding, and residual stresses each pull real column strength below the elastic Euler stress [04:07][45:14].
### Spec References
The talk is behavior-focused and cites few clause numbers verbatim. The AISC column curve is described as the single fitted curve used for all shapes, with the transition near a slenderness of about 113 and the long-column branch set at 0.877 (87.7 percent) of the Euler buckling stress [69:23][69:55]. The speaker names the AISC Specification Commentary effective-length table for support conditions and K factors [71:57], references Appendix 1 for using a user-developed column curve that accounts for residual stresses [83:41][83:10], and mentions the direct analysis method and its tau (stiffness reduction) factor [59:11][81:08]. He cites the SSRC "Guide to Stability Design Criteria for Metal Structures" (about 1,100 pages) and a Ray Tide background paper in the AISC Engineering Journal [68:23][68:53]. No AISC 360 chapter, AISC 341, AWS D1.1, or RCSC section is stated by number.
### Technical Details
Euler buckling load is n-squared times pi-squared EI over L-squared, controlled by the first mode, giving Euler stress of pi-squared E over (L/r)-squared once divided by area using radius of gyration [18:33][20:37]. Adding a sine-shaped initial out-of-straightness of about L/1000 produces a midspan amplification factor of 1/(1 - P/P_Euler), so deflections grow unbounded as load approaches the Euler load [29:51][31:26]. Residual stresses, on the order of 30 to 50 percent of yield in heavy jumbo shapes, arise from uneven cooling: flange tips cool first and end in compression while the web-flange junction ends in tension, and these compressive flange tips yield early and cut effective EI [50:20][54:02][62:13]. Minor-axis strength is consistently below major-axis strength because losing the flange tips to yielding hurts weak-axis stiffness far more [62:43]. K factors of 0.5, 0.7, 1.0, and 2.0 follow from the differential-equation solution and can be estimated from the spacing of inflection points on the buckled shape [75:29][76:00].
### Fabrication Notes
The most fabrication-relevant content is the residual-stress discussion. Built-in stresses come from uneven cooling after rolling, from welding built-up shapes (where the welded-shape residual pattern is more severe than rolled shapes), and from cold bending [50:20][54:02]. An audience exchange clarifies that mechanical straightening of a column (cold cambering or gagging past yield) often reduces rather than adds residual stress because it takes the section past yield and relaxes it, though cold-forming can introduce its own residual stresses [65:48][66:19]. No shop tolerance numbers, fit-up steps, or QC procedures are given; this is theory, not shop practice.
### Erection Notes
No erection sequencing, bracing, crane, rigging, or site-coordination content appears. The only field-adjacent point is conceptual: real end restraint is hard to know (the Walt Disney Concert Hall example), so the assumed K factor for an erected column depends on the actual rotational and lateral stiffness the connections provide, which alignment charts approximate under stated assumptions [77:32][78:35].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
No inspection or rejection criteria are named. The implied design errors are conceptual: treating a real column as perfectly straight, ignoring residual stresses (which the speaker warns makes a finite-element column analysis unconservative), and misjudging the K factor when end restraint is uncertain [83:41][81:08]. He notes a single AISC curve cannot capture every shape, so it slightly over-predicts minor-axis strength and under-predicts major-axis strength relative to finite-element results, a modeling limitation rather than a field failure [70:25].
### Bid / Cost Implications
No pricing, scheduling, or estimating content appears. The only economic remark is general: structural steel has an excellent strength-to-weight and stiffness-to-weight ratio, so economical designs use less material and produce slender members, which is exactly why nearly every strength limit state must check some form of instability [05:09]. This is background context, not a bid input.
### Your Company Application
This is foundational theory behind the compression-strength values that bridge/aisc_validator.py already encodes, not a source of new numbers. For Ivan takeoff and estimating, the lecture confirms why column capacity falls with slenderness and end restraint and why minor-axis controls, but tonnage and member weights must continue to come from aisc_validator.py per Hard Rule 5, never from any hand math shown here. For Mario shop and welding, the practical takeaway is that welded built-up sections carry heavier residual-stress patterns than rolled shapes, and that mechanical straightening past yield tends to relax residual stress rather than add it. For our in-house PE stamp, the references to the SSRC guide, the AISC Commentary K-factor table, Appendix 1 column-curve provisions, and the direct analysis method with its tau factor are worth pulling when a stamped stability check needs backup. Doctrine flags: NONE. No supplier names, no PEMB language, no rate or AISC weight is asserted, and nothing here overrides the validator or BID_RATES.

## Five Useful Stability Concepts
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=k30_FSEhXIE | Duration: 1:17:42 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
Dr. Joseph Yura (UT Austin emeritus, 32 years on the AISC specification committee) walks through five stability concepts for steel members and frames. The first is that an imperfect member loses stiffness as axial load approaches the buckling load, so deflections grow toward infinity and give visible warning before collapse [03:08]. The amplification-factor relation takes an initial displacement delta-zero (from initial curvature or lateral-load moments) and grows it as axial load rises, with second-order P-Delta moments triggering yielding at roughly 85% of the Euler load [02:38][04:13]. The remaining four concepts are inelastic column behavior from residual stresses, the summation-of-P method for system buckling, the effect of end-connection details in built-up columns, and the stiffness and strength required for bracing [09:26][16:48][33:35][54:54][63:15].

### Spec References
The talk is academic and cites the AISC specification and manual by general reference rather than by clause. Named items: the AISC column curve and its two design equations (Euler/0.877 branch and the inelastic branch) [29:54]; the stiffness reduction factor tau, equal to the tangent modulus over elastic modulus, published as a table in the 13th edition manual with a slightly different formula in the newer manual [29:20][32:32]; the squash-load ratio threshold P/Py of 0.35 that separates elastic from inelastic [30:25]; the alignment chart for K factors [36:39]; the AISC column tables with K=2 for a cantilever column [47:34]; the two built-up-member equations for snug versus tightened intermediate fasteners [60:34]; the LRFD specification curves for double angles [61:39]; and the bracing rule that required brace stiffness is twice the ideal value with a brace strength of 1% of the compressive force at an initial out-of-straightness of 1 in 500 [65:56][66:27]. No single AISC 360 section number, AISC 341 seismic section, AWS D1.1 clause, RCSC clause, or Design Guide number is stated aloud.

### Technical Details
Residual stresses from differential cooling of rolled shapes are compression at the flange tips and tension near the web-flange junction; when applied P/A stress drives the tips into yield, those yielded zones have E=0 and contribute no stiffness, effectively shrinking the elastic I and reducing buckling capacity [18:55][20:28]. A built-up epoxied specimen of 70 ksi core plus 40 ksi outer pieces showed the added area gave 38-40% more capacity for a long (low-stress) member but identical capacity to the bare core for a short member once the outer steel yielded [22:30][24:05]. The summation-of-P concept states that for sway buckling of a story, the sum of the column loads must be at or below the sum of the column P-criticals (stiffness contributions), and the load distribution among columns is nearly irrelevant in the elastic range [35:37][41:53]. When one column is inelastic (tau reduced) a lightly loaded elastic neighbor can supply the missing stiffness; in the worked example column A at P/Py=0.75 had tau=0.414, and the elastic column B raised the system sum to 606 kips against a 509 kip total load [44:58][47:02]. For built-up columns, fully fixing only the ends (with slip allowed along the length) gives the same buckling load as a fully connected member because the equivalent K is about 0.5 [56:58].

### Fabrication Notes
The central shop-relevant point is that rolled sections arrive with locked-in residual stresses from differential cooling, present "like it or not," and these reduce inelastic buckling strength independent of any shop work [18:55]. The Quebec Bridge case captures a fabrication-versus-field dispute: the chief engineer insisted the lower chords were already bent when they left the shop, while the field rep insisted they only deflected after installation, a classic argument over whether distortion is a fabrication defect or a service-load effect [06:51]. The lesson is to document member straightness leaving the shop so an out-of-straight member is not wrongly blamed on fabrication or field. The bracing basis assumes an initial out-of-straightness of 1 in 500 [66:27].

### Erection Notes
The double-angle tests show that end-connection tightness governs built-up capacity in the field: end bolts tightened by turn-of-the-nut to develop slip resistance roughly doubled capacity versus snug-only ends, where snug or lubricated (low slip-coefficient) ends let the angles buckle as two independent members at about half the load [59:33][61:39]. Intermediate fasteners matter much less for strength; their main role is to cut the unbraced length of the individual angle, and tightening them versus snugging them had little effect in these tests [60:03][61:06]. For bracing during erection, a brace and its connection must reach at least twice the ideal stiffness and carry 1% of the braced compressive force, and the Q&A distinguishes a relative brace (cuts across the unbraced length, typical of truss X-systems, defines the unbraced length) from a nodal brace (controls one point, needs two locations to define a length) [65:56][76:59].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The headline failure is the 1907 Quebec Bridge collapse: chord 9 went from 3/4 inch out of line to 2-1/4 inches over a week while work continued and workers stayed on the bridge, and two anchor-arm chords buckled and the span totally collapsed just as engineers were still debating whether the bend was a shop defect or a field condition [07:22][08:26]. The recurring design error named is assuming a beam framing into a column top gives reliable rotational restraint and a K factor below 1; in a real frame the beam is not designed for the roughly 50% moment amplification needed to push the column past the Euler load, so the restraint does not exist and a plastic hinge forms in the beam instead [14:40][16:14]. A second error is treating an alignment-chart K-factor column "capacity" as a hard load limit on that column rather than as a stiffness contribution to the story [51:10].

### Bid / Cost Implications
This is a methodology webinar with no pricing, schedule, or estimating figures. The economic angle is indirect: correctly crediting an elastic neighbor column's stiffness through the summation-of-P method can show a frame is adequate with smaller members than a member-by-member K-factor check would allow, and column-strengthening by welding flange-tip plates can fail to deliver expected capacity if the existing core is already highly stressed and yields under added load [44:58][25:06].

### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, this is a reminder that AISC weights and member sizes from bridge/aisc_validator.py remain the system-of-record; the talk is engineering theory, not a source of shape data, and nothing here changes validated tonnage. For Mario's shop and field crews, the double-angle result is the practical takeaway: end connections on built-up compression members must be tightened (turn-of-the-nut, good slip resistance) or the member buckles at half its intended load, while intermediate fasteners are mainly for unbraced-length control [59:33]. For Paul's safety program, the Quebec narrative is a usable training story on heeding growing deflection as a collapse warning rather than waiting on a paperwork debate. For the in-house PE stamp and Tekla detailing, the K-factor cautions (do not claim K below 1 from a load-carrying beam; do credit a fixed foundation base) and the bracing rules (twice ideal stiffness, 1% strength, relative versus nodal) are direct design-review checkpoints. Doctrine flags: NONE. The content is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language and no supplier names.
