## Structural Fire Engineering
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hsJEqMUDFac | Duration: 1:29:06 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
Alan Jowsey teaches structural fire engineering as a performance-based alternative to picking a prescriptive hourly rating off a code lookup table [32:34]. The thesis is that fire is a load case in its own right with its own load combination, equal in standing to wind, snow, seismic, and vibration, and it should be designed for rather than left as an afterthought [43:19], [80:13]. The workflow is three steps: define the fire load, run heat transfer to learn how the steel heats up, then run a structural analysis at elevated temperature to check stability [07:21]. The central design lever is the limiting steel temperature, defined as the temperature the steel can reach while still carrying its applied load, which then sets how much passive fire protection is actually needed [60:01].

### Spec References
ASTM E119 and UL 263 are the named North American furnace test standards [31:33], [67:51]; the speaker also names BS 476 (UK), and BS 9999 as the UK rating lookup table [32:03], [66:18]. The International Building Code (IBC) and NFPA are cited as the prescriptive rating sources, with IBC construction types I through V and occupancy group B used in the worked example, and IBC's italic frame definition quoted as columns, girders, beams, trusses, and spandrels carrying gravity loads [31:03], [34:34]. AISC and CSA are cited as having an appendix titled "structural design for fire conditions," with the stated fire load combination 1.2D plus the load effect from an extraordinary event plus 0.5L or 0.2S [62:36], [63:07]. The SFPE Handbook is cited for the 538 C derivation as a 60 percent yield-strength reduction [63:38], [64:41]. Eurocode steel-fire parts and ISO, ABS, and API oil-and-gas standards are named generically [59:01]. No AISC 360 section, AISC 341 seismic section, AWS D1.1 clause, or RCSC clause is cited in this webinar.

### Technical Details
Limiting temperatures cited: ASTM E119 holds columns to 538 C (1000 F) and beams with a concrete slab to 593 C (1100 F) [40:44]. UK limits are 520 C for tubulars, 550 C for wide-flange columns, 620 C for slab-supported beams; mainland Europe caps at 500 C and offshore at 400 C [41:15]. The 538 C value sits between a yield intercept near 469 C and a buckling intercept near 550 C at the 60 percent stress level, and it assumes a member fully stressed to its design limit; a member governed by deflection or vibration at 20 to 30 percent utilization can justify 650 to 700 C and thinner protection [64:41], [66:16]. Protection options named are intumescent coatings, boarding, cementitious/SFRM, insulation blankets, bolt caps, concrete fill of tubulars, and concrete encasement of I-sections [29:27]. Cellular/web-opening beams ("smart beams") add failure modes: web-post bending, buckling, horizontal shear, bearing, and top-T bending around openings [61:02]. Tensile membrane action lets unprotected secondary beams in a bay be carried by the slab at high deflection [18:13], [74:00].

### Fabrication Notes
The webinar treats fire protection largely as a shop-or-field applied coating decision rather than a fit-up or weld-prep topic. Jowsey notes that reducing an intumescent system from a three-coat to a one-coat application improves constructability and gives greater control when applied off site in the shop versus in the field [73:28], [74:00]. The optimization graph trades steel weight against fire-protection cost: a heavier section has greater inherent fire resistance and needs less coating, so the lightest frame is not always the cheapest once coating material and application labor are added [56:58], [58:00]. He flags that connection bolts and plates lose strength and gain ductility as they heat, so fabricated connections checked only at ambient may be under-evaluated for fire [27:52].

### Erection Notes
Construction sequencing is named as a benefit driver: thinner or eliminated fire protection is quicker to apply and means less time on site [20:16], [43:51]. Thermal expansion during heating and contraction during cooling generate forces that can fail joints and redistribute load to adjacent members, which is an erected-frame behavior to be aware of [10:54], [23:49]. The fire hose test (a North American requirement) checks whether the assembly survives the sudden cooling and contraction forces from firefighting water after a fire [82:45]. No crane, rigging, or bracing sequencing is covered.

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The recurring error named is treating fire protection as an afterthought rather than designing it early, which is where problems arise [80:43]. A second is the unchecked assumption that a connection that works at ambient works in fire, with nobody verifying bolt strength loss, plate ductility, or heating and cooling forces [27:52]. A third is structural engineers disowning hot design as the architect's responsibility, leaving the limiting temperature on the tender drawings unverified by the engineer of record [38:41], [44:54]. There are no AISC 360, 341, or weld-inspection rejection criteria in this lecture; the "failures" here are design-process gaps, not shop or field NDE rejections.

### Bid / Cost Implications
The cost case is explicit and quantified. Dropping a coating from a 3-hour to a 2-hour rating cut intumescent thickness from 0.42 in to 0.26 in, a 39 percent reduction; 2-hour to 1.5-hour was 14 percent; 1.5-hour to 1-hour was nearly 60 percent, all product-specific [52:12], [52:42]. A combined structural-plus-fire-engineering case took a column coating from 3.4 mm to 1.15 mm, a 66 percent material saving, multiplied across every column and floor [73:28]. A fabricator-proposed lighter cellular beam saved 9 percent weight but raised cost about 8 percent once coating was included, showing weight savings can increase total cost [77:07]. High-rise office buildings with high required ratings and uniform floor plates give the biggest savings; low buildings needing only 15 to 60 minutes often do not [85:19].

### Your Company Application
This is a fire-engineering design webinar, not an AISC 360/341/AWS fabrication standard, so it does not feed Mario's welding WPS or Paul's site safety directly. It is most relevant to Ivan's takeoff and bid posture: when a set specifies SFRM or intumescent fireproofing, the coating thickness and number of coats are a real cost line, and a heavier-but-cheaper-to-coat member can change the all-in number, so weight selection has a fire-protection cost tail that Ivan should flag rather than always chasing the lightest frame. For the in-house PE stamp, the AISC appendix "structural design for fire conditions" and its 1.2D-plus-extraordinary-event load combination [62:36] are worth keeping on file, since a hot-design check is a quick hand calc that can justify a thinner coating spec. The bolt and weld strength-reduction-with-temperature point [81:44] is a reminder for Tekla connection design that fire-rated connections may need verification beyond ambient. Doctrine flag: this content names fireproofing coatings and design methods only, with no supplier names and no PEMB language, so NONE.

## Designing Members for Torsion
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=y71tWRmnCZg | Duration: 1:35:57 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
The webinar, presented by Dr. Daniel Linzell of the University of Nebraska Lincoln, teaches how to design steel members for torsion, with the focus on thin-walled open cross-sections (W-shapes, channels, angles, tees) that are torsionally weak [04:06][14:22]. The central message is that torsion in open shapes reduces to an elastic stress-analysis problem: you compute the angle of twist theta and its first, second, and third derivatives, convert those into St. Venant (pure) shear, warping shear, and warping normal stresses, then superimpose them with the direct axial, bending, and shear stresses and check against yield limits [34:58][37:33]. Key terms developed are shear flow, shear center (the point through which a load causes no twist), St. Venant torsion (planar, in-plane shear only) and warping torsion (out-of-plane flange movement that generates additional shear and normal stresses when restrained) [22:36][27:14][32:25].

### Spec References
AISC Steel Construction Manual Part 16 (the Specification), Chapter H combined-forces provisions, with HSS torsion handled in interaction Section H3.2 and open-shape torsion in Section H3.3 where the torsion term appears squared and torsion may be neglected if required torsion is under 20 percent of capacity for closed sections [35:29][36:31][37:02]. AISC Design Guide 9 (Torsional Analysis of Structural Steel Members), including its Section 2.3 statement that open shapes are torsionally poor, its Appendix A torsional properties (polar moment of inertia, warping constant, parameter a, warping statical moment, normalized warping function), and its Appendix B nomograph plots of theta and its derivatives by case [17:58][39:34][50:23][51:24][51:56]. The Q&A references Specification Section F2 (lateral-torsional buckling critical moment) [92:46]. Bridge-side references named: AASHTO LRFD Part 6 steel members, the NSBA/AASHTO Guidelines for Steel Bridge Analysis, and the AISC/NSBA Steel Bridge Design Handbook (warping figures in roughly Chapter 12) [20:33][56:01][57:34].

### Technical Details
The worked example is a W8x24, 50 ksi, 15 ft simply supported lintel over a bearing-wall opening, carrying CMU dead load plus an eccentric facade load applied 8 inches off the web centerline that produces a uniform applied torque tu [58:05][61:12][68:27]. Boundary conditions are taken as twist-pinned/warping-free (Appendix B Case 4): twist is prevented at the supports because the beam bears on block, but warping is left unrestrained as the conservative choice since end warping restraint could not be guaranteed [64:47][66:50][73:05]. Theta double prime at midspan is nonzero due to natural warping restraint from continuity, so warping normal stress exists where bending is maximum [74:39]. Computed results: strong-axis bending normal stress 8.5 ksi plus warping normal stress 9.5 ksi sum to 18 ksi against the 50 ksi yield limit; web direct shear 2.23 ksi plus pure-torsion web shear 4.67 ksi give about 6.9 ksi, while flange warping shear 0.45 ksi plus flange pure-torsion shear 7.62 ksi give about 8 ksi; the controlling 8 ksi is checked against 0.6Fy of 27 ksi, so the section passes [80:21][84:31][87:35]. The free Windows tool WinTorque (steeltools.org, version 1, DG9-era) computes theta and its derivatives and outputs two text files of twist values and element stresses [70:30][78:48].

### Fabrication Notes
This is a design and analysis webinar with no shop fabrication, fit-up, tolerance, or QC content. The only fabrication-adjacent point is the recommendation to proportion a member so that torsional (pure-twist) buckling is not a concern rather than relying on a buckling check, since crucshaped sections are the weakest and are not normally used [38:34][39:04].

### Erection Notes
No erection sequencing, bracing, crane, rigging, or field-coordination content appears. The closest field-relevant detail is that the lintel's torsional end fixity depends on whether the member bears tight against adjacent CMU with no gap, which controls whether warping is restrained; an open gap means warping is free [91:42][92:12].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
No inspection or rejection content. The recurring design pitfalls named are wrongly ignoring torsion when it cannot be explained away, mis-defining the warping boundary condition (twist-fixed versus twist-free changes the rotation curve and the warping stresses), losing track of stress signs when superimposing on non-I shapes since W-shapes conveniently always have a location where bending and warping stresses simply add, and a units slip in the example (kip-ft/ft label) that cancels out [18:28][64:47][41:38][76:11]. Several failure photos (a rigid frame collapse and the 2003 Marcy Bridge lateral-torsional/stability failure) are shown to argue torsion can be a real contributor, though not the sole cause [21:35].

### Bid / Cost Implications
No direct cost, schedule, or estimating content. The implicit takeaway for pricing is methodological: a member that looks adequate for vertical bending can be governed by warping, since in this torsionally weak W8x24 the warping normal stress (9.5 ksi) exceeded the bending stress (8.5 ksi) and roughly doubled the demand, so an eccentrically loaded lintel, spandrel, or facade-carrying beam may need a heavier section than a bending-only check suggests [80:52].

### Your Company Application
This maps directly to Ivan takeoff and the in-house PE stamp on any eccentrically loaded member: facade-carrying spandrels, CMU lintels, channel ledgers catching joist or bar-joist reactions off the shear center, and canopy framing where the load does not pass through the web all need a DG9 torsion check before the section is locked, because warping can double the stress demand and drive a heavier shape than aisc_validator.py weight selection alone would flag [19:31][42:11][80:52]. The free WinTorque tool plus DG9 Appendix A and B give the stamping engineer a defensible, low-cost path to compute theta derivatives and combined stresses, useful as a verification step on flagged eccentric members [70:30][51:24]. For Tekla detailing, the end condition matters: detailing a lintel tight against block with no gap can justify warping restraint and lower stresses, so the connection detail is a structural decision, not just a clearance choice [91:42]. Doctrine flags: NONE. The content is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language, no supplier names, and uses AISC weights and spec sections only, consistent with the verify-do-not-generate posture and the aisc_validator.py weight rule.

## Practical Implementation of Composite Floor Designs
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rIqBZvYeLow | Duration: 1:30:30 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
William Jacobs of Stanley G. Lindsay and Associates covers field problems in composite steel floor design that the codes do not address cleanly, organized in three parts: conduit and penetrations and openings through the slab and their effect on composite beam effective width [01:34], strengthening in-place composite beams including load history and welding under load [33:37], and ten best-practice tips [67:54]. The unifying technical claim is that because composite W-shapes are braced by the slab and are compact under Chapter I, they develop full plastic strength, so load history and mixed steel grades do not reduce flexural strength as long as plasticity is achievable [43:55]. This is a practical estimating and field-coordination talk, not a connection-design lecture.

### Spec References
AISC Chapter I composite provisions and the compactness limit web slenderness less than or equal to 3.76 times sqrt(E/Fy) [51:45]; the alternate plastic-web limit cited as "B4.1b case 16" and the column lower bound H/tw less than 1.49 [53:18]; cover-plate provisions in "F13.3" for shear flow, extension, and attachment [56:55]; stitch-weld spacing s-max of 24 times the thinner part joined and not more than 12 inches, with each weld at least 4 times the leg size and not less than 1.5 inches [60:33]; the de-facto 25 percent minimum composite from the manual charts and commentary, with the 2016 spec adding a stud-ductility requirement and 50 percent commentary recommendation [61:03]; the 2010 spec stud-projection limit of not more than 1.5 inches above the deck and a half-inch minimum cover over anchors [80:13]. Non-AISC references named: retired ASCE 3-91 composite-slab standard, SDI Floor Deck Design Manual first edition 2014, ACI 318 (cited as 318-11), OSHA 29 CFR 1926.754(e)(2), AISC Design Guide 3 (ponding 10 percent slab-weight increase) [79:12], AISC Design Guide 18 (galvanized welding) [81:46], the AISC web-openings Design Guide (number not stated), SCI Technical Note 350, ASCC Position Statement 23, SDI 2012 position statement on sloped-roof fastening, and AWS limiting puddle welding on roofs steeper than 15 degrees [83:17].

### Technical Details
Conduit baseline from the retired ASCE 3 and unchanged in SDI 2014: 1 foot 6 inch minimum spacing, max conduit diameter of 1 inch or cover-over-3, no crossing, three-quarter-inch minimum cover below conduit [04:41]. Denser conduit requires reinforcing the slab to ACI 318, which allows down to three diameters spacing [06:46]. For massed pipe per SCI TN350: keep conduit out of 8 inches each side of the beam centerline, run transverse pipe in the outer thirds, discount studs within roughly 1.75 stud heights (about 8 inches) and remove the displaced strip from the compression block [08:51]. Effective-width manipulation near openings uses Wiseman's 1996 method springing a 14-degree alpha angle past openings, with eccentric compression forces resisted by added slab tension reinforcing [22:48]. The sectional approach cuts at each stud and sums the smaller QN side to build a stepped capacity diagram for openings, stepped-back slabs, or uneven stud layouts [27:25]. The specification requires enough anchors between a concentrated load and the nearest zero-moment point to develop the moment at that load [33:06].

### Fabrication Notes
Stud burn-off is the key shop number: studs shorten about 3/16 inch welded to bare steel and up to 3/8 inch welded through deck, so the installed length, not the ordered length, should be on the drawings to stay under the 1.5-inch projection limit [80:13]. Galvanized beams should not have studs welded directly because of fumes and weld inclusions; Design Guide 18 says remove or mask the coating, and the practical galvanizers' method is a two-stud shot, the first burning off coating and bin-tested, the second placed in the same spot if the first fails [81:15]. Reinforcing options run from a welded bottom plate (down-hand weld, clampable, modest gain) to a WT (overhead weld, hard to hold) to a recommended W8 or W10 section that clamps and welds down-hand while still placing steel far from the neutral axis [37:11]. Welding under load reduces section properties: stick welding renders about 1 inch of section ineffective, so the reduced mono-symmetric section must carry the load present at the time of welding or the member must be shored [55:22].

### Erection Notes
Deck openings should not be field-cut until the slab reaches 75 percent of design strength, because the deck carries the wet concrete weight and was not designed with a hole [13:29]. OSHA 1926.754 requires floor and roof openings be decked over until immediately before use [13:29]. Skewed or mis-broken deck causes field crews to pile studs into pods or shoot them through high-flute holes, which is wrong; the fix is a deck closure piece with studs welded uniformly, and Jacobs repeatedly recommends just designing such beams non-composite [72:31]. Camber only 80 percent of the pre-composite dead load, since shear-tab supports have some rotational restraint and full camber over-lifts the beam and pushes studs out of the slab top [82:16]. Coring through an existing slab to add shear transfer is messy, needs water lubricant, creates a stud-weld fire hazard, and is best reserved for making non-composite beams composite [40:48].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The opening example is a massive conduit bundle with studs poking between it that destroyed composite action and damaged the slab, fixed only with filler beams, slab reinforcing, and a girder cover plate [03:06]. Another job had a slab cored 16 times in a row mid-span, effectively cantilevering the slab and forcing a post-installed steel frame [11:56]. Contractors welding all studs into one half of the span (13 placed where 10 were called, but useless) [73:31], notching the horizontal leg of an edge bent plate at shear connectors and then cutting the deck to fit [75:34], and violating the 1-inch minimum lateral clear distance to a stud by shoving deck over [75:03] are all named field failures. Studs ruptured and "unzipped" when composite percentage was too low, dropping capacity back to non-composite, which is why 50 percent minimum composite is recommended [61:38].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Strengthening is described as generally expensive, so the first move is to change the load path (relocate the load, add a post) before adding steel [35:09]. Concrete ponding from member deflection drives overruns; Design Guide 3 advises increasing slab weight 10 percent, mostly from beam and girder deflection rather than deck, and Jacobs adds a general note warning contractors to carry the overrun in base bids so there is no later add [78:41]. Air entrainment of 4 to 7 percent required by some UL ratings draws contractor pushback and can complicate finishing, a coordination cost to anticipate [68:25]. Specifying deck-fastener pins (mechanical anchors) in lieu of puddle welds is favored on large or high-sloped jobs for quality control and speed [83:17]. Edge conditions need wider flanges (a 5-inch minimum, so a W14x22 or W12x26 rule of thumb) to fit studs and bent plates, a member-selection cost driver [75:34].

### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, the burn-off rule (order studs longer to land at the specified installed length) and the 5-inch-minimum-flange edge rule (W14x22 or W12x26 at perimeters and openings) are direct estimating inputs that should flow through aisc_validator.py rather than being assumed, and the Design Guide 3 ten-percent concrete-overrun note belongs in our slab-on-deck quantity and our general notes so we are not exposed to a concrete add. For Mario's shop and welding crew, the under-load welding reduction (1 inch ineffective for stick welds), the galvanized two-stud method, and the bin-test discipline are AWS-adjacent field-welding checks for any strengthening or stud work; deck-stud puddle welds on roofs steeper than 15 degrees are limited by AWS, so Mario should plan mechanical fasteners there. Paul's safety scope picks up the OSHA 1926.754 opening cover-over rule and the stud-weld fire hazard when coring. For Tekla detailing, the 75-percent-strength field-cut sequence, stud installed lengths, edge bent-plate geometry, and uniform stud layout on skewed deck are model and field-issue items to flag. No anchor-rod, joist, in-house-PE-stamp, or ACP-specific content appears in this talk. Doctrine conflict: NONE. This is conventional structural-steel composite floor content with no PEMB language and no supplier or rate data to surface.

## 01 22 16 History of the AISC Specification
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=G112fvQ9kiY | Duration: 1:03:43 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is an informal history of the AISC Specification told by Dr. Theodore Galambos, who has sat on the AISC Committee on Specifications for more than 40 years [00:31]. The core lesson is why a single national steel specification exists at all: at AISC's 1921 founding the construction industry had numerous and different proprietary manuals, and the inaugural objective was to establish a single code authority recognized by building-code bodies and designers to eliminate that confusion [04:43]. The talk traces how the document grew from a 23-page pocket volume with a 9-page spec costing 25 cents [05:13] to roughly today's size, driven by new research, new steels, and new construction practices. The recurring theme for a fabricator is that every allowable, column curve, and connection rule in current AISC 360 carries decades of test-backed history, not arbitrary numbers.
### Spec References
The speaker names editions and methods by year rather than the clause numbering a modern detailer cites. Named items: the first AISC specification (1921, 23-page pocket volume, 9-page spec) [05:13]; the first AISC manual (about 1928, 476 pages, $2) [08:18]; the 1936, 1949, 1961, 1963, 1969, 1978, and 1989 ASD editions [12:24] onward; the 1986, 1993, and 1999 LRFD specifications [52:27]; the combined LRFD-plus-ASD unified specification that followed [52:59]; the 1989 ninth-edition ASD green book [53:29]; and the 2016 specification where the Q-factors are retired and effective length is moved into an appendix (he recalls it as "appendix 7") [39:21]. He also cites ASCE 7 load factors superseding the old one-third wind/seismic stress increase [31:56], and AASHTO composite-bridge standards from 1957 that fed AISC's 1963 composite rules [44:35]. No AISC 360 section number, AISC 341 seismic provision, AWS D1.1 clause, RCSC clause, or numbered Design Guide is cited verbatim; this is editions and methods, general principles, no section cited.
### Technical Details
Column strength history runs from the Rankine first-yield curve used roughly 50 years [10:21], to the 1936-1949 two-branch parabola-plus-Rankine curve splitting primary and secondary members at L/r [18:42], to the 1961-63 curve built on the tangent-modulus average of strong- and weak-axis buckling of a W8x31 with a variable factor of safety from 1.67 to 1.92 (5/3 to 23/12) [19:47], to the present curve covering both initial imperfections and residual stresses, derived from reanalyzed Lehigh tests and simplified by Ray Tide [21:55]. Lateral-torsional buckling moved from a Rankine-type allowable to the 1949 Ld/bt formula from Bethlehem Steel research, then to the Timoshenko elastic-buckling formulation split into St. Venant and warping-restraint terms, taking the maximum of two formulas [22:59]. Combined axial-plus-bending stress evolved from simple addition to the interaction ratio formula, then the 1961-63 Cm moment-gradient factor and the 1/(1 - fa/Fe') amplification with the effective-length term [27:43]. Slender-element Q-factors arrived in 1969 borrowed from the cold-formed specification [30:19]. Plastic design entered in 1963 with moment redistribution [32:26], and post-buckling (tension-field) plate-girder strength, block shear, and compactness limits all came from Lehigh research [37:46].
### Fabrication Notes
This is a history talk, so it gives no shop tolerances, fit-up rules, or QC procedures. The only fabrication-adjacent thread is the long shift from riveted to welded construction: welded plate girders replaced riveted ones after Lehigh testing [37:14], and the talk notes the political "noise abatement of riveting" complaints that helped push welding forward [41:25]. Welding and high-strength bolts entered the specification in 1949 along with friction connections [35:36]. General principles, no fabrication tolerance or section cited.
### Erection Notes
No erection sequencing, bracing, rigging, or crane procedure is covered; the webinar is about how the design specification evolved, not field work. Bracing appears only as a research and specification topic that AISC has studied for a long time [41:25], and ponding and vibration were handled by telling the designer to take care of them with the specification declining to give numbers [33:01]. General principles, no erection section cited.
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The talk frames "errors" historically rather than as modern inspection rejections. The original problem was inconsistent column formulas where the basic unit stress was not a consistent index of the so-called factor of safety, with allowable strength varying by about 10 ksi depending on which manual you used [09:20]. Block shear and certain compactness limits were written specifically as responses to observed failures [37:46]. A recalled full-scale steel-joist floor test at a John Deere plant in Davenport, Iowa failed when the first compression member buckled, and that embarrassment drove Steel Joist Institute specification changes [56:38]. Ponding failures prompted the ponding provisions [33:01].
### Bid / Cost Implications
Economy is a stated through-line: the speaker says the specification was always concerned about economy, and the growth in provisions reflects wider use across more industries, not an attempt to "make things fat" [54:31]. Incomplete (partial) composite action was adopted in 1969 specifically because it gave designers economy [34:31], and plastic design was promoted because it gives a better understanding of behavior under load and yields economy [47:42]. The takeaway for estimating is that method choice (ASD versus LRFD, full versus partial composite, plastic versus elastic) historically changed member sizes and therefore tonnage and cost.
### Your Company Application
This is background and culture, not a takeoff or detailing input, so it does not change any validated number; Ivan's member takeoff still runs through bridge/aisc_validator.py against the v16.0 database and Tide's present column curve and the modern composite rules described here are exactly what that validator encodes. For the in-house PE stamp it reinforces that current AISC 360 allowables, the effective-length and amplification terms, and partial-composite economy all rest on the test history Galambos recounts, so our engineer is verifying against settled provisions rather than novel theory. For joists, the Davenport John Deere joist-floor failure [56:38] is a useful reminder to Mario and the shop that joist compression members govern and SJI rules came from real collapses, and the riveted-to-welded and 1949 high-strength-bolt history [35:36] situates our welded and field-bolted connections in their lineage. There is no anchor-rod, Tekla, AWS D1.1, RCSC, AISC 341 seismic, or ACP-controls content to map. Doctrine flags: NONE. The talk is conventional structural steel and even notes that slender-section provisions were pushed by metal-building people [14:59]; that is cited as historical fact about the specification, not as PEMB positioning, so no brand conflict.

## Sustainability 2015 What's New with Steel and Sustainability
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tI88sRhdqBw | Duration: 1:15:59 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
John Cross (AISC VP of Marketing) and Erica Winters Downey (Great Plains Regional Engineer) walk through the 2015 state of green building as it touches structural steel: the shift away from single-attribute material credits toward Environmental Product Declarations (EPDs), whole-building Life Cycle Assessments (LCAs), and the competing rating systems. The central argument for a fabricator is that steel is a multi-attribute material (recycled, recyclable, reusable), and that LCA quantities for steel must come from a licensed structural engineer's bill of materials, not a parametric estimator [46:38][47:10]. This is a market and documentation webinar, not a connection-design or AWS/RCSC technical session.
### Spec References
No AISC 360, AISC 341, AWS D1.1, RCSC, or AISC Design Guide sections are cited; the talk is about sustainability standards. The documents named are LEED 2009 and LEED v4 (LEED BD+C), ASHRAE 189.1, the International Green Construction Code (IGCC), Green Globes (an ANSI consensus standard in development), and the Living Building Challenge. ASHRAE 189.1 material path is stated as a comparative LCA or meeting two of four criteria: 10% recycled content, 15% regional materials, 5% bio-based, or 10 products with industry EPDs [50:18]. A Product Category Rule (PCR) under international standards governs the forthcoming steel EPDs [33:10].
### Technical Details
Recycled content for steel is calculated as post-consumer plus half of pre-consumer, by mass, with the credit contribution weighted by cost; 25% is the default claim with no documentation, though domestic mills publish actual figures online [22:20]. Regional materials use a 500-mile radius with three competing distance methods (mill-as-scrap-origin, scrap-allocation percentage, and actual transport distance where truck counts a full mile, rail one-third, barge one-half, ship one-fifteenth) [24:22][25:23]. AISC is producing three industry-average cradle-to-gate EPDs (hot-rolled sections, hollow structural sections, plate), built from a fabricator data survey of 1,100 members with 300 returns covering 1.1 million tons, showing about 7% fabrication waste and roughly 10 pounds of welding electrodes per ton of steel, with electricity as the dominant impact [33:42][37:54]. An industry-average EPD counts as only half a product toward credit thresholds.
### Fabrication Notes
The fabrication-shop data tied to EPDs is directly relevant: fabrication waste averaged about 7% of tonnage, consumables (welding electrodes near 10 lb/ton) and electricity drive the shop environmental impact, supplies generally come from within 50 miles of the shop, and steel scrap is sold, never landfilled, because buyers pay for it [37:23][37:54]. The cost basis for the recycled-content credit is material plus fabrication (material as delivered to site), not the mill price alone, and that is where Cross says fabricators most often submit LEED paperwork wrong [22:52].
### Erection Notes
Erection is named only to exclude it: the LEED material-cost basis is material plus fabrication and does not include erection [23:22]. No field sequencing, bracing, crane, or rigging content appears in this webinar.
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The recurring documentation error is fabricators reporting only the mill cost of steel rather than mill plus fabrication when claiming the recycled-content credit [22:52]. A second class of error is trusting parametric LCA estimators: the Athena estimator, run against 100 Steel Solutions Center projects, scattered with no pattern, underestimating steel by as much as 40% and overestimating by as much as 80% [44:05]. Cross argues an LCA that omits impact categories such as land use and habitat disruption is itself just a single-attribute assessment in disguise [47:40].
### Bid / Cost Implications
Building green adds cost (LEED Silver near parity historically, Gold or Platinum roughly 5 to 10% more), and the market now justifies green on operating-cost payback (about 11% first-year and 28% five-year operating reductions, seven-year payback targets) rather than principle [06:50][09:57]. For estimating, the load-bearing point is that structural steel quantity is a function of the framing system, bracing, and loads, not square footage, so a valid takeoff requires a licensed structural professional and cannot be backed out of a simple area sketch [45:07][46:38]. Material cost is defined as 45% of overall project cost in the LEED math, so a steel package near 9 to 10% of project cost already sits close to the 20% recycled-content threshold [23:22].
### Your Company Application
This webinar validates the count-gap and verify-don't-generate doctrine head-on: AISC's own finding that the Athena estimator missed steel quantity by 40 to 80% is the same failure mode our pipeline guards against, so Ivan's takeoff through aisc_validator.py (measured member takeoff from schedules and framing marks, never SF times psf) is exactly the licensed-professional bill of materials Cross says an LCA needs. The CLAUDE.md rule that SF is a controlling input but steel tonnage comes from a member takeoff is reinforced verbatim by the SF-is-not-a-proxy argument [45:07]. Practical fabricator actions: capture mill recycled-content figures and report cost as material plus fabrication (Ivan), retain the three AISC industry-average EPDs and the per-ton tonnage figure to hand a GC for LEED or ASHRAE 189.1 documentation, and have Mario's shop track electrode usage (about 10 lb/ton) and scrap diversion since those feed any EPD or waste-minimization credit. For ACP controls, a recycled-content or EPD line can be added to the register if the GC pursues a green credit. No conflict with Your Company doctrine; no PEMB language and no supplier names appear. Doctrine flag: NONE.

## Development and Large Scale Testing of Long Span Floor Systems
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XTymILVzkTk | Duration: 59:44 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is a two-part AISC webinar on long span composite floor systems for multi-story residential steel framing. Devin Huber presents Purdue research (Dr. Varma, AISC Faculty Fellowship) on deep composite deck systems that span up to 30 ft and eliminate intermediate filler beams to cut floor-to-floor height [01:36][04:43]. The driver is vertical real estate: a conventional 1.5 to 3 in deck plus filler beams and girders runs 17 to 21 in total system depth, while the deep deck systems get structural depth down to 10 to 11 in [02:37][32:25]. Erica Winters Downey then surveys deep composite floor deck products available in the market and their span, fire, acoustic, and vibration ratings [33:27].

### Spec References
Cited generally, not by clause number: SDI, ACI, and AISC codes for code-based design [16:02]; an AISC Design Guide frequency equation for floor vibration evaluation, named only as "the design guide" with no number stated [22:43][23:13]; IBC acoustic targets of STC 50 and IIC 50 [39:38]; UL fire assembly numbers stated verbatim, D951 for the CSI deck, D903 for United Steel Deck and for Epic [38:33][41:11][42:11]; an ASTM E119 ("ASTM curve") fire time-temperature exposure for the heat transfer tests, spoken as "ASM curve" [28:20]. No AISC 360 section, AISC 341 section, AWS D1.1 clause, or RCSC reference was cited.

### Technical Details
Systems tested: a composite cellular deep deck, 7.5 in deep with a cellular bottom panel, 10 in overall depth on lightweight concrete, no shoring required, spanning 20 to 30 ft [09:52][10:23]. A non-cellular deep deck variant ("candidate 1A") uses a single line of shoring at midspan to push past 30 ft, since deflection scales with span to the fourth power [11:54][12:26]. A third "load balancing" system jacks the bare beam up about 1 in before the pour to counterbalance dead load, letting a W8x35 replace a W16x31 or W18 at a 30 ft span, 8 ft filler spacing [13:58][14:28][14:48]. Five specimens were tested at 30 ft spans, loaded at third points to approximate uniform moment [17:35][18:36]. Measured first natural frequency was 5.8 to 6 Hz across specimens [22:43]. A 27x86 girder dropped a 6.4 Hz floor to about 5.6 Hz, so the girder matters [24:13]. Self weights run 50 to 60 psf [32:25].

### Fabrication Notes
End attachment is either shear studs or a 5/8 in puddle weld; shear studs delay deck-to-concrete slip and preserve composite action [10:53][11:23]. AISC-spec 9 in shear studs are required for these deep profiles and are readily available [11:23]. The thicker cellular deck cannot be reliably stud-welded through: arc blow and blasted galvanizing drop weld quality, so holes were pre-cut with a plasma cutter and studs shot through to the beam with the deck held by bearing [11:23][49:31]. Rule of thumb stated: you can shoot through up to 16 gauge without a problem, anything thicker needs a pre-cut hole [50:02]. One marketed product uses a crimping tool that forms a shear key at the side lap to lock slip without studs [50:02].

### Erection Notes
The presenters stress erection is not a big departure from conventional practice: end conditions use simple closures, seated connections at columns, and standard closure panels [30:55][31:25]. Eliminating infill beams reduces the number of crane picks an erector bids, since erectors bid by picks [33:58]. Shoring, where used, is one line at midspan or at quarter points, not closely spaced lines like cast-in-place, and was left in roughly 7 days before stripping [05:14][19:08]. Panels are light enough for two men (each about 24 in wide), and there is interest in assembling several panels on the ground and craning them up as a unit to save crane time [44:49][47:27].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The named failure modes are structural test behaviors, not field inspection rejections. Specimens without shear studs showed a brittle shear-bond failure: once the deck started to slip it could not be arrested, the concrete cracked under the load point and slid back toward the support, and composite action was lost completely [26:19][27:19][27:50]. Stud-welding through thick deck risks arc blow and a poor weld through the galvanizing [49:31]. Bare unprotected deck warped severely in the heat transfer test (bottom plate reached about 650 C), while a protected specimen stayed near 200 C [28:20][57:09].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Cost was the hardest figure to pin down and was debated openly. The Corus slim deck material was quoted around $5 per square foot delivered [44:17][52:35]. An audience member estimated the finished CSI system at $10 to $12 per square foot all in (deck plus concrete) versus precast plank installed near $8 per square foot, so the system is not automatically cheaper on a slab-only basis [52:35]. The real offset comes from removing filler beams, their connections, and their fireproofing, plus saving 6 to 8 in per floor that compounds to roughly 10 ft of cladding and piping over a 20 story building [33:58][34:30][48:29]. Thinning the deck to 18 gauge where shoring or span allows saves real steel cost versus 14 gauge or cellular [48:29]. Lead times run 4 to 6 weeks on long span deck, so it is an early design decision and can beat precast plank where plank availability is poor [40:10][54:36].

### Your Company Application
This is residential deep-deck floor technology outside Your Company's typical conventional structural steel and is informational, not a doctrine change. For Ivan's takeoff and estimating, the durable lessons are that deck gauge and shoring choice swing cost materially (18 vs 14 gauge), that erector pricing is per-pick so removing infill beams is a real line-item saving, and that eliminating filler beams also drops fireproofing scope. For Mario and AWS D1.1 welding, the arc-blow caution on shooting studs through thick galvanized deck is directly transferable to our field stud and puddle-weld work; pre-cut holes are the fix above 16 gauge. For our in-house PE stamp, note the floor-vibration check should account for girder flexibility, not just the deck, and the AISC design-guide frequency method is not calibrated for deep decks (about 3.5 percent damping was needed to stay conservative). The $/SF comparisons here are residential precast-versus-deck and do not touch BID_RATES; treat them as context only. No conflict with Your Company doctrine.

## Around the Bend - What You Need to Know about Steel Bending
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UjaHYlX3b-M | Duration: 48:48 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is an AISC Bender-Roller Committee webinar (TD Alwood, AISC regional engineer; Barry Feldman, president of Cotler Metal Products) on cold and hot bending of structural shapes [00:01][03:09]. The committee is 13 member firms (11 US, 2 Canada) formed to fill an information gap because curved steel had been treated as a "black box" with no published tolerance or specification guidance [00:34][03:40]. The central message is that bending is a craft and proprietary process that varies by shop, so the controlling deliverable is complete, unambiguous shape, radius, orientation, and end-use information given to the bender before material is purchased [01:37][08:50][09:20].
### Spec References
Almost no formal code sections are cited. The speakers name architecturally exposed structural steel (AES, called "AESS" generically) as the highest-quality finish baseline [04:11][10:54], and reference ASTM A500 by name as the HSS tube standard whose dimensional tolerances are "exhaustive" and can leave tube shape and radius off [32:42]. They point to AISC resources: the Bender-Roller web page (cited as aisc.org/benders), the Steel Solution Center / "think tank," the curved-steel brochure, the nomenclature chart, and a cold-bending paper. No AISC 360 chapter, AISC 341 section, AWS D1.1 clause, RCSC provision, or Design Guide number was stated, and no bending tolerance standard exists per the speaker [36:15].
### Technical Details
Six bending methods are described: rotary draw (compression) bending for very tight radii and high repetition, limited by machine and tooling size [05:43][06:13]; rolling (pyramid/three-roll) bending, the most common in structural work, done in XY coordinates up to 360 degrees [06:43]; point or gag (ram) bending applying point loads at measured increments [07:16]; synchronized incremental cold bending with internal support for tight-radius HSS [07:47]; hot bending around pins and acorn plates at full chrome points [07:47]; and induction bending with an electric coil heating a short length for large-diameter pipe and heavy wall, common in oilfield work [08:19]. Required inputs are shape, size, radius, chord or depth dimension, angle, and orientation (easy way vs hard way, leg/flange in vs out, odd-leg angle leg position) [09:20][09:52][10:23]. Examples shown include W27x146 rolled easy way, W18x40 hard way with no web or flange distortion, W24 Hummer-dealership beams bent hard way, and spiral stairs needing arc degree, rise, run, and overall rise [06:43][14:58][16:29].
### Fabrication Notes
Hold and tail stock is required between the rolls, so the bender needs extra material beyond the finished arc length: roughly 6 ft (3 ft per end) for W8-W10 easy way and W6-W24 easy way, about 11 ft (5.5 per end) for W6-W24 hard way, and 10 ft easy / 14 ft hard for W27-W40 [13:27][13:57][14:27]. Trimming and whether straight ends are needed must be stated, and a customer who supplies exactly the arc length leaves the piece short, forcing welds or splices [12:57][13:27]. QC is a visual inspection with XY coordinates marked on the floor and the piece checked against a square every 12 inches before shipment; tank work can hold an eighth-inch on chord over a 40 ft piece, sometimes by tack-welding an angle across the chord to hold dimensions while the piece relaxes [27:29][37:48]. A500 tube variation argues for ordering all pieces in an assembly from the same mill and heat number for consistent initial shape [32:42]. Galvanizing or painting after bending must be disclosed because some benders heat-correct parts, which affects coating [33:13].
### Erection Notes
The session is shop-focused, but transport is treated as an erection-handoff risk. Curved pieces must ship flat, never with the legs in the air, because road bounce opens the curve, and over-tight strapping twists hard-way beams or opens the bend, so blocking and tie-down must respect the built-up stress in the member [34:45][35:15]. Even crane handling of a heavy section (example: 7-inch tee at 55 lb/ft) can change a tight-tolerance bend, which is why tack bars are added to hold geometry through handling [37:48]. Field fit-up to a defined point A to point B should be flagged to the bender so they engineer a support to keep the chord-and-depth geometry in place on delivery [38:19].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Named failures include web and flange distortion, oil canning, and interior ripples on tube (acceptable if wall-encased, rejectable on AES) [11:25][11:55][27:00]. A spiral stair was bent to a 38 ft radius when the design meant 38 ft diameter, delaying a restaurant opening (nomenclature error) [16:59]. An audience member reported large G-shaped pieces that should have matched arriving with 6 to 8 inch field fluctuation with no change-order relief [28:00]. The presenter cited his own shop failing a 20x12x0.5 wall tube at a $3,800 replacement cost, and noted bends too tight to roll were instead fabricated from bent plate and welded up [29:04][45:31]. Standard tolerances do not exist, and AES not stated up front cannot be recovered after the fact [36:15][33:44].
### Bid / Cost Implications
Bending is an added process cost on top of base steel, and the increment scales with method, radius tightness, wall thickness, and shape complexity [18:34][26:28]. Tighter and multi-radius or parabolic curves cost more than a single constant radius [43:00]. AES specified after quote raises cost because it may require a different machine, a heavier wall, or different internal support [33:44]. Estimators must include hold-and-tail material in the buy, since being a couple feet short on 100 beams is a costly rework [30:06]. The recurring guidance is to consult the bender and price the curve before the buyer sees it, so steel is not priced out of a job by a surprise [43:00][08:50].
### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, treat any curved or rolled member as a separate line with a bending-process adder and explicit hold-and-tail material (about 3 ft per end easy way, 5.5 per end hard way for wide flange per [13:57][14:27]); aisc_validator.py gives the base shape weight, but it does not price bending, so a curved-steel job is a LOW-confidence ROM until a bender confirms feasibility and cost. Tekla detailing should output a 3D model plus clear radius, arc, chord, and easy/hard-way orientation in standard nomenclature, since the speaker prefers a 3D model when dimensions are unambiguous [47:03]. Mario's shop should hold the AES-versus-encased distinction on the traveler so distortion and ripple acceptance are explicit, and Paul's transport and rigging plan must enforce flat shipping, careful blocking, and controlled strapping to protect the bend [34:45]. If ACP has any curved canopy or feature steel, flag it early to the in-house PE and a bender, and consider the bent-plate-and-weld fallback when a radius is too tight to roll [45:31]. Doctrine conflict: NONE. This is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language, and naming a "proprietary bender" on a drawing per [44:31] is a vendor-routing practice, not a supplier callout on a client proposal, so it does not breach the no-supplier-names rule.

## Design with Damping
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PHg89myYVzw | Duration: 1:06:12 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
Robert J. McNamara of McNamara Salvia argues that structural damping is poorly understood and should be replaced in practice by deliberately designed dissipative systems [02:06]. He frames damping as the C velocity term in the dynamic equilibrium equation, a mathematical convenience that does not exist in nature, and notes the seismic world's universal 5 percent damping assumption has no real correlation or origin [05:40][06:11]. His central thesis is that added energy-dissipation devices should be treated as corrective forces with a defined load path back to the structural frame, not as a hidden percent-of-critical number you guess at [17:58][18:30].
### Spec References
General principles, no section cited. This is a conceptual NASCC expert-essay lecture on dynamics and damping; no AISC 360, AISC 341, AWS D1.1, RCSC, or Design Guide section numbers are stated by the speaker. He references his own engineering journal and ASCE-published papers generically and names product types and one wind-load condition (146 mph, ASCE exposure C or D, stated informally) but cites no code section [32:19][23:35].
### Technical Details
He categorizes dissipative systems by mechanism: friction dampers and viscoelastic dampers (displacement dependent), yielding dampers (yield real material, displacement dependent), viscous dampers/shock absorbers (velocity dependent, peak force when displacement is zero), and inertia/tuned mass dampers including sloshing dampers [11:49][12:51][14:22]. Inherent steel damping is cited as roughly 0.5 to 2 percent of critical, dropping near 1 percent on very tall towers, and he warns that a rigid-diaphragm assumption or a soft load path negates the damper entirely [10:17][24:37][19:31]. Project examples include a viscous-damper toggle-brace system (lambda-shaped) that amplifies small inter-story drift roughly three times so the shock absorber sees larger velocity, with force scaling as the square of the amplification [40:30][42:02][55:26].
### Fabrication Notes
No structural-steel fabrication, fit-up, or shop QC content is presented. The only shop-adjacent detail is an improvised tuned mass damper at Mass General Hospital built from a scrap piece of metal deck used as the spring, plumber's lead for the mass, and duct tape, with a vendor-supplied viscoelastic element for secondary damping [29:15][30:17]. Members named in examples are W36 cantilevers with W24 infill beams and W36x300 floor members, but these are design sizes, not fabrication instructions [33:52][35:25].
### Erection Notes
No erection sequencing, bracing, crane, or rigging content. The closest field point is placement of dampers: because a damper carries no gravity and no overturning to the base, it can be located arbitrarily in plan and elevation, for example every other floor in the Boston tower, as long as the corrective-force load path reaches the lateral system [40:30][41:00][21:03].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The recurring failure he names is a soft or neglected load path: a well-designed damper produced essentially no response reduction under simulated seismic time history because of stiffness loss in the connecting parts, and rigid-diaphragm analysis overestimates damper effectiveness [20:01][19:31]. He also flags that serviceability dampers in stair towers are not fireproofed and require no inspection, but seismic damage-control dampers that cut design base shear (for example 5,000 kips to 2,500) demand inspection and raise unresolved fireproofing questions [63:52][64:22].
### Bid / Cost Implications
He is blunt that this work is not covered by standard structural fees: the special-systems fee can equal the entire structural fee on a tall building, and seismic time-history analysis with site filtering on deep soil (200 ft of Boston blue clay) consumes large effort [54:24][55:56]. A concrete cost data point is the Boise airport terminal, where roughly 12 installed Taylor Devices dampers provided seismic damage control for about 100,000 dollars and cut expected displacement near 50 percent [52:51][47:12]. He also shows that the assumed damping value drives wind-tunnel force reductions of 30 to 40 percent, a direct cost lever on base shear [23:35][25:08].
### Your Company Application
This webinar sits well outside Your Company's conventional structural-steel scope. The firm fabricates and erects framing, joists, deck, and connections; it does not engineer viscous dampers, tuned mass dampers, or seismic dissipative systems, and our in-house PE stamp covers connection and erection engineering, not high-rise dynamic damping design. The one transferable idea for Ivan's takeoff and the in-house PE work is the load-path discipline: any specialty device shown on a drawing set (damper, isolator, slide bearing) is a corrective-force element with a defined connection back to the frame, so it must be flagged as an engineered-by-others item with its own connection demands rather than priced as ordinary brace steel. For Tekla detailing, a toggle or damper bracket carries amplified squared forces and out-of-plane demands and should be treated as a delegated-design connection, not a stock detail. Doctrine conflict: NONE.

## Structural Integrity of Buildings
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_JPqOSwT8oA | Duration: 1:28:13 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
This webinar (session E4, Ronald Hamburger of SGH and Kurt Gustavson of AISC) covers the new structural integrity provisions added as Section 1614 to the 2009 IBC, applicable to high-rise buildings in occupancy categories III and IV [25:42, 37:32]. Hamburger gives the history (Ronan Point gas-explosion progressive collapse in 1960s London, Oklahoma City 1995, WTC 9/11, the NIST recommendations) and explains the provisions were deliberately written by the NCSEA ad hoc committee to satisfy the political push without changing how engineers actually design or what construction costs [19:37, 20:07]. The technical heart is a set of minimum tie/connection tension requirements: column splices must carry tributary dead plus live load in tension, and beam/girder shear connections must have a minimum nominal axial tensile strength tied to the vertical reaction [30:49, 31:49]. These are minimum interconnection rules, explicitly not progressive-collapse member-removal analysis [66:07].

### Spec References
Cited verbatim by the speakers: IBC Section 1614 (with subsections 1614.1 applicability, 1614.2 definitions, 1614.3 frame structures, 1614.4 bearing-wall structures) [25:42, 27:48]; ASCE 7 Section 1.4 disproportionate-collapse language and ASCE 7 Seismic Design Category A tie/continuity provisions [09:20, 09:51]; ACI 318 structural integrity reinforcement (two bottom bars or PT cables through the column core, Class A splices) [08:17, 28:48]; AISC Specification Chapter B and Chapter J limit states [42:12, 45:22]; the 2010 AISC Specification ballot (third ballot, adding "normal usage" language) [44:49, 91:00]; SCI Publication 212 and the SCI/BCSA manual "Joints in Simple Construction" [50:33, 54:41]. The 75-ft high-rise threshold ties to the IBC fire-department-access definition [76:28].

### Technical Details
For steel frame structures the two requirements are: each column splice has minimum design strength in tension to transfer the tributary dead plus live load between splices (example: 50-kip loads at each floor, splices every second floor, so 100 kips tributary tension) [31:19]; and all beam and girder connections have a minimum nominal axial tensile strength equal to the required vertical shear for ASD, or 2/3 of the required shear for LRFD, but not less than 10 kips [31:49, 39:34]. A composite-slab exception with specified shear studs reduces these to half (ASD) or 1/3 (LRFD) [32:20, 40:35]. The check is at nominal strength (no phi or omega factor), evaluates rupture and bolt-shear limit states rather than yielding or bearing-deformation serviceability states, and the axial force is not concurrent with the vertical reaction [35:58, 42:44, 73:20]. Connection performance was drawn from UK testing: single-plate shear works well, all-bolted double angles yield then rupture near the heel, end-plate connections work, while single-angle connections and angles welded to the support are untested or problematic [49:31, 53:08, 59:16].

### Fabrication Notes
The speakers note the shop trend away from welding toward bolted/punched connections: beam shops favor single-angle and single-plate shear connections because their beam lines punch everything and they prefer to do very little welding [57:45, 61:22]. Connections with the angle welded to the outstanding leg put the weld in torsion and will peel off, so they are flagged to avoid for axial tension [59:16, 86:54]. The provisions create an inducement to detail composite slabs (with adequate shear studs and welded wire fabric or reinforcing) because that halves the required tie force [32:52, 40:35]. No preheat, electrode, or WPS specifics are given; this is a design-provision webinar, not a welding-procedure session.

### Erection Notes
The webinar does not cover field erection sequencing, bracing, crane, or rigging. The only erection-adjacent point is that the 75-ft applicability threshold derives from fire-truck access height, not from erection method [76:28]. General principles only, no erection sequencing cited.

### Bolting Requirements and Welding Requirements
Bolting: the check looks at bolt shear and bolt bearing/tear-out at nominal strength; bolt tension was shown by Gustavson's calculations to never control the double-angle case when 80% of nominal bolt tensile strength is used per SCI Publication 212, which lets the prying force be neglected [54:41, 55:11]. A proposed 2010 spec change permits bearing bolts in connections with short-slotted holes parallel to the force direction for the integrity check only, with the bolt assumed at the end of the slot, waiving the normal slip-critical requirement [46:56]. Welding: CJP/PJP, electrode, and NDE specifics are not addressed; the relevant welding caution is that welds across the outstanding angle leg act in torsion with no reliable capacity and should be avoided [59:16, 86:54].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The named failure modes are tensile fracture of double-angle legs near the heel under axial tie force [53:08]; weld peel-off when a tee stem or angle is welded to the support and the weld is loaded in torsion, which progressively rips off [86:54]; seated connections that carry large vertical reactions but have limited horizontal tie capacity [62:26]; and inadequate edge distance along the beam axis on single-plate connections, which Hamburger calls out as "something stupid like put no edge distance" [83:50, 75:28]. Single-angle and welded-to-column connections are untested and flagged to avoid until research is published [62:26, 78:39].

### Bid / Cost Implications
The explicit design intent was provisions with little effect on the cost of construction and little change to how connections are designed [20:07]. Gustavson's 39-page conference paper and limit-state studies conclude the horizontal tie requirement almost never controls connection design, so most single-plate, double-angle, and end-plate connections meet the requirement without modification [64:01, 66:37, 85:22]. The practical cost driver is detailing discipline rather than added steel: the engineer states the vertical reaction on the plans and the fabricator's detailer designs for 2/3 or 1/3 of it, same as current practice [80:45]. Seated connections and welded-to-support angles may need detail changes or reinforcement, which carries some cost [64:01].

### Your Company Application
For Ivan, this confirms member takeoff and connection design rarely change tonnage from these provisions, so they should not inflate an estimate; the cost exposure is detailing and a few problem connection types on tall occupancy-III/IV jobs, not extra steel. For Tekla detailing and the in-house PE stamp, the takeaway is to state the beam vertical reaction on the plans and let the detailer carry 2/3 (LRFD) or full (ASD) of it in tension per IBC 1614, preferring single-plate or all-bolted double-angle shear connections and avoiding seated connections and angles welded to the support leg where axial tie capacity is needed. For Mario, the welding lesson is concrete: do not weld across an outstanding angle leg or a tee stem where it sees the tie force, because that weld works in torsion and peels off. This aligns with conventional structural-steel positioning and Hard Rule 5 (AISC weights from aisc_validator.py, never LLM math); the integrity check uses nominal strength and Chapter J rupture limit states, which our connection design should reference, not generate. Conflict with Your Company doctrine: NONE.

## Unified Design of Steel I-Section Flexural Members in the 2005 AISC and 2007 AASHTO Specifications
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4q7xXjnxBo8 | Duration: 1:23:20 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is Don White's TR Higgins award lecture on the unified flexural strength provisions that were harmonized between the 2005 AISC Specification and the 2005/2007 AASHTO LRFD Bridge provisions [00:00][01:04]. The core idea is one consistent framework for the flexural strength of I-section members covering doubly and singly symmetric sections, compact, non-compact, and slender webs, hybrid webs and flanges, and non-prismatic geometry, built so the complicated cases stay tractable without making the simple cases harder [03:09][03:43]. The whole picture reduces to a single strength curve plotted against a slenderness term (lateral-torsional or flange-local), anchored by a plateau strength (Fmax / Mmax), an inelastic anchor point, and an elastic buckling branch [06:20][07:21]. This is research and code-development theory, not a fabrication or erection how-to.
### Spec References
The talk cites specification editions and provisions rather than fabrication clause numbers: AISC 2005 Specification and AISC 1999 (AISC 99) Provisions [18:43][19:16]; AISC ASD 89 (1989) for comparison curves [34:19][34:49]; AISC 2009 LRFD [33:46]; AASHTO 2004/2005/2007 LRFD bridge provisions [33:14][48:19]; AASHTO LRFD 1998 [72:05]; the SSRC Guide elastic-LTB equations [20:50][30:39]; and AISC Design Guide 25, design of frames using web-tapered members [44:42][47:18]. Parameters named aloud include RPC and RPT effective shape factors, RTS in the AISC manual, Cb moment-gradient modifier, and the slenderness limits Lambda-pw and Lambda-rw (HC/Tw of 137 as the non-compact web limit for Grade 50) [12:00][13:33][28:25]. No connection, bolting, or welding clause numbers (J-series, RCSC, AWS) are cited because the lecture is about member flexural strength.
### Technical Details
Strength is built from three segments: a plateau to anchor point 1 (the compact limit), an inelastic transition where flange stress reaches roughly 0.7 Fy (FL = 7/10 Fy) due to residual plus flexural stress, and the elastic LTB or flange-local-buckling branch [07:52][08:56]. The plateau Mmax is a function of web slenderness HC/Tw through the effective shape factors RPC and RPT, which equal one at the non-compact web limit and rise toward Mp/My at the compact limit [12:31][13:03]. For singly symmetric sections the speaker shows extreme cases where Mp can fall below My of the compression flange, so tension-flange yielding must be checked as a separate limit state [14:04][16:09]. Elastic LTB uses the rt (RTS) radius of gyration based on the compression flange plus one-third of the web depth in compression, with KY and KZ end-restraint factors set to one in the spec but allowed by the commentary, and Cb for moment gradient [22:53][23:24][27:00]. Shear post-buckling uses Basler tension-field action with a Vincent shear-buckling coefficient; moment-shear interaction was removed from AISC 2005 except where flanges are small (web-to-flange area ratio above 2.5 or web depth to flange width above 6), in which case post-buckling shear strength is disallowed [50:21][52:24][53:27]. Curved-girder and lateral-bending effects are handled by the AASHTO one-third rule, treating the flange as an equivalent beam-column [65:23][69:29].
### Fabrication Notes
The lecture does not address shop fabrication, fit-up, or QC. The only fabrication-adjacent points are member type distinctions that matter to a fabricator's catalog choices: the provisions make no strength distinction between rolled and welded shapes even though welded three-plate girder test data sit slightly lower [40:32][41:06], and hybrid built-up girders (different web and flange yield strengths) and web-tapered built-up members are explicitly covered [04:13][44:42]. A simple welder-warping detail is mentioned: boxing in the end of a beam creates warping restraint (KZ less than one) to raise LTB strength [21:52].
### Erection Notes
No erection sequencing, crane, or rigging content. The one field-relevant warning is on bracing: the bracing provisions are written to develop the K=1 LTB strength, so if a designer squeezes capacity by using K less than one for lateral-torsional buckling, the bracing requirements are not covered by code and lab tests have shown braces failing before the member [31:39][32:12]. There is also discussion of construction-stage loading on bridge girders (wind, eccentric overhang bracket loads, skew, horizontal curvature) that drives flange lateral bending before the deck is composite [05:15][68:28].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
No weld or bolt inspection failures are discussed. The errors named are design and code-application errors: applying the doubly symmetric RTS equation to a singly symmetric section, which does not work [23:56]; the AISC 99 anomaly where an extreme section checked as both compact and slender web simultaneously, resolved conservatively in 2005 by classifying it slender [18:43][19:16]; discretizing long members into many elements in software that lacks warping torsional stiffness, producing a fictitious flexural-torsional buckling that the analysis is not actually modeling [29:37][30:09]; and the false magnification of moment-shear interaction that results from evaluating moment at a shifted location for high shear but at the peak for low shear [62:46][63:17].
### Bid / Cost Implications
No direct cost, schedule, or estimating content. The indirect implication for an estimator is capacity, not price: the unified 2005 provisions recover real strength over ASD 89 (the speaker shows up to 72 percent greater capacity at extreme moment-gradient points and additional flange-local-buckling strength for compact flanges) [38:26][35:20], which can mean a lighter member satisfies the same demand. That is a member-weight and tonnage lever, but it is the engineer of record's call, not a takeoff input.
### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff this video changes nothing in aisc_validator.py: the AISC weight per shape is fixed catalog data and this lecture is about flexural strength capacity, which is the PE's design check, not a takeoff number. The clearest in-house PE stamp note is the bracing caution at [31:39]: do not let a stamped design lean on K less than one for LTB without separately justifying the bracing, because code bracing only develops the K=1 strength. The boxed-end warping-restraint detail at [21:52] is a real Mario shop fabrication option for a beam that needs more LTB capacity. Hybrid and web-tapered built-up girders and the rolled-versus-welded strength equivalence [41:06] are relevant if a job specifies plate girders rather than rolled W shapes, which affects Mario's welding scope and AWS D1.1 weld volume even though the design strength is the same. There is no joist, anchor-rod, field-bolting, or ACP-controls content here, and no AWS, RCSC, or AISC 341 seismic citation to map. No conflict with Your Company doctrine: NONE. The verify-don't-generate posture is reinforced, since every strength claim here traces to a cited test database and spec edition rather than generated math.

## Design of Frames Using Web-Tapered Members
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nRJoDUtlCz4 | Duration: 1:02:05 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This webinar (session E9) walks through AISC Design Guide 25, "Frame Design Using Web-Tapered Members," presented by Dick Kaylor of Computerized Structural Design and Don White and Yuck Kim of Georgia Tech [01:41][16:43]. The guide fills a gap left when the 2005 AISC specification dropped the older George Lee web-tapered provisions from the 8th and 9th editions [02:43][06:49]. The unifying method is stated in one sentence: map the elastic buckling strength of a web-tapered member to the elastic or inelastic buckling strength of an equivalent prismatic member [17:13]. The mapping turns on a parameter gamma-e, the multiplier on the applied loads that brings the member to its elastic buckling state, evaluated where flange stress f-r over Fy is highest [08:21][19:16].

### Spec References
Cited references are AISC Design Guide 25 (the subject document) [02:12]; the AISC 2005 specification column strength equations, with the inelastic-elastic transition at KL/r limit 4.71 times sqrt(E/Fy), equivalently F_e/Fy at the 0.44 limit [17:44][18:46]; AISC 2005 Chapter A (design basis terms), Chapter C (stability, second-order analysis), Chapter D (axial tension), and beam-column interaction equation H1-1 [07:19][08:21][40:58]. Speakers also cite the AISC Commentary story-buckling concept and the B2 amplification approach [25:27], and an AASHTO 2007 Cb equation written in terms of stress rather than moments [11:24][37:44]. The frame is identified as ASCE 7 Seismic Design Category B and C, R equal to 3 [57:11]. The successive-approximations (Marks) method from 1920s-1930s Timoshenko is referenced for in-plane buckling of non-prismatic members [13:29][51:57].

### Technical Details
The scope is limited to a maximum taper angle of about 15 degrees; beyond that the user is extrapolating [05:46][50:23]. The method avoids K factors entirely by computing the elastic buckling stress F_e directly and plugging it into the 2005 column equations [12:25]. For out-of-plane checks each unbraced length is treated as a simply supported segment with K equal 1, using I_y at the segment midspan [33:10][69:00 region near 33:40]. Torsional buckling need not be checked for a doubly symmetric section when K_z*L is less than or equal to K_y*L [34:11]. Constrained-axis torsional buckling (the speakers joke "cat buckling") is the controlling case when the top flange is braced at close spacing (purlins or joists at 5 ft) while the bottom flange has kickers at much wider spacing such as 20 ft; the real unbraced behavior falls between the two and is computed at the segment midspan cross-section [13:59][35:42]. The example is a modular metal-building gabled frame with 55 ksi steel, interior leaning columns pinned at the base, exterior double-symmetric tapered columns at a 4.37 degree taper, and slender or non-compact webs and flanges checked cross-section by cross-section [20:50][21:22].

### Fabrication Notes
The document is oriented toward metal-building-manufacturer practice, where members are heavily computerized built-up plate girders rather than rolled shapes, so fabrication is implied to be shop welding of tapered plate sections [04:15][05:16]. An audience question raised that most of these sections are welded on one side of the web; the speakers noted one-sided welded prismatic tests at UT Austin and in the Lee research, with residual-stress patterns that can add some benefit but also introduce welding distortion [58:42][59:15]. Research imperfection magnitudes used were on the order of 1/1000 for local distortions [60:49][61:23]. No AWS D1.1 clause, electrode, preheat, or NDE requirement is cited; the welding discussion is research context, not a fabrication spec.

### Erection Notes
No erection sequence, crane, rigging, or field-bracing procedure is taught in this webinar. The only field-relevant content is the bracing assumption baked into the analysis: top-flange bracing from purlins or joists at roughly 5 ft on center and bottom-flange kickers at wider spacing, which the constrained-axis torsional buckling check models [13:59][35:42]. Brace point locations and the unbraced-length definition drive the member checks but the talk does not cover how those braces are installed in the field.

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
No weld rejections or bolt inspection failures are named; this is a design-methodology talk. The closest analog is design-side error: assuming a fixed effective length factor (the old habit of "K is 1.5, doesn't matter how many leaning columns") gives a unity check of about 0.68, while a proper effective-length method that knocks down Cb for the many leaning columns yields 1.1, a violation, against 0.75 from the direct analysis method [44:42][46:16]. The lesson is that ignoring leaning-column destabilization understates demand. The speakers also caution against checking a thousand points along a tapered member; instead check only where f-r over Q*Fy is maximum and at segment ends and midspan [40:25][54:35].

### Bid / Cost Implications
The direct analysis method gives substantial savings over the effective-length method for non-rectangular gabled geometries, and for wide modular frames with heavy gravity load on many leaning columns the sidesway amplification can exceed the 1.5 limit that bars the effective-length method outright [47:49][48:20]. On rafters the two methods land at practically the same strength ratio, with the direct analysis method often a shade higher (about a 0.01 penalty) because it adds frame-imperfection moments [46:47][49:20]. The method is presented as easier to program and integrate into in-house spreadsheets or software because the successive-approximations buckling solution avoids eigenvalue packages [13:29][47:49].

### Your Company Application
Web-tapered built-up members are a metal-building-manufacturer technique; Your Company positions as conventional structural steel and does not use PEMB language, so this content is reference for engineering literacy, not a product line to adopt. For Ivan's takeoff it is a flag: a tapered built-up frame is fabricated tonnage of welded plate girders, not catalog rolled shapes, so aisc_validator.py rolled-shape weights will not apply and tonnage must come from plate dimensions and weld volume. For Mario's shop the one-sided web-to-flange weld and the distortion-versus-residual-stress trade-off [60:49] matter for fit-up and camber control if such work is ever quoted, governed by AWS D1.1 in our own WPS rather than anything stated here. For an in-house PE stamp the takeaway is that any tapered-member or heavily leaning-column gabled frame should be designed by the direct analysis method, not a guessed K factor, since the 1.5 sidesway limit and leaning-column knockdown can flip a passing check to a failure [45:14][48:20]. Doctrine conflict: NONE, provided we treat this as internal estimating and engineering methodology and keep all outward language conventional-structural, not PEMB.
