## Ethics and Accountability
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CkdX6_eRm-0 | Duration: 1:25:22 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is a facilitated professional-ethics session for structural engineers, fabricators, and detailers, not a code-clause technical seminar. The throughline is that ethics risk drops when a firm pairs a strong ethical culture with an actively supported code of conduct, and that "doing the right thing" holds even when it costs schedule or a client relationship [05:05][14:31]. The presenter, a Minnesota structural engineer of ~55 years in practice, builds toward a real connection-design case study where an engineer of record reported under-designed steel connections to the building official rather than let them be covered with sheetrock [56:21][59:53].
### Spec References
The speaker references the AISC Code of Standard Practice, specifically Part 3.1.2, on the option that allows a fabricator to design connections from loads shown on the design drawings, tied to a Charlie Carter presentation earlier in the conference [03:01][03:34][04:35]. He names the word "allow" versus "require" as the controlling distinction in that provision. No AISC 360 chapter, AISC 341 seismic section, AWS D1.1 clause, RCSC pretension method, or numbered Design Guide is cited in this session. Treat the takeaway as general principles, with only the Code of Standard Practice Part 3.1.2 cited verbatim.
### Technical Details
The core technical thread is delegated connection design under the Code of Standard Practice: the engineer of record shows loads, the fabricator may design connections to those loads, and the EOR remains responsible for those connections even when their design is delayed or delegated [04:05][61:55][62:25]. The case study involves a five-story structural steel frame building with girder and collector connections to braced frames that did not match the design drawings [56:21][57:22]. The presenter also voices a personal preference against post-installed connectors in tension and notes finding fasteners he could turn and pull out of a building by hand, an inspection-quality point [63:15][63:47].
### Fabrication Notes
The pivotal fabrication failure is sequencing: steel shop drawings were started off the DD-phase (mill order) set, while connections were finalized only in the CD set, so the submitted shop drawings carried inaccurate connections and were rejected [57:22]. Portions of the shop drawings were rejected for the girder and collector-to-brace-frame connections specifically. The broader lesson for shop drawing handling is to not accept incomplete submittals pushed out under schedule pressure, and to cycle an incomplete set back rather than process it [69:53][70:24].
### Erection Notes
Construction advanced on unapproved, rejected shop drawings, and the rejected connections were erected as shown and then re-evaluated at 40 to 50 percent under design even after taking all code-allowed reductions [57:52][58:22]. The fix was field remediation: the general contractor hired its own PE to design field fixes for the connections, which were submitted as shop drawings, reviewed, and approved, with no schedule interruption [60:23]. A separate site-safety anecdote covers an untied worker hanging out a nine-story window, framing field safety as a moral duty even outside contractual scope [22:37].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The named failures are connections built under design (40 to 50 percent), construction proceeding on rejected shop drawings, and a general contractor that stopped returning calls and pressed ahead on schedule while the owner was kept unaware of the defect [57:52][58:22][58:52]. Plan stamping (signing for work one did not design) is flagged as a prohibited practice, summarized as "he who designs signs" [09:20]. The presenter also calls out special inspectors not actually performing the work, including fasteners that pulled out and backfill that settled six inches despite a passing test report [63:15][64:47].
### Bid / Cost Implications
Schedule incentives and liquidated damages drove the bad behavior: completion bonuses plus penalties pushed the contractor to bury a defect, raising whether liquidated damages themselves create an ethical pressure that values completion over safety [56:51][67:20][67:50]. The remediation cost (re-evaluation PE, fabricator material, erector labor) was carried by the general contractor with no claims, and the project still finished on time [66:49]. The operational cost lesson is to write reasonable shop-drawing review time into the specification and to log every shop drawing in and out, since slow review can itself become the basis of a delay claim [69:22][69:53].
### Your Company Application
For Ivan in takeoff and estimating, the Part 3.1.2 delegated-connection option is the live issue: when Your Company designs connections to EOR loads, the in-house PE stamp carries real responsibility, so bids should price connection engineering and shop-drawing review honestly rather than compress them to win schedule. For Tekla detailing, the case study is a direct warning to not start production details off a DD or mill-order set and submit them as final, and to never let rejected connection details get fabricated, which ties to the count-gap and verify-don't-generate discipline. Mario's shop crew lead role maps to the "cycle back an incomplete set" rule, and Paul Guerrero's safety authority maps to the nine-story untied-worker example as a stop-work moral duty. For ACP project controls, adopt the shop-drawing log (every drawing in and out, weekly status) so review turnaround is defensible against a delay claim, and treat liquidated-damage clauses as a flag to protect inspection and connection integrity. No conflict with Your Company doctrine: the session reinforces verify-don't-generate, in-house PE accountability for delegated connections, and honest scoping. DOCTRINE FLAG: NONE.

## Safety by Design
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Sep7EBrzIkI | Duration: 56:11 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is a policy and practice webinar by Mike Toole of Bucknell University on Prevention through Design (PtD), which he calls Designing for Construction Safety (DFCS) or Safety by Design [04:08]. The thesis is that structural engineers and architects can voluntarily make decisions during design and detailing that make a building easier and safer to erect, the same way constructability and quality are designed in [04:39]. Toole frames the case three ways: an ethical duty under the ASCE and NSPE codes of ethics to hold paramount the safety of the public, including workers [08:15]; a sustainability triple-bottom-line argument where worker safety is the social-equity leg [09:18]; and a dollars argument of lower workers comp, fewer delays, and higher productivity [10:51]. Research is cited loosely: studies linking roughly 22 percent and 42 percent of construction fatalities to design factors, attributed to Mike Behm of East Carolina University and a European study, presented as contributory not causal [07:13].

### Spec References
This session is about safety policy, not connection design, so it cites almost no AISC or AWS technical sections. The one explicit code reference comes from an audience structural engineer at [49:39] who notes the AISC Code of Standard Practice requires the designer to identify the lateral-load-resisting system, and observes that bid documents rarely comply, leaving it vague or missing. Named external instruments and bodies, none being an AISC 360/341 or AWS clause: the UK CDM (Construction Design and Management) regulations of 1994-95 revised 2007 [13:26]; OSHA, NIOSH, and NIOSH's NORA Construction Sector Council [04:39][15:58]; the CII (Construction Industry Institute) design-for-safety checklist tool built by Jimmy Hinze with about 457 items [22:39]; Australia's free SHARE/CHAIR-style work product [35:22]; and the NISD (National Institute of Steel Detailing) and National Erectors Association joint safety-in-design manual for steel [25:40]. General principles, no AISC section cited.

### Technical Details
The steel-specific design measures are detailing moves, all common-sense and low cost: pre-punching holes in columns at the right locations for safety rail and intermediate rail so erectors can stand a guardrail as soon as the deck is on [44:36]; adding clips on columns so ironworkers can tie off when working a cantilever [44:36]; avoiding hanging connections in favor of seated/bearing connections so the ironworker is at less risk while landing the first two bolts [26:42]; chamfering sharp corners; and leaving enough clearance at connections to fit a torque wrench [27:13]. Built-in fall-protection anchorage in the structural frame is the headline low-hanging fruit, useful for both erection and later window washing and maintenance [11:53]. A non-steel example is raising parapets a few inches above the code 30-inch minimum so the parapet itself becomes fall protection [25:10].

### Fabrication Notes
The strong recurring theme from the fabricator and erector voices in the room is that the fabricator and detailer, not the design engineer, are the right party to embed erection-safety features, because they know the erection sequence, the standards, and the field practice [54:48]. One fabricator describes columns arriving with holes whose purpose a junior structural engineer could not explain, which is exactly the detailing knowledge that should drive the safety features [55:18]. Prefabrication is presented as a primary safety strategy: moving work off elevation to the ground or, better, into the shop where machines and automation do it, reduces exposure and often saves time and money [12:25]. Modular work platforms and lifting points fabricated on the ground and set in place are given as the Bechtel example [30:46].

### Erection Notes
Erection safety is the entire point of the design moves above. The lived erector account at [44:36] is the clearest: pre-located rail holes and tie-off clips let a worker stay safe without climbing down to order and rig temporary barricade that is often not on site. Bechtel's process embeds temporary platforms, lifelines, lifting clips, and climbing rungs in the model so erection is easier and faster [30:46]. The CDM discussion stresses the constructor side: a site-specific erection plan plus a site-specific safety plan and a hazard analysis as a legal duty [50:41]. Multiple speakers insist personal responsibility and ironworker ingenuity remain first, and that schedule pressure is what makes crews cut corners, which good design should relieve rather than replace [44:06][52:13].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
No weld rejections, bolt-installation failures, or NDE findings are discussed, since this is not an inspection talk. The named failure is a documentation and compliance gap: the AISC Code of Standard Practice requirement to identify the lateral-load-resisting system is rarely met in bid documents, showing up vague or missing [49:39]. A second recurring failure mode is the fabricator not being given all the information needed to make the critical connection [46:37]. The broader systemic error Toole names is the industry's slow uptake driven by liability fear, the 800-pound gorilla, and by structural engineers lacking any safety training in their education [17:29][20:36].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Toole concedes a real added cost: designers need training, design takes more time, and there is QC overhead for safety review, so the work is hard to sell to a low-bid owner [19:33]. His counter is life-cycle: a dollar spent in design fees can save ten in construction and shorten schedule, which lands best with sophisticated owners, design-builders, owner-controlled insurance program (OCIP) owners, and process/industrial clients, and poorly with commercial design-bid-build [20:04][29:14]. A fabricator at [47:07] makes the operational point directly: if a fabricator builds the safety features in, that cost can be included in the price, so it is a quotable line of scope rather than a hidden burden. Middle East process clients are cited as already refusing proposals that do not show a prevention-through-design program [36:23].

### Your Company Application
This maps cleanly onto Your Company's conventional structural steel positioning and gives Paul Guerrero (NCCER safety director) a design-stage safety vocabulary to bring into bid review and the erection plan: push for pre-punched guardrail holes and tie-off clips at columns, bearing/seated connections over hanging connections, and adequate wrench clearance, all of which Tekla detailing can carry and Mario Gutierrez's crew benefits from in the field. Ivan's takeoff and the bid can treat these erection-safety features as priced scope rather than free, echoing the fabricator at [47:07], which fits our verify-don't-generate discipline of naming the source of every cost. The Code of Standard Practice point at [49:39] is a concrete intake check for Ivan and the drawing-completeness gate: confirm the bid set identifies the lateral-load-resisting system, and RFI the GC when it is vague or missing, since that gap is both a compliance and a pricing risk. Anchor-rod work, joists, and field bolting all sit inside this same erection-safety frame, and the ACP project controls register is the right home for a per-job erection-safety and tie-off plan. Doctrine flags: NONE. The session uses no PEMB language for steel, and the lone "pre-engineered buildings" mention at [12:56] is the speaker's generic prefabrication example, not Your Company outward copy.

## Robust Structures
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YRjJqLr8MeE | Duration: 1:30:40 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
This webinar (session E22, two speakers: Prof. Chris Foley of Marquette and Kirk Marchand of Protection Engineering Consultants) is about structural robustness and resistance to disproportionate (progressive) collapse in steel framing after a key member is lost to blast, vehicle impact, gas explosion, or construction defect [01:37][02:08][45:33]. The central idea is that a conventional steel frame is inherently robust "out of the box" and the engineering task is to quantify that latent capacity, not to add exotic detailing [05:08][36:48]. Robustness is framed three ways: acceptable probability of loss, acceptable probability of collapse, or acceptable risk and consequence, and a robust system is characterized by redundancy, reliable ductility, and the ability to accommodate load reversals [10:09][10:40]. The mechanics center on a transition from a flexural (plastic-hinge) mechanism to a geometric-stiffness or catenary/membrane mechanism as a damaged span deforms vertically, with both mechanisms linked and active together [11:10][19:53].

### Spec References
The speakers cite documents and guidance rather than AISC 360 chapter-and-section numbers. Named references: ACI 318 (cited for structural-integrity and continuity-reinforcement provisions as a model for steel) [06:08][26:01]; GSA progressive-collapse guidance and DOD UFC 4-023-03 "methods to mitigate progressive collapse," being merged into one holistic approach [47:39][48:10]; FEMA 356, now ASCE 41 (referred to repeatedly as "asc41"), used for the flexure-based modeling curves, allowable plastic rotations, and the life-safety and collapse-prevention acceptance limits [61:07][64:47][79:16]; ASCE 7 occupancy tables, proposed as the basis for risk level in the emerging SEI guidance [50:47]; the 2008 UFC update [79:16]. AISC is cited as the funding sponsor for the blast and connection research, not as a clause source [02:38][37:49]. No AISC 360, AISC 341, AWS D1.1, RCSC, or Design Guide numbers were stated.

### Technical Details
Foley's analysis manipulates connection moment strength (term beta) and stiffness to show that partially restrained (PR) connections accumulate vertical deformation faster, which activates geometric stiffness earlier and generates large horizontal tension forces sooner, raising the risk of tensile rupture at the connection if those forces cannot be carried [13:15][15:16][15:48]. Strong-column-weak-beam behavior caps the moment funneled into columns and is favorable here as it is in seismic design [23:29][24:59]. The floor slab and deck matter: ACI-style continuity reinforcement, welded-wire mesh membrane action, and the steel deck acting as one-way tension reinforcement (deck spans one direction only, unlike a two-way cast-in-place slab) provide catenary capacity, but only with adequate anchorage at panel ends [26:01][27:02][28:34]. Marchand's DTRA test program ran four phases on exterior perimeter-bay specimens: base-plate and connection blast response, column blast response, full beam-girder-column system blast, and a phase-four ram push-down test on the damaged (or pristine "immaculate removal") double-span condition [52:21][53:21][54:25]. Tests measured ram force, axial force via load pins, and beam strain, then derived shear, moment, chord rotation, and flexural-versus-axial energy split [65:47][66:18].

### Fabrication Notes
The webinar is research-oriented and does not give shop fabrication tolerances or fit-up procedures. The fabrication-relevant takeaway is connection type selection: the connections tested were simple shear tabs, double-angle (web) connections, WTs, bolted cover-plate ("bolt wind moment"), bolted split-T, side plates, and welded-flange ("woof"/seismic moment) connections [35:46][54:55][59:35]. Foley's MSOE connection tests ran 27 specimens of three-, four-, and five-bolt simple shear connections and showed 17 inches of deformation over a 14-inch span with no fracture, with angles flattening and pulling off bolt heads as the limit state [36:16][36:48]. The practical fabrication point is that a few extra bolts per connection (the ACI-style "minimum two or three bolts per connection" idea) can materially raise integrity [06:38].

### Erection Notes
There is little direct erection or rigging content. The relevant systems-level point for the field is that anchorage at the ends of damaged spans, the in-plane shear stiffness of the deck diaphragm, and continuity of tie members govern whether catenary action can develop, so deck attachment (puddle welds, headed studs) and connection completeness in the as-erected condition carry real structural-integrity weight [30:37][39:53]. Marchand stresses that corner and perimeter bays often cannot develop catenary action because there is nothing to react the membrane force against, so the as-built tying scheme around the building perimeter matters [45:02][45:33].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
No code rejections or QC inspection failures are named since this is research, not a shop or field QA talk. The named failure modes from testing are the connection degradation sequences: bottom-flange failure, then sequential bolt failures, then top-flange failure for welded-flange connections, and web tear-out and angle failure for cover-plate connections at roughly 12 percent rotation [71:28][74:00][75:06]. The cover-plate connection behaved unpredictably and is flagged as the "oddball" that should give pause in setting acceptance criteria [83:27][84:29]. A recurring analyst error called out is discounting residual capacity: a blast-damaged column can retain up to about 30 percent of its vertical load capacity, contrary to the assumption that a visibly deformed column is finished [60:06][60:37].

### Bid / Cost Implications
The cost theme is that imposing full seismic requirements purely to chase robustness makes buildings much more expensive without true equivalency to a disproportionate-collapse event [88:07][89:10][89:41]. The research lets a practitioner credit the inherent capacity of conventional connections through nonlinear inelastic analysis instead of buying seismic detailing wholesale [89:41]. A second cost-relevant result: the dynamic increase factor for alternate-path analysis drops from a factor of 2 (elastic worst case) to about 1.2 when inelastic connection behavior is allowed, which reduces demand and therefore steel weight in integrity design [62:41][63:45][64:15].

### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff and estimating, the message is to resist scope-creep pricing: a disproportionate-collapse or integrity requirement does not automatically mean full seismic detailing, and conventional shear tabs and simple connections carry meaningful inherent ductility and energy, so the bid should price the specified analysis approach (ASCE 41 / UFC alternate path) rather than defaulting to seismic moment frames [80:19][89:10]. For Mario's shop and welding, the takeaway is that bolt count and weld completeness at simple connections drive integrity capacity, so connection details should be fabricated exactly as detailed, with full bolt complement and sound deck puddle welds and stud anchorage [06:38][30:37]. For Tekla detailing and the in-house PE stamp, any project carrying explicit progressive-collapse or tie-force provisions (GSA, DOD UFC, or an owner spec) needs the controlling document confirmed before detailing, since acceptance limits trace back to ASCE 41 rotations, not AISC 360 connection design alone; flag such a job for engineering review at intake. For ACP project controls, none of this is triggered unless the contract documents call out integrity or progressive-collapse provisions, so the action is to screen specs for those references at takeoff. Doctrine conflict: NONE. The webinar uses conventional structural-steel language throughout and cites no rate, supplier, or AISC weight that would conflict with Your Company doctrine; nothing here overrides aisc_validator.py weights or bid_rates.py.

## Rules of Thumb for Steel Design
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TM25D8RGiyk | Duration: 43:54 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
Dr Socrates Ioannides (Structural Affiliates, Nashville) presents a set of closed-form approximations for preliminary steel sizing so an engineer can answer depth, weight, column-size, and tonnage questions on the spot in a design meeting and sanity-check computer output [02:01][04:38]. The rules are explicitly Allowable Stress Design based, developed before LRFD, and use service (un-factored) loads directly because the allowable-stress safety margin is already baked into each constant [06:38][07:08]. They are approximations, not always conservative, and the speaker repeatedly says to verify with full analysis [06:38][10:15].
### Spec References
No code section, table, or Design Guide number is cited verbatim; these are general design rules of thumb, no AISC section cited. The talk names the steel-shape weight tables generically ("the AISC table" of economy sections, "the steel book") at [09:13][20:07] and references UL fire-rating assembly designations spoken aloud for composite floors: UL 902, UL 925, and UL D916 ("9259 16") depending on the spray-fireproofing supplier [35:17]. It also references LRFD versus ASD as design methods generally [06:38][17:29], not a clause.
### Technical Details
Key approximations, all in conventional units (moment in foot-kips, depth in inches, weight in pounds per foot): area of any shape = weight / 3.4 [08:11]; moment of inertia I = d squared times weight / 2 [08:42]; elastic section modulus = depth times weight / 10 [09:13]; radius of gyration rx is about 0.45d, ry is about 0.25 times flange width [10:15][10:46]. The flagship beam rule is weight = 5M/d for 36 ksi and 3.5M/d for 50 ksi (the "5M over d" story) [13:52][15:25]; composite beams use 70 to 75 percent of that [16:26]. Shear-stud count is about 1.1 times the weight in ASD or 1.25 times the lighter LRFD weight, using 3/4 inch studs, and more than three studs per square foot signals a design problem [16:58][17:59]. Truss-chord force is about 1.3M/d, chord weight about 2M/d, total truss about three times the chord weight [21:08][22:13]. Column allowable stress straight-line fit: Fa = 22 minus 0.1(KL/r) for 36 ksi, with a 0.15 factor for 50 ksi [23:17]. Depth rule: roof members about half the span (inches per foot of span), floor beams a bit more, roughly half an inch per foot [24:53]. High-rise floor weight estimate: psf = stories/3 + 7 [31:07].
### Fabrication Notes
The talk is preliminary design oriented and gives no shop fit-up, tolerance, or QC procedure. The only fabrication-adjacent items are the 3/4 inch shear-stud convention and the rule that more than three studs per square foot is a red flag [16:58], and the fillet-weld capacity check that the weld strength is a little less than 1 kip per sixteenth of an inch of weld size per inch of length [33:46]. No NDE, WPS, or weld-procedure content.
### Erection Notes
One erection-rate planning figure is given: a crew erects roughly 40 to 60 tons per week, derived as an average that depends on piece count, typical piece weight, and connection type [32:44]. Worked schedule example: a 12-story, 36,000 SF building at (12/3 + 7) psf comes to about 2,000 tons, with about 10 weeks mill/delivery lead and about 16 weeks to erect, totaling roughly six months [33:15]. No bracing, rigging, or sequencing detail beyond the rate.
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
No inspection-failure or rejection catalog is presented. The speaker flags design-judgment errors instead: shear-stud counts above three per square foot indicate a flawed composite design [16:58], and engineers commonly over-estimate simple-beam deflection because real bolted "simple" connections provide rotational restraint, so actual deflection is about 80 percent of the calculated value [34:16]. He also warns the rules go unconservative on the heaviest sections in each column group [10:15].
### Bid / Cost Implications
Several rules feed estimating directly: tonnage from psf = stories/3 + 7 gives a fast structural-weight order of magnitude for a high-rise [31:07]; the 40 to 60 ton/week erection rate plus mill lead time gives a schedule estimate [32:44][33:15]. Economy guidance: optimum bay is about 30 by 40 for beam-and-joist framing (beams short way, joists long way) and 40 by 40 for joist-girder/truss systems [26:56]; composite framing runs about one shape size lighter than non-composite [17:29]. The speaker notes mill/service-center delivery is no longer 8 to 10 weeks but more like 14 to 20 weeks [32:12].
### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff and ROM estimating, this is a useful cross-check layer on top of the measured aisc_validator.py member takeoff, never a replacement: weight = 5M/d (or 3.5M/d at 50 ksi), area = weight/3.4, and S = d times weight/10 let Ivan reasonableness-check a member before it hits the validated tonnage, and the stories/3 + 7 psf and 40 to 60 ton/week rules give a fast sanity figure for schedule and a $/SF gate. This stays consistent with Your Company doctrine: these are verify-don't-generate sanity checks, ROM-grade only, and any number that feeds a price must still come from the measured schedule-plus-framing-plan takeoff through aisc_validator.py, not from M/d arithmetic. The shear-stud rule (1.1 times weight, 3/4 inch studs, three-per-SF ceiling) is a Mario shop-side QC sniff test, and the fillet-weld 1 kip per sixteenth per inch figure is a quick capacity check for the in-house PE and Mario's weld sizing, both subordinate to the actual WPS and AWS D1.1 qualification. The 14 to 20 week mill lead time is a procurement input for ACP project controls. Doctrine flags: NONE, with the caveat that all constants here are ASD service-load approximations and must not override validated weights, locked BID_RATES, or AISC database values.

## Cool Castings and Green Ideas from Europe
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-AP02Bzql_Q | Duration: 1:00:05 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is a research and innovation lecture by a fatigue and fracture specialist from the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology (EPFL), framed around sustainable steel construction in Europe rather than a code-application clinic [01:02]. The central technical thread is steel castings (cast nodes) as an alternative to welded tubular joints for better fatigue durability and complex geometry [19:48]. Three secondary topics follow: structural glass used as a load-bearing and bracing element [35:04], stainless steel (austenitic and duplex) for fire resistance and corrosion durability [40:46], and a new grout-and-embossed-plate connection for fast composite-bridge erection [43:59]. The recurring argument is to compete on life-cycle value and durability rather than being the lowest bidder [05:11].

### Spec References
This talk cites the European standard system, not AISC, AWS, or RCSC. The speaker references EN 1090 (delivery condition and execution of steel structures, with Part Two for execution) and Eurocode 3 / EN 1993 with its many parts including general rules, fire, thin-wall products, stainless steel, plate buckling, and shells, plus structure-specific Parts 2 through 6 for bridges, towers and masts and chimneys, silos and tanks, piling, and crane-supporting structures [06:45][07:15][07:47]. Eurocode 3 Part 14 is cited as the stainless steel design code [42:21][42:55]. Eurocode 4 (steel and concrete composite) is named, and the speaker states the overall Eurocode set is 53 parts with roughly 27 to 30 being steel or composite [51:46][52:47]. Material grades named: cast steel grade GS 20Mn5 compared by the speaker to ASTM A572 Grade 52 [24:02][24:34], and stainless grade 316 versus a structural carbon reference of A36 [42:55]. A 2003 NSCC conference paper by "Scher" on cast-node application is cited [21:54]. No AISC 360 section, AISC 341 seismic section, AWS D1.1 clause, RCSC provision, or AISC Design Guide is referenced anywhere; treat all design provisions here as European, not the codes Your Company bids under.

### Technical Details
Modern steel castings are made by a vacuum argon refinement (VAR) process that yields high-strength low-alloy grades with good weldability, some weldable without preheat [22:28][23:01]. Cast material reaches yield strengths up to roughly 900 MPa (140 ksi) via quench and temper, though such grades are not yet used in construction [25:36][26:08], and toughness is shown meeting and exceeding the 27 joule code requirement [26:39]. The fatigue case for cast nodes is smoother stress flow and lower stress concentration than a welded tubular joint, where cutting and welding geometry is suboptimal [27:11][27:44]. In welded tube-to-tube joints cracks typically initiate at the weld toe of the tension diagonal, and welders in Switzerland use backing bars or backing rings so root cracking is uncommon [28:14][28:45]. For the cast-node-to-tube weld the speaker compared several joint preparations and found the simplest detail, a beveled cast-node end acting as its own backing bar, gave the best relative fatigue strength versus fabrication cost; an eccentric detail putting compression at the root (offshore-industry practice) is even better but architects prefer the flush detail [30:52][31:54][32:28]. For structural glass, tempered glass carries surface compressive residual stress of 100 to 180 MPa so the controlling failure criterion shifts from compression to tension and from stress to stress-intensity factor; glass can be designed as a structural element on that basis [38:40][39:41]. Duplex stainless (austenitic plus ferritic) is presented as lower nickel, lower cost, good strength, toughness, and corrosion resistance, with circular sections only currently available in duplex [40:46][57:32].

### Fabrication Notes
The core fabrication message is to move complexity into the shop where it can be done in a controlled environment with low tolerances and prefabrication [03:05][19:48]. Castings let you form very complex or very large nodes in one piece, with one example part weighing about 16 tons [24:34]. The connection problem is tolerance control between a cast node and a tube: machining the cast-node face for a steel or ceramic backing is described as good but very expensive, so the preferred low-cost approach is a beveled cast-node end that compensates for tolerance and self-backs the root [30:19][30:52][31:54]. Good root penetration must still be ensured [31:54]. For the composite-bridge connection, fabrication involves an embossed steel plate welded to the beam top flange, an optional epoxy-plus-sand bonding layer for roughness, water-jet roughening of the precast slab rib, and a cement grout placed under confinement, with tubes to keep grout from escaping [45:03][45:33][46:03].

### Erection Notes
Erection appears mainly as a selling point for steel (fast erection, high strength-to-weight, less material to transport) and as a caution about castings [03:05][03:37]. The St. Kilian bridge in Germany is cited as a case where using cast nodes everywhere cost a lot and caused difficulty during erection, the speaker's example of over-using castings [34:01]. The composite connection system is promoted explicitly for high erection speed and a clean field operation, using precast slab elements with glued joints between prefabricated pieces and the grouted shear connection rather than cast-in-place studs [43:59][44:31][46:35]. No crane, rigging, sequencing, or bracing procedure is given in code terms.

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Inspection of the weld between the casting and the normal steel is raised from the floor as an open problem, and the speaker concedes he has no good answer: production qualification has been done for research but characterizing root penetration by non-destructive examination is still an active project, and any backed butt weld makes the root hard to verify [48:41][49:12][49:43]. The named recurring defect mode in welded tubular joints is fatigue cracking at the weld toe of the tension diagonal, sometimes from the root depending on geometry [28:45][29:17]. Cast nodes themselves contain casting defects but are more fatigue resistant, so cracking moves to the weld between node and tube rather than the casting [29:49][30:19]. Cost-driven over-use of castings on simple standard nodes is presented as a design error to avoid [33:30].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Casting cost is dominated by mold reuse: the producers want 10 or more identical parts to be cost effective, and four identical nodes (the Berlin stadium quarter-symmetry example) is still not enough and runs more expensive [54:23][54:55]. The cast steel price runs about a factor of four higher per kilogram than steel used in a normal connection, partly offset because better stress flow lets you use less material [54:55][55:27]. Castings are roughly one project in 100 in Europe, and casting producers carry 12 to 18 month backlogs, so lead time and availability are real constraints on specifying them [55:57][56:28]. The broader bid argument is to sell life-cycle value, durability, reuse, and recyclability over lowest initial cost, with the reminder that on buildings the structure is only about 30 percent of total cost and equipment or envelope is 70 percent [05:11][59:35].

### Your Company Application
This is a European research talk with zero AISC, AWS D1.1, or RCSC content, so it does not change any Your Company takeoff, validator, or rate input. The usable takeaways are estimating and methodology, not code. For Ivan, the cast-node economics are a clean bid heuristic: a custom one-off connection casting is roughly four times the per-pound steel cost and only pencils at 10-plus identical parts, with 12 to 18 month lead times, so any RFI proposing cast nodes on an ACP-type job should trigger a long-lead and cost flag rather than a routine takeoff. For Mario, the practical welding point is that a cast-node to tube weld, like any backed butt weld, has a root that is hard to inspect, which reinforces the in-house PE stamp and AWS D1.1 discipline of getting root penetration and NDE right on any cast or backed detail. The structural-glass-as-bracing and duplex-stainless-column material is outside Your Company's conventional structural steel scope and is informational only. Doctrine flag: NONE. Nothing here conflicts with Your Company doctrine; note only that the GS 20Mn5 to A572-52 and 316 to A36 comparisons are the speaker's approximations and must not be treated as validated AISC material data.

## A New Approch to Design for Stability
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iOH6kaXX3Mk | Duration: 52:10 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is the 2007 T.R. Higgins award lecture by Shankar Nair of Teng and Associates, explaining the stability provisions of the 2005 AISC specification and the new Direct Analysis Method [00:00]. The thesis is that buckling as a pure bifurcation is a theoretical abstraction that does not occur in real structures, because every real member or frame carries an initial imperfection, an out-of-plumbness or out-of-straightness, that produces a starting displacement y-sub-0 [02:02][05:38]. Failure of a member loaded in nominally pure compression is therefore always a combined compression-and-flexure event, never pure crushing and never pure buckling [08:09]. The lecture argues the profession had been designing for stability "by rote" and walks through why the traditional method of neglecting imperfections and inelasticity in the analysis, then compensating with an effective-length factor K greater than one, is unconservative on moments [00:31][24:36].
### Spec References
2005 AISC specification (360) is the subject throughout. Cited explicitly: Chapter B general design requirements [30:14], Chapter C stability analysis and design requirements [31:17], Chapter E column compressive strength for flexural buckling [15:50], Appendix 7 for the Direct Analysis Method [40:33][33:22], Sections C2.2a (effective length method) and C2.2b (first order analysis method) [40:33]. The B1/B2 amplified first order analysis is referenced as the long-standing second order method [12:46]. The Code of Standard Practice out-of-plumbness tolerance of L/500 is cited [23:35]. The speaker notes the commentary lists nine conditions for the alignment chart, condition eight being simultaneous column buckling [26:08]. He previews the 2010 AISC spec making Direct Analysis the base method [51:17].
### Technical Details
Three prescriptive methods account for P-Delta effects, geometric imperfections, and residual stresses [32:50][33:22]. Direct Analysis applies to all structures and makes no distinction between braced frames, moment frames, or shear wall systems [40:03]. It requires a second order elastic analysis capturing both P-Capital-Delta (load through displaced node location) and P-small-delta (load on deformed member shape) [33:52]. Geometric imperfections are handled by a notional lateral load of 0.002 times the story gravity load, equivalent to an out-of-plumbness of 1 in 500 [34:54][35:24]. Inelasticity from residual stress, of order 0.3 times yield, is handled by reduced stiffness EI-star and EA-star using a 0.8 factor plus a tau-b factor on flexural stiffness that drops below one when axial force exceeds half of yield [13:17][38:00]. With these in the analysis, members are checked at K equals 1 using the ordinary Chapter E column curve [39:33]. Delta over Delta-0 above 1.5 forces Direct Analysis as the only option [40:33].
### Fabrication Notes
This is an analysis-and-design webinar with no shop fabrication, fit-up, cutting, or QC content. No fabrication detail to extract.
### Erection Notes
The lecture connects to erection only through tolerance. The L/500 out-of-plumbness limit from the Code of Standard Practice is the field tolerance that the strength curve and the 1-in-500 notional load are calibrated against [23:35][35:24]. The speaker notes 1 in 500 is roughly a quarter inch over 12 feet [35:24]. No sequencing, bracing, crane, or rigging content.
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The central named error is the traditional pre-2005 practice of neglecting imperfections and inelasticity in the analysis, which understates member demand on sidesway frames and yields a reported base moment of zero on a loaded column that in reality fails largely in flexure [24:06][24:36]. That understated moment propagates into underdesigned beams and connections, an unconservative result [25:06]. The second named failure is misuse of the sidesway alignment chart: few real buildings meet its simultaneous-buckling assumption, and leaning columns, unequal restraint, unloaded columns, and unsymmetrical plans all violate it, so K is rarely computed correctly for a real three-dimensional structure [26:08][27:40]. The speaker states he does not know anyone who calculates K correctly for a real 3D frame [28:10].
### Bid / Cost Implications
No direct pricing, bid, or estimating content. The implication for a fabricator is indirect: the new method demands the engineer of record run a proper second order analysis with reduced stiffness and notional loads, which surfaces real base moments that drive larger or more developed beam-to-column connections than the old K-greater-than-one shortcut implied [25:06]. The ASD note matters for any in-house design: under stability-governed ASD you must analyze at 1.6 times the ASD load combination and divide results by 1.6, because member force does not scale linearly with load, and skipping this yields an undersized, less safe member [48:12][49:45].
### Your Company Application
For our in-house PE stamp this is the governing method to apply on any moment-frame or combined braced-and-moment-frame job: run the Direct Analysis Method per AISC 360 Appendix 7, model the 0.002 notional load, use the 0.8 and tau-b reduced stiffness, and check members at K equals 1, rather than chasing alignment-chart K values [33:22][38:00]. The payoff for Tekla detailing and for Mario's shop is that the analysis now reports the true base and connection moments, so connection design and the fabricated detail match the real demand instead of an understated one [25:06]. The L/500 out-of-plumbness tolerance ties directly to our anchor-rod setting and field plumb tolerance, and to the Code of Standard Practice we already cite [23:35]. The ASD 1.6 multiply-then-divide rule is a concrete checklist item for any stamped ASD calc [49:45]. No conflict with Your Company doctrine: NONE.

## Basic Introduction to Nonlinear Analysis
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y5aCcybCX4g | Duration: 1:30:55 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This webinar teaches how a structural analysis program actually computes nonlinear behavior, with the standing reminder that "the function of a structural engineer is to design not to analyze" and that analysis is a means to an end [00:01]. The speaker walks the audience through the direct stiffness method, the basis of every commercial frame program and of the finite element method, where the computer enforces equilibrium and compatibility at each degree of freedom and uses a force-displacement relationship F = K Delta as the translator between forces and displacements [16:30, 17:02]. He stresses that the only way these programs model real behavior is by modifying member stiffness, so material nonlinearity, second-order effects, and buckling are all just stiffness modifications [18:03, 88:38]. The lecture builds from material nonlinear analysis (plastic hinges) to geometric nonlinear analysis (P-Delta) to combined second-order inelastic analysis and elastic critical (buckling) load analysis. All these methods are described as approximate and a complement to, never a substitute for, good engineering [04:13].

### Spec References
The speaker cites the AISC steel specification Chapter C, which requires accounting for P-Delta (P-cap-Delta and P-small-Delta) second-order effects [01:35, 02:07], and Appendix 1, which permits inelastic analysis and design [02:07, 40:45, 41:15]. He references the direct analysis method as the future alternative to back-calculating K factors [78:54]. He names hand methods B1 and B2 moment amplification factors for second-order effects [03:10]. He mentions LRFD design reaching M-sub-p for a fully braced member [33:34]. No AISC 341 seismic section, AWS D1.1 clause, RCSC provision, table number, or numbered Design Guide is cited in this lecture; it is an analysis-theory webinar, not a connection or welding talk.

### Technical Details
The material model assumed throughout is elastic-perfectly-plastic: the program monitors member stress and, when it reaches yield (for example 50 KSI), switches the modulus of elasticity from 29,000 KSI to zero [26:45, 27:54]. A plastic hinge forms in axial members when P over the yield load Py equals one, and in flexure when the moment reaches the plastic moment M-sub-p (plastic section modulus times yield strength), with the ratio M over M-sub-p equal to one [29:29, 33:34, 35:06]. Combined axial force and bending are governed by a yield surface, where staying inside means elastic and reaching the surface forms a hinge; a section at the surface can shed bending moment to neighbors to take more axial force [46:25, 47:25]. Second-order stiffness equals first-order elastic stiffness modified by a geometric stiffness term that is negative for compression (the "backpacker" analogy) and positive for tension (the "guitar string" analogy) [61:18, 62:18, 62:50]. Buckling occurs when the stiffness matrix determinant goes to zero, solved as an eigenvalue problem where eigenvalues are load factors and eigenvectors are buckling modes [74:14, 80:58]. The worked example is a continuous W21x65, 24 ft and 12 ft spans, 100 Kip load, where moment redistribution let load grow about 16 to 17 percent past first yield before a three-hinge mechanism [37:09, 40:45].

### Fabrication Notes
This webinar covers analysis theory only and states no fabrication requirements, tolerances, shop processes, fit-up, or QC procedures.

### Erection Notes
The lecture does not address erection procedures, sequencing, bracing, or rigging. Its only physical connection to the field is the underlying behavior the analysis predicts, such as lateral stiffness loss under gravity compression, which is relevant to how a frame stands during erection but is not discussed as field procedure.

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The speaker flags analysis-tool errors rather than shop or field rejections. He warns that a program labeled "P-Delta" may capture only P-cap-Delta and miss P-small-Delta, so the user must confirm both are included [53:05]. He cautions that software must account for axial-force-bending interaction on the yield surface, since ignoring axial force in the W21x65 example overstated capacity by failing at 73 percent of load versus 100 percent [50:32, 51:02]. He warns against using a buckling analysis to back-calculate K factors and to be careful when the elastic critical load ratio approaches one [78:54, 79:25]. He also notes columns may need subdivision into two elements for adequate second-order and buckling accuracy [68:38, 81:29].

### Bid / Cost Implications
The cost theme is computational expense versus accuracy in choosing an analysis method. Concentrated-plasticity plastic-hinge models are cheaper and a good starting point, while distributed-plasticity (plastic zone) analysis is more accurate but computationally more expensive, with the gap between them shrinking as a structure becomes more redundant [35:38, 36:09, 36:39]. Full 3D brick-element finite element analysis is described as the "full enchilada," appropriate for component study but beyond what basic frame analysis needs [36:39, 37:09]. The practical bid-side lesson is that inelastic analysis can justify more capacity from the same steel (the example carried roughly 16 percent more load past first yield), but second-order effects cut the other way and reduced the same beam to about 67 percent of its first-order capacity [40:45, 70:10].

### Your Company Application
This is engineer-of-record analysis methodology and sits with the in-house PE stamp, not with Ivan's member takeoff. Your Company's takeoff stays a measured member count through bridge/aisc_validator.py, which holds the validated AISC weights and section properties (area, moment of inertia, plastic section modulus) that any such analysis consumes; this video does not change those numbers and the verify-do-not-generate rule still applies. The relevant doctrine point is that the PE must run a true second-order analysis per Chapter C and may use Appendix 1 inelastic analysis, and our estimate-grade coordinate model in bridge/fabrication.py remains visualization and QC only, never an analysis substitute. The content is general structural theory with no PEMB language and no connection, bolting, or welding detail, so it does not touch Mario's AWS D1.1 scope, Paul's safety scope, anchor rods, joists, field bolting, or ACP project controls. ## Fatigue and Fracture Control in Steel Structures
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QCGPPFiNrUc | Duration: 1:02:57 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
The talk is not about fracture mechanics theory or design math but about what the engineer and fabricator can do to prevent brittle fracture and fatigue failure in steel structures [00:01]. The controlling thesis is that constraint (a triaxial state of stress) matters as much as notch toughness, and constraint is set by the people who detail, load, and build the structure, not the metallurgist [04:37][05:09]. Brittle fracture is sudden and catastrophic, propagating up to 5,000 ft per second, so once it starts it is over [01:02]. The repeated message is that excessive notch toughness will not compensate for poor design, poor details, or poor fabrication [60:54][61:24].
### Spec References
The speaker cites general principles and history more than clause numbers. Named references: the AASHTO fracture control plan with the 15 ft-lb transition temperature criterion from the WWII Liberty ships [11:15][16:57]; AASHTO Charpy V-notch values for a 1-1/4 in A36 plate at Zone 1 / 0 degree service temperature requiring 25 ft-lb at +70 F for fracture critical members, rising to 35 ft-lb for A514, and to 45 ft-lb above 2-1/2 in thickness, with very thick plate disallowed in Zone 3 (down to -60) [16:57][20:32][21:04]; ASTM E399 valid K1c plane-strain fracture toughness test [15:25]; the AISC manual passage stating triaxial tensile stresses tend to cause brittle fracture and should be avoided [29:47][50:36]; AASHTO fatigue design categories A through E developed by John Fisher [54:14]. Material grades A36, A514, A517, A588, and A533B are named. No AISC 360 chapter, AISC 341 section, AWS D1.1 clause, or RCSC section is cited.
### Technical Details
K1 (applied stress intensity, a function of nominal stress times the square root of pi times flaw size) must stay below K1c, the material critical toughness, in the same way calculated stress stays below yield [02:35][03:06][45:28]. Constraint elevates the stress-strain curve: under full triaxial tension (Sigma 1 = Sigma 2 = Sigma 3) the Mohr circle shrinks to a point, shear stress approaches zero, and the steel cleaves before it can yield [23:36][25:08][29:47]. Toughness rises with temperature and falls with thickness and loading rate; AASHTO tests above service temperature to account for the rate shift between impact and the intermediate rate bridges actually see [17:27][18:27]. Shallow cracks (a/W near 0.15) show higher measured toughness than deep laboratory cracks (a/W near 0.5), a conservatism in standard test specimens [31:50][35:59]. Case studies: Point Pleasant bridge eyebar (1967, 47 dead), Bryte Bend box girder Sacramento, Ingram Barge (1972, no pre-existing flaw, 55 ft-lb Charpy, failed purely from a triaxial detail) [11:45][14:20][25:38][28:45], and the Hoan bridge (2000, no pre-existing crack) [51:08].
### Fabrication Notes
Detail geometry is decisive: improving riveted-era square corners and thick-plate details corrected most of the Liberty ship problem [10:45][11:15]. Highly constrained welded junctions (deck plate, bulkhead, ring and stiffener all meeting at one point) create a triaxial state that fractures with adequate Charpy and no pre-existing crack [27:12][28:13]. For moment connections the backup bar left in place is a built-in discontinuity, and the welder must stop and start at the beam web center where residual stresses peak [38:37][39:41][40:11]. Modified pre-Northridge fixes: specify a weld electrode with minimum Charpy toughness, remove the bottom flange backup bar, gouge out the root weld to remove cracks, and add a fillet weld at top and bottom flanges [44:57][45:28]. Following the WPS precisely (watching preheat and interpass) was confirmed on the cover-plate specimens [50:06]. Fatigue life is improved by reducing initial flaw size a-zero and by fabrication quality, not by adding toughness [55:15][57:17].
### Erection Notes
Field welding posture is a named failure driver: the fabricator sets the assembly, it is bolted up, and the welder straddles the joint with a backup bar, welds across, must stop at the web, then comes back left-handed across the highest-residual-stress region at the center [38:37][39:41]. Educating the designer so the field welder is not forced to weld backwards in an awkward position is listed as a fabrication and fatigue control measure [60:23]. No crane, rigging, or sequencing detail beyond field weld access is discussed.
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Named failures: WWII Liberty ships (several hundred brittle fractures), Point Pleasant eyebar, Bryte Bend with out-of-spec plates at a Category E fatigue detail, Ingram Barge, and pre-Northridge moment connections where backup bars were left in, electrodes had no minimum specified Charpy, and pre-existing cracks acted as the initial flaw [10:45][14:20][40:42][41:13]. A structural trend is named: as scrap-car recycling pushed A36 actual yield up to 48-52 KSI, the strong-column weak-beam intent inverted toward a stronger beam, removing the ductile rotation the design relied on [43:54][44:26]. Inspection finding: herringbone (chevron) patterns trace back to the triaxial origin, and several origins had no pre-existing crack at all [27:42][51:40].
### Bid / Cost Implications
Engineering design is framed as an optimization of performance, safety, and cost [60:54][61:24]. Higher-strength steel was historically supplied at no added charge, which the designer accepts even though more strength is not what the connection needs [43:54][44:26]. Minimizing Category E details is called a cost-effective way to handle a fatigue situation [60:23]. Over-design is also penalized: too much conservatism (the OSHA Kansas Cowboy example) makes a project too expensive and poorly performing even though it is safe [62:24]. Specifying excessive notch toughness is wasted cost that does not fix poor design or fabrication [60:54].
### Your Company Application
For Mario as AWS D1.1 welding lead, the moment-connection lesson is direct: a minimum Charpy electrode, root-weld gouging, and removal of the bottom flange backup bar are concrete WPS and procedure controls, and the stop-start-at-the-web problem argues for planning field weld access and posture before the joint is in the air. For Tekla detailing and the in-house PE stamp, the constraint thesis says avoid junctions where deck plate, stiffeners, and connection plates pile into one point creating triaxial stress, and prefer reduced-constraint moment details (dog-bone RBS, elongated cope, free-flange) when a moment frame is in scope. For Ivan on takeoff, the actual-versus-specified yield drift means a stated A36 grade can deliver 48-52 KSI, which is a flag when connection behavior depends on a yield mismatch, not a tonnage input. For Paul on safety, the brittle-fracture cases reinforce that detail geometry and field weld conditions, not just material certs, drive catastrophic failure. No conflict with Your Company doctrine; the conventional structural-steel framing aligns, and nothing here touches PEMB language, supplier names, or locked rates. Doctrine flag: NONE.

## Steel Design After College - Part 12
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MbrFNxg9jJM | Duration: 34:11 | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This webinar segment covers three practical topics: anchor-rod placement tolerances and field-fix options at column bases, the design and connection economics of steel trusses, and computer-model verification practice. The unifying theme is closing the loop between analysis, design, and what actually gets built, plus controlling cost by controlling connections and field problems before they happen [00:01], [06:39], [27:45].
### Spec References
The speaker cites the AISC Code of Standard Practice anchor-rod placement tolerances versus ACI 117 (stated as "112 over 114," the concrete placement tolerance standard) and stresses they do not agree, with the AISC steel tolerances being much tighter [01:33], [02:03]. He references weldable anchor-rod material as "grade 55" and A36 as weldable grades [05:05], grade 50 and grade 65 steel for long-span truss chords [25:42], and the slenderness provisions of Chapter F for slender tee compression elements [18:06]. No AISC 360 section numbers, AISC 341 seismic sections, AWS D1.1 clauses, RCSC sections, or Design Guide numbers were stated by number; treat the rest as general principles, no section cited.
### Technical Details
A truss is framed as a beam: diagonals and posts carry shear, chords carry the flexural couple, so chord force equals the moment diagram divided by truss depth (M/D) [07:42], [10:49]. Economical truss depth runs 1/10 to 1/12 of span, with a flat cost curve in that range [11:51]. Truss types named: king post, scissors, bowstring, and a "Brunel" teardrop catenary truss after engineer I. K. Brunel [08:44], [09:14]. Panel points should be set so loads frame in at the joints, keeping chords as axial-only columns rather than beam-columns, and uniform load on a top chord should be avoided because it adds moment to an already heavily loaded compression chord [13:26], [13:58]. Secondary bending moments in pin-modeled chords are generally negligible and may be ignored, but if chords are modeled continuous, the connections must be designed continuous to match [15:30], [16:02].
### Fabrication Notes
The shop-versus-field rule: if the truss is 16 feet deep or less it can ship over the highway (about 13 feet routine, up to 16 with a special permit), so make all joints shop welded, ship in one piece, and use a bolted splice only every 60 to 120 feet; deeper trusses force field-bolted connections [16:33], [17:05]. Connection cost dominates heavy trusses, where connection weight (gusset plates, bolts, stiffeners, welds) can be 30 to 35 percent of total truss weight, so simplifying connections and even spending more on members can be the cheaper path [12:23], [12:54]. Connection options scale with load: single gusset for double-angle or tee members, slotting and perimeter-welding HSS pipe or tube to a single gusset, single-gusset wide-flange with claw angles for medium loads, and double gusset plates (one each side, bolted flanges) as the standard for heavy W12/W14/W16 chords [16:33], [18:37], [20:39], [21:09]. Tees that deepen the stem let web members bolt or weld directly and save a gusset, with the trade-off of slender-element checks per Chapter F [18:06].
### Erection Notes
The engineer should carry a preconceived erection procedure and show it as a suggested sequence on the drawings, since for long-span roofs the heaviest loads can occur during erection [22:41], [23:11]. Long-span design should model an out-of-straightness (built-in P-Delta) because the truss will end up that way regardless [24:12], [24:42]. Slip-critical bolts with oversized holes are recommended to absorb fit-up and reduce field fixes and hole wallowing, though fabricators argue the cost both ways and the fabricator-erector team should settle it [24:42], [25:12]. The Miller Park "Big Blue" crane collapse is referenced as an erection-load lesson, attributed primarily to operating the crane outside acceptable wind conditions [26:45], [27:15].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The headline failure is a mislocated anchor rod, for example a 2-inch rod set 3 inches off, which is an expensive, schedule-killing fix because the column usually cannot move [00:01]. Contractors exploiting the looser ACI concrete tolerance to dodge the tighter AISC tolerance is named as a recurring contractual trap [02:03]. Model-side errors named: designing one steel grade on the drawings (grade 50) while the analysis used another (A36) or vice versa, wrong unbraced length assumed by the program (it often defaults to member length when the real value may be half or twice that), ignoring the roughly 5 percent friction at "frictionless" pot bearings or Teflon sliding supports which can crack supports under large axial force, and stopping at first-order analysis instead of running second-order [27:45], [30:51], [31:52], [28:45].
### Bid / Cost Implications
In heavy long-span trusses the money is in the connections, not the member sizes, so design simplicity at the joints drives bid price more than tonnage [12:23]. Engaging the fabricator and erector early to capture shop preferences yields the best bid price, and grouping repetitive truss member sizes can trade a little extra tonnage for detailing and fabrication savings [22:09], [22:41]. Grade 65 steel for long-span chords costs only 0 to 3 percent more than grade 50 and reduces member sizes, effectively free strength, with the caveat of overseas sourcing and a possible shipping delay that pre-ordering can absorb [25:42], [26:12].
### Your Company Application
This maps directly to Your Company anchor-rod doctrine: specify AISC Code of Standard Practice tolerances explicitly so a GC cannot fall back on looser ACI 117 numbers, require top and bottom templates and a qualified surveyor at the pre-construction meeting, and design rods with extra extension length so a pushed-down rod still takes a nut. Ivan's takeoff should treat heavy-truss connection steel (gussets, stiffeners, claw angles) as up to 30 to 35 percent of truss weight rather than pricing bare members, and should flag grade 65 chord material with its overseas lead time on long-span jobs. Mario's shop benefits from the 16-foot ship-depth rule that keeps welding in the shop with only periodic field-bolted splices, and the field-welding caution (wind, rain, inspector required) supports our shop-weld field-bolt default; Paul's safety scope picks up the Miller Park wind-condition crane lesson for long-span erection. Tekla detailing should sketch the connection first then size members, and our in-house PE stamp work should keep analysis-to-drawing grade consistency, correct unbraced lengths, the 5 percent sliding-support friction force, and a first-order versus second-order comparison flagged when the difference exceeds 10 to 15 percent. DOCTRINE FLAGS: NONE. The content is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language and no supplier names beyond a generic mention of overseas mill sourcing.

## Steel Design After College - Part 11
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=F-IsJMmRqWI | Duration: 31:26 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24

### Core Concept
This session is a fast overview of column base plate and anchor rod design, framed as a preview of the reissued AISC Design Guide 1 authored by Jim Fisher and Larry Kloiber [00:32]. The base plate is presented as a critical element because it is the interface between the steel frame and the foundation, and a frequent earthquake failure point where bases rotate inelastically and fail in a non-ductile manner if not detailed properly [01:33][02:05]. The speaker walks through three load cases (axial compression or tension, axial plus shear as in braced frames, and axial plus moment as in moment frames), bearing and bending of the plate, anchor rod tension development, shear transfer, and the combined axial-plus-moment case ending in a quadratic solution for the bearing length Y [09:49][29:24].

### Spec References
Cited by the speaker: AISC Design Guide 1 (reissued, column base plate design) [00:32]; ASTM F1554 anchor rod spec with grades 36, 55, and 105 [07:13]; AISC manual Part 14, Figure 14-3 for base plate bending discussion [12:19]; the A2/A1 square-root bearing increase with a phi factor of 0.65 [05:37][15:25]; ACI 318 Appendix D for anchor design (embedded and post-installed), referenced to editions 318-02 and 318-05 [16:29][17:01]; ACI 318 Chapter 11 shear friction [18:36][20:09]; PCI Handbook corbel design analogy for an edge-loaded column [27:21]; OSHA four-anchor-rod minimum with the 300 lb load at 18 in eccentricity [10:19]. The speaker also references an unnamed higher-strength ASTM rod grade ending in BD reaching about 150 KSI Fu but states he does not recall its full designation [07:45].

### Technical Details
Base plate steel options given: A36 available to 8 in thickness then a lower grade above that, or A572 Gr 50 to 4 in and Gr 42 from 4 to 6 in, with A36 preferred as more economical and increasing thickness preferred over increasing strength [03:36][04:06]. Anchor rod material of choice is F1554 Gr 36 because it is weldable; Gr 55 can be special-ordered weldable; Gr 105 is not weldable under any circumstances [07:13][07:45]. F1554 is color coded blue for 36, yellow for 55, red for 105, with a white paint mark at the embedded end for weldable Gr 55 [09:17]. For high uplift, the preferred load path extends anchor rods up the side of the column into a pocket so the rod takes tension directly to the foundation, leaving the base plate to carry compression only and sparing the perimeter weld [13:20][14:23]. ACI Appendix D shear limit states named are anchor shear strength, concrete breakout in shear, and concrete pryout, with pryout generally not governing for the deep 18 to 72 in rods used in steel buildings [20:41][21:42]. Combined shear and tension uses an Appendix D interaction surface, linearized with a free zone where small tension may be ignored [24:18].

### Fabrication Notes
A36 plate is the shop default to control cost; higher grades are reserved for architectural thickness limits [04:06]. Fillet welds are always preferred over PJP or CJP welds for cost wherever forces allow, with PJP or CJP used only when fillets cannot carry the load [04:36]. In high seismic zones, CJP is preferred over PJP because of the built-in root defect in a PJP [05:07]. Galvanized anchors and nuts must be purchased from the same supplier and shipped as a matched assembly [08:46]. The combined-action anchor rod calculations near concrete edges are described as nasty and error-prone, justifying an in-house spreadsheet because the hand calc is worth doing only once [23:14][23:46].

### Erection Notes
Grout transfers base plate load to the foundation and is normally non-metallic; metallic grout is reserved for vibratory equipment and costs more [05:07][05:37]. Grout strength by cube test at 28 days is kept at twice the supporting concrete strength so the A2/A1 bearing increase is always satisfied without rechecking [05:37][06:09]. Double-nutted anchor rods in outdoor or exposed conditions are not grouted, because trapped grout cracks, holds moisture, and corrodes the rod, which is why highway light poles are nutted rather than grouted [06:09][06:40]. Post-installed anchors suit only very small loads and are discouraged for building columns unless drilled and epoxy grouted [08:15]. Anchor rod placement should use a template so rods land in the right location and shear can be designed straight through the rod [26:19].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Earthquake column base failures occur when bases are not detailed for inelastic rotation: the plate fractures, the anchor rods rip out, or high brace-frame shear is not handled [02:05]. Modeling a base as purely pinned or fixed while ignoring real rotational stiffness produces errors in computed drift and P-delta [03:06]. A missed failure path is the inclined 1 to 1.5 tension crack at the embedded nut, where lost development length on the hooked rebar up the pier means the uplift is not carried [17:31][18:36]. The speaker repeatedly flags that concrete contractors frequently set anchor rods wrong, requiring exotic field fixes covered in a separate lecture [25:49][26:19]. An edge-loaded heavy column can fail along a corbel-like diagonal plane that some engineers do not recognize [26:51].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Cost guidance is explicit: A36 plate over A572, thickness over strength, and fillet welds over PJP or CJP all reduce cost [04:06][04:36]. Taking large uplift through the base plate and perimeter weld is called too expensive a place to spend money; routing the rod up the column side is cheaper and stronger [13:20]. Four-inch rods at Gr 105 or the special high-strength grade are noted as very expensive and as demanding heavy foundation development [07:45][08:15]. For high shear, the office default is to bite the bullet with heavy anchor rods and shear friction rather than detailing shear lugs, because lugs invite both concrete placement and weld errors [25:18][25:49].

### Your Company Application
For Ivan takeoff, this maps to anchor rod scope: capture F1554 grade, weldable callouts, galvanizing, the OSHA four-rod minimum, and rod length, since 18 to 72 in deep rods and Gr 105 versus the higher grade swing material cost sharply. For our in-house PE stamp, the A2/A1 bearing rule with phi 0.65, the ACI 318 Appendix D shear and breakout limit states, the shear friction path, and the kern-based axial-plus-moment quadratic for Y are the governing checks, and the speaker's advice to computerize the edge-anchor calc aligns with a validator-backed spreadsheet rather than trusting hand or LLM math. For anchor rod setting and tolerance, the template-set requirement and the no-grout-on-double-nutted-exposed-rod rule should be standing field notes for Mario and the erection crew, with Paul tracking the OSHA four-rod, 300 lb at 18 in stability condition during column raising. Mario's welding rules confirmed here: prefer fillets, use CJP not PJP in seismic, all under AWS D1.1 practice. Conflict with Your Company doctrine: NONE. This is conventional structural steel, no PEMB language used in the entry, and all spec numbers are quoted as stated rather than generated.

## Steel Design After College - Part 10
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=k8KGJ2mnf5E | Duration: 31:58 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This part covers diaphragm modeling in multistory and high-rise steel buildings, and the analysis errors that flow from the rigid-diaphragm assumption [00:00]. The speaker explains that programs like ETABS assume an infinitely rigid diaphragm to cut degrees of freedom and shorten solution time, but anything connected to that rigid diaphragm becomes effectively rigid, undergoes no axial shortening, and therefore picks up no axial force [00:33-01:36]. The central teaching point is the load path: forces in the diaphragm, collectors, drag struts, and brace beams must be tracked by hand or by correctly modeling the diaphragm, because a postprocessor blindly trusts whatever the model fed it.

### Spec References
General principles, no section cited. The lecturer does not call out any AISC 360 section, AISC 341 seismic clause, AWS, RCSC, or Design Guide by number in this segment. The content is analysis-modeling theory (diaphragm rigidity, collectors, drag struts, Vierendeel action) rather than code-clause recitation.

### Technical Details
A brace beam (the horizontal beam connecting the two columns at the top of a Chevron, or the beam in a diagonal-braced bay) shortens under diaphragm shear, and that shortening can contribute as much as 15% of the total story drift of a braced frame [02:38-03:09]. If both end joints are tied to a rigid diaphragm there is no relative in-plane displacement, so no deformation and no axial force [08:21-08:54]. The worked free-body shows a collector growing to 142 kips horizontal brace component plus 7.1 kips/ft line load over 10 ft, summing to 213 kips axial in the collector [07:15-08:21]. Modeling the diaphragm as in-plane shell elements (a crude 30 ft by 30 ft mesh is acceptable) captures diaphragm shear, hot spots, and tributary collection; flexible diaphragms can be modeled as shell or membrane elements [04:10-06:11]. Special cases flagged: large stair or atrium openings forcing shear into narrow neck regions, Vierendeel bending across atrium openings, L/T/Y-shaped plans with neck-down high-shear zones, and basement perimeter walls that are far stiffer than the assumed core load path [15:06-29:31].

### Fabrication Notes
No fabrication, shop fit-up, or QC content appears in this segment. The lecture stays in the analysis and design-modeling domain.

### Erection Notes
No erection, sequencing, bracing, or rigging content appears in this segment.

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The closing top-10 list names the recurring diaphragm errors [29:31-31:33]: diaphragm shear capacity never checked; connections not designed for chord and collector forces; collector force transfer into the vertical system ignored with no clear load path; chord and collector beams not designed for their axial shear forces; diaphragm not modeled at all; brace-beam axial force wrong because the beam was not released from the diaphragm; large floor openings ignored; basement walls wrongly assumed conservative to ignore; vertical lateral elements that transfer in plan with unrecognized horizontal shear transfer; and the root error, garbage in garbage out, where the engineer trusts the computer output without checking statics. Two named near-failures: a transfer-truss chord shown as a 14x90 against 14x400 diagonals because the chord was never released from the diaphragm, which would have collapsed when shoring was removed [22:22-24:55]; and a mezzanine-core column designed as braced at a floor that had no vertical bracing, giving it twice the unbraced length and a buckling failure under 12,000 kips [17:09-19:17].

### Bid / Cost Implications
The cost signal here is member sizing driven by correct force capture. A brace beam designed only for gravity reads as a W18x35; once the axial collector load is captured it jumps to a 14x120 [13:01-13:31], a large weight and cost swing that a takeoff would miss if it trusted unverified analysis output. Atrium, neck-down, and offset-brace conditions add reinforcing steel in the slab or supplemental steel members under the slab to carry diaphragm shear [16:08-26:25], all of which affect tonnage and cost.

### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, the lesson is that member weights coming off an analysis postprocessor can be silently wrong when the diaphragm assumption hides axial force, so a chord or collector that looks light next to its diagonals (the 14x90 against 14x400 tell) is a flag to query the EOR rather than price as-shown. This reinforces Your Company doctrine: verify, do not generate, and never trust unguarded model math; aisc_validator.py confirms the shape weight but cannot confirm the force was captured, so an undersized collector is a design-input risk to surface, not a number to silently price. For the in-house PE stamp, the segment is a direct caution that whoever stamps owns the statics check behind the computer output. No conflict with Your Company doctrine. NONE.
