## Steel Design After College - Part 9
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HliH5COHYi4 | Duration: 33:49 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This session teaches horizontal diaphragm behavior and design: how a floor or roof deck collects in-plane wind or seismic shear and distributes it to the vertical lateral-load-resisting (VLR) elements. The speaker classifies diaphragms as rigid, semi-rigid, or flexible and shows that this classification depends not only on the material (concrete slab vs metal deck) but also on the spacing of the VLR elements, that is the diaphragm aspect ratio [03:37][07:15]. The controlling idea is to treat a simple rectangular diaphragm as a deep beam spanning between VLR supports, with a shear and moment diagram, chord forces at the edges, and a verified load path from the field of the deck through collectors and connections into the bracing [11:55][32:28].

### Spec References
The speaker cites IBC 2003 and IBC 2006 for the code definition of a flexible diaphragm: flexible when the maximum diaphragm lateral deformation (Delta D) exceeds two times the average story drift (Delta VR) of the associated story [04:08][04:40]. He references the Steel Deck Institute (SDI) for an alternate classification based on shear stiffness G Prime [05:12][06:12], and ACI 318 Chapter 21 with ACI equation 21-10 for the nominal shear strength of a concrete-slab diaphragm [28:52]. He names the SDI diaphragm design manual and research by Larry Luttrell of West Virginia University [22:11][27:50][28:20], and Jim Fisher's book "Designing with Steel Joists, Joist Girders and Steel Deck" for joist-seat shear capacity [17:32]. No AISC 360 section, AISC 341 section, AWS D1.1 clause, or RCSC reference was cited.

### Technical Details
Diaphragm shear stiffness is expressed as G Prime, equal to deck thickness T times the shear modulus G, and is tabulated in deck catalogs for both bare and concrete-filled decks [21:06][23:14][24:16]. Shear deflection generally controls over flexural deflection because diaphragms are very deep in their own plane; the shear deflection of a uniformly loaded shear beam goes as q L squared over 8 B T G [20:36][21:06]. Diaphragm shear strength S is governed by four phenomena: edge fastener strength, interior panel strength, corner fastener strength, and shear buckling of the deck, tabulated in pounds per linear foot of attachment [24:48][25:19]. Typical bare-deck shear capacity runs about 150 to 200 up to roughly 1200 lb/ft, with most decks in the 400 to 500 lb/ft range; California high-seismic work uses fillers to raise capacity [25:19][25:49]. Terminology covered includes drag struts, collector beams, chord (tension and compression) elements, the field of the diaphragm, support fasteners, side-lap fasteners, and the deck fastening pattern notation such as 36/3, 36/4, and 36/9 [08:47][30:24].

### Fabrication Notes
The session is design-oriented, but fabrication-relevant points are the deck-to-purlin attachment pattern and side-lap fastening, since the chosen pattern (welds or screws, 36/3 through 36/9) dictates the transferable shear per running foot and the published G Prime value [22:43][30:54]. The speaker notes safety factors of about 2.75 to 3.25 depending on whether the diaphragm is welded, screwed, or filled, reflecting test scatter [26:50][27:20]. He warns that catalog strengths must be read carefully for whether they are stated as ASD or LRFD values and whether the one-third ASD wind increase is already built in, to avoid taking the increase twice [25:49][27:20].

### Erection Notes
Standing-seam roofs have no diaphragm capacity and act only as linear vertical-load elements, so the erector must install a separate horizontal diaphragm, commonly rod bracing, angles, or T's woven between bar joists and over, under, or through purlins, which the speaker calls expensive and no fun to erect [00:33][01:35][02:05]. Where joist seats create a 2.5 in or 5 in gap between the concrete slab plane and the steel beam, filler elements (an angle, a tube section, or a channel) are field-added to supplement the limited joist-seat shear capacity and complete the load path down into the beam [16:29][18:02]. The erector must respect the load path through collector beams, beam-to-column connections, and across to the brace frame so high diaphragm shears actually reach the ground [15:29][16:29].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The repeated failure mode is an incomplete or invalid diaphragm load path: forgetting that a standing-seam roof carries no shear, or failing to supplement joist seats in a high-wind or high-seismic condition, which has produced documented diaphragm failures in earthquakes [01:04][18:32][19:04]. Offsets where a brace frame steps from one plane to another dump the full accumulated shear from above into the diaphragm at that level, an easily missed high-shear condition [11:23][11:55]. Large floor openings act like a cope and create local shear and bending concentrations that need added reinforcing steel and a shear check across the reduced width [19:35][20:06].

### Bid / Cost Implications
The speaker is explicit that supplemental diaphragm steel is a real cost. Adding a horizontal rod or angle diaphragm under a standing-seam roof, weaving steel between joists and purlins, is described as expensive and labor-intensive to erect [01:35][02:05]. Filler tubes, angles, or channels to bridge joist-seat gaps in high-shear roofs are added pieces and added fabrication and field labor [18:32]. The takeoff must reflect that the deck fastening pattern (36/3 vs 36/9) and side-lap count drive both connection labor and required deck strength, so a denser pattern in a high-seismic or high-wind zone carries more installation cost [30:54][31:25].

### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff this is a reminder that on any standing-seam or untopped-deck roof, the diaphragm steel (rod bracing, edge angles, collector and drag elements, joist-seat fillers) is a separate line item that the deck quantity alone does not capture; harvest it from the framing plan and lateral notes, not from SF x psf. For Mario's shop and field crew, the deck-to-purlin weld or screw pattern and side-lap fastening are the diaphragm load path, so the specified 36/x pattern and any filler tubes or angles must be installed exactly as detailed. Tekla detailing should carry collector beams, drag struts, chord/edge angles, and joist-seat fillers as modeled members so they appear in the takeoff. For the in-house PE stamp, the diaphragm classification (IBC flexible-when-Delta-D-exceeds-twice-Delta-VR), the G Prime stiffness source, the deck shear strength S, and the chord-force design are the items to verify, and any concrete-fill diaphragm chord can be rebar per ACI 318 Chapter 21. No supplier name should reach client output even though the speaker references a manufacturer catalog generically; that is internal sourcing only. DOCTRINE CONFLICT: NONE. The standing-seam and metal-building references are the speaker's general engineering examples, not a positioning statement, so no PEMB-language issue arises in our outward copy.

## Steel Design After College - Part 8
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VIi2Ka3Zv-s | Duration: 36:54 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This part covers composite and non-composite steel deck selection and then transitions into the role of floor and roof diaphragms in lateral load resistance. The central economic thesis is that labor cost now dominates material cost, so "least weight is least cost" is no longer true; in-place steel price is driven by manhours per ton and piece count, not pounds per square foot [00:32][01:33][02:05]. The deck discussion runs from depth and gauge economy through attachment for wind uplift, and the diaphragm discussion treats the floor as a deep horizontal beam spanning between the vertical lateral force resisting system [34:08][34:38].

### Spec References
The speaker cites the AISC specification limiting composite-action deck to a 3 inch maximum depth because deeper composite decks had not been tested [00:01]. He cites the Steel Deck Institute (SDI) composite deck design handbook 1997 and SDI minimum attachment of 18 inches on center in the field and 12 inches on center at perimeter and corners when rib spacing is less than or equal to 6 inches, otherwise at every rib [07:13][17:58]. He cites Factory Mutual roof live-load criteria of 200 lb per foot at midspan with a deflection limit of L/240, the FM uplift class system (I-90 means 90 psf uplift), Underwriter Laboratories span requirements, and the AISC Code of Standard Practice column out-of-plumb tolerance of L/500 [15:53][18:29][20:33][35:42]. Coating callouts G60 and G90 galvanizing and ASTM A992 / A36 material grades are named, as are coating designations G60 and G90 [10:14][29:58]. No AISC 360 chapter, AISC 341 seismic section, AWS D1.1 clause, or RCSC section was stated.

### Technical Details
Composite deck comes in 1.5, 2, and 3 inch depths; cellular decks serve office under-floor access and Epic-type slotted decks allow hanging loads [00:01][04:06]. Non-composite decks split into narrow rib, intermediate rib, and wide rib (type A, type F, type B), with vented form deck required under lightweight insulating concrete so moisture can cure out [12:48][23:08]. The SDI procedure for a heavy concentrated load on a composite slab projects the B2 loading footprint through the topping to a B-sub-m effective width, then checks punching shear, one-way shear, and flexural capacity with added perpendicular reinforcing over the W distance [07:43][08:43]. Diaphragm theory treats the floor deck as the web of a deep beam and the spandrel or edge angle as the chord, transferring in-plane shear to brace frames, moment frames, or shear walls [34:38][35:09].

### Fabrication Notes
The shop and material economy points dominate over fab tolerances here. The speaker observes that 18 gauge is the practical economic floor for deck thickness; 19 and 20 gauge price well, but 16 gauge jumps sharply in cost, so heavier deck rarely pencils out even when it could span farther [05:08][05:38]. Coating selection is a fabrication-spec decision: G90 for all roofs because the deck serves as positive reinforcement and must resist corrosion, G60 or a phosphatized painted finish acceptable on floors at the owner's accepted risk [11:15][24:09]. A field-experience note: heater kerosene oil contaminating the underside of deck prevents paint adhesion and forces a re-clean, so a cleanliness clause belongs in the spec [26:24].

### Erection Notes
Piece-count reduction is framed as the primary erection-cost lever; erectors report that cutting handled pieces by a quarter to a third yields meaningful savings, achieved by longer-spanning deck that widens purlin and floor-beam spacing [02:05][02:35]. The counter-issue is that deep heavy decks (a 7 inch 15 or 16 gauge sheet) exceed safe two-man manhandling when the crane lands them, where 2 and 3 inch sheets are handled by two men per end [03:06][03:36]. Curved long-span roofs create a gap between the deck and a flat purlin top; either a continuous bent plate is run along the member so the deck bears flat, or a power-actuated fastener manufacturer will not warrant capacity unless the deck bears flat, which required field load testing on one project [30:28][31:30].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Failing to specify a vented form deck under insulating concrete leaves the concrete permanently mushy because moisture cannot escape, taking weeks or months to dry [23:39]. Hurricane-region roof membrane blow-offs are attributed to decks not attached properly at corners and edges where uplift pressures peak; engineers who say nothing about fastening get only SDI minimums from the roofing contractor, "you don't get anything you don't pay for" [18:29][24:40]. Power-driven pins gave early field trouble where varying steel hardness changed the required pin type and driving power, improved somewhat by the more consistent A992 material [29:28]. Crimped side-lap fasteners historically gave almost no diaphragm capacity unless a patented crimping process is used [28:57].

### Bid / Cost Implications
The recurring estimating message is that two designs at 12 vs 14 psf are not ranked by weight but by manhours per ton and dollars per ton across fabrication, shipping, handling, and erection, so a heavier longer-spanning system with fewer pieces can be cheaper in place [01:33][02:05]. Deck cost premiums are non-linear: gauge above 18 jumps disproportionately, and exotic coatings or paints raise unit deck cost, so spec choices directly move the deck line item [05:38][19:29]. Form deck with bar joist at 2 to 3 foot spacing remains slightly cheaper than composite deck with composite beams at 8 to 10 foot on center per the speaker's market, a comparison worth pricing both ways [22:06][22:37].

### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff and the aisc_validator.py member workflow, this confirms our doctrine that piece count and manhours, not least weight, govern the bid; when two framing schemes are close on tonnage, Ivan should flag the lower-piece-count option and let labor rates decide rather than picking the lighter one. The deck rules feed our roof-deck $[ROOF DECK RATE]/SF and composite $[COMPOSITE DECK RATE]/SF gates directly: gauge above 18, G90 coating, and hurricane-zone fastening at corners and edges are real cost adders Ivan should not absorb silently, and a vented form deck under insulating concrete is a spec item to confirm with the GC. For Mario's shop crew and field bolting, the manhandling limit on deep 15-16 gauge sheets and the puddle-weld vs power-driven-pin attachment choice are crew-safety and method questions to route through Paul Guerrero, especially Houston Gulf Coast hurricane uplift detailing. The diaphragm-as-deep-beam material is a Tekla detailing and in-house PE stamp concern where spandrel-to-column connections must carry diaphragm shear through the joint, which our PE should verify on stamped sets. Doctrine conflict: NONE. The video names bar-joist manufacturers (Vulcraft, Mercor) generically as the speaker's own examples; per our rules those names stay internal and never appear on any Your Company client output.

## Steel Design After College - Part 7
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=btZZXEZbESo | Duration: 32:58 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This part covers the analysis and modeling of steel lateral load resisting systems for wind, then transitions into metal deck design. The presenter walks through how to model moment frame joints and panel zone deformation, how to take the correct unbraced lengths for brace beams in concentric braced frames, how foundation rotational stiffness reduces drift, how to set serviceability drift and strength P-Delta limits, and how a low lateral load combined with high gravity load can produce a story stability problem even when a drift limit is met [00:02 to 29:58]. The closing section covers composite deck, form deck, and roof deck basics [30:28 to 32:32].

### Spec References
The presenter cites the AISC LRFD specification generically and names specific items: the alignment chart nomograph G factor (a base rotational stiffness of G equal to 10 for a reasonably fixed footing, and G equal to 1 for a so-called rigid foundation) attributed to a paper by Ted Galambos [11:25 to 12:55]; the 1999 LRFD spec brace-frame stiffness requirements [19:07]; the 2005 AISC specification direct analysis method in Chapter C and Appendix 7, which reduces member EI to 80 percent of gross and uses the notional load concept [19:37 to 21:08]. He also references the PCI Handbook for modeling footing and base-plate/anchor-bolt rotational stiffness [13:27], and his own 1993 Engineering Journal article on a drift damage index [21:40]. No bolting, welding, or seismic detailing sections were cited.

### Technical Details
For moment frame joints, the recommendation is to model center-to-center of joint rather than treating the panel zone as infinitely rigid, because a rigid-joint plus clear-span model underestimates drift from panel zone shear deformation; for tube buildings with columns at 10 to 15 feet on center, explicitly model panel zone deformation [00:33 to 03:41]. Brace beams in Chevron and X-braced frames carry both gravity and large axial load, so they are designed as beam-columns, and the controlling point is that torsional buckling (KLz) is often ignored by software postprocessors even though a slab can make KL minor zero; the fix is to trick the software by setting K minor to the actual torsional unbraced length (for example 30 feet, or 15 feet with a mid-span kicker) [04:13 to 09:51]. He warns against counting a non-fireproofed elevator divider beam as a brace point, and against the rigid diaphragm assumption inhibiting axial shortening of a brace beam [05:13, 09:51 to 10:52]. Serviceability uses a drift limit of 0.0025 (one over 400) under 10-year or 50-year wind, including P-Delta and composite stiffness; strength P-Delta is held to a Q of 0.25 (a 1.33 amplification), and under factored gravity Q is limited to 0.375 (1.6) [14:59 to 21:40]. The story stability index is Q equals P-Delta over VH; a narrow face with low wind area but full gravity mass can be a soft, unstable direction, as in the Boston Hancock building, which was stiffened and fitted with a tuned mass damper [24:15 to 29:28].

### Fabrication Notes
This webinar is design-and-analysis focused and gives no shop fabrication, fit-up, tolerance, or QC content.

### Erection Notes
No erection, sequencing, bracing, crane, or rigging procedures are covered.

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The errors named are analysis and design errors, not inspection rejections. The main ones are taking a beam-column joint as infinitely rigid and then using clear-span member properties, which underestimates drift [02:08]; designing a brace beam for KL major with KL minor of zero and forgetting torsional buckling as a limit state [08:17]; relying on a non-fireproofed elevator divider beam as a code-valid brace point [10:21]; letting a rigid diaphragm assumption suppress real brace-beam axial shortening [05:13]; and assuming a drift-limit-satisfying frame is automatically free of a story stability problem [24:45]. The Boston Hancock building is cited as a real case of an undetected stability and motion-perception problem [27:57 to 29:28].

### Bid / Cost Implications
No direct cost, schedule, bid, or estimating discussion appears. The indirect implication for a fabricator is that lateral-system member sizes, and therefore tonnage, are sensitive to how the engineer of record models drift and stability, which can move column and brace-beam weights between an early and a final design.

### Your Company Application
This is reference material for the in-house PE stamp and for anyone reviewing an engineer-of-record lateral package, not for shop or field crews. For Ivan's takeoff it is a reminder that brace-beam and column weights on a moment or braced frame can shift with the EOR's drift modeling, so a lateral-frame tonnage carried before the design is final should be tagged medium confidence and reconciled against the stamped member schedule through aisc_validator.py rather than scaled. The deck section maps to Your Company's standing scope that deck supply and install stays in-house: it confirms composite deck acts as positive slab reinforcement except under forklift or vibratory loading, where the slab must be reinforced conventionally, and distinguishes form deck (a stay-in-place form, not reinforcement) from roof deck. The torsional-buckling and panel-zone notes are EOR design concerns that do not change validated AISC weights or rates. Nothing here touches Mario's welding, Paul's safety scope, Tekla detailing, anchor rods, joists, field bolting, or ACP controls. Doctrine flags: NONE.

## Steel Design After College - Part 6
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K0G-6EdO0ho | Duration: 26:33 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This lecture covers lateral analysis of steel buildings for wind, focused on the practical modeling and limit-state decisions a structural engineer makes when designing the vertical lateral load resisting system (abbreviated VLR throughout) [00:31]. The speaker frames the work around three numbered analyses: analysis one serviceability, analysis two strength, and analysis three stability under sustained gravity load [07:42]. The recurring theme is that all-steel moment frames are almost always controlled by wind drift or seismic drift rather than strength, so the engineer designs for stiffness and gets strength for free, while brace frames are the reverse and end up lighter [05:08][06:10].

### Spec References
ASCE 7 chapter 6 commentary is cited for a table that converts a 50-year mean recurrence wind event to a 10-year, 25-year, or other return period, and chapter 6 is cited again for the four required wind load cases shown in figure 6-9 [15:17][16:19]. ACI 318 chapter 10 is cited as the concrete code that also uses the symbol Q for the stability index [09:43]. Strength load combinations are stated as 1.6 times nominal wind, and the stability analysis mass uses 1.2 dead plus 1.6 live [08:12][26:01]. No AISC 360, AISC 341, AWS D1.1, RCSC, or Design Guide section was cited in this segment.

### Technical Details
The interstory stability index Q is defined as P times Delta divided by V times H, where P is the sum of gravity load on the story, Delta is the story drift relative to the story below, V is the story shear, and H is the story height [10:13]. The leaning-column P-Delta effect can weaken a frame by 10 to 15 percent, so a moment-frame-only model must carry a dummy column holding the tributary gravity load to capture it [03:35]. The four ASCE 7 wind cases run from full load on the projected area in each orthogonal direction, to a 25 percent base-shear reduction paired with a 15 percent eccentricity for torsion, to a quartering diagonal wind at three quarters value, to the combined diagonal-plus-eccentric case [16:50][17:50]. Torsional behavior is checked through mode shapes, wanting the first two modes translational and the third torsional, and the speaker recommends counting on real foundation rotational stiffness rather than assuming a pinned base, which over-stiffens the tall first story [22:26][12:14].

### Fabrication Notes
This is a structural design lecture with no fabrication, fit-up, shop-process, or shop-QC content.

### Erection Notes
No erection, field sequencing, bracing, or rigging content appears in this segment. The only field-adjacent note is a reminder to check foundation load for net uplift under brace frames [06:10].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The speaker names design modeling errors rather than fabrication or weld inspection failures. The main ones are running straight to the computer model without sanity-checking whether the frame deflects logically under wind, a garbage-in garbage-out risk [04:37]; omitting leaning-column gravity load and underestimating drift and member sizes by 10 to 15 percent [03:35]; assuming a pinned foundation base and oversizing first-story members [12:14]; and concentrating all lateral resistance at the building core, which produces torsional instability that has caused real earthquake damage [21:26].

### Bid / Cost Implications
The cost lever in this lecture is steel weight. Brace frames are designed for strength and pick up drift control for free, so they yield a lighter steel building than moment frames, which are designed for drift and pick up strength for free [06:10]. Architects resist brace frames because they occupy space, so the engineer negotiates placement early, and a combined brace-plus-moment-frame system is offered as efficient [06:40][07:11]. Assuming a pinned base instead of crediting real foundation stiffness pushes extra steel into the first-story beams and columns, a direct weight and cost penalty [12:14].

### Your Company Application
This content sits with the design engineer and the in-house PE stamp, not with the shop or field crews, so Mario and Paul gain nothing here and Tekla detailing is downstream of these decisions. For Ivan and takeoff, the usable signal is that frame type drives tonnage: a brace-frame solution generally tonnages lighter than an equivalent moment frame, which is a sanity check on a competitor or design assumption when estimating, though our member takeoff still runs through aisc_validator.py and never substitutes a rule of thumb for a measured count. On the Asian City Plaza project controls, the wind-case and torsional-distribution discussion is a reminder that a low-rise multi-wing job should confirm the EOR's lateral system before we price secondary and bracing steel. No conflict with Your Company doctrine: this is structural-design methodology and the no-PEMB positioning is untouched. NONE.

## Steel Design After College - Part 5
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=e4Gejxd4ROQ | Duration: 29:08 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This segment covers composite beam design under the 2005 AISC spec, focused on deflection limits, the revised shear-stud capacity equation, and using composite action to control moment-frame drift [02:04][16:29]. The speaker walks through why the US lowered stud capacities after Virginia Tech testing, how to place studs in the strong versus weak position, and how to strengthen existing composite beams when a floor's live-load requirement increases [22:40]. The throughline is that composite floors are robust and conservative in practice but the stud equation and connection forces still need disciplined detailing.

### Spec References
The speaker cites AISC Design Guide 3 for serviceability deflection limits on beams supporting CMU, brick, or cladding [01:01][01:33]. He references the AISC 2005 specification and its Chapter I commentary for the revised shear-connector equation and the lower-bound moment of inertia equation [06:12][07:16][19:04]. The earlier 1999 spec is named for comparison, including its now-removed 10-kip LRFD and 6-kip ASD minimum connection reaction requirement [15:29]. Bolt grades A307, A325, and A490 are cited by grade [24:43][25:14]. Specific deflection ratios stated: L/240 total load, L/360 live load with a 1.5 inch cap, 3/8 inch under live load plus 50% superimposed dead for cladding, and L/600 under live cladding plus 60% superimposed dead [00:01][01:01][01:33].

### Technical Details
The new stud equation keeps the historic upper bound of 0.5 times stud area times the square root of f-prime-c times E-concrete, then applies two reduction factors: Rg (stud geometry condition) and Rp (stud position factor) [05:40][06:12][06:44]. Rp is 0.6 in the weak position, 0.75 in the strong position, and 1.0 only for a stud welded directly to steel with no deck [07:16][07:47]. Rg is 1.0 for a single stud per rib, 0.85 for two studs per rib, and 0.7 for three or more [08:18][08:48]. The net effect is roughly 5 to 15% lower stud capacities than the 1999 spec, but capacity is not very sensitive to small shortfalls in connector count [08:48][11:50]. For drift, the beam is split into three zones (bare-steel negative-moment zone assumed over half the span, a composite positive-moment zone using the lower-bound I, and a bare-steel zone next to the column defined by a 45-degree line to the effective flange width), then reduced to one effective I that raises bare-beam stiffness about 10 to 30% [18:03][19:35][20:07][21:39].

### Fabrication Notes
The deck stiffening rib in the flute center forces the field welder to place the stud on one side, creating the strong-versus-weak position problem; deck manufacturers will not remove that rib [03:37][04:08]. Strengthening an existing composite beam can be done by coring down, welding a stud by hand, and grouting back with non-shrink grout to add connectors, or by welding a wider cover plate with a downhand stitch fillet weld, or welding a tee to the bottom [22:40][23:11][23:43]. If the beam already has deflection, a tee profile must follow the bow, sometimes needing a shear tab to close the gap [24:13]. The speaker references David Ricker's and John Miller's Engineering Journal papers on strengthening and welding to existing beams [23:11][24:43].

### Erection Notes
Stud placement in the field is the central erection issue: a welder told to alternate strong and weak will reliably alternate, but if told to put all studs in the strong position he may carry over to the weak side near the end unless watched, so the engineer must show the placement scheme on the drawings [04:08][04:38][05:08]. Shear-connector spacing limits are unchanged at 3D, 4D, and 6D [13:26]. For uniformly loaded beams studs go on uniformly; for girders with three-point loading, the constant-moment center region theoretically needs no studs, so the drawings must state whether the program upsized for uniform placement or gives only the minimum count [11:50][12:24][12:55].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The named risk is a field welder placing studs in the weak position when the design assumed strong, leaving insufficient shear connectors for the intended live-load capacity [05:08]. Software that auto-designs moment-frame beams as non-composite is conservative but leaves drift capacity unclaimed [16:29][26:46]. A questioner raised a real case where 4 feet at the end of a 36-foot span had no slab; the answer is to draw the moment diagram and confirm the bare steel beam carries the moment at the non-composite location, accounting for moment development past the opening [25:44][26:15][27:16]. Quality checking of beams and cambers in the shop is normally the owner's testing laboratory under a plan prepared by the engineer of record, not the engineer's own job [27:49][28:19].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Counting composite action in moment-frame drift can lower beam sizes 10 to 30% for free since drift, not strength, usually governs moment frames [17:00][21:39]. Putting actual reactions and axial loads on the drawings rather than load-table values avoids the conservative inflated forces fabricators dislike and keeps connection material from being oversized [14:26][14:56][15:59]. Upgrading an existing floor's live-load rating may hinge on the connection, for example replacing 3/4 inch A307 bolts with A325 or A490, switching slip-critical to bearing, or going bolted to welded, each carrying different shop and shoring cost [24:43][25:14].

### Your Company Application
For Ivan's takeoff, the stud Rg and Rp reductions and the 3D/4D/6D spacing mean stud counts and the composite-deck supply line should follow the EOR's stated placement scheme, not a generic uniform assumption, so the takeoff reads the typical detail before pricing connectors. For Mario's shop and field crew, the strong-versus-weak stud placement is a welding-discipline item to flag in fit-up and field stud-welding, and the alternate-them rule is the safe default to call out. The reactions-on-drawings preference aligns with our practice of designing connections from actual forces under the in-house PE stamp rather than conservative load tables, which trims connection steel. For ACP controls, the moment-frame drift method and any existing-beam strengthening (cored studs with non-shrink grout, cover plates, welded tees) are scope and cost items to capture if a live-load change arises. No conflict with Your Company doctrine; this is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language.

## Steel Design After College - Part 4
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0OqYe8Uqn9Q | Duration: 32:35 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This webinar segment (slides 79 onward) covers composite beam design strength and serviceability under the 2005 AISC specification, with the bulk of the time spent on camber and floor levelness as the dominant real-world problem in composite floor construction [00:01], [07:13]. The speaker frames composite design around a plastic stress distribution model that lets you tune shear connectors to less than full composite action for economy [02:05], [02:35], and warns repeatedly that the precomposite construction stage, not the composite stage, often controls beam size [01:34].
### Spec References
The speaker cites AISC specification Chapter F for bare-steel and precomposite strength provisions [00:32], [05:11]; Chapter I and its commentary for composite moment-of-inertia options [27:32], [28:33]; the AISC Code of Standard Practice for camber tolerances [17:12], [19:48]; Design Guide 11 for floor vibration [22:56], Design Guide 5 (low and medium high-rise buildings) for a camber section [23:29], and Design Guide 3 for serviceability [26:31]. Load references are ASCE 7 load combinations including the 1.4 dead-alone case [06:43] and ASCE 7-02 Appendix B serviceability combinations [26:31]. The 25% minimum composite action is described as a suggestion, not a specification requirement [01:02].
### Technical Details
Plastic stress distribution requires a compact web meeting the h/tw limit; a non-compact web forces design by superposition of elastic stresses, an issue mainly for thin-web plate girders [00:32]. Effective flange width remains 1/8 of the span, half the distance to the adjacent beam centerline, or for spandrels the distance to the slab edge [03:38]. Short-term deflection uses an effective I equal to 75% of the transformed moment of inertia, the 25% reduction accounting for creep; long-term creep is sometimes estimated using 50% of E [28:33], [29:34]. Partially composite I is reduced by a summation-Q term, and the manual offers a lower-bound moment of inertia as a conservative simplified check [29:34], [30:37]. Total deflection is Delta 1 (precomposite bare beam under wet concrete) plus Delta 2 (composite section, superimposed dead and long-term live) plus Delta 3 (composite section, transient live) minus camber [31:07].
### Fabrication Notes
Camber is an imperfect hydraulic-ram process applied by trial and error, and identical beams can come out level, high, or low [19:48]. The speaker insists camber be measured and inspected at the fabrication plant in the unstressed condition, never in the erected field condition, because beams lose camber in transit and it is unfair to hold the fabricator to a field check; the Code of Standard Practice states this unstressed basis [17:43], [19:16]. Practical limits: round camber down to 1/4-inch increments, hold a 3/4-inch minimum (fabricators will not give a 1/2-inch camber), and treat anything over about 2 to 2-1/4 inches with caution [22:24], [10:54]. Welded cover plates and shop-welded edge angles change camber because welding heat alters it [08:14], [23:59].
### Erection Notes
The metal deck braces the top flange only when its flutes run perpendicular to the beam, so girders should be taken as unbraced over the distance between framing composite beams unless special construction bracing is provided [05:11], [05:41]. The pour method is an erection-stage decision the engineer controls by specification: pour to constant thickness (floor follows deck and beam deflection profile) or pour to a level floor with extra concrete as needed; multi-story contractors will give only the specified thickness and no more unless told otherwise, because extra concrete on every floor of a 60-plus-story building adds up [14:36], [15:38], [16:11].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
Over-camber is called the worst case: studs can end up exposed above the floor, which an inspector flags as a missing 2-hour fire rating, and a thinner-than-designed cover (2+3 instead of 2+4-1/2) can erode the composite flange strength you calculated [20:19], [21:22]. A real spandrel-beam case is described where a tube post and continuous sill turned the cambered beam into a vierendeel truss that stiffened it, the camber never came out, the curtain wall would not meet tolerance, and the posts had to be cut off and releveled at cost [09:18], [09:51]. A separate lawsuit involved floor vapor emission attacking reformulated low-VOC adhesives on structural floors [24:29], [25:30]. Common design oversights named: forgetting that chases and floor openings in hotels and condos cut effective flange, and forgetting that a bent-plate deck stop adds moment of inertia and kills the camber [04:41], [10:23].
### Bid / Cost Implications
The composite model lets cost track the client: developers wanting code-minimum office buildings get minimum composite action and the fewest studs, while an institutional owner planning future load increase may pay for full composite action and reserve capacity [02:35], [03:07]. Designing non-composite-and-heavier to avoid camber is a valid but more expensive option for clients willing to pay for a stiffer floor [12:28]. Shoring is rarely the most economical choice per contractors and adds long-term creep deflection [13:01]. Floor vibration design (Design Guide 11) for retail, convention, or ballroom floors can control and force upsizing of the whole framing, a direct cost driver [22:56].
### Your Company Application
For Mario's shop crew, the load-bearing takeaway is that camber must be checked at the plant in the unstressed condition with someone measuring each beam, since field camber checks are off the table once a beam ships; on any composite-deck job Your Company fabricates, build a shop camber-inspection step into the traveler and round camber to 1/4-inch with a 3/4-inch floor. For Ivan's takeoff, composite action percentage and stud count are a cost lever to confirm against the EOR drawings, not to assume, and Chapter F precomposite strength often sizes the beam, so the bare-steel weight is the governing tonnage input. For Tekla detailing, cover plates, bent-plate deck stops, and edge angles welded in the shop alter camber and must be modeled before the camber call is finalized. This is a structural composite-floor topic with no PEMB language and no conflict with Your Company doctrine. DOCTRINE FLAGS: NONE. Per Hard Rule 5, any beam weight or section property referenced from this material must still come from bridge/aisc_validator.py, not from the webinar.

## Steel Design After College - Part 3
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JbG64heJ3TE | Duration: 36:09 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This segment closes lateral-torsional buckling of flexural members and opens composite beam design, the speaker calling composite floor construction the bread and butter of steel building design [12:25]. Two ideas anchor the LTB wrap-up: local buckling is rarely an issue for rolled A992 beams but matters for built-up and a few wide-flange sections, and understanding the Cb moment-gradient factor often yields real savings in non-composite beam design [00:01]. The composite section is framed as practical problem-solving (floor flatness, levelness, camber, weak versus strong studs, ponding) rather than hand calculation, since most engineers run computer programs now [12:25].

### Spec References
Cited by the speaker: AISC 2005 specification (then-current) and its new stud capacities [10:55][13:58]; Chapter B compactness table for B/t ratios tied to rotation/ductility [05:39]; the Cb upper limit of 3.0 introduced in the 2005 spec [10:55]; AISC Design Guide 19 (fire), authored by John Ruddy [25:19]; AWS requirement that the stud ferrule be removed after welding and the bend (hammer) test for stud verification [15:33][16:04]; an AWS rule that unless the stud is over the web, stud diameter shall be no more than 2.5 times the flange thickness [18:34]; Steel Deck Institute minimum deck-attachment requirements [07:15][10:25]; UL fire listings D916, D902, and D925 for composite construction [26:20]. Material specs named: A992 (50 ksi), A36 and A572 (described as obsolete for rolled shapes), shear studs to ASTM A108 at 60 ksi, and steel fibers to ASTM C1116 [17:04][18:04][18:34].

### Technical Details
A992 rolled beams at Fy 50 ksi are standard; composite decks run 1.5, 2, or 3 inches deep with embossments, made composite by 3/4 inch headed studs, one to three per flute [15:02][15:33]. Normal-weight concrete is 3 ksi minimum to 10 ksi maximum, lightweight 3 to 6 ksi, with strengths above the cap usable for stiffness only, not strength [20:43]. Back-slab cracks over supports are expected because the slab is designed as simply supported but behaves continuously; tests show the cracks do not materially reduce flexural capacity, so the fix is extra mesh or bars cheered up over the support for crack control [21:13][22:15]. Minimum composite action: the speaker keeps it above the common 25% floor because at 25% the studs are strained hard and can break if poorly welded [35:04].

### Fabrication Notes
Stud welding quality is the recurring shop and field concern. The AWS ferrule must be hammered off after welding, and a bend test per AWS confirms a sound weld [16:04]. Stud guns left uncalibrated, especially in early-morning moisture on the deck, produce studs that are not properly welded, a dangerous condition [16:34]. To honor the AWS 2.5-times-flange-thickness rule when studs are not reliably placed over the web, the speaker's practice excludes composite beam webs thinner than about 0.3 inch, ruling out light sections such as W10x12, W10x15, W8x13, and W12x16 [19:06][19:39]. Deck-to-beam attachment uses 5/8 inch puddle welds in higher uplift zones (I60/I90) and 3/4 inch in high-seismic zones [07:45].

### Erection Notes
Deck welding pattern provides compression-flange bracing, with a roughly 12 inch on-center support spacing and wider field spacing, per the project spec and SDI minimums [10:25][29:29]. Decks should be laid as two- or three-span conditions, not simple spans; the detailer can almost always arrange this, and simple-span deck (for example across an elevator lobby) is a safety hazard because it can slip off its support, so high-rise records advise turning the deck to run parallel to the elevator front for a multi-span layout [31:31][32:01]. Decks are generally sized heavy enough to span the beams unshored [31:00].

### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
A documented girder collapse during construction killed a worker: the engineer assumed the girder was fully braced for the wet-concrete load, but where deck ran parallel the contractor placed only a couple of tack welds on a pan, leaving the long span effectively unbraced between third-point beams, producing a lateral-torsional buckling failure and a lawsuit [08:48][09:21]. Other named failures: shoddy stud welds with the ferrule left on [15:33], uncalibrated stud guns yielding unwelded studs [16:34], concrete strength below D916's 3500 psi normal-weight minimum (some use 2500 or 3000) [27:55], and lightweight concrete density above the UL listing limit [34:01].

### Bid / Cost Implications
Concrete ponding is the headline cost item: a 2 or 3 inch deck spanning 9 to 12 feet deflects 5/8 to 3/4 inch at midspan, and that extra concrete over a million square feet of floor is real money [32:31]. The fix is a specification clause making the contractor responsible for the added concrete from ponding and deck deflection, otherwise it returns as an RFI plus change order [33:01]. Vendor catalogs setting load tables at 110 pcf lightweight concrete understate real 115-plus pcf density, requiring load adjustment [34:01]. Stiffening a section to solve a bracing question is unpopular with fabricators but is the quick path when analysis time is short [04:35]. West Coast seismic jobs trim slab thickness (2 plus 2.5 instead of 2 plus 3.5) to cut mass over many floors and accept spraying the deck [26:52].

### Your Company Application
Mario's shop and welding lead role maps directly: enforce the AWS ferrule-removal and bend-test on every stud lot, and watch stud-gun calibration on damp morning decks, since unwelded studs are a safety and capacity failure [16:04][16:34]. Tekla detailing should screen composite beams against the 2.5-times-flange-thickness stud rule and avoid thin webs (W10x12 class) where studs may not land over the web [19:06]. Ivan's takeoff should carry a ponding-concrete allowance and a spec note assigning that extra concrete to scope, and should not trust 110 pcf vendor load tables [33:01][34:01]. Paul's safety oversight applies to deck layout: require two- or three-span deck and forbid simple-span deck at lobbies given the documented slip and collapse history [09:21][32:01]. The in-house PE stamp must verify wet-concrete construction-stage bracing of girders, the exact assumption that killed a worker in the cited case [08:48]. For ACP controls, fold a ponding-concrete and deck-attachment line into the structural spec early so it does not surface as a change order. Doctrine flags: NONE. The content is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language, and AISC weights and rates remain sourced from aisc_validator.py and bid_rates.py, not from this video.

## Steel Design After College - Part 2
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=94UR-cjVWyQ | Duration: 27:32 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This webinar teaches the flexural strength of wide-flange beams governed by lateral-torsional buckling (LTB) and the lateral-bracing rules that control it. The speaker, a former student of Dr. Joseph Yura at the University of Texas, builds the three LTB zones (full plastic, inelastic, elastic) and then drives most of the session into the Cb moment-gradient factor, showing it is a multiplier that recovers real flexural capacity when the moment is not uniform across the unbraced length [03:09], [07:50]. A recurring theme is what actually counts as a brace point: an inflection point is NOT a brace point because the cross-section can still twist and the compression flange can still displace laterally [01:33].
### Spec References
The speaker cites these AISC 360 Chapter F items by name: equation F2-1 for the full-plastic zone where Lb is less than Lp [03:09]; equation F2-5 defining Lp as 1.76 ry times sqrt(E/Fy) [03:09]; the inelastic linear-degradation equation between Lp and Lr [03:39]; equation F2-3 for the elastic LTB zone where Lb exceeds Lr [05:46]; equation F1-1 for Cb with the term Rm introduced in the 2005 specification [11:58], [14:01], [14:31]; and Table 3-1 in the manual tabulating Cb for practical load cases [15:02]. He also references the manual beam charts (moment capacity versus unbraced length) per section [04:42]. The two uplift and continuous-beam Cb expressions are attributed to Dr. Yura and Dr. Helwig and are explicitly stated as NOT in the specification [20:15].
### Technical Details
In the elastic zone (equation F2-3) the flexural capacity contains no Fy and no E, so a higher-strength steel buys nothing once the unbraced length is long enough; the section buckles elastically before the extra yield can be used, the same behavior as a long column [05:46], [06:46]. Cb = 1.0 is the worst case of a uniform moment across the full unbraced length [07:17]. Equation F1-1 uses Mmax plus the quarter-point, centerline, and three-quarter-point moments (Ma, Mb, Mc) and Rm, where Rm = 1 for a symmetric I-beam and takes another value for a singly-symmetric plate girder in composite action [14:01], [14:31]. The Yura continuous-beam equation can return Cb up to 3.0, which is the specification cap, and is also capped by Mp [17:39], [18:09]. A separate set of three sign-sensitive Yura equations handles roof members under wind uplift, where deck braces the top flange but the bottom flange goes into compression [18:09], [19:10]. For a wind-uplift roof purlin braced by deck, a quick rule of thumb is Cb = 2 [20:47].
### Fabrication Notes
This is a design-and-analysis webinar with no shop fabrication, fit-up, or QC content. No fabrication tolerances or shop processes are discussed.
### Erection Notes
Bracing detailing rules surface that affect field and connection layout. At every support the specification requires preventing twist of the cross-section and lateral displacement of the compression flange for the support to count as a brace point [02:05]. For a cantilever, brace both top and bottom flange at the support; a free unbraced tip gives Cb = 1, but bracing the free end top and bottom lets you use equation F1-1 for Cb = 1.67 [22:21], [23:23]. The preferred cantilever bracing order is a full-depth connection at support and tip, then a full-depth stiffener plus kicker, then full-depth stiffeners relying on slab flexural stiffness [23:54]. The speaker also warns a thin beam web running over a column can behave like a column and kick out, calling for a web stiffener or a deck kicker bracing the column top [22:21].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
The central named error is engineers defaulting to Cb = 1.0 out of habit or because the manual and textbooks encourage it, leaving real capacity on the table [11:26], [16:05]. A second named error is counting an inflection point as a brace point, which is invalid because the cross-section still twists [01:33]. The speaker recounts a real dispute on a one-million-square-foot project where the engineer of record's design checked out fine once Cb was properly calculated, while the peer reviewer rejected it using Cb = 1.0 by default; the correction would have beefed up hundreds of beams for hundreds of thousands of dollars [25:26], [26:28].
### Bid / Cost Implications
Properly computing Cb instead of assuming 1.0 raises flexural capacity by tabulated factors from 1.14 up to 1.67 (and a noted 1.3, 1.32, 1.56) [15:33], [16:05], meaning lighter or fewer beams for the same loads. A 30 percent capacity gain (Cb = 1.3) is cited for a simple roof purlin braced at midspan [21:18]. The million-square-foot dispute shows the dollar stakes directly: the difference between Cb = 1.0 and a calculated Cb was hundreds of thousands of dollars in steel reinforcement avoided [26:28]. For takeoff this means a member schedule built on conservative Cb = 1.0 may carry tonnage that a correct LTB check would remove.
### Your Company Application
This is design intelligence for the in-house PE stamp and for Tekla detailing, not a change to Your Company's validated-tonnage workflow. The bracing rules feed detailing: where the PE relies on Cb above 1.0, the brace points (support twist restraint, cantilever-tip top-and-bottom bracing, deck-as-tension-flange-brace on uplift) must actually appear in the Tekla model and connection details, or the assumed capacity is fictional. For Ivan's takeoff this is a verify-don't-generate flag: member weights still come from bridge/aisc_validator.py against the schedule and framing-plan marks, never from any LTB or Cb math; Cb only explains why an engineered member is lighter than a Cb = 1.0 assumption, it never sets a weight. The uplift and continuous-beam Yura equations are NOT in the AISC specification [20:15], so any use is engineering judgment owned by the stamping PE and must not be auto-applied by the estimating tool. No conflict with Your Company doctrine. NONE.

## Steel Design After College - Part 1
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BJffavTtBz8 | Duration: 32:31 | Upload: NA | Tier: 2 | Watched: 2026-06-24
### Core Concept
This is the opening session of an AISC course modeled on a design firm's in-house program to bring new and returning engineers up to speed on the 2005 AISC specification [00:32][01:33]. After a roadmap of seven sessions (non-composite flexure, composite beams, lateral/wind design, metal deck, diaphragms, base plates and anchor rods, trusses, plus computer modeling), the bulk of Part 1 teaches the strength limit states for non-composite flexural members [08:47]. The three governing strength limit states taught are local buckling (flange and web), lateral-torsional buckling (LTB), and yielding, all keyed to the slenderness parameter Lambda [09:19][11:56]. The central practical message is that taking Cb equal to 1.0 by default is needlessly conservative, and a few minutes of calculation can yield real economy [10:21].
### Spec References
AISC 2005 specification (360-05), cited generically as "the new 2005 specification" [02:05]. Table B4.1 for limiting slenderness parameters (Lambda p compact, Lambda r non-compact) [16:04][19:40]. Chapter B for the slenderness parameter Lambda [14:00]. Chapter F for the moment-capacity reduction equations on non-compact and slender sections [20:12]. AISC Design Guide 3 (second revision, serviceability for steel building structures, authored by Jim Fischer and Mike West) [12:58]. The AISC base-plate/anchor-rod design guide, second revision, referenced for a later session [04:40]. AISC seismic provisions and seismic manual (2005) named but deferred to seismic-specific seminars [03:37][18:08].
### Technical Details
Local buckling uses b/2t for the flange (b is flange width, t is flange thickness) and h/t for the web (h is web depth, t is web thickness); for channels the flange ratio is b/t [16:04][16:35]. If Lambda is less than Lambda p the section develops full plastic capacity (forms a hinge); between Lambda p and Lambda r it reaches initial yield before buckling; above Lambda r it is a slender compression element, rare in wide-flange building design but common in light-gauge metal [14:32][15:33]. The plain (non-seismic) b/t limits target an inelastic rotation capacity of 3, sufficient for wind and low-to-moderate seismic; seismic provisions impose stricter ratios [17:06][18:08]. The b/t limits derive from finite-element analyses and can be reproduced by meshing a section (a W6x15 was the worked example) and loading it until local ripples appear [18:38][19:09]. LTB capacity depends on section properties (Z, r, S, J, etc.), modulus E, yield strength Fy, and Cb, but the major driver is unbraced length, divided into three zones by Lp (full plastic) and Lr (inelastic vs elastic LTB) [22:49][24:21][26:23]. Weak-axis bending of wide flanges, channels, tubes, pipes, and plates cannot produce LTB; it is a strong-axis phenomenon only [25:22]. A brace point exists where lateral displacement of the compression flange OR twist of the cross-section is prevented; a point that prevents twist counts as braced even if the compression flange can still translate, demonstrated by two parallel beams laced with X-bracing every 3 ft that reach full plastic capacity despite lateral movement [27:27][28:29][29:33].
### Fabrication Notes
This is a design-theory session and does not cover shop fabrication, fit-up, or QC. It touches fabrication only indirectly: when an engineer builds a plate girder or a custom built-up wide-flange section, thin webs or thin flanges make local buckling a real check rather than a non-issue, so member proportioning at design time constrains what gets fabricated [21:45][22:17]. No tolerances or shop processes are stated.
### Erection Notes
No field erection, sequencing, crane, or rigging content appears; the bracing discussed is permanent design bracing of the compression flange, not temporary erection bracing. The practical bracing examples (metal deck or concrete slab bracing the top flange, stiffeners plus anchor bolts at the base to prevent twist, kickers, or X-braces) describe the in-service braced condition that the designer must identify, not an erection procedure [30:35][31:09].
### Common Errors / Inspection Failures
No inspection or rejection content; the errors named are design mistakes. Defaulting Cb to 1.0 for simplicity is flagged as overly conservative and economically wasteful, since Cb can reach 1.5 to 3 [10:21]. The recurring conceptual error is misjudging what constitutes a brace point: engineers wrongly assume beams with an unrestrained compression flange are unbraced when prevented twist alone provides the brace [28:29][30:05]. The closing session warns against over-reliance on software, letting the computer think for the engineer, and skipping checks of input data and output before placing it on drawings [05:40][06:11][06:41].
### Bid / Cost Implications
The economic theme is design optimization, not bid pricing. Properly computing Cb instead of assuming 1.0 lets a section carry more moment over the same unbraced length, which can downsize members and save steel weight [10:21]. Recognizing that prevented twist counts as a brace point can shorten the effective unbraced length and unlock full plastic capacity without adding bracing material [29:33][30:05]. No dollar figures, fabrication rates, or schedule data are given.
### Your Company Application
This session is design-side education with no fabrication or erection procedure, so the direct shop/field links are limited; the value to Your Company is in QC of incoming designs and member-takeoff sanity. For Ivan's takeoff through aisc_validator.py, the worked sections (W6x15 as the one 36 ksi shape sensitive to local buckling) confirm that standard rolled wide-flange shapes almost never trip local buckling, so a takeoff that flags many slender-element reductions signals a built-up or plate-girder set worth a second look. For Tekla detailing and the in-house PE stamp, the brace-point rule (twist restraint counts even without compression-flange restraint) is the kind of judgment our PE applies when reviewing where deck, slab, stiffeners, kickers, or X-braces establish unbraced length; the base-plate stiffener-plus-anchor-bolt example ties to our anchor-rod workstream as a twist-restraint detail at column bases. Joists and roof deck appear here as continuous-bracing elements for the top flange, reinforcing that deck supply stays in scope as it also serves a structural bracing role. No conflict with Your Company doctrine: this is conventional structural steel with no PEMB language, no supplier names, and all spec citations are verbatim from the speaker. DOCTRINE FLAG: NONE.

# SYNTHESIS

Cross-cutting findings synthesized across the watched corpus. Spec citations and any numbers here are study aids drawn from the videos and must be re-verified against the current AISC Manual, the controlling Specification, and bridge/aisc_validator.py before they enter a bid or a stamped calculation.

## Connection Design and Detailing

Connection design is where a steel building is actually won or lost, because everyone buys the same mill steel and the connection method is the only real differentiator between fabricators (Last Bastion). The cost pie from Connection Design as the Fabricator's Representative puts erected structural steel at roughly material 28 percent, fabrication 46 percent, erection 26 percent, so less weight is not less cost, repetition pays, and connection material alone runs 5 to 30 percent of total tonnage that aisc_validator.py does not carry. For Ivan that is the governing estimating posture: enumerate connection types, treat connection steel as a real percentage of tonnage rather than a flat allowance, and price by complexity, not by weight alone. The unifying design theory across every entry is the lower-bound theorem of limit analysis (Vertical Bracing, Last Bastion, Night School 6 Session 1): any internal force field that satisfies equilibrium, violates no limit state, and has enough ductility to redistribute is safe, and among valid admissible fields the one giving the highest predicted capacity is closest to the true collapse load and usually the most economical. Ductility is the non-negotiable caveat. Steel works because it deforms and sheds load to stiffer elements rather than fracturing, so ductile limit states must precede brittle ones. Every connection calc Your Company's in-house PE authors should rest on this framework, and the method discipline (uniform force method over KISS for column-web bracing) is itself a cost lever: Last Bastion cites a worked detail where the UFM force field gave about 320 kips of capacity where the parallel-force field on the same hardware gave only about 30 kips, and a 40-story job showed roughly a quarter-million-dollar fabrication swing between KISS and UFM.

Simple shear connections are designed as pins even though a real moment-rotation curve shows some end moment, and this only holds when the connection is detailed for rotational ductility (Shear Connections Part 1 and 2, Fundamental Concepts Part 1). The ductility rules a detailer and shop must hold are concrete: keep plate and angle material thin (a 5/8 in cap), use wide bolt gauges or widely spaced welds, never weld across the top of an angle or end plate (doing so destroys the pin assumption), and detail the shear tab thin enough that bolts "plow" (bear-deform) the plate before fracture. Brad Davis teaches the four simple types as single angle, single plate (shear tab), unstiffened seat, and stiffened seat. The shear tab is the default because it eliminates drilling thick column flanges, needs no prying check, and erects easiest on a drift pin (Night School 6 Session 3, where switching from double clips to shear tabs took a power-plant job about two million dollars under estimate). Conventional shear tabs are limited (one bolt column, 2 to 12 bolts, a not over 3.5 in, weld at least 5/8 of plate thickness both sides, plate no thicker than the Table 10-9 max); past those limits the extended single plate adds plate buckling per Section F11 (with a Cb floor of 1.84) and a von-Mises shear-flexure interaction. Block shear and shear yielding/rupture are checked under J4.3 and equations J4-3/J4-4/J4-5; weld ductility and minimum size come from Table J2.4. A controlling fabrication input is the plus-or-minus 1/4 in beam-length tolerance, absorbed by a 1/2 in setback and by deducting 1/4 in from the design end distance in block-shear and tensile-rupture checks. Slot orientation is a hard detailing rule: support-side holes on a single angle stay standard (never slotted) so the angle cannot rotate the beam out of bearing, while beam-side holes may be standard or short slots, and horizontal slots in web angles let one angle pattern fit many beam web thicknesses. Slot orientation also gates the count-gap work, since horizontal slots quietly mark a connection the detailer assumed carries no axial.

Coped beams are a frequent shop-cut feature whose controlling limit states shifted in the 15th-edition Manual from elastic allowable stress to a strength-based procedure that credits inelastic capacity and removes the old cope-geometry limits (New Developments in Connection Design). Single-cope flexure is now modeled as local buckling of a short WT cantilever per Chapter F, and double-cope flexure as lateral-torsional buckling per F11 with Lb taken as the average of top and bottom cope lengths; shear uses the 0.6 von-Mises factor on the reduced depth Ho, and axial uses an effective area per E7 with tension yield per J4.1, J4.4 governing flexural buckling below KL/r of 25. This is the governing method whenever a cope is deep, long, or skewed (a 45-degree skew lengthened one cope about 40 percent), and the deep/long-cope warning that an unbraced coped beam has greatly reduced LTB strength is a real erection-stage check before decking goes on. Connection Design as the Fabricator's Representative gives the matching count-gap trigger: a shallow W8 beam framing into a deep W36 over a 12 in cope risks flexural buckling and block shear and may force a W12 upsize. Both the Manual Cb errata (read greater-than-or-equal-to 1.84) and the roughly 1/16 in of out-of-flatness a cope cut leaves are detailing and QC items for Tekla and Mario's crew.

Fully restrained moment connections decompose the beam end moment into a flange force couple, with the flanges carrying the moment and a single web plate carrying only direct shear (Moment Connections Part 1). The directly welded flange detail puts CJP flange welds with backing in the field downhand; PJP is explicitly not recommended on a directly welded flange because filling a beveled flange from one side leaves a root crack and stress riser. The column-side governs through the six J10 limit states (flange local bending J10.1, web local yielding J10.2, web local crippling J10.3, web compression buckling J10.5, transverse stiffener design J10.8, and panel-zone shear J10.6), with Design Guide 13 the force-distribution reference. The worked W24x103-to-W14x159 example is the lesson for Ivan: a normal-looking 882 kip-ft joint still required full-depth transverse stiffeners top and bottom plus two 3/4 in doubler plates, real priced plate and weld that a beam-and-column takeoff misses. Bolted FR connections (T-stub and end-plate, Moment Connections Part 2) are governed by prying action: the strategy is to size the plate for thick-plate behavior (thickness reaches t-NP, derived setting Mu = phi Mp of the flange using Fu not Fy) so no fulcrum forms and the prying force Q goes to zero. The counterintuitive levers polled in that session matter on the shop floor: increasing bolt gauge or decreasing flange thickness increases prying, and the correct way to reduce it is higher specified Fu. End-plate flexural strength uses Design Guide 16 yield-line tables (parameters Y and s, with the gamma = 1.25 flush versus 1.0 extended factor and the FR classification check at the connection-classification curve), so the detailer pulls Y and s by configuration rather than minimizing by hand. Bolt prying detail (Night School 6 Session 3) follows the Part 9 method (T-sub-C, alpha-prime, rho, delta, Fu not Fy, J3.7 bearing and J3.8/J3.9 slip-critical interaction), and the column flange must be checked on both sides, since a thin column flange can govern even with an adequate clip or end plate.

Stiffeners (continuity plates) and doublers (column web reinforcing plates at the panel zone) are explicitly described as expensive and undesirable, and the controlling design move is to verify the actual panel-zone shear under the real dead/live/lateral moment breakdown and column axial load per J10.6, not the full beam moment capacity (Stiffeners and Doublers, Moment Connections Part 1). Drucker's office cost study found that assuming full beam capacity put roughly 100 percent of columns into doublers where actual moments needed only about 26 percent. The economical hierarchy she gives is direct: a thickened doubler prepped to clear the column radius and fillet-welded saved about 25 percent over groove-welding into the radius, a modest column upsize (about 20 lb/ft) saved about 15 percent, and the cheapest option was upsizing the column to drop the stiffeners entirely while using a thickened doubler with a single-pass 5/16 fillet. The fabricator-relevant welding rules: AWS D1.8 prequalifies a 30-degree-prep PJP doubler weld that avoids UT (the recurring inspection failure is UT rejection of doublers groove-welded into the radius, where a gap forms behind the override), welding in the k-area is restricted on low-toughness rotary-straightened W-shapes, and the effective thickness of a thickened doubler is taken at the toe of the fillet, not the full plate. Panel-zone strength drops sharply once column axial approaches the squash load (the reduction triggers above alpha Pr / Py of 0.4). For Houston low-seismic work most of this stays wind/low-seismic, but the standing estimating flag for Ivan is that Code of Standard Practice 3.1.1 now requires conceptual doubler/stiffener details and quantities (or an allowance) at bid time, so he must read for contrary spec exclusions before pricing or risk an unfunded RFI fight over who pays for doublers.

Bracing and gusset connections are the most indeterminate family and the source of the most common and most dangerous detailing errors (Bracing Connections, Vertical Bracing Connections, Performance and Behavior of Gusset Plate Connections). The critical-section sizing tool is the Whitmore section, a 30-degree load spread off each side of the connection length; gusset compression checks under J4.4 yielding when Lc/r is at or below 25, otherwise E3 buckling with K from Design Guide 29 (often 0.5 for a corner gusset, up to 1.2 for a gusset welded only to the beam, or K = 0.65 corner and K = 1.2 midspan per the gusset-performance tests). The uniform force method routes all interface resultants through the work point so each gusset face sees only normal and shear forces with no moment, with the alpha-beta geometry constrained by Manual equation 13-1 and four special cases (Case 2 shifts the vertical brace component to relieve an overloaded beam-web joint, the new Case 4 takes the eccentric distance out to the first bolt column to connect to a column web as if it were a flange). The single most actionable QC gate across these entries is the slotted-hole warning: detailers throw default horizontal short slots into gusset-to-column shear plates and corner shear tabs by habit because they look like ordinary shear connections, when in fact these carry large axial transfer force (one live job had about 50 such connections needing reinforcement). For Your Company that means any gusset-to-column shear plate or corner shear tab carrying transfer force must not get default horizontal slots, and the PE stamp must confirm the EOR provided the beam reaction Rb, the transfer force Ab, and column HSS status, not just brace axial. Two more firm rules: the gusset-to-beam fillet is increased 25 percent for non-uniform force distribution even when the design says no moment, and an unauthorized field or shop weld the engineer did not assume sucks load into adjacent bolts and can rupture them (Vertical Bracing), so never add a weld outside the assumed force field. The gusset-performance tests add the counterintuitive seismic lesson that a stronger, stiffer gusset performs worse, so the elliptical 8tp corner clearance and 6tp midspan band keep yielding in the brace and cut plate size 30 to 40 percent.

Transfer force is the recurring root cause of bad bracing connections and a direct bid risk (Connection Design: Load Path and Transfer Forces). Transfer force across a joint equals the member axial load only when the bay has no vertical bracing, so a beam or purlin with zero axial can still carry a large transfer load from a brace's horizontal component, and a detailing routine (SDS2 was named) can silently substitute the full member axial load and produce connections far heavier than needed. The standing rule for Your Company's connection PE is to request transfer forces from the SER per Code of Standard Practice 3.1.2 and never let Tekla substitute full member axial load. Communication discipline ties the same theme to the bid (Effective Communication Connections): classify every job against Code of Standard Practice 3.1 option one, two, or three at intake, state explicitly whether the fabricator PE must sign and seal calculations and, separately, shop drawings (each raises cost and risk), and treat any UDL or full-plastic-moment load posted instead of actual reactions as a conservative LOW-confidence load that inflates connection size, continuity, and doubler cost. The recurring abuse is a girder forced to carry 147 kips when the infill beams delivering load were good for only 70 (back-calculating to 700 to 947 psf on a commercial floor), or a beam designed for half-UDL carrying a phantom reaction 8 to 25 times any realistic load. The Last Bastion frames the same point as the verify-do-not-generate gate it is: specify and RFI actual reactions, separate gravity from lateral moments, and avoid silently pricing conservative phantom loads.

Base connections, splices, and seismic detailing close the body of knowledge. Exposed column bases are far more ductile than design assumes (8 to 10 percent drift) and behave between pinned and fixed, so pinned is the conservative column-sizing assumption (Column Base Connection); the hard correction is that the Design Guide 1 shear-lug 45-degree cone method is unconservative by roughly a factor of two and must apply the ACI concrete size-effect penalty, while DG1 is fine for friction (mu about 0.45) and anchor-rod bearing. Base plates fail because engineers oversimplify them as P over n; the real distribution is stiffness-driven, so small geometry changes swing forces 30 to 100 percent, and the routinely-missed limit state is bearing on the partial flat of the A563 nut, which can control over rod steel strength even for grade 36 rods (Got Stiffness, with a worked example where stiffness-based demand was 63 percent above P/n and pushed F1554 grade 55 to grade 105). The fixes are a plate washer, higher-strength concrete, or a larger rod diameter, and continuous special inspection of grout is a real held inspection point because voided grout invalidates the bearing the model assumes. Splices are for shipping and constructability, and the doctrine is weld-in-shop, bolt-in-field, prefer PJP over CJP in the shop to cut volume, and keep the field splice simple and direct (The Splice is Right): the headline number is a W14x730 tension chord where a bolted splice needed about 6,900 lb of extra steel and 128 bolts while a welded version used roughly 70 lb of weld metal for a 79 percent cost reduction. Seismic connections (Introduction to Seismic Connections, the chevron and corner-connection Night School sessions) are capacity-designed to the brace expected strength (tension RyFyAg, compression the lesser of RyFyAg and 1.14 Fcr Ag, post-buckling 0.3 times buckling) under AISC 341, with prequalified moment connections per AISC 358, demand-critical CJP welds, protected zones (no attachments, tacks, or arc strikes in the brace middle quarter, brace ends, and the entire gusset), a 2t hinge fold-line clearance for out-of-plane brace buckling, brace slots cut gusset-thickness-plus-1/8 with reinforcing plates that restore the net section, and backing-bar removal at beam-bottom-flange welds per the Northridge lesson. The standing rule from every seismic entry is to confirm the seismic system before pricing connections: high-ductility systems add continuity plates, gusset reinforcement, knife plates, demand-critical filler metal, and added NDE that a plain gravity-frame takeoff never shows, and a chevron SCBF can force a large beam upsize from the mechanistic two-load-case analysis (a W24x84 jumping to W24x176 in the worked example) that Ivan must price as real tonnage. Houston is mostly low-seismic, so most Your Company work including ACP will not be SMF or SCBF, but the cost and detailing premium is exactly why the seismic system has to be read off the structural notes before a connection bid.

Every spoken weight, force, plate thickness, and percentage in these sessions is a study aid. AISC member weights and shape properties come from bridge/aisc_validator.py per Hard Rule 5, rates stay CEO-locked in bid_rates.py, and any connection capacity gets re-derived and stamped, never generated from a webinar number.

### Re-Watch and Ivan callout

For the in-house PE stamp and Tekla detailing, the deepest-value re-watches are, in order: Connection Design as the Fabricator's Representative (the COSP Option 3 playbook and the count-by-type bid method), Vertical Bracing Connections and Bracing Connections (UFM, lower bound, Whitmore, the slotted-hole gate), Stiffeners and Doublers (the actual-moment panel-zone check and the column-upsize cost study), and Moment Connections Parts 1 and 2 (J10 limit states, prying, thick-plate design).

For Ivan's takeoff specifically: carry connection steel at 5 to 30 percent of tonnage rather than a flat allowance; flag braced bays, moment frames, and seismic systems for separate connection-labor pricing; treat any UDL or Mp load (instead of actual reactions) and any horizontal-slotted gusset-to-column plate as RFI triggers before pricing; and price the chevron-SCBF beam at its mechanistic-analysis size, not its gravity size. Confirm the seismic system, the COSP option, and the sign-and-seal scope at intake, because each one is a cost line the estimate must carry, and route every member weight through aisc_validator.py.

## Fabrication and QC Requirements

Fabrication begins with the right material called out by the right ASTM standard, and the two material-spec sessions ("Are You Properly Specifying Materials" with Kruth, and the same-titled Carter session) converge on a single default grade set Ivan should hold in aisc_validator.py lookups: W shapes are A992 (always 50 ksi, no grade suffix, so never carry the string "A992 Grade 50"); HP shapes moved to A572 Grade 50 in 2016 and are no longer A36; rectangular and square HSS are A500 Grade C at 50 ksi while round HSS at the same Grade C is only 46 ksi; steel pipe is A53 Grade B at 35 ksi and is not interchangeable with round HSS; plate and bar are A36 or A572 Grade 50; and connection material rebased from 36 ksi to 50 ksi in the 16th edition Manual, so a 15th-edition connection takeoff assumes the wrong default. The single most common mis-spec Carter names is "A325 anchor bolts," because anchor rods are not bolts and the supplier then quietly furnishes A449 rod cut to length; the correct callout is F1554, and per Kruth the standing default is F1554 Grade 55 with supplement S1 (weldable) so the field crew can weld a threaded extension when a rod is set low, while Grade 105 is high-strength but never weldable and a low-set Grade 105 rod cannot be field-corrected. These grade and CSI Division 5 spec callouts (section 05 12 00 per "Steel Specifications Unraveled") govern the cost of the steel, so source them off the spec and general notes together rather than harvesting one number from one place. Any grade, weight, or rate quoted here is a study aid and must be re-verified through aisc_validator.py and bid_rates.py before it touches a real bid.

The manufacturing sessions ("The Manufacturing of Structural Steel Shapes" and "Practical Steel Metallurgy") matter to fabrication because they tell Ivan and Mario what the Mill Test Report certifies and why. Strength comes from controlled microalloy additions (vanadium, columbium/niobium) and rolling reduction rather than carbon, so weldability and Charpy toughness are preserved; A992 carries a max carbon equivalent of 0.45 (0.47 above 2 inch flange) and a 0.85 yield-to-tensile cap specifically for seismic ductility, and A913 reaches Grade 65/70 properties through in-line quench-and-self-temper while keeping A992-Grade-50 weldability and needing no preheat at grades 50 and 65 (grade 70 still needs preheat), a real shop saving on heavy sections in cold weather where preheating can take up to 24 hours. Two metallurgy facts protect the shop from disputes: a single rolled shape can simultaneously certify A36, A572-50, A709-50, and A992, so grade names are context labels on the same steel; and MTR values are nominal not exact, so a third-party retest that substitutes a 0.505 round coupon on a thick shape samples the coarse-grained, segregated core and reads misleadingly low against the full-thickness A370 plate coupon. Mario confirms chemistry and carbon equivalent off the MTR before setting preheat and filler (standardize FEXX 70 ksi filler per AWS A5.20/A5.29/A5.36 and drop stale A5.1/A5.5 stick-welding references), and never weld high-strength heat-treated bolts.

The full-shop tour ("Steel Fabrication: A Virtual, Detailed Tour") frames production as "drawings and steel" first, then a flow of receiving, cutting, hole-making, layout, fitting, welding or bolting, cambering, cleaning, coating, and shipping, all under an AISC-certification quality management system.
