Material identification and traceability run from receiving to assembly per AISC 360 Section 2.1/A3 and Code of Standard Practice Section 6.1: each piece is marked with heat number, PO, job number, and size, MTRs are filed behind the PO back to heat, and a visual receiving inspection per ASTM A6 rejects kinked, bent, or flange-tilted material for QC disposition. Cutting is by horizontal bandsaw for wide flange and channel, CNC plasma or oxyfuel for plate (oxyfuel for thick), with thermal-cut quality per AISC 360 Section M2 and holes drilled or punched per M2.5 and RCSC Section 3.3. Connection type (double-angle clip, shear tab) is chosen by the shop's own equipment and crew skill, not by load alone: an automated drill-line shop bolts faster, a high-skill welding shop welds faster, so the standard detail is set to the plant. Shipping limits constrain assembly size (standard flatbed 8 ft 6 in wide, 48 or 53 ft; permit to 14 ft wide and 85 ft), which decides what ships as a shop assembly versus stick-built and therefore the crane and crew. The PE-stamp question is answered cleanly: design documents and any Option 3 fabricator-engineered connections need a PE stamp, but shop drawings themselves are an interpretation and should not be stamped; when an EOR asks for a seal, the right move is an RFI requesting a review letter, which Joseph and the in-house PE should adopt as standing policy.

Camber and bending are the two shop forming operations. Per "Specifying Camber," camber is induced in the shop (not the mill) by cold cambering on a third-point ram jig (deflecting past yield so the elastic portion springs back) or by hot cambering with 1100 to 1200 degree wedge heats, with hot running roughly ten times the cost of cold (about 3 man-hours cold versus 30 hot). It is verified in the shop in the unstressed horizontal position to the Code of Standard Practice Section 6.4.4 tolerance: minus-zero, plus-one-half-inch for beams 50 ft or less, with an added 1/8 inch per 10 ft over 50 ft, and a beam already holding 75 percent of specified camber needs no further work. Camber only pays above a 5 lb/ft weight saving, must be specified in 1/4 inch increments rounded down (never below 3/4 inch because transport loses up to 25 percent), and must be kept off moment connections where the differential pinches one weld root closed; over-camber is corrected with 200-to-500-degree heat, never by reverse-pressing. Bending and curving ("Around the Bend") is a proprietary craft with no published tolerance standard, so the bender needs shape, radius, chord, angle, and orientation (easy-way versus hard-way) before steel is bought, plus hold-and-tail material beyond the arc length (roughly 3 ft per end easy way, 5.5 ft per end hard way for wide flange). Curved members are a separate LOW-confidence ROM line until a bender confirms radius and cost, must ship flat with controlled strapping, and fall back to bent-plate-and-weld when a radius is too tight to roll.

HSS handling and tolerances deserve their own discipline because the tube wall, not the member, often controls the connection. "What Your Fabricator Wishes You Knew About HSS" ranks the wide-flange-to-HSS-column shear connections least to most expensive as shear tab, WT, double angle, then through plate (about four times the single plate), and the through-plate detail copied set-to-set is the headline error, including cases where an all-around weld symbol forced an interior weld and the shop had to chop and reweld a column top. A single through plate adds a full hour of shop time per connection, and bumping a 3/16 inch wall to 1/4 inch to avoid the through plate is often cheaper overall; a tube-to-tube fillet is about two hours of fit-up versus one to one-and-a-half days plus inspection as a CJP, so push fillet up to about 1/2 inch before stepping to PJP and reserve CJP for genuine need. A500 wall tolerance (the 0.93 design factor tied to AISC B4.1) can stack roughly a quarter inch of slop across an HSS 12x4 end-plate joint; A1085 holds a tighter 5 percent wall tolerance, a single 50-to-70 ksi yield, and CVN 25 ft-lb at 40 F, removing the 0.93 factor, and is the path when capacity is tight or the load is dynamic (A500 is not rated for dynamic loading). Tekla should default to shear tab and stepped truss joints, fix HSS seam orientation per Code of Standard Practice 10.2.8 on AESS, and size welds to the applied load, not full member yield. Concrete-filled HSS ("Concrete Filled HSS," AISC 360 Chapter I) adds shop scope: a 3-to-5-foot free-fall limit to avoid segregation, cap-plate vent holes when bottom-pumping, self-consolidating concrete where rebar crowds the section, and a load-transfer detail (bearing plate, headed studs, or channel anchors) over the connection length plus 2B or 2D.

Surface preparation, coatings, and AESS are where margin is won or lost. "SSPC Surface Preparation" makes the controlling point that coating performance is bought at the prep stage, not the can: SP 1 solvent cleaning is mandatory first, then blast to the specified class with an angular grit profile (SP 10 near-white typically strips all mill scale on new steel, SP 6 commercial allows 33 percent staining, and SP 6 versus SP 10 is a real labor and abrasive cost difference), then airless-spray coat for production with brush reserved for repair; the written SSPC standard always outranks the reference photographs. Zinc-rich primers are the workhorse because zinc sacrifices itself, ISO 12944 ties dry-film thickness to environment and life, and intumescent fire coatings are section-factor driven so heavier steel needs less thickness. "Steel Specifications Unraveled" adds two shop-floor catches: galvanizing must be specified no-quench when the member will later be painted (the water bath leaves impurities that defeat primer adhesion), and relief holes in galvanized closed shapes need a named party responsible for plugging or trapped water can freeze and split the member. Metallizing ("Metallizing - From A to Zinc") is bridge-industry but carries one transferable rule: unsealed metallized faying surfaces meet RCSC Class B slip-critical (0.5 minimum slip coefficient) per the FHWA finding, which is the coating-versus-connection check Mario and the PE should confirm on any coated slip-critical joint. AESS scope ("Buyer Beware" and the AESS portion of the SSPC session) is an hours-per-ton labor modifier on validated weights under 2016 Code of Standard Practice Section 10, not a tonnage add: categories run AESS 1 (ground sharp edges, weld spatter removed, continuous weld appearance, SP 6), 2 (tolerances halved, markings removed, smooth welds, 25 to 35 percent over non-AESS), 3 (mock-up, all mill marks removed, HSS seams oriented and hidden, button welds ground and filled), 4 (welds contoured and blended, HSS coil seam ground smooth), and AESS-C custom. The cost matrix must never appear on a client document or contract, which aligns with Hard Rule 4; price welds-ground-smooth and tight coping only where the occupant actually sees them, and RFI the GC when a set says AESS but omits which Section 10.2 items apply.

QC and QA are governed by AISC 360 Chapter N, the single IBC-recognized source for steel special inspection ("Quality Control and Quality Assurance"). The dividing line is that QC is the fabricator's and erector's control of their own work while QA is provided by others (third party, EOR, or AHJ), every Chapter N task is tagged Observe (random or intermittent) or Perform (each joint, weld, or bolt), and the standing rule is that an undocumented inspection counts as not performed. QC inspects against the approved shop and erection drawings; QA additionally checks against the design drawings and specifications to confirm information transferred correctly, which is exactly the cross-check the in-house PE and Tekla checker should run rather than just matching the model. The pre-weld gate is Table N5.4-1 (WPS available per AWS D1.1 6.3, consumable certs and material ID per 6.2, qualified welder per 6.4, fit-up: root opening, root face, bevel, cleanliness, tack quality, backing fit), and the post-weld gate is Table N5.4-3 (Perform on weld size, length, location, and the visual list of crack prohibition, fusion, crater section, profile, undercut, porosity, measured with gauges per AWS D1.1 6.5.3). Field bolting maps to RCSC pre-installation verification: three bolts per lot (not per keg) in a Skidmore-Wilhelm calibrator, with DTIs permitted as the calibrator to avoid a Skidmore on every site, bolts stored in dust-tight containers because lubrication is critical, and the standing real failure is CAR #008, where a missing field-weld section bubble on the erection diagram let a temporary erection bolt carry a permanent load and fail; the corrective action is a detailing-standard note putting a section bubble at every field-welded joint, which Tekla should carry as a permanent rule. The seismic supplements ("Weld Inspection" and "NDE and Special Inspection of Seismic Welding") add that acceptance criteria are workmanship limits, not failure boundaries (AWS D1.1 Commentary C-6.8 lets a qualified welder disposition cosmetic discontinuities instead of over-repairing), that NDT scope scales with ASCE/SEI 7 Risk Category (100 percent UT on tension CJP for Risk III/IV versus 10 percent for II) and must be priced from the contract not assumed, that the SAC round-robin found about 16 percent false-call rejections so disciplined VT and right-sized NDT avoid paying for repairs that fix nothing, and that seismic work triggers AISC 341 J5 k-area MT plus AWS D1.8 backing-bar removal, protected zones, and technicians tested on real flaw samples. Across the shop the same theme holds: trace every weld to a welder ID and every bolt to a lot, document acceptance or rejection per item, and measure nonconformance as cost-percent-of-sales, not raw count.

### Ivan and team callouts

- Ivan (takeoff/estimating): lock current grades into aisc_validator.py (A992 W, A572-50 HP and connection material on the 16th-edition basis, A500 Gr C rectangular HSS at 50 ksi, round HSS 46 ksi, A53 Gr B pipe at 35 ksi); carry connection material as 5 to 30 percent of tonnage, not a flat allowance; price surface-prep class (SP 6 versus SP 10), ISO 12944 DFT, AESS hours-per-ton, through-plate and CJP shop-hour deltas, camber, and bending as distinct lines; flag CVN supplements, A588 weathering, and A913 as cost and lead-time premiums; flag any curved or filled member as added scope and LOW confidence until confirmed. Every quantity stays a study aid pending re-verification.
- Mario (shop, AWS D1.1): confirm grade and carbon equivalent off the MTR before setting preheat and filler; standardize FEXX 70 ksi filler; prefer fillet then PJP over CJP; run the Table N5.4-1 fit-up gate and Table N5.4-3 visual gate as the in-house checklist with welder-ID stamps; claim the A913 no-preheat saving on heavy sections; for seismic work, separate D1.8 qualifications, k-area awareness, and access-hole technique.
- Paul (NCCER safety): blast and coating respiratory and silica/lead hazards; controlled concrete placement and pump positioning on CFT; protected-zone coordination so safety-cable holes and pins stay clear on seismic frames; flat shipping and controlled strapping on curved members; rigging plans for heavy cast nodes or large assemblies.
- Tekla detailing and in-house PE: every field-welded joint gets a section bubble (CAR #008); default to shear tab and stepped HSS joints; carry AESS category-by-elevation and weld-finish callouts per member; size welds to applied load; stamp design and Option 3 connection calcs but not shop drawings (answer an EOR seal request with a review-letter RFI).
- Anchor rods and ACP: F1554 Grade 55 S1 weldable as default, never "A325 anchor bolts," with washer holes per Manual Table 14-2 and ACI 117 placement coordination so rods set by others land the base plate clean; adopt a Chapter N quality manual, NCR-as-percent-of-sales metric, and Code of Standard Practice Section 4 submittal and RFI logs in the project register.

## Erection and Field Operations

The first principle running through every erection video is a scope boundary: the engineer of record designs only the completed structure, while the erector owns stability of the bare frame at every intermediate stage, and that duty falls to Your Company whenever we erect. AISC 360 Section M4.2 directs the erector to secure the frame for dead and erection loads with temporary bracing per the Code of Standard Practice, and COSP Section 7.10.3 requires temporary supports sufficient to secure the bare frame against loads likely during erection including wind, while exempting unpredictable events (hurricane, tornado, earthquake, explosion, collision); 7.10.4 keeps that bracing in place until the permanent lateral-force-resisting system and its connecting diaphragm are installed (Erection Engineering of Low-Rise Buildings, Stability During Construction, The Science Behind the Art). COSP 7.10.1 obligates the EOR to identify the lateral system and any required erection sequence, and 3.1.2 to show shears, moments, axial and transfer forces; when a set is silent on the lateral path, anchorage fixity, or how long bracing must stay, that is an early RFI, not an assumption (Stability During Construction). Because Your Company carries an in-house PE, the erection-stability check, the engineered cable-brace plan, pick analysis, and temporary-splice loads are stamped deliverables we own rather than wash out under a generic means-and-methods note (The Science Behind the Art, The Erector's Perspective). The Erector's Perspective lists COSP Section 7 in full (7.1 method, 7.3 foundations, 7.5 anchor-rod installation, 7.7 grouting, 7.10 temporary support, 7.12 and 7.13 tolerances, 7.14 correction of errors), and the correct answer to "when is a stamped stability plan required" is both: when the contract specifies it and when the structure cannot resist environmental plus erection loads before completion.

The controlling and most counterintuitive load is construction wind on the bare, unclad frame, which routinely exceeds the finished-building design wind. The bare frame is a lattice of high-drag exposed members, so even with relief it draws more force. ASCE 37 Section 6.2.1 gives a wind-speed reduction keyed to construction duration (0.75 under six weeks, 0.8 for six weeks to one year, 0.85 for one to two years, 0.9 for two to five years), but because pressure scales with velocity squared the 0.75 speed factor only buys about a 0.50 to 0.56 force factor (Low-Rise, Stability During Construction, The Science Behind the Art). ASCE 37 Section 6.2.2 shielding applies full wind to the first three rows and a 15 percent reduction (85 percent) on the fourth and later, and AISC Design Guide 10 adds a stacking factor eta from its Figure 2-2 keyed to spacing-to-depth and solidity ratio; a worked W21x50 bay landed eta near 0.36, rounded to 0.4 (Low-Rise). That relief is offset by open-framework force coefficients of roughly 1.6 to 2.0 (about 1.95 for a single wide flange) from ASCE 7 Figure 29.5-2. The result is dramatic: the AISC 14th-edition example building ran a construction base shear of about 429 to 600 kips against a final design shear near 170 kips, two and a half to three times the permanent case (Stability During Construction, The Science Behind the Art). Practical consequence for our crews, which Paul should hold: engineered temporary cable bracing is sized to that probable event, not to a 20 to 25 mph site wind, which is why a properly braced frame looks over-braced; braces designed for 25 mph are expected to fail above it, and slender trusses cannot be set above a stated 15 mph until guyed to dead men (The Erector's Perspective). On high-rise work ASCE 37 Section 6.5 allows up to 80 percent reduction on mapped spectral accelerations with R=2.5, reflecting that a partially connected ductile system may fracture before developing full ductility (High-Rise), though most Your Company work is the low-rise case.

Sequencing runs from the braced bay outward so the permanent lateral system engages as early as possible. Each erection stage is analyzed as its own standalone building with wind applied per sequence, modeled tier by tier from column-splice to column-splice, and temporary cable bracing sized to the resulting base shear and removed only when the permanent diaphragm for that portion is in (Low-Rise, Stability During Construction). Starting erection at a braced-frame line, as on the 300 Tryon braced-core tower where plumbing the core plumbed the building, minimizes stability cables (It Doesn't Get Built Without the Erector). Cable detail matters: wire rope with a turnbuckle wrapped about 18 inches up the column, terminated against a welded keeper angle so the choker cannot ride up under load, with erectors preferring two 5/8-inch lines over going to 3/4 inch; a choker that only bites on itself has no test basis and will slide (Low-Rise, Stability During Construction). For long-span trusses the on-hook versus at-set check governs: orient the top chord web horizontal so the compression chord is stable to lift (a 145-ft, 160,000-lb truss with a W14x370 chord is unliftable web-vertical and erectable web-horizontal at identical weight), and use the L/r slenderness screen of under 80 likely stable, 80 to 100 needs a stability analysis, over 100 likely collapses after release and needs bracing (Stability During Construction, What Engineers Need to Know, Constructability Part 2 and Part 4). The Constructability Part 4 industrial-roof case (a 120-ton truss at L/b 180 against an 80 target, erected three feet out of plumb) and the Science Behind the Art barrel-truss kink (picked at midspan, finished with a 7-foot kink matching the predicted buckled shape) are the cautionary failures: slender-member instability is invisible to the naked eye even to seasoned erectors, so the pick analysis must be a stamped calculation. Temporary splices on long trusses shipped in pieces were sized for the final building, not the erection condition, so field CJP welds often get a temporary bolted connection so the crew moves on while welders finish (The Science Behind the Art, Working with Large Trusses).

Anchor-rod setting and tolerance is the single most recurring field-fix topic; Fisher spends a half hour on it because the problems repeat far too often (Field Fixes and Solutions). The hard rules: OSHA 1926.755 requires a minimum of four anchor rods per column with the assembly and column-to-base-plate weld designed for a 300 lb load 18 inches eccentric, and 1926.756(d) holds column splices to the same load (What Engineers Need to Know, Low-Rise). That OSHA floor is an erection-stability minimum, not a wind design: anchor rods sized only for the 300 lb at 18 inches resolve to about 0.6 ft-kip against roughly 9.7 ft-kip at 15 psf wind, eight to sixteen times too small, and Fisher's Utah collapse (a 40-ft HSS column building that went over in a 30 to 35 mph wind with a joist girder left unattached) shows the consequence. Design anchor rods for the real free-standing-column wind face, not the OSHA floor (What Engineers Need to Know). Detailing choice is decisive: placing the four rods outside the column footprint took a temporary-wind base anchorage from 146 percent concrete breakout down to a workable utilization by only enlarging the base plate, not the anchors, and reserving an inch or two of base-plate edge distance allows field slotting if a rod is off (Low-Rise, Stability During Construction, What Engineers Need to Know). Specify ASTM F1554, default to Grade 36 (color-coded blue) over high-strength 105 ksi (red) precisely because Grade 36 is weldable and ductile enough to cold-bend up to 45 degrees or heat-straighten, while you cannot weld to or bend 105 ksi rods, which must be replaced; a buried-nut (headed) rod develops full strength and resists pullout where a hooked rod can straighten and pull out, and thread engagement is roughly linear so a nut flush with the rod top is the check (Field Fixes Part 2, Field Fixes and Solutions, Welding Special Applications via F1554/S1). Templates must be wood or steel firmly fastened to the formwork so the pour does not drift the pattern, and problems multiply when the concrete contractor rather than the erector sets the rods (Field Fixes and Solutions). Set rods are reconciled against ACI 117 concrete tolerances, which are looser than the AISC COSP, so the steel detail absorbs the difference (Field Fixes Part 3). The crane-runway kink (a 280-ft box girder permanently deformed because rods at one end were set 6 inches out of straight) is the lesson that a setting error at one point propagates into an unfixable member (Field Fixes Part 9). Kanvinde's column-base test program confirms the validated detail: F1554 rods with leveling nuts, standard slightly-oversized holes, washer plates, and embedment deep enough that concrete pullout does not govern, a PJP-on-flange-outside plus reinforcing-fillet-inside toughness-rated weld sized to develop the flange, and the warning that exposed bases are flexible (8 to 10 percent drift, between pinned and fixed) and that the Design Guide 1 45-degree cone overpredicts shear-lug capacity by about a factor of two, so a shear lug must use the concrete size-effect method (Column Base Connection).

Field fixes and remediation share one doctrine: labor is the cost and material is cheap, so the cheapest fix is prevented by detailing and the second cheapest adds steel rather than chasing an overstressed member (Field Fixes and Solutions, Field Fixes Part 3, Part 8, Part 11). The diagnostic order is get accurate information first, act immediately to limit delay charges, determine whether a fix is even required, then settle the paperwork before engineering the repair. Tolerance accumulation is the common root cause: ASTM A6 lets a beam over-run theoretical depth up to 1/4 inch and a web sit off center, so continuity and embed plates are detailed oversized (continuity plates thicker than the beam flange, embeds 1/2 inch for deck and 3/4 inch for beam bearing, made larger in plan because they are routinely mislocated), and end plates detailed short about 1/8 inch each end with finger shims (Field Fixes and Solutions, Part 3, Part 4). Continuity plates must match the A992 50 ksi member; a real moment frame was invalid until 36 ksi plates were replaced (Field Fixes Part 3). Weld shrinkage shortens a CJP about 1/8 inch and accumulates into out-of-plumb columns and short moment lines (a 165-ft line drawn 2.5 inches short), corrected by plumbing the center column and leaning outward as welds shrink; AWS D1.1 requires a buildout pass when the root exceeds about 3/8 inch (Field Fixes Part 4). Column splice gaps of 1/16 inch or less need no action, up to about 1/4 inch may be shimmed with flat mild-steel shims, and the H/500 (L/500) plumb tolerance from the COSP with Appendix 6 bracing forces governs out-of-plumb columns (Field Fixes Part 4, Field Fixes and Solutions). The AISC 2005 spec permits 50 percent bolt-weld load sharing in shear connections with longitudinally loaded fillet welds, so a missing bolt row is fixed by reducing remaining bolts to 50 percent and welding the difference; hole misfits are reamed an eighth inch to the next bolt size with edge distance rechecked, with fill-and-redrill the least desirable since AWS has no general hole-restoration procedure (Field Fixes Part 6). Camber is shop-induced past yield and verified unstressed by string line in the shop, cannot be checked in the field, runs minus 0 plus 1/2 inch, pays only above a 5-lb/ft saving, and is kept off moment-connected, braced, spandrel, short (under 25 ft), light, and thin-web (1/4 inch) beams (Field Fixes and Solutions, Part 4, Part 5). Existing-joist and RTU remediation is gated on SJI load-table capacity, not SF: identify web and chord type with a micrometer, design reinforcement for the full panel shear, land concentrated loads at panel points (inverted channel plus web angle when off-panel), order reinforcing joists no-camber with a shallow 2-inch seat, and never cut the end compression diagonal or bridging without restoring it (Field Fixes Part 7, Part 8, Part 9).

Crane, rigging, and weld-type economics drive the erection bid more than tonnage. Erectors price in pieces and crane picks, not tons: count columns, beams, girders, joists, studs, vertical and horizontal bracing, deck SF, edge angle and bent plate, then add a weld-weight calculation on heavy splices (It Doesn't Get Built Without the Erector, The Erector's Perspective). Hoisting governs the plan; on 300 Tryon the tower crane was limited not by radius but by an 11,000-lb two-part hoist with an 85 percent safety derate, so the fix brought in a hydro to set first-tier full columns and cut upper columns in half. Heavy picks are both calculated and weighed on the operator's load cell before the swing, since rigging, paint, bolts, and welds push a pick over chart at the margins, a direct verify-do-not-generate confirmation that a calculated weight alone is not trusted. Lifting lugs use a factor of safety near 5 (between ASME BTH-1 categories B and C) on an exact unfactored assembly weight that captures all supplemental plates (High-Rise). The headline value-engineering lever appears in three videos: a full-capacity CJP column splice on heavy W14 shapes runs roughly 690 cubic inches and 193 lb of weld, about 35 lb deposited per shift, for a 6.5 man-day splice, and converting to a PJP sized to the actual design demand plus a 200 kip-ft erection moment (research confirmed CJP was not required) cuts it to about 1.9 man-days and saves on the order of 1,800 dollars per joint plus large schedule gains, with magnetic-particle plus visual replacing the UT every CJP otherwise carries (The Erector's Perspective, It Doesn't Get Built Without the Erector, The Splice is Right). Field fillet welds run flux-cored arc with 5/16 inch as the optimum and typical maximum since production is governed by passes not throat (3/8 inch jumps to two passes and 67 percent more cost), and seismic moment-connection welds add AWS D1.8 with a separate welder qualification (What Engineers Need to Know, It Doesn't Get Built Without the Erector). All of these are study aids: actual weld weights, deposition rates, man-days, and dollar figures must be re-verified for a live bid, and all member weights route through aisc_validator.py.

The Code of Standard Practice scope split is the framework that ties this together and the posture Your Company should adopt at bid. COSP Section 7 assigns the erector foundations-as-found, anchor-rod and embed installation, grouting, field connection material, temporary support, safety protection, frame and erection tolerances, and correction of errors, while the EOR carries the completed-structure design, the lateral-system definition, the erection-sequence requirements, and the connection forces (The Erector's Perspective, It Doesn't Get Built Without the Erector, Constructability Part 4). Two recurring documentation gaps generate out-of-bid cost and belong in the drawing-completeness gate: a nonstructural-only lateral system (precast shear wall or tilt-up) where the precast designer never accounted for incidental steel lean-on load, which forced a hard W14x74 brace and a 5-kip lean-on limit not in the original bid; and a specification that references both the COSP and ASCE 37 and so contradicts itself on hurricane loading, which the erector must red-flag and resolve by RFI, exclusion, or bid clarification (Low-Rise, Stability During Construction). Bringing the erector to the table early is repeatedly tied to schedule (a hospital compressed 52 weeks to 35, another 17 weeks saved) by substituting bolted for welded moment connections, choosing anchor-rod layouts that avoid temporary cable bracing, and modeling cranes, shoring, and bracing in the shared Tekla model (Constructability Part 3 and Part 4, It Doesn't Get Built Without the Erector). For ACP, the actionable controls are a stamped, signed-and-sealed erection-sequence plan authored under our PE; a confirmed lean-on limit and bracing responsibility in writing where any nonstructural lateral element exists; anchor rods set from firmly fastened templates with the four-rod minimum treated as a floor and the real wind face designed; and the every-couple-of-days brace-and-plumb cadence OSHA expects on slotted-end joist and joist-girder framing (Field Fixes Part 4). None of these sources introduce PEMB language or supplier names, and every quantity here is a study aid to be re-verified, with weights from aisc_validator.py and rates from bid_rates.py.

### Re-Watch and Ivan callout

- Highest-value erection re-watch in order: The Erector's Perspective and It Doesn't Get Built Without the Erector (full COSP Section 7 scope split, piece-and-pick estimating, CJP-to-PJP weld economics), then Erection Engineering of Low-Rise Buildings and Stability During Construction (per-sequence ASCE 37 wind, Design Guide 10 shielding/stacking, cable-brace sizing and anchor-rod-outside-the-footprint detail), then Field Fixes and Solutions (anchor-rod half hour, camber, A6 tolerance fixes).
- Ivan takeoff flags: price erection in pieces and crane picks, not tons; flag any long-span truss, transfer element, crane-runway bay, arched or cambered-HSS roof, or rolled member for an erection-engineering and tolerance-accumulation line; carry the 1.1 to 1.25 (up to 1.5 heavy-bolted) connection factor when converting analytical truss weight to picked weight; add a weld-weight calc on heavy column and truss splices and price the CJP-to-PJP conversion as a value-engineering option; and treat a nonstructural-only lateral system or a spec that cites both COSP and ASCE 37 as a drawing-completeness RFI before pricing. All member weights through aisc_validator.py; all rates from bid_rates.py; every quantity above re-verified for the live bid.

## Bolting and Welding Standards

The bolt-grade and joint-class decision is the first cost lever Ivan controls, and the recurring lesson across the bolting videos is do not over-specify. High-strength structural bolts come in two families: Group A at 120 ksi tensile (ASTM A325 and the twist-off F1852) and Group B at 150 ksi (A490 and twist-off F2280), per the matrices in High Strength Bolting: The Basics and Fastener Fundamentals. A307 common bolts run about 60 ksi and remain a sound, cheaper choice for static, non-fatigue work, while A325 and A490 are reserved for fatigue, seismic, load reversal, or pretensioned slip-critical joints (Bolting Primer Part 7). The single most expensive default error is calling slip-critical when snug-tight bearing would serve. Bolt Primer Part 9 and Part 8 make this quantitative: bolt shear strength is independent of pretension, so a bearing connection does not need pretension verification at all, and no-slip-at-factored-loads (phi = 0.85) is the costlier exception to no-slip-at-service-loads (phi = 1.0) and must be justified, not defaulted. For Your Company building frames this means bearing-type snug-tight is the estimating default and slip-critical pricing (extra bolts, faying-surface prep, pretension inspection) is triggered only by documented fatigue, reversal, or geometry sensitivity. All bolt shear, tension, slip, and bearing capacities come from AISC Table J3.2 and the RCSC Specification, never from LLM arithmetic, which is the direct bolting analog of the aisc_validator.py weight rule (High Strength Bolting: The Basics).

Pretension, when required, is delivered by one of RCSC's four methods and verified by procedure, not by measuring tension after install. Fastener Fundamentals and Bolting Primer Parts 10 and 11 name them as turn-of-nut, calibrated wrench, twist-off tension-control (TC) bolts to ASTM F1852, and direct-tension-indicator (DTI) washers to F959. Turn-of-nut works because it drives the bolt past yield onto the flat plateau of the load-elongation curve, so widely varying snug elongations converge on nearly the same pretension; the rule is snug then add one-half, one-third, or two-thirds turn by bolt length, half-turn typical, with large rotational tolerance remaining before fracture (Primer Part 11). The minimum required pretension is 70 percent of bolt ultimate tensile strength, and field measurements run above specified (turn-of-nut A325 about 35 percent over, A490 about 26 percent, calibrated wrench about 13 percent, the 1.13 Du factor), so that conservatism is already in the rule and is not extra capacity to spend. Mario's crews must run a Skidmore-Wilhelm pre-installation verification once per day and on any change of lot, length, or diameter, and on a slick-coated bolt a twist-off spline or a closed DTI gap does not by itself prove pretension, calibration does (Primer Parts 10 and 11). Torque-to-tension "cheater" tables are banned by RCSC because they run roughly 40 percent off (High Strength Bolting - Why isn't it Simple, Bolting Primer Part 10). The strongest field-tool recommendation in Fastener Fundamentals is to move off impact wrenches to non-impacting, non-reacting electric or pneumatic tools, which preserve coating on coated bolts where impacting drives it off corners and threads.

Three bolting failure modes deserve a standing place in the in-house PE review and Paul's QC briefs. First, prying action: a bolt loaded in tension through a flexible flange sees force well above the naive P/n division, easily 20 to 30 percent higher (Bolting Primer Part 7, High Strength Bolting basics, the Kemper Arena collapse), so any hanger, moment, or tension-bolted connection needs the prying calculation, and a count-based takeoff will undersize bolts. Second, loss of pretension from soft or gapped grip: dished flanges, insulation, or excess galvanizing inside the grip kill fatigue life and can let bolts fall out, fixed by shimming at the bolt line and barring non-steel material from the grip (Why isn't it Simple, the crane-girder and Hartford arena cases). Third, the long-joint penalty: past 50 inches of bolt line the per-bolt shear capacity drops about 20 percent, plus a further reduction for threads in the shear plane, so long field splices must carry the code reduction rather than load divided by count (Bolting Primer Parts 8 and 9). For coated Group B bolts, shop receipt inspection should screen for quench cracks (which rise with coated A490) and scrap the lot, while not panic-rejecting cosmetic seams and bursts that ASTM permits (Fastener Fundamentals).

On the welding side, every AISC-governed building project is automatically governed by AWS D1.1 for material 1/8 inch and thicker, with AWS D1.3 for sheet/deck under 3/16 inch and AWS D1.8 plus the AISC Seismic Provisions attaching only on seismic moment-frame scope (Bolting Primer Parts 1 and 2). D1.8, D1.5 (bridge), and D1.6 (stainless) do not belong in a standard Houston conventional bid by default. The dominant cost error in welded design, named in nearly every welding video, is the default CJP groove weld specified to avoid sizing a fillet. Weld Details: The Good, The Bad and The Ugly quantifies it on a real joint: 24.5 kips on a 5-inch rod is 0.23 ksi over the CJP, while a minimum 5/16 fillet carries it at 11 times demand using 0.23 pounds of weld metal versus 26 pounds for the CJP, a 96 percent reduction in deposited metal. The standing estimating and detailing rule is long-and-small fillets at the minimum prequalified leg, never below it, because doubling length doubles strength while doubling leg quadruples deposited metal. A CJP call-out on incoming drawings is therefore a cost flag Ivan should price the fillet alternate against, since the demand check is a short hand calc against AISC 360 Chapter J. Matching weld metal is required only on CJP groove welds in tension; everywhere else undermatching is permitted and actually lowers residual stress (Bolting Primer Parts 2 and 4). The engineer owns the effective throat E while the shop owns depth-of-prep S, process, and bevel angle, so Tekla details carry the S dimension, not E (Bolting Primer Part 3, Tables J2.1 through J2.4).

WPS qualification, welder qualification, electrodes, and preheat are Mario's domain under D1.1, and the prequalified-joint logic is the governing discipline: a prequalified standard joint can be used as-is, but any deviation (changed root face, skipped backgouge, non-steel backing) forces requalification by PQR, and a prequalified detail still requires engineer-of-record suitability judgment per the D1.1 note added after the El Paso lamellar-tearing failure (Weld Details, FHWA Bridge Welding Manual). Welders are qualified by process, so a flux-core shop cannot switch to SMAW without requalification, and a fresh welder qualification is required for each backing material since only steel backing is prequalified (Bolting Primer Parts 2 and 3). Hydrogen control runs through all of it: low-hydrogen electrodes (the E7018 reference, E for electrode, 70 for 70 ksi deposited tensile) ship sealed and live in heated rod ovens with exposure-time limits, because hydrogen cracking needs the coincidence of diffusible hydrogen, yield-level residual stress, and a hard microstructure (Primer Parts 1 and 2, FHWA manual). The prequalified minimum-fillet-size table routinely governs over the strength-calculated size, with low-hydrogen welding keying the table off the thinner part (A992 is welded low-hydrogen), so a 3/16 calc commonly becomes a 1/4 installed and any weld-quantity estimate built only off demand will under-bid (Bolting Primer Parts 3 and 4). Fit-up must be measured before deposit: D1.1 allows 1/16 of root gap, beyond which the fillet leg is enlarged by the gap amount, and the throat-stress jump is steep (21 ksi at fit, 84 ksi at a 3/16 gap left uncorrected), so backing must stay continuous on CJP joints (Bolting Primer Part 5). Distortion control is its own shop discipline: smallest adequate weld, fewest passes, lowest heat input, weld on or balanced about the neutral axis, sub-assemble at each sub-neutral-axis, and backstep where later welds would crack earlier ones on partly erected steel (Bolting Primer Part 6).

NDE scope and weld acceptance are where the bid must read the building's risk category rather than assume a flat add. Per AISC 360-10 Section N5.4 and the inspection-task tables N5.4-1 (before welding) and N5.4-3 (after welding), QC belongs to the fabricator and erector and QA to the owner's special inspector, and the two must agree the NDE scope from the contract before any weld is made, because the IBC and the code forbid imposing UT or RT after the fact (Weld Inspection: What Matters, NDE and Special Inspection of Seismic Welding). The Risk Category drives the line item: UT is required on 100 percent of CJP groove welds in tension butt, T-, and corner joints in material 5/16 inch or greater for ASCE/SEI 7 Risk Category III or IV, but only 10 percent for Risk Category II (Weld Inspection, Section 5b). The five NDE methods (VT, PT, MT, RT, UT) each have a lane: PT and MT find surface and near-surface flaws (PT only on ground-smooth surfaces such as cope access holes), UT is the workhorse for interior CJP volume but is not appropriate for PJP or fillets under 5/16, and re-checking a UT finding with RT gives conflicting calls because the two see different things (NDE of Seismic Welding). The governing philosophy from Weld Inspection is that D1.1 acceptance criteria are workmanship limits reflecting what a qualified welder can produce, not a structural-failure boundary, so cosmetic discontinuities are dispositioned under Commentary C-6.8 rather than over-repaired; the SAC UT round-robin found 16 percent of rejectable indications were false calls at locations with no real flaw, so disciplined VT plus right-sized UT avoids paying for repairs that fix nothing, and the repair-cost curve rises sharply from shop to field to completion. The visual reject list under Table N5.4-3 is cracks, lack of fusion, bad crater cross-section, out-of-tolerance profile and size, undercut, and porosity. Cited rates, percentages, and quantities here are study aids and must be re-verified against the live spec edition and the actual project documents before they touch a real bid (verify, do not generate).

### Anchor rods (Ivan, Mario, PE stamp)

Welding - Special Applications (AISC Design Guide 21 Chapter 12) is the anchor-rod authority. Standardize on F1554 grade 36 and, where a set-too-deep risk exists, order to Supplement S1 up front so a welded extension is defensible; grade 55 has no chemistry limit unless ordered to S1 and grade 105 is essentially uncontrolled and a near-guaranteed weldability problem. Never call out A325 for anchor bolts (use F1554), and Mario verifies weldability by chemistry and carbon equivalency off the MTR before any field weld. A welded extension uses a weldable doughnut washer, chisel-ground point, weld-one-side then backgouge then weld-two, ground flush; never a plug weld (no tension capacity) and never a tack on the inboard nut side (can crack the rod). The first fix for a misset rod is mechanical (coupler nut, mill the base plate), not a field weld.

### Re-watch shortlist

- Weld Details: The Good, The Bad and The Ugly (mRJp75pN0Ho): the twelve weld-design principles and the 96-percent CJP-versus-fillet cost case.
- High Strength Bolting: The Basics (PmXMTt_JPb8): joint-class decision, Table J3.2, pretension by RCSC, prying.
- Weld Inspection: What Matters (jhxRagJo644): N5.4 inspection tables, NDE by Risk Category, false-call discipline.
- Welding - Special Applications (Oq85-3nZsZQ): F1554 anchor rods, jumbo access holes, coated-steel WPS-by-test.
- NDE and Special Inspection of Seismic Welding (gIBim_sQXUk): QC/QA split, backing-bar UT, D1.8 if seismic work is ever taken.

## Spec Compliance (AISC 360 and AISC 341)

The specification backbone for every Your Company job is a layered code system, and the most repeated lesson across the seismic series (Sabelli Parts 1 through 8, Engelhardt Non-West-Coast Parts 1 and 2) is that you must know which layer governs which decision before you price or detail anything. ASCE 7 supplies the loads, the seismic design category, the risk category, the response modification factor R, and the analysis method. AISC 360 supplies member and connection strengths for every project, seismic or not. AISC 341 is a supplement that applies only when the job is a seismic project, meaning one that ASCE 7 forces to meet ductile detailing (Drawing and Specification Requirements, Muir and Sable, frames AISC 341 as a supplement to AISC 360, with AISC 360 applying to all projects). AISC 358 supplies the prequalified moment connections, and AWS D1.1 plus its seismic supplement AWS D1.8 supply the welding rules. The poll in Sabelli Part 5 made the point bluntly: seismic QA is not one document but AISC 360 Chapter N, AISC 341 Chapter J, AISC 358 Section 5.7, AWS D1.1 Section 6, and AWS D1.8 Section 7 all at once. For Houston and the ACP project this matters because Harris County is low-seismic, typically SDC A or B, where undetailed systems at R equal to 3 are designed essentially like wind and AISC 341 does not bind (Non-West-Coast Part 2; Seismic Design for Non-West Coast Engineers Part 1). The standing rule for Ivan is to read the seismic design category and R off the structural general notes first, confirm whether AISC 341 is invoked, and never assume seismic scope is absent or present.

AISC 360 Chapter C is the stability backbone, and Design for Stability (Geschwindner, AISC 360-10) lays out the structure cleanly: Section B3.5 sends you to Chapter C, where C1 lists the five effects that must be considered (member deformations, second-order P-big-delta sway and P-little-delta member effects, geometric imperfections, stiffness reduction from inelasticity and residual stress, and uncertainty in stiffness and strength), C2 gives required strength, and C3 gives available strength, with the analysis method chosen for one dictating the other. The three permitted methods are the Direct Analysis Method (C2 with C1.1), the Effective Length Method (Appendix 7.2), and the First-Order Analysis Method, and the Direct Analysis Method is the foundation because it sets the applicability limits on the others. The Direct Analysis Method reduces all stiffnesses to 0.8 and applies tau-sub-b to flexural stiffness, which earns K equal to 1 and removes the K calculation as a source of error; loads run at LRFD level or 1.6 times ASD so the higher second-order amplification is captured, and notional loads of 0.002 times alpha times the gravity load at each level model out-of-plumbness. Two tolerances anchor the analysis to real steel and carry into Your Company's field survey: out-of-straightness L over 1000 from ASTM A6, already baked into the column curves, and out-of-plumb L over 500 from the Code of Standard Practice. Stability Design of Low- and Medium-Rise Steel Buildings (White) confirms that for practically all multi-story buildings under wind and earthquake combinations the structure comes out stability non-critical with B2 at or below 1.7, so notional loads are not required with the lateral combination, but moment-frame spandrels and columns can be drift-governed and grow late in design (his spandrel jumped from W24x62 to W24x68 purely for stiffness). Ivan should flag moment-frame members as drift-sensitive and not treat strength-sized members as final.

AISC 360 member design runs through the chapter map the connection and seismic videos cite repeatedly: Chapter D and Table D3.1 for tension and shear lag, Chapter E for compression and column buckling, Chapter F for flexure, Chapter H for combined forces with interaction equation H1-1a, and Chapter J for connecting-element yielding, block shear, and the J10 concentrated-force limit states at panel zones and continuity plates (Introduction to Seismic Connections, Atherton; Seismic Part 6). Chapter I governs composite members, and New Composite Design Provisions (Jacobs) is the reference for concrete-filled HSS, encased columns, the load-transfer equations I6-1 and I6-2, and the steel-anchor section I8 that replaced the old shear-stud language for ACI 318 Appendix D consistency. Across all of these the controlling Your Company doctrine is fixed: member weights come from bridge/aisc_validator.py, never from any number spoken in a webinar, and the example sizes in these talks are study aids only that must be re-verified for real work.

AISC 341 is built on one idea taught from every angle in the seismic set: capacity design. You designate a ductile fuse, detail it to yield, then make everything else stronger than the fuse so it yields first (Underlying Concepts, Wong; Basic Concepts in Ductile Detailing; Malley TR Higgins lecture). The fuse is sized using expected yield strength, not minimum specified, through F-y-e equals R-y times F-y; for A992 that is 50 ksi specified, an R-y of 1.1, an expected 55 ksi, and a defined upper bound of 65 ksi (Sabelli Part 1). The fuses differ by system: the beam plastic hinge in special and intermediate moment frames (SMF, IMF), the brace yielding in tension and buckling in compression in special concentrically braced frames (SCBF), the shear-yielding link in eccentrically braced frames (EBF), and the steel core in buckling-restrained braced frames (BRBF), which yields in both directions because a grout-filled casing prevents buckling. R factors stated across the series are SMF, BRBF, EBF, and steel plate shear walls at 8, SCBF at 6, IMF at 4.5, OMF at 3.5, OCBF at 3.25, and undetailed at 3 (Sabelli Part 1; Non-West-Coast Part 2). The cost message is consistent and load-bearing for Ivan: a higher R buys smaller base shear but the ductile detailing more than offsets it, with an informal study in Drawing and Specification Requirements putting an SMF near R equal to 8 at roughly 2.5 times the cost of an R equal to 3 system, and To-3-or-Not-To-3 putting the connection-fabrication premium at 1.5 to 2.5 times. Capacity-protected surrounding members (columns, collectors, beams in chevron bays, gussets, base plates) run heavier than an elastic read of the plans suggests, so a seismic job is not priced like a gravity job and tonnage scaled off square footage alone misses it.

The fabricator and the in-house PE have distinct verification duties, and the clearest single list comes from Drawing and Specification Requirements (Muir and Sable): on any AISC 341 set, confirm the contract documents state the seismic force resisting system, the R factor, the demand-critical weld locations, the protected zones, the backing-bar treatment, and a confirmed AISC 358 prequalified connection. The named "public enemy number one" is designing an IMF or SMF without first confirming a prequalified AISC 358 connection exists for the chosen members, which forces an expensive owner-funded testing program under AISC 341 Chapter K. An SMF or IMF without a confirmed prequalified connection is a LOW-confidence, change-order-prone bid that gets an RFI, not a price, consistent with verify-do-not-generate. AISC 358 prequalification carries real limits the detailer must respect: no prequalified connections to the weak axis of a column, limited HSS options, and the RBS menu requires rolled or built-up I-shapes within depth, weight, flange-thickness, span-to-depth and width-to-thickness limits (Seismic Part 7 cites AISC 358 Section 5.3 for RBS member restrictions; A992 is not mandatory, A36 plate and Grade 50 are explicitly allowed). The 358 menu of prequalified moment connections includes RBS, welded unreinforced flange-welded web (WUF-W), bolted flange plate, and bolted and welded end plate, plus proprietary types, and SMF connections must demonstrate 0.04 radians of story drift while retaining 80 percent of nominal plastic moment, IMF 0.02 radians (Atherton; Malley).

Demand-critical welds, protected zones, and the post-Northridge weld details are where Mario's AWS scope and the in-house PE stamp meet, and the entries are specific. Demand-critical welds are required only where AISC 341 lists them, principally the CJP groove welds at beam-to-column joints and at column splices and bases in the higher-ductility systems, with the note that beam-to-column groove welds are demand-critical even in an ordinary moment frame (Drawing and Specification Requirements). They carry two toughness tiers from the FEMA/SAC research, roughly 20 ft-lb at 0 degrees F for all seismic welds and 40 ft-lb at 70 degrees F for demand-critical welds (Malley; Sabelli Part 5 ties the 40 ft-lb at 70 F to inelastic-strain locations and a service temperature above 50 F). AWS D1.8 governs backing bars, WPS, weld-access-hole welder qualification, and continuity-plate clip geometry that the older 2005 Appendix W carried. Backing treatment is location-dependent: to the inside of a section the backing may stay with a reinforcing fillet, while to the outside (the bottom flange) the backing must be removed, back-gouged, and a smooth transition provided, and a butt-splice CJP at a column splice generally needs no backing removal (Drawing and Specification Requirements; Seismic Part 2 details remove-backgouge-reweld-grind at the bottom flange, no weld dams, correct pass count, enlarged access holes, CJP web welds). Non-Destructive Examination of Seismic Welding (Mays) adds the inspection reality: NDE has no inherent IBC requirement and applies only when the contract documents or seismic provisions call for it, so Ivan must price NDE from the S-notes and the Division 05 spec rather than assume it, and the code forbids imposing UT or RT not in the documents. UT is the workhorse for CJP welds but is wrong for PJP and for fillets under 5/16 inch; the lower-flange backing-bar corner and the web-flange "gimme zone" blind spot are tied to many Northridge fractures, which is why backing comes off seismic lower-flange joints. AISC 360 Chapter N is the IBC-recognized special-inspection source, splitting QC (fabricator and erector) from QA (third party), and AISC 341 Chapter J plus the AISC 341 Appendix Q quality plan layer the seismic requirements on top, with AISC-certified-fabricator status able to drop shop welds from continuous to periodic inspection on non-seismic work.

Protected zones are a coordination hazard that crosses Mario's shop, Paul's safety brief, and Tekla detailing. They are no-attachment zones (the middle quarter of a brace, brace ends and the full gusset per AISC 341 Section F2.5c, and roughly one beam depth from the column face on moment frames) where no tack, shot pin, deck puddle weld, safety-cable hole, or curtain-wall attachment is allowed (Atherton; Seismic Part 2; Malley shows a Lehigh test where a stud over a plastic hinge fractured the beam top flange). The fix when violated is to cut and redo, and the prevention is to mark the zones on the model and resolve them at the pre-fabrication and pre-erection meeting (Mays). For braced frames the gusset must keep a free fold line, minimum twice the gusset thickness plus tolerance for the linear case, and that fold line must not be encased by a slab or composite deck or the hinge cannot form; a compressible material about 1.5 inches must surround a gusset embedded in concrete (Sabelli Part 3; Wong; Drawing and Specification Requirements). For Your Company anchor rods, the seismic rules are direct: column bases are designed to develop the member capacity and the amplified seismic load, weldable Grade 55 rods with the ASTM S1 supplement allow a field-welded extension fix per AISC Design Guide 1, Grade 36 is always weldable and Grade 105 is never weldable so a misplaced Grade 105 rod is very hard to correct, and shear at the base is best taken by bearing or friction rather than through the rods (Sabelli Parts 5 and 7; Drawing and Specification Requirements). Bolted joints in a seismic force resisting system are fully pretensioned with a Class A faying surface but designed for bearing, with standard holes the default and oversized holes allowed at braces for fit-up (Malley; Seismic Part 8). None of these entries conflict with Your Company doctrine; all are conventional structural steel with no PEMB language, and every weight, factor, and member size quoted here is a study aid that must be re-verified through bridge/aisc_validator.py and the stamped structural drawings before it touches a real bid.

### Re-Watch

For a live AISC 341 bid, re-watch in this order: Drawing and Specification Requirements for Seismic Design (gr3G7fNniVI) for the fabricator's bid-screen checklist and the AISC 358 prequalification trap; Introduction to Seismic Connections (gqCdO8zB0gA) for the SMF and SCBF connection rules and exact detail dimensions; Non-Destructive Examination of Seismic Welding (gIBim_sQXUk) for the NDE-scope pricing and protected-zone enforcement; and Seismic Design Part 2 (nR_4iv_Mboo) for the Northridge weld-detail catalog Mario's crew must reproduce.

### Ivan Callout

On takeoff, gate the structural general notes for SDC, risk category, R, the named seismic force resisting system, and a confirmed AISC 358 connection before pricing. If AISC 341 is invoked, add line items the tonnage hides: demand-critical high-toughness filler, backing-removal labor, continuity and doubler plates, gusset reinforcement, UT on every moment connection, NDE per the S-notes, and proprietary BRBs priced off the manufacturer brochure rather than aisc_validator.py. An SMF or IMF without a confirmed prequalified connection is LOW confidence and gets an RFI, not a price. All conventional member weights still route through bridge/aisc_validator.py; nothing in these videos overrides that.

## Bid and Estimating Intelligence

The single most consistent message across this corpus is that steel is priced wrong when it is priced by the ton. Every constructability speaker says the same thing in different words: material has flattened to roughly 25 to 30 percent of delivered cost while shop and field labor drive the rest, so the controlling estimating metric is dollars per square foot and piece count, not dollars per ton (Constructability Part 1, Part 2, Part 3, Part 4). Ruby and Associates prove it with a bay-size study where 30, 40, and 60 foot bays carry nearly identical tonnage but the 30 foot scheme generates far more trusses, joists, struts, connections, and joints, so "throw a blanket over the tonnage difference" and the man-hours still swing hard (Constructability Part 1). A four-option lateral study ran 1,000 to 2,100 dollars per ton but 88.80 to 113.75 dollars per SF, and the material spread was 40,000 to 50,000 dollars against a labor swing near 120,000 (Constructability Part 2). For Ivan this is direct confirmation of the existing doctrine that SF is the controlling input and that a measured member takeoff through aisc_validator.py beats SF x psf: an AISC sustainability webinar (Index sr line, Sustainability 2015) showed parametric estimators miss steel tonnage by 40 to 80 percent, which is exactly why we run a member-by-member count and carry separate fab and erection labor rather than one blended ton number. These quoted percentages and dollar figures are study aids and must be re-verified against BID_RATES for any live bid; they never override the CEO-locked rates.

Connections are where the money actually lives, and the corpus is unanimous that they are the largest single cost driver and the most common place to over-spend. Schwinger (50 Tips, SteelDay 2012) estimates roughly half the cost of a steel frame is connection-related because once mill steel reaches the shop nearly everything that follows is connection work, and a delegated-connection session put fab labor at 46 percent of cost (Index, Connection Design as the Fabricator's Representative). The mechanism that converts a connection into wasted money is over-specification: the drawing note "design connections for the full shear strength of the member" or "150 percent of the Table 3-6 uniform load" forces a coped, hole-punched grade-50 beam to carry two-to-four times its real reaction, and Schwinger's W24x76 example shows a 113-kip connection demanded where the real reaction near a concentrated load was actually 234 kips, so the blanket UDL note is both wasteful and occasionally dangerous (50 Tips). The single most economical thing an EOR can do is show actual reactions, moments, and axial forces on the contract drawings; most fabricators will accept actual design load plus 10 to 20 percent rather than a blanket UDL (Field Fixes Part 10). For Your Company the actionable rule is a drawing-completeness gate before pricing: if a set lacks reactions, stiffener and doubler locations, or reduces connections to a general note, that is a low-confidence RFI, not a minimum-connection assumption silently carried into the price (Constructability Part 3, Field Fixes Part 10, 50 Tips). The 30-story shear-wall embed that no bidder priced and the New York chevron with diagonals undersized because the software checked gross not net area are precisely the count-gaps our member takeoff and completeness gates exist to catch (Constructability Part 2).

Weld type is the sharpest cost lever the corpus quantifies, and it favors Your Company's in-house PE stamp directly. The erector sessions both walk a CJP-to-PJP column-splice conversion on heavy W14 shapes: a full-capacity CJP flange weld runs roughly 690 cubic inches and 193 pounds of weld, about 230 pounds of flux-core wire at 35 pounds deposited per shift, for 6.5 man-days per splice, while converting to a PJP sized to the actual design tension plus a 200 kip-ft erection moment cuts it to about 1.9 days and saves roughly 1,800 dollars per joint plus large schedule gains, with magnetic-particle and visual testing replacing 100 percent UT (Erector's Perspective, It Doesn't Get Built Without the Erector). Default-CJP over-welding is repeatedly named the costliest common error; a fillet alternate can cut weld metal dramatically (Index, Weld Details: The Good, The Bad and The Ugly). On HSS the deltas are explicit and bookable: a through plate adds a full extra shop hour per connection, a tube-to-tube fillet is about two hours of fit-up versus one to one-and-a-half days as a CJP, round HSS roughly triples truss connection cost, and bumping a 3/16 inch wall to 1/4 inch to avoid a through plate is often cheaper overall (HSS, What Your Fabricator Wishes You Knew). The shop economics behind this are concrete: the maximum single-pass fillet is 5/16 inch, so a 5/8 fillet takes six passes, meaning twice the strength costs six times the labor, and fabricators switch to PJP above about 3/4 inch (Secrets of the Manual). Mario's role maps onto all of this: prefer fillet then PJP over CJP, size welds to the applied load not full member yield, watch all-around weld symbols that can force an interior weld, and flag D1.8 plus separate welder qualification on any seismic moment connection (HSS, both erector sessions). Deposition rates, pass counts, and the 1,800-dollar figure are study aids to re-verify, not bid inputs.

Erection engineering and temporary-condition scope is the most commonly missed and mis-allocated cost in the corpus, and it is exactly the scope Your Company's in-house PE stamp should own. The bare, incomplete frame draws far higher engineered wind than the finished building (Index, Erection Engineering: Stability During Construction), so a frame stable when done can collapse under a 30 mph gust mid-erection. Fisher catalogs the failure modes: a 40 ft HSS-column building in Utah collapsed in 30-to-35 mph wind because a joist girder sat unattached on a column top, and the OSHA 1926.755 four-anchor-rod minimum plus the 300 lb at 18 inch eccentric load gives erectors a false sense of stability because rods sized only for that load will not hold a frame against wind (Field Fixes and Solutions, Field Fixes Part 1, Field Fixes Part 3). The L-over-b screen is the bookable rule: under 80 the member is stable as set, 80 to 100 needs a stability analysis, over 100 will likely collapse after release and needs erection bracing, and the industrial roof erected 3 feet out of plumb had an L-over-b of 180 against a target of 80 (Constructability Part 2, Constructability Part 4). The erection engineer should be priced as real scope: a stamped plan runs from a few thousand dollars for one truss to tens of thousands on a large project, and temporary shoring towers, welding enclosures counted by how many times a welder is re-enclosed, crane sharing, and soil-improvement timing are all line items, not overhead (Erector's Perspective, Constructability Part 4). Ivan should add a constructability screen to every set that computes truss and girder L-over-b, flags concrete-core lateral systems as brace-frame substitutions that grow our erection scope, and budgets temporary sway frames and cable bracing before the field hits them.

Anchor rods are the recurring field-cost sink the corpus spends the most time on, and the discipline is consistent enough to standardize. Default to F1554, never "A325 anchor bolts," because a supplier will quietly furnish A449 rod cut to length and the buyer thinks they got A325 (Are You Properly Specifying Materials, both sessions). Prefer fewer, larger, lower-strength Grade 36 rods over many small high-strength rods, both because four rods place far more accurately than eight or twelve and because Grade 36 and Grade 55-S1 are weldable for field correction while Grade 105 is never weldable, so a low-set 105 rod cannot be saved by welding (Field Fixes and Solutions, Field Fixes Part 1, Field Fixes Part 2, Steel Design After College Part 11). Use the AISC Manual Table 14-2 oversized base-plate hole sizes coordinated with ACI 117 placement tolerance so rods set by the concrete contractor land the base plate clean, and dimension templates center-to-center explicitly to avoid the misread that put 1,300 rods out of position and forced a re-drill to adhesive anchors (Are You Properly Specifying Materials, Field Fixes Part 1, Secrets of the Manual). The cost case is that a 6-inch setting error at one end of a 280-foot crane runway propagated into an unfixable S-kinked girder, and that a labor-not-material rule governs every field fix, so the cheapest fix is the one prevented by detailing and the second cheapest is the one solved by adding steel (Field Fixes Part 9, Field Fixes and Solutions). These table numbers (14-2, 1-22, J3.3) are 15th-edition citations that predate the 16th-edition basis aisc_validator.py wraps and must be re-confirmed before quoting; the 16th edition also rebased connection-material tables from 36 to 50 ksi, so a 15th-edition connection takeoff assumes the wrong default grade (Are You Properly Specifying Materials).

Camber, composite floors, and the construction-stage condition are the bid traps that surface later as change orders, so they belong in the estimate up front. Camber pays only above a roughly 5-pound-per-foot weight saving, runs about 35 to 200 dollars cold per infill beam and roughly ten times that for hot, and a cambered W21x44 jumping to a W21x83 when camber is removed shows the weight-versus-labor trade (Specifying Camber). The do-not-camber filters are bookable: skip spans under about 24 feet, depths under 14 or over 44 inches, webs a quarter inch or thinner, and anything under 3/4 inch, and never camber moment-frame, braced, or directly-welded members (Specifying Camber, Field Fixes and Solutions, 50 Tips). The composite-floor change-order pattern repeats across Field Fixes Part 5 and the Steel Design After College composite sessions: chasing a level pour on near-zero-camber beams accumulated 3 to 3.5 inches of extra concrete mid-span on one medical job, over-camber left studs protruding above the slab and cost a fire rating, and a deck spanning 9 to 12 feet deflects 5/8 to 3/4 inch and that extra concrete over a million SF is real money. The fix is a specification note assigning extra concrete from deck and beam deflection to the GC's scope so it does not return as a back-charge to Your Company (Steel Design After College Part 3, Part 4, Field Fixes Part 5). Two construction-stage items are life-safety and must be PE-verified: wet-concrete girder bracing where a deck running parallel left a girder effectively unbraced and a worker was killed in a lateral-torsional buckling failure (Steel Design After College Part 3), and a flat-roof ponding check, since most economical roofs fail the AISC 360 Appendix 2 Cp + 0.9 Cs less than 0.25 stiffness check and the quarter-inch-per-foot slope is not a guaranteed safe harbor (Recent Developments in Design for Ponding).

The fabricator-versus-erector pricing dynamic is the connective tissue under all of this. The fabricator buys raw steel by the ton then loads man-hours for detailing, drilling, coping, welding, bolting, surface prep, and shipping; the erector sells labor and hoisting and prices in pieces, crane picks, bolt counts and sizes, and weld weight, never tons, with GCs converting to dollars-per-ton only as a negotiating metric (Erector's Perspective, It Doesn't Get Built Without the Erector, Constructability Part 4). Because Your Company is both fabricator and erector, our bid must reconcile both lenses: count columns, beams, girders, joists, studs, bracing, deck SF, and deck-edge bent plate, compute moment-connection and column-splice weld weight as explicit drivers, run every member weight through aisc_validator.py rather than LLM math, and weigh heavy picks the way the QC director describes because rigging, paint, bolts, and welds can push a pick over chart at the margins (Erector's Perspective). The repeated case against splitting a job between two fabricators, where the absent shop-fit check forced air-arcing out CJP welds in the field at very high cost, argues for single-fabricator scope plus a mandatory pre-erection fit verification as a coordination gate on ACP (Field Fixes Part 3, Field Fixes Part 6). The early-fabricator-collaboration evidence is strong enough to use as a sales argument: a 144,000 SF hospital under the constructability method saved 17 weeks against design-bid-build, and a Georgia crane building moved trusses from 25 to 50 foot spacing, removed about 835 tons, and saved close to a million dollars and 16 weeks while making the structure stiffer (Constructability Part 3, Part 2). Across every video the throughline matches our own doctrine: verify, do not generate, source the SF, price the connections and the construction-stage scope, and never let a tonnage-times-rate number stand in for a member-and-labor takeoff.

### Re-Watch and Ivan callout

The highest-value estimating watches, in order, are the four Constructability sessions (Part 1, Part 2, Part 3, Part 4) for the dollars-per-SF-over-dollars-per-ton and piece-count doctrine, the two erector sessions (Erector's Perspective, It Doesn't Get Built Without the Erector) for the CJP-to-PJP weld-cost model and the piece-and-pick estimate template, 50 Tips for the connection-over-specification RFI catalog, the HSS fabricator session for connection-hour deltas, and Field Fixes Parts 1, 2, and the main Field Fixes and Solutions for the anchor-rod discipline. For Ivan specifically: run the drawing-completeness and reaction-presence gate before any number, compute truss and girder L-over-b against the 80/100 thresholds, flag every through-plate, tube-to-tube CJP, AESS, blanket-UDL, full-MP, and 4-inch-spandrel-flange condition as a cost driver or RFI, default anchor rods to F1554 Grade 55-S1 or larger Grade 36 with Table 14-2 holes, carry an extra-concrete deflection note on composite floors, and treat every spec number quoted from these videos (table numbers, deposition rates, dollar figures, percentages) as a study aid to re-verify against the 16th-edition Manual, aisc_validator.py, and BID_RATES before it touches a live bid.

## Doctrine Flags

This corpus is AISC and SJI education recorded by named presenters at named employers, so it is dense with supplier and manufacturer names that must never migrate onto a Your Company client document under Hard Rule 4 and the Tier 1 brand stance. The Simple Connections Simplified session is presented by a Canam Buildings engineer and a Vulcraft-Verco engineer and names proprietary deck side-lap clinch fasteners by brand; Composite Steel Joists carries a "Vulcraft district office" reference; Metallizing is delivered entirely by Can-Am Bridges and turns on their in-house arc-spray practice; Steel Design After College Part 8 names Vulcraft and Mercor as joist and deck sources; the Steel Construction Process role-map names Nucor, "New Core," and Butler as metal-building examples; and both materials webinars name mill sources, with Properly Specifying Materials (Kruth) citing ArcelorMittal, Nucor Yamato, Gerdau, and Steel Dynamics as the A913 rolling mills. Every one of these is an internal estimating or methodology input only. Ivan may use them to size lead times and sources, but they stay off proposals, GP reports, and capability sheets exactly as Vulcraft, Canam, Nucor, and Ayamsa already do.

The single largest verify-do-not-generate exposure in this corpus is the AISC Manual edition gap. Many of the most useful entries were recorded against the 15th edition, while aisc_validator.py wraps the v16.0 database, and the table numbers and default grades do not carry across cleanly. Field Fixes and Solutions (Fisher) explicitly cites Table 14-2 anchor-rod washers, Table 1-22 A6 depth tolerance, and Table J3.3 reaming as 15th-edition numbers and the entry flags them for re-confirmation before any live quote. Properly Specifying Materials (Kruth) states the headline shift directly: the 16th edition rebases all connection-material tables from 36 ksi to 50 ksi, so any connection takeoff priced off a 15th-edition default assumes the wrong grade. The doctrine action is that no table number, washer size, edge distance, or default Fy spoken in these videos is a bid input until it is re-verified against the current Manual and the validator; the videos are study aids, not the system-of-record. This is the same posture that protects every rate, weight, and quantity in the corpus, and several entries name that trap on themselves: the deck-attachment patterns, weld leg sizes, and bolt grades in Simple Connections trace to SJI, SDI, and AISI tables rather than a generated figure, and Rules of Thumb for Steel Design is entirely ASD service-load approximation (weight equals 5M/d, area equals weight/3.4) that must never override a validated member takeoff.

Material-spec doctrine across the two Carter and Kruth webinars and Field Fixes converges on a hard anchor-rod rule that maps straight onto Your Company's anchor workstream. Never call out "A325 anchor bolts": Carter notes the supplier then quietly furnishes A449 rod and the buyer believes they bought A325, and anchor rods are governed by ASTM F1554, defaulting to Grade 55 with supplement S1 for weldability so a low-set rod can take a field-welded extension. Grade 105 is high-strength and never weldable, so a mis-set Grade 105 rod cannot be field-corrected, a point Field Fixes and Field Fixes Part 2 both stress alongside the F1554 color code (A36 blue, Grade 55 yellow, Grade 105 red). Current preferred grades are A992 for W shapes (never "A992 Grade 50"), A572 Grade 50 for HP and the 16th-edition connection-material basis, A500 Grade C at 50 ksi for rectangular HSS and 46 ksi round, A53 Grade B at 35 ksi for pipe (not interchangeable with round HSS), and A513 is a banned handrail tube because it carries no minimum strength level. Ivan should lock these into aisc_validator.py lookups rather than trust an LLM grade string, and the Properly Specifying Materials entry confirms this is a verify-don't-generate reinforcement, not an override of any locked value.

The most systematic doctrine boundary in the corpus is the bridge-versus-building code firewall, which runs through roughly a quarter of the deep-read entries and must keep AASHTO and AWS D1.5 citations out of any AISC 360 building bid. Steel Bridge Fabrication (Karl Frank) runs under AASHTO and AWS D1.5 with preheat and amperage from D1.5 Section 1.5 and Table 5.1, not the AWS D1.1 building code Mario certifies under; the entry notes any bridge work would need separate D1.5 procedure and welder qualification. Fatigue and Fracture Design, Loads and Analysis, That's Not Fracture Critical, the two Fracture-Control Plan lectures, and Challenging Bridge Projects are all AASHTO LRFD with HL-93 live load, detail categories A through E-prime, the 0.8 and 1.75 fatigue factors, the FHWA 2012 SRM memo, and AWS D1.5 clause 12, none of which apply to building steel. The doctrine each entry encodes is identical: tag the content bridge-domain, treat its spec numbers as reference only, and never let an AASHTO fatigue category, fatigue-limit value, or load factor be cited as an AISC 360 or aisc_validator.py number. Most Your Company building steel is strength-governed, not fatigue-governed, so this is knowledge literacy rather than a routine takeoff input. The bolting carryover also needs a caution: these bridge entries reference A490 field welding and AASHTO practice that do not override the building-side RCSC and AISC 360 defaults.

PEMB and metal-building language is the Tier 1 brand line, and three entries carry framing that must be firewalled out of outward copy. Design of Underhung Hoist and Crane Girders repeatedly references pre-engineered metal buildings as the host structure for underhung cranes; that is the speaker's context, and the entry flags that it must not migrate into Your Company language, which stays conventional structural steel. Design of Frames Using Web-Tapered Members is built on Design Guide 25 metal-building-manufacturer practice with a 55 ksi gabled modular frame of welded tapered plate girders; the entry treats it as engineering literacy only and flags that a tapered built-up frame is welded-plate tonnage that aisc_validator.py rolled-shape weights will not cover, so tonnage must come from plate dimensions and weld volume, not the validator. The Steel Construction Process role-map names metal building systems and their manufacturers generically. In all three the methodology is usable internally for estimating and screening (internal framing-type identification is allowed), but the outward positioning stays "conventional structural steel, concept to completion" with no PEMB, pre-engineered, or metal-building-manufacturer wording. AESS, by contrast, is fully consistent with the brand because it is engineered architecturally exposed conventional steel, per the SSPC and Code of Standard Practice Section 10 entry.

Rate and pricing discipline is its own flag because several entries quote concrete dollar figures that are presenter regional numbers, not Your Company pricing. Design Tips for Constructible Steel in High-Seismic Regions states special moment frame around 30 dollars per SF, brace frame around 18, transfer beams at 20,000 to 40,000 dollars each, and caissons around a million each; the entry explicitly notes any rate transfer to a Your Company bid must still use the CEO-locked BID_RATES in bid_rates.py and that these are the presenters' regional figures. Metallizing quotes 12 to 14 dollars per SF, Challenging Bridge Projects quotes metallizing at 0.50 per pound, and Rules of Thumb gives a 40-to-60-ton-per-week erection rate and a stories-over-3-plus-7 psf weight rule. None of these are Your Company numbers and none touch the locked fab, erection, joist, roof-deck, or composite rates. The connection-cost split that does recur as durable doctrine is the cost pie from Connection Design as the Fabricator's Representative (roughly material 28 percent, fabrication 46 percent, erection 26 percent) and the rule that connection material alone is 5 to 30 percent of tonnage; these support the existing posture that SF times psf is ROM only and that the validator carries base-shape weight, not connection steel, doublers, or stiffeners.

Two cloud-connector and confidentiality cautions sit underneath all of this. First, several entries cite Manual section and Design Guide numbers from memory or mis-state them on the recording: Field Fixes Part 2 mis-numbers the base-plate guide as Design Guide 3 when it is Design Guide 1, Constructability Part 3 says "SSP5" for SSPC-SP 5, and That's Not Fracture Critical labels an AWS clause "C15 class 12" as approximate transcript audio. Any such citation must be verified against the actual standard before it is quoted, which is the connector-security least-privilege principle applied to ingested content: do not act on a number embedded in a source file without confirming it. Second, the SF-is-the-controlling-input and ask-before-guessing rules are reinforced repeatedly. Steel Bridge Fabrication's 3/8-inch flange case is the headline verify-don't-generate lesson, where an estimator assumed a stated dimension was a misprint and bid 3/4 inch, then was forced to build the failing 3/8 inch members; the doctrine is to RFI rather than auto-correct a stated value. Constructability Part 3 and Connection Design as the Fabricator's Representative both demand refusing to price incomplete connection information and running a drawing-completeness gate before pricing, treating general-note connections and blanket UDL or full-strength specs as low-confidence RFI items rather than silent assumptions.
