The Designing for Membrane Architecture entry adds the Dallas Cowboys fabric-roof collapse as the cautionary case for never crediting unverified bracing, the same principle behind sourcing tonnage from a measured member takeoff rather than an assumed area or bracing condition. Every one of these reinforces, never contradicts, the verify-do-not-generate core.

## Ivan's Takeoff Direct Callouts

The first standing rule across this whole library is that member tonnage is the smaller half of the cost story, so Ivan's takeoff cannot stop at the wide-flange and HSS weights that aisc_validator.py returns. The Fabricator's Representative session puts the erected-steel cost pie at roughly material 28 percent, fabrication 46 percent, erection 26 percent, and states connection material alone runs 5 to 30 percent of total tonnage that estimators routinely miss (Connection Design as the Fabricator's Representative, COSP Section 16.3, AISC 360 Chapter J). Constructability Part 4 and the HSS session reach the same place from the labor side: material has flattened near 25 to 30 percent of total cost while shop and field labor drive the bid. The operational consequence is that every braced bay, moment joint, splice, base, and AESS face must carry a separate connection-material and connection-labor line that aisc_validator.py does not produce, because the validator carries shapes, not gusset plates, doublers, stiffeners, reinforcing bars, or weld volume. Treat any flat per-ton connection allowance as ROM only and flag it.

The concrete count-and-price list for connection steel breaks out as follows, each item grounded in an entry. Continuity plates (transverse stiffeners) and web doubler plates at moment-frame column panel zones are the headline add: Moment Connections Part 1 worked a routine W24x103-into-W14x159 joint at 882 kip-ft and still needed full-depth stiffeners plus two 3/4-inch doublers, sized through the six J10 column-side limit states (J10.1 flange local bending, J10.2 web local yielding, J10.3 crippling, J10.5 compression buckling, J10.6 panel-zone shear, J10.8 stiffener design). Stiffeners and Doublers cautions that pricing the panel zone off full beam moment capacity instead of the actual moment breakdown can put doublers on nearly every column (the office study went from about 100 percent to about 26 percent of columns needing doublers when actual moments were used), so Ivan should carry doublers and stiffeners as a flagged scope item, not a default, and read the spec for who designs them. Gusset reinforcement and seismic detailing items are the next block: continuity plates, gusset plates, slotted-HSS reinforcing plates, knife/hinge plates, and demand-critical welds appear on any set tagged AISC 341, 358, SMF, SCBF, or IMF (Introduction to Seismic Connections; Chevron Brace Part 2; Night School 6 Session 5). The Chevron Part 2 example shows the real tonnage risk: the mechanistic two-load-case capacity-design analysis forced a beam upsize from W24x84 to W24x176, which Ivan must price at the seismic size, not the gravity size. Whitmore-section gusset buckling, the 2t (or 3t) hinge fold-line clearance, slot-plus-1/8-inch HSS net-section loss, and the slot reinforcing plates per AISC 341 F2.5b are all detailing-driven quantities flowing from these jobs.

Bolting, weld, and anchor quantities each have their own callouts. For bolts, lock the two-bolt-size rule with a 1/4-inch diameter gap to prevent wrong-bolt installation (Fabricator's Representative: 3/4-inch A325 Group A and 1-inch A490 Group B, both ASTM F3125), and price slip-critical only where the EOR demands it because faying-surface prep (Class A mu 0.30, Class B mu 0.50) plus pretension and inspection make it materially costlier than snug-tight bearing (Fundamental Concepts Part 1; Bracing Connections; The Splice is Right notes bearing bolts in oversized holes can cut truss-splice bolt count by 50 percent versus slip-critical). For welds, the 5/16-inch fillet is the economic threshold: it lays in one pass, 3/8 needs roughly three passes (about 3x cost), 1/2 about six passes (about 6x), so cost scales with passes not leg size (Fundamental Concepts Part 1, Manual equation values). CJP is the most expensive weld because of prep, backing, NDE, and certified welders; the Splice session quantifies the swing with a W14x730 chord where a welded shop splice used about 70 lb of weld metal versus a bolted version's roughly 6,900 lb of steel and 128 bolts, a contractor-priced 79 percent cost cut, so the splice method assumption materially swings both tonnage and bolt count through aisc_validator.py. The HSS session adds that a tube-to-tube CJP runs one to one-and-a-half days versus two hours for the fillet equivalent, and a single through-plate adds about an hour of shop time each. For anchor rods, default to F1554 (never "A325 anchor bolts," which quietly yields A449 rod per Are You Properly Specifying Materials, both Carter and Kruth versions), standardize Grade 55 with supplement S1 weldable so a low-set rod can be field-corrected, and flag any Grade 105 callout as field-uncorrectable. Freestanding columns need four anchor rods resisting the OSHA 300 lb force at 18 inches from the face (Fabricator's Representative; The Splice is Right, OSHA Subpart R), and washer holes follow Manual Table 14-2 coordinated with ACI 117. Joist end anchorage and deck fastener patterns are separate buyout-adjacent scope: joist member weights come from SJI tables, not aisc_validator.py, and deck profile, gauge, yield, and fastener pattern drive cost and even allowable unshored span (Steel Specifications Unraveled flags the 8'-9" versus 9'-9" swing when deck yield is omitted), so deck supply and installation stay always in Your Company scope and get priced item by item rather than assumed.

The scope-gap RFIs to raise before pricing are the other half of this work, because the recurring root cause across the connection series is incomplete EOR force data. Bracing Connections is explicit: the EOR often hands only the brace axial load and omits the beam reaction Rb, the transfer force Ab, and whether the column is HSS (needed for Qf), so the detailer cannot see that axial even exists in a joint, and the speaker was on a live job with about 50 gusset-to-column shear plates that got default horizontal slots and needed reinforcement. Missing transfer forces are therefore RFI number one: transfer force does not equal member axial load unless the bay has no bracing, and the connection PE must request true transfer forces from the SER per COSP Section 3.1.2 rather than letting Tekla substitute full member axial. Envelope-loading confusion is RFI number two: a building with many load combinations produces apparent through-forces and nodes that lack equilibrium, plus eccentric work lines (the Fabricator's Representative example showed an 8-inch offset generating 347 ft-k with no moment listed), both of which should trigger a confirm-true-forces RFI and possibly member up-sizing. Seismic system confirmation is RFI number three: confirm the SFRS, R value, demand-critical welds, protected zones, and the prequalified AISC 358 connection before bidding, because Houston is mostly low-seismic SDC A/B with R=3 undetailed, but any out-of-region or higher-risk job pulls in 341/358 detailing and AWS D1.8 welds as real cost adders (Introduction to Seismic Connections; the joist-girder session notes SDC and R drive per-bay tonnage more than span, so Ivan must read SDC/R off the structural notes first). SF and gross-area confirmation remains the controlling-input RFI per house doctrine, since a structural-only subset rarely states gross area. AESS category is RFI number four: AESS escalates labor not tonnage, priced item by occupant-proximity category per COSP 10.2 (categories 1 within touch, 2 within 20 ft, 3 above 20 ft), and a set that says AESS but omits which items (welds ground smooth, mill-mark removal, tighter coping) needs a clarification before any blast/finish line is priced (SSPC Surface Preparation; HSS session). Two more worth a standing RFI: stair and platform bracing or drift connections that are invisible on incomplete drawings, since if it is not shown it is not in the price (Steel-Framed Stairway Part 2), and the surface-prep class itself (SP 6 commercial versus SP 10 near-white), which directly drives the blast line item and should sit LOW until confirmed.

Several secondary-quantity formulas are worth encoding into the count-gap engine as study aids, every one re-verified before it touches a real bid. From the seismic capacity-design entries: brace expected tension Tu = RyFyAg, connection-design compression at 1.1 times nominal buckling, post-buckling at 0.3 times buckling, with the frame mechanistic analysis dividing the connection compression back by 1.1 (Chevron Part 2; Night School 6 Session 5). HSS net-section loss at a slotted brace is the wall area lost to a slot equal to gusset thickness plus 1/8 inch per wall, computed on nominal (not 0.93 design) wall, which usually forces a reinforcing plate whose effective net area must at least equal the brace gross area (Chevron Parts 1 and 2). A1085 HSS removes the 0.93 design-wall factor that A500 carries, a real wall-area difference Ivan should reflect when capacity is tight (Are You Properly Specifying Materials; HSS session). The Whitmore section spreads brace load 30 degrees each side over the connection length to set the critical gusset width, a directly codeable geometry rule (Bracing Connections, Manual Figure 9-1; Fundamental Concepts Part 2). Shear-lag U = 1 minus xbar over L reduces tension-rupture area on angles and WT stems (a long-leg double angle gave U = 0.85, a 15 percent reduction), and effective hole diameter for net-area math is bolt diameter plus 1/8 inch (Fundamental Concepts Parts 1 and 2). The thermal-growth rule for fit-up allowance is about one-eighth inch per 100 feet per 15-degree shift from the 60-to-70-degree shop temperature, relevant for Houston summer sets (Constructability Part 4, DG23 Section 6.8). For temporary-bracing budgeting, screen truss and girder L-over-b against the 80 threshold to flag where temporary sway frames and cable bracing are needed (Constructability Part 4). The gusset-to-beam fillet gets a 25 percent length increase for non-uniform force even when the design says no moment (Bracing Connections, Hewitt-Thornton). And for engineering-hours folded into the fab and erection rates, the worked corner-connection figure of roughly one hour per connection (about 20 minutes when pictures reuse) is a usable count-times-rate basis (Night School 6 Session 4). Every one of these is a verify-don't-generate input: the formula shapes the count, but the member weight and the final capacity still route through aisc_validator.py and the in-house PE stamp, never through any number quoted in a webinar.

For ACP specifically, the priorities are reading SDC and R off the structural notes before pricing connection labor, screening the column bases for the four-rod F1554 Grade 55 S1 pattern with Manual Table 14-2 hole sizes against the concrete contractor's ACI 117 tolerances, confirming any AESS items per face before pricing finish, and filing the transfer-force and SF-confirmation RFIs early rather than absorbing them as change orders later.

## Recommended Re-Watch List

From the 232-video index, these 18 carry the most direct operations value for Your Company and reward a full second viewing by a named person. They cluster around the work that actually moves a bid number or prevents a field problem: delegated connection design, erection stability under our own PE stamp, bolting and welding discipline, base plates and anchor rods, seismic connection premiums, and the Code of Standard Practice scope split. The selections favor the high spec-reference, high-density sessions over the broad theory lectures, because the theory backstops the validator but does not change a takeoff line or a shop hour.

The single highest-priority re-watch is "Connection Design as the Fabricator's Representative" (zEUATyZFOEo, sr=45), which Joseph and Ivan should watch together. It is the densest entry in the entire index and it defines our whole delegated-design posture under AISC Code of Standard Practice Option 3: count connection types, write RFIs to strip costly geometry, choose repetition because fab labor dominates cost, and design to AISC 360 Chapter J, RCSC, and AWS D1.1. Pair it directly with "Understanding the Code of Standard Practice" (2uGymrKGkcU) for Joseph, which sets the drawing-completeness gate, the three connection-responsibility options, the 6.4.4 camber tolerances, and the erection-disclosure rules that anchor our verify-do-not-generate bid posture. Together these two are the doctrinal spine for how ACP and every future set gets screened before pricing.

For the connection-design engineering itself, the PE and Ivan should re-watch "Moment Connections, Part 1" (L6R9bqhxrnM) and "Bracing Connections" (LPUhN4zoZaA) in sequence. Part 1 works the six J10 column-side limit states with a real W24x103-to-W14x159 example and maps panel-zone, stiffener, and doubler additions straight onto takeoff and Tekla; the bracing session gives the Whitmore, lower-bound, and uniform force method basis plus the actionable rule to block default horizontal slots in axial-carrying gusset and corner shear plates and to RFI missing EOR transfer-force data. Reinforce both with "Connection Design: Dealing with Load Path, Transfer Forces and Apparent Lack of Joint Equilibrium" (-_1h4muNI7k), which carries the load-bearing rule that transfer force does not equal member axial load unless the bay is unbraced, so our connection PE must request transfer forces from the SER per COSP 3.1.2 and never let Tekla substitute full member axial load. "Vertical Bracing Connections - Analysis and Design" (Qr2mYsXSR4s) on Design Guide 29 belongs in the same block for the lower-bound plus UFM special cases and the firm rule never to add welds the engineer did not assume.

For erection engineering, which is stamped work Your Company owns rather than buys, the PE should re-watch "Erection Engineering of Low-Rise Buildings" (TJP57O8XudU). It ties per-sequence wind via ASCE 37 construction-period factors and Design Guide 10 shielding, temporary cable bracing, and anchor-rod and moment-connection details directly to our Tekla erection-procedure and PE-stamp deliverable, which is the low-rise envelope most of our work lives in. Add "The Erector's Perspective" (tDl6_Y8_XlI) for Paul and Mario: an ironworker QC director shows how erectors re-price a set against crane reach, weld access, and construction-stage stability, with a CJP-versus-PJP splice cost model and the COSP Section 7 scope split mapped across all five of our streams.

Bolting and field welding deserve two dense re-watches. "Fastener Fundamentals" (rt6D-p5BgO8, sr=18) is the right one for Paul on field bolting and shop receipt inspection: torque-tension-angle, the RCSC snug-tight and four pretension methods, Group A versus B grades, coatings, and documented field failures. "Weld Details: The Good, The Bad and The Ugly" (mRJp75pN0Ho) is Mario's: twelve welded-connection design principles where the costliest common error is default-CJP over-welding, with the fillet alternate cutting weld metal roughly 96 percent, which is real money on every joint we detail. For the seismic-weld and NDE side that any out-of-region job triggers, re-watch "Quality Control and Quality Assurance" (C2PFj9YZ_mw), which establishes AISC 360 Chapter N as the single IBC-recognized special-inspection source, splits QC from QA with every task tagged Perform or Observe, and carries the rule that undocumented inspections count as not performed.

Base plates and anchor rods get two targeted re-watches for Ivan, the PE, and the anchor-rod setting crew. "Got Stiffness? Designing Better Base Plates" (x_P1EezPXGI) corrects the P-over-n shortcut and forces sizing of F1554 anchor rods, washers, and grout on a stiffness, prying, and nut-head bearing check with stamped current calcs and held grout inspection. "Field Fixes and Solutions" (yI69Nu6pwQI) is Fisher's catalog of anchor-rod, camber, fit-up, and tolerance rules where prevention through detailing beats costly field labor; it is the most directly field-useful of the many Field Fixes entries and pairs well with "Field Fixes - Part 2" (RD-lPTNaH9s), which catalogs anchor-rod, base-plate, spandrel, and bolted-connection problems we can pre-draw as standard repair details under our stamp.

Two more round out the seismic and economic judgment that ACP-grade and out-of-region bids demand. Ivan should re-watch "Introduction to Seismic Connections" (gqCdO8zB0gA) for the rule to price connection labor, continuity plates, gusset reinforcement, and demand-critical welds separately and to confirm the seismic system before bidding, and "To 3 or Not To 3" (hJVsZLSvfTA), which quantifies that high-R systems buy a 50 to 62 percent base-shear cut but force AISC 341/358 detailing and a 1.5 to 2.5x connection-fabrication premium, making the seismic R choice a connection-cost and foundation decision priced separately from tonnage. Finally, the whole estimating team benefits from re-watching "Steel Fabrication: A Virtual, Detailed Tour of the Steel Fabrication Process" (6CFDIBILmZ8), which walks detailing, mill ordering, production, and QC against exact Manual tables and the COSP, AISC 360, RCSC, and AWS D1.1 sections, and gives a clean answer on what needs a PE stamp. Every rate, weight, splice-saving, or connection-hour figure cited in any of these sessions is a study aid and must be re-verified through aisc_validator.py and bid_rates.py before it touches a real bid.
